# Sūrah al-Baqarah (Chapter 2) — Expanded Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:1

> Alif-Lãm-Mĩm.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Three Letter Names That Refuse Translation**

The longest chapter of the Qur'an — 286 verses — opens with a line that is not a sentence. *Alif. Lām. Mīm.* are the names of three Arabic letters, recited by name and not by sound: the reader says *alif*, not *a*. Twenty-nine of the Qur'an's 114 chapters begin with such letter sequences, and this particular trio heads six of them — al-Baqarah, Āl ʿImrān, al-ʿAnkabūt, al-Rūm, Luqmān, and al-Sajdah. Nothing in the line parses as ordinary Arabic: no verb, no subject, no predication. It arrests the listener at the threshold of the Book with material rather than message, and fourteen centuries of readers have taken that arrest seriously, treating the letters as one of the Qur'an's most deliberate enigmas. Any account of them must admit two facts at once. They were recited from the first day and preserved with the text — nothing so conspicuous survived by accident. And no explanation of them has ever commanded consensus, which is itself information about their function.

**A Mystery the Caliphs Acknowledged**

The earliest Muslims did not solve the letters; they located them. Abū Bakr is reported to have said that every book has a mystery, and the mystery of the Qur'an is in the openings of its chapters. ʿAlī's formulation runs in parallel: every book has a quintessence, and the quintessence of this Book is in the spelled-out letters. Ibn ʿAjībah went further and confined the knowledge to the elite among Allah's friends. These sayings are not evasions but claims about the architecture of revelation — that the Book possesses a layer held back from casual grasp, positioned where every reader must pass it. The tradition that stacks the secrets of the learned, the successors, the prophets, the angels, and finally Allah Himself makes the same point as a hierarchy: each rank is surpassed by a knowledge it cannot carry, and the letters stand at the border where reading turns into reverence. A book entirely transparent would demand nothing but comprehension; these openings demand something else first.

**Al-Rāzī's Riverbeds and the Measure of Capacity**

Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī pictured the problem as water. The sea pours into rivers, rivers into streams, streams into rivulets; force a rivulet to carry the river's whole volume and it bursts its banks and is destroyed. He grounded the image in the Qur'an itself: *"He sends down rain from the sky, causing the valleys to flow, each according to its capacity"* (13:17). Revelation on this picture is apportioned — the same downpour fills each bed only as far as its walls allow. The letters then function as a marker of the surplus: the part of the sea no rivulet carries. The doctrine protects both sides of the relationship. Allah's speech is not diminished by human limits, and human beings are not crushed by contact with what exceeds them. Capacity becomes a spiritual category rather than an insult: the valleys differ in width, and the rain does not complain of any of them.

**The Objection: A Book That Calls Itself Clear**

Theologians pressed the other way. The Qur'an describes itself as clear, as guidance, as revealed in a plain Arabic tongue; a Book part of which no one can read would address Arabs in what amounts to a foreign language, and al-Rāzī himself records the objection. The Qur'an anticipates the tension and legislates a posture toward it: *"He is the One Who has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book, of which some verses are precise—they are the foundation of the Book—while others are elusive… but none grasps their ˹full˺ meaning except Allah. As for those well grounded in knowledge, they say, 'We believe in this ˹Quran˺—it is all from our Lord'"* (3:7). The letters belong to the elusive class by design. The mature response in that verse is not solution but inclusion — belief extended to what remains sealed. Clarity and mystery are therefore not rivals in this Book's self-description; the clear carries the weight of practice, and the sealed carries the weight of awe.

**Trust Without Transparency: Al-Rāzī's Compromise**

Al-Rāzī resolved the standoff with an analogy from practice. Some of the Law's wisdom is legible — the harms behind the prohibitions of wine and gambling can be argued. Other requirements, like particular rites of the pilgrimage, are performed without any accessible reason at all. The unreadable portion of the Qur'an belongs to this second kind: obeyed, recited, carried, but not cashed out into understanding. Far from being a defect, the arrangement trains a faculty that transparent religion never exercises — trust. A person who acts on wisdom he can see is partly relying on himself; a person who recites *Alif. Lām. Mīm.* morning and evening without grasping it relies on the Speaker alone. Al-Rāzī adds that the practice keeps the heart oriented beyond the world and beyond what it already knows. The letters are thus pedagogy through opacity: they teach the reader where his knowledge ends while his recitation continues.

**Building Blocks, Oaths, and a Standing Challenge**

Concrete interpretations multiply. Some read the letters as abbreviations — *alif* for Allah, *lām* for Jibrīl, *mīm* for Muḥammad, the whole descent of revelation compressed into three signs. Some mapped them onto speech itself: *alif* the origin of sound, *lām* its middle in the mouth, *mīm* its consummation on the lips. The numerologists counted values — *alif* one, *lām* thirty, *mīm* forty. Others hear an oath, Allah swearing by the letters as He elsewhere swears by created things. Strongest of all is the reading woven into this very sūrah: the Book is built from the same letters its hearers command, so the challenge stands open — *"produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true"* (2:23). The raw material lay in every Arab mouth; the composition defeated them all. What the letters precede, the next verse declares: a Book beyond doubt.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:2

> This is the Book! There is no doubt about it—a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺,

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Declaration That Argues Nothing**

After the sealed letters, the first sentence of al-Baqarah claims everything and demonstrates nothing: *this is the Book*, and there is no doubt in it. The Qur'an's method at its longest chapter's threshold is declaration, not proof — the certainty is stated in the tone before any evidence is arranged. The demonstrative itself invites argument. "This" points at something present, yet many exegetes read it as "That," a distant pointer, and both readings have ground. Al-Baqarah is Madinan, revealed when most of the Qur'an already existed, so "That Book" can gather the revelations already in the community's hands. Or the pointer aims higher, at the heavenly original: *"In fact, this is a glorious Quran, ˹recorded˺ in a Preserved Tablet"* (85:21–22). "The Book" functions as a proper name here, one of several the Qur'an carries — among them the Standard, *al-Furqān*: *"Blessed is the One Who sent down the Standard to His servant, so that he may be a warner to the whole world"* (25:1). A thing named this many times by its Maker does not introduce itself defensively.

**Where to Pause: Two Grammars, Two Meanings**

Arabic readers of the first generation located a fork in the sentence's rhythm. Pause after "the Book," and the line reads: This is the Book — no doubt exists in it — a guidance for the God-conscious. Pause after "doubt," and it reads: This is the Book without doubt, containing guidance for the God-conscious. Both pauses are licit; combining them is not, and the classical rule that one may stop at either point but never treat both readings at once shows how carefully the sentence's joints were studied. The two parsings shade the claim differently. The first makes doubtlessness a property asserted of the Book — a statement about its content, immune to suspicion. The second makes "without doubt" part of the Book's identification — the Book, that unmistakable one, is now declared a guidance. Neither reading survives alone in the tradition, and the ambiguity is productive: the sentence has been recited both ways for fourteen centuries, carrying both claims at once.

**Rayb: The Doubt That Carries Suspicion**

The word negated here is not the neutral term for uncertainty. *Rayb* is doubt with an edge — suspicion, misgiving, the uneasy doubt that accuses. The verse does not merely say the Book is certain; it says the kind of doubt that darkens into distrust has no foothold in it. The negation is categorical in form — *lā rayba fīhi* — and the Qur'an backs such confidence elsewhere not with assurance but with a standing challenge: produce a chapter like it (2:23). A text that invites its critics to falsify it can afford an unqualified negative. Exegetes also note the social shape of *rayb*: it is the doubt of the hearer who suspects manipulation, and the verse answers precisely that suspicion — this Book does not work on you by hidden leverage. Its claims are on its surface, its proofs are public, and its demand on the reader is stated in the same breath as its promise.

**Taqwā: A Word Built Out of Guarding**

"Those mindful ˹of Allah˺" renders *al-muttaqīn*, and the root *w-q-y* means to guard, to shield, to put something between yourself and what you fear. The *muttaqī* is a person who has installed a protection between himself and Allah's displeasure — wariness made habitual, awareness of the divine presence kept constantly switched on. Taqwā is not one virtue among others but the Quranic name for the whole posture of the soul toward Allah, sitting alongside trust, hope, fear, and contentment in the classical lists. The Qur'an makes it the measure of rank: *"Surely the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous among you"* (49:13). And it is demanded without ceiling: *"O believers! Be mindful of Allah in the way He deserves, and do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission ˹to Him˺"* (3:102). A guidance promised to the *muttaqīn* is therefore promised to a character, not to a curiosity — to those already in the habit of guarding.

**Guidance Attached to a Posture, Not an Intellect**

The verse conditions its gift, and the condition explains much of the Qur'an's uneven effect on readers. Guidance here is not information transferred but direction received, and reception depends on the receiver's stance. The Qur'an states the asymmetry plainly: *"We send down the Quran as a healing and mercy for the believers, but it only increases the wrongdoers in loss"* (17:82), and it names itself *"a cure for what is in the hearts"* (10:57). The same rain falls on every valley; each valley flows according to its capacity (13:17). Taqwā is that capacity in moral terms — the guarded heart is the vessel guidance fills, while the heart turned wholly outward hears the same words and hardens on them. This is why the sūrah will spend thirteen verses dissecting people who received the guidance and deflected it: the danger it diagrams is not ignorance but the posture that makes knowledge useless.

**Character Before Code**

Al-Baqarah will legislate for a newborn state — war and debt, marriage and fasting, inheritance and dietary law. Its first word about its own guidance is that guidance lands on character before code. The people described are not defined by what they have been commanded but by how they stand: mindful, guarding, aware. The five-verse opening of the sūrah builds its portrait in that order — a Book beyond doubt, a posture of taqwā, then the acts that flow from it — and every ruling that follows in the remaining two hundred and eighty-odd verses addresses people so defined. Law given to the unguarded breeds evasion; law given to the *muttaqīn* breeds practice. The verse thus states the sūrah's operating assumption: revelation is a guide, and a guide is only as good as the willingness of the traveler to be led.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:3

> who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and donate from what We have provided for them,

**Expanded Commentary**

**Faith Begins Where Sight Ends**

The first quality of the God-conscious is belief in *al-ghayb* — the unseen, literally "the absent": realities beyond the reach of the ordinary senses. Allah, the angels, Paradise, Hell, and the Day of Judgment all belong to it. The definition matches the one the Prophet ﷺ gave when Jibrīl came in human form and asked what faith is: to believe in Allah, His angels, the meeting with Him, His messengers, and the Resurrection (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 50). Every item on that list is unseen in the verse's sense, and the ordering of al-Baqarah agrees with the ḥadīth — belief in the unseen heads the list of acts, because nothing else on the list can be done sincerely without it. The verse is not demanding credulity. Belief in the unseen is belief on a warrant: the report of the One whose truthfulness has been established. It transfers trust from the eye to the Witness, and that transfer is the first act of every religious life.

**Two Kinds of Unseen**

Commentators split the category along a useful line. Some realities are invisible in principle — Allah, whose nature no sense could grasp even if the senses were willing. Others are visible in principle but withheld in fact — the Hour, whose timing belongs to Allah alone; when Jibrīl asked about it, the Prophet ﷺ answered that the one asked knows no more than the one asking, and recited: *"Verily, with Allah (Alone) is the knowledge of the Hour"* (31:34, cited in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 50). The distinction protects the doctrine from two errors. Against the rationalist who denies what cannot be seen, the first class says: the most real thing in existence is precisely the thing no eye contains. Against the enthusiast who claims private access to hidden things, the second class says: some of the unseen stays sealed until Allah opens it, and speculation about it is not faith. Believing the unseen therefore includes believing its edges — accepting both what revelation discloses and what it withholds.

**Iqāmah: Prayer Erected, Not Merely Performed**

"Establish" translates *yuqīmūn*, from a root meaning to set upright, to make stand — the same verb used of raising a building or straightening a leaning thing. Prayer that is *established* differs from prayer that is merely performed: it has structure, continuity, and support, and it holds other things upright with it. The word *ṣalāh* itself carries a range the technical usage narrows. In the Qur'an it names the canonical prayer of recitation and bowing, but it also names invocation — Allah and His angels make *ṣalāh* upon the Prophet, and believers are commanded to join them: *"Indeed, Allah showers His blessings upon the Prophet, and His angels pray for him. O believers! Invoke Allah's blessings upon him"* (33:56). The prophets before Muḥammad ﷺ were charged with the same institution — ʿĪsā recounts that Allah enjoined prayer upon him (19:31), and Mūsā receives the command at Ṭuway (20:14). To establish prayer is to join a structure older than the qiblah.

**Spending From, Not Spending All**

The third quality is *infāq* — expending, giving out — and two small words do the theological work. "From" renders a partitive: what is donated is a portion, not the whole, and the portion is defined by need and capacity rather than by exhaustion. "What We have provided for them" fixes prior ownership: the wealth in a believer's hand arrived as provision (*rizq*) from Allah, so spending gives away what was never absolutely his. The pairing with prayer is deliberate and runs through the whole Qur'an — ṣalāh and zakāh are joined so often that classical exegesis treats them as a single institution with two limbs, one vertical and one horizontal. The Prophet's ﷺ definition of Islam to Jibrīl bundles the same acts: worship Allah alone, establish the prayers, render the obligatory charity, fast Ramaḍān (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 50). Donation here covers the obligatory due and the voluntary gift alike; the verse praises the disposition before the ledger.

**A Ladder From the Inner to the Outer**

The three qualities descend a graded staircase, and the commentators map it precisely. Belief in the unseen is an inward act with an invisible object — nothing of it appears on the body. Prayer stands in the middle: its motions are visible, its recitation audible, yet its object remains unseen. Donation completes the descent — an outward act with a visible object, wealth passing from hand to hand. Read in order, the verse constitutes the whole human being: the heart, the body in time, and the possessions in the world, each given its assignment and each anchored to the one before. The gradation also guards against two amputations. Faith that never becomes prayer is sentiment; prayer that never becomes spending is ritual. By the verse's architecture, the inner conviction is incomplete until it has walked all the way down into the street.

**Character Named Before Any Law Is Given**

No command has been issued yet in this passage. The sūrah — the Qur'an's longest and most legislative — opens its human portrait with three qualities of the heart and hand, described rather than demanded. The God-conscious are identified by what they already do before they are addressed by statute, and the identification sets the terms for everything that follows: when the rulings arrive, they arrive to a people already shaped by unseen-faith, standing prayer, and open-handedness. There is a lesson in the order for every reader of the long sūrah. Law lands differently on character than on raw will — the same commandment produces evasion in one person and worship in another, and the difference was made before the commandment was heard. Al-Baqarah begins by showing the kind of person its two hundred and eighty-six verses are written for.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:4

> and who believe in what has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what was revealed before you, and have sure faith in the Hereafter.

**Expanded Commentary**

**One Faith Across Many Books**

The fourth quality extends belief from the unseen in general to revelation in particular — and not to one revelation but to a chain. A Muslim is required to believe in the Torah given to Mūsā, the Gospel given to ʿĪsā, and the scriptures before them; belief in prior books is a condition of the faith, not a courtesy toward it. The Qur'an grounds this requirement in the unity of the message itself: *"He has ordained for you ˹believers˺ the Way which He decreed for Noah, and what We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what We decreed for Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, ˹commanding:˺ 'Uphold the faith, and make no divisions in it'"* (42:13). One religion, delivered in installments, with each installment obliging belief in all the others. The verse therefore draws the community's boundary unusually: it excludes nobody who accepts the whole chain, and it admits nobody who accepts only their preferred link. Belief here is loyalty to a single divine project across centuries rather than subscription to a single text.

**Why the Last Book Is Named First**

The order of the clause is chronologically reversed: what was revealed *to you* is named before what was revealed *before you*. The reversal is a statement of rank. The final revelation stands at the head of the list because it functions as the guardian of the earlier ones — confirming, correcting, and completing what time and human hands had altered in their transmission. The Qur'an claims exactly this office for itself: Jibrīl *"revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah's Will, confirming what came before it—a guide and good news for the believers"* (2:97). A confirming book logically precedes the books it confirms in the order of belief, since the believer's access to the earlier revelations now runs through its testimony. Naming the Prophet's book first also personalizes the chain: revelation is not an abstract library but an address delivered to a man in the hearer's own generation, continuous with the deliveries before it.

**One List — or Two Groups Merged Into One**

A grammatical question with communal consequences runs through the classical commentaries. Does the "and" that opens this verse continue the description of verse 3 — one group of God-conscious, bearing all four qualities — or does it introduce a second subject: *and those who* believe in the two revelations, with verse 5's verdict covering both? Al-Ṭabarī favored the second reading and gave it historical content: verse 3 describes the believers from the Arabs, verse 4 the believers from the People of the Book who accepted the earlier revelations and now accept the Prophet ﷺ. The Qur'an attests such people exist: *"Indeed, there are some among the People of the Book who truly believe in Allah and what has been revealed to you ˹believers˺ and what was revealed to them"* (3:199). Weighing the readings, the difference matters less than it appears. Verse 5 gathers everyone described into a single "they," and the reward attaches to qualities rather than genealogy. The stronger effect of the passage is unifying: two streams of belief pouring into one guidance.

**Yaqīn: Faith That Has Stopped Negotiating**

The verse ends not with belief but with certainty — *yaqīn*. Arabic distinguishes grades of assent: conjecture (*ẓann*), knowledge acquired by report or inference, and *yaqīn*, the settled certainty that leaves no room for renegotiation. The God-conscious are described as having *sure faith* in the Hereafter specifically. The specification is meaningful. Of all the unseen realities named in verse 3, the Hereafter is the one most contested and most easily deferred — a doctrine whose consequences are all in the future and whose evidence is entirely in report. Certainty about it is therefore the hardest faith, and the verse demands it not as intellectual achievement but as a condition of character: the heart that has stopped arguing with the Last Day. Classical spirituality treated *yaqīn* as the pivot of the religious life — belief that has hardened into conviction moves the limbs, while belief that remains opinion only moves the tongue.

**The Hereafter Anchors the Whole Portrait**

Structurally, the five-verse opening of al-Baqarah closes its description of the God-conscious with a horizon. Taqwā, prayer, and donation are practices stretched across a lifetime; belief in the two revelations fixes their source; certainty in the Hereafter fixes their destination. Without the destination the earlier qualities lose their peculiar rationality — why guard, why stand at dawn, why let go of wealth, if the ledger closes at the grave? The verse answers by naming the closing of the ledger as the object of certainty. Exegetes connect this to the essay-worthy theme of the Qur'an as a whole: guidance functions as guidance only for someone going somewhere. By placing the Hereafter last in the list, the sūrah makes eschatology the frame of ethics — every act of the *muttaqīn* is read, by them, as a deposit against a Day they hold as certain.

**The Prophet Written Into the Definition**

One more feature deserves notice: the community is defined around its messenger. The verse says "what has been revealed *to you*" — the second-person address to the Prophet ﷺ inside a description of believers inserts him into their identity. In the Madinan setting this was a live boundary question: Jews and Christians accepted revelation in general while rejecting this messenger, and the verse forecloses the option. Acceptance of the chain terminates in its final link. At the same time the formulation refuses triumphalism — the same breath that names the Prophet's revelation first names the earlier revelations as objects of belief. The sūrah will later state the tension frankly: *"Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith. Say, 'Allah's guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance'"* (2:120). Here at the opening, the balance stands complete: a distinct community, gathered around a final messenger, believing everything heaven ever sent.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:5

> It is they who are ˹truly˺ guided by their Lord, and it is they who will be successful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Pointers and One Restriction**

The verse pronounces its verdict with unusual grammatical weight, and the weight is the meaning. It opens with *ulāʾika* — "those," "it is they" — a demonstrative of distance that Arabic rhetoric uses to elevate: pointing at people as one points at something raised on a platform. Each of the two clauses then locks in a restriction. "It is *they* who are truly guided" fronts the pronoun so that guidance is confined to the described group — they, and not the claimants who will follow in the sūrah's next thirteen verses. "It is *they* who will be successful" repeats the lock on a second prize. The doubled structure is not ornament; it is exclusion by syntax. The same sūrah will describe disbelievers and hypocrites at length, and none of them receives either pointer. The opening portrait of al-Baqarah ends, therefore, not with a summary but with a verdict sealed twice — once over guidance, once over success — and the seal is grammatical.

**Falāḥ: Success With Roots in a Plowed Field**

"Successful" renders *mufliḥūn*, from *falāḥ*, and the root's memory is agricultural: to plow, to cleave the earth, to farm. The *fallāḥ* is the cultivator, and *falāḥ* is what cultivation eventuates in — the harvest at the end of long labor. The etymology colors every Quranic use of the word. Success in this vocabulary is not luck and not seizure; it is the yield of a field that was broken open, seeded, watered, and guarded through seasons. Read back into the verse, the metaphor quietly recapitulates verses 3–4: the plowing was taqwā, the seeding was faith in the unseen, the seasons were prayer and donation. The harvest named here belongs to that labor and to nothing else. The Qur'an's choice of an agricultural word for the soul's ultimate attainment is exact — farming is the human activity that most visibly combines effort with dependence, where the worker does everything and the increase comes from elsewhere.

**The Word the Adhān Carries Into the Street**

*Falāḥ* is not confined to scripture; it is shouted into Muslim streets five times a day. The call to prayer, after the testimony, rings out *ḥayya ʿalā al-ṣalāh, ḥayya ʿalā al-falāḥ* — come to prayer, come to success — welding the word to the act the previous verses described. The adhān's origin is fixed in history: when the Madinan community gathered for prayer by guesswork, some proposed a Christian bell, others a Jewish horn, and ʿUmar suggested a human caller; the Prophet ﷺ then ordered Bilāl to rise and call (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 604). Every recitation of al-Baqarah's opening thus has an echo in daily sound: the mosque announces in the same vocabulary that success is reached through prayer. The verse and the adhān mutually interpret each other — the call is the verse in the imperative mood, and the verse is the call with its grammar explained.

**Not Rescue but Arrival**

Translators sometimes render *falāḥ* as "salvation," and the substitution imports a frame the word does not carry. Classical usage does not sort humanity into saved and damned as its first division; it sorts the thriving from the lost, the arrived from the failed. *Falāḥ* is attainment of the good a thing was made for — in this world and in the next — rather than rescue from a verdict. The difference shows in what the word promises. Rescue is negative: escape from danger. Arrival is positive: possession of the harvest, nearness to the Provider, the settled state of one whose labor bore fruit. The Qur'an spreads the term across both horizons; the believer prospers in his soul here and inherits the Garden there. Reading verse 5 with this frame keeps its two clauses in proportion: guidance is the arriving life, success is the arrived one.

**Guidance They Ride, Not Guidance They Made**

The middle phrase deserves exact attention: they are *upon* guidance *from* their Lord — *ʿalā hudan min rabbihim*. The preposition "upon" pictures guidance as a mount or a vehicle the travelers ride; it is under them and carrying them, not something they manufactured or own. The source is then named: *from their Lord* — using *rabb*, the Lord who nurtures and manages, the same title that headed al-Fātiḥah's second verse. Possession is carefully refused. The guided do not hold their guidance as property; they receive it as provision, continuously, the way the field receives rain. The echo of the Qur'an's opening prayer is exact — the petition *"Guide us along the Straight Path"* (1:6) is answered here in the declarative: the God-conscious are the people that petition describes in motion. Verse 5 of al-Baqarah can thus be read as the first fulfillment of al-Fātiḥah, the Book showing what an answered prayer looks like from outside.

**Description, Then Verdict: The Method of the Opening**

The five-verse unit now displays its whole shape. Verse 2 names the Book and the posture it requires; verses 3–4 describe the people in four qualities; verse 5 judges them. The sequence — describe, then seal — is the Qur'an's characteristic method, and it teaches by contrast: when the disbelievers and the hypocrites appear next, they too will be described before any verdict falls, and their portraits will end in loss rather than *falāḥ*. The double reward in this verse also distributes across time: guidance is granted now, in this life, as a state the traveler inhabits; success is promised at the end, as an arrival. Neither is earned as wages — both are pronounced over people whose defining act was belief in what they could not see. The constitution of the community is complete before al-Baqarah turns to its histories and its laws, and everything after verse 5 addresses the people this verdict has defined.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:6

> As for those who persist in disbelief, it is the same whether you warn them or not—they will never believe.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Verdict on Persistence, Not on Possibility**

The verse swings from the guided to a second company, and its opening word fixes the charge: *kafarū* — those who disbelieved, in the settled sense the translation marks with "persist." The grammar describes a state achieved rather than a door being shut. When the sentence adds "they will never believe," it reports an end reached through its own road, the way a physician reports a disease that has passed its treatable stage. Nothing in the verse claims these people were barred before they chose; the negation of belief is the sum of their negations. The Qur'an elsewhere keeps the two ideas in tension without collapse — guidance offered to all, acceptance determined by each — and this verse states the second term only. Read as description rather than decree, it answers a pastoral problem rather than a metaphysical one: what should a warner do when warning demonstrably no longer works on particular hearts?

**Nadhīr: An Office Measured by Delivery**

Warning is one of the two names the Qur'an gives the prophetic office, and its logic is contractual: the messenger delivers, the hearer decides, Allah judges. The verse releases the Prophet ﷺ from the burden of outcomes by defining his commission in terms he can always fulfill: *"We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ only as a deliverer of good news and a warner to all of humanity"* (34:28). The adverb "only" does real work — the office does not include manufacturing belief in other people's chests. Prophetic biography supplies the cost of forgetting this: the Makkan years show a messenger grieving over every refusal, and revelation repeatedly consoles him with the limits of his jurisdiction. A warning that changes no one has still succeeded as a warning, because the act was owed to the hearer and to Allah, not to the result. The verse is the doctrine of the office stated at its sharpest edge — the case where delivery and reception fully part company.

**Consolation in a Hard Shape**

There is mercy in the sentence's bluntness, addressed to a man who grieved over every soul that refused him. The precedent runs back to Nūḥ, told after nine and a half centuries of refusal: *"None of your people will believe except those who already have. So do not be distressed by what they have been doing"* (11:36). The information arrives as relief — once the closed cases are known to be closed, the heart stops paying for them daily. Expectation honestly lowered is a form of care for the one who carries the mission, and the Qur'an applies that care here without softening the fact. The verse does not say warning is worthless; it says warning has done all it can do with these particular hearts, and the warner may set that portion of his grief down. Consolation and verdict arrive in one sentence, and the consolation depends entirely on the verdict being true.

**A Sentence Spoken Over Many Peoples**

The formula is not unique to al-Baqarah, and its repetitions show that the Qur'an is describing a type rather than a roster. Of the Makkan elite who mocked the messenger it says: *"It is the same whether you warn them or not—they will never believe"* (36:10) — nearly the same words, a generation and a city away. The exegetical lists gather further parallels where warning is declared spent (7:193; 26:136; 63:6). Each recurrence marks a threshold crossed by a community: repeated refusals compacted into a fixed disposition, after which new evidence no longer reaches the faculty that weighs evidence. The generality matters for reading this verse inside the sūrah's opening. The five-verse unit before it described the guided as a type too — qualities, not names — and now the second type appears in the same style. Al-Baqarah is building a taxonomy of souls, and "the ones for whom warning has closed" is its second entry.

**Warning Still Reaches the House Next Door**

The futility declared here is local, and the verse does not license silence. The command to warn stands; what changes is the distribution of results. In any assembly the same words fall on three kinds of ground — the guarded heart of verse 2, the settled refusal of this verse, and everything between — and no warner can see the boundaries from where he stands. The call is therefore universal while the outcome remains per soul. This arrangement also protects the message from becoming salesmanship. If the warner's success were measured in conversions, he would temper the warning to make it sellable; measured in delivery, it can stay exactly as sharp as it was sent. The Qur'an records the futility openly, in the same Book that commands the warning, so that neither truth is lost: some hearts will never open, and the call must still reach every ear.

**Foreknowledge That Does Not Bind the Will**

A difficulty remains, and honesty requires stating it: if Allah declares they will never believe, in what sense were they free not to? The classical answers distinguish God's knowledge from God's coercion — knowledge of a choice is not a chain on it, any more than a witnessed event is caused by the witness. The verse's own framing supports the distinction: it is spoken *about* people who have already persisted long enough to be predictable, the way a prognosis follows a history. The Qur'an never presents this knowledge as the mechanism of their refusal; the mechanism, in the sūrah's coming verses, will be shown as something they do — and something that is then confirmed over them. How knowledge and confirmation relate to the will is a question the revelation states rather than systematizes. The following verse shows what this settled refusal looks like from the inside.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:7

> Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and their sight is covered. They will suffer a tremendous punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Qalb: The Organ That Thinks**

The Qur'an's heart is not primarily the seat of feeling. *Qalb* — a word whose root means to turn and flip — names the organ of consciousness, knowledge, and decision, the place where evidence becomes conviction. It is where revelation itself landed: Jibrīl *"revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah's Will"* (2:97). Because it thinks, it can malfunction in cognitive modes: it can be veiled from comprehension — *"We have cast veils over their hearts—leaving them unable to comprehend it—and deafness in their ears"* (6:25); it can be stained by accumulated acts — *"their hearts have been stained by all ˹the evil˺ they used to commit"* (83:14); it can harden past feeling — *"your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder"* (2:74). Sealing stands at the far end of this pathology. The choice of the heart as first object tells us what kind of loss the verse describes: not missing information, but a disabled faculty — the organ that converts seeing and hearing into believing has been closed at the source.

**One Verb, Three Locks**

The Arabic syntax divides the verse's action, and the division is deliberate. One verb, *khatama* — He has sealed — governs two organs, the hearts and the hearing, as if a single act closed both. Sight is handled separately: upon it a *ghishāwah*, a covering, is placed, arriving in the sentence as its own accusative object. The translation renders the second clause passively — "their sight is covered" — and the effect in recitation is a slight widening of the picture: two organs sealed shut, a third draped over. The three channels named are the three by which guidance enters a human being. The heart decides; the ear receives the word, and revelation is above all a heard thing; the eye receives the sign, and the Qur'an constantly points at horizons and bodies and ruins as āyāt. With decision, hearing, and sight all disabled, no input remains — which is why the previous verse could declare warning useless. The anatomy and the prognosis fit each other exactly.

**A Seal Set by Allah — and Earned**

Two readings of the verse have run through the tradition since the first century. The predestinarian reading takes the seal at face value: faith and its absence issue from God's prior command, and the human will is not the author of either. The other reading makes the seal a consequence — spiritual punishment, following choices already made. The Qur'an itself arbitrates, and it arbitrates for the second reading by showing the order of operations: *"Have you seen ˹O Prophet˺ those who have taken their own desires as their god? ˹And so˺ Allah left them to stray knowingly, sealed their hearing and hearts, and placed a cover on their sight"* (45:23). Desires enthroned first; the seal follows, marked by "and so." The same sequence appears in the description of the constricted chest (6:125). Allah's action is real and sovereign in both readings — He is the one who seals — but the sealing ratifies a self the person built. The verse punishes by confirming: what they chose becomes what they are.

**Sealing as a Family of Images**

The Qur'an does not rely on one metaphor for this closure but on a family, and the variety is diagnostic. Rock-hardness after repeated refusal (2:74). A veil laid over comprehension, paired with manufactured deafness (6:25). Rust — the word *rān*, a staining that accrues deed by deed until the surface no longer reflects (83:14). Tightness, as of a chest forced to climb into the sky (6:125). Each image carries the same two claims: the closure is real, and it was built incrementally. No one wakes sealed. The heart hardens by refusals the way metal oxidizes by exposure, and the seal of this verse names the finished state of a long process. That is why revelation, which heals one constitution, worsens another: *"it only increases the wrongdoers in loss"* (17:82). The same downpour that fills the guarded valley of verse 2 runs off the sealed surface, and the running-off is itself recorded as increase.

**A Punishment Matching the Closure**

The verse ends on its second sentence: theirs is a *tremendous* punishment — *ʿadhāb ʿaẓīm*. The adjective is the largest the passage has used, and its scale answers the scale of the loss. These are not people who missed a favor but people who closed the organ by which any favor is received; the penalty-word matches the crime-word in magnitude. The same pairing recurs wherever deliberate rejection is judged: those who open their chests to disbelief after belief are answered with condemnation and *"a tremendous punishment"* (16:106). There is also a harder reading available in the verse's own structure — the closure itself already functions as penalty. A sealed heart is not merely scheduled for punishment; it is living inside one, cut off from the only thing that could rescue it. The final sentence then adds what the soul has lost the equipment to fear. The Qur'an's economy is exact: the tremendous punishment belongs to those who made tremendous the shutting of their own doors.

**A Diagnosis Facing Inward**

Readers have always known the verse's danger lies in its direction. Nothing in it invites the reciter to inventory other people's hearts and pronounce them sealed; its function in the sūrah — and in the prayer where al-Baqarah is recited — is to make the hearer examine the processes that end here. Every image in the family hardening, veiling, staining, tightening — describes something that begins small and ordinary: one refused truth, one desire enthroned, one sign looked past. The seal is the terminus of a road whose early miles feel weightless. That is the pedagogical terror of the verse: it exists so that the reciter never arrives at it. And the door the verse leaves open is the one it never mentions — while life lasts, repentance pries at what refusal has closed, since the confirmation described here operates on the living, not the dead. The next verses turn to a third company, whose hearts are sick rather than sealed.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:8

> And there are some who say, “We believe in Allah and the Last Day,” yet they are not ˹true˺ believers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Third Company That Hides Its Name**

The sūrah's opening has sorted souls into two groups — the guided, described in four verses, and the settled disbelievers, dispatched in two. Now a third company appears, and the space given to it is startling: thirteen verses, from this one through verse 20, more than both earlier groups combined. The group is also the only one not named at its introduction. The word that will crystallize for it — *munāfiqūn*, the hypocrites, those whose inside contradicts their outside — is held back here; the verse offers only "some among the people" and a quoted claim. The withholding is method. Nifāq is defined by concealment, so the description proceeds the way detection proceeds: behavior first, label later. By the time the sūrah names them outright, the reader has watched them lie, deceive, sicken, claim reform, sneer, mock, and trade — and can recognize the type without the name. The longest portrait in the opening belongs to the least self-identifying people, because they are the hardest to see.

**A Two-Pillar Claim, Cheap to Make**

The quoted creed is orthodoxy in miniature: belief in Allah and in the Last Day — the origin and the destination, the two poles between which the whole of Islamic doctrine stretches. Nothing in the wording is heretical; recited sincerely it would be the beginning of faith. That is precisely the verse's point: the formula costs nothing to say, and saying it is not believing it. The rebuttal arrives without argument, evidence, or qualification — *yet they are not believers* — because the case does not turn on the sentence they uttered but on the heart that declined to stand behind it. Belief in the Qur'an is located below speech; the tongue can carry a creed the chest has never signed. The verse thus installs the distinction that governs the whole passage: between *qawl*, saying, and *īmān*, believing. The hypocrites own the first completely and the second not at all, and no amount of fluency in the first converts into the second.

**Madina Made Them; Every Age Remakes Them**

The historical referent is fixed. In and around Madina, after the Hijrah, a circle of people professed Islam while collaborating at need with its enemies, or cooled into inaction when the faith demanded cost. The tradition gathers the leadership of this camp around ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, a chief whose standing in the city was eclipsed by the Prophet's ﷺ arrival — though the Qur'an never names him, keeping the description portable. The commentaries insist on that portability: the verses refer to such people wherever and whenever they live. Every generation that has a dominant faith produces its compliance class — people for whom belief is a social costume rather than a conviction, worn while it pays. The Madinan hypocrites had specific motives: recovered influence, protected wealth, insurance against the Quraysh. The type outlives the motives. Any community whose orthodoxy brings social advantage will contain people buying the advantage without the orthodoxy, and this verse is their permanent file.

**Speech as Costume**

The verb the verse chooses for their faith is *yaqūlūn* — they say. Their entire religious identity fits inside a verb of tongue. The Qur'an returns to this structure in its sūrah named for them: *"When the hypocrites come to you ˹O Prophet˺, they say, 'We bear witness that you are certainly the Messenger of Allah'—and surely Allah knows that you are His Messenger—but Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are truly liars"* (63:1). The anatomy of the lie there is exact: the sentence itself is true, and it is still a lie, because a testimony is constituted by the witness behind it. Take the believing heart away and the words remain while the testimony dies. That is what it means to wear speech as costume — the garment of the creed draped over an absence. The verse in al-Baqarah states the same discovery from the other end: they say the true sentence, and the divine verdict calls them non-believers, because what makes belief belief was never in the saying.

**Why Thirteen Verses for People Who Say So Little**

The asymmetry of coverage answers a question of danger. Open enemies stand outside the fence: they can be seen, counted, and guarded against, and their hostility harms the body. Hypocrites stand inside: they pray in the row, sit in the council, marry into families, hear the plans, and know where the community is soft. Their harm runs to trust itself — a community that cannot believe its own members' creeds has been wounded in its organ of cohesion. The sūrah's investment matches the threat: thirteen verses of detection equipment, listing the signs by which the hidden type becomes visible — the disease that shows in hesitation (2:10), the corruption dressed as peace-making (2:11–12), the contempt dressed as sophistication (2:13), the two-faced speech (2:14). None of this arms an inquisition into hearts, which remain Allah's jurisdiction; it arms ordinary believers with patterns. The length of the passage is a measure of how seriously the Qur'an takes the enemy who arrives smiling and agreeing.

**Anatomy of an Exposure**

The sentence itself is built as a miniature exposure, and its parts deserve notice. It opens with a partitive — *wa-min al-nās*, "and among the people are some" — locating the type inside humanity, indistinguishable from outside, a subset you cannot point to by appearance. It then quotes their claim in direct speech, letting the creed stand in their own words with no editorializing. Finally it delivers the verdict in four words: they do not believe. Claim, then contradiction; maximum contrast, minimum commentary. The rhetoric teaches suspicion of costless creeds without teaching suspicion of persons — the target is the structure of saying-without-being, not any named individual. In the taxonomy the sūrah is building, this verse occupies the hinge: belief (verses 2–5) and disbelief (verse 6) were each defined straightforwardly, and now the type that borrows the vocabulary of the first while sharing the state of the second steps into the light for thirteen verses of examination.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:9

> They seek to deceive Allah and the believers, yet they only deceive themselves, but they fail to perceive it.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Deception Aimed at the Undeceivable**

The verse names the operation behind the costume: *yukhādiʿūn* — they deal in deception, in a verb form that carries attempt and reciprocity, deceiving or trying to deceive in exchange. The first object of the attempt is Allah. The absurdity is the diagnosis. Deception is a technique that works on limited perceivers — you conceal what another cannot see — and Allah is the Knower of the unseen, from whom nothing is concealed in the heavens or the earth. To attempt deception against omniscience is not merely to fail; it is to demonstrate what the attempter actually believes about his target. The classical commentaries draw the inference cleanly: you only scheme against someone you think can be fooled, and the hypocrite's scheme exposes a practical atheism inside his professed creed. He says he believes in Allah and the Last Day (2:8) and behaves as though neither were watching. The verse treats the attempt itself as evidence — the deception declares the deceiver's real theology better than his testimony does.

**The Trick That Lands Only on the Trickster**

The second clause delivers the reversal in the tightest possible grammar: *wa-mā yakhdaʿūna illā anfusahum* — they deceive *none but* themselves. The particle of exception confines the entire effect of the scheme to the schemer. Every hour of performance, every calculated creed, every managed appearance subtracts from the one self the deceiver actually owns; the mask is worn at the cost of the face. The Qur'an states the same reversal elsewhere with the verb turned around: *"Surely the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He outwits them"* (4:142) — the attempted deception returns as their being outwitted, and the sūrah al-Nisāʾ adds the detail of prayer performed half-heartedly, purely to be seen. The mechanism deserves precision: the self-deception is not an accidental side effect but the substance of the act. To live inside a false self-presentation is to lose access to the true self; the hypocrite's most successful deception always has exactly one victim, and he is standing behind the mask.

**The Recurring Grammar of the Counter-Plan**

Where creatures plot, the Qur'an repeatedly answers with divine plotting, and the pairing is a fixed motif: *"They planned, but Allah also planned. And Allah is the best of planners"* (8:30). The exegetical lists run the motif through the Book — in Yūnus, al-Raʿd, Ibrāhīm, al-Naḥl, al-Naml — always in the same shape: a human scheme, a divine response, the response described as better rather than greater. The comparison is qualitative. Human planning works by concealment and speed; divine planning needs neither, since it operates through truth taking its time, letting the scheme unfold until its own logic undoes it. To call Allah the best of planners is not to accuse Him of trickery — the word in these verses carries the sense of arranging outcomes the arranger of evil did not intend. The hypocrites' deception in Madina did eventually undo itself exactly this way: no counter-mask was needed, only events, and each event pulled another thread from the costume.

**Wa-lā Yashʿurūn: The Blindness Built Into the Trick**

The verse closes on a verb of perception: *yashʿurūn*, from *shuʿūr* — the finest grade of awareness, sensation so subtle that Arabic connects it with *shaʿr*, hair, the sensitivity of skin that feels a hair's touch. Its negation is therefore not "they do not know" but "they do not feel it" — the reversal is happening at a level below their noticing. This is the built-in blindness of self-deception: the trick requires the trickster to half-believe the performance in order to sustain it, and the half-belief anesthetizes precisely the faculty that could catch him out. The closing clause reads as diagnosis rather than insult. A deceiver who perceives his own deception is in torment and usually stops; the hypocrite's peace of mind is the symptom of the disease. The verse has located the mechanism by which a person can spend years defrauding himself and call the years successful — perception itself has been spent in buying the mask.

**Concealment, Lying, and Deception: The Passage's Taxonomy**

Read against its neighbours, this verse advances the exposure by one precise step, and the steps form a taxonomy. Verse 8 recorded the lie — saying with the tongue what the heart withholds; that is *kidhb*, falsehood in speech. Verse 9 records the operation — active double-dealing directed at Allah and the community; that is *khidāʿ*, deception as a practice with objects and goals. Between and beneath both runs *kitmān*, concealment: hiding what one knows, which the sūrah will later charge against People of the Book who suppress revelation. The distinction matters because the sins have different centers. The lie is a sentence; the deception is a career. A person may lie once from fear and remain sound; a person who organizes his life around managing other people's beliefs has built a structure that now builds him. The passage proceeds act by act — claim, operation, disease — assembling the type out of behaviors before it ever needs the name.

**What the Community Is Owed by All This**

The believers were the second object of the deception, and the verse quietly assigns them their posture. No community can fully screen hearts — the interior belongs to Allah, who alone bears witness that the hypocrites are liars (63:1). What the community receives instead is pattern recognition: the signs by which the hidden type leaks — the claim without cost, the deception whose only victim is the deceiver, the absence of felt awareness. With those signs the believers are neither naive nor inquisitorial; they hold the outward by the profession and leave the inward to its Knower, while Allah undertakes the counter-plan. The verse's final irony arms them with patience: a deception that devours only its author needs no hurried exposure. It will ripen. The community's task is to remain what the deceiver cannot fake — and the following verse explains why the faking itself is a sickness that grows.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:10

> There is sickness in their hearts, and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase. They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Disease With No Fever**

The verse changes register from courtroom to clinic: *fī qulūbihim maraḍ* — in their hearts is a sickness. *Maraḍ* is the general Arabic term for a morbid state that weakens and unsettles whatever it occupies, and the commentators identify the heart's version as doubt and double-mindedness — the divided condition of a person running two beliefs at once. The Qur'an consistently thinks about the soul in medical terms: hearts sicken, and hearts are cured. The Book names itself the treatment — *"a cure for what is in the hearts"* (10:57) — and states the differential effect of the same dose: *"We send down the Quran as a healing and mercy for the believers, but it only increases the wrongdoers in loss"* (17:82). Whether revelation heals or aggravates depends on the organ it meets. The guarded heart of verse 2 receives it as medicine; the divided heart receives it as irritant, and the irritation is recorded as increase. A disease with no fever is still a disease — invisible symptoms do not make health.

**The Increase Attributed to Allah**

The second clause assigns the disease's growth to divine action: Allah *increases* them in sickness. The attribution parallels the sealing of verse 7, and the mechanism is the same shape — confirmation rather than manufacture. Each lie widens the wound; each performance deepens the split between the said self and the lived self, and the widening is decreed as penalty while operating as nature. The Qur'an has a name for this pattern in its doctrine of *istidrāj*: the sinner is given latitude that feels like success while it accumulates ruin, drawn on stage by stage toward an end he cannot see. Unpunished sin, on this picture, is not paused sin but compounding sin — the interval of apparent immunity is itself part of the sentence. The verse refuses to let evil stagnate. Sickness left to itself does not hold steady; it grows, and its growth passes through the divine will as everything does, here in the mode of justice: what they chose to become is being ratified as what they are becoming.

**Two Readings of the Cause: Lying, or Denying**

The final clause grounds the punishment in a speech act, and the Arabic allows two forms of it. Read as *yakdhibūn*, the cause is "their lies" — falsehood told. Read as *yukadhdhibūn*, the intensified form, it becomes "their denying" or "their calling the truth a lie." The exegetes weighed the readings, and al-Ṭabarī's preference for the first has textual support inside the Qur'an: the sūrah named for the hypocrites flatly declares them liars in the plain sense — *"Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are truly liars"* (63:1). The distinction is not pedantry. On the first reading the crime is the verse-8 claim itself: the recited creed was a lie the moment it left the mouth. On the second the crime extends to rejecting the truth they privately recognized. Both readings describe the same people, but the first ties the punishment more tightly to the passage's sequence — claim (2:8), deception (2:9), and now the sickness named as the wage of the original lie.

**Alīm After ʿAẓīm: The Adjectives Escalate**

Compare the two verdicts the passage has issued. The disbelievers of verse 7 received *ʿadhāb ʿaẓīm* — a tremendous punishment, an adjective of scale. The hypocrites receive *ʿadhāb alīm* — a painful punishment, an adjective of penetration. The shift is a judgment about the two conditions. The sealed disbeliever's loss is vast and outer: faculties closed, a tremendous penalty answering a tremendous refusal. The hypocrite's penalty is designed for an interior crime — a pain that reaches where the disease lives, since the sickness was itself an inner thing. The adjectives also track the sūrah's argument that hiddenness aggravates rather than softens guilt: the open denier sinned in daylight; the hidden one sinned while professing the opposite, adding treachery to rejection. The Qur'an's later verdict on the group confirms the direction of travel — Allah *"condemned them and prepared for them Hell"* for harbouring evil thoughts of Him (48:6). Painful is the fitting adjective for a crime committed against one's own heart.

**The Diagnostic Question Asked Again**

The Qur'an comments on itself, and its own later passage supplies the symptom list for this verse's disease. When a decision is referred to Allah and His Messenger for judgment, the sūrah al-Nūr observes the divided heart recoiling: *"Is there a sickness in their hearts? Or are they in doubt? Or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will be unjust to them?"* (24:50). The verse equates *maraḍ* with doubt and then gives it a behavioral test — the reaction to being judged by the truth one professes. Health welcomes the verdict even when it costs; sickness negotiates, delays, resents. This is how a disease with no fever becomes visible: not by inspection of the heart, which belongs to Allah, but by the flinch at the moment of decision. Al-Baqarah names the condition in verse 10; al-Nūr hands the community its symptom. Between them the portrait needs no clairvoyance — only occasions when the truth asks for a choice.

**From Act to State to Trajectory**

The three verses have now completed a pathology, and its stages deserve to be seen together. Verse 8 recorded an act: they said what they did not believe. Verse 9 recorded a practice: the saying hardened into a scheme of deception aimed at Allah and the community. Verse 10 records a state and its direction — the practice has become a disease, and the disease is increasing. This is sin read as medicine rather than as bookkeeping: not a ledger of infractions but the biography of a condition, with each stage generated by the last. The punishment clause then reads less like retribution than like prognosis — the painful end of a painful process, continuous with it rather than bolted onto it. The moral weight of the sequence falls on the earliest stage. A lie is still cheap to retract at verse 8; by verse 10 the retraction would have to fight a disease that Allah is increasing. The passage is telling its reader where the only easy exit stood, and how quickly it narrowed.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:11

> When they are told, “Do not spread corruption in the land,” they reply, “We are only peace-makers!”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Answer Arrives Before the Accusation Is Digested**

The verse is staged as dialogue, and its tempo is part of its content. "When they are told" — the speaker left indefinite, the charge delivered: do not spread corruption in the land. The reply comes at once, complete and unexamined: *we are only peace-makers*. No pause, no question about which acts are meant, no offer of account. The syntax of instant defense is on display: the accused answers the accusation not with facts but with a self-portrait. The reflex matters because it exposes where these people live — inside a prepared narrative, where every rebuke has a script waiting. An honest person hears "you are corrupting" and first asks *how*; the hypocrite hears it and first reasserts who he claims to be. The verse records the smallest unit of the passage's diagnosis: the disease of verse 10 speaking in real time, converting correction into an occasion for more of the costume.

**Fasād: Un-Making, Not Mischief**

The charge uses *fasād*, and the word is heavier than "mischief." From a root meaning to spoil or rot, it names the undoing of *ṣalāḥ* — the soundness, right order, and fertility of a thing. Corruption in Quranic usage is entropy with a moral cause: what disobedience does to the fabric that holds a land together. Ibn ʿAbbās defined corruption in the land as open disobedience against Allah, and the definition extends to its consequences, since the moral state of inhabitants registers in their world. The Qur'an states the registration at planetary scale: *"Corruption has spread on land and sea as a result of what people's hands have done, so that Allah may cause them to taste ˹the consequences of˺ some of their deeds and perhaps they might return ˹to the Right Path˺"* (30:41). Land and sea are not neutral stages on which sins occur; they carry the sins, spoil with them, and testify. A charge of *fasād* is therefore never a charge of mere rule-breaking — it is a charge of un-making the world's order from inside.

**The Speaker Deliberately Left Unnamed**

Classical exegesis noticed what the verse withholds: who says "do not spread corruption"? Al-Rāzī canvases the options — the Prophet ﷺ himself, a party of believers, or a victim of the corruption speaking rebuke to the corrupters — and the openness is the point. With the speaker indefinite, the scene becomes universal: every generation's corrupters hear this sentence from someone, and a society that still produces people who say it has not wholly died. The passive construction — *idhā qīla lahum*, "when it is said to them" — makes the rebuke ambient, a standing feature of the moral atmosphere rather than one prophet's campaign. The verse thus captures a permanent confrontation: the land's corruption generates its own protest somewhere, and the corrupter's reply, in every age, follows the same script. What is being tested is not the identity of the speaker but the reflexes of the one accused.

**“Only Peace-Makers”: Two Ways to Read the Claim**

The reply admits two readings, and the commentators supply both. On the first, the claim is sincere self-perception: they genuinely regard their course as reconciliation — mediators between camps, keepers of a workable peace, men of moderation in a polarized city. On the second, associated with al-Rāzī, the claim is strategy: positioned between the believers and the disbelievers, they present their lukewarmness as bridge-building, their hedging as peacemaking, and charge the price of the bridge to both sides. Weighing them, the next verse decides: the divine retort calls them corrupters *who fail to perceive it* (2:12) — correcting a perception rather than unmasking a known lie. That verdict fits the first reading: at this stage the blindness is real. The two readings are not rivals so much as layers — the strategic position of the bridgekeeper, maintained long enough, generates the sincere belief that bridgekeeping is righteousness. The costume of verse 8 has grown into the skin.

**Salmān's Warning: The Verse Has Not Peaked Yet**

An interpretation attributed to the Companion Salmān al-Fārsī runs through the commentaries: the people this passage fully describes have not yet come. Al-Ṭabarī records it, and the tradition accepts it in the sense that these verses are not confined to the Prophet's ﷺ contemporaries — the description awaits fuller populations in later ages. The reading has modern extensions: some contemporary Muslims find in *fasād* upon the land a direct verdict on the destruction of the natural environment, and 30:41's coupling of land and sea with the works of human hands supports the extension. The combined effect lifts the verse out of its Madinan scene without emptying the scene. There were hypocrites there, named in the histories, rebuked in these words; and there will be — are — corrupters elsewhere answering the same rebuke with the same self-portrait. A verse with no historical floor would float free; a verse with no future would be dead. Salmān's reading keeps both.

**A Virtuous Word Worn as Camouflage**

*Muṣliḥūn* — the word they claim — means those who set things right, who repair and put in order; the exegetes caution that it is not "reform" in the modern programmatic sense but the active maintenance of *ṣalāḥ*. The claim is therefore a seizure of vocabulary: the corrupters dress in the language of repair, and the dressing is tactical. Whoever controls the word "peace-maker" controls the verdict before any evidence is weighed. The Qur'an's answer, in the next verse, strips the label and reinstalls the test — claims are read against consequences, words against acts. The pattern this verse installs recurs wherever power learns moral language: oppression announced as order, plunder announced as development, betrayal announced as realism. Against all of it the verse preserves the oldest rebuke in the land's own defense — *do not spread corruption* — and records, for the diagnostician, the exact reflex by which the corrupter betrays himself: instant, total, self-portraiture.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:12

> Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Divine Interruption in the Middle of the Dialogue**

The previous verse ended with the hypocrites' claim still hanging in the air; this verse answers it before any human reply can arrive. The answer comes from above the dialogue: *alā* — the particle that arrests attention — followed by *inna*, the particle of emphasis, and then the verdict. No argument is offered, no evidence marshalled, no interlocutor appointed to debate. The case is simply declared settled by the only party whose knowledge covers interiors. The interruption has a formal effect worth noticing: the Qur'an has been reporting what they say and what they are told, and now it drops the reporting and speaks. Third-person narration becomes direct address to the reader. The device concedes nothing to the claim it answers — a self-portrait does not merit a rebuttal, only a correction — and it relocates the trial. The hypocrites argued their case to the community; the community is now informed of how the case actually stands in the court that never adjourns.

**The Restriction That Refutes**

The grammar of the verdict is a machine of three parts. *Innahum* — indeed they — with emphasis. *Hum* — the pronoun fronted from inside the sentence, where Arabic places it to restrict: *they, and no others*. *Al-mufsidūn* — the definite active participle: *the* corrupters, the people the noun truly names. Assembled: it is precisely they who are the corrupters. The restriction refutes by reassignment. The claim of verse 11 was not that corruption doesn't exist but that its authors are peace-makers; the retort accepts the charge's reality and hands it back to the claimants. They had assigned themselves the title *muṣliḥ*, repairer; the verse installs them in its exact opposite, *mufsid*, un-maker — and the definite article closes the office to anyone else: whatever corruption is being done in that land, its registered practitioners are these. The verse thereby legislates how labels are read in the Qur'an: the name follows the act and its consequences, never the advertisement, and no self-description survives contact with the divine ledger.

**Corruption by Way of Neutrality**

The hardest question the verse poses is honest: how is peace-making corruption? The answer is structural. In a conflict between truth and falsehood, a party that positions itself between them moves the center of gravity toward falsehood — every step the middle takes away from the truth is a step the falsehood did not have to take. The bridgekeeper supplies corruption with respectability: while the *muṣliḥ*-claim stands, the un-making proceeds under cover of a virtue no one wants to investigate. Ibn ʿAbbās's definition — corruption as open disobedience against Allah — extends naturally to those who dress disobedience in reconciliation language, since the dressing multiplies the harm: it misleads observers about what obedience costs and what compromise buys. The verse judges by outcome, and the outcome of this particular peace is *fasād* spreading through the land of verse 11. Neutrality that favors the corrosive party is not a third position; it is the corrosive party's most useful position.

**The Unperceiving, Named Twice**

The closing clause repeats verse 9's almost word for word: *wa-lākin lā yashʿurūn* — but they do not perceive it. The repetition is the passage's signature now. In verse 9 the unperceived thing was the self-deception; here it is the corruption. One blindness, two objects, and the recurrence tells the reader that insensitivity itself is the group's defining symptom — more than the lying, more than the scheming. Perception, *shuʿūr*, was the fine-grained awareness that feels a hair's touch; its absence at both hinges of the passage means the type is unified by what it cannot feel: not the trick returning on the trickster, not the rot spreading under the peace-making. The two blindnesses are one disease — the *maraḍ* of verse 10, which Allah increases. The verse's structure thus completes the diagnosis begun there: a sickness whose specific power is to anaesthetize its own symptoms, so that the sufferer's comfort becomes the physician's gravest datum.

**The Land Tastes What the Hands Send**

Corruption in this vocabulary is never victimless abstraction, and the Qur'an's widest statement of the theme gives verse 12 its scope: *"Corruption has spread on land and sea as a result of what people's hands have done, so that Allah may cause them to taste ˹the consequences of˺ some of their deeds and perhaps they might return ˹to the Right Path˺"* (30:41). The sentence carries verse 12's whole theology in miniature. The corruption is theirs — their hands, their peace-making, their un-making. The medium that carries it is not opinion but land and sea: soil, water, social order, the physical and moral habitat that spoils with its inhabitants. And the purpose clause remains medicinal — *so that they may taste* and *perhaps return*: even the consequences are arranged toward repentance, the only exit the diseased perception of verse 12 cannot see. The hypocrites of Madina corrupted a city; the verse's grammar corrupts no city alone. Every land gets the taste of what its peace-makers spread.

**A Standing Answer to Every Euphemism**

The verse's afterlife is its point. Every age produces corrupters who hold the vocabulary of repair — wars fought under the word peace, plunder under development, betrayal under realism — and every age needs the retort that strips labels back to acts. The Qur'an supplies it once, in eleven words of Arabic, and installs it as a permanent test: when claim and consequence diverge, the consequence is the truth of the claim. The closing clause sharpens the test into a warning about its users. The worst position in this passage is not the corruption but the imperceptible corruption — the un-maker who feels like a repairer, whom no rebuke reaches because every rebuke is metabolized into self-portrait. The community that reads this verse is armed and cautioned at once: armed, because the euphemism now has a fixed answer; cautioned, because the answer was needed twice — verse 11 was not enough — and the perception that fails at *fasād* may already be failing in the reader who flinches at the diagnosis.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:13

> And when they are told, “Believe as others believe,” they reply, “Will we believe as the fools believe?” Indeed, it is they who are fools, but they do not know.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Plainest Command, the Scornful Refusal**

The charge of corruption is followed by a simpler sentence, and the reply to it unmasks the group more completely than any argument could. The command carries no content to dispute: *believe as the people believe* — join the faith of the community around you, the faith already tested in lives you can see. No doctrine is expounded, no proof is demanded, no condition is attached; the invitation is to company. And the answer refuses precisely the company: *shall we believe as the fools believe?* The interrogative form in Arabic — *a-nuʾminu* — is rhetorical, and rhetorical questions of this shape carry scorn rather than inquiry. The verse thus locates the root of this unbelief with clinical accuracy. It is not evidential — no objection to a sign or a proof appears anywhere in the reply. It is social: the objection is to the believers. When faith's cost is association with the despised, the costume of verse 8 becomes unbearable to wear in public, and the contempt that the costume was hiding speaks.

**“The Fools” Aimed at the Best on Earth**

The referent of "the fools" is fixed by the historians and the commentators: the Prophet's ﷺ Companions — the community of the early believers, who in Madinan and Makkan terms were largely the poor, the young, the clients, and the unprestigious. The sneer is one of sophistication: faith read as vulgarity, belief as the resort of simple people who could not manage doubt. Some exegetes add a harder layer — that these speakers privately recognized the intelligence of the believers and applied the word "fools" anyway, to perform superiority before their circle. On that reading the insult is deliberate slander layered over private knowledge, which would place the speakers beyond mere blindness. The verse's own verdict, however, ends with *they do not know*, and the commentaries weigh this: a purely strategic slanderer knows exactly what he is doing. The stronger reading makes the contempt genuine — they truly ranked the Companions beneath themselves — which is why the verdict can pronounce them fools without reservation. You cannot strategically slander your way into sincerely missing the worth of the best people on earth; only a broken scale does that.

**The Verdict Flips in the Same Breath**

The retort reuses the machinery of verse 12 — *alā*, *inna*, the fronted pronoun — and aims it at the insult itself: *indeed, it is they who are the fools*. The word thrown at the Companions returns, with restriction, onto the throwers: they, and no others, hold the title. The term deserves its lexicon. *Sufahāʾ* is the plural of *safīh*, from a root meaning lightness — the light-witted, the weak in judgment, and in legal Arabic the person placed under interdiction because he squanders his estate. The *safīh* is not stupid in the modern sense of raw capacity; he is a bad evaluator who misprices things and spends accordingly. That is the exact shape of the verse's reversal. The Companions, called fools for buying the eternal with the temporal, made the only solvent purchase on the market; the sophisticates, congratulating themselves on the deal they refused, were the ones trading at a loss — squanderers of the only capital a self owns. The Qur'an does not answer the insult with a counter-insult; it answers it with an audit.

**From Unperceiving to Unknowing: The Closure Deepens**

The passage's cycle closes on a shifted negation, and the shift is a descent. Verse 9 ended: they do not *perceive* — *lā yashʿurūn*, the failure of fine sensation. Verse 12 repeated it. Verse 13 ends: they do not *know* — *lā yaʿlamūn*, the failure of the cognitive faculty itself. Perception is the surface instrument; knowledge is the settled possession. A man who does not feel the rot under his peace-making might still, in principle, be shown it; a man who does not know his own folly has lost the organ by which showing would work. The two negations map the passage's whole trajectory — from costume (they say) through operation (they deceive) and disease (sickness increased) to the completed closure of judgment. The escalation also explains the sequence's arrangement: the earlier verses described acts a person could stop; this verse describes a condition in which stopping has become unthinkable, because the thinker is the casualty. The cycle of the first diagnosis is finished, and its subject now carries both negations at once.

**Safah as the Qur'an Defines It**

The reversal works only with the Qur'an's own definition of folly, and that definition is consistent wherever the root appears: *safah* is misvaluation — the selling of the lasting for the fleeting, the preference of a moment's position for an eternity's substance. The fools of this passage are not mocked for ignorance of facts; they are convicted of ignorance of worth. The Companions knew what they were buying; the despisers did not know what they were refusing, and their refusal was priced by rank, fashion, and the opinions of their circle. This is why the Qur'an can call knowledge and folly by these inverted names throughout: the person who knows the market of the eternal is the intelligent one whatever his social standing, and the person ignorant of it is the *safīh* whatever his sophistication. The verse legislates a revaluation of the word itself. "Fool" ceases to name the simple and begins to name the misplaced — and by that statute, the sneer of verse 13 was a confession.

**An Egalitarian Epistemology**

What remains is the verse's largest claim: truth is not graded by the social standing of its carriers. The objection "as the fools believe" is an objection to believers, not to belief — an epistemology of status, where a proposition's weight equals the prestige of its holders. The Qur'an's answer dismantles the instrument.
