If belief were validated by the rank of its adherents, the earliest Muslims — poor, young, unprestigious — would have carried the weakest creed in Arabia, and the chiefs of Quraysh, who made exactly this objection in exactly these terms, would have been its soundest critics. The verse sides permanently against that reasoning: the company of truth is often the company the world despises, and the reflex to measure a message by its messengers' standing is here named what it is — the lightness of the *safīh*. The closing negation makes the diagnosis final. They do not know — and a person who does not know what knowledge is cannot be argued into knowing; he can only be watched, by readers warned that the same scale operates, silently, in every age.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:14

> When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But when alone with their evil associates they say, “We are definitely with you; we were only mocking.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Rooms, Two Creeds**

The verse is staged as a diptych of rooms. In the first, the hypocrites meet the believers and produce two words — *we believe*. In the second, alone with their own company, the profession is retracted in full: *we are definitely with you; we were only mocking*. The contrast is total — same speakers, same day, opposite creeds — and the verse lets both statements stand unedited, side by side, with no narrator between them. What emerges is a definition of nifāq more precise than any label: faith that exists only in an audience. In the believers' room the creed is a ticket; in the private room the ticket is described aloud as a fraud. The sūrah has been cataloguing this group's acts — the lie, the deception, the sickness, the corruption-claim, the sneer — and now it produces the group's own transcript, the one document that cannot be reinterpreted, because both versions of it were spoken by the same mouths.

**The Occasion That Sealed the Transcript**

The commentaries preserve the scene behind the verse. A hypocrite boasted to his circle: watch how I divert these fools from you. He went to certain Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, loaded them with praise, then returned to his own companions and instructed them — when you see them, do as I do. The Companions went to the Prophet ﷺ and reported what had happened, and this verse came down, exposing the intention behind the performance (recorded by Ibn Kathīr and others). The occasion explains the verse's documentary quality: revelation functioning as evidence in a live dispute. It also fixes a permanent feature of the prophetic community — its founder was given no police of hearts, but he was given a Book that overheard the back rooms. The boast "watch how I divert these fools" is the private text of which every public creed of verse 8 was the performance, and the two were now read aloud together.

**Shayāṭīn With Human Faces**

"With their evil associates" renders *shayāṭīnihim* — their satans, plural of *shayṭān*. The plural does most of the work. The singular in the Qur'an usually names the one tempter; the plural ranges widely, and exegetes read it here as the hypocrites' leaders and confederates, their fellow travelers in disbelief, or even the inner demons each carries into the private room. The Qur'an itself licenses the human application: *"And so We have made for every prophet enemies—devilish humans and jinn—whispering to one another with elegant words of deception"* (6:112). Shaitanic function, on that verse, is not a species marker but a job description, and humans hold the post. The possessive in "their satans" adds a final stroke: every man's company of deviation is somehow his own — chosen, cultivated, and addressed with the intimacy of *we are definitely with you*.

**“We Were Only Mocking”: The Clause That Convicts**

The private confession has three movements, and the last is the fatal one. *We are definitely with you* — loyalty reassured, the emphatic particle doing double duty after a public day of apparent betrayal. Then the disclosure: *we were only mocking*. Mockery, not doubt, is what the public profession concealed. The distinction matters theologically. The doubter withholds assent pending evidence; the mocker has already seen the evidence and chosen derision. Mockery is contempt in its purest verbal form — it does not argue with faith, it performs superiority over it, and it recruits the audience into the performance. The "only" — *innamā* — minimizes the act even while confessing it, the reflex of men for whom the mockery was entertainment rather than position. The verse records that self-minimizing tone verbatim because it is diagnostic: nothing feels cheaper than a joke, and the sūrah will show what the joke costs.

**The Taxonomy's Sixth Entry**

Read inside the passage that began at verse 8, this verse adds a new specimen to the collection. The lie stated a false creed; the deception organized it into a scheme; the sickness named its interior condition; the peace-making claim showed its social rhetoric; the fools-retort exposed its contempt for believers; now the mockery reveals its emotional core — not fear of the truth but amusement at it. The progression is from act to disposition, and mockery sits closest to the root. A man who lies to the believers still takes them seriously enough to manage them; a man who mocks them has placed them below seriousness entirely. That is why the sūrah treats this verse as the turning of the passage: after it, the description stops accumulating their sayings and starts pronouncing what will be done about them. The private room has said everything; the case is complete.

**A Revelation That Abolishes the Back Room**

The verse's permanent effect is on the geography of secrecy. Before it, the hypocrites possessed what every hidden type possesses: a space where the self is unobserved and the real creed can be spoken. This verse cancels that space — not by surveillance they can see but by a text that quotes their closed-door sentences with quotation marks intact. The community that received it learned that its Scripture hears rooms. For later readers the lesson generalizes past the historical hypocrites: every person maintains a private room where the day's professions are reviewed and revised, and the verse stands as the reminder that the room is not private in the only sense that finally matters. The believers in the first room could not tell the difference between the two creeds; the difference was nonetheless written down, preserved, and recited — and the next verse answers the mockery in its own idiom.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:15

> Allah will throw their mockery back at them, leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Mockery Returns to Its Sender**

The answer to the private room is one verb: *yastahziʾu bihim* — Allah mocks them, in the same measure and the same mode as their *innamā nastahziʾ*, "we were only mocking." The Qur'an attributes mockery to Allah, and the attribution troubled exegetes enough to generate two reconciliations. One reading holds that the disgrace the disbelievers bring upon themselves is the mockery in substance — recompense arriving in the deed's own shape, not an act of derision originating in God. The other, al-Rāzī's, treats the prolonged ignominy in which Allah leaves them as tantamount to mockery: a scheme permitted to run its full course until the schemer is exposed. Weighed against the Qur'an's wider idiom — plotting answered by plotting, deception answered by outwitting — both readings describe one law: the moral universe returns acts in kind. The joke of verse 14 was told at the believers' expense; this verse announces that its punchline was reserved, from the first syllable, for the tellers.

**The Law With a Second Witness**

The formula is not local to al-Baqarah, which is what makes it a law rather than an incident. Sūrah al-Tawbah records the same exchange over alms: *"˹There are˺ those who slander ˹some of˺ the believers for donating liberally and mock others for giving only the little they can afford. Allah will throw their mockery back at them, and they will suffer a painful punishment"* (9:79). Two settings — Madinan hypocrisy in the sūrah's opening, Madinan hypocrisy around the charity drives years later — one identical verdict. The recurrence shows mockery being treated as a category with a fixed consequence, not a sin singled out for local color. It also refines the category: in al-Tawbah the object of the joke is generosity measured against the giver's means, the sneer of the ledger-keeper at sincerity. What is mocked in both sūrahs is never the powerful; it is faithfulness in its unimpressive forms. The returned mockery therefore has a target list, and the list is compiled by the mocker himself.

**Ṭughyān: The Overflow That Becomes a Vehicle**

"Wandering blindly in their defiance" ends on *ṭughyān* — defiance, rebellion, transgression — a noun from *ṭaghā*, to pass beyond a limit, the way water passes beyond a bank. The word family carries its hydrology into the theology: transgression is an overflow, a quantity exceeding the vessel that contained it. The Qur'an's exemplar is Pharaoh, and the command to confront him states the charge in the word itself: *"Go to Pharaoh, for he has truly transgressed ˹all bounds˺"* (20:24). The hypocrites of this passage have their own overflow: a public creed they do not believe, a private loyalty they do not confess, and mockery poured over the gap between the two. Ṭughyān names the condition of living past one's own limits — beyond sincerity, beyond consistency, beyond the point where the performance can be sustained. What the verse says of them is that they are left *in* it: the overflow becomes the medium they now move through.

**Yaʿmahūn: Staggering Inside the Sentence**

The closing verb, *yaʿmahūn*, has no clean English equivalent, which is why translations reach for "wander blindly" or "continue blindly." It describes the staggering of a person whose vision has gone — movement without orientation, effort without direction, the walk of one who circles. The Qur'an keeps the word as a fixed formula and deploys it across settings: *"Whoever Allah allows to stray, none can guide, leaving them to wander blindly in their defiance"* (7:186), with further instances in al-Anʿām, Yūnus, and al-Muʾminūn. The pairing with *ṭughyān* in each case is the point: the wandering is not punishment imposed on an innocent activity but the interior experience of the transgression itself. To live past your limits is to lose the horizon; the rebel's reward is vertigo. The hypocrites mocked believers who walked a straight path toward a known destination; the returned mockery leaves the mockers in motion and the mockers' destination unknown to the mockers.

**The Heaviest Judgment Is Withdrawal**

Read carefully, the verse's verb structure makes Allah's action a leaving: *wa-yadharuhum* — He leaves them, abandons them to the wandering. Nothing is struck; no bolt falls. The mockery returned is not God performing a joke on them but God withdrawing the hand that steadies, and letting the joke complete its own circuit. This is the Qur'an's recurring economy of judgment — the sinner's greatest danger is not divine intervention but divine permission, the respite that reads as success while it accumulates ruin. The withdrawal answers the mockery with exact justice: they treated faith as a game played before an inattentive audience; they are given what their creed assumed — an audience that has stopped intervening. And the verse locates the duration inside the leaving: *yamadduhum*, He extends them, stretches the rope while the staggering continues. The mockers of verse 14 asked, in effect, to be taken unseriously. Verse 15 grants the request literally.

**Justice Paid in the Same Currency**

The exchange between the two verses is a closed circuit, and its symmetry is the theological claim. They said: we were only mocking. The answer: Allah will throw their mockery back at them — the same noun, the same activity, redirected. The moral order this assumes is not mechanical but articulate: it knows the currency of each deed and pays in it. The liar is undone by a discovered lie; the deceiver becomes the deceived; the mocker inherits the joke. That is why the verse offers the hypocrites no new information about Allah — only a mirror with a verdict attached. For the reader outside the scene, the circuit carries a second charge: every mockery spoken at sincerity, generosity, or prayer is registered as a loan, and the repayment schedule is not published in advance. The sūrah's opening movement ends here, its taxonomy complete, and turns next from what the hypocrites are to what they have done with what they had — a transaction stated in the vocabulary of the market.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:16

> They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance. But this trade is profitless, and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Soul Stated as a Ledger**

The verse re-describes everything the passage has shown in the vocabulary of the market. The hypocrites are *alladhīna ishtarawū* — the ones who purchased, who struck a bargain — and the goods exchanged are named: misguidance bought, guidance paid. Commerce is the Qur'an's favored idiom for the soul's decisions, and al-Baqarah will return to it: of another group it says *"These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world"* (2:86), and the sūrah al-Ṣaff opens its counter-offer in the same register — *"O believers! Shall I guide you to an exchange that will save you from a painful punishment?"* (61:10). The metaphor is chosen with care. A market presumes free buyers, real alternatives, known prices, and a moment of decision; sin read as commerce keeps all four. Nothing here is fate or weakness — it is a transaction, entered by parties who preferred one commodity over another, and the verse's judgment is an audit of that preference.

**Buying Can Mean Preferring**

The verb *ishtarā* carries a documented ambiguity, and the exegetes worked both sides of it. In standard usage it means to purchase; in an established extension it means to prefer, to choose one thing over another regardless of payment — as when Thamūd is described in Fuṣṣilat: *"We showed them guidance, but they preferred blindness over guidance"* (41:17). Al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī note the preference-reading here, and also note what weakens it: the verse itself goes on to mention *tijārah*, commerce, which pulls the metaphor back toward the literal market. Both readings survive, and they are not rivals so much as two exposures of one photograph. Preference describes the interior act — the tilt of the will toward misguidance. Purchase describes its structure — something held was surrendered to obtain it. Guidance was genuinely in the hypocrites' hands: they had the creed, the community, the prayers. You cannot prefer away what you never possessed, and the verse's economics depends on that prior ownership.

**An Audit With Three Findings**

The commercial frame lets the verse issue its verdict as findings of fact. First: the goods. What they acquired, misguidance, they already had — it was the state of their private rooms before the purchase; what they surrendered, guidance, was the one asset they could not regenerate. The trade is therefore not an exchange of values but a surrender of value for possession of what was never lost. Second: the result — *their commerce has not brought them profit*. Not "brought little profit" or "brought tainted profit": no profit at all, the ledger closed at a loss beyond recovery of the purchase price. Third: the standing of the traders — *they are not rightly guided*, which reads in commercial terms as the revocation of their license. A merchant whose entire inventory is counterfeit is not merely poorer; he is outside the market. The three findings move from the deal to the balance sheet to the trader's status, and each is final in a way that leaves no appellate language in the verse.

**The Double Verdict at the End**

Why does the verse need both closing clauses — profitless, *and* not guided? The first is economic, the second existential, and together they answer a question the market metaphor invites. A failed trader can remain a trader; a loss can be absorbed by reserves. The second clause forecloses that reading: the loss consumed the reserves. Guidance in the Qur'an is not an asset held alongside the self — it is the condition of the self's orientation, and its sale leaves the seller disoriented toward every subsequent deal. There is also a structural echo in the doubling. Verse 5 of this sūrah ended its portrait with two locked clauses — *it is they* who are guided, *it is they* who are successful — and this verse inverts the architecture for the opposite type: *it is they* whose trade failed, *it is they* who stand unguided. The sūrah is keeping parallel ledgers, and the restriction-pronouns mark each entry as complete.

**Everyone Trades at This Market**

The hypocrites are the verse's named clients, but the transaction type generalizes, and the Qur'an applies the same verb elsewhere to whole communities. Thamūd preferred blindness to guidance (41:17). Another group in this very sūrah trades the covenant and its oaths for a paltry price (2:86; 3:77). The common structure is visible once named: some possession of truth surrendered for some advantage of position, appetite, or safety. The hypocrite version is the paradigm case only because it trades at the highest price difference known to the market — the whole of guidance for the whole of its opposite, undertaken by men who could recite both sides fluently. Every reader who has ever softened a conviction to suit a room, or traded honesty for standing, has transacted here in smaller denominations. The verse is terrifying not because the trade is exotic but because the market is universal and its currency is what each person is holding.

**The Counter-Offer Left Standing**

A market verse implies a rival offer, and the Qur'an makes the counter-trade explicit: *"O believers! Shall I guide you to an exchange that will save you from a painful punishment?"* (61:10) — belief and striving in Allah's cause presented as the commerce that rescues. Set beside verse 16, the two transactions share everything but direction: both require surrendering something held, both promise an acquisition, both are entered knowingly. The difference is that the profitable exchange buys the lasting with the fleeting, while this one does the reverse and calls the reversal profit. Verse 16 of al-Baqarah is the negative plate of that offer — the photograph of the trade that fails — and the sūrah keeps it in circulation for a pastoral reason: no one enters a bad deal intending to; the hypocrites believed they were managing risk. The audit published here exists so that later traders can price their goods before the sale rather than after.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:17

> Their example is that of someone who kindles a fire, but when it lights up all around them, Allah takes away their light, leaving them in complete darkness—unable to see.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Passage Turns From Description to Image**

After seven verses of direct characterization — they say, they deceive, they are sick, they mock — the sūrah changes instruments and begins to draw. *Mathal*, example or parable, is the Qur'an's method of making a moral condition visible: the type is not re-described but staged inside a scene the body can picture. Two scenes follow, the kindled fire and the storm, and the first is domestic in scale — one person, one flame, one night. The switch to image is itself a claim: the hypocrite's condition resists definition and yields to depiction, because its essence is not a proposition but an experience — the feel of light that is not yours, and of its withdrawal. The parable also transfers the diagnosis from courtroom to campfire. Every listener has sat by a flame that guttered; the verse recruits that memory as evidence, and the memory convicts without argument.

**A Fire That Lit the Surroundings, Not the Self**

The verbs are exact. *Istawqaʿada nāran* — he sought, kindled, sat down by a fire: the effort is real, and so is the settling-in beside it. *Falammā aḍāʾat mā ḥawlahu* — when it illuminated *what was around him*. The light's reach is specified as the surroundings, and the specification is the parable's first cut: the fire lit his situation — the ground, the faces, the immediate world — but nothing inside him; the man himself stands in the scene unchanged by its brightness. Commentators map the correspondence: the fire is the hypocrite's professed faith, the *shahādah* he recited, which lit up his legal and social surroundings — membership granted him protection, inheritance, marriage, standing in the community — while his heart stayed where it was. Borrowed light behaves exactly this way. It makes everything visible except its source, and it flatters the borrower with the sense of sight while the eye itself learns nothing.

**Allah Removes the Light, Not the Fire**

The extinction clause chooses its noun with care: *dhahaba Allāhu bi-nūrihim* — Allah took away *their light*. Not the fire — the light. The distinction matters because fire and light are separable in experience: the flame can remain while its illumination goes, as the hypocrites' formal membership remained while its meaning drained. The removal is attributed directly to Allah, and the attribution continues the theology of verse 7 — the sealing there, the extinguishing here — where divine action confirms a state the subject built. The timing clause completes the picture: the light goes *when it has lit up all around them*, at the moment of maximum usefulness and maximum confidence. Classical exegesis places that moment at death, when the mask comes off and the communal light of the profession no longer reaches the soul. The sūrah al-Ḥadīd stages the sequel: *"On that Day hypocrite men and women will beg the believers, 'Wait for us so that we may have some of your light'… Then a ˹separating˺ wall with a gate will be erected between them"* (57:13).

**Darkness in the Plural, Sight Intact**

The aftermath is described in two clauses that do different work. *Tarakahum fī ẓulumāt* — He left them in darknesses, plural: not one absence of light but layered darkness, the grammatical plural suggesting darkness folded over darkness, the stacked condition of a night that has no single source to fix. Then *lā yubṣirūn* — unseeing. The verb form keeps their sight: the faculty is intact and functioning; there is simply nothing for it to find. This is a sharper punishment than the sealed organs of verse 7. The man whose heart was sealed could not process evidence; the men of this parable can see perfectly and are surrounded by night. They retain the capacity to know that they cannot see — awareness of the loss preserved inside the loss. Every human darkness is tolerable until the eyes work, and the verse leaves them working.

**Light Is Allah's to Give, and Fire Is Man's to Strike**

The parable sits inside a larger grammar of light the Qur'an develops, whose center is the verse of Light itself: *"Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth"* (24:35). In that grammar, light in the true sense is not a substance but a relation — illumination that belongs to Allah and is extended, guided to whomever He wills. Against it, the kindled fire of verse 17 is what a creature can produce unaided: a local, fuel-fed flame, genuine as warmth and useless as a sky. The hypocrites' error, in the parable's terms, was mistaking a struck fire for given light — assuming that a profession they manufactured would illuminate like a grace they received. That is why the removal is attributed to Allah rather than to wind or fuel: only the Giver can withdraw the given, and what He withdrew had never been theirs. The fire was their work; the light was always a loan.

**Why the First Parable Is Small**

Of the two images this passage deploys, the fire comes first and is deliberately modest — one man, one flame, one dark plain. The smallness serves the diagnosis. Hypocrisy begins domestic: a creed recited in a room, a prayer performed for an audience, a lamp kept burning because the neighbors see it. The parable refuses the type any grandeur — no storm yet, no thunder, just a guttering flame and a man standing in his own extinguished evening. Read in sequence with the verses before it, the image gathers their content: the lie of verse 8 was the striking of the flame; the deception of verse 9 was sitting down beside it; the mockery of verse 14 was boasting of how well it lit the room. The extinction of verse 17 is not a new event in the passage but the same events seen from the end. And the sūrah is not finished: a second parable follows, widening the scene from one flame to a whole sky, because the condition has more than one weather.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:18

> They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Three Adjectives and No Verb**

The verse is a nominal sentence — Arabic's construction for states rather than events. It does not say they *became* deaf, dumb, and blind, or that something *was done* to them; it says: deaf, dumb, blind — full stop. The nominal form in Arabic carries the sense of fixity and continuance, and the three adjectives arrive without a single verb to soften them into process. What the syntax states is a achieved condition: the disabilities have hardened from history into nature. The bracketed *˹wilfully˺* in the translation marks the exegetical consensus that supplies the missing history — these are not afflictions that befell innocent organs but disabilities manufactured by their owners' choices, now past the point where choice is needed to maintain them. The verse thus stands between the parable of verse 17 and the storm of verse 19 as the passage's one-line medical report: what began as conduct has completed itself as constitution.

**Words Whose Sound Enacts Their Sense**

The commentaries note a feature that survives recitation better than translation. Read aloud in Arabic, *ṣummun bukmun ʿumyun* performs what it says: three heavy, closed-syllable words, each ending in a doubled consonant that shuts the mouth — no open vowels to release them, no verbs to move them along. The line sounds the way the condition feels: sealed, weighted, without exit. The Qur'an's reciters have always treated sound as semantic material, and this triad is one of its clearest cases — a diagnosis delivered in phonetics as well as lexicon, so that the ear receives the closure before the mind parses it. In the prayer where these verses are recited, the congregation's own mouths form the words; the description of the hypocrites is uttered in the voices of the people warned against resembling them. Few verses so completely fuse their form to their content.

**Each Organ and the Faculty It Abandoned**

The triad maps onto the channels of guidance with clinical neatness. Deaf: the ear is closed, and revelation in the Qur'an is above all a heard thing — the Prophet ﷺ received it as recitation, and faith enters through listening. Dumb: the tongue is disabled, and the tongue is the organ of the *shahādah* — the very instrument that lied in verse 8 can now speak nothing true even if it wished. Blind: the eye is shut, and the Qur'an's world is dense with *āyāt*, signs to be seen in the sky, the earth, and the self. The three losses answer the three closures of verse 7 — the sealed heart, the sealed hearing, the covered sight — and complete them outward: what was locked inside is now dead at the surface. The order in Arabic puts deafness first, matching the priority of hearing in a religion of recited revelation; the translation's "deaf, dumb, and blind" preserves the sequence, and the sequence itself is an anatomy lesson in how guidance arrives and how it can be refused.

**A Signature the Qur'an Signs Twice More**

The triad is not improvised here; it is a recurring formula the Book applies to the same human type in two other settings, and the recurrences fix its meaning. Later in this sūrah, the disbelievers who will not respond to the messenger are compared to livestock: *"˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb and blind so they have no understanding"* (2:171) — the same three words, now attached to a flock that hears the shepherd's call as noise. In al-Isrāʾ the formula is projected onto the Resurrection: *"And We will drag them on their faces on the Day of Judgment—deaf, dumb, and blind. Hell will be their home"* (17:97). The two extensions do real interpretive work. Al-Baqarah 171 confirms the disabilities are spiritual insensibility, not bodily fate — the organs work; the understanding is elsewhere. Al-Isrāʾ 97 shows the condition's terminus: what was acquired by choice in this life is ratified as the body's posture in the next. Between acquisition and ratification, this verse holds the hinge.

**“They Will Never Return”: The Last Door**

The closing clause — *fa-hum lā yarjiʿūn* — names what the triad forecloses: the return, *rujūʿ*, the Qur'an's word for repentance as a turning back. The exegetes specify the object variously: they will not return to guidance, to Islam, or to repentance and heed — and the three readings collapse into one, since each names the same lost motion. The finality particle *lan* is not used here; the negation is the plain *lā* with the imperfect, stating continuation rather than decree — they do not return, and the not-returning is their present tense. The clause explains itself by the triad before it: return requires hearing the call, speaking the confession, seeing the road, and the organs of return are precisely the organs disabled. This is the verse's most severe claim — not that return is forbidden but that it has become unperformable, the way a burned-out bridge is not prohibited, only absent. The door did not close on them; they dismantled it from inside.

**Acquired Disability, Preserved as Warning**

Everything in the verse's placement argues against fatalism. These are not men born deaf, dumb, and blind — the passage has just narrated the manufacturing, step by step: the lie, the scheme, the sickness increased, the mockery, the trade. The triad is the scar tissue of those acts, which is why the translation's "wilfully" belongs to the sense and not merely to the gloss. And the verse exists to be heard by the un-afflicted. In the liturgy of the mosque, in the private recitation of al-Baqarah, the description passes over the tongues of people whose organs all function — the warning operating on the principle that a disability is preventable only while it is still recognized as a choice. The hypocrites of Madina are long dead; the triad is not, because the acts that build it are perennial. Every refused truth deposits something; the verse states the endpoint of the deposits so that the first refusal can be recognized for what it is — the down payment on a silence that will not end by itself.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:19

> Or ˹those caught in˺ a rainstorm from the sky with darkness, thunder, and lightning. They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap for fear of death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Parable Widens the Scene**

The particle *aw* — "or" — links this image to the fire of verse 17 as a second exposure of the same subject: another parable, or their case is like the case of people caught in a storm. The scale change is total. The first image was domestic — one man, one flame, one plain; this one is cosmological — a sky, a downpour, a weather system with the victims inside it. The bracketed *˹those caught in˺* in the translation states the grammar's implication: the hypocrites are no longer standing beside a fire they lit but enclosed in a rainstorm they did not make and cannot leave. Commentators have read the two parables as complementary states — the extinguished flame depicting the end of borrowed light, the storm depicting the daily weather of a life lived under revelation one refuses. Together they cover the type in both tenses: what hypocrisy ends in, and what it feels like from inside while it lasts.

**One Sky, Three Weathers**

The storm carries darkness, thunder, and lightning together — *ẓulumāt wa-raʿd wa-barq* — and the traditional mapping of the three is consistent: the darkness is the doubt and denial the hypocrites live in; the thunder is the warning, the menace of the message that makes them flinch; the lightning is its proof and clarity, the flashes of truth their eyes cannot deny. The image's precision lies in the simultaneity. This is not darkness relieved by occasional light, but one sky producing all three at once — exactly as one revelation reaches the hypocrites as guidance and threat and dazzle in a single text. The plural darkness matches verse 17's layered dark; the storm now gives it weather — moving, loud, active. Revelation, in this reading, is not a lamp offered in a neutral room. It is a storm system: the same event that waters the valley of the God-conscious (13:17) deafens and blinds the men standing against it.

**Fingers in Ears: The Posture of the Verse**

The middle of the parable is pure body language: *yajʿalūna aṣābiʿahum fī ādhānihim* — they put their *fingers* into their ears. Not hands over ears, but fingers driven in — the gesture of panic precision, the anatomy of someone trying to seal a passage that cannot be sealed. The reason given is *mina al-ṣawāʿiq*, from the thunderclaps, literally the stunning bolts; and the motive beneath the reason is *ḥadhara al-mawt* — fear of death. The verse has captured the hypocrites' entire religion in one reflex: their relationship to revelation is not assessment but survival. They do not argue with the thunder; they plug against it. Fear of death, in the Qur'an's moral vocabulary, is not piety but the engine of every compromised creed — the attachment to a life whose terms are set by the world explains the lie of verse 8, the deception of verse 9, and the mockery of verse 14 alike. Men who stuff their ears at the truth are not refuting it; they are surviving it, thunderclap by thunderclap.

**Raʿd: A Sound, and a Question About an Angel**

The exegetical tradition attaches one curious debate to the word for thunder. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās has the Prophet ﷺ, asked about *al-raʿd*, describing it as the name of an angel who drives the clouds; other scholars rejected the attribution as gratuitous, since the Arabs knew *raʿd* perfectly well as the sound of thunder, and the Qur'an's usage needs no celestial bureaucrat behind it. The debate is worth less than what both sides share: the Qur'an made thunder a named presence in revelation — Sūrah 13 takes its title from it, and that sūrah's verse describes the sound's true status: *"The thunder glorifies His praises, as do the angels in awe of Him"* (13:13). Whether *raʿd* is an angel or an acoustics, the thunder in the Qur'an's universe is a worshipper — a voice engaged in *tasbīḥ*, the same act the hypocrites' creed lacked. That is the parable's quiet irony at full depth: the men stuffing their ears are not shutting out noise but doxology. The sky over their heads is praying; their fingers are pressed against a hymn.

**Encompassed: The Clause That Closes the Sky**

The verse ends by stepping out of the image to state the doctrine the image performs: *wa-Allāhu muḥīṭun bi-l-kāfirīn* — Allah encompasses the disbelievers. The word *muḥīṭ* carries encirclement on every side, the way an ocean surrounds an island or a siege surrounds a city. Inside the parable the meaning is spatial: there is no edge to the storm, no horizon they can run for, because the weather is not local but total. Outside the parable the meaning is the divine attribute: knowledge and power that leave no exterior, no back room, no exit — the same encompassment that heard the mockery of verse 14 now stated as cosmology. The men in the storm fear death from above while the verse informs them that what is above is not merely lethal but enveloping. Death they might outrun; an encompassing God is the condition of every direction they could run. The clause is the parable's wall of sky made explicit — and it names its occupants not as hypocrites here but as disbelievers, filing them under the genus their private creed always held.

**Samāʾ: The Word Above the Scene**

One lexical note sharpens the whole image. The storm comes *mina al-samāʾ* — from the *samāʾ*, a word whose range runs from sky to heaven to firmament to simply "above," chosen by context. The commentators flag the range, and the parable exploits it: what descends on these men is meteorological and revelatory at once. In the Qur'an's consistent vertical grammar, guidance comes down — water from the sky, books sent down, angels descending — and the storm obeys the grammar while inverting its mercy: the descent that waters the believer's valley arrives at the hypocrites as darkness, concussion, and dazzle. Their response completes the inversion. Instead of receiving what comes down, they press inward and downward, fingers into ears, the only motion available to people who have refused to look up. The verse's geography is therefore moral: a sky full of revelation, a ground full of men whose entire posture is defined by what they will not take from it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:20

> It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight. Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still. Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Brightness That Nearly Takes the Eye**

The verse continues the storm and fixes on its most violent element: *yakādu al-barqu yakhṭafu abṣārahum* — the lightning all but snatches away their sight. The particle *yakādu*, "it almost does," governs the clause, and its work is precise: the snatching is imminent, deserved, begun — and withheld. The lightning here is proof at full intensity, the clarity of revelation in its most dazzling mode, and the parable says something severe about clarity: to eyes adapted to darkness, light itself is dangerous. The hypocrites did not choose blindness by shutting their eyes; the brilliance they refused to live by now threatens the organs they kept. Exegetes connect the clause to the fire parable's ending — light taken away there, sight nearly taken here — as one movement in two tempos. The *yakādu* keeps the stroke pending, which means the verse is not describing a finished punishment but a suspended one, and suspension is where every warning lives.

**Walking by Flashes: The Gait of Hypocrisy**

Between the flares, the parable records the men's locomotion, and the locomotion is the diagnosis: *kullamā aḍāʾa lahum mashaw fīhi* — whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it; *wa-idhā aẓlama ʿalayhim qāmū* — when it darkens over them, they stand. Their movement has no internal source. They do not walk toward anything; they walk when conditions permit, and the condition is brightness they did not kindle. The verb chosen for the dark intervals, *qāmū*, is deliberately flat — they stood, halted, stalled — the posture of men paused rather than resting. Read morally, this is opportunism drawn as physics: advance while faith pays, freeze when it costs. The hypocrite's progress through life is therefore intermittent by construction, a series of sprints between eclipses, and every pause is longer than the last until the darkness of verse 17's ending closes over the whole road. No one in the parable is traveling; they are being flashed forward.

**The Conditional That Will Never Fire**

The third movement states what is *not* happening: *wa-law shāʾa Allāhu la-dhahaba bi-samʿihim wa-abṣārihim* — had Allah willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight outright. The construction is the unreal conditional, the grammar of a possibility deliberately left unactualized, and it recontextualizes everything before it. The thunder that deafens, the lightning that nearly blinds — these are mercy operating at reduced voltage. The full stroke exists in the divine capacity and is being withheld in real time. The verse thus answers an objection the storm provokes: if God were merely hostile to these men, the parable would end in the first flash. Instead the withholding is stated as the fact that governs the scene — the organs remain functional, the flashes keep coming, the walking remains possible. The restraint is also the proof that the disability is moral and not physical: eyes that could have been taken are still being addressed.

**Qadīr: Power as the Frame of the Whole Scene**

The closing clause names the attribute that holds the parable together: *inna Allāha ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr* — surely Allah is Most Capable of everything. The word *qadīr* shares its root with *qadr*, measure as well as power — the capacity to do a thing and the ordaining of its amount. Both senses are at work in the verse's logic. The storm's violence is *measured*: the lightning stops short of the eye, the thunder stops short of the heart, because power here operates with a scale in its hand. And the withheld stroke is *possible* at every moment: the conditional of the third movement depends entirely on this attribute. Omnipotence stated after a description of restraint is not a threat but a definition — the difference between cannot and will-not, which is the whole difference between a victim of nature and an addressee of God. The hypocrites are not caught in weather; they are inside a governed demonstration, and the Governor is named in the last sentence.

**Two Parables, Two Tempos of One Condition**

Set side by side, the fire and the storm divide the hypocrites' condition along time. The first parable is singular and final: one flame kindled, one extinction, a man left in completed darkness — the end state, which the tradition associates with the unmasking at death. The second is rhythmic and repeated: flash, walk, dark, stand, flash again — the daily gait, the condition as it is lived before the end arrives. The pairing is pedagogically exact. A warning that showed only the extinction would let every borrower of light say *not yet*; a picture that showed only the rhythm would let him say *never ends, so never comes*. Together they give the type both of its tenses — the intermittent present and the terminal past — and the *yakādu* of this verse sits at the seam, the almost that keeps the rhythm from becoming an excuse. Some commentators extend the division to persons, reading one parable of hypocrisy's leaders and the other of its rank and file; the grammatical evidence is thin, but the two-tempo reading stands on the text alone.

**The Parables End; the Address Begins**

With this verse the thirteen-verse diagnosis that began at verse 8 is complete. The passage has moved through the group's speech, scheme, sickness, social claims, mockery, and commerce, and finished with two images that hold the whole type in one night — a small extinguished fire and a sky in concussion. Nothing further will be said about the hypocrites for some time; the sūrah turns. The next verse leaves parable, third person, and diagnosis behind and addresses the entire species directly with its first command — worship — moving from what these men are to what all men are for. The structure is deliberate: al-Baqarah exhausts the description of the diseased type before it issues the universal call, so that the call arrives with its negative examples already filed. The storm is still sounding when the invitation goes out, and the invitation is addressed to everyone standing inside it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:21

> O humanity! Worship your Lord, Who created you and those before you, so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Command Falls on the Whole Species**

The sūrah's opening twenty verses sorted people into files — the God-conscious, the disbelievers, the hypocrites — and the taxonomy could have bred a comfortable reading: every reader locating himself in the good file and continuing. Verse 21 forecloses that move by its address. *Yā ayyuhā al-nās* — O humanity — gathers all three files back into one room, and the first direct command of al-Baqarah is issued to the species as such, not to the believers alone. The vocative is the Qur'an's widest; it excludes no one capable of hearing it, including the men just described as deaf. The command that follows is equally universal in its object: *uʿbudū rabbakum* — worship your Lord. Not a new ritual, not a Madinan regulation, but the primordial obligation, restated at the head of the Qur'an's longest legislative sūrah so that every law that follows is received inside it. Structure before statute: the whole book of rulings will be addressed to people first defined as worshippers.

**ʿIbādah: The Verb That Contains a Whole Life**

"Worship" here is the Qur'an's comprehensive term, *ʿibādah* — the same word al-Fātiḥah put at the center of the prayer, *"You ˹alone˺ we worship"* (1:5). Its root covers servitude, obedience, and adoration at once, and its scope in Quranic usage is a life's entire orientation rather than a liturgical segment. The creation of the two orders is stated as its purpose elsewhere without ambiguity: *"I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me"* (51:56). Read with that verse, the command of 2:21 is not adding an activity to human life but naming the activity human life is for. The exegetes' standard gloss — worship as the utmost humility joined to the utmost love — keeps the term from collapsing into either fear alone or affection alone. And the command's justification is embedded in its own relative clause: *Who created you*. The Maker's claim on the made is the argument; nothing else is offered, because nothing else is needed. A thing that was made owes its making its orientation, and *ʿibādah* is that orientation with a name.

**“Your Lord”: The Title That Argues**

The command names its object *rabbakum* — your Lord — and the choice of title carries the verse's whole persuasion. *Rabb* is not primarily a word of power; it is the nurturer-owner, the one who raises what he possesses from stage to stage, the title al-Fātiḥah set over the worlds. To command worship in the name of the *rabb* is to ground obligation in received care: you are not addressed by a stranger with force but by the party who developed you from what you were. The relative clause then widens the nurture across generations — *Who created you and those before you* — so that the addressee inherits the claim along with the lineage. No one is self-originated and no one's ancestors were; the chain of makers everyone appeals to terminates in one Maker, and the verse simply walks the reader up his own family tree to the point where gratitude has an address. The prohibition that will close verse 22 — no equals — is already prepared here: a Lord who created your fathers cannot have partners invented by sons.

**Laʿalla: A “Perhaps” That Functions as a Promise**

The purpose clause — *laʿallakum tattaqūn*, so that you may become mindful — uses one of the Qur'an's characteristic particles, *laʿalla*, which classical grammarians gloss as expectation: perhaps, perchance, with the hope that. The particle raised a theological question the commentaries address directly: hope implies uncertainty, and uncertainty implies a heart in suspense — states unfitting to God. Two reconciliations dominate. One holds that God's "perhaps" is equivalent to a promise, since nothing can stand in its way; the expectation is certain from the divine side. The other attaches the hope to the subject of the sentence rather than to God: *you* are the ones for whom the outcome stands open, and the particle describes your position, not His. The second reading has the better grammar and the richer effect. The command genuinely hands the worshipper something to become: taqwā is offered as a real possibility that the act of worship genuinely produces, and the openness in the particle is the space where human freedom lives inside a divine sentence.

**Taqwā as the Destination, Not the Prerequisite**

The purpose clause performs a quiet reversal of the sūrah's opening. In verse 2 the Book is guidance *for* the God-conscious — taqwā appeared as the condition of receiving. Here worship is commanded *so that* taqwā may result — the same quality now appears as the fruit of practice. The two positions are not contradictory but sequential, and between them lies the sūrah's moral psychology: a minimum of guarding brings a person to the prayer, and the prayer manufactures the guarding it required. Taqwā is thus both door and destination, and the circle is how growth works — each turn through worship deepens the mindfulness that enabled the worship. This is also why the command is plural and general: taqwā is not reserved to a spiritual elite who arrived before the address; it is held out to humanity as an achievable state, produced by an available act. The God-conscious of verse 2 were described as if finished; verse 21 opens the workshop where they are made.

**Why the Call Comes After the Parables**

The placement of this verse is an argument in itself. Immediately before it stand the two most claustrophobic images in the sūrah's opening — an extinguished fire and a concussion of sky — and immediately after it comes the furniture of the world: earth as resting place, sky as canopy, rain as provision. The sequence moves from the fate of counterfeit light to the summons toward the real, and the summons is issued with the evidence assembled in the next breath. Diagnosis preceded prescription, so that the prescription arrives to an audience that has just seen what untreated looks like; and evidence follows the command, so that the command is not bare authority but authority that shows its work. The whole opening of al-Baqarah now reads as one designed movement: five verses of portrait, thirteen of exposure, two parables of night — and then the lights come on and the entire species is addressed by name, with the first word it is given being the first word of every prophet's message.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:22

> ˹He is the One˺ Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy; and sends down rain from the sky, causing fruits to grow as a provision for you. So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah ˹in worship˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Evidence Is the Furniture of the World**

The verse answers the command of verse 21 not with syllogism but with surroundings. Its argument is a list — earth, sky, rain, fruit — and every item is something the addressee is already using. The rhetorical strategy is worth naming: revelation does not here prove God from abstractions but points at the furnished condition of the listener's life and asks him to read the furniture as evidence. Each piece carries a maker's mark. The earth is *firāsh*, a spread resting place; the sky a *bināʾ*, a built canopy; the rain a descent with a purpose; the fruit an output with a beneficiary — "for you," stated twice. The list moves from structure to supply: first the house, then its provisioning system. By the time the verse reaches its prohibition, the reader has walked through his own daily life as an exhibit, and the prohibition lands not as decree but as the only conclusion the exhibit supports. This is the Qur'an's most characteristic argument form — cosmology as testimony, geography as witness stand.

**A Bed and a Building: Domestic Words for Cosmic Things**

The two nouns chosen for earth and sky collapse the cosmic into the domestic. *Firāsh* is bedding, a place spread for rest — the earth described not as a planet but as a mattress laid out for the addressee, fitted to his body, neither too hard nor too hostile. *Bināʾ* is construction, an edifice — the sky as a raised roof, and the same root the Qur'an uses for buildings humans erect. The pairing produces a house: floor and ceiling, and the inhabitant between them. The register is deliberate and it does theological work. A house implies a householder; bedding implies someone who cared whether the sleeper was comfortable; a built roof implies a builder who calculated loads. The extended furnishing continues elsewhere in the Book — mountains set as stabilizers so the earth does not shake, and broad pathways for finding the way (21:31) — each feature an installed fixture. The verse's argument from design is therefore not Paley's watch found on a heath but something more intimate: you are not examining a mechanism, you are lying in a bed someone made.

**The Provision Chain: Rain Sent, Fruit Brought**

Between the structure and the prohibition the verse inserts the supply line: water sent down from the sky, fruits brought out by it, the whole chain ending in the word *rizq* — provision, sustenance, what is apportioned to a creature by another. The verb forms keep the agency exact: Allah *sends down* the water and *brings forth* the fruit; the earth grows, the tree yields, but the verse assigns both motions to the hand above the sky. *Thamarāt*, fruits, carries its double range into the theology — the commentators read it as natural produce for the body and, by extension, as the spiritual sustenance drawn from the same created order for the soul. The double range makes every meal a two-channel communication: calories and testimony arriving together. Provision in the Qur'an is never neutral matter; it is *rizq* — a gift with a Giver named in the grammar — and the verse positions the listener inside an unbroken delivery system whose sender signs every package.

**“Knowingly”: The Adverb That Turns Prohibition Into Indictment**

The final sentence is short and its last word is the blade: *fa-lā tajʿalū li-llāhi andādan wa-antum taʿlamūn* — do not set up equals to Allah *while you know*. The circumstantial clause does not restrict the prohibition — setting up equals is forbidden to the ignorant as well — but it aggravates the case against the addressee. After the list of verses 21–22, no one can plead ignorance of the Builder; the knowledge is built into the furniture, delivered with the fruit, recited in the very verses being read. The word *andād*, equals or rivals, names the specific idolatry of partnership: not denying Allah but assigning peers beside Him — intermediaries credited with independent power, causes treated as causes-in-themselves, favors thanked to the wrong hand. The verse thus converts its whole preceding argument into a legal instrument: you have been shown the house, the builder, and the deliveries; a rival credited in this house is now credited *knowingly*, and the adverb registers the exact weight of every such credit.

**The Greatest Sin, in the Prophet's Own Ranking**

The prohibition's rank is fixed in a verified report. ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd asked the Prophet ﷺ directly: what is the greatest sin in the sight of Allah? The answer: *"That you set up a rival unto Allah though He alone created you"* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4477). The ḥadīth's logic is the verse's logic compressed — creation cited as the very ground that makes rivalry monstrous — and Bukhārī filed this report under a chapter headed by this verse of al-Baqarah, joining the two texts officially. The rest of the ranking sharpens the first place: asked what comes next, the Prophet ﷺ named killing one's child for fear of sharing food, then adultery with a neighbor's wife. The triad is coherent: a sin against the Creator, a sin against life, a sin against lineage — the three orders this verse's world rests on. That the greatest of the three is theological rather than bloody tells the reader how the Qur'an prices harm: the misdirection of worship outranks murder because it corrupts the source from which every other right flows.

**Where the Equals Actually Hide**

Idolatry in a furnished house is subtler than statues. The verse's own list suggests the hiding places: provision is the most dangerous rival precisely because it is most real — the hand that feeds is thanked before the Hand that sends the food, the salary eclipses the Provider, the rain is credited to the climate. The classical commentators note that *andād* covered the idols of the Arabs, but the Qur'an's usage extends the term to anything granted independent agency beside Allah — and the knowledge clause applies with full force to the modern reader, who knows the food chain, the water cycle, and the astronomy better than any previous generation and is therefore *more* without excuse, not less. Deeper knowledge of the furniture does not refute the Builder; it multiplies His signatures. The verse's demand is finally one of credit assignment: every comfort received is to be traced, consciously, to its source, and every tracing that stops early — at the market, the state, the self — sets up, knowingly, an equal.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:23

> And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Challenge Issued at the Level of Doubt**

The verse addresses a specific interior state and takes it seriously: *wa-in kuntum fī raybin* — if you are in *rayb*, the doubt-with-suspicion named in this sūrah's second verse as having no place in the Book. The challenge does not wait for denial or hostility; it descends to the earliest stage of resistance and offers it a test. That pedagogical choice is worth weighing. A prophet confronting deniers might demand belief or pronounce judgment; this verse instead proposes an experiment, phrased as a fair conditional — if such is your doubt, then attempt such-and-such. The invitation converts an interior fog into an exterior task with a public outcome. Doubt that will not test itself is revealed, by the refusal alone, to be something other than doubt. And the task is calibrated to be attemptable by anyone: it requires no faith, no purity, no membership — only the ability to write. The verse is, in form, the most open door the Qur'an offers its critics, and the most exacting.

**“Our Servant”: The Title That Carries the Claim**

The revelation is described as *mā nazzalnā ʿalā ʿabdinā* — what We have sent down upon Our servant — and the single word *ʿabd* carries the verse's whole biographical argument. The Qur'an does not name Muḥammad ﷺ here but titles him, and the title is the lowest and highest a person can hold: slave, servant, one who owns nothing and speaks for Another. The choice answers the objectors' actual case, which was never that the text lacked beauty but that its author was visible — a known man, in a known town, with a known history of neither scribal training nor poetic apprenticeship. The Qur'an supplies that biography as evidence rather than embarrassment: the *unlettered Prophet*, *"whose description they find in their Torah and the Gospel"* (7:157), who could not read the scriptures he is said to have absorbed. A forgery requires sources; this author had none. The servant-title therefore does humility-work and argument-work in the same breath — the man is small enough that the book cannot be his.

**One Sūrah: The Deliberately Minimal Quantum**

The demand is graduated down to its floor: *bi-sūratin min mithlih* — one sūrah of its like. Not the whole Book, not ten chapters — a single unit, and the Qur'an elsewhere records the demand having been pitched higher before: bring ten sūrahs like it, forged if you must (11:13); bring a Book like it (28:49 — cited in the classical lists of the graduated challenge). The gradation is a documented feature of the challenge verses, which appear in Yūnus, Hūd, and al-Isrāʾ as well, and the Isrāʾ formulation removes the final limit of even collective effort: *"If ˹all˺ humans and jinn were to come together to produce the equivalent of this Quran, they could not produce its equal, no matter how they supported each other"* (17:88). One sūrah is thus the minimum testable unit of a claim whose maximum version spans two species. The commentators note this verse is Madinan while its parallels are Makkan — the challenge was not exhausted by its first audiences but re-issued to a new city with new doubters, and stands re-issued to every century since.

**“Call Your Helpers Other Than Allah”**

The second clause extends the challenge from the individual to his whole alliance: *wa-dʿū shuhadāʾakum min dūni Llāh* — summon your witnesses, your patrons, your gods-beside-Allah. The phrase *min dūni Llāh* is the same construction verse 22 used for the equals set up in worship, and the reuse is a hinge: the helpers invoked in the literary test are of the same order as the rivals forbidden in the creed. The verse quietly argues that every false god is now on trial as a co-author — if the idols are real powers, let them co-sign a sūrah. The objectors are invited to mobilize everything their worldview contains: poets, soothsayers, ancestral deities, jinn confederates of the kind the Qur'an names as whisperers of elegant deception (6:112). The demand is phrased as generosity — bring all the help you trust — and functions as exposure: the challenge will be refused by the same mouths that professed the helpers, and the refusal will itself testify which of the two claims the claimants actually believed.

**Iʿjāz: The Doctrine This Verse Built**

From verses of this shape the Islamic sciences developed the doctrine of *iʿjāz* — the Qur'an's inimitability — a technical term the Qur'an itself does not use, built by scholars out of the challenge's fourteen-century record. The root means to incapacitate: a *muʿjizah*, miracle, is what disables the opponent's capacity to respond, and the Qur'an is Islam's central miracle in precisely this sense — not a staff turned serpent but a standing public test that no one has passed. The classical analysis locates the inimitability in several simultaneous registers: the linguistic surface — eloquence and a prose form that is neither poetry nor speech; the structural layer — coherence across a text revealed piecemeal over twenty-three years; the semantic depths — layers of meaning that reward centuries of reading without exhaustion. Each register was separately attemptable; their combination was not. And the miracle's modality suits its claim: a staff can be watched only by those present, while a text challenges every generation with the same demand, at the same floor of one sūrah, in the reader's own lifetime.

**The Silence of Fourteen Centuries as Evidence**

The challenge's career is part of its argument, and the verse leaves that career open on purpose. The condition — *in kuntum ṣādiqīn*, if you are truthful — converts every subsequent century into testimony. Hostile regimes possessed the motive, the poets of two classical golden ages possessed the craft, and the Arabic grammatical tradition itself grew up around this text with every tool needed to imitate it; the record contains no surviving work accepted as meeting the demand, from enemies who would have gained everything by meeting it. Skeptics can discount the record — victors preserve archives — but the burden the verse assigns is public and permanent: the test remains runnable today, by anyone, with the floor still at one sūrah. That permanence is rare among miracles and deliberate among claims. A wonder that expired with its witnesses requires faith in a report; a challenge still standing requires only an attempt. The verse's final word to the doubter is therefore not *believe me* but *try* — and the next verse states what follows when the trying fails, as the verse already knows it will.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:24

> But if you are unable to do so—and you will never be able to do so—then fear the Fire fuelled with people and stones, which is prepared for the disbelievers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Conditional That Answers Itself**

The verse opens by completing the test of verse 23, and completes it before anyone has taken it: *fa-in lam tafʿalū* — but if you have not done it — *wa-lan tafʿalū* — and you will never do it. The second clause, set off in this translation by dashes, is an interruption of the conditional by certainty. The particle *lan* is Arabic's strongest future negation, and the commentators draw the grammatical-theological point precisely: a conditional from Allah is not an expression of uncertainty, just as the "perhaps" of verse 21 was not an expression of anxiety. Divine "ifs" state the logic of the situation from the human side while the divine side already holds the outcome. The effect on the reader is singular — the challenge is issued in full seriousness *and* its failure is announced in the same breath, so that the trial functions as revelation rather than information: the point was never to learn whether they could, but to let them discover, by trying or by flinching, what they are.

**An Aside Spoken Over Their Heads**

There is a shift of addressee inside the dash that deserves attention. "If you do not" addresses the doubters; "and you will never do it" is spoken about them — a confidence delivered past them, to the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, in the middle of a sentence directed at the objectors. Rhetorically the aside is devastating: the doubters are being examined and, simultaneously, their exam results are being read aloud to the proctor. The device also protects the challenge's sincerity. Had the verse said simply *you will fail*, it would be a taunt with no test; had it said simply *if you fail*, the confidence would be absent. Holding both in one sentence, the Qur'an performs perfect knowledge and perfect fairness at once — the door genuinely open, the outcome genuinely known, and the known outcome stated publicly so that the failure, when it arrives, arrives without excuse. The hypocrites of this sūrah's opening lived by managing appearances; this aside announces a courtroom where appearances are read before they are worn.

**A Fire With Fuel Named**

The consequence clause introduces the Fire with an engineering detail: *allatī waqūduhā al-nās wa-l-ḥijārah* — its fuel is people and stones. The commentators identify the stones as sulfur, the burning mineral of the classical imagination, and as the idols themselves, the objects of the worship that led their votaries in — and the Qur'an elsewhere states the idol reading outright: *"Certainly you ˹disbelievers˺ and whatever you worship instead of Allah will be the fuel of Hell"* (21:98). The fuel list is thus a moral equation: the worshipper and the worshipped burn together, and the false god becomes, in the only transformation it ever manages, an aggravator of its devotee's fire. The same phrase is turned on the believers elsewhere as pastoral warning — *"Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones"* (66:6) — which confirms the description is meant to be taken concretely by every party. A hell of abstraction frightens no one; a hell with a fuel specification is designed for the imagination, and the imagination is where choices are actually made.

**“Prepared”: A House Already Furnished**

One verb in the closing clause does quiet, heavy work: *uʿiddat* — it has been prepared, made ready in advance, for the disbelievers. The passive points to a preparation completed before any inhabitant arrives; the Fire is not improvised at the judgment but kept ready, stocked, waiting — the inverted mirror of verse 22. There the world was furnished for the addressee: a bed of earth, a canopy of sky, a supply chain of rain and fruit. Here the counter-house is furnished too: fuel laid in, appointment made, address written. The two houses stand in the same passage a verse apart, each with its provisions and its tenancy terms, and the reader of the sūrah is being shown that he is already a resident of one — by worship or by rivalry, by the direction his gratitude flows. The preparedness of the Fire also answers the preparedness of the Garden that follows in verse 25: neither destination is under construction; both are standing, and the only unfinished item in the cosmos is the choice.

**Ittiqū: The Command the Threat Actually Issues**

The main verb of the verse is easy to skim past: *fa-ttaqū* — then guard yourselves, then fear — the imperative of the very root that named the sūrah's opening people, the *muttaqīn*. The structure is worth stating plainly: the threat is not the verse's point; the command is. "Fear the Fire" is taqwā given an object, and the whole verse exists to move taqwā from disposition to decision. The God-consciousness of verse 2 was described as an achieved character; here its manufacture is shown — mindfulness made urgent by a named danger, made possible by an open test, made reasonable by a prepared alternative. The Qur'an's use of fear is instrumental and never terminal: fear of the Fire is prescribed the way a smoke alarm is installed, to produce motion toward exits, not paralysis. That is why the verse ends by naming the Fire's appointment — *for the disbelievers* — a class with membership rules and therefore with resignation procedures. The fear commanded here is, in its full function, hope wearing work boots.

**Threat Positioned After a Failed Test**

The verse's location in the argument completes its mercy. The sequence has been: command (worship, v. 21), evidence (the furnished world, v. 22), test (produce a sūrah, v. 23), verdict and consequence (v. 24). The threat arrives only after the intellect has been addressed and the experiment offered — it is not the opening move of revelation but its fourth, spoken to people whose doubt has been given every instrument to resolve itself and who are now shown the shape of the alternative. This ordering answers the commonest misreading of Quranic warning: the Fire is not a bludgeon wielded against the unexamined but the last honest datum given to the examined. And the paragraph does not end in the dark. The very next verse pivots from the prepared Fire to the Gardens prepared for belief and good works, so that the two houses stand side by side and the reader — the real addressee of both — is left where the Qur'an always leaves him: not informed about destinations but standing at the switch.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:25

> Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow. Whenever provided with fruit, they will say, “This is what we were given before,” for they will be served fruit that looks similar ˹but tastes different˺. They will have pure spouses, and they will be there forever.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Counter-Announcement, in the Same Breath**

One verse after the Fire is prepared, the imperative turns: *wa-bashshir* — and give good news. The command is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ and through him to everyone who will ever carry a message of joy, and its recipients are named in the Qur'an's standing formula: *alladhīna āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt* — those who believe and do righteous deeds, faith joined to its works in the pairing this sūrah used at 2:3. The juxtaposition with verse 24 is not decoration but structure: the two announcements share one grammar of preparedness, one audience of the living, and one present moment in which the hearer must locate himself. Good news in the Qur'an is never generic comfort; *bashārā* is announcement of a specific, named, delivered good — here, gardens — and its force depends entirely on the specificity of the alternative announced one verse earlier. The sūrah has now completed its two horizons, and every subsequent ruling it issues will be issued between them.

**Rivers Under the Gardens: An Inverted Desert**

The gardens are described as *tajrī min tahtiha al-anhār* — rivers flowing from under them — and the commentators are careful with the preposition: the water is not buried, as the English might suggest, but runs *below the greenery*, visible and audible from beneath the canopy of the trees. For the first audience the phrase was not scenery but inversion. In Arabian experience water hides — in wells, in underground channels, in rock — and greenery is bought at the price of digging. Paradise is announced as the country where the terms are reversed: the water flows openly, on display, underfoot and everywhere, with the gardens standing on top of an un-concealed abundance. The formula then becomes the Qur'an's most repeated description of reward, recurring in dozens of sūrahs as a fixed refrain — each repetition re-addressing people whose daily relation to water was fear, and promising them its opposite. The rivers are also, in the exegetical reading, the visible form of provision no longer rationed: *rizq* without scarcity, flowing where verse 22's rain fell only at intervals.

**“This Is What We Were Given Before”: Memory Inside Paradise**

The strangest and richest clause in the verse is the dwellers' own remark. Given fruit, they say: *this is what we were given before*. The majority reading takes "before" as the earthly life — the fruits of Paradise arriving in the forms of the fruits of this world, so that the first bite in eternity triggers recognition. The commentators then draw the theology out of the homesickness: the world's fruit was the sample, Paradise is the delivery; the familiar form is kept so that the reward is *recognizable as the fulfillment of a life actually lived* — this world is not forgotten there, only its bitterness removed, which is why the Qur'an's standing description of the dwellers is that no fear comes upon them and they do not grieve (2:62). A minority reading places "before" inside Paradise — each fruit resembling the one previously tasted there. Both readings serve one purpose: continuity of personal memory across the boundary of death. The reward is not absorption into novelty but the completion of a biography the dweller still owns and can quote.

**Mutashābih: Same Face, Different Taste**

The verse explains the recognition with one loaded word: they are given fruit *mutashābih* — resembling, similar, the translation glossing it *looks similar ˹but tastes different˺*. The exegetes read the resemblance three ways: identical appearance with transformed taste; or uniform excellence — no fruit of Paradise has an inferior grade, so every specimen resembles every other in perfection; or the remark as wonderment rather than comparison, since the dwellers are recognizing names and forms while the realities exceed both. The word choice carries a second cargo for the attentive reader: *mutashābih* is the same term Sūrah 3 will use for the Qur'an's elusive verses (3:7) and that Sūrah 39 uses for a Book whose parts resemble each other in harmony (39:23). A lexicon links Paradise's fruit to the Book's texture: familiarity on the surface, inexhaustible difference underneath, recognition that deepens instead of exhausting. The dwellers' conversation over fruit is, in miniature, the reader's conversation with revelation — every return to the familiar thing yields an unfamiliar taste.

**Pure Spouses: Purity as Completed Companionship**

The verse's third gift is *azwāj muṭahharah* — spouses made pure. The commentators define the purification concretely and consistently: freedom from menstruation, from excreta, from every bodily process the classical lists call distasteful, and from injury and defect of every kind — purity as the completion of companionship, everything that strains or interrupts human intimacy removed from it. One scholarly caution deserves preservation: the major commentators do not attach sexual purity or virginity specifically to this verse; the purification named is comprehensive, of body and condition, not a single attribute. The gift also answers a loneliness in the passage: the men of the parables stood alone in a dark plain, and the storm's victims were described only as a plural of fear; here companionship is named as part of the reward, and the plural becomes company. Whatever the modern reader makes of the imagery's cultural skin, the verse's structural claim is plain — Paradise is furnished with persons, not only produce, and the highest created good listed here is a companionship that cannot spoil.

**Khulūd: The Clause of Permanence**

The verse closes on the word that seals both houses: *hum fīhā khālidūn* — they will be there abiding, *khulūd* the Qur'an's standing refrain for the inhabitants of the Garden and the Fire alike. Lexically the root denotes staying, duration, a thing's persistence in its place; from the mouth of Allah the commentators read it as the promise that upgrades duration into eternity, since His word cannot expire. The Qur'an sometimes reinforces the clause — abiding *forever* — and sometimes qualifies it, *as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills* (11:108), which the exegetical tradition debates without dissolving, ending in a verse the same passage supplies: *a generous giving, without end*. This verse states the permanence flatly, and the flatness is part of the good news: a joy announced as temporary would not be news at all, since the heart's objection to every earthly good is exactly its expiry. The rivers flow, the fruit recurs, the spouses remain, and the clause of *khulūd* removes from all of them the one defect that made every provision of verse 22 bittersweet — the deadline.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:26

> Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito or what is even smaller. As for the believers, they know that it is the truth from their Lord. And as for the disbelievers, they argue, “What does Allah mean by such a parable?” Through this ˹test˺, He leaves many to stray, and guides many. And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious—

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Parable Defended Before the Attack Lands**

The verse opens in the middle of an argument its hearers were having: *inna Allāha lā yastaḥyī an yaḍriba mathalan mā baʿūḍatan* — Allah is not ashamed to strike a parable of a mosquito, or of anything above it, which the commentators read as anything beyond it in smallness. The occasions reported behind the verse name the objectors and their objection: the hypocrites, stung by the parables of verses 17–20; or Jews scoffing that God would deign to compare idols to a fly (22:73) or the protectors taken beside Him to a spider's house (29:41); or idolaters pressing the same complaint. In every version the charge is one of dignity — such images are beneath divine speech. The verse answers not by raising the images but by lowering the objection: *lā yastaḥyī*, He does not shy away, does not hold back out of propriety. The answer implies a principle of revelation that runs through the whole Book: truth selects its own images, and the selection is made by fitness to the point, not by the social rank of the objects. A God who furnished the world with gnats can speak with gnats.

**The Mosquito and the Scale of Signs**

The choice of *baʿūḍah* — mosquito, gnat — is exact for the argument being answered. The objectors measured divine speech by the grandeur of its contents; the verse answers by naming one of the smallest creatures that nonetheless exists, is formed, feeds, reproduces, and does work in the world no elephant can do.
