If the objection is that small things cannot carry meaning, the mosquito refutes it by existing at all: the creature that is beneath dignity in the objectors' scale is not beneath creation in the Maker's. The classical scholars drew the corollary into the doctrine of signs — every existent, at every scale, is an *āyah*, and the sign-value of a thing lies in its craftedness, not its size. The clause "or what is even smaller" then pushes past the limit of the visible: whatever lies below the mosquito's scale — what the ancients could only posit, and later ages would actually see — belongs to the same field of signs and the same freedom of divine speech. The verse is, incidentally, one of the Qur'an's standing answers to every aesthetics of the sublime that excludes the small.

**Two Hearers, One Sentence**

The middle of the verse splits its audience with surgical symmetry: as for the believers, they know it is the truth from their Lord; as for the disbelievers, they say, *what does Allah mean by such a parable?* The same utterance produces knowledge in one group and objection in the other, and the verse's point is that the divergence locates itself entirely in the receivers. The believer's clause is worth parsing: he knows *that it is the truth*, and *from his Lord* — recognition of content and of source together, the parable received as both true and sent. The disbeliever's clause is a question that is not a question — *mādhā arāda Llāhu bi-hādhā mathalan* — phrased as inquiry, functioning as protest; the classical commentators note that had the objection been genuine seeking, the verse would have answered it with explanation, which it does not. The sorting happens in real time, in the ear. This is the verse's own claim demonstrated performatively: readers have just watched themselves receive it — some finding in it a principle, some finding in it a difficulty worth arguing with, and the difference between those two responses is the subject matter.

**A Message That Actively Divides**

The verse then states its most difficult doctrine without softening: *yuḍillu bihi kathīran wa-yahdī bihi kathīran* — by it He leaves many astray and guides many. The "it" is the parable — the same small utterance functioning as guidance and as straying simultaneously, and the commentators press exactly this: the effect described is stronger than being ignored. Revelation denied is not neutralized in the denier; it works on him, moving him further from what it says. The verse echoes the sealing of 2:7 and the sickness-increased of 2:10 as one continuous mechanism: divine speech is active substance, and the moral condition of the receiver determines the direction of its action — medicine or irritant, light or dazzle, the same sky that waters the valley deafening the men of the storm. Many scholars read here the Qur'an's fullest statement that guidance and misguidance both pass *through* revelation rather than around it: no one is misled by the Book who was not already positioned to be. The doubles — many astray, many guided — refuse the comfort of rarity in both directions.

**Al-Fāsiqūn: Straying With a Qualification**

The final clause restricts the damage: *wa-mā yuḍillu bihi illa al-fāsiqīn* — He leaves none astray by it except the rebellious, the *fāsiq*. The word comes from a root meaning to exit, to break out — used of the date that bursts its skin, of the animal that leaves the herd — and in Quranic usage names the person who has stepped outside a binding order: the covenant-breaker, the one who transgresses while knowing the line. The restriction answers the charge latent in the verse's own doctrine. If the same parable guides and misleads, is the outcome arbitrary — does God darken whomever He pleases? The clause says no: the straying has a qualification, and the qualification is prior conduct. The *fāsiq* is misled *by* the parable because he was already out of position relative to truth; the parable reveals and completes the exit he began. The exegetes identify the *fāsiqūn* of this passage with the hypocrites just described — men whose rebellion was not ignorance but breach — and the verse thereby hands its reader the test in advance: what this speech does to you will tell you where you are standing.

**An Open Verse, Deliberately Unclosed**

One formal feature of this verse is visible in every printed Qur'an and in this translation's final dash: it does not end its sentence. The description of the rebellious begun here is completed by the next verse, which lists their three breaches — and the sūrah thereby enacts at the level of syntax what the passage teaches at the level of meaning: the *fāsiq* is not defined in a word but in a continuation, his definition running on past the boundary of a single unit. The device also binds the two verses into one reading act; the listener cannot receive verse 26's restriction and stop — the sentence pulls him into the catalogue. Qur'anic verse-ends are famously flexible, sometimes closing a thought, sometimes leaving it mid-stride, and the classical sciences of recitation track these joints with care. Here the open ending serves the argument: straying was just described as a direction rather than an event, a going-out that continues; the grammar performs it by continuing. The dash is not a printer's convenience but the verse's last word — unfinished, on purpose.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:27

> those who violate Allah’s covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained, and spread corruption in the land. It is they who are the ˹true˺ losers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Rebellious, Defined in Three Breaches**

The open sentence of verse 26 closes here, and it closes with a definition: the *fāsiqūn* are those who do three things — break a covenant, sever what Allah ordered joined, and corrupt the land. The definition is entirely behavioral. No creed is inspected, no interior is probed; the rebellious are identified by breaches, and the three breaches share a single shape. Each is the cutting of a connection that ought to hold: the vertical bond with Allah, the horizontal bonds among creatures, and the condition of the ground on which both stand. Sin, in this verse's grammar, is not primarily violation of a rule but severance of a relation — and the sequence is causal, running from the highest bond downward. The definition also universalizes the passage: whatever its occasion among the hypocrites and scoffers of Madina, the three breaches are available to every community and most of them are committed daily somewhere by someone. The Qur'an defines its worst human type not by a name but by a list of acts anyone can check against a life.

**Which Covenant? Three Candidates and a Preference**

The exegetes identified the broken covenant variously, and the range is instructive. The widest reading takes it as the primordial covenant of human nature — the scene in al-Aʿrāf where Allah drew the descendants of Adam from his loins and asked *"Am I not your Lord?"* and they answered, *"Yes, You are! We testify"* (7:172) — a pact every person signs before birth and can breach after. A second reading, favored by al-Rāzī, takes it as the sworn expectation of the pre-Islamic Arabs: *"They swore by Allah their most solemn oaths that if a warner were to come to them, they would certainly be better guided than any other community"* (35:42) — an oath broken the moment the warner arrived. A third confines it to the specific covenants made with the People of the Book. Weighed together, the readings are not rivals but concentric rings of the same offense: every human being holds the first covenant, the Arabs of the revelation's audience added the second, and the scriptural communities the third. "After it has been affirmed" — *baʿda mīthāqih* — fits all three: in each case the bond was established, witnessed, and confirmed before the breaking. The verse prosecutes no one for ignorance; it prosecutes the confirmed and betrayed.

**Severing What Was Ordered Joined**

The second breach — *yaqtaʿūna mā amara Llāhu bihī an yūṣala* — severs what Allah commanded to be connected, and the commentators' first application is kinship: the ties of blood whose maintenance the Qur'an legislates from its opening pages — *"Be mindful of Allah—in Whose Name you appeal to one another—and ˹honour˺ family ties"* (4:1) — and whose severance it pairs, exactly as here, with corruption in the land: *"Now if you ˹hypocrites˺ turn away, perhaps you would then spread corruption throughout the land and sever your ˹ties of˺ kinship!"* (47:22). The pairing in both sūrahs is not accidental but analytic: kinship is the first society, the training ground of every bond, and a person who can cut the ties he was born into has rehearsed the cutting of all the rest. Other exegetes widen the referent to everything Allah ordered joined — faith and practice, the prophets as one brotherhood, the community and its teachers, the People of the Book and the confirmation of their own scriptures in this Qur'an. One classical note adds a barb for Madina's Jews: the tie to this Prophet was itself kinship, Isaac and Ishmael being brothers. Every reading keeps the same structure: a commanded connection, deliberately cut.

**Corruption in the Land — the Passage's Third Return**

The third breach is *yufsidūna fī al-ard*, and the phrase is by now a signature of this sūrah's opening: the charge the hypocrites deflected while claiming to be peace-makers (2:11), the verdict that stripped the claim from them (2:12), and now the defining trait of the *fāsiq*. The recurrence completes an identification — the peace-making of verse 11 and the covenant-breaking of verse 27 are the same phenomenon at two depths, and the land's corruption is what both produce. Read with the two breaches before it, the corruption has a precise etiology: when the bond with Allah is cut and the bonds between people are cut, the ground itself inherits the severance, since the land in Quranic thought is not a neutral stage but a participant that registers the moral state of its inhabitants — corruption spreading on land and sea by what human hands have done (30:41). The three breaches form one ecosystem of damage: vertical, horizontal, environmental. A generation that keeps covenants and kinships farms a different earth than one that does not, and the verse states the farming as fact rather than metaphor.

**Al-Khāsirūn: The Ledger Closed at a Loss**

The verdict uses the market vocabulary the passage has been accumulating: *ulāʾika humu al-khāsirūn* — it is they who are the losers, *khāsir* being the merchant who returns from a venture with less than he carried out, bereft, or in the word's other shade, simply *lost* — having mislaid the road or the self. The restriction grammar — *ulāʾika hum* — repeats the sūrah's verdict formula, and the repetition lets the opening's ledgers be compared side by side: the God-conscious who are the successful (2:5), the traders who bought error with guidance and profited nothing (2:16), and now the covenant-breakers who are the losers. The three entries share one economy. Loss here is not deprivation inflicted from outside but the arithmetic of the breaches themselves — a covenant broken spends a bond, kinship cut spends a society, corruption spread spends the land, and the spender arrives at the audit holding nothing, having consumed every asset that was not his to consume. The verse thus needs no added penalty clause; the loser's inventory is the penalty, read aloud.

**The Inverse Portrait of the Opening Five**

Set against the sūrah's first portrait, this verse reveals its construction: it is the God-conscious described in reverse. Where those believed in the unseen, these break faith with a covenant affirmed. Where those maintained prayer — a commanded connection kept on schedule — these sever the connections commanded. Where those spent from what they were provided, enriching the land's circulation, these corrupt the land. Where those were sure of the Hereafter and thereby joined themselves to the largest bond of all, these live as though the vertical bond were optional. The two portraits are one map read in opposite directions, and that is the verse's pastoral instrument: every quality of the *muttaqīn* has its exact negation here, so the reader can locate himself not by feeling but by checking the bonds — which connections he keeps and which he cuts. The losers are not a people apart; they are the same diagram walked backwards, and the direction is chosen bond by bond, daily, by everyone the verse is recited over.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:28

> How can you deny Allah? You were lifeless and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die and again bring you to life, and then to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question That Is an Argument**

The verse opens with an interrogative of impossibility: *kayfa takfurūna bi-llāh* — how can you disbelieve in Allah? Not "will you," not "do you dare," but *how* — the question that challenges the mechanics rather than the audacity of a position. The implication is that disbelief, examined against the believer's own biography, becomes incoherent: not wicked, which it also is, but unperformable with open eyes. And the argument the question unfolds is not cosmological or scriptural but autobiographical — it is built entirely from things that happened *to the addressee*. You were dead. You were given life. You will die. You will live again. You will be returned. Every clause is a stage of the reader's own record, known by direct experience or by the experience of every person he has ever lost. The verse thereby relocates the debate about God from the sky to the self: the evidence is not out there at a distance to be assessed; the evidence is the assessor. The "how" now has its full force — with what instruments, drawn from whose life, is this denial being conducted?

**Four Stages and a Return**

The commentators count the verse's itinerary in stages: lifelessness before birth; life given for the world; death at the term; life restored at the resurrection — and then, governing all four, the return to Allah. The Qur'an states the same arithmetic from the other side, in the confession the dead will make: *"Our Lord! You made us lifeless twice, and gave us life twice. Now we confess our sins. So is there any way out?"* (40:11). Two deaths, two lives, one unanswered question. The symmetry is the verse's engine: resurrection is not a new kind of divine act requiring new evidence but the repetition of an act the addressee has already been the object of. Whoever finds the second giving of life incredible must first explain the first — and the first is not in dispute between the verse and its hearer, since the hearer exists. The argument's structure is thus *a fortiori* in the oldest sense: if the harder thing (life from no life at all) has been done to you, the easier thing (life again from a life already lived) cannot coherently be denied by you.

**What “Dead” Means Before the Beginning**

The first stage — *kuntum amwātan*, you were dead things — required the exegetes to define a pre-biographical death, and their readings converge on hiddenness. One strand takes it materially: the person's existence in the substance of the body — in the loins of the parents, in the dust of the earth, as raw material not yet a someone. Another takes it lexically: the Arabs called a thing "dead" when its traces were effaced and it was not mentioned or remembered — death as unremembrance — and the Qur'an supplies the gloss in its own idiom: *"Is there not a period of time when each human is nothing yet worth mentioning?"* (76:1). Ibn ʿArabī read the stage metaphysically: not sheer nothingness but non-manifestation — the person held, unexpressed, in divine knowledge, "dead" only to the world, fully real to the Knower. The readings agree on what matters for the argument: before the first life there was a true state of absence from the world, and the passage from that absence to a speaking, denying self was not performed by the self. Every person's first predicate, in the verse's grammar, is *was not* — and every subsequent claim to independence is made from borrowed existence.

**Life as a Loan From the Hand Being Denied**

The hinge of the verse is its second clause: *fa-aḥyākum* — then He gave you life. The verb is Allah's, the object is the reader, and the gift is the very capacity being used to refuse it. There is a compressed indictment in the sequence: the life with which the denial is thought, spoken, and defended is the gift whose Giver the denial targets. Disbelief, on the verse's showing, is not a neutral cognitive stance but an act performed with embezzled funds — the denier's existence is the denier's chief evidence against denial, and he cannot set it down while he uses it. The Qur'an elsewhere generalizes the point into a doctrine of total dependence: provision, hearing, sight, and hearts are all loaned faculties whose loan can end (as in 67:23's inventory — He produced your hearing, your sight, your faculties, and little thanks you give). Verse 28 keeps the inventory to its two largest items — being and being-again — because two are enough: a creature who did not originate himself and does not terminate himself is bracketed at both ends by the Giver, and the middle he calls his own is a span between two donations.

**“To Him You Will Be Returned”: The Preposition of Destination**

The final clause compresses the whole eschatology into a grammar: *thumma ilayhi turjaʿūn* — then *to Him* you will be returned. The passive verb removes the traveler's control: returns of this kind happen to people, like the first life did. And the destination is not a place but a person — *ilayhi*, to Him. The commentators note the Qur'an's habit of describing the Last Day as return precisely because return implies an origin and an owner: you go back to where you came from, to whom you belonged. The phrase re-reads everything before it — the four stages were never a cycle but a trajectory with an address, and every stage was movement toward the meeting. Judgment, in al-Fātiḥah's name for its Day, is the settling of accounts; here it is the arrival of the loan at the Lender. The preposition also answers the denial named in the verse's first word: disbelief in Allah is, at bottom, living as though the return were to nowhere — as though the trajectory had no address. The verse's last word says otherwise, and says it as grammar rather than threat: *to Him*.

**Why the Personal Argument Comes Last**

The verse's placement completes the sūrah's evidential architecture, and the placement is the argument's final turn. Verse 21 commanded; verse 22 proved from the world — earth, sky, rain, fruit; verses 23–24 proved from the Book and its unmet challenge; verse 25 painted the two destinations. Only then does verse 28 arrive with the evidence no one can dispute at arm's length, because it is not at arm's length: your own death and your own beginning. The order moves from the furthest evidence to the nearest — cosmos, scripture, eschatology, self — and reserves the self for last, where arguments are strongest. The address remains the plural of verse 21, all humanity, and it includes, without exception, everyone who has ever lost a parent or been lost by one: the middle two stages of the verse are public knowledge in every family on earth. The denial the verse calls incoherent is therefore not a philosopher's position but a lived contradiction, and the verse leaves its hearer holding it — a being who cannot explain his own first morning, arguing against the explanation offered for it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:29

> He is the One Who created everything in the earth for you. Then He turned towards the heaven, forming it into seven heavens. And He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Everything in the Earth — For You**

The verse's first clause is a deed of gift: *khalaqa lakum mā fī al-ard jamīʿan* — He created for you whatever is in the earth, *all of it*. The preposition *lakum*, "for you," is the operative word; the Qur'an repeats the gift-formula across sūrahs — cattle, crops, the sea's yield, the night and day — and states its general principle elsewhere: *"He ˹also˺ subjected for you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth—all by His grace"* (45:13). The comprehensive *jamīʿan* forecloses every carve-out: not some resources, not the useful ones, not the ones a particular civilization happens to exploit — everything in the earth, including what no generation has yet found a name for. The clause therefore reads forward as well as backward: ores no ancient market knew, forces no classical physics dreamed of, are inside the gift's scope. The verse is the Qur'an's ground-title for human use of the world, and its breadth is matched only by its condition — a gift *for you* is a gift with a purpose, and the purpose was stated ten verses earlier, in the command to worship the Giver.

**The Jurisprudence and the Limit of “For You”**

Islamic law built on this clause, and the building has two walls. The first is permission: what was created for human use is presumptively lawful — the default of things in the world is permissibility until a text restricts it, a principle the jurists derive from exactly this verse's generosity. The earth is not a sacred untouchable; it is a furnished estate handed to a tenant with instructions to live. The second wall is limit: "for you" states a beneficiary, not an owner absolute. The gift-formula appears in a sūrah whose opening command was worship and whose next verse announces a vicegerent — and a vicegerent administers property in the name of the Principal. The classical ethic of the gift follows: use without waste, extraction without corruption, possession held as trust — the same three bonds verse 27 listed, now seen from the property side. A covenant-breaker corrupts the land (2:27); the land corrupted is the gift misused; the misuse is not primarily economic but theological, a tenant redecorating the house as if he held the title. Modern readers hear the verse's ecology here: an endowed earth creates duties, not merely appetites.

**Istawā: Turning Toward the Heaven**

The second movement begins with a verb the Qur'an deploys in creation contexts with deliberate weight: *thumma istawā ilā al-samāʾ* — then He turned toward, or directed Himself to, or established Himself over the heaven; the translations vary because the verb's range is wide, and this very verse renders it "turned towards" while elsewhere — *the Most Compassionate, ˹Who is˺ established on the Throne* (20:5) — the same word pictures enthronement. The commentators' shared minimum is purposeful attention: *istawā* carries the sense of addressing a task completely, the way a builder turns from the foundation to the frame. The *thumma*, "then," marks an order of disclosure rather than divine delay — the Qur'an's creation sequences consistently narrate stages for a hearer who can only take them in sequence. The movement of the verse is architectural: the floor furnished first (the earth, for you), then the raising of the structure above it — canopy in verse 22, seven-fold edifice here. The reader is being walked through his house in the order a house is made: ground, then roof, then the inspection clause that closes the verse.

**Seven Heavens: The Numbered Sky**

The heaven's formation is given a number: *sabʿa samāwāt*, seven heavens — stated flatly, without explanation, and the Qur'an returns to the figure with structural detail: *"˹He is the One˺ Who created seven heavens, one above the other. You will never see any imperfection in the creation of the Most Compassionate"* (67:3), the layered construction also appearing in the six-days narrative of Fuṣṣilat (41:12) and in al-Ṭalāq's pairing of seven heavens with the like thereof in earths (65:12) — earths upon earths, as the early commentator Mujāhid read the cosmology: heavens above heavens, earths above earths. The classical exegetes ranged freely over the figure — atmospheric layers, celestial spheres, orders of being — and the Qur'an's own usage declines to legislate among them, fixing only three claims: the sky is plural in order, layered rather than a single dome; the layering is flawless, an engineered perfection the eye can test (67:3 challenges it directly); and the structure, however many of its floors lie beyond human sight, was built with the same "for you" orientation as the floor the reader stands on. Seven, in Semitic usage, is also the number of completeness — and the completeness claim is exactly the one the verse's closing clause will ratify.

**The Knower of All Things Signs the Blueprint**

The verse ends by stepping back from its own cosmology to name the Cosmologist's remaining attribute: *wa-Huwa bi-kulli shayʾin ʿalīm* — and He has knowledge of all things. The placement answers a question the grandeur of the scene raises unasked. A creation this vast — seven heavens over an earth stocked with everything — invites the worry that haunts every large house: does the Builder still know what happens in the small rooms? Is a creature this minor inside a cosmos this layered actually registered? The clause answers with the Qur'an's standard universal: *kull shayʾ*, every thing, with no scale floor and no scale ceiling. Omniscience here is not an abstract perfection but the guarantee of the gift's governance — the provisions are delivered by a Provider who tracks the delivery down to each recipient, and the return of verse 28 will be a return to precisely this knowledge. The same clause also underwrites the challenge two sūrahs-earlier verses and the census of verse 26: the God who parables with mosquitoes knows mosquitoes. Vastness and minuteness are held in one sentence, and the sentence is signed by the attribute that holds them: knowledge of all things.

**The Stage Is Set; The Appointment Follows**

Read in sequence, verses 21–29 form one complete movement — the sūrah's grounding — and verse 29 is its final stroke. The command to worship was issued (21), the furnished house shown as evidence (22), the Book's own claim tested and the alternatives prepared (23–25), the parable's sorting explained and the covenant-breakers defined (26–27), the reader's own biography produced as the nearest evidence (28), and now the cosmos inventoried as a gift with a Giver who knows every item (29). Everything required for the next scene is in place: an endowed earth, a layered heaven, an omniscient Owner, and a species under a worship-command. The verse that follows opens with the announcement that gathers all four threads — a declaration, made to the angels, about a placement upon this very earth. The cosmology of verse 29 is thus not an interlude but a stage set, furnished in detail so that the drama of the next verses can begin with everything already built, endowed, and known.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:30

> ˹Remember˺ when your Lord said to the angels, “I am going to place a successive ˹human˺ authority on earth.” They asked ˹Allah˺, “Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood while we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness?” Allah responded, “I know what you do not know.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Khalīfah: A Word That Named an Office and an Era**

The announcement's key term is *khalīfah*, and its semantic range shaped Islamic political vocabulary for a thousand years. The word comes from *khalafa*, to come after, to succeed, to replace — and it carries both directions of the relation at once: one who comes *after* another, and one who stands *in for* another, a deputy. The title *khalīfat rasūl Allāh*, successor of the Messenger of Allah, shortened to *khalīfah* and anglicized as caliph, is the historical deposit of this verse's word. But the Qur'an's own usage is wider than any throne. Here and in al-Anʿām the term spans the species: *"He is the One Who has placed you as successors on earth and elevated some of you in rank over others, so He may test you with what He has given you"* (6:165) — succession as the human condition, coupled to testing. In Ṣād it narrows to an office with a job description: *"O David! We have surely made you an authority in the land, so judge between people with truth"* (38:26). Both layers are present in the announcement: humanity as such succeeds — on the earth, after its prior orders of life — and particular humans deputize, administering justice in the name of the One who placed them.

**An Announcement Made, Not a Question Asked**

The divine speech here is declarative: *innī jāʿilun fī al-ard khalīfah* — I am placing, I am about to place, a vicegerent in the earth. The active participle states a matter resolved, and the angels are informed rather than consulted. The distinction was important to the commentators, because it frames everything that follows: the angels' reply is not a vote against the decree but a question within it, and the divine response treats it as such — answering, not rebuking. There is a model of speech in the scene worth noticing. Allah includes creatures in the knowledge of His decisions without transferring to them the authorship of those decisions; He makes angels and, later, prophets and communities, parties to information about what He will do. The announcement also fixes the theater: *in the earth* — the same earth verse 29 described as created for humanity, now receiving its announced heir. The gift and the heir are matched before the heir exists; the endowment of verse 29 reads backward as preparation for this sentence.

**The Angels' Question: Two Readings and a Weighing**

The reply is the scene's puzzle: *Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood?* The question quotes two specific crimes, and the exegetes split on where such specifics came from. The first reading gives the angels experience: the earth had prior inhabitants — the jinn-tribes of the Ibn ʿAbbās narrative, who spread corruption and shed blood before being driven off — and the angels generalize from a known record. The second reading, al-Rāzī's preference, makes the question an expression of wonder rather than doubt or objection: the angels marvel at a wisdom that wills a blood-shedder for vicegerent, without impugning the wisdom. Weighing them, the question's precision favors the first — corruption and bloodshed are named, not guessed — while angelic impeccability favors the second, since wonder cannot sin. The tradition harmonizes: they knew the type because Allah had disclosed it to them, and they asked to understand, not to object. Notably, the two crimes they name are this sūrah's own charges — corruption in the land (2:11, 2:27) and the shedding of blood it will legislate against — as if the angels quoted the file on humanity that al-Baqarah is in the middle of documenting.

**The Iblīs Material and How the Tradition Grades It**

The commentaries attach a body of narrative to this verse — Ibn ʿAbbās's report of Iblīs as al-Ḥārith, an angel of the tribe called al-ḥinn, custodian of Paradise, sent against the earth's earlier corrupters, filled with pride at the victory, taunting Adam's lifeless clay body for forty years, flying in and out of it: *you are nothing*. The reports are vivid and they are graded by the tradition itself. Al-Rāzī and others note that the angelic-tribe specifics cannot be relied upon — they carry the fingerprints of popular narrative — because the Qur'an settles the question of Iblīs's kind in its own text: *"but not Iblîs, who was one of the jinn, but he rebelled against the command of his Lord"* (18:50). An authority like Ibn ʿAbbās would have known that verse. The method lesson is preserved inside the exegetical tradition rather than imported into it: lore is weighed against the Qur'an's explicit statements, and where they diverge, the lore is demoted. What survives the grading is the order-of-creation datum the Qur'an itself supplies — the jinn fashioned earlier, from scorching fire, while man was made of sounding clay (15:26–27) — enough to ground the prior-inhabitants reading without the mythology.

**“While We Glorify and Sanctify”: The Credential in the Question**

Embedded in the angels' question is their self-description: *wa-naḥnu nusabbihu bi-ḥamdika wa-nuqaddisu lak* — while we glorify Your praise and proclaim Your holiness. The two verbs name the angelic office: *tasbīḥ*, declaring Allah beyond every defect, and *taqdīs*, the related sanctification — some commentators read the pair as one act, we glorify You while praising You. The credential sharpens the question into its real form: the sky already has worship in it — ceaseless, sinless, unanimous — so what does the earth gain by a worshipper who sheds blood? The Qur'an's own cosmology deepens the puzzle: *"The seven heavens, the earth, and all those in them glorify Him. There is not a single thing that does not glorify His praises"* (17:44). If everything already glorifies, the angels' worship is not unique in kind. The answer the scene will develop — taught names, a tested creature, worship chosen where it could be refused — supplies what universal glorification lacks: the *tasbīḥ* of a being that could have corrupted and shed blood, and did neither. The credential in the question is therefore honest and incomplete, and the verse lets it stand unrebutted.

**“I Know What You Do Not Know”**

The divine reply is the scene's whole theodicy, and it declines to argue. *Innī aʿlamu mā lā taʿlamūn* — I know what you do not know: not a refutation of the record on corruption and blood, which the reply leaves standing, but a reserve entered against it. The commentators fill the reserve with contents: prophets, saints, martyrs, knowers of Allah, generations of the just — goods the announcement will produce that the angels' data cannot yet contain. Al-Rāzī's summary holds the logic: despite the inevitability of bloodletting, good will come of this creature, and what that good is, is known to Allah alone. The reply thus establishes the epistemics of human history in one sentence: the species is justified by hidden contents, its ledger balanced by entries no observer — angelic or human — can total. It also answers backward into the sūrah: the God who knows the unshown good in a blood-shedding species is the same who overheard the mockery in the closed room (2:14) and reads what hearts conceal (2:28's Lender). The angels were told, in effect, that their information was accurate and their conclusion premature — a distinction every reader of this verse is living inside.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:31

> He taught Adam the names of all things, then He presented them to the angels and said, “Tell Me the names of these, if what you say is true? ”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Answer Arrives as a Curriculum**

The reply to the angels' question — *I know what you do not know* — is now unpacked, and the unpacking is not an argument but a lesson plan: *wa-ʿallama Ādama al-asmāʾa kullahā*, He taught Adam the names, all of them. The vicegerent's qualification is announced in the medium of instruction. Not power, not sinlessness, not seniority in creation — taught knowledge, comprehensive in scope, is what the office runs on. The verse's verb choice deserves weight: *ʿallama*, the intensive form of teaching, the same verb the angels will use of themselves in their confession — *what You have taught us* — so that the scene establishes one epistemology for every creature present: all knowledge in the room is taught knowledge, differing in scope, not in kind. And the scope given to Adam is total — *kullahā*, all of them. The demonstration to follow will show why the announcement of verse 30 was made in confidence: the being the angels questioned has just been equipped with something the questioners do not possess, and the equipment is public, examinable, and about to be examined.

**Which Names? The Exegetical Range**

The commentators debated the inventory, and the debate maps the verse's reach. Ibn ʿAbbās read the names as the vocabulary of human discourse — man, sea, mountain, down to the kettle, the whole working lexicon by which people name and address their world. Mujāhid took the widest scope: the names of everything, a complete nomenclature of existence. Others proposed narrower lists — the names of the angels, or of Adam's descendants. Al-Ṭabarī preferred the last, partly on a grammatical ground worth recording: the pronoun used for the presented things is *hum*, the plural reserved for persons, where non-persons normally take the feminine singular — though the commentators concede the rule is not absolute, citing counter-instances like the beasts referred to by *hum* in 24:45. Al-Rāzī drew the linguistic corollary: Adam was taught all the languages of the earth, and his descendants specialized into particular tongues over time. Weighing the readings, the grammatical argument for persons is strong but defeasible, and the safest construal keeps both poles — the names of things and of people, objects and offspring, the lexicon and the genealogy. The verse is claiming, at minimum, that the first man was given the complete naming-capacity: everything in his world could be called, classified, and addressed.

**Adam From the Earth's Whole Surface**

The exegetes attach to this scene a report about Adam's making that explains humanity's variety. His name is derived by some from *adīm*, the surface of the earth, and a prophetic saying preserved in the ḥadīth collections states the derivation as fact: Allah created Adam from a handful taken from the entire earth — and the children of Adam correspond to the earth, some red, some black, some white, some in between, and so in temperament: ease and difficulty, good and bad. The report does three things for the verse. It grounds the first human in the whole planet rather than a locality — the vicegerent is made of the estate he will administer, sampled from every province of it. It explains difference within the species as compositional rather than hierarchical: the handful was mixed at the source. And it ties Adam's creation to the earth of verses 22 and 29 — the soil furnished for humanity is the soil humanity is furnished from. The naming-knowledge of this verse is thus given to a creature whose body is already a catalogue of the earth, microcosm holding macrocosm, fitted to name what he is made of.

**The Presentation and the Demand**

The scene's staging is precise: *thumma ʿaraḍahum ʿalā al-malāʾikah* — He presented them to the angels. What was presented, the commentators note, is either the named objects themselves or the names — the exhibit is deliberately not itemized, and the omission is the point of the following clause: *anbiʾūnī bi-asmāʾi hāʾulāʾ*, tell Me the names of *these*. The demonstrative "these" presumes a display the angels are looking at and the reader is not shown; the narrative withholds the inventory from everyone except the parties being tested. The demand's closing condition — *in kuntum ṣādiqīn*, if you are truthful — imports the sūrah's idiom of testing: the same conditional closed the literary challenge of 2:23, *if what you say is true*. Truth-claims in the Qur'an are consistently cashed out in performance — produce a sūrah, name the exhibits — and the condition here is not a doubt of angelic honesty but the standing rule of the scene: what you claim to know, demonstrate. The angels made a claim in verse 30 about their glorifying and sanctifying, and about the corruption of the announced heir; the demonstration will sort the claim.

**The Test the Angels Cannot Pass — and Its Fairness**

The demand is not a trick. It measures a real difference the verse has already installed: Adam was taught *all* the names; the angels, as their coming confession will state, hold only what they were taught for their functions. Ibn ʿArabī's reading sharpens the difference into a metaphysics: the angels in relation to the world are like the faculties of a person — each fixed to its office, each limited to what it is, and each thereby veiled from what is above it; Adam alone was given the synthesis, the capacity to hold all the names together and through them to know the Namer in a way no single-faculty knower can. On that reading the test is fair because it asks each party only for what was given it: the angels cannot name the exhibits because their knowledge is functional, and functional knowledge is exactly what verse 30's question was built on — they reasoned from their office. The superiority being demonstrated is therefore not moral but structural: the vicegerent's rank rests on comprehensive naming, the capacity to classify the whole and address it — which is also, not coincidentally, a description of what science, law, and language do.

**Naming as the Root of the Human Estate**

The verse's largest claim is anthropological. What distinguishes the human being in the Qur'an's founding story is neither sinlessness — the angels hold that — nor strength, nor age in creation, but taught, comprehensive, articulable naming. Every human science extends this endowment: taxonomy, grammar, law, medicine, astronomy are unfoldings of *al-asmāʾ*, the capacity to fix a name to a thing and thereby to hold the thing in discourse, transmit it, deliberate about it. The Islamic tradition read the verse exactly so — the superiority of knowledge over worship-only, the scholar's rank above the merely devout — and the story's outcome institutionalized the lesson: the demonstration of naming settled the hierarchy of the scene without conflict, without a single act of power. Authority in this narrative is decided by curriculum. The vicegerency announced in verse 30 turns out to be an epistemic office — deputy of the One Who knows all things (2:29), equipped with the names, installed over the earth that was furnished for him — and the reader inherits the estate with the capacity that conveys it: whatever you can truly name, you can truly steward.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:32

> They replied, “Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Answer Begins by Exonerating the Questioned**

The angels' reply opens before it confesses: *subḥānaka* — glory be to You, Allah be declared beyond every defect. The word order is protocol, and the protocol is doctrine. Faced with a demand they cannot meet, the angels' first act is not self-defense and not despair but the vindication of the wisdom that framed the test — the same *tasbīḥ* they named as their office in verse 30, now performed at the exact moment it costs something. The exegetes note the pattern the Qur'an keeps: whenever divine action could be misread as defective — a decree, a judgment, an attribution of guidance and straying — *subḥānaka* or *subḥānahu* intervenes to sever the act from every imperfection. Here the glorification does specific work: it says, before the confession, that a test we will fail was still rightly designed. The sentence thus models the only posture the Qur'an recognizes for a creature at the limit of its knowledge — not the suspension of judgment but the prior acquittal of the Judge, held while the limit is admitted.

**One Negation, One Exception: The Epistemology in a Clause**

The confession itself is the Qur'an's most compressed statement of creaturely knowledge: *lā ʿilma lanā illā mā ʿallamtanā* — we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. The grammar is a total negation governed by a single exception, and the form is exact: no underived knowledge belongs to any creature — not to the angels, whose sinlessness and antiquity might have argued for self-sufficiency, and by the verse's silent inclusion, not to anyone else. Every cognition in existence is loaned. The clause also settles the scene's comparison without disparaging either party: the angels and Adam differ not in kind of knowing — both are taught — but in curriculum. Adam received the names, all of them; the angels received their functions. The exception-clause therefore does double duty. It absolves the angels of the failed demand (they cannot name exhibits outside their instruction), and it locates Adam's superiority inside the same principle (his instruction was comprehensive). One epistemology governs the whole room, and its first article is that ignorance, rightly confessed, is not a defect in the creature but a property of createdness.

**The Limitation the Verse Exists to Record**

The commentators draw the scene's formal conclusion from this reply: the verse records the limitation of angelic knowledge — not its weakness but its boundedness, specifically in universal comprehension. The angels know truly what they know; their knowledge simply does not extend to the whole, and verse 30's question was generated from inside that boundary. Read against the reply of verse 33 — *I know what you reveal and conceal* — and against the announcement of verse 29 — *He has knowledge of all things* — the scene arranges three epistemic ranks in one frame: the Knower of all things; the creature taught all the names; the creatures taught their functions. The ranking retroactively absolves the angels' question in verse 30 of every charge of insolence: it was the honest output of a bounded knower contemplating an unbounded decree. And it establishes the Qur'an's standing treatment of angelic error-adjacent speech — wonder, question, confession — as the behavior of knowers who are certain of their limit and therefore never pretend past it. The limitation is not their shame; it is their *tasbīḥ* in epistemic form.

**Two Names to Close: The Knower and the Wise**

The confession ends by naming the resolution the angels cannot articulate: *innaka anta al-ʿalīm al-ḥakīm* — You are truly the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. The two names answer the two difficulties of the scene with surgical fit. *Al-ʿalīm* answers the knowledge gap — what we cannot name, You know; the exhibits are inside Your science even when they are outside ours. *Al-ḥakīm* answers the wisdom gap of verse 30 — the placement of a blood-shedding vicegerent, the withholding of comprehensive naming from sinless worshippers, the design of a test its first-takers will fail: every item has a purpose the Wise holds even where the knowing cannot trace it. The pairing is one of the Qur'an's most frequent closings, and its logic here is that knowledge and wisdom are the two attributes a bounded creature must posit whenever he meets a boundary: that the Knower has the fact I lack, and that the Wise has the reason I lack. The angels model the complete act of confession — limit admitted, both perfections affirmed — in a single sentence, and the sentence becomes the pattern.

**The Sentence the Tradition Learned By**

This reply entered Islamic practice as the learner's standing prayer. The classical etiquette of study opens sessions with *subḥānaka* and this confession, and the great Qur'anic supplication for increase — *My Lord, increase me in knowledge* (20:114) — is recited in the spirit of a verse that makes all knowledge a taught gift to be requested rather than a possession to be displayed. The liturgical reuse is not incidental; it reads the scene as normative. Every student occupies the angels' position at some hour: confronted with material he cannot name, tempted either to bluff or to despair, and this verse supplies the third option the scene enacted — glorify, confess the exact limit, name the Teacher's two perfections, and wait for the instruction. The prayer of al-Fātiḥah, *Guide us along the Straight Path* (1:6), is the same posture in petition form; the angels' confession is its declarative twin. A tradition that begins every circle of learning with these words has made the failed test of verse 31 into its pedagogy: the demonstration every learner must first pass is that he knows what he does not know.

**Humility as the Highest Knowledge in the Scene**

There is an irony the verse completes, and it is the story's hinge. The angels pass the test by failing it. Asked for names they do not have, they produce the truest sentence available in the situation — a confession exact in its limit and complete in its theology — and the narrative treats that sentence as the right answer to the wrong question. The demonstration of verse 31 established the vicegerency's ground: comprehensive taught knowledge. This verse establishes the worshippers' ground: comprehensive taught *ignorance*, known as such and correctly related to its Teacher. Both grounds are sound, and the scene needs both — a deputy who can name the estate, and attendants who will not overreach it. The final effect on the reader is a redefinition of rank: in this narrative, knowing is honored, but knowing-one's-not-knowing is honored first, because it is the only knowledge no curriculum can confer and no exam can fake. The angels, senior in creation and sinless in function, speak the verse that every later knower — Adam's children included — must be able to say at the edge of his own instruction, and the saying of it is not defeat but the exact posture the Teacher designed the edge for.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:33

> Allah said, “O Adam! Inform them of their names.” Then when Adam did, Allah said, “Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Act of Office Is Instruction**

The demonstration proceeds by command: *yā Ādamu anbiʾhum bi-asmāʾihim* — O Adam, inform them of their names. The verb is *anbiʾ*, from the root of *nabaʾ*, news, and *nabī*, prophet — the announce-verb the Qur'an reserves for significant disclosure, here in its first human instance. The vicegerent's inaugural act is thus not governance, not judgment, not worship in the liturgical sense, but teaching: he addresses the angels, and what he gives them is information they lack. The scene's inversion is complete and gentle — the questioned are answered by the one they questioned, and the answer takes the form of instruction rather than triumph. Nothing in the verse narrates a humiliation of the angels; the narrative records only the transfer of names. Read with verse 32's confession, the exchange is a liturgy of two offices: the functionaries confess their limit, the namer supplies it, and the gap between them is closed by knowledge moving in the direction the Teacher set. Authority in this story has now shown its operating mode — it informs.

**The Delivery the Narrative Withholds**

Between the command and its outcome stands one of the Qur'an's most consequential silences: *fa-lammā anbaʾahum bi-asmāʾihim* — then when he had informed them of their names. The content is not given. No list, no sample, no inventory of what Adam said; the narrative records the fact of the delivery and skips the delivery. The exegetes' inventories — kettle and mountain, offspring and angels, the languages entire — are reconstructions around this withheld center, and the withholding itself instructs. Had the verse itemized the names, the demonstration would be a closed catalogue, a finite list examinable once; by suppressing the list, the text makes the naming-capacity itself the exhibit, a power whose contents unfold across the whole subsequent history of the species. Every classification, every definition, every true naming from the first fire-drill to the last element is, on this reading, inside *anbaʾahum bi-asmāʾihim* — the verse is a seed-paragraph for the human sciences, and its silence is the room the sciences will occupy. The narrative economy is exact: the point was never the nouns but the faculty, and faculties are not enumerated, only exercised.

**“Did I Not Tell You”: The Reserve Unsealed**

The divine speech returns to the angels with a self-quotation: *a-lam aqul lakum innī aʿlamu* — did I not say to you that I know? The reference is to verse 30's reserve, *I know what you do not know*, and the quotation marks the demonstration as the reserve's unpacking: what the angels did not know was the naming-capacity now exercised in front of them. The knowledge claimed is then given its full scope in two pairs — *ghayb al-samāwāt wa-l-arḍ*, the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and *mā tubdūna wa-mā kuntum taktumūn*, what you reveal and what you were concealing. The first pair is cosmological: nothing hidden in either order of creation — the seven heavens of verse 29 and the furnished earth — falls outside this knowledge; the Qur'an states the same scope as a standing attribute, *"˹He is the˺ Knower of the seen and the unseen—the All-Great, Most Exalted"* (13:9). The second pair is personal: the knowledge turns from the cosmos to the addressees' own interiors. The verse thus welds the two orders the reader is tempted to separate — the vast and the private — into one claim, held by one Knower, in one sentence.

**What Was Concealed: The Exegetical Candidates**

The final phrase — *what you used to conceal* — generated a literature, because the narrative does not name the concealed thing. One strand reads it as Iblīs's pride: if the tradition's placement of him among the prostrators is accepted, his interior refusal was present in the scene and known, the concealed item being the self-preference that his later open defiance will display. A second strand, recorded by al-Ṭabarī, reads it as a thought attributed to the angels themselves — that Allah never creates a thing nobler than them — with the counter-observation that on this reading what they "concealed" was a virtue, their settled knowledge of their own rank, and their acceptance of Adam's excellence in the scene was then without objection. Weighing the candidates, the text's refusal to specify is itself informative: the demonstration's force does not depend on which interior is meant, because the claim being proved is the *knowledge*, not the inventory. The Knower cites concealment generally, and every hearer supplies his own instance — which is how the verse achieves its pastoral aim: it is addressed to a reader who also has an unspoken item, and the reader knows which one it is without the text telling him.

**The Scene's Real Audience**

The address in the second half of the verse slides, and the slide is deliberate. *Mā tubdūna wa-mā taktumūn* — what *you* reveal and conceal — is grammatically the angels' interior, but the sūrah's first audience hears it inside a frame just built: the hypocrites of verses 8–20, whose two rooms the Book overheard; the mockers of verse 14 whose private transcript was published; the covenant-breakers of verse 27 defined by breaches nobody witnessed at the time. The naming-demonstration and the concealment-knowledge are one claim about the same God: He who knew the unnamed contents of Adam's instruction knows the unspoken contents of every chest in Madina. The story of Adam, in other words, is not an interlude from the sūrah's opening but its ratification — the cosmic scene supplies the metaphysics the earlier portrait assumed. And it arms the community: the believers who cannot see into their neighbors' rooms are told, in the first story of their Book, that the rooms are lit from above. What they cannot audit, the Knower of *ghayb* audits; what they must take at word, He takes at heart.

**The Trial Closed, the Estate Confirmed**

Verses 30–33 form a complete movement, and its parts interlock: announcement (30), question (30), reserve (30), curriculum (31), test (31), confession (32), demonstration (33), ratification (33). The vicegerency stands at the end on three pillars the scene has exhibited — comprehensive taught knowledge, confessed limitation, and interiors transparent to the One who placed them. The angels' question is answered not with information about the future but with an installed fact: the blood-shedder exists now, and he can name everything in the room. The reserve of verse 30 — *I know what you do not know* — is discharged as far as discharge is possible for a bounded knower: the hidden good was shown in its first specimen, and the rest remains with the Knower, which is exactly where the angels' confession left it. For the reader at the end of the first juzʾ-section of al-Baqarah, the estate is now fully titled — earth furnished (29), heir announced (30), heir equipped (31–32), heir installed and the installation ratified by omniscience (33) — and the narrative is ready to record what the heir did with the estate, beginning with the command that comes next.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:34

> And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,” so they all did—but not Iblîs, who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Command That Tests Obedience, Not Knowledge**

The naming-demonstration of verse 31 established Adam's rank by curriculum; this verse confirms it by command. Allah orders the angels — the same company that confessed its bounded knowledge two verses earlier — to prostrate before the new creature. The prostration is one of honor and submission to the divine order, not of worship, which the Qur'an reserves for Allah alone; it is a ceremonial ratification of the appointment announced in verse 30. What the command tests is therefore not information — the angels have just watched the demonstration — but the will's posture toward a decree whose wisdom they have seen only in outline. Their question of verse 30 had been reasonable; the answer of verse 31 was empirical; now the answer arrives as an order, and orders are where creatures discover what their questions were made of. The angels' response — *so they all did* — is total and immediate, and the totality sets up the exception the verse is built to isolate.

**One Exception, and the Qur'an Names Its Species**

*Illā Iblīs* — except Iblīs. The exception is grammatically tiny and cosmologically enormous, and the Qur'an elsewhere removes all ambiguity about its nature: *"but not Iblîs, who was one of the jinn, but he rebelled against the command of his Lord"* (18:50). He was no angel who fell; angels in the Qur'an's doctrine do not rebel — they do not possess the equipment. He was a creature of the jinn, made of fire before man's clay (15:26–27), elevated by long worship into the company of angels, and addressed with them by the command. The distinction matters for everything that follows. A sin committed by an angel would impugn the order of heaven; a sin committed by a will-bearing creature among sinless company locates the fault exactly where the verse places it — in a freedom misused. The scene is thus staged with precision: the only being in the assembly capable of saying no is the one who says it.

**Refusal, Arrogance, Unfaith: Three Steps in One Sentence**

The verse narrates the fall in three verbs, and their order is a causal chain. He *refused* — *abā*, the plain withholding of the act. He *acted arrogantly* — *istakbara*, a verb of self-magnification, the tenth-form that carries the sense of considering oneself great. And the result: *he was among the unfaithful* — enrolled, by his own act, in a category that did not previously include him. The sequence states the Qur'an's anatomy of apostasy: disobedience is not first a theological position but a postural one — a refusal generated by an inflated estimate of the self, and the estimate, sustained, hardens into unbelief. Nothing in the verse suggests Iblīs doubted Allah's existence or power; he disputed Allah's judgment in appointing. The sin is not against information but against rank as Allah assigned it — which is why the verse files it under *kufr* rather than under error.

**The First Sin Was a Comparison**

The Qur'an records Iblīs's reasoning wherever it retells this scene, and the reasoning is a syllogism: *"What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you? He replied: I am better than he is: You created me from fire and him from clay"* (7:12). The sentence contains the whole pathology — a measurement of origins, a ranking of materials, and a verdict against the decree that outranks it. The exegetes' rebuttal is also embedded in the materials: clay receives, nurtures, and grows what is planted in it, while fire consumes what it touches; the comparison that flattered Iblīs was defective on its own terms. But the deeper indictment is structural. The first act of disbelief in the Qur'an's human-facing history is *qiyās* against a command — private judgment installed as a court of appeal over revelation. Every subsequent "I know better than the text" descends, in the Qur'an's genealogy of error, from this one sentence spoken standing while everyone else was prostrate.

**A Scene the Book Retells Five Times**

No narrative moment in the Qur'an is repeated more insistently: the command, the prostration, and the refusal appear in al-Aʿrāf (7:11–25), al-Ḥijr (15:28–44), al-Isrāʾ (17:61–65), al-Kahf (18:50), and Ṣād (38:71–78), each retelling adding a facet — the respite granted, the oath of ambush, the strategy against the straight path. Al-Baqarah's version is the most compressed of the five: the sin named, the ranking stated, the scene closed. The compression itself is a choice — this sūrah needs only the fact of the refusal, because its subject is the community that will face the refuser's war. The repetitions across the Book function as emphasis by distribution: the fall of humanity begins not at the tree but at the prostration, and every generation that reads any of the five accounts is told where its oldest enemy enlisted. Ṣād preserves his answer in the same six words (38:76) — the syllogism is stable across every retelling, which is how fixed ideas appear in transcripts.

**The Enemy Was Hired Before the Fall**

Structurally, the verse plants the Adamic drama's antagonist inside the vicegerency narrative. The angels feared corruption and blood from the new appointment (2:30); the first corruption in the story is committed by neither man nor angel but by the third party who has now declared war from inside the assembly. Humanity's temptation is thus older than humanity's sin: the whisperer was positioned before the fall, and his motive — the refused prostration — is recorded before the tree appears. The verse also carries a standing warning to its readers about the company sin keeps. Iblīs was no stranger to worship; the tradition describes aeons of devotion before this moment. Nearness, antiquity, and piety of record did not immunize the one act of rank-dispute. The prostration scene is the sūrah's first case file in its long study of how knowledge and standing fail to protect a heart — and the next verses move the case file to the garden, where the same enemy will find a softer target than a commanded angel.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:35

> We cautioned, “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please, but do not approach this tree, or else you will be wrongdoers.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Charter of Four Clauses**

The address to Adam is a residence charter, and its proportions are the first thing to notice. Four elements: a dwelling — *live, you and your wife, in Paradise*; a company — the wife named inside the address; an open permission — *eat as freely as you please*, unrestricted as to place and kind; and a single prohibition — *do not approach this tree*. The ratio is deliberate and it is the moral shape of life as the Qur'an will legislate it for Adam's children: a vast field of the permitted crossed by one thin line of the forbidden. Readers of later law recognize the pattern — the ḥalāl comprehensive, the ḥarām minimal — and its origin is this verse. The permission's generosity is also strategic: the prohibition will be tested against a background of abundance, so that the transgression cannot plead necessity. Nothing about the tree is needed; everything else is given. The trial is therefore not of appetite cornered but of will indulged — the hardest kind, and the fairest.

**“Do Not Approach”: A Boundary With a Margin**

The prohibition's verb is *lā taqrabā* — do not *approach* — and the choice of verb over "do not eat" builds a safety margin into the command. The forbidden act lies at the end of a path; the prohibition begins at the path's entrance. Islamic ethics drew the principle directly from this grammar: guard the haram by guarding its approaches — the glance before the look, the meeting before the act, the conversation before the commitment. The margin also sharpens the coming failure. When the tree is eaten, the couple did not merely cross a line but traversed a whole protected distance to reach it, which is why the temptation narrative in Ṭā Hā dwells on the approach — the whisper that walked them toward the tree step by step. A command framed as *do not approach* makes every deliberate nearness a partial transgression, and it teaches the reader of the verse that moral boundaries in this Book are defended in depth, not painted at the edge of the cliff.

**Which Tree? A Name the Qur'an Withholds**

The exegetical literature is full of candidates — wheat, the grapevine, the fig — and the Qur'an itself never names the tree, using only *shajarah*, a word broad enough for any tree, shrub, or woody growth. The commentators are candid about where the candidates come from: Jewish and Christian oral traditions, and perhaps Arabian lore, filtered into the tafsīr collections, much of it weakly attested in ḥadīth and some of it, as al-Ṭabarī's own material shows, no better than folklore. The withholding is a lesson in exegetical method that al-Rāzī states as a rule for the whole story: certain details are neither knowable from the text nor needed by it — *one should cease and refrain from being categorical, and God knows best*. What the narrative requires is not the tree's species but its function: one object, arbitrarily chosen by the Commander, made the visible form of obedience. A named species would invite arguments about fruit; an unnamed tree keeps the test where it belongs — on the command, not the commodity.

**Which Garden? The Dispute and Its Weighing**

A larger question divides the commentators: is this the Garden of Reward promised to believers, or a garden of trial prepared elsewhere? The consensus holds the first — it is *al-Jannah*, the definite, well-known Paradise — and answers the objections: Iblīs may have whispered from outside its bounds, and the promise that its dwellers are never expelled (15:48 — *"nor will they ever be asked to leave"* (15:48)) applies to those admitted as reward after the earthly test. The minority position, al-Rāzī reports and presses, notes real difficulties: Satan's lie inside a garden where *"never to hear any idle talk or lying therein"* is promised (78:35); the tempter's offer of a *"Tree of Immortality and a kingdom that does not fade away"* (20:120), which would tempt no one already immortal; and the descent-verb *ihbiṭ*, used in this sūrah for ordinary travel (2:61) without implying vertical fall. Al-Rāzī's verdict is his method again: the proofs on both sides are weak and contradictory, so certainty is withheld — and the story's meaning survives either answer intact.

**The Wife Addressed Inside the Command**

The Qur'an does not name her in this verse or any other; she is *your wife*, and the traditions supply the name Ḥawwāʾ and the details of her creation. What the verse's grammar does supply is joint address: the command is spoken over both of them, the permission belongs to both, and the prohibition binds both. This is a structural departure from the Genesis account's sequencing, and its consequences run through the Quranic story. The temptation in Ṭā Hā is directed at Adam by name (20:120); the eating is joint; the confession is joint and in the dual and plural — *"Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers"* (7:23). No woman is singled out as the entry-point of sin, no man as its victim; the responsibility is shared in the same sentence that shares the pardon. The unnamed wife of this verse is, in the Qur'an's moral universe, a co-addressed moral agent — present in the command, present in the slip, present in the received words of verse 37.

**The Warning Label Stated Before the Trial**

The charter closes with its consequence announced in advance: *or else you will be wrongdoers* — *fa-takūnā mina al-ẓālimīn*. The warning does three things. It makes the coming failure informed: the couple will eat knowing what the eating classifies them as, which removes entrapment from the story entirely. It supplies the vocabulary of the aftermath — *ẓulm*, wronging, the word their own confession will use in al-Aʿrāf: *we have wronged ourselves*. And it defines the sin's essence before the act: approaching the tree is not primarily rule-breaking but self-wronging, a damage whose first victim is the doer. The verse thus installs the theology the whole Adamic cycle will demonstrate — a broad permission, one marked line, a stated consequence, an enemy on the ground, and two free agents who will shortly discover that the only thing the tree could take from them was themselves. The next verse records how the enemy worked the space this charter left open.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:36

> But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in, and We said, “Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other. You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Azallahumā: He Made Them Slip**

The verse's first verb is exact about agency: *fa-azallahumā al-shayṭān* — Satan caused them both to slip, using the same root the English metaphor "to fall" shares with the Arabic — a foot losing purchase, a slip into error. The verb form is causative, not creative: he produced the slipping; he did not create the fall. The Qur'an never grants Iblīs power over human choice — his own later confession in the Book is that he had no authority except the call (14:22's declaration, paraphrased in his speech on the Day). What he owns is the invitation; what the couple owns is the step. The verse holds both truths in one clause without letting either dissolve the other: the enemy's action was real — he *made them slip*, an achievement the text does not soften into mere suggestion — and the responsibility remains theirs, which is why the descent-command that follows is addressed to them and not to their tempter. Every reader inherits the same two facts about every sin: it was worked for, and it was chosen.

**How the Deception Worked: Selling Certainty**

The mechanics of the slip are supplied by the parallel accounts, and they show an attack on the one vulnerability the charter of verse 35 had left open. The Garden offered everything except guaranteed continuation — and Satan sold exactly that: *"O Adam! Shall I show you the Tree of Immortality and a kingdom that does not fade away?"* (20:120). The offer targeted not appetite but fear of loss, and al-Rāzī's observation sharpens it: a promise of eternal life is tempting only to someone whose eternity feels contingent — which is also one of his arguments that the garden of trial was not yet the Garden of Reward, where permanence is the floor and no such bait could work. Ṭā Hā adds the second instrument: he swore to them that he was their sincere adviser (20:119 — the oath recorded in al-Aʿrāf and Ṭā Hā). The deception thus ran on two rails — a guarantee against the terror of ending, and a sworn claim of goodwill — and both rails are still in service in every temptation since.

**“Descend, All of You”: The Plural and the Enmity**

The command *ihbiṭū* is plural, and the exegetes read the addressees as Adam, his wife, and their progeny — sometimes with Iblīs and his progeny included — the couple standing as representatives of the whole company. The descent is thus not a private exile but the installation of a species and its enemy on one ground, and the command legislates the terms: *as enemies to each other*. The enmity is not an accident of the fall but part of the charter of the earth — announced, expected, and built into the arrangement. Ṭā Hā carries the same formula: *"Descend, both of you, from here together ˹with Satan˺ as enemies to each other"* (20:123). Readers of the verse are thereby told something about their own residence: the war declared in verse 34 did not end at the expulsion; it was given a new theater with a permanent garrison. To live on earth is to live inside a declared enmity, and the guidance promised in verse 38 is the supply line for the side that keeps the covenant.

**A Residence and Provision — With a Clock**

The earth's description is two nouns and a deadline: *mustaqarr* — a dwelling place, a settled station — and *matāʿ* — provision, enjoyment, furnished means; both *ilā ḥīn*, until a time. The commentators range over the dwelling: the earth as abode, in the sense of 40:64 — *"It is Allah Who made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy"* (40:64) — or the graves as the true *mustaqarr* of the body. The readings can stand together, since every dwelling before the grave is provisional and the grave itself is a station on the way. The deadline is read as death, or the Resurrection, or an appointed term known only to Allah. The effect of the clause on the whole story is to make the earth a furnished leasehold: comfort is real — provision is promised in the same breath as the enmity — and comfort is terminal. The verse that expelled humanity from a garden also outfitted the exile: residence, rations, a clock, and an enemy. Three of the four are mercies; the fourth is the test.

**No Inherited Guilt: What the Verse Refuses to Say**

One doctrine is conspicuous by its absence, and the absence is load-bearing. The Qur'anic fall is not tied to original sin: nothing in this verse or its sequel transmits the slip as a stain on the descendants. What the children of Adam inherit from the garden is the situation — the earth, the enmity, the guidance to come, the clock — and not the guilt. The guilt was personal, the repentance was personal, and the acceptance of verse 37 will cancel it at the source before the descent is even narrated to its end. Islam's account of the human condition therefore starts elsewhere: not from an inherited corruption needing ontological repair, but from weakness (*ḍaʿf*), forgetfulness, and an exposed position in an enemy's theater — conditions treated with law, reminder, and repentance rather than with atonement. The difference explains much of the two religions' divergent vocabularies: where one tradition speaks of washing an inherited stain, this verse speaks of guarding a rented house against a declared adversary, with forgiveness available on demand for every breach.

**An Expulsion That Was Also an Installation**

Read back through verse 30, the descent changes character. The original announcement was never "I am placing a vicegerent in the Garden" but *"I am placing a successive ˹human˺ authority on earth"* — the earth named as the office's seat before the man existed. The garden residence and the slip and the descent were all, on this reading, stages in a single appointment: the vicegerent was educated, tested, forgiven, and then installed at his post, with his adversary also on site and his guidance also en route (2:38). The angels' question of verse 30 receives its fullest answer here — the corruption and blood they feared are real possibilities of the office, but the office was never designed for the innocent; it was designed for the repentant, for creatures who slip and receive words. The verse is thus an expulsion only in its grammar. In its function inside the sūrah it is an induction: humanity enters the earth not as a convict but as a posted deputy, briefed on the enemy, provisioned for the term, and expected at every fall to do what Adam is about to be shown doing — take the words and turn.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:37

> Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord, so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Words Received, Not Composed**

The verse's pivot is a single verb: *fa-talaqqā Ādamu min rabbihi kalimāt* — Adam *received* words from his Lord. The reception is from a direction the reader must not miss: the words of repentance were authored on the divine side first and handed down, so that the sinner's first true act of return was itself a gift. A person cannot repent with his own resources, the verse teaches, because the fall has damaged precisely the resources repentance needs; so Allah supplies the sentence. The commentators identify the words variously, and the identifications form a small library of the tradition. The dominant reading takes them as the confession preserved in al-Aʿrāf: *"Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will certainly be losers"* (7:23). Others report Adam's plea in three questions — Did You not make me a vicegerent? Did You not breathe into me of Your spirit? Does Your compassion not outstrip Your wrath? — with the divine "yes" to each as the received words. Others again say the words were the rites of the pilgrimage taught to him, or a formula of tawḥīd and self-accusation recorded by al-Rāzī: *There is no god but You; glory be to You and praise; I have wronged myself, so forgive me*. The plurality is itself informative: the tradition agrees on the mechanism — repentance is taught before it is offered — while leaving the syllables open.

**One Verb, Two Directions**

Arabic compresses the whole theology of repentance into a single root. *Tāba* means to turn or return, and the same verb serves both parties in the transaction: the servant turns back to Allah, and Allah turns back to the servant. English needs two words — repent and relent, or repent and accept — because the actors differ; Arabic needs one verb and a preposition, because the motion is one. The verse displays both uses in sequence: Allah *turned* to Adam — *fa-tāba ʿalayhi*, He relented toward him, accepted his turning — and the intensive divine name *al-Tawwāb* at the verse's close names the One for whom this turning is a repeated, habitual act. The Biblical parallels the commentators note — passages where a kind of relenting is predicated of God — mark a shared Semitic intuition; the Qur'an's formulation is precise about direction: *ʿalā*, upon him — the divine turning descends onto the human one, covering it. Repentance, in this grammar, is a single movement with two ends, and the end that starts it is the one above.

**The Acceptance Runs Ahead of the Return**

Sequence the clause carefully: Adam received the words, *then* He turned to him. The acceptance is attached to the receiving, not to a completed program of amendment — no penance is interposed, no waiting period, no expiation enumerated. The verse's two closing names ratify the speed: *al-Tawwāb*, the Accepter of Repentance in the intensive form — the repeatedly-turning, the One whose nature is to accept — and *al-Raḥīm*, the Most Merciful, the particular mercy of al-Fātiḥah's third verse now at work at the lowest point of human history.
