**Why This Warning Falls on Israel First**

The addressees of verse 48 are the children of Israel of verse 47, and the warning is aimed at the specific theology of rescue their community held. Chosenness had hardened, in some of its popular forms, into a doctrine of genealogical immunity — a people that at one point claimed for itself the very title of Allah's children and beloved (5:18), and that trusted in the merit of the fathers, the covenant of the bloodline, the interceding patriarchs. Verse 48 dismantles the machinery clause by clause: the fathers cannot avail (no soul helps another), the patriarchs cannot intercede uncommissioned (no intercession accepted), the treasury of accumulated merit cannot ransom (no ransom taken), and the community's power cannot defend (no help given). Lineage, in this verse's arithmetic, delivers no exit on the Day — which converts verse 47's favor into verse 48's responsibility: the remembered blessings were a trust audited individually, not an inheritance cashed collectively. The Madinan occasion sharpens the aim: scholars selling the signs for a paltry price (2:41) were transacting in exactly the currencies this verse voids — position, patronage, price — and the recital that follows will show their ancestors, at the sea and at the mountain, warned in the same words.

**The Individualized Soul and the Justice It Makes Possible**

Stripped of its four exits, the soul of verse 48 stands alone — and the aloneness is as much gift as terror. A day of no proxies is a day when no one's fate is decided by someone else's: not by a father's sin, not by a community's collapse, not by a patron's defection. The verse is the eschatological twin of the sūrah's legal principle that no bearer of burdens bears another's burden, and of its charter to Adam's children that each departs the descent on his own response (2:38–39). Individualization is the precondition of perfect justice: only a court where every soul appears in person, unrepresented and unbought, can render a verdict with nothing in it but that soul's own case. The verse therefore completes the covenant logic of the unit it closes. The covenant was bilateral (40); its carrying was made possible by help sought through patience and prayer (45); the disposition that carries it is certainty of the meeting and the return (46); and the meeting's setting is this Day — no availing, no mediation, no price, no force. Between verse 40 and verse 48 the sūrah has built the entire moral universe its recital will populate: a contract, a method, a certainty, and an unpostponable hearing. The recital of favors and failures begins at the next verse, and it begins *after* the warning, so that every blessing about to be remembered is remembered as evidence in a case already scheduled.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:49

> ˹Remember˺ how We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with dreadful torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women. That was a severe test from your Lord.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Ledger Opens With a Rescue**

The bracketed "remember" at the head of the verse is supplied by the grammar: *idh*, "when," hangs on the *udh-kurū* of verse 47 — remember My favors... *and when* We delivered you. The recital of favors has begun, and its first entry is not a gift of property or status but an act of extraction: deliverance from a tormentor. The choice determines the reading of everything that follows. Before the sūrah records a single one of this community's failures — and it will record many, beginning a few verses on — it files the rescue that made them a people. Israel's national existence in the Qur'an is dated from the Exodus: a delivered community, born in the act of being taken out. The ledger's order is also the order of gratitude's logic: the favor remembered first is the one no later merit contributed to, since a slaughtered infant and an enslaved mother had nothing to offer. Whatever the covenant will demand, it demands from people whose first line-item was pure rescue — and the verse states the rescue with Allah as its only actor: *We delivered you*, no intermediary named, no human verb in the sentence's main clause.

**The People of Pharaoh: Deliverance From a System**

The object of the deliverance is *āl Firʿawn* — the people, household, and following of Pharaoh, not Pharaoh alone. The word *āl* gathers a tyrant's apparatus: the court, the officers, the army, the overseers, the informants — the whole machine through which one man's will becomes a population's torment. The deliverance is thereby political in the full sense: it ends not a person but a regime, and the Qur'an's phrasing everywhere keeps this collective frame — Pharaoh and his soldiers pursuing at the sea (10:90), Pharaoh and his hosts drowned, the lands and honors left behind passing to the delivered people, as the wider recital in al-Shuʿarāʾ records. The same favor is rehearsed in Sūrah Ibrāhīm with Moses as the preacher, addressing the same people with nearly the same sentence: *"Remember Allah's favour upon you when He rescued you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with dreadful torment—slaughtering your sons and keeping your women. That was a severe test from your Lord"* (14:6). The double filing — Moses reciting the favor to them in the wilderness, Allah reciting it to their descendants in Madina — shows the memory being instituted as worship: a delivered people are commanded to keep the deliverance in speech, generation after generation, because the favor operates only while it is remembered.

**The Two Torments: Slaughter and Keeping**

The torment is itemized in two participles. *Yudhabbiḥūna abnāʾakum* — slaughtering your sons: the systematic killing of male infants, the verb of ritual slaughter applied to children, which is the word's full horror. *Wa-yastaḥyūna nisāʾakum* — keeping your women alive: the deliberate sparing of the females, not mercy but policy — life reserved for servitude, the women kept as the instrument of a people's reduction. The pair is a demographic strategy: kill the future (the sons), own the present (the women), and the nation dissolves within a generation. The verse's summary verb above them — *yasūmūnakum sūʾa al-ʿadhāb*, they afflicted you with dreadful torment — carries the sense of *sām*: to make someone taste repeatedly, to impose and re-impose; the torment was not an episode but a regimen. And no reason is given. The Qur'an records Pharaoh's motives elsewhere — the fear of a boy who would end his rule, the arrogance of a king who styled himself his people's supreme lord — but this verse presents the torment in its bare form, unmotivated in the telling: power afflicting because it can. The gratuitousness is part of the indictment; a torment with a grievance invites argument, and the verse declines to let Pharaoh have one.

**Balāʾ: The Torment Was Also a Test**

The final sentence reassigns the event: *wa-fī dhālikum balāʾun min rabbikum ʿaẓīm* — and in that lay a trial, immense, from your Lord. The torment, in its full wickedness, is simultaneously filed as *balāʾ* — trial — and the filing is from Allah: *min rabbikum*, from your Lord, using the name of care. The two readings do not cancel: Pharaoh's crime remains wholly Pharaoh's, and the trial remains wholly Allah's — the Qur'an's standing structure for evil, in which the perpetrator acts freely and is judged for it, while the Event enters God's governance as examination. Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ states the principle universally: *"Every soul will taste death. And We test you ˹O humanity˺ with good and evil as a trial, then to Us you will ˹all˺ be returned"* (21:35) — evil is test-material as much as good is, and the test of evil is the hardest form, because it asks faith to survive without evidence of care. The verse thus binds the Exodus to the sūrah's wider theology of trial — the tests of Adam in the garden, of Ibrāhīm at the altar, of the believers at Badr to come — and it quietly arms the reader for the recital's next movements: the manna and the quail will be a test of gratitude, the wilderness commands a test of obedience, and the sea itself a test of trust. Deliverance does not end the examination; it changes its syllabus.

**Why Egypt Comes First in the Recital**

The sequence of the coming verses — rescue, sea, calf, pardon, book, manna, water from rock — is not merely chronological; it is pedagogical. Egypt is filed first because it is the fact that every later failure aggravates. The people who build the calf (verse 51) are people who watched the sea drown an army; the people who demand to see Allah plainly (2:55) are people who were fed without sowing; the people who refuse the city (2:58) are people who were carried out of a furnace. Each breach in the recital is committed by witnesses of verse 49, and the verse's position at the head makes that witness permanent: no failure can be read here without the rescue already on file. The order also teaches the sūrah's readers the anatomy of ingratitude — kufr al-niʿma, covering the favor — by showing its precondition: a favor this complete, received this helplessly, forgotten this fast. The recital is thus structured as a single argument across eighty verses: here is what was given; here is what was done with it; here — in the covenant of verse 40 and the warning of verse 48 — is the frame that makes both matter.

**“You”: The Descendants as Parties**

The verbs are all second-person plural — *We delivered you, they tormented you* — spoken to people centuries after the events, and the grammar is the verse's deepest claim. The Madinan children of Israel are addressed as the direct objects of the Exodus because a community that inherits a covenant inherits its history as its own: the favors flow to the descendants through the same channel as the obligations, and the Qur'an will not let the inheritance be taken one-sided. The collective personhood at work here — the ummah across generations as a single moral subject — is the same structure that lets verse 47's favor and verse 48's audit bind people who never stood at the sea. It also extends beyond Israel by design: al-Baqarah recites the Exodus to Muslims who are not its biological descendants, files it in their scripture, and makes its memory their own — which is why the sūrah addresses *them* with the same "remember." Every reader of verse 49 inherits the ledger: the rescue was for you too, in the only sense the Qur'an finally cares about — that the God who extracted a slaughtered people from Pharaoh's machine is the God your covenant runs through, and the test that began in Egypt has not ended; it has only changed addressees.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:50

> And ˹remember˺ when We parted the sea, rescued you, and drowned Pharaoh's people before your very eyes.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Three Verbs, One Subject**

The verse compresses the Exodus into three first-person plural verbs — *We parted, We rescued you, We drowned* — and keeps a single subject across all three: Allah. The wider recitals name the instruments: the staff, the strike, the inspiration to Moses (26:63); the pursuit, the drowning's timing (10:90). Here the instruments are withheld, and the withholding is theology. The sea did not part because a staff was waved; a staff was waved because the sea had been ordered to part. The Qur'an's habitual grammar of miracle operates at exactly this register — human action fully real, divine agency fully primary — and verse 50 states the primary alone. Note too the structure of the middle verb: *parted the sea* takes no human object in form, but the Arabic carries *bi-kum* — "with you," "through you," "for you" — and the commentators divide between the readings without needing to choose: the sea parted *for your sake*, and it parted *as you entered it*, the miracle completing itself through their walking. A delivered people is not a spectator of its deliverance; the road opened under their feet and closed behind them, and the verse's grammar keeps both facts — Allah's sole doing, their bodily passage — in one clause.

**The Mechanism: A Mountain on Each Side**

The Qur'an's fuller filing of the same event supplies the scene this verse's audience already held: *"So We inspired Moses: 'Strike the sea with your staff,' and the sea was split, each part was like a huge mountain"* (26:63). The simile is the verse's most deliberate stroke — water standing as geology, the fluid made structural, each wall a *ṭawd*, the word for a great mass of mountain. The image accomplishes two things. It fixes the crossing as a passage *between* standing things, not a ford or an ebb-tide: the sea did not recede but rose into architecture, and the road ran through a canyon of held water. And it slows the miracle down to visible duration — walls like mountains do not flash and vanish; they stand long enough for a nation to walk through, and for an army to walk in after. The deliberateness is the point of the whole staging: a fleeing people could have been lifted over the water or hidden from pursuit, but the crossing was arranged at walking pace, in daylight visibility, with both parties on site — a sign engineered for witnesses rather than an escape engineered for survival. Verse 50's summary verb *rescued* rests on that staging; its final verb, *drowned*, completes it in the same corridor.

**Wa-Antum Tanẓurūn: The Clause of Watching**

The verse ends with a circumstantial clause — *wa-antum tanẓurūn*, and you were looking on. The drowning of Pharaoh's people happened in the sight of the delivered: from the far shore, the rescued watched the corridor close on their pursuers. The clause is the recital's recurring instrument of aggravation and honor at once. Aggravation, because a sign witnessed binds harder than a sign reported: the coming failures — the calf above all — will be committed not by people who heard of the sea but by people who stood at its edge and saw an army go into it. Honor, because being made a witness is itself a favor: Allah staged the greatest of the Exodus signs with this community in the front row, and the Qur'an's repeated appeals to sight (*do they not see, do they not look*) treat vision as the highest-bandwidth channel of evidence. The clause also does quiet work on the verse's audience in Madina: their ancestors were eyewitnesses, and the eyewitness generation is the generation the recital will hold most accountable — which converts the honor of descent into the liability of inheritance. A community that claims the witnesses' covenant is answerable at the witnesses' standard.

**The Confession That Arrived Late**

The drowning the verse summarizes is unfolded elsewhere with a detail that belongs to any reading of it: Pharaoh's end was not silent. As the water closed, Sūrah Yūnus records his confession — *"I believe that there is no god except that in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am ˹now˺ one of those submit"* (10:90) — the tyrant adopting, at the last second, the exact formula of the people he had been slaughtering. The Qur'an's answer to the confession is refusal: belief at the sight of punishment, when the test's conditions have collapsed, is no longer faith but recognition — the knowledge compelled by evidence no longer avoidable, worth nothing in the ledger because it costs nothing. And the aftermath is filed as a standing sign: *"Today We will preserve your corpse so that you may become an example for those who come after you. And surely most people are heedless of Our examples!"* (10:92). The body of the drowned king — displayed, preserved, made an *āyah* — is the Exodus's epilogue for later generations: the man whose machine slaughtered sons now a public exhibit of the machine's end. Verse 50's audience watched him go in; the Qur'an's later audiences were told the corpse stayed. Both facts are in the favor: the delivered were shown, with their own eyes, the total and permanent closing of the threat.

**Two Rescues in One Verse**

The rescue of verse 50 is double, and the doubling matters. Extraction alone — a fleeing people across a fordable gap — would have left the threat alive and the pursuit resumable; the deliverance is completed only by the drowning, which ends Pharaoh's people as a power. One instrument performed both: the same water that was a road for the delivered was a grave for the pursuers, and the corridor's two verdicts fell along a single line of division. The structure makes the sea the Qur'an's densest image of divine justice — not justice as balancing but as separating: a people and their tormentors placed in one element, and the element itself sorting them. It also explains why the Exodus functions throughout the Qur'an as the standing promise to the oppressed: the pattern is not escape-with-luck but deliverance-with-completion, in which the mechanism of pursuit becomes the mechanism of the pursuer's end. For the sūrah's first Muslim hearers — a small community newly settled in Madina after an exile of the same shape — verse 50 was not history recited but precedent published: the God who parted the sea before witnesses had already demonstrated, in the fullest public form, how He handles a people cornered at water.

**The Honor and the Liability of the Watching**

Verse 50 closes the first movement of the recital — torment (49), deliverance (50) — and leaves the witnesses standing on the far shore with everything still to be asked of them. The verse's final clause will govern the reading of every entry that follows: a sign seen is a sign owned, and ownership runs in both directions. The generation that watched the sea become mountains received the strongest evidence any community was ever given — and the recital will show what that generation did forty nights later, at the foot of a mountain of a different kind. Nothing in verse 50 excuses them, and nothing in it condemns them yet; the verse simply fixes the epistemic condition under which their whole history will be judged: *you were looking on*. The same clause extends, by the inheritance logic of verse 49's "you," to every reader the recital reaches — the Qur'an puts its audience behind the eyes of the witnesses and holds them to what sight obliges. Between the sea and the audit of verse 48 stands the rest of the recital: favors itemized, breaches itemized, pardons offered — the case file of a people delivered before their very eyes, and of the covenant they carried out of the water.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:51

> And ˹remember˺ when We appointed forty nights for Moses, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Appointment of Forty Nights**

The recital's second entry opens with a divine appointment: *wāʿadnā Mūsā arbaʿīna laylah* — We set a term for Moses of forty nights. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf files the same appointment with its arithmetic exposed: *"We appointed for Moses thirty nights then added another ten— completing his Lord's term of forty nights. Moses commanded his brother Aaron, 'Take my place among my people, do what is right, and do not follow the way of the corruptors'"* (7:142). The term was the miqāt — the tryst at the mountain for the giving of the Torah — and its length carries the Qur'an's numerology of completion: forty is the number at which a thing ripens, the span of formation before reception. The nights are named rather than the days because Arabic reckoning runs by the moon — the night precedes and gives its name to the day — and because the vigil's interior is a night-work: Moses fasting, watching, waiting on revelation. The appointment's structure matters for what follows: a prophet called away for a fixed term, a deputy installed with instructions, and a people left in the interval. Every element of that arrangement becomes material in the crisis the same verse reports, and the verse reports both halves in one breath — the appointment *and* the calf — so the reader holds the gift and the failure together.

**Ittakhadhtum: The Calf Was Taken**

The verb of the sin is *ittakhadhtum* — you took, adopted, took up. The translation renders it *worshipped*, and the rendering is right about the act, but the Arabic keeps the act's grammar of acquisition: idolatry here is not something that happened to the people but something they *took*, the way one takes a position, a tool, or a side. The taking was manufactured. Sūrah Ṭā Hā stages the scene: *"Then he moulded for them an idol of a calf that made a lowing sound. They said, 'This is your god and the god of Moses, but Moses forgot ˹where it was˺!'"* (20:88). The ḥadīth of the Qur'an's telling is in the details — the calf was moulded, not found; it lowed by artifice, a sound engineered into a hollow body; and the proclamation wrapped the new god in the old religion's language, claiming it for Moses himself. The people did not abandon their vocabulary; they re-pointed it. This is the anatomy of the taken idol: it arrives wearing continuity, announced in the idiom of the faith it replaces, and its adoption feels to the adopters like fidelity rather than defection — *Moses forgot*, they said, and thought themselves the better keepers of his god.

**The Sin of the Interval**

The temporal clause is the verse's quiet center: *in his absence* — the calf was taken while Moses was away, inside the forty nights, in the interval between the prophet's departure and his return. The people had everything they needed for the interval: a deputy installed by the prophet himself, explicit instructions against the corruptors' way (7:142), a fixed term — the appointment was announced, not open-ended. The failure was therefore not of information but of duration: a faith that held under the prophet's visible mediation did not hold under his announced absence. The verse exposes the difference between believing in Allah and believing in a prophet's presence — the second collapses at the first miqāt, and the first is what the covenant of verse 40 actually contracted for. The interval is also where the Sāmirī worked: the Qur'an's fuller accounts show him gathering, melting, shaping — craftsmanship performed in public over time. The calf was not a sudden panic but a project, built unhindered across days of the prophet's absence by a people who watched it take shape and said nothing until it lowed.

**Ẓālimīn: The Wrong Landed on the Wrongdoers**

The verse closes its accusation with a circumstantial participle — *acting wrongfully*, *wa-antum ẓālimūn*. Ẓulm is the placement of a thing outside its proper place: the word for injustice, for tyranny, and for the mislocation at the heart of sin. Applied to shirk it is the Qur'an's standing diagnosis — shirk is named the great ẓulm (31:13) precisely because it puts worship where worship does not belong. The participle's form is equally precise: *you* were wrongdoers — the sentence's subject and its wronged party coincide. The calf did not injure Pharaoh's memory, the Egyptians, or the desert; the taking of it injured the takers, severing them from the favor that had just defined them as a delivered people. Sūrah al-Baqarah returns to the same event with the wrongness filed in the heart's own hydraulics: *"Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully"* (2:92) — the charge restated almost word for word later in the sūrah — and then, in the verse after that, the interior mechanism: *the love of the calf was rooted in their hearts because of their disbelief* (2:93), a people made to drink the idol as one drinks water, the calf's love soaking the heart through the disbelief that opened it. The act was public; the ẓulm was capillary.

**The Charge Refiled on the Descendants**

Verse 51 addresses the wilderness generation as *you* — and the sūrah will file the identical charge against the Madinan descendants in the same second person (2:92), which is the inheritance logic of verse 49 operating in the negative direction: the favors flow down the line, and so do the liabilities of the family record. Sūrah al-Nisāʾ states the descendant generation's version of the pattern plainly: the People of the Book who demanded a revelation in writing from heaven are reminded that their forebears demanded greater — make Allah visible to us — and that they *"took the calf for worship after receiving clear signs"* (4:153). The verse's own structure anticipates the refiling: clear proofs precede the taking in every account (the sea still wet behind them, the manna still arriving), which makes the calf not a failure of evidence but a failure of the interval. And the refiling answers the objection every descendant raises about ancestral crime — that no soul bears another's burden — by identifying what actually descends: not guilt but pattern. The same heart-drink is offered in every generation; verse 51 is read by Madinans as a mirror because their own interval — a prophet's absence by death, a community's custody of his deposit — runs the same test in slower time.

**What the Interval Tests**

The forty nights are therefore a fixture of the Qur'an's moral pedagogy, and verse 51 installs it: the interval tests what the presence cannot. Under a prophet's eye, obedience and awe are indistinguishable; under his announced absence, only what was actually faith remains standing. The verse pairs with verse 45's method clause — patience and prayer are exactly the equipment of intervals, the disciplines that hold a person on the line when the line's author is not visibly walking it — and the calf is what patience and prayer were not called in to prevent. The Qur'an's communities after this one live wholly inside such an interval: the final Prophet ﷺ has died, the miqāt of history runs on, and the lowing shapes are moulded in public by craftsmen who claim continuity with him. Verse 51's value to that condition is diagnostic before it is hortatory: it tells the waiting community where the failure will present — not in the open denial of verse 41, not in the sale of verse 41's signs, but in the taken thing, adopted during the wait, dressed in the vocabulary of the faith, and loved before the prophet returns. The audit of verse 48 hangs over the interval; the pardon of the sūrah's next movement meets it — and between the two stands this verse, the interval's own case law.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:52

> Even then We ˹still˺ forgave you so perhaps you would be grateful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Pardon Files Itself After the Fall**

Two verses after the calf, the recital records its discharge: *thumma ʿafawnā ʿankum min baʿdi dhālika* — then We pardoned you after that. The Arabic keeps the temporal marker the English compresses: *min baʿdi dhālika*, after that — after the taking, after the wrong, after everything verse 51 filed. The pardon is not announced before the sin as a blanket guarantee, which would make obedience optional; it follows the sin as its actual answer, and the sequence carries the sūrah's whole economy of mercy: the breach is real, the record is real, and the pardon arrives into a completed case rather than an anticipated one. The narrative's chronology folds — the repentance demanded of the people and its cost are recorded two verses further on — but the verse's logic does not depend on the fold: what is stated here is the divine side's movement, and it is stated as fact accomplished. *ʿAfanā ʿankum*: We pardoned you, with the preposition *ʿan* doing its lexical work — pardoning *away from* you, the fault removed from the pardoned party's person rather than merely suspended over it. The recital's first crisis closes, in other words, not with a punishment balanced against a crime but with a deletion — and the deletion has a purpose clause, which is the verse's second half and its real subject.

**ʿAfw: The Strongest Word for Forgiveness**

Arabic distributes forgiveness across a family of terms, and the verse's choice is the family's most radical member. *Maghfira* is covering — the fault concealed and protected from consequence, the root's image of a helmet or shield; *tawbah* is return — the human turning met by the divine turning, the Accepter of Repentance receiving what the repentant brings; *ʿafw* is effacement — the trace obliterated, the ground wiped clean, the word used elsewhere in Arabic of wind smoothing sand until the footprint is gone. To be granted *maghfira* is to be sheltered from what one did; to be granted *ʿafw* is to have what one did deleted from the ledger's face. The Qur'an reserves this strongest deletion for exactly this kind of case — the calf, whose enormity the recital has just measured in the starkest terms it has — and Sūrah al-Nisāʾ confirms the scope when it refiles the event: they took the calf after the clear signs, *"Still We forgave them for that ˹after their repentance˺ and gave Moses compelling proof"* (4:153). The pardon after the greatest of the wilderness sins thus becomes the recital's precedent-law: if ʿafw reached the calf, no fault of the interval sits outside its range. The verse is the sūrah's answer, filed before the question is asked, to every reader who assumes their own case is the exception.

**Li-ʿallakum: The Particle of Purpose**

The pardon's second half is a purpose clause: *li-ʿallakum tashkurūn* — so perhaps you would be grateful, that you may prove grateful. The particle *laʿalla* runs through the Qur'an's legislation and recital as the marker of divine intent toward human transformation: laws given *laʿallakum tattaqūn*, that you may become god-fearing; signs shown *laʿallakum taʿqilūn*, that you may reason; the next gift of the recital given *laʿallakum tahtadūn*, that you may be guided. The particle carries hope and purpose at once — the grammarians debate its exact force in divine speech, and the settled reading takes it as stating the end for which the act is done, from the position of the recipients for whom the end is hoped rather than guaranteed. Its presence here is theologically precise: the pardon does not *produce* gratitude by fiat, because gratitude is a free act that cannot be caused; the pardon *opens the room* in which gratitude becomes possible. A people crushed by an unpardoned calf could not thank — the weight of the debt would occupy the whole of worship. The deletion of verse 52 clears the ledger so the cleared people can do the one thing the ledger was for: acknowledge the Giver. Every *laʿalla* in the recital works this way — divine acts as the preconditions of human responses the acts do not compel.

**Shukr: Where the Pardon Was Headed**

The destination named is *shukr* — gratitude, the word the classical lexicographers define as the imagining of the favor and the showing of it: gratitude that perceives the gift accurately and then deploys it in the direction the Giver set. The definition matters here because the calf was, in this exact sense, failed shukr. A delivered people — verse 49's rescue, verse 50's sea — answered the favor by taking a manufactured god, which is the favor's deployment in the direction the favor came against. Ingratitude in the Qur'an is not rudeness but misdirection: *kufr al-niʿma*, covering the favor, spending the gift against the Giver's purpose. The pardon of verse 52 therefore restores more than standing; it restores capacity. The pardoned are re-tasked with the same vocation the calf interrupted — to be a people whose existence runs as acknowledgment — and the verse states the re-tasking as the pardon's own end. Gratitude is thus not the emotional afterglow of forgiveness but its structural purpose: the reason the deletion happened is that a deleted ledger can be written on again, and what is wanted on it is a people who use deliverance, sea, interval, and pardon itself as material for thanks. The sūrah will test the restored capacity immediately and often — provision after provision in the wilderness, each with its own accounting — because shukr restored is shukr to be exercised.

**A Recital Built on Renewals**

Verse 52 is the first instance of the pattern that will shape every subsequent movement of the wilderness recital: demand or favor, failure, consequence, pardon, purpose clause. The people will quarrel and be provisioned, refuse a city and be given a way back, thirst at the rock and be given twelve springs — and at each turn the divine side's response closes with *laʿalla*, the next capacity to be formed. The pattern's cumulative argument is about the covenant itself: a bond that survived the calf did not merely tolerate small defaults, and the recital's repetitions are the sūrah's demonstration that verse 40's *I will fulfil Mine* is operational history, not rhetoric. This is also why the recital can be severe without being despairing — its accusations land inside a structure whose fixed point is renewal. The reader of verse 52 is being taught how to read the next seventy verses: every failure about to be filed has already been filed once, at the calf, and the calf's case closed with ʿafw. The severity of the coming audit (verse 48's Day stands over all of it) and the recurrence of the pardon are not competing messages but the two terms of a single covenant — binding because breach is real, standing because pardon is real.

**The Only Exit Left Standing**

Four verses earlier the sūrah sealed the Day's four exits: no availing soul, no accepted intercession, no taken ransom, no given help (2:48). Verse 52 shows what remains when the exits are shut — and what remains is not an exit at all but an arrival: pardon initiated from Allah's own side, unrequested by price, unmediated by patron, untransferred by proxy. The two verses together state the Qur'an's complete economy of salvation. Nothing can be *paid* — the ransom of a world of gold is refused (3:91); nothing can be *arranged* — intercession exists only as permission (2:255); but everything can be *given*, and the giving is ʿafw, the strongest deletion the language has. The difference between the refused ransom and the granted pardon is the difference between transaction and mercy: the first treats fault as debt, which misprices it, and the second treats the sinner as a person to be restored, which is what the fault actually damaged. Gratitude is then the only possible return — not payment but acknowledgment, the receipt a gift can accept. For the verse's first addressees, weighing in Madina whether a lifetime of ancestral standing could be traded for a new confession, verse 52 published the terms of every divine dealing on record: the calf pardoned, the ledger wiped, the purpose stated. Whatever else the covenant demanded, its pardon-side had already been demonstrated at maximum difficulty — and demonstrated, like everything else in the recital, before their very eyes.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:53

> And ˹remember˺ when We gave Moses the Scripture—the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺ that perhaps you would be ˹rightly˺ guided.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Nouns, One Gift**

The verse records the recital's central donation: *wa-idh ātaynā Mūsa al-kitāba wa-l-furqān* — and when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion. The two nouns stand joined by *wa*, and the exegetes have read the join three ways, each with its support. The first reading takes them as one gift under two names — the Book, which is the Criterion, the Torah itself functioning as the divider between truth and falsehood; the translation's appositive rendering ("the Scripture—the standard") follows this reading. The second takes them as two gifts: the Book, and separately the furqān understood as the concrete acts of separation that accompanied it — the parting of the sea, the rescue, the distinctions performed before witnesses, the deliverance as the Credential of the Law. The third reads furqān as the clear proofs and the victory, the evidences by which the Book was authenticated. The three readings converge on a single claim whichever way the grammar falls: the giving at Sinai was not the delivery of text alone. A book arrives with its divider — the power to separate — and a divider arrives with its book — the standard by which the separations are made. What Moses brought down from the forty nights was, in every reading, a machine for telling things apart.

**Furqān: The Word That Divides**

The noun comes from *f-r-q*, to split, part, separate — the same root as the recital's own verb two verses back: *We parted the sea*, *faraqnā*. The word-family connection is the Qur'an's theology of revelation in miniature. The sea was split with water; the furqān splits with meaning — a criterion that divides truth from falsehood, lawful from unlawful, the clean case from the corrupt, the way from the wandering. Arabic names the divider by its action: something is *furqān* not because of its material but because of what it does to a confused situation — it makes two things out of one muddle. The Qur'an generalizes the term accordingly. Sūrah 25 takes its title from the opening declaration that the Furqān was sent down to the servant — the Qur'an naming itself by the function this verse assigned to the Torah. The day of Badr is named in Sūrah al-Anfāl as the day of discrimination, *yawm al-furqān* (8:41) — the battle where the community's case was separated from its enemies'. And ʿUmar's honorific al-Fārūq — the one who divides — descends from the same root's moral sense. Across all these filings the word keeps its Sinai meaning: the gift that makes distinctions is the gift that makes a people, because a community is exactly a body that can tell its cases apart. The people of verse 51 — who could not, for forty nights, distinguish a lowing idol from the God of the sea — are the diagnostic case for why the furqān came.

**The Same Gift Filed for Two Brothers**

Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ records the donation with Aaron joined to the address: Moses and Aaron were given the Criterion, the light, and the reminder — the same threefold gift expanded (21:48). The joining matters for this verse's argument. The furqān was given to a *prophetic pair*, which is to say to a community's leadership as an instrument of government — the criterion is what deputies hold when the principal is at the mountain. Verse 51's crisis was precisely a failure of held distinction in the deputy's interval: the people had the deputy but not yet the book, and the calf's lowing divided nothing. The giving of verse 53 answers that gap in the recital's economy — after the interval's failure and its pardon, the permanent divider is installed, so the next absence will be met not by a man alone but by a standard the man and the people hold jointly. The al-Anbiyāʾ filing adds the gift's third name, the *dhikr* — the reminder — and the addition completes the machine: a criterion divides cases, a light shows them, a reminder keeps both from being forgotten between applications. The Torah at Sinai is thus described with the same triple vocabulary the Qur'an will use of itself, and the description is the sūrah's quiet claim of continuity: what Madina's scholars carry and what Madina's Prophet ﷺ recites are filings of one gift.

**The Purpose Clause: For Guidance**

The verse ends with the recital's standing particle: *laʿallakum tahtadūn* — that perhaps you would be guided. The purpose clause does three pieces of work. It states the gift's end: the Book and Criterion exist for guidance, not for possession — a furqān held and not applied has missed its purpose clause as surely as a favor held and not acknowledged missed verse 52's. It universalizes the addressee: the plural *you* covers the wilderness generation and every inheritor of the gift, which is why the sūrah can file the same donation to the descendants directly (2:87) and why al-Baqarah's own opening describes itself by the identical function — a book, no doubt in it, guidance for the God-conscious (2:2). And it subordinates the gift to the sūrah's running argument with the scholars: guidance is the Book's purpose, and verses 41–42 charged exactly the men whose profession was that purpose — selling its signs, mixing its truth, concealing what they read. A criterion in the hands of concealers produces the precise inversion the recital documents: the machine for telling things apart operated to tell them apart wrongly, distinctions manufactured rather than found. The purpose clause is the verse's built-in audit of every subsequent holder, and it is filed here, at the giving, so that no later custodian can claim the function was added by critics.

**The Book After the Pardon**

The verse's placement in the recital is itself an argument. The order runs: rescue (49–50), failure (51), pardon (52), gift (53). The Torah is given *after* the calf and *after* the ʿafw — the law arrives to a pardoned people, not to a clean one. The sequence forecloses two readings of revelation at once. Against legalism: the Book is not the condition of the pardon but its consequence — mercy came first, unearned, deleting the greatest sin on record, and the standard was installed in the cleared space. Against antinomianism: the pardon was not the end of the matter either — the pardoned were immediately handed the divider, because a wiped ledger that receives no standard will be written on again by whatever calves are moulded next. Law-after-mercy is the Qur'an's whole ordering of the covenant, and it is also the ordering of this sūrah's own legislation: al-Baqarah will spend two hundred verses detailing command and prohibition to a community already assured, at its head, that the guidance is mercy (2:64's renewals, 2:160's openings, 2:173's necessities). Verse 53 files the principle in history before the sūrah applies it in law: the standard is given to forgiven people precisely because forgiven people are the only ones who can hold a standard without either worshipping it or selling it.

**The Furqān's Last Filing**

The gift of verse 53 is the recital's pivot from memory to institution. Everything before it happened *to* the people — delivered, rescued, pardoned; the furqān is what is placed *in* their hands, and the recital's remaining movements will test the hand: the quarrels over commanded things, the refusals at the city's gate, the thirst at the rock, and finally the great charge of the following verses — the killing of prophets and the selling of signs, which are crimes of the divider's custodians, possible only where a furqān is held. The verse therefore reads forward as the enabling fact of every later accusation and backward as the answer to verse 51: the interval's failure was met with a permanent instrument, the absence's crisis with a present standard. And the instrument's history does not end in this sūrah or this community. The Qur'an's self-naming as Furqān, the Prophet's ﷺ title for the revelation he received, the sūrah's placement of this gift in its covenant unit — all file the last installment of one donation: the divider given at Sinai, renewed in every prophet's hand, and recited now in Arabic to a new custodian community whose whole commission, in verse 43's row of bowers and 3:110's charge, is to hold it and apply it. Verse 53 is where the recital hands the reader the tool the recital itself was made with — and the audit it installs runs on every holder until the Day of verse 48, when the divisions made with it are read back, case by case, before the eyes that watched.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:54

> And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “O my people! Surely you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf, so turn in repentance to your Creator and execute ˹the calf-worshippers among˺ yourselves. That is best for you in the sight of your Creator.” Then He accepted your repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Repentance With a Price Attached**

The verse files the calf's settlement, and the settlement is not a word. Moses addresses his people with the diagnosis first — you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf — and then commands a repentance with two movements: turn to your Maker, and execute among yourselves. The first movement is the interior return the word *tawbah* always names; the second is its public cost, a death-penalty carried out inside the community on the guilty. The pairing states the verse's whole theology of atonement: a sin of this size — shirk committed after the sea, under the mountain's shadow — is not dissolved by sentiment. The turn must be real, and its reality is measured by what the turners are willing to do. The sūrah's earlier filings had already shown the divine side moving fast: pardon filed at verse 52, the Book given at verse 53. Here the human side's movement appears, and it is the hardest thing the recital asks of anyone: a community asked to run the sword through its own calf-takers. The verse does not soften the command and does not explain it away; it reports the command, reports the acceptance, and ends on the two names that make both possible.

**“Execute Yourselves”: Whom the Swords Actually Found**

The literal phrase is *fa-q-tulū anfusakum* — kill yourselves — and the exegetes divide on who died and by whose hand. The dominant reading, and the strongest, is that the innocent executed the guilty: the calf-worshippers were killed by their own kinsmen and neighbors, which made the punishment more terrible than any external execution, since every stroke fell inside the camp and inside the family. The biblical account runs the same shape — Moses at the gate calling for whoever is for the Lord, and the sons of Levi taking swords against their brothers and companions (Exodus 32:27) — and the Qur'an's phrasing, read with 2:85's later charge that this community kills its own and expels its own, fits the same event. A second reading softens the distribution: the killed were martyrs, and the killers had their repentance accepted through the killing, so that all were forgiven and the episode functioned as collective purification rather than the innocent punishing the guilty. A third, esoteric reading takes the killing inward: slay your own egos, the command's real object being the passions that built the calf. The first reading carries the plain sense and the historical parallel; the third is devotion, not exegesis — it preaches the verse rather than reading it.

**Why the Verse Says Maker, Twice**

The address names Allah twice as *Bāriʾ* — your Maker, your Creator — and the repetition is the verse's chosen instrument. *Baraʾa* is creation in its fashioning sense: the making of a thing whole, sound, fitted — the same name that stands in the divine triad of Sūrah al-Ḥashr, the Creator, the Maker, the Fashioner (59:24). Against a community that had just manufactured a god with its own hands, the name does precise work. The calf was made; the Maker of the camp was not made. The verse insists on the distinction by putting the unmade Fashioner's name in both hinges of the sentence — turn in repentance *to your Maker*; that is best *in the sight of your Maker* — so the whole settlement runs between the people and the One who fashioned them, with the fashioned thing excluded from the grammar entirely. There is also a claim of jurisdiction in the name: the One who fashioned the body has standing over the body, including its death. A command to execute is bearable only from the Fashioner; from anyone else it would be murder. The name chosen twice is the name that makes the verse's severity lawful and its acceptance credible.

**The Better Thing in the Maker's Sight**

Between the command and the acceptance stands a valuation: *that is best for you in the sight of your Maker*. The demonstrative covers the whole package — repentance plus execution — and calls it *khayr*, better, the same comparative the Qur'an uses for the eternal against the temporal, for prayer against trade. The verse thereby inverts the obvious arithmetic. To the living, the killing of kin is the worst available outcome; in the Maker's sight, for this people at this moment, it was the best — best because it was the only route back, and because the alternative was not acquittal but the settled citizenship of verse 39. The valuation also answers a standing objection to costly repentance: that it is God demanding suffering for its own sake. The verse says the opposite — the suffering is instrumentally *best*, valued not in itself but as the road, and the road ends in acceptance within the same breath. Divine severity here is bounded by divine purpose on both sides: the command is severe because the sin was total, and the acceptance is immediate because the purpose was restoration, not payment. The sūrah's economy of verse 48 holds — no ransom is taken — but repentance is not ransom; it is the return the covenant always priced in.

**Tawwāb: The Name That Keeps Accepting**

The acceptance clause carries the sūrah's signature pair: *He accepted your repentance; surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful* — Tawwāb, Raḥīm. *Tawwāb* is the intensive form: not one who accepts once but one who accepts repeatedly, whose accepting is a settled attribute rather than an occasional act — and the word's double direction matters, since tawbah in Arabic runs both ways: the servant turns, and Allah turns back toward the servant. The pair appeared earlier in the sūrah at the first great fall: Adam received words from his Lord, and the same sentence closed his case — *"Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord, so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful"* (2:37). The identical names thus bracket the two founding repentances of the recital — the species' first and Israel's greatest — which is the sūrah telling its readers that the calf sits inside the human story rather than outside it. What Adam did at the tree and what Israel did at the calf are the same motion, and the same two names receive both. No sin in the recital is filed as unprecedented, and none as unforgivable while the pair is on the record.

**A Case File Still Addressed to You**

The verse is framed inside the second-person address that runs from verse 40: Moses speaks to *his people*, but the sūrah files the speech as *your* history — the Madinan descendants inherit the scene the way they inherited the sea and the manna. The inheritance is not guilt transferred across generations, which the Qur'an's own principle of burdens would forbid, but membership: a community that claims the covenant claims the case file, and the case file's first entry on repentance is this one. For that community in Madina, the verse also carried a pointed relevance — scholars who knew a prophet's description and had not yet confessed it were, in the sūrah's argument, standing at the same fork: a diagnosed wrong, a commanded return, and a valuation that called the costly road *best*. The verse's closing names are the ones every reader carries out of it. The Accepter of Repentance is not a name reserved for the wilderness generation; it is the standing title of the One who took this confession — the most expensive confession in the recital — and answered it with acceptance before the verse ended.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:55

> And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses! We will never believe you until we see Allah with our own eyes,” so a thunderbolt struck you while you were looking on.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Faith Offered a Condition**

The verse records a sentence with a structure worth holding still: *we will never believe you until we see Allah with our own eyes*. This is not a request for evidence — the speakers had the sea, the manna, the mountain — but a condition attached to faith itself, a demand that belief suspend until the unseen becomes visible. The grammar is emphatic at every joint: *lan*, the particle of never; *ḥattā*, until; and the object not a sign but Allah. The sūrah's opening had defined the God-conscious as believers *in the unseen* (2:3); this sentence is that definition refused. And the refusal targets Moses in his office: *we will never believe you* — not "we doubt this sign" but "your word, as such, is not creditable until our terms are met." The verse thus names a posture the Qur'an returns to constantly — faith negotiated from the position of the skeptic, with the terms set by the skeptic — and answers it not with argument but with event. The negotiation collapses in the same verse that reports it: the condition was seeing, and what arrived instead was a stroke that ended sight's bargaining.

**Jahratan: The Demand to See Openly**

The demand's manner-word is *jahratan* — openly, plainly, manifestly. The same word qualifies speech elsewhere in the Qur'an, describing what is said aloud rather than in secret, and applied to seeing it carries both senses the commentators draw out: seeing with the eye in plain sight, and seeing publicly — a theophany witnessed, undisputed, available to the whole camp. Either sense convicts the demand. If *jahratan* means with our own eyes, the speakers are asking the invisible to submit to the organ of a creature — sight, the faculty that grasps surfaces and finite things, set as judge over the One whom, as the Qur'an states, vision does not grasp while He grasps all vision (6:103). If it means publicly, they are asking God to perform — to appear on demand, before an audience, on their schedule — which converts the Lord of the covenant into a supplier of spectacles. The two readings share one root fault: the demand reverses the direction of disclosure. In the covenant, Allah shows what He wills, when He wills, through signs He chooses; *jahratan* asks that choice to be handed over. The thunderbolt's arrival inside the same sentence is the answer to a demand framed as ultimatum.

**Ṣāʿiqah: A Word Wider Than Lightning**

The instrument is *ṣāʿiqah* — rendered thunderbolt, but the word's range in Arabic and in Qur'anic usage is wider: a stroke of destruction, a deafening cry, fire from the sky, an earthquake's shock, a swoon-inducing blast. The Qur'an sends it upon ʿĀd and Thamūd as the punishment that overtook them (41:13, 51:44), and it names with the same root the collapse of Moses at the mountain — when his Lord manifested to the mountain and levelled it to dust, *"Moses collapsed unconscious"* (7:143), *ṣaʿiqa*, struck down by what the mountain could not stand. The same root describes creation's swoon at the Trumpet on the Day of Judgment (39:68). The breadth matters for reading this verse: the *ṣāʿiqah* here is whatever it needs to be — fire, blast, shock — to accomplish one stated effect, the death of the speakers, reported flatly in the next verse's premise. The word choice also ties the scene to its own precedent. Moses asked to see, and the seeing was refused with a mountain's demolition and his own unconsciousness (7:143); the people here demand to see, and the demand is answered with the same family of stroke. One prophet asked once, in private, and was answered with a lesson and a repentance; a community demanded as ultimatum, and the answer arrived without the lesson's softening.

**Seventy Men, or a Separate Scene**

The exegetes divide on whether this verse and the scene in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf are one event. Al-Aʿrāf reports that *"Moses chose seventy men from among his people for Our appointment and, when they were seized by an earthquake, he cried"* — and there pleads for them, attributing the seizure to the foolish among them and asking pardon (7:155). One side identifies the two: after the calf's destruction, Moses took seventy of the choicest — including calf-worshippers seeking reconciliation — and their demand to see Allah drew the stroke of this verse. The other side keeps them separate, noting that al-Aʿrāf's instrument is *rajfah*, an earthquake-shock, while this verse's is *ṣāʿiqah*, and that the contexts differ: seventy chosen men at an appointment, against a communal demand filed to Moses in the camp. The identification reading has to explain the word-difference; the separation reading has to accept two stroke-scenes in one wilderness. Neither is decisive, and the Qur'an's habit of filing one event twice with varied detail — the sea, the mountain, the manna all appear in multiple sūrahs with different instruments named — makes identification entirely plausible. What both readings agree on is the event's substance: a demand to see, a stroke from the unseen, witnesses present. The identification question changes the cast list, not the case.

**Struck While Watching**

The verse's final clause — *while you were looking on* — is the same circumstantial phrase that closed the sea's drowning at verse 50, and its reuse is exact in function. There, a people watched their pursuers drown; here, the demanders watched each other fall. The clause removes every buffer between the sign and its witnesses: the stroke did not happen in the distance, in the dark, or to a generation that could be mythologized later — it landed inside the field of vision of the people it is now being recited to. The Qur'an's epistemology of signs treats sight as the highest-bandwidth evidence and charges accordingly: what is seen binds absolutely, and a community struck down *while watching* has no epistemic escape left. The clause also does a quiet work of self-implication. The speakers said *until we see* — and they saw. They saw the thing they demanded the impossible version of: not Allah disclosed, but Allah's judgment disclosed, visibly, immediately, at the moment of the ultimatum. The demand for sight was answered with sight, and the sight was of the demand's own consequence.

**Why the Sight Was Refused**

The refusal behind the stroke is doctrine, and the Qur'an states it in the scene this verse echoes. Moses asked — reverently, once, as a prophet at the appointed meeting: *My Lord! Reveal Yourself to me so I may see You* — and the answer was a demonstration: *"You cannot see Me! But look at the mountain. If it remains firm in its place, only then will you see Me"* (7:143). The mountain, levelled to dust by a manifestation it could not bear, published the reason: creaturely substance does not survive direct disclosure in this life, and the demand of verse 55 was therefore a demand for the impossible dressed as a condition for faith. The sūrah itself files the same impossibility as eschatology: *"Are they waiting for Allah ˹Himself˺ to come to them in the shade of clouds, along with the angels? ˹If He did˺, then the matter would be settled ˹at once˺"* (2:210) — full disclosure ends the test, and the test is the point of the descent. Sūrah al-Nisāʾ confirms the verdict on this very demand: the people who asked for a book from heaven had asked greater of Moses — make Allah visible to us — and the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing (4:153). The stroke of verse 55 is thus not anger interrupting negotiation but the covenant's boundary marked in the only medium an ultimatum understands: the unseen staying unseen, visibly.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:56

> Then We brought you back to life after your death, so that perhaps you would be grateful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Resurrection Filed in History**

Eleven words in the translation carry an event the Qur'an nowhere softens: after the stroke, the struck were raised. *Thumma baʿathnākum min baʿdi mawtikum* — then We brought you back to life after your death. The death is stated as death, not swoon or near-death; the raising is stated as Allah's act in the first person, with no instrument, no prophet's prayer narrated, no mechanism supplied. The verse is one of the small number of places where resurrection — the raising of the dead to life — happens inside history, to a named community, as a reported event rather than a promised one. Its position in the recital gives it argumentative weight: it follows immediately the demand to see Allah and the stroke that answered it, so the sequence reads as demand, judgment, reversal — the same community that tried to force disclosure receives the disclosure's most extreme form instead: not the sight of Allah but the experience of death and its undoing. The verse states the reversal flatly because its flatness is the point. A resurrection that required elaboration would be a story; a resurrection filed in one clause, between a stroke and a purpose, is a precedent.

**Baʿatha: The Verb That Raises and Sends**

The verb *baʿatha* does double duty in Arabic, and the double duty generated a minority reading of this verse. The root means to rouse, to raise up, to set in motion — and in Qur'anic usage it carries both the raising of the dead and the sending of prophets: Allah *baʿatha* messengers among peoples (2:213 among many), and Allah *baʿatha* the dead at the Last Day. One reading takes this verse accordingly: the raising after the stroke was the sending of prophets among the Israelites — their revival understood as institutional, the community resuscitated through renewed guidance rather than resuscitated in its bodies. The majority reading takes the plain sense: bodily resurrection, because the verse's own premise is a literal death (*after your death*) and a literal stroke, and because the Arabic idiom of the resurrection from the grave uses this same verb. The minority reading has one thing in its favor — the word's documented range, familiar to Muslims from the celebration of the Prophet's ﷺ commissioning, ʿĪd al-Mabʿath, named from this root. But it has to read *your death* metaphorically to work, and the previous verse supplies no metaphor: the thunderbolt struck, and the people watched. The plain reading is stronger, and it is the one the recital's logic requires.

**The Proof of the Last Day, Demonstrated Early**

The verse's resurrection is doing eschatological work in a historical file, and the sūrah states the connection itself. Its opening argument for the Last Day runs on exactly this grammar: *"You were lifeless and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die and again bring you to life, and then to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned"* (2:28). The four-step sequence — lifelessness, life, death, life again — is the sūrah's proof that return is not novel for Allah but habitual: the God who ran the sequence once on a species runs it again on a community at the sea's edge, and will run it finally on everyone. Verse 56 is thus the middle filing of the sūrah's resurrection argument: 2:28 states the rule, 2:56 shows the rule executed on witnesses, and the rule's final execution is the Day of verse 48. For the recital's addressees the demonstration has an edge — a community that demanded to *see* Allah received instead the one sight that proves the unseen's power over their own bodies: death reversed on themselves. The demand of verse 55 failed; the evidence that actually arrived was stronger than what was demanded, because it was lived rather than viewed.

**Gratitude as the Purpose of Return**

The purpose clause — *so that perhaps you would be grateful* — is the recital's second filing of the same formula: verse 52's pardon ended with *so perhaps you would be grateful*, and verse 53's gift of the Scripture will end with its own *laʿalla*, that perhaps you would be guided. The particle states the divine intent behind the act without guaranteeing its landing: the raising makes gratitude possible, not automatic. The clause also identifies what resurrection is *for* in this recital. The raised are not raised as trophies of power — the verse does not end with "so that you would know that I am able," though the knowledge is implied — but as debtors restored to the capacity of thanks. A dead man cannot be grateful; a forgiven calf-taker cannot serve; a struck-down community cannot keep a covenant. Every reversal in the recital reopens the same closed circuit between gift and acknowledgment, and gratitude is the circuit's name. The verse thereby binds the resurrection to the sūrah's economy of verse 47: favors are remembered or lost, and the greatest favor — life returned from death — is filed here with its purpose attached, so that no later reader can receive the story as spectacle without receiving its claim.

**A People Who Have Seen Their Own Death**

The recital's coming accusations all acquire their weight from this verse. The community addressed in the second person — *We brought you back* — is a community whose members died and returned, and whose descendants inherit the file. Whatever this people later does in the wilderness, it does as people who have been on the far side of death and came back with the covenant still standing: a position no other nation in the Qur'an occupies. The severity of the recital's later charges — refusing the city, trading the manna for onions, breaking the Sabbath — is calibrated against this fact, and the verse is why the charges stick. But the same fact runs in the other direction as comfort, and the Qur'an intends both. A people raised after a stroke are a people whose worst moment was reversed: the demand that deserved permanence received instead a second life, which publishes the sūrah's standing rule that Allah's dealing with covenant-breakers runs through reversal before it runs through ruin. For the individual reader the verse installs the same logic: the death of a soul — in sin, in despair, in the stroke of its own demands — is not outside the range of the verb *baʿatha*. The One who filed this resurrection has the form on record.

**Reversal Is Allah's Standing Method**

Verse 56 does not stand alone in the Qur'an, and its companions fix its genre. Later in this same sūrah, a man passing a ruined city asks how Allah could bring it back to life, and is answered by being killed for a century and raised — *"So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years then brought him back to life"* (2:259) — with his food unfresh and his donkey's bones reclothed in flesh as the evidence laid out around him. Abraham asks to be shown how the dead are given life, and is walked through four birds scattered on hilltops and called back in haste (2:260). ʿĪsā is given the raising of the dead as a sign of his mission, *by Allah's Will* (3:49). The pattern across the filings is constant: reversal is demonstrated to a questioner, a passerby, a prophet, a community — always to witnesses, always with the same verb-family, always as proof of the general rule rather than as exception to it. Verse 56 is the filing addressed to a whole people at once. Its placement here — before the manna, before the city, before the rock — makes reversal the foundation of the wilderness narrative: everything the recital gives this community afterward is given to people who have already been dead and returned, which is the sūrah's way of saying that every favor in the file arrives on top of the first one.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:57

> And ˹remember˺ when We shaded you with clouds and sent down to you manna and quails, ˹saying˺, “Eat from the good things We have provided for you.” The evildoers ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Provision That Nobody Produced**

The verse files the wilderness economy in its purest form: shade from above, food from above, and between them a people that farms nothing. No sowing precedes the manna, no herding precedes the quails, no labor stands anywhere in the sentence — the verbs are all divine (*We shaded, We sent down*), and the only human verb is the one commanded: *eat*. The desert is the setting the Qur'an chooses deliberately, because it is the one habitat where provision cannot be mistaken for production: no rain-cycles, no soil, no stored harvest to credit. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf files the same provision with the same grammar — *"We shaded them with clouds and sent down to them manna and quails, ˹saying˺, 'Eat from the good things We have provided for you'"* (7:160) — and both filings attach the same concluding principle. The structure makes this the recital's clearest case of unconditioned niʿma: the people had just died and been raised (verse 56), had not yet been asked for anything, and the provision arrived before any demand. The verse's placement in the sequence — after resurrection, before the city's test — puts pure gift at the center of the wilderness years, so that every failure around it is measured against a baseline that cost the recipients nothing.

**Ghamām: The Cloud That Shelters and Splits**

The shade is *ghamām* — a word the Qur'an reserves for clouds with theological careers. This is the cloud-cover under which Allah will appear at the end of the age: the sūrah itself asks whether the deniers are waiting for Allah to come *in the shade of clouds, along with the angels*, at which point the matter is settled (2:210). It is the cloud into which the sky splits on the Day the angels descend (25:25). The same noun shading a camp in the desert and framing the final theophany is not accidental vocabulary: *ghamām* is Allah's chosen medium of presence-with-veil — near enough to shelter, opaque enough to protect. For a people who had demanded to see Allah plainly and been struck for it (verse 55), the arrival of the shading cloud is a second answer to the same demand: you asked for unveiled sight and received stroke; here is the unveiled impossible thing given in its bearable form — His provision covering you as a roof, His presence near you as shade. The wilderness tradition of a cloud leading and covering the camp thus enters the Qur'an as doctrine rather than logistics: the ghamām is the mercy-version of the manifestation the demanders asked for.

**What Manna Was, and What the Qur'an Declines to Say**

The Qur'an never describes the manna. It names it, sends it, and pairs it — always with quails, in every filing, in both sūrahs — and declines to say what it was. The exegetes fill the silence with reports of varying confidence: a honey-like substance, a delicate bread falling like snow, an exudate of the tamarisk, even something of the ginger family; the biblical account of bread from heaven, gathered daily and described as wafer-like with honey's taste, runs alongside these identifications. The Qur'an's silence is the more instructive datum. A provision whose nature is undescribed cannot be naturalized: every attempt to fix the manna as this or that known food converts a sign into a commodity, and the text refuses the conversion by refusing the description. What is stated is its direction — *sent down*, from above — and its function — the good things, *ṭayyibāt*, wholesome and lawful. The pairing with quails completes the diet's grammar: bread from the sky and birds delivered into the camp, staple and protein both arriving without hunt or harvest. The reports of identification are the tradition's curiosity; the verse's own claim is simpler and harder — for a generation, the food supply of an entire nation fell out of the sky.

**Eat: The Command Against Prohibition**

The speech inside the verse is an imperative with a strange object: *eat from the good things We have provided for you*. Strange because eating requires no command — hunger commands it — and because the Qur'an elsewhere has to argue against the opposite impulse: *Who has forbidden the adornments and lawful provisions Allah has brought forth for His servants?* (7:32). The command to eat the ṭayyibāt is a standing ruling against religious self-starvation, and the sūrah's addressees knew both failure modes the ruling targets: communities that forbid their own lawful foods in the name of piety (4:160 will file the prohibition as punishment-shaped-law), and communities that receive provision without receiving it as provision. The word *ṭayyibāt* carries the whole ethic: the good, the wholesome, the clean, the lawful — one Arabic term doing the work of four English ones, naming food that is simultaneously sound in substance and sound in permission. To be commanded to eat the ṭayyibāt is to be told that the good thing given is to be enjoyed, not merely consumed, and not ascetically refused. The verse's manna is therefore doctrine as much as diet: grace arrives as good things, and the correct response to good things is to eat them gratefully, which is the only command the speech contains.

**The Wrong That Lands on the Wrongdoer**

The verse closes with the principle the whole recital runs on: *the evildoers did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves*. The sentence is the mirror of verse 54's diagnosis — you wronged yourselves by taking the calf — and of the wider Qur'anic rule that Allah is beyond the reach of harm, so every sin's damage settles in the sinner's own account. The grammar of the clause is worth its precision: the wronging verb appears twice, once with Us as object and once with themselves, and the first is negated to establish the second. No sin diminishes Allah; no ingratitude shortens His provision; the manna falls on the grateful and the ungrateful alike until the term of the test ends. What ingratitude destroys is the ingrate — the capacity for enjoyment, the standing in the covenant, the self that the favor was building. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf's parallel filing ends identically (7:160), which marks the principle as the fixed frame of the wilderness narrative rather than a comment on one lapse. The clause also answers the question verse 55's stroke raised about divine severity: the stroke, like the sin it answered, harmed its recipients and not its Sender — severity and provision run through the same arithmetic, in which Allah's acts are pure giving or pure ordering, and the entire variable of harm sits on the human side of the ledger.

**Fed Without Plowing, Tested Without Knowing**

Between the provision and the principle stands the verse's unstated function: the manna was a test wearing the costume of a gift. The recital's structure makes this explicit in retrospect — the same provision that verse 57 files as pure niʿma becomes, in the verses that follow, the occasion of complaint and exchange, and the wilderness generation's handling of the sky-food is what the file remembers. But even within this verse the test is visible in the command's shape. Eat *from the good things We have provided for you* — the sentence keeps the Provider inside the eating: the food is not to become ordinary, is not to be received as weather or luck or nature's yield, but as provided, with the Provider named in the provision's own title. That is the discipline unearned food imposes — daily dependence made visible, since nothing in the camp can be credited to the camp. A people fed without plowing cannot develop the amnesia of harvest peoples, who mistake the yield for the work of their hands; the desert's bareness keeps the source in view. The evildoers of the closing clause are precisely those who managed the amnesia anyway — proof that provision, however pure, tests the same faculty every favor tests: whether the receiver keeps the Giver in the gift.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:58

> And ˹remember˺ when We said, “Enter this city and eat freely from wherever you please; enter the gate with humility, saying, ‘Absolve us.’ We will forgive your sins and multiply the reward for the good-doers.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Second Entry Into a Given Land**

The verse's command has the shape of a gift with a liturgy. A people fed for a generation in the open desert is told to enter a city and eat freely, wherever they please, from what it holds — and the entry is fenced with two small requirements: a posture and a word. The first half of the command is deliberately unrestrictive — *eat freely from wherever you please* places no boundary on the table — and the restrictions attach not to the eating but to the entering. The structure replays, with a difference, the first entry-command of the sūrah: Adam was placed in the garden with the same open table, *eat as freely as you please* (2:35), and one restriction — the tree. Here the restriction is inverted into a positive rite: instead of one thing withheld, one thing asked — humility at the gate, absolution on the lips. Both scenes are entries into unearned abundance, and both make the entry itself the test rather than the residence. The wilderness generation stands at the city's threshold as Adam stood at the tree's: everything given, one small thing required, and the required thing aimed at the posture of the receiver rather than at the property of the gift.

**Which City the Command Named**

The city is unnamed in this verse, and the exegetes' candidates follow the geography of the conquest: Jerusalem, Jericho, other cities of Syria or Jordan, and — al-Rāzī's minority reading — Egypt itself. The identifications turn on a historical problem the verse leaves open: Moses never entered the Holy Land, so a command spoken under his leadership would either predate the conquest or belong to Joshua's campaign at Jericho. Al-Rāzī's Egypt reading dissolves the problem by relocating the scene: the punishment of the following verse, he reasons, fits the period before any entry into the Holy Land, and Egypt — the land of their torment — would then be re-entered as a land of provision, the reversal complete. The stronger evidence runs the other way. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf files the same command with the city named: *"Enter this city ˹of Jerusalem˺ and eat from wherever you please"* (7:161), and Sūrah al-Nisāʾ joins the gate-entry to the covenant's catalogue: *"We raised the Mount over them ˹as a warning˺ for ˹breaking˺ their covenant and said, 'Enter the gate ˹of Jerusalem˺ with humility'"* (4:154). The identification with Jerusalem — or with a city of the Holy Land entered at the conquest — carries the Qur'an's own explicit glosses, while the Egypt reading rests on inference. The unnamed city of this verse is named twice elsewhere in the Book, and the naming settles it.

**The Gate Entered With the Head Lowered**

The posture required at the gate is *sujjadan* — prostrating, or in the broader lexical range of the word, bowing low. The exegetes note the ambiguity and its reason: in Islamic rite *sujūd* is precisely the forehead to the ground, but the word's root covers any deep bodily lowering, and the command here is read on both registers — entering the gate in a bow, or entering in full prostration. Either way the requirement is the same in substance: the body performs what the heart must hold at the moment of arrival. A people entering a promised city have one natural posture — upright, victorious, claiming — and the command installs the opposite at the threshold itself. The humility is not general piety but entry-specific: it governs the exact moment when possession begins, when the risk of reading the gift as achievement peaks. The sūrah's wider argument explains why the moment needed engineering. This was a community that had demanded to see Allah as an ultimatum, that had taken a calf while its prophet was away, and that was about to eat freely from a city it had not built. The bowed gate is the covenant's prophylactic against the theology of arrival: enter as recipients, not as conquerors, and let the body say it where everyone can see.

**Ḥiṭṭa: One Word for the Whole Liturgy**

The spoken requirement is a single word: *ḥiṭṭah* — rendered here *Absolve us*, literally an unburdening. The grammarians' reading of its force is exact: al-Zamakhsharī takes it as a cognate-accusative invocation, "unburden us an unburdening" — the way Arabic compresses a whole petition into its verbal noun, so that the word is not a description but a request in its shortest legal form. The word's content completes the posture's work.
