A bowing body could still carry a boasting heart; the prescribed speech forecloses it, because *ḥiṭṭah* names the speaker's condition — burdened, in need of removal — and names nothing about the speaker's merit. There is no room in the word for *because we fought*, *because we kept the law*, *because our fathers were righteous*; the entire entry-theology of the covenant is compressed into a noun meaning take this load off. The verse thereby makes the liturgy a doctrinal instrument: what a people says at its threshold of blessing discloses what it believes about the blessing. Islamic practice keeps the pattern in its own entry-formulas — the duʿāʾ of the mosque's door, the greeting of peace at every threshold — and the ancestor of the whole genre stands here: one word, spoken entering, that assigns the gift to the Giver and the burden to the only Remover.

**Forgiveness and Increase at the Threshold**

The promise answering the word is double: *We will forgive your sins and multiply the reward for the good-doers*. The first half meets the petition — *ḥiṭṭah* asks for removal, and removal is pledged, maghfira for their line of sins: the calf, the demand, the wilderness record. The second half exceeds it, and the exceeding is attached to a named group: the *muḥsinūn*, the good-doers, the people whose worship carries excellence. The promise's structure is thus the sūrah's whole economy of grace in two clauses — the floor is forgiveness for the asking, and the ceiling is multiplication for the excellent — with both opened by a bowed entry and a four-letter word. The multiplication clause also does specific work in this context. The city's table was *eat freely from wherever you please*; the promised increase says that the material gift is the lesser half of what the threshold offers. A community entering in humility receives not only the city but a rising curve inside the covenant — reward that compounds for those who do the asking well. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf's filing carries the same double promise (7:161), which marks it as the standing terms of entry rather than a one-time offer: wherever the gate of a divine gift is opened, forgiveness and increase are posted on it together.

**Every Blessing Has a Gate**

The verse's permanence lies in its form. Blessings, in the Qur'an's moral geography, are not open fields but walled cities with gates, and the gate has requirements: a posture that says *I did not earn this* and a word that says *remove what I brought*. The wilderness generation's file will be read against these two requirements, but the requirements themselves are addressed to every reader standing at a threshold — of provision, of position, of a house, of a season of ease. The command's economy is its mercy: nothing is asked at the gate but humility and absolution-seeking, both of which cost the asker nothing and save him everything. The verse also completes the recital's arc of arrival. The descent from the garden began the human file with an exit; the entry of verse 38 opened the earth as residence; and here a delivered people is brought to the first re-entry — a city given, a table spread, a rite prescribed — the descent's counter-movement staged inside history. What Allah asks at the gates of His gifts has not changed since this verse: come down off the camel of self-sufficiency, bow at the door, say the word that names your need. The city beyond is already paid for; the gate only checks who is entering.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:59

> But the wrongdoers changed the words they were commanded to say. So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them for their rebelliousness.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Changed Word**

The verse's first clause reports one of the smallest sins in the Qur'an and one of the most heavily answered. The command had been a posture and a word (verse 58); the response was a substitution — *the wrongdoers changed the words they were commanded to say*. The verb *baddala* is the Qur'an's technical term for replacement: not mispronouncing, not forgetting, but swapping the commanded thing for another thing in its place. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf files the same clause with the same verb and adds the qualifier that sharpens it: *"But the wrongdoers among them changed the words they were commanded to say"* (7:162) — *among them*. The substitution was not the whole camp's act but a faction's, and the naming matters: the recital indicts precisely and does not smear. What the qualifier also exposes is the social anatomy of the sin — a liturgy commanded to everyone, corrupted by some, and not corrected by the rest, since the punishment that follows lands on the community's file as a whole. The changed word is the smallest possible act of covenant-breaking, and that is why the verse treats it as the largest kind of sign: what a people does with one commanded syllable discloses what it will do with a scripture.

**What They Said Instead**

The reports supply the substituted words, and they supply two versions. The famous reading has them replacing *ḥiṭṭah* — absolve us — with *ḥinṭah*, wheat: the petition for forgiveness turned into a request for grain, the liturgy of the gate converted into shopping. Al-Zamakhsharī pressed the obvious objection: these people did not speak Arabic, so a wordplay between two Arabic nouns cannot be what happened, and the report's wit does not survive translation into the scene. The objection is sound as far as it goes, and the hadith literature preserves the Prophet's ﷺ own version of the substitution, which is different in wording and identical in kind. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī records it: the Children of Israel were told to enter the gate in prostration and say *ḥiṭṭah*, *"but they changed (Allah's Order) and entered, dragging themselves on their buttocks and said, 'Habatun (a grain) in a Sha'ratin (hair)'"* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4641). The substitution in the ḥadīth is still a food-word — a grain, in a hair — but the mechanism the Prophet ﷺ emphasizes is the change itself, whatever the syllables: the commanded petition was replaced by a trivial phrase, and the commanded posture by its inverse. The stronger reading holds both reports together at the level they agree on: the word was changed because the word was the test, and a people unwilling to ask for absolution will always find a smaller sentence to say in its place.

**Entering on Their Backsides**

The ḥadīth's postural detail completes the picture. The gate required a bow or prostration — heads lowered, entering in humility (verse 58). What the Bukhārī report describes instead is a people entering *dragging themselves on their buttocks*, the body's inversion of the commanded reverence performed in a way that could only be deliberate: one does not accidentally slide through a gate seated. The two changes mirror the two commands exactly — posture reversed, word replaced — which converts the incident from lapse into liturgy-of-mockery, a counter-rite performed at the threshold of the gift. The verse's own summary word names its character: *fāsuq*-conduct, rebelliousness, the root that carries leaving-the-bounds. Mockery of a commanded form is not a lighter version of disobedience but its concentrated form, because it adds to the refusal a statement about the Refuser: that the command is a joke. The Qur'an treats that statement as decisive everywhere it appears, and the punishment clause of this verse — descending, as the mockery did, on the whole scene — is filed under the same heading the gate-posture was meant to prevent: a people who would not lower themselves at a gift's threshold were answered from above.

**A Punishment From the Heavens**

The response arrives as *rijz min al-samāʾ* — punishment from the heavens. *Rijz* is the Qur'an's word for penal affliction: the same noun names the plagues sent upon Pharaoh's people when they broke each promise (7:134), the affliction sent on the people of Lūṭ's cities (29:34), and — in its other register — the whispering pollution of Satan (8:11). The commentators read the heaven-sent rijz here as a plague, the identification supported by the word's use for the Egyptian plagues and by al-Rāzī's related reasoning that this punishment belongs to the period before any entry into the Holy Land. The clause's direction — *from the heavens* — answers the scene's geography: the sky had been this community's benefactor for a generation, dropping shade (verse 57) and dropping food; the same sky now drops the penalty, and the verse states the symmetry without comment because the symmetry is the comment. Nothing on earth mediated the punishment; no army, no famine-cycle, no natural cause is named. A liturgy mocked at a gate is answered by a dispatch from the direction the gift came, and the answer's precision — *upon them for their rebelliousness*, the cause stated in the sentence — keeps the punishment inside the covenant's own logic: not rage but consequence, filed against a named act.

**Why a Word Carries This Weight**

The disproportion between the sin's size and the punishment's weight is the verse's deliberate lesson, and the sūrah explains it by pairing this scene with a later charge against the same community's scholars: *"a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it"* (2:75). The gate-substitution and the text-corruption are one crime at two scales — the single commanded word changed at the threshold, the received Book changed in the study — and the Qur'an's insistence on filing both says that the handling of words is this recital's central diagnostic. Words are the covenant's medium: promises are words, liturgy is words, scripture is words, and the demand to *say* ḥiṭṭah was a demand to let the mouth ratify what the heart knew — that the city was gift, the table was provision, and the guests were burdened sinners at a merciful Lord's door. To change that word was to change the covenant's terms from the human side, an act small in syllables and total in direction. Verse 42 had already legislated the principle for the scholars — do not mix truth with falsehood, do not conceal it knowingly — and verse 59 shows the principle's wilderness origin: the first corruption of a divine word on this community's record was committed with the mouth, at a gate, in a single substituted sentence.

**The Sky Keeps Both Ledgers**

Read inside the recital, the verse closes the entry-scene with the sūrah's governing arithmetic on display. The sky's ledger for this people now holds shade and manna on the credit side (verse 57) and rijz on the debit side (verse 59), with one community drawing from both columns. That is the verse's pastoral severity: proximity to grace does not immunize against penalty, and the penalty arrives through the same channel as the grace, which is the covenant's way of saying that the channel was never the point — the handling was. The wrongdoers are distinguished *among them*, the punished act is named, the cause is stated, and the file moves on: the recital will next record necessity rather than luxury answered — a thirsting camp and a prophet's prayer — because the covenant's dealings track need with the same precision they track insolence. For the sūrah's second audience, the verse's edge is unchanged. Every community lives at gates of given things, and every liturgy of entry — the word said over a meal, the prayer at a threshold, the confession that keeps a gift assigned to its Giver — has its substituted syllables. The changed word is never only a word; it is the heart's verdict spoken aloud, and verse 59 records what the heavens do with verdicts.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:60

> And ˹remember˺ when Moses prayed for water for his people, We said, “Strike the rock with your staff.” Then twelve springs gushed out, ˹and˺ each tribe knew its drinking place. ˹We then said,˺ “Eat and drink of Allah’s provisions, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Prophet's Prayer for Water**

The verse opens with need rather than command: Moses sought water for his people — *istisqā*, the seeking of drink, a prophet reduced to the desert's one question. The Qur'an states the prayer and moves immediately to the answer, and Sūrah al-Aʿrāf files the same sequence with the same economy: *"We revealed to Moses, when his people asked for water, 'Strike the rock with your staff.'"* (7:160). The form of the scene became Islamic practice: the prayer for rain, ṣalāt al-istisqāʾ, established in the Prophet's ﷺ sunnah and performed to this day when the rains fail — a community asking its Lord for water through its imam, in the grammar this verse first wrote down. The detail worth holding is the direction of the asking. The people's thirst is real; the prophet does not lecture them about it but carries it upward. The recital elsewhere shows this community's needs expressed as complaint (the food fatigue that follows in the file); here need is expressed as intercession, and the answer comes through the intercessor's channel. The verse thus distinguishes, without naming the distinction, two ways of being needy before Allah — the way that asks Him through His appointed, and the way that demands of Him as a customer — and grants the first without a word of rebuke.

**The Staff Again**

The answer is an instruction addressed to a tool: strike the rock with your staff. The staff is by now the recital's standing instrument. At the sea the same command produced the same grammar — *"Strike the sea with your staff," and the sea was split, each part was like a huge mountain* (26:63) — and the two filings together establish the pattern of prophetic miracle in the Qur'an: the extraordinary act is routed through an ordinary object wielded by an obedient hand. Nothing in the staff parts seas or opens stone; the verse's theology is that divine power does not bypass means but honors them, so that the means stay visible and the power stays unmistakable. The staff's own history deepens the choice: it was Moses's shepherd's stick — the one he leaned on and beat down leaves with for his flock, as he told the One who spoke to him at Ṭuwā (20:18) — and it became the sign-object of his mission. A herdsman's tool, retained through prophethood, is now the instrument of a nation's water. The Qur'an keeps selecting for its signs the objects people already carry, which is its standing answer to demands for spectacle: the miracle is not the absence of ordinary things but what obedience does with them.

**Twelve Springs for Twelve Tribes**

The struck rock yields structure, not just water: twelve springs gush out, and each tribe knows its drinking place. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf supplies the correspondence explicitly — *"We divided them into twelve tribes— each as a community"* (7:160) — so the water-system mirrors the camp-system, spring for tribe, and the miracle includes its own administration. The commentators elaborate with reports of a portable stone — carried through the wilderness, struck on each of four faces, three streams from each face, twelve in total — and with the reading that each tribe's spring was assigned by lot or by marking; the reports are tradition's furniture rather than the verse's content, and the verse's own point stands without them: grace arrived organized. A camp of twelve tribes at one water source is a riot; a camp of twelve tribes with twelve springs is a settlement. The detail answers the desert's second scarcity after food — not water alone but water without conflict — and it prefigures the verse's closing prohibition, since competition at wells is where corruption in the land typically begins. Some exegetes add that each tribe knew its place because the springs were marked to them or because each stream followed its tribe's banner; whatever the mechanism, the stated outcome is a provision that arrives with peace built into its plumbing.

**The Rock in Two Scriptures**

The scene has a biblical twin, and the comparison is instructive in what each scripture emphasizes. Exodus 17 places the striking at Horeb, with the place named Massah and Meribah — testing and quarreling — because the people quarreled and tested the Lord there, asking whether He was among them or not. The Qur'anic filing removes the quarrel-frame entirely: the people ask, Moses intercedes, the water comes. What the Qur'an adds is the twelve-springs correspondence and — decisively — the speech attached to the water: eat and drink, and do not corrupt. The two testaments thus remember the same rock with different centers of gravity: one preserves the scene as a story about Israel's testing of Allah, the other as a story about Allah's provisioning and its ethics. Neither emphasis is absent from either text's wider corpus, but the Qur'an's version is the one this recital needs, because the recital is building a case about how provision is handled. The naming difference does real work: a scene remembered as Meribah teaches the danger of testing God; the same scene remembered as twelve springs teaches the responsibility that rides on organized grace. The Qur'an files the second and lets the wilderness's later verses — the complaint, the exchange, the refusal — supply the testing.

**Eat and Drink, and Do Not Corrupt**

The speech the water arrives with is the verse's law in miniature: *eat and drink of Allah's provisions, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land*. The first half is permission with a possessive attached — the provisions are Allah's, and the eating is of them, a formulation that keeps the Provider inside every meal the way verse 57's ṭayyibāt-command did. The second half converts the meal into a covenant term. *Corruption in the land* — fasād — is the Qur'an's name for the whole family of public wrongs: injustice, violence, fraud, the breaking of the social order through which provision flows. Joined to eat-and-drink in a single sentence, the prohibition states the ethics of receiving: grace licenses enjoyment and forbids predation, and the two halves bind each other — the people who eat Allah's provision are the people who may not corrupt Allah's land. The wilderness setting makes the join concrete. A camp fed by manna and watered by twelve springs has no economy of its own to exploit; its only possible corruption is against each other and against the terms of the gift. The verse thereby universalizes while it particularizes: every community living on provision it did not produce — which is every community — receives here its two-clause constitution. Take what is given, thankfully; do not turn the given land into a corrupted one. The spring-fed camp is the model polity of the recital, legislated in a sentence spoken over water.

**The Rock and the Heart**

The verse carries a second reading the sūrah itself authorizes. Fourteen verses later the same sūrah compares this community's hearts to stone — and to stone that waters: *"Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers; others split, spilling water; while others are humbled in awe of Allah"* (2:74). The comparison presumes exactly what verse 60 staged: rock is not barrenness in the Qur'an's mineralogy but potential — the hard thing that, struck in obedience, pours. The Sufi commentators drew the inference explicitly: Ibn ʿAjībah reads the stone as the heart, the staff as spiritual resolve (*himmah*), and the striking as the discipline that breaks the ego's hardness so wisdom and unveiling flow — twelve streams for the twelve faculties of a restored soul. The esoteric reading is legitimate precisely because verse 74 installs the rock-heart equation in the text; the historical event remains the verse's primary sense, and the symbolic reading rides on it rather than replacing it. Both registers converge on one claim: the water came from the hardest thing present, at a stroke performed in obedience, through a stick that was only a stick. The camp drank from a rock that day, and the recital keeps the scene on file for every later reader whose own hardness is waiting for the same command — strike, and what was stone will water twelve directions.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:61

> And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses! We cannot endure the same meal ˹every day˺. So ˹just˺ call upon your Lord on our behalf, He will bring forth for us some of what the earth produces of herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions.” Moses scolded ˹them˺, “Do you exchange what is better for what is worse? ˹You can˺ go down to any village and you will find what you have asked for.” They were stricken with disgrace and misery, and they invited the displeasure of Allah for rejecting Allah’s signs and unjustly killing the prophets. This is ˹a fair reward˺ for their disobedience and violations.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Complaint Against Heaven's Table**

The verse opens with the longest direct speech any wilderness generation addresses to its prophet in this recital, and the speech is a complaint about the menu. *We cannot endure the same meal* — the manna and quails, provision that fell from the sky without sowing, has become unbearable through repetition. The complaint's structure is worth naming precisely, because the verse's verdict depends on it. Nothing in the speech accuses the food of being bad: the manna was ṭayyib, sent with a command to eat (verse 57). What the speakers cannot bear is *uniformity* — one food, day after day, with no market, no variety, no Egypt. The sin is not appetite, which the law of provision permits, but the refusal of a gift's *form* while demanding its continuation — keep feeding us, but on our terms, with the crops we remember. The biblical record preserves the same complaint in the same wilderness: the people weeping for the fish and cucumbers and melons and leeks and onions and garlic of Egypt, and the quails granted in answer turning into judgment on the cravers (Numbers 11). The Qur'an's filing compresses the episode to its moral geometry — heaven's food rejected for earth's — and lets the geography speak: the menu they demand is literally the menu of the land they were delivered from.

**The Requested List**

The five crops are named one by one — herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, onions — and the naming is the verse's rhetoric. These are not delicacies but garden-commons, the cheapest produce of any village plot, listed with a specificity that reads like a shopping order. One word in the list carries its own exegetical history: *fūm*, rendered garlic, which classical lexicography also reads as wheat — either way a field-crop, either way ordinary. The list's function is contrast: against manna, food that arrived daily from above the sky, the demand is for food that arrives annually out of dirt, cultivated, stored, traded, priced. The demanders are not asking for more; they are asking for *normal* — for the economic world they recognize, where food has human mediation and the eater stands in a market rather than under a cloud. That is why the complaint is theological before it is culinary. Manna made dependence visible every morning; onions make it invisible in a supply chain. A people who cannot endure the same meal are, in the verse's diagnosis, a people who cannot endure being visibly dependent — and the recital's later dealings with this community will repeatedly expose the same nerve: the demand to see Allah plainly, the demand for a visible substitute while Moses is away, the demand now for a food-system that hides its Giver.

**Moses's Rebuke: The Direction of the Exchange**

The answer comes as a question that contains the whole verdict: *Do you exchange what is better for what is worse?* The verb is *istibdāl* — substitution, the same family the recital used for the changed word at the gate (verse 59) — and the question's force is in its direction-words. Better and worse here are not flavors but stations: the heavenly provision is the better, the earth's commons the worse, and the exchange is therefore a descent dressed as a purchase. The second half of the rebuke drives it home: *go down to any village and you will find what you have asked for*. The verb is *habaṭa*, to go down — the sūrah's word for Adam's exit from the garden (*descend from the heavens*, 2:36) and for every fall from a given station to an earned one. The crops are available; they have always been available; they grow wherever people farm, and the camp can have them the moment it accepts descent into the ordinary economy. The word *miṣr* in the command — rendered *any village* — carries the pun the exegetes debate: as a common noun it is a town, any town; as the proper name it is Egypt, and al-Ṭabarī notes that the verse's orthography requires the indefinite reading (*miṣran*, not *Miṣra*), so the command is go down to a town, not return to Egypt — though early readers heard the second meaning humming under the first. Both readings converge: what the demanders want is available anywhere below heaven, and getting it means leaving the table where heaven serves.

**Stricken With Disgrace and Misery**

The verdict arrives in two coverings and a burden. *They were stricken with disgrace and misery* — *ḍuribat ʿalayhim al-dhillah wa-l-maskanah*: abjection and destitution struck over them as a tent is struck over a camper, or a tax is struck on an account. The imagery of the verb is enclosure: the two conditions wrap the community, and the recital is not describing one bad season but a standing condition — the same sentence will be refiled in Sūrah Āl ʿImrān with the addition that the covering holds wherever they are found, except under a covenant with Allah and a covenant with people (3:112). The third element is active rather than passive: *they invited the displeasure of Allah* — *bāʾū bi-ghaḍabin min Allāh*, and the verb *bāʾū* is commercial in its root sense: they returned home carrying it, the way a trader returns carrying his goods. Wrath is filed as acquired property, earned and borne back, which is the sūrah's market idiom applied to the worst possible cargo. The two coverings and the burden together answer the complaint's logic exactly: the people who could not endure heaven's monotony receive earth's monotony as a permanent estate — disgrace that does not rotate, misery that does not vary — and the displeasure they carry is the receipt.

**Rejecting Signs, Killing Prophets**

The verdict names its grounds, and the grounds exceed the meal: *for rejecting Allah's signs and unjustly killing the prophets*. A complaint about onions is being answered with a charge sheet of murder, and the connection is the recital's method rather than disproportion. The verse addresses the community across its whole history in the second person — the same inheritance logic that made descendants parties to the sea and the calf — and files the two capital crimes of that history: the signs rejected (the demand for sight, the changed word, the calf taken after the sea) and the prophets killed without right, a charge the Qur'an repeats across sūrahs (2:87, 2:91, 3:21, 3:112, 3:181, 4:155, 5:70) with the same *unjustly* — since no prophet's killing could ever be just, the adverb marks the killings as done against known truth. The sūrah will turn the charge into an argument at verse 91: a community that says *we believe in what was sent down to us* is asked why it killed Allah's prophets before, if belief is the claim (2:91). The meal-complaint sits inside that larger indictment because it shares its root: the rejecting of what Allah sends, in the form He sends it. The manna rejected was a sign handled exactly as the prophets were handled — received, resented, replaced.

**Disobedience and Violations: The Summary Clause**

The verse closes its case file with a summary in two nouns: *this is for their disobedience and their violations* — *ʿaṣaw wa-kānū yaʿtadūn*. The first is the refusal of command, the plain disobedience; the second, from *ʿudwān*, is crossing the set bound — the transgression that does not merely decline a limit but overruns it. The pair covers the verse's whole material: wanting the sky's food replaced is disobedience to the provision's terms; demanding it while demanding heaven's continuation, mocking the gift's form, is violation. The exegetical tradition also hears in the double formula an escalation — habitual disobedience ripening into aggressive excess — and the recital supports the hearing: the changed word became the mocked gate, the mocked gate became the calf, and the calf's generation became the killers of prophets. The summary clause is therefore not a redundancy but a diagnosis of trajectory: a community is being shown where its small refusals were walking. For the sūrah's permanent readership the verse keeps its double edge. Every generation has its manna — the provision arrived in a form it did not choose — and every generation hears the same market call from the village below. The question the verse files is the rebuke's question, unchanged: which direction is your exchange running, and what will you be carrying home?

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:62

> Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians—whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Four Names on One Promise**

The verse lists four communities and hangs one promise on all four: the believers — the Muslim confessors — the Jews, the Christians, and the Ṣābiʾūn. The third name is the verse's historical puzzle, and the exegetes' candidates map the puzzle's shape. *Ṣābiʾ* derives from a root meaning to leave one religion for another — or, in a second etymology, to rise, as stars rise — and pagan Arabs used it as a slur for the Prophet ﷺ himself, who had left the religion of his forefathers. The commentators propose identifications across a spectrum: monotheists with no book, rites, or prophet, saying only *there is no god but God*; angel-venerating worshippers who faced a qiblah and recited the Psalms; defectors from the People of the Book; followers of the religion of Noah; or star-influenced monotheists whom some classify as unbelievers. History supplies two concrete groups: the people of Ḥarrān, who adopted the name Ṣābiʾ in the early Islamic centuries to claim the Qur'an's protected status for their Hellenized Near-Eastern religion, and the Mandaeans of southern Iraq and Iran — monotheists who revere John the Baptist, practice frequent baptism, and are still called ṣābiʾa today. The list's fourth slot thus names either a specific community or a category of the in-between, and the verse's ruling is framed to work either way.

**The Condition Is Creed and Conduct, Not the Label**

The list is immediately overridden by a relative clause, and the clause is the verse's actual ruling: *whoever truly believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good*. The four names enumerate; the condition defines. Three elements constitute it — belief in Allah, belief in the Last Day, and righteous action — and the verse attaches the promise not to any name in the list but to whoever meets the three. The structure does deliberate theological work. A reader expecting communal soteriology — Jews saved as Jews, Christians as Christians — finds instead individual criteria stated in the terms the Qur'an uses everywhere for the substance of faith: the two beliefs that orient a life (its Lord and its end) plus the conduct that proves them. The adverb the translation supplies — *truly* — renders the Arabic's own emphasis device, and it guards the clause against nominal membership: the Jew, Christian, or Ṣābiʾun in view is the one whose belonging has become belief. The verse is therefore not a list of saved communities but a statement that salvation runs through persons and their creed-and-conduct, with the communities named as the addresses among whom such persons are found.

**Their Reward With Their Lord**

The promise is stated in the Qur'an's fixed eschatological idiom: *their reward is with their Lord*, and *no fear upon them, no grief*. The two halves are the charter formula of this sūrah — the same pair that closed the descent's guarantee to Adam's children: whoever follows the guidance, *"there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve"* (2:38). The reuse is the verse's strongest structural signal: the people of verse 62 are being admitted to the charter's own promise, in the charter's own words, which places the verse inside the sūrah's first architecture rather than beside it as an exception. The formula's two negatives are precise about what salvation removes — fear of what is coming, grief over what was left — covering the future and the past in one stroke, the exact double anxiety the Last Day generates. And the reward's location — *with their Lord*, stored in His custody rather than distributed by any community's gatekeepers — removes the promise from every institutional claim: no priesthood, no lineage, no confession holds the keys to this verse's treasury. The reward is with the Lord of the four named groups, which is the verse's quiet way of saying He is one and His custody is single.

**The Parallel Filing in al-Māʾidah**

The Qur'an states this ruling twice, and the second filing confirms the first's permanence: *"Indeed, the believers, Jews, Sabians and Christians—whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve"* (5:69). The parallel is near-verbatim, with one variation — the Ṣābiʾūn move ahead of the Christians in the order — and variation of order without variation of content is the Qur'an's way of filing a principle rather than an occasion. A concession to a moment is stated once; a standing rule is restated in a later sūrah, in a different context, with the same clause carrying the same weight. Al-Māʾidah's filing sits among verses on communal difference and judgment — God will decide between the communities on the Day of Judgment — which frames the rule there as eschatological business belonging to Allah alone. The double filing also answers the historicist reduction from within the text: whatever historical group the Ṣābiʾūn were, the ruling's grammar — whoever believes and does good — is built to outlive every candidate identification, and the second sūrah's repetition publishes that intent.

**Before Islam or After? The Abrogation Debate and Its Better Answer**

The exegetes ask whether the verse's promise runs past the Prophet's ﷺ mission, and three answers have their grounds. The first limits it: the verse concerns Jews, Christians, and Ṣābiʾūn who kept their original faith before Islam and, when the Prophet ﷺ came, acknowledged him — people like Salmān al-Fārsī, Abū Dharr, and the monks Waraqa ibn Nawfal and Baḥīra; on this reading the labels name communities, and the condition names their faithful members' completion in Islam. The second claims abrogation: a view cited from Ibn ʿAbbās holds that 3:85 — whoever seeks a religion other than submission, it will not be accepted — cancels this verse. The counter-principle defeats it on the tradition's own terms: abrogation applies to legal rulings and commands, not to descriptive statements, and least of all to statements about persons' standing with Allah in the hereafter; verse 62 is description, not legislation, and survives. The third, al-Zamakhsharī's, reads *those who believe* ironically as the hypocrites — outward confessors lumped with the named groups, against whom the verse's second half then defines true believers. The reading collapses without it: nowhere else in the Qur'an does *those who believe* mean hypocrites, and a Jew who followed Muhammad's law would simply no longer be called a Jew. The stronger construction keeps the plain sense and reads the condition as the verse does — creed, eschatology, and good works as the substance the labels stand for, with the commentators' common gloss that true belief after the mission's publication includes acceptance of the Messenger, since rejecting a prophet one has truly known is not belief in Allah but belief on one's own terms.

**Al-Ghazālī's Latitude and the Verse's Placement**

The verse's hardest question — who counts as having truly believed and done good, judged across barriers of information — received its most careful Islamic answer from al-Ghazālī. In his *Fayṣal al-tafriqah* he argues that whole populations fall inside divine mercy: the Byzantine Christian or the Turk who never met the Prophet's ﷺ message except as caricature — who heard only that a man called Muhammad claimed prophethood and was, as presented to them, a liar — cannot be convicted of rejecting him, because what they rejected was not him. Birthplace, upbringing, and the quality of one's informants mediate every person's knowledge of religion, and al-Ghazālī gives those mediators full weight: denial deserving of condemnation requires access to the thing denied. The argument is the verse's condition applied with epistemic honesty — *whoever truly believes* is a statement about hearts and their actual information, which belongs to Allah's audit and not to human label-checking. The verse's placement makes the same point structurally. It stands in the middle of the Israel recital — between the wilderness verdicts and the covenant of the mountain — inside the sūrah's most particular prosecution, and it interrupts the prosecution with a universal principle. The recital audits a community by name; the verse declares that reward runs by creed and conduct in four communities at once. Particular judgment and universal criteria are thus filed adjacently, each guarding the other: the audit prevents the principle from becoming indifference, and the principle prevents the audit from becoming exclusion.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:63

> And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from you and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Covenant Taken Under the Mountain**

The verse files the covenant's most physical scene: Allah takes the pledge from the community and raises the mountain over them in the same breath. The two acts are joined by a single *wa* — took a covenant, raised the mountain — and the joining is the verse's whole subject, because a covenant normally has a signing and this one has a setting. The word for mountain here is *ṭūr*, which the commentators note as a loan from Syriac meaning simply mountain, fully naturalized into Arabic — the same word that names the Sinai of Sūrah al-Ṭūr and the valley where Moses received his mission. The covenant being taken is the covenant of verse 40, the one the sūrah's whole address exists to renew: the Torah's obligations accepted by the community that will carry them. And the acceptance happens under a raised mountain, which the exegetes agree was raised *to frighten them* — the pledge extracted at the moment of maximum seriousness, with the community's standing literally under question. The scene's strangeness is its content: this is what covenant-signing looks like when the covenant is not a contract between merchants but the constitution of a people, received from the Lord of the worlds, by a generation that had just spent its wilderness years testing every alternative.

**Raised Over You: The Exegetes' Two Readings**

How the mountain stood over the camp divides the commentators, and both sides have grounds. The majority reading is literal and total: the mountain — Sinai itself, or a mass torn from Palestine — was uprooted, made to move, and held suspended above the Israelites like a canopy, the fear of its fall the sanction behind the pledge. The alternative reads the phrase as idiomatic: the mountain loomed above them, the way English says a danger *hung over* a people, and the looming was the theophany's terror — the thick cloud, the smoke like a kiln's, the violently shaking mountain of the Exodus account, with its standing order that whoever touches the mountain dies. The Qur'an's own elaboration settles the question toward the literal. Sūrah al-Aʿrāf describes the scene with two details no idiom needs: *"We raised the mountain over them as if it were a cloud and they thought it would fall on them"* (7:171). A mountain *like a cloud* — spread above them as shade is spread — and a community that *thought it would fall*: both details belong to a suspended mass, not to a looming landscape, and the second detail records the camp's own perception, which is exactly what the literal reading claims. The looming-idiom reading remains possible as language but must explain away 7:171's specific imagery; the stronger reading keeps both verses at face value. The mountain was held over them, and they looked up.

**Hold Firmly, With Strength**

The speech under the mountain is the covenant's clause: *hold firmly to that which We have given you, and observe what is in it*. The first verb — *khudhū*, take, seize — is governed by *bi-quwwah*, with strength, which the exegetes read as earnestness, seriousness, and settled resolve: take the Scripture the way a drowning man takes a rope, with the whole body's commitment. The strength is not intellectual assent but grip. The second command — *remember what is in it* in one reading, *observe its teachings* in this translation's rendering of *udh-kurū mā fīh* — makes memory a term of the covenant: the contents are to be held in recall, recited, kept present, because a book unremembered is a book not held. The same command is filed at verse 93 with the mountain scene repeated and the covenant's object named as obedience, and again in al-Aʿrāf with the identical words and identical purpose clause (7:171) — three filings of one signing. The object held is *what We have given you*: the Torah, as the commentators state plainly, the book given at the forty nights' end (verse 53). The verse thereby connects the recital's two mountain scenes — the gift received by Moses above and the covenant gripped by the people below — into one transaction: the Book descended, and the descent's condition was strength of hold and permanence of memory.

**So Perhaps You Will Become Mindful**

The clause of purpose is the covenant's stated end: *laʿallakum tattaqūn* — so that you may become god-fearing. The recital's purpose clauses have been accumulating — pardon for gratitude (52), the Book for guidance (53) — and this one names the deepest target, the virtue the sūrah opened with: guidance is for the mindful (2:2), and the Scripture's holding is for mindfulness. The sequence inside the verse is exact: strength of grip, then memory of contents, then taqwā as the formed disposition. Scripture does not produce god-fearing by being owned but by being held hard and kept in recall until its categories become the holder's reflexes — which is the verse's definition of what the covenant actually is: not a signed document but a training regime with an eschatological objective. The taqwā named here is also the covenant's only adequate sanction, which reorders the mountain scene: the mountain hanging overhead produces fear of falling, but the verse wants fear *of Allah* — and the difference between the two fears is the distance the Scripture must carry the community. The raised mountain gets the pledge spoken; the held Book gets the pledge lived. Verse 63 is thus the sūrah's statement of how a people under terror becomes a people under conscience: the terror is the door, the grip is the road, and mindfulness is the arrival.

**Consent Under the Canopy**

The scene raises the question every reader brings to it: what is a covenant worth if the mountain is hovering? Islamic thought has resources for the tension, and the verse's own text supplies the main one. A contract signed under compulsion is void in the law men make; this covenant is different in kind, because the compulsion is not a party extracting advantage but the Truth making its weight visible once — and the thing consented to is not a burden imposed for the imposer's benefit but the community's own constitution, whose terms the verse states in full: hold the Book, remember it, become mindful. The exegetical reports add the context that sharpens it: the mountain was raised because the community was balking — hesitating at the obligations, inclined to decline — and the raising was the mercy that made the decline impossible to complete. Fear here functions as the arrest that stops a worse choice, the way a parent's shout stops a child at the well's edge. The sūrah's later filings keep the tension honest: verse 93 records the same mountain raised and the same covenant taken, and the community's answer there — *we hear and disobey*, with the calf's love rooted in their hearts (2:93) — proves that the canopy did not manufacture inner assent. The mountain could compel the tongue; only the Scripture, held with strength, could compel the heart. The verse files both facts in one sentence: the most overwhelming signing scene in revelation, and a signing whose real ratification was left to memory and grip.

**The Sūrah's Covenant Register**

Verse 63 is the third filing of the covenant in this sūrah's first hundred verses, and the register is cumulative by design. Verse 40 states the covenant bilaterally — fulfil yours and I will fulfil Mine. Verse 53 files its instrument — the Scripture and Criterion given. Verse 63 stages its signing — the pledge taken under the canopy, with the terms spoken: hold, remember, become mindful. Verse 93 will refile the same scene with the community's answer recorded, and al-Nisāʾ gathers the whole package — the Mount raised for the covenant, the gate entered with humility, the Sabbath kept, the firm pledge taken (4:154) — into a single indictment list. The repetition is the covenant's own method: a bond of this weight is not signed once but re-read at every station, and the Qur'an's habit of refiling Sinai across sūrahs treats the covenant as a living instrument each generation re-enters. That is why the address is second-person — *We took a covenant from you* — spoken to Madinans about a mountain they never stood under: the pledge runs with the Scripture, and every community that receives the Book receives the scene. The verse's last word is its first demand: mindfulness. Everything else — the fright, the grip, the memory — is scaffolding around a single objective, and the scaffolding comes down, in the sūrah's own telling, the moment the community lets go.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:64

> Yet you turned away afterwards. Had it not been for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you, you would have certainly been of the losers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Turning Away After Everything**

Three words carry the verse's indictment: *turned away, afterwards*. The verb *tawallā* is not the glancing-off of inattention but the deliberate turn of the back — the same verb the Qur'an uses for the one who hears the call and walks the other way. Its object here is everything verse 63 assembled: the covenant taken, the mountain raised, the command to hold with strength. And the temporal marker *baʿda dhālik* — after that — is the aggravator. This was not a people who turned away in ignorance, before the demonstration; they turned away after the canopy, after the sea, after the resurrection of verse 56, after the pardon of verse 52. The recital's whole accumulation of favors stands behind the adverb, and the adverb converts the turning into the sūrah's definition of ingratitude: not failing to see, but walking away from what was seen. The verse states the turn in the barest grammar available — a verb, a pronoun, a time-word — because elaboration would soften it. Every defense a reader might reach for (we did not know, we were not shown, we were never asked) has been pre-filed in the preceding twenty verses, and *afterwards* closes the file.

**The Counterfactual of Loss**

The second sentence is a conditional about a history that did not happen: *had it not been for Allah's grace and mercy upon you, you would have certainly been of the losers*. The *lawlā* construction — were it not for — states the community's actual position by naming the alternative it escaped. The turn away deserved a consequence, and the verse identifies the consequence precisely: loss, *khusr*, the sūrah's commercial word for the soul that trades its capital for nothing. The counterfactual does two kinds of work at once. Juridically, it establishes that the turning-away merited ruin — the grace was not the payment of a debt but the interception of a verdict. Pedagogically, it teaches the community to read its own survival: everything this people still has after the turning — covenant, scripture, posterity, the standing offer of repentance — exists inside the intercepted alternative, on loan from two divine attributes. The Qur'an's counterfactuals are among its sharpest instruments, because they force gratitude to reckon with what was deserved. A community that reads only its blessings grows entitled; a community that reads the sentence suspended over its blessings grows careful. The verse is the recital's balance-sheet moment: here is what you did, here is what you earned, here is the two names standing between you and it.

**Faḍl and Raḥma: The Two Names That Intercepted**

The interception runs through a pair: *faḍl* and *raḥma* — grace and mercy. The two nouns are not synonyms stacked for emphasis; they name distinct operations, and the pair's division of labor is exact. *Faḍl* is surplus: giving beyond what is owed, beyond what is earned, beyond the measure of the deed — the word the Qur'an uses for provision granted without accounting, for reward multiplied past the act's worth. *Raḥma* is tenderness toward the miserable: care that reaches a recipient in a condition it cannot remedy itself — the womb-root's mercy, moving toward need rather than toward merit. The turning-away community stood in need of both operations at once: it had earned less than it had (so surplus was required — faḍl), and it was in a condition it could not exit unaided (so descending care was required — raḥma). The pair appears across the Qur'an as the standing formula of rescue — the believers hold their direction of prayer through Allah's faḍl and raḥma, the sūrah's own verse on the qibla test closes on Allah as Raʾūf and Raḥīm toward humanity (2:143) — and its filing here, immediately after the turning-away, makes the theological point the recital keeps proving: the covenant survives its breaches because its divine side runs on grace-and-mercy rather than on match-and-mirror. The human side turns; the divine side's response is governed by names that do not.

**What the Mountain Could Not Do**

Verse 63's canopy produced a pledge; verse 64 records that the pledge did not hold. The pair of verses states, in the Qur'an's own sequence, a limit on terror: fear compels the tongue but does not convert the heart, and a covenant signed under a hovering mountain requires a different power to keep. The sūrah had already legislated the alternative — verse 45's method clause: seek help through patience and prayer, the disciplines that hold a person on the line after the line's terror has faded. Verse 63's own purpose clause said the same thing from the other end: hold firmly, remember, *so perhaps you will become mindful* — taqwā formed by grip and memory, not by fright. Verse 64 is the demonstration of why the purpose clause was needed. The raised mountain is thus given its exact weight in the recital's theology: enough to arrest a refusal, not enough to found a fidelity. What fidelity requires is the pair of this verse — grace that gives the turning-away community a second standing, mercy that keeps working on hearts the mountain could only shake. The sequence fright → pledge → turn → grace is the sūrah's whole account of how law alone fares with human beings, and it is why the recital never relies on severity twice: every terror in the file is followed by provision, every collapse by an intercepted verdict.

**Of the Losers**

The verdict intercepted is named in the sūrah's market idiom: *you would have been of the losers* — *la-kuntum min al-khāsirīn*. Loss, in this sūrah, is never vague misfortune but failed exchange: its opening portraits buy misguidance at the price of guidance and complete the purchase without profit (2:16); its hypocrites deal in deception that returns on the dealers; its deniers trade the eternal for the fleeting. To be *of the losers* is membership in that company — the people whose ledger shows capital spent on nothing. The commercial frame sharpens the counterfactual's arithmetic. The turning-away was itself a transaction: the covenant's obligations set down, the covenant's benefits retained as far as possible, the direction of trade reversed. What grace intercepts is not a mood but a deal — the completed sale of a delivered people's standing for the price of an unkept pledge. And the *min* of membership does its habitual work: the losers are a class, and the intercepted community was one clause away from enrollment. The sūrah's readers stand inside the same grammar. Every turning-away is a small purchase in the same market, and the verse states what keeps any buyer out of the losers' roll: not the buyer's discipline, but the two names that move before the transaction settles — grace upon you, mercy upon you.

**The Mercy That Keeps the Case File Open**

The verse's placement makes it the recital's refrain in miniature. Between the mountain and this sentence, the file has already run its cycle once: sin, consequence, pardon, purpose (the calf, the stroke, the reversal, the gratitude-clauses). Verse 64 compresses the whole cycle into two sentences — the turn stated, the interception stated — and thereby publishes the rule by which the rest of the recital will be read. Nothing after this verse surprises: the gate's mockers, the table's complainers, the calf's builders are all communities turning away afterwards, and all of them are still being addressed, which means the interception is still standing. The final audience of the verse is the individual reader, and its grammar is built for that transfer: *upon you* is second-person, and the counterfactual is addressed to anyone who has ever walked away from a covenant they signed under conviction. The sūrah's answer to every such walk is this verse's answer — not a demand to un-walk it by willpower, but the naming of what has been holding the file open the whole time: faḍl that keeps giving past the deserving, raḥma that keeps descending into the condition. The turning-away is real, the loss is earned, and the two names are greater than both — which is the only reason verse 65 can go on to address the same community again.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:65

> You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath. We said to them, “Be disgraced apes!”

**Expanded Commentary**

**“You Are Already Aware”**

The verse opens by assuming knowledge: *you have known* — *wa-laqad ʿalimtum* — those of you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath. The addressees are not being told a story; they are being reminded of a case in their own communal memory, one their tradition preserved and their scholars recited. The assumption of shared knowledge does rhetorical work no new information could: a charge the accused already knows cannot be met with denial, and the verse proceeds directly to the verdict. The *of you* — *alladhīna iʿtadaw minkum* — keeps the inheritance logic of the whole address: the Sabbath-breakers are filed inside the community's own *you*, ancestors whose case belongs to the descendants as the sea and the calf did. And the word for their act is *iʿtadaw* — from the same root as verse 61's closing charge, violations, the crossing of set bounds. The recital has been accumulating this root: transgression at the table, transgression at the gate, and now transgression in the calendar. The verse names the specific bound — *fī al-sabt*, in the matter of the Sabbath — because the Sabbath was the one commandment written into time itself: a weekly border, recurring, unmissable, equally binding on the rich and the poor. The bound chosen for this case file is the one no member of the community could claim not to see.

**The Test Engineered at the Seaside**

Sūrah al-Aʿrāf preserves the scene in full, and its details explain why the Qur'an calls the event a test: *"Ask them ˹O Prophet˺ about ˹the people of˺ the town which was by the sea, who broke the Sabbath. During the Sabbath, ˹abundant˺ fish would come to them clearly visible, but on other days the fish were never seen. In this way We tested them for their rebelliousness"* (7:163). The arrangement is deliberate provocation by arrangement: a fishing town whose fish appeared, visibly, in abundance, only on the one day work was forbidden — appetite maximized exactly where law interdicted. The exegetes read the visible abundance as the test's precision instrument: the fish were not merely present but *shurraʿan*, surfacing in plain sight, engineered temptation in the town's own harbor. The Sabbath itself carried the covenant's weight — al-Nisāʾ lists its keeping among the terms of the firm pledge taken under the mountain (4:154) — so the weekly surfacing was a weekly audit of the pledge. The verse in al-Baqarah assumes the whole apparatus and states only the breach and the sentence, because for its first audience the apparatus was known: the town by the sea was a case recited in their own houses, and the Qur'an's reminder needed only the case number.

**The Town's Three Companies**

Al-Aʿrāf's filing adds the social anatomy of the breach, and it belongs to any honest reading of the sentence. The town held three groups: the transgressors, who fished; a company that warned and forbade; and a company that questioned the warners — *"Why do you ˹bother to˺ warn those ˹Sabbath-breakers˺ who will either be destroyed or severely punished by Allah?"* — answered by the warners with the sūrah's whole doctrine of public admonition: *"Just to be free from your Lord's blame, and so perhaps they may abstain"* (7:164). The answer defines the warner's two reasons: discharge — the obligation of forbidding evil falls on the one who knows, whatever the target's response — and hope — *perhaps* they will abstain, the same particle that governs the recital's purpose clauses. Verse 65's audience in Madina had just been addressed about this exact obligation: the scholars who preach righteousness and exempt themselves (2:44). The town scene is that verse's case law. When the warning was ignored, the outcome sorted the companies: *"We rescued those who used to warn against evil and overtook the wrongdoers with a dreadful punishment"* (7:165). The rescued are named by their warning — not by their fishing-abstinence alone but by their standing in the breach and speaking. The third company's fate the exegetes debate; the text's emphasis falls where the warners' answer put it: the blame discharged is the blamer's own salvation.

**“Be Disgraced Apes”**

The sentence is four words: *kunū qiradatan khāsiʾīn* — be apes, disgraced. The imperative of being — *kun* — is the Qur'an's creative command, the word that makes rather than requests; the transformation is filed as divine speech act, instantaneous and total. *Khāsiʾūn* adds the condition attached to the new form: driven away, disgraced, banished — the word used elsewhere of a dog slinking off and of the punished cast out from favor. Al-Aʿrāf files the same sentence with its precondition: *"But when they stubbornly persisted in violation, We said to them, 'Be disgraced apes!'"* (7:166) — persistence first, transformation second; the sentence lands after the warning was refused and the violation hardened into custom. The exegetical debate over the transformation's mode is old: the majority reads it bodily and literal — the Qur'an's plain statement, confirmed by al-Māʾidah's mention of people Allah reduced to apes and pigs (5:60); Mujāhid read it as hearts transformed while bodies remained, comparing the metaphor of 62:5 — *"The example of those who were entrusted with ˹observing˺ the Torah but failed to do so, is that of a donkey carrying books"* — where the animal is admittedly likeness. The bodily reading is stronger: the Qur'an distinguishes clearly between its *mathal*-parables, which announce themselves as likenesses, and its *masakh*-transformations, which are stated as events; 5:60's phrasing — reduced to apes and pigs — describes a fate, not a figure. The metaphorical reading keeps the moral truth the literal one contains: the form followed the nature. A people whose humanity had become purely appetitive — surfacing fish as the only object of thought — received the body of the appetite they lived by.

**No Progeny: The Line That Ends**

The sentence raises the question every generation asks of it, and the Prophet ﷺ answered the question directly. When the metamorphosed peoples were mentioned before him — the monkeys, and as one narrator recalls, the pigs — he said: *"Verily, Allah did not cause the race of those which suffered metamorphosis to grow or they were not survived by young ones. Monkeys and swine had been in existence even before"* (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2663b). The ruling has two clauses, and each does theological work. The metamorphosed left no offspring: the transformation was terminal for the transformed, a dead end rather than a new species — which answers the naturalist objection that today's apes would then be human descendants, and preserves the punishment's character as extinction-of-a-people rather than origin-of-a-kind. And monkeys and swine already existed: the animal forms were not created at the transformation but entered by it. The ḥadīth thereby fixes the punishment's semantics: *masakh* is not evolution but verdict — a soul's removal from the human register, complete with the loss of what makes human life continue, posterity. The transformed did not become ancestors; they became a case, which is exactly how verse 65's continuation files them. For the town's story the clause adds its final severity: the Sabbath-breakers did not merely change shape. Their line ended with them, and the fish they surfaced for found no heirs.

**The Sin's Shape: Law Kept, Intent Broken**

The exegetical tradition preserves the mechanism of the breach, and the mechanism is the verse's permanent warning. The townsfolk, the reports relate, did not simply cast nets on the Sabbath: they engineered around it — channels dug and pools dammed before the holy day, so the surfacing fish would be trapped by Saturday's tide and gathered on Sunday. The letter stood; the intent was gutted. The Qur'an's own text supports the reading of engineered breach: the fish came *on* the Sabbath visibly and not on other days (7:163), and the response was *iʿtidāʾ* — transgression, working the bound rather than keeping it. Islamic jurisprudence built its doctrine of *ḥiyal* — legal fictions, contrivances that preserve a form while defeating its purpose — in the shadow of this case: the jurists cite the Sabbath-town as the archetype of the sin that keeps the words and kills the ruling, and the transformation as its verdict. The shape matters beyond its history because it is the most portable sin in the catalogue. Table-complaints and mocked gates are sins of appetite and insolence, visible in the act; the contrived breach is a sin of jurisprudence — committed by people who know the law precisely enough to route around it, and who are therefore the hardest to convict before men. Before Allah the routing is the aggravation: the town that studied its harbor's calendar and built its workaround had not failed to understand the Sabbath. It had understood it well enough to defeat it, and the sentence that fell on understanding of that kind was not a fine but a species-change.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:66

> So We made their fate an example to present and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Nakāl: The Punishment Designed to Be Seen**

The verse's central word is *nakāl* — rendered here *an example*, and carrying in its root the whole logic of exemplary punishment. *N-k-l* names a penalty imposed not only on its bearer but on its audience: the punishment that makes an example, that others look at and are restrained by — the same root as the ankle-shackle, the restraint worn by the one who must not move. A punishment as nakāl is therefore doubled in its economy. It pays the debt of the punished — the sentence deserved, the verdict executed — and it works on everyone who ever hears of it, converting a completed event into a standing deterrent. The Qur'an uses the word sparingly and always at its heaviest scenes: Pharaoh's punishment is nakāl for the hereafter and the first life, the double-term severity of a tyrant made into permanent exhibit. The Sabbath-town's fate receives the same instrument. The transformed people are gone — no progeny, the line ended — and what remains of them is exactly what the verse says: a case. The event has been converted from history into equipment, and the conversion is divine action: *We made it* — the nakāl is not what audiences happen to do with the story but what Allah filed the story as.

**“To What Is Before It and Behind It”**

The nakāl's range is stated in a spatial-temporal formula the exegetes read three ways: *li-mā bayna yadayhā wa-mā khalfahā* — for what is between its hands and what is behind it. The dominant reading is temporal: for the generations present at the event and the generations after — the punishment's deterrence running forward through time, every later community a beneficiary of the town's sentence. The second reading keeps the idiom spatial — *between the hands* meaning ahead, in front: for the surrounding settlements of that region and those behind them, the deterrent working geographically across the neighborhood that watched the fish-traps fill. The third reads the referent as sins rather than people: an expiation and restraint for the offenses before it and after it — the punishment settling the town's earlier trespasses and foreclosing later ones in the same stroke. The readings are compatible rather than competing, and their compatibility is the formula's point: the nakāl's jurisdiction is total in every dimension — the town's own past, its region's present, posterity's future. The temporal reading carries the verse's main weight, because verse 66 exists to explain why the story is being recited in Madina centuries later: the audience of the recital *is* the *mā khalfahā*, the behind-it, receiving the sentence as it was designed to be received — at a distance, through speech, as restraint.

**Mawʿiẓah: The Admonition and Its Addressees**

The second filing of the punishment is *mawʿiẓah* — admonition, exhortation, lesson — and its addressees are named: *li-l-muttaqīn*, for the God-fearing. The word carries both registers the classical lexicons record: counsel that draws the hearer toward good, and reprimand that pushes from evil — the single term covering the lesson's two faces, because a warning is simultaneously an invitation. The addressee-naming is the verse's most deliberate stroke. A punishment made nakāl addresses everyone through fear; the same punishment made mawʿiẓah addresses the muttaqīn through recognition. The distinction is the sūrah's own opening distinction — the Book as guidance *for the God-conscious* (2:2), a benefit that lands only where the landing-conditions exist. A lesson requires a faculty to receive it, and taqwā is that faculty: the settled carefulness about Allah's bounds that lets a person hear an old sentence as addressed to himself. Without it the same story is anecdote — entertainment at the ancestors' expense, or tribal polemic, or nothing. The verse thus splits its own audience: the nakāl restrains the outward person in whoever hears it, and the mawʿiẓah reforms the inward person in whoever fears. Both are mercy; the second requires cooperation, which is why it is restricted by name rather than by exclusion — the God-fearing are not a tribe but a condition, and the condition is open to every hearer the recital reaches.

**How a Punishment Becomes a Lesson**

The mechanism by which an event centuries dead performs this double work is the recital itself, and the verse is the recital's statement of purpose. The town's transformation is inaccessible to the senses now — no ruins of apes, no surviving witnesses — yet the nakāl operates because the event was preserved in revelation and is being read aloud in Madina. The Qur'an's own narration is the delivery system of the lesson: the same speech that files the punishment enacts its forward reach, carrying it across the generations the formula names. This is why the Qur'an insists on its stories as *aḥsan al-qaṣaṣ*, the best of narrations (12:3), and files its penalties with narrative care — the punishment of Pharaoh's body preserved explicitly so that it may become a sign for those who come after (10:92), the Sabbath-town narrated across three sūrahs. Every major penalty in the Book carries its transmission clause, and verse 66 is the clause in its purest form: the event's afterlife as lesson is part of the sentence. The reader's position in the mechanism deserves exact statement, because it defines what reading this verse is doing: to receive the mawʿiẓah is to be the *mā khalfahā* functioning as designed — the punishment completing its second purpose in the heart of someone the town never met. A lesson unlearned is a nakāl half-executed; the verse files the audience as the sentence's remaining half.

**The Saved Companies and the Lesson's Full Text**

The mawʿiẓah's content is larger than the transformation, and the fuller filing in al-Aʿrāf shows why. That sūrah's account preserves the town's three companies — the breakers, the warners, and the questioners of the warning — and preserves the outcome's sorting: the warners rescued, named by their warning (7:165). Read as one lesson, the case teaches more than *do not break the bound*. It teaches the structure of a community under test: that transgression in a town is never only the transgressors' affair, that standing in the breach with a spoken warning is itself a form of keeping the Sabbath, and that the rescue is attached by name to the warning rather than to private abstention. The questioners of al-Aʿrāf's account — why bother warning the doomed? — voice the fatigue the lesson exists to answer, and the warners' reply (discharge before Allah, hope for the target) is the lesson's positive text. Verse 66's two nouns thus divide the case's teaching cleanly: the nakāl is the negative half, the fate of the breakers restraining every hearer from the engineered breach; the mawʿiẓah is the positive half, the fate of the warners instructing every God-fearing hearer what to do in a town where the fish surface on the forbidden day. A lesson with only its first half produces fear without direction; the Qur'an files both.

**Deterrence and Mercy in One Sentence**

The verse's pairing of nakāl and mawʿiẓah states the Qur'an's whole philosophy of penalty in one sentence, and the pairing is not balanced by accident. Deterrence alone would make the punishment pure power — a display for its effect on others, using the punished as instrument. Admonition alone would make it pure speech — a lesson detachable from any consequence. Joined, they keep each other honest: the lesson is serious because it was purchased with a real sentence, and the sentence is purposeful because it was filed as teaching. The same structure runs through the recital's whole treatment of this community — severity that is always also pedagogy, from the stroke that answered the demand for sight through the covering of disgrace that answered the table-complaint. And the structure extends to the verse's position in the address to Madina: a community being audited across twenty-odd verses of its ancestors' file is receiving, in the audit's form, exactly what the Sabbath-town received — the record of penalties made into forward-facing instruction. The difference is the audience's advantage. The town learned nothing until the sentence fell; Madina is being given the sentence before its own breach, and every reader after Madina inherits the same precedence. That is the mercy inside the mechanism: the nakāl travels ahead of the sin it restrains, so the generations behind the town can keep the bound the town broke — warned by a punishment already paid for.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:67

> And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow.” They replied, “Are you mocking us?” Moses responded, “I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sūrah Named for a Cow**

The longest sūrah of the Qur'an takes its title from this episode: al-Baqarah, the Cow. The naming is itself an exegetical act — of the sūrah's hundreds of rulings, narratives, and arguments, the tradition's chosen identifier is a story about a commanded sacrifice and the reception it met. The episode is also, as the commentators note, unusually detailed by Qur'anic standards: where the Book typically compresses a narrative to its moral geometry, this one runs across several verses of dialogue, question and answer, specification and response. The detail is the reason for the naming. The sūrah's central subject is how a covenant community handles what it is given — scripture, provision, commands — and no scene in the recital displays the handling's failure mode as precisely as a command received with a sarcasm-question. The cow-episode is al-Baqarah in miniature: a divine order, minimal in its terms; a human reception that converts the order into an occasion; and a negotiation that costs the receivers everything the order was going to give them cheaply. A sūrah that legislates prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, marriage, debt, and war names itself after this exchange because the exchange determines whether any legislation will be carried at all.

**A Command With No Specifications**

The order arrives in six words: *Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow*. Its remarkable feature is what it lacks. No age, no color, no lineage, no number — an indefinite noun, *baqarah*, any cow. In a law-code whose later sūrahs will specify sacrificial animals down to their condition and season, this command is maximally general, and the generality is the test's design. A specific command tests obedience's precision; a general command tests obedience's willingness. Any cow would have discharged the order, which means the entire difficulty of the episode was manufactured by the receivers: the command's ease was total, and everything hard about it entered through the response. The exegetical tradition preserves the Prophet's ﷺ verdict on the exchange in exactly these terms: had they taken the nearest cow and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed them — the report standing as the tradition's summary of the whole negotiation. The indefinite command also frames what follows as revelation's standing lesson on the cost of interrogation: every question put to a general order has the power to narrow it, and narrowing an easy command converts ease into difficulty. The order said *a cow*; the dialogue will end with a cow so specified that only one in the region answers the description — and the distance between those two points is the verse's moral geography.

**“Are You Mocking Us?”**

The response to the command is a question about the commander's sincerity: *a-tastahziʾu bi-nā* — are you mocking us? The word is *istihzāʾ*, jest, derision — the accusation that a deadly-serious divine order is a joke. The inversion in the response is total and worth stating exactly: the most serious possible speech — *Allah commands you* — is received as the least serious possible speech. Nothing in the exchange yet justifies the reading; the command is plain, its source is named, its prophet is the one who parted the sea before their eyes. The mockery-accusation therefore tells the reader about the accusers rather than the accusation: these are hearts for which a divine command has become unsayable in plain terms, so it must be deflected as humor before it can be either accepted or refused. Deflection is the response's function. To accept the order means to slaughter; to refuse it outright means open rebellion under a covenant just re-signed at the mountain; to call it mockery means neither — the command is suspended in the ambiguity of a joke, and the receivers keep their options. The Qur'an names this exact posture elsewhere as the habit of hearts hardening after long acquaintance with signs, and the recital's placement of the scene — directly after the covenant filings and the turning-away — files the mockery-question as the sound a turning-away heart makes when addressed again.

**The Prophet's Refuge**

Moses's answer is not anger, correction, or argument — it is *istiʿādha*: *I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant*. The prophet treats the mockery-accusation as a contagion to be fled rather than a charge to be answered, and the refuge-formula reveals his diagnosis: to trade jest for jest, to meet derision with heat, is to join the *jāhilūn* — and the word in Qur'anic usage names far more than missing information. *Jahl* in this Book is a disposition: the settled preference for one's own way over known truth, the active state the prophets are warned against joining — *do not be one of those ignorant* is the address to a prophet grieving others' denial (6:35); Noah is warned not to ask *about what you have no knowledge of*, lest he fall into ignorance (11:46); Joseph prays to be kept from yielding *and falling into ignorance* (12:33). In all three the ignorance is moral motion, not cognitive lack — and the same word, in its social form *jāhiliyyah*, will name the entire pre-Islamic order of tribal insolence. Moses's refuge therefore answers the mockery-question at its root: you ask whether I jest; I seek Allah's protection from the condition that would make me jest with a command of Allah, or answer your jest in kind. The prophet models the only safe handling of derision aimed at revelation — neither absorbing its frame nor returning its tone — and the model became Islamic etiquette: the answer to *are you joking?* is not a joke but a refuge.

**Excessive Questioning Destroys**

The scene the verse opens is the Qur'an's case law for a principle the Prophet ﷺ stated as legislation. Asked, when Hajj was made obligatory, whether it applied every year, he declined the question three times and then said: *"Leave me with what I have left to you, for those who were before you were destroyed because of excessive questioning, and their opposition to their apostles. So when I command you to do anything, do it as much as it lies in your power and when I forbid you to do anything, then abandon it"* (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1337). The ḥadīth names the cow's questioners explicitly as the destroyed-people archetype — *those who were before you* — and states the mechanism: questioning multiplies obligation, and multiplied obligation breaks compliance. The man who asked *every year?* risked making Hajj annual by asking; the people who asked *what cow?* made their one-cow order into a unique-cow hunt.
