For the believers of Madina the scene was evidence of a specific kind: the Prophet ﷺ had not attended those councils, and no informant could have carried their content in this compression; the recital's reach into the private room was itself the argument that its source stood outside every room. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān files the same exposure with the same anatomy — *"When they meet you they say, 'We believe.' But when alone, they bite their fingertips in rage"* — and draws the verse's general law: *Surely Allah knows best what is ˹hidden˺ in the heart* (3:119). The two rooms are, before Allah, one room; the partition the conspirators built runs between themselves and each other, never between the scene and its Recorder. That is the verse's permanent edge for every reader: the counsel of closed doors is already transcribed, the disclosure they feared has occurred in the only forum that decides — and the believers' advantage in that forum was never information but the fact that they said the same thing in both rooms.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:77

> Do they not know that Allah is aware of what they conceal and what they reveal?

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Shortest Sentence, the Widest Surveillance**

Seven words in the translation close the scene the previous verse staged at length. The two rooms — the public confession, the private counsel — are collapsed into a single question: do they not know that Allah knows what they hide and what they show? The compression is the verse's method. After the conspirators' argument has been quoted in full, with its premises, its fear, and its internal rebuke, the recital does not answer it point by point; it asks whether the arguers have noticed the audience. Every calculation in the private room assumed a bounded disclosure — knowledge dangerous only if it reached the believers, a case lost only if the evidence surfaced before people. The verse removes the boundary: the disclosure they were managing has already happened, continuously, to the only party whose knowledge decides anything. A rhetorical question of this brevity functions as a verdict rather than an inquiry — the facts are not in dispute, only the defendants' awareness of the facts — and its placement makes it the hinge of the whole passage: verses 75–76 built the case of informed concealment, and verse 77 states the condition that makes concealment incoherent. The sūrah's longest argument with a community is here reduced to its smallest form, and the smallest form is the strongest.

**A Theme With No Exception in the Book**

The knowledge of hidden and manifest is the Qur'an's most ubiquitous divine attribute after mercy, and its ubiquity is the verse's warrant. Sūrah al-Naml states it in the same pairing: *"And surely your Lord knows what their hearts conceal and what they reveal"* (27:74) — hearts specified, the seat of the private room named as transparent. The same declaration recurs across the revelation — Allah knows what is in the souls, knows the secret and the more secret, knows what the breasts conceal — in verse after verse the recital could cite (21:110, 24:29, 28:69, 33:54, 36:76). The divine names gather it: Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Great, the Exalted — the pairing that closes the sūrah's own verse of the Throne (2:255). The cumulative effect is a cosmology without interior walls: there is no category of the concealed that functions as concealment before Allah, and every human institution built on that category — secrets, cabals, double scripts, the managed disclosure of verse 76 — is built on a local fiction. The verse's question form (*do they not know?*) presumes the answer is available knowledge: this is not esoteric doctrine but published revelation, stated so often that ignorance of it is itself a choice. The conspirators of the previous verse knew it as text and forgot it as fact — which is the precise failure the question exposes.

**The Practical Atheism of the Private Room**

The question's target is not unbelief but inoperative belief. The men of verse 76 affirmed the Lord, the revelation, and the Day — their counsel quoted all three. What their conduct denied was the bearing of those affirmations on the room they were sitting in: a plan built to keep knowledge from Allah's witnesses, as if the witnesses were the whole jury. Islamic moral theology has a name for the structure — living as though the unseen were absent, the practical atheism of hearts whose creed is sound and whose calculations exclude it. The sūrah's opening had diagnosed the same condition from the other side: the disbelievers warned that a seal has been set (2:7), the organ of reckoning closed; verse 77 describes its softer variant, where the reckoning is acknowledged verbally and omitted operationally. The distinction the verse installs is between knowledge-that and knowledge-in-force: they know *that* Allah knows, and the question asks whether they know it in the way that reorganizes behavior. The answer their counsel gave is on record — a disclosure policy with no line-item for divine awareness — and the policy is the verse's indictment. This is why the question is addressed to *them* in the third person rather than as a rebuke spoken to their faces: it is diagnostic speech, filed for the believers' education, describing a condition the recital's audience is being inoculated against.

**The Collapse of the Two Rooms**

The verse's two objects — what they conceal, what they reveal — name the distinction the private room lived by, and the single verb governing both abolishes it. Before people, concealment and disclosure are different acts with different consequences; the hidden word travels no further than its hearers, the public word goes on record. Before Allah the two stand in one field of knowledge, equally present, equally preserved — and the verse's grammar enacts the leveling: one knower, two objects, no difference in the knowing. The collapse has an immediate practical reading, which the tradition made into a virtue's definition: sincerity is the private room behaving like the public one, the believer whose concealed and revealed are the same substance because both are addressed to the same Witness. It also has a judicial reading, which the recital is running: the evidence the conspirators feared disclosing is not being gathered from informants but from the field itself — nothing needs to leak where nothing was ever sealed. The verse thus completes verse 76's exposure from inside its own logic. Their question was *will you tell them?* The recital's answer is that telling was never the mechanism: the knowledge is not moving toward Allah, because with Allah it never moved. Every reader inherits the architecture — the rooms everyone keeps, the words budgeted for privacy — and the verse states the only fact about them that finally matters: the budget is imaginary, the rooms are one, and the audit verse 74 announced — Allah's never being unaware of what we do — has been running the whole time.

**One Attribute, Two Readings of the Same News**

The knowledge verse 77 announces is the recital's most double-edged fact, and its two edges are filed in the sūrah itself. Against the concealer it is threat without remainder: no strategy survives contact with an omniscient opponent, and the litigation posture of verse 76 — managing evidence before the Lord — is revealed as the one unwinnable case. Toward the sincere it turns as comfort with the same remainder: the nearness the sūrah will state in its own terms — *I am truly near. I respond to one's prayer when they call upon Me* (2:186) — is the identical attribute experienced from the other side. The heart's concealed prayer, the unspoken grief, the goodness nobody witnessed: all of it is known, which means none of it is lost. The two readings are not different doctrines but one fact meeting two postures — the hidden contents of a soul that fears exposure, and the hidden contents of a soul that trusts. The verse's placement between the exposure of hypocrisy and the recital's continuing audit fixes its function as the passage's ground rule: everything filed after it — the ransom, the distortions, the claims about the Fire, the covenant breaches to come — is evidence in a court whose judge reads the sealed file as easily as the open one. *Do they not know?* The question is the recital's standing invitation to move from the first room to the second, and to discover that there was only ever one.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:78

> And among them are the illiterate who know nothing about the Scripture except lies, and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Class: The People Below the Scholars**

The recital completes its social anatomy. Verse 75 indicted a group that heard Allah's word and distorted it knowingly; verse 76 recorded the closed-door counsel that managed what the confession would concede. Now the camera widens: *and among them are the illiterate* — a third class inside the same community, the people who never heard, never read, and never distorted anything, because the Book never reached them except through other mouths. The sūrah is describing the structure of a scriptural religion as it actually exists on the ground: a literate clerical class holding the text, and beneath it a vast population whose religion is what the class transmits. The verse's charge is not the heavy one — no distortion, no conspiracy — but it is a charge nonetheless: their knowledge of the Scripture runs to nothing but lies, and what they hold is wishful speculation. The illiterate are indicted for the shape of their knowing: a religion held without verification, received without the capacity to check, resting where its teachers left it. The three verses together file the whole pyramid, and the sūrah's point sharpens: the call now being made in Madina cannot pass through this structure, because the structure itself is what the verses describe.

**Ummī: What the Word Carries**

The term — *ummiyyūn* — is doing careful work. In the usage the exegetes settle on, an *ummī* is one who cannot write, or cannot write well: the condition of the majority in a world where literacy was a trade. The commentators note the qualification honestly: literacy in Arabia, Jewish and Arab alike, was partial — some read and wrote fluently, some managed a rudimentary script, and the fully literate were a small fraction of the whole. A minority opinion attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās reads the word differently — a people acknowledging no prophet and no revealed book, called *ummiyyūn* precisely for that opposition to the Books of Allah — but the tradition itself marks this reading as unconvincing against the ordinary sense of the word. The term carries a second life in the Qur'an that makes its appearance here resonate: the coming Prophet is announced as *the unlettered Prophet* whom they find written in their own Torah and Gospel (7:157), and Sūrah al-Jumuʿah describes a Messenger raised *from among the unlettered* (62:2). Illiteracy in the recital's vocabulary is neither insult nor virtue but a condition — and the verse's illiterate are defined by it tragically: cut off from the Book by the very lack that, in another people, would make the Book's arrival among them the miracle it became.

**Amānī: The Lies and the Stories One Wants**

What the illiterate have instead of the Scripture is named in the Arabic *amānī* — rendered here *lies* — a word the tradition reads from two sides, and both sides belong to the verse. On one reading it means the reports they are told: their knowledge of Scripture is exactly what their scholars choose to say it is, religion received secondhand from the same class the previous verses convicted. On the other it means the things invented and wished for — the doctrines of comfort the community prefers: that the Fire will hold them only a counted number of days, that the Garden admits no one outside their own two communities. The word can be rendered lies, hearsay, hopes, or desires, and its semantic field — stories heard and stories wanted — is precisely the material an unverified religion runs on. The double sense is the verse's diagnosis in a single term: without access to the Book, the laity cannot distinguish what was transmitted from what was consoling, and the class above them, as verses 75–76 established, has both the means and the motive to blur the line. *Amānī* is scripture-by-rumor plus scripture-by-wish, and the illiterate hold it with full confidence and zero ground.

**“They Wishfully Speculate”**

The closing verb fixes the epistemic status of the whole: they *speculate* — wishfully, as the translation marks it — the Arabic *yaẓunnūn*: they conjecture, suppose, and guess. The exegetes gloss it sharply: they lie about Allah, or they think false things about Him — conjecture that has hardened into assertion. The Qur'an's epistemology runs on a distinction this verb draws cleanly: knowledge (*ʿilm*) rests on revelation received and verified; *ẓann* is everything short of it — inference, hearsay, presumption — and when *ẓann* occupies the place of knowledge in religion, the occupation is itself the sin. The illiterate's tragedy is that their conjecture is involuntary in origin: they cannot read the Book, so guessing is all the machinery they have. Yet the verse does not excuse them, and the reason is the verse's transferable lesson: they accepted a religious certainty whose warrant they never sought, from custodians whose trade the recital has just exposed. Conjecture filed as conviction is the layperson's taḥrīf — the same slant between word and meaning, produced below stairs by credulity instead of above by design. The sūrah's running audit of reason — the repeated *do you not understand?* — has its negative case here: a community whose majority has stopped needing reasons at all.

**The Corruption Chain, Top to Bottom**

Read in sequence, verses 75 through 78 describe a system, and the system is the verse's real subject. At the top: scholars who heard Allah's word, understood it, and distorted it knowingly. Around them: a private council governing what may be admitted in public, afraid of their own scripture's contents reaching rival hands. Beneath them: the illiterate majority whose entire religion is what the council permits to circulate — hearsay shaped above, conjecture held below. The flow runs one way: the literate manufacture the distortion and the unlettered consume it, and the consumer's inability to check is what makes the manufacturer's crime profitable. Accountability in the recital attaches at both ends of the chain — the verse files the illiterate's condition as culpable ignorance, the ignorance of those who took a religion on terms that made verification impossible by construction. For the young Muslim community hearing this recitation, the anatomy was immediate equipment: they were being told why the scholars of Madina would not simply hand their congregations the truth if it were shown them — the congregations had no independent access to the truth to begin with, and the custodians' position depended on keeping it that way.

**The Unlettered Nation and the Book It Cannot Alter**

The verse's irony completes itself in the community addressed. The Prophet ﷺ described his own people in the same term: *"We are an illiterate nation; we neither write, nor know accounts"* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1913) — the ḥadīth's context is the lunar calendar, a ruling that fasting follows the seen crescent rather than calculation, and its self-description is exact: an *ummī* ummah. Yet the Qur'an's preservation runs through precisely this condition as its instrument. The revelation given to the unlettered Prophet was lodged not in manuscripts held by a class but in mass-recited memory — thousands of chests carrying the same text, generation upon generation, a transmission model in which the hearsay chain of verse 78 is structurally impossible: where every layperson carries the Book itself, no council can manage what the laity know. The contrast is the recital's quiet argument for its own audience. Israel's Scripture became, in the verse's description, a text the many could not check and the few could slant; the Qur'an answers by making its whole community the manuscript. The illiterate of verse 78 are pitiable and culpable at once — and the ummah hearing the verse is being shown, in the same breath, what its own unletteredness was arranged to prevent.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:79

> So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, “This is from Allah”—seeking a fleeting gain! So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they have earned.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sentence of Wayl**

The recital's diagnosis ends and its verdict begins, in the heaviest single word the Qur'an deploys against a crime of the pen. *Wayl* — woe — is an ordinary Arabic cry of ruin, the exclamation of one who has seen the bottom drop out, and the Qur'an uses it as a standing formula of condemnation across dozens of verses. Here it falls three times in two sentences: woe to those who write; woe for what their hands have written; woe for what they earn. The triple structure is itself the ruling — the crime is cursed in its commission, its product, and its proceeds, with no remainder left unjudged. Some commentators, drawing on a report the tradition itself flags as disputed — Ibn Kathīr among those who contested it — read *wayl* as a proper name: a valley in Hell so deep that a falling denier descends forty autumns before reaching its bottom, or a mountain of blood and pus, or the very cry the punished will utter when the word becomes their only language. Whether curse or toponym, the term's function is fixed: this is the recital's maximum sentence, and it is filed not against violence or disbelief in the open field but against forgery — the manufacture of false scripture for money.

**With Their Own Hands**

The phrase the verse builds on is physical: the Scripture distorted *with their own hands* — and the Arabic beneath the translation is more literal still, naming those who write the book with their hands. The emphasis is deliberate and it narrows the indictment to an act of production. Verse 75 charged distortion of a word heard; this verse charges authorship — hands putting ink where Allah put nothing. The phrase *with their own hands* strips the crime of every mediating excuse: not inherited error, not drift in transmission, not the entropy of copying, but original composition by identifiable people at identifiable desks. The exegetes preserve the historical forms the charge took: accounts of writings composed and pawned off on the unlettered for small profit, and the graver account — the alteration of the prophecies describing the coming Prophet, the very portraits lodged in the Torah (7:157) reshaped so that the descriptions would fit something else. The mechanism is the fullest form of the slant the sūrah has been tracking: first the meaning is rotated inside the text, then, when rotation is not enough, the hand writes a new page and the new page enters circulation wearing the old warranty. The verse's specificity is its universality: it is addressed to every age's forgers, and every age has produced candidates, inside every tradition that keeps its faith in books.

**“Then They Say: This Is from Allah”**

The writing alone is not the crime's summit; the attribution is. *Then they say, "This is from Allah"* — the manufactured page is issued with the divine warrant attached, and the lie acquires its full structure: not merely falsehood but falsehood sold as revelation. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān states the same act in the same terms and adds the aggravation: *"They say, 'It is from Allah'—but it is not from Allah. And ˹so˺ they attribute lies to Allah knowingly"* (3:78). The theological gravity is in the direction of the lie. To deceive a person is to wrong a person; to speak in Allah's name without Allah is to enlist the divine authority itself as the instrument of the wrong, making God — in the eyes of the deceived — the sponsor of the fabrication. The buyer of the forged page does not merely hold an error; he holds an error he believes Allah guaranteed, which immunizes it against every future correction: to question the text becomes, for him, to question God. This is why the recital ranks the crime above the distortions before it. Distortion slants a truth still present; authored attribution replaces the truth with a counterfeit wearing omnipotence as its seal — and the counterfeit's victims defend it with the sincerity real faith deserves.

**The Fleeting Gain**

The clause of commerce supplies the motive and completes the indictment: the distortion is done *seeking a fleeting gain*. The forgery is an industry — composition, warranty, sale — and the Qur'an files it under the sūrah's running economics of the sacred, which began at verse 41 with signs exchanged for a cheap price and will recur wherever the recital weighs spiritual capital against worldly cash. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān joins the two crimes in one sentence: *"Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture to make it known to people and not hide it, yet they cast it behind their backs and traded it for a fleeting gain"* (3:187) — the same custodians, the same covenant to disclose, the same small money on the other side of the scale. The phrase *fleeting gain* is the verse's own commentary on the transaction's arithmetic: an infinite authority, borrowed without right, liquidated for cash that will not outlive the seller. The tradition's historical gloss — writings sold to the unlettered of Arabia at small profit, the altered prophecies preserving a position and its revenues — keeps the motive concrete: this is not error seeking truth but truth's costume seeking income. And the price being paltry does not soften the verdict; it sharpens it. The recital's repeated astonishment is that the sacred is sold cheap — that hands which have touched the warranty of heaven settle for so little.

**Capital and Proceeds, Both Cursed**

The second sentence divides the ruin into its two accounts: woe for *what their hands have written*, and woe for *what they have earned*. The writing and the earning are cursed separately, and the separation carries a ruling. The product bears guilt even where the sale fails — the forged page is wayl's object before anyone buys it; the proceeds bear guilt even where the writing went unchallenged — income from false revelation corrupts what it touches, feeding households, purchasing standing, seeding influence from a poisoned root. The doubling also closes a circuit with the verse before it: the illiterate of verse 78 knew nothing of the Book but hearsay, and this verse shows what the hearsay was made of — pages written by hands, warranted by tongues, sold to people who could not check. Producer and market, capital and demand, in one economy of fabrication, and the woe falls on the supply side where the intelligence lives. The economic precision is the verse's enduring edge for its own community: religious income is audited by its source. What is earned by carrying a true revelation is provision; what is earned by writing a false one is wayl — and no volume of sincere buyers converts the second into the first.

**The Standing Indictment**

The verse was revealed about forgers in Madina's Scripture-market and has never since lacked addressees. Every tradition that keeps its faith in texts breeds the verse's crime: fabricated reports composed for patrons, rulings purchased, histories written to order and warranted with the sacred name — and the Islamic tradition's own response to verse 79 is its proudest institutional achievement. The sciences built to police attribution — the criticism of transmission chains, the grading of narrators, the discipline that made a report's warrant a researchable object rather than an asserted one — exist because this verse exists: a revealed immune system against the forgery of the sacred, developed by a community that took the woe personally and spent centuries engineering the checks the illiterate of verse 78 never had. The verse thereby reads in three registers at once: a historical indictment of specific hands, a permanent law of religious economics in which the counterfeit's price is always paltry and its woe never partial, and a standing instruction to every generation to keep the question verse 76's conspirators feared alive in their own houses — what Allah has actually revealed, distinguished by evidence from what hands have written and tongues have warranted. The organs named in the two sentences, the hand and the tongue, remain the only instruments of the crime, and the audit of both remains open.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:80

> ˹Some of˺ the Jews claim, “The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Have you taken a pledge from Allah— for Allah never breaks His word—or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Tariff on Hell**

The recital quotes the claim itself now, third-person as before, and the claim is a doctrine: *the Fire will not touch us except for a number of days* (2:80). The formula is precise in its comfort — the Fire is real, its touch is conceded, but its duration is capped, and the cap is national: a fixed term, after which the community's stay ends. The exegetes preserve the figures the claim circulated with. Some report forty nights, set equal to the days spent at the foot of the calf, after which another people would inherit the Fire's remainder — and some add the bitter twist that the successors named were the followers of Muhammad ﷺ. Others report forty years; others seven days, one day for each thousand years of the world's existence. Whatever the arithmetic, the structure is identical: punishment converted into a tariff, eschatology into a schedule, and the schedule set by identity rather than by deeds. The verb *touch* is the claim's own softening — contact, not residence; a brushing of the Fire against a people who have already decided, on their own authority, exactly how long the contact lasts. The recital has been documenting a community's management of revelation; here it documents the management of its consequences — a self-issued amnesty, drafted below stairs and signed in Allah's name.

**The Parallel File in Āl ʿImrān**

The same claim is quoted again in the Qur'an, and the second filing supplies the diagnosis the first leaves for the rebuttal to deliver: *"This is because they say, 'The Fire will not touch us except for a few days.' They have been deceived in their faith by their wishful lying"* (3:24). Two additions carry weight. The deception is located *in their faith* — not beside it, not in politics or profit, but inside the piety itself, which is where a false assurance does its damage: the doctrine of numbered days did not merely misdescribe the hereafter, it reorganized a community's relationship to its own sins, making repentance optional and reform affordable. And the origin is named: *their wishful lying* — fabrication with a history, a doctrine built rather than received, which connects this claim directly to the economy of verses 78–79: the illiterate holding hearsay as certainty, the hands writing what tongues warrant as divine. The numbered days are the output of that machine — an *amānī*-doctrine in the full sense of verse 78, both a story told and a story wanted, the wish for a cheap exit from the Fire wearing the dress of a revealed schedule.

**The Two-Pronged Rebuttal**

The answer comes as a command — *Say* — and it is a disjunction that leaves the claim nowhere to stand. First prong: have they *taken a pledge from Allah* (2:80)? If the numbered days are a divine promise, produce the covenant — the document, the warrant, the moment Allah committed Himself to the term. And the prong carries its own trap: *Allah never breaks His word* — if such a pledge existed, it would indeed be honored; the rebuttal does not question Allah's fidelity but the pledge's existence. No scripture given to this community contains the term, and the community whose file the sūrah has been building holds a documented history of covenant-breaking from its own side (2:40 and 2:63 among them) — a party in default invoking a contract it never signed. Second prong: or are they *just saying about Allah what you do not know* (2:80)? If there is no pledge, then the claim is not a disputed interpretation but speech about God without knowledge — the epistemological crime the recital has been charging since verse 75, where distortion followed understanding, and verse 78, where conjecture replaced the Book. The disjunction is exhaustive and both exits are convictions: either you hold a covenant you cannot produce, or you are authoring eschatology without a source. The claim's advocates have no third option, and the verse's brevity is the confidence of an argument that knows its ground.

**Where the Number Came From**

The tradition's genealogy of the claim exposes its machinery. Forty nights is not an arbitrary figure — it is the length of Moses' appointed term at the mount, the period at the end of which the community below built the calf; the claim takes a completed historical punishment, the discipline of a generation, and reissues it as a permanent eschatological ceiling: we sinned for forty days, so we burn for forty days, and then we are out. The seven-day variant runs the same operation on a larger frame — one day per millennium of the world's age, the calendar of history converted into the tariff of the Fire. In both cases the method is legible: find a number somewhere in the tradition, detach it from its context, and re-attach it to the afterlife with the force of a promise. This is taḥrīf in its speculative register — the slant applied not to a text's wording but to a number's jurisdiction — and 3:24's verdict — deception *in their faith by their wishful lying* — names the psychology: a community under the weight of its own record wanted a bounded sentence, found materials for one in its scriptures, and built the bound. The recital files the wish-doctrine with the same seriousness it files the forged page, because a purchased assurance is the most consequential counterfeit of all: it is spent at the exact moment it is needed.

**Temporary Fire — the Precise Line Islam Draws**

The verse must be read with a precision the Islamic tradition itself drew, because mainstream Islamic theology does hold that some who enter the Fire eventually leave it. The position rests on Qur'anic exceptions — *"staying there forever, as long as the heavens and the earth will endure, except what your Lord wills"* (11:107) — and on the mass of ḥadīth describing intercession for the Fire's inhabitants, believers whose sentence ends. Al-Rāzī's treatment of this verse is the tradition's sharpest instrument for keeping the two things apart. First: the verse does not deny that a soul might reside in the Fire temporarily — it rebukes this specific claim, its absurdly small number, and the impudent certainty voiced without any explicit promise from Allah. Second: no one may assume such release for themselves or their people as an entitlement, but that does not bar Allah's forgiving an individual after a period. Third — the distinction on which everything turns — there is a difference between saying *Allah will not remove a believer from the Fire* and saying *Allah never promised to remove him*: Allah may act beyond His promises, and the absence of a pledge does not bind His mercy. The sin verse 80 indicts is therefore not the hope of release but the claim of a contract: the numbered-days doctrine is a self-issued covenant, and the rebuttal's first prong — a *pledge from Allah*? — is the permanent test of every cheap assurance in every age: release belongs to Allah's mercy, which He may extend; it cannot belong to a schedule, which no one can sign for Him.

**Saying about Allah What You Do Not Know**

The second prong outlives its occasion and becomes the verse's general law. *Saying about Allah what you do not know* (2:80) is the recital's formal charge against ungrounded theology — speech about God without warrant, the sin that sits beneath the forgery of verse 79 and above the conjecture of verse 78, naming in one clause the whole corruption chain's common root. The verse installs a rule of procedure for religious claims: assertions about Allah's dealings — His promises, His punishments, His terms — require a source from Allah, and where the source is absent, the assertion is not opinion but attributed lie. The pastoral transfer to the recital's audience is immediate and uncomfortable. Every religious community generates its numbered days: assurances of national exemption, calculations that cap the consequences of collective behavior, doctrines that let a people sin on schedule. The forms change — the structure of verse 80's claim is the structure of every "God would not punish us, His people, beyond this" ever preached. The rebuttal does not change either. Have you taken a pledge? If yes, produce it. If no, then know that the mercy you are counting on is real — 39:53 forbids despairing of it — but it is Allah's to give on His terms, not yours to schedule on your own, and the difference between hoping in an unbound mercy and claiming a bound one is the difference the verse's two prongs were revealed to draw.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:81

> But no! Those who commit evil and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Balā: The Word That Overturns**

The verse opens with a single particle that answers the claim before it: *balā* — rendered here *But no!* — a word whose whole function is to reverse a preceding denial. The numbered days have just been quoted and rebutted by question; now the rebuttal becomes pronouncement. The dialogue form drops — there is no *Say* here, no argument addressed to arguers — and the recital speaks in the register of settled fact: the schedule is void, and the actual rule is filed in its place. The particle's force is corrective rather than merely negative: *balā* does not only deny the tariff, it asserts the opposite of what the denial implied. They said the Fire's touch would be brief and bounded; *balā* — the Fire's residence is real and, for the persons about to be described, without end. The shift from question to pronouncement marks the passage's judicial structure: verse 80 cross-examined the claim and found it unwarranted; verse 81 delivers the finding. And the delivery begins by defining, with surgical narrowness, exactly whom the forever binds — which is the verse's mercy to every reader not inside the definition, and the reason Islamic theology has argued over its two conditions for fourteen centuries.

**Two Conditions: Earning and Encompassment**

The persons the verdict names are defined by a double formula, and each term is load-bearing. First: *those who commit evil* — the verb is *kasaba*, to earn, to acquire, the sūrah's commercial idiom turned on the self: sin as something a person produces and takes ownership of, wages in the exact sense, the same earning-language verse 79 used for the proceeds of forgery. Second: the sinner *engrossed in sin* — the Arabic *aḥāṭat bihi khaṭīʾatuhu*: his sin has encompassed him, surrounded him, closed over him, the imagery of water over a drowned man or walls around a besieged city. The two conditions are not redundant; the second narrows the first. Not every earner of evil is encompassed by it — the formula describes a completion, and the exegetes' glosses converge on that point: the sin that encompasses is, in Ibn Kathīr's terms, the sin of one who dies in rejection; in al-Ṭabarī's reported reading, the sin of shirk, of one who meets Allah having set up rivals with Him; in another gloss, the sin that has left no good deed standing to counterbalance it. What the conditions together describe is not a lapse but a settled estate: a person whose earning has become an enclosure, whose choices have completed a character with no opening left in it. The verdict that follows — residents of the Fire, forever — is pronounced on that estate and only on it, and the precision is why the verse's first word can be *balā* without contradicting every promise of mercy in the Book.

**Residents, Forever**

The verdict itself uses the sūrah's standing eschatological formula: evildoers become *the residents of the Fire*, and they are *there forever*. The same sentence closed the recital's opening portrait of denial — those who disbelieve and reject the signs are the Fire's residents, there forever (2:39) — and its reappearance here ties the numbered-days claim to the denial it sprang from: the doctrine of a bounded Fire was a privilege claimed by people whose position the sūrah has already ruled on. *Residents* — *aṣḥāb*, companions, the people of a place, belonging to it as it belongs to them — is the verse's psychology in one word: this is not visitation but citizenship, and citizenship in the Fire is the fixed form of the character the two conditions described. *Forever* — *khālidūn… abadan* — doubles the permanence, and the doubling answers the claim's arithmetic exactly: against days numbered, duration without number. The justice of the formula reads through the encompassment: what the person built around himself in a finite life is made the shape of his infinite one, the enclosure he earned becoming the residence he keeps. The Qur'an's eschatology does not present the Fire as a caprice imposed on strangers to it but as the consummation of an encompassed self — which is also why the door the verse leaves open, in the word *encompassed*, has been the hope of every sinner who has not yet been closed over.

**The Verse in the Theological Wars**

Few Qur'anic sentences were argued over as fiercely in Islam's formative centuries, and the argument defines the verse's reception. Read maximally — *evil* meaning any grave sin — the verse became the Khārijī and Muʿtazilī proof-text: the unrepentant major sinner, they held, is the Fire's resident forever, the Muʿtazilah assigning him an intermediate station in this world and perdition in the next. The mainstream position read the two conditions together and refused the maximization: the evil that encompasses is disbelief and association, not the failures of a believer struggling inside his faith, and the Qur'an's own texts bound the reading. *"Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating others with Him ˹in worship˺, but forgives anything else of whoever He wills"* (4:48) — the unforgivable named, everything below it placed inside the divine will. And the recital's own open door: *"O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah's mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins"* (39:53) — a verse addressed to the exceeded-limit people precisely so that no encompassment short of final rejection would be read as sealed. The mainstream synthesis keeps both edges: the believer's grave sin does not make him the Fire's resident forever, and no sinner may presume the mercy while continuing the earning — because the verse's terror is real, its conditions are exact, and the space between a lapse and an encompassment is the space repentance exists to keep open.

**The Anatomy of Encompassment**

The image at the verse's center — sin closing over its owner — describes a process the sūrah has already documented from the adjacent side. The hardened hearts of verse 74 were hardened *after* the signs, layer upon layer, each unresponded evidence depositing stone; the encompassment of verse 81 is the same accumulation seen from inside the water. A first sin is a wound; repeated, unrepented, defended, it becomes a habit; the habit becomes a character; the character becomes an enclosure — the point at which the person no longer has his sins but is had by them, and the verse's second condition is met. The tradition's moral psychology takes the image literally as diagnostic: a ḥadīth of Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim pictures trials presented to hearts as a reed mat is woven stick by stick — every heart impregnated by them takes a black mark, every heart that rejects them a white one — until hearts sort into two kinds, and the engrossed state is reached not by a single enormity but by the refusal of many small breaches (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 144a). This is why the verse's terror is pastoral rather than merely judicial. It is not filed to make readers despair of their lapses — a lapse is not an encompassment — but to make them afraid of the direction: of the earning that continues after the conscience protests, of the breach defended instead of repaired, of the slow hydraulic work by which a sinner's own choices close over his head. *Balā* overturns the numbered days, and the overturned claim's lesson survives in inverted form: there are no cheap schedules, and the only number that matters is how long the encompassment is allowed to continue before it is no longer possible to leave.

**The Audit of Earning**

The verse closes the numbered-days episode by installing its permanent law: the Fire is not a tariff but a wage, and wages follow work. The *kasaba* that opens the formula is the recital's whole economics of the self in one verb — every person earning, daily, the residence he will occupy, the sūrah having just indicted a community for earning its religion as revenue (79) and its eschatology as comfort (80). The encompassed sinners of verse 81 are the final case of the same principle stripped of its excuses: no forged warranty, no national exemption, no schedule — only the closed account of a self that earned enclosure and receives it. The verdict's symmetry with the promise the recital keeps beside it is the verse's balance for its audience: the same formula, the same forever, stands ready on the other side of the ledger for belief and righteous work, and the sūrah will file it immediately. For the reader under audit — and the recital addresses every reader as audited — the verse's function is to destroy the two false comforts it was revealed against. Against presumption: identity purchases no term, and no people has a pledge it cannot produce. Against despair: the encompassment is not the state of the struggling, and 39:53 remains open until the water actually closes. Between the two, the verse leaves the only ground the recital ever offers — the earning, today, in whichever direction the hands are moving.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:82

> And those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Pair Completed**

The verse begins with a conjunction and that conjunction is its theology: *and* — the promise filed immediately beside the verdict, so that the recital's ruling on the hereafter reaches the reader as a pair and never as a half. Verse 81 overturned the numbered days with the Fire's eternity; verse 82 sets the Garden's eternity in the same grammatical frame — the same formula of residence, the same word for forever — and the symmetry is exact by design. The Qur'an's method of instruction runs on this pairing throughout: threat and promise, *takhwīf* and *tarġīb*, fear and hope, filed in adjacent verses so that neither operates alone on the heart. A recital of verdicts without the promise would produce despair, which the Book forbids; a recital of promises without the verdicts would produce presumption, which verse 80 has just dismantled. The pair together produce the only posture the recital ever asks for — a soul that fears its earning and hopes in its Lord simultaneously — and verse 82 is the pair's second half, the half addressed to the audience actually hearing the recitation in Madina: the believers, for whom the forever of the Fire has just been defined by exclusion and the forever of the Garden is now defined by inclusion.

**Two Conditions: Belief and Work**

The formula's subjects are defined, like the verdict's, by a double condition: belief joined to good works. The pairing is the sūrah's standing definition of the saved — it opened the Book's own portrait of the God-wary, who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and give from their provision (2:3–4), and it carries the sūrah's first promise of the Garden: *"Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow"* (2:25). The two terms are joined in every instance because neither completes the formula alone: belief without righteous work is a claim the recital has just spent verses auditing — the confession of verse 76's meeting-room, true-sounding and empty in practice; work without belief is the charity of a heart encompassed by something other than Allah. *Āmanū wa-ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt* — believed and did the ṣāliḥāt, the things that set right, the acts that repair — is Islam's shortest complete description of a human being in proper order: the heart anchored in the unseen, the limbs discharging what the heart holds. The verse's conditions are thereby the mirror of verse 81's: against earning that encompasses, belief that grounds and work that rectifies; against a character closed over itself, a character open upward and outward, and the two characters receive their two eternities.

**Residents of the Garden**

The verdict's wording is reused and its change of object changes everything: *they will be the residents of Paradise* — *aṣḥāb al-jannah*, the companions of the Garden, the same word of belonging that verse 81 gave to the Fire. Belonging is the verse's psychology as it was the verdict's: the Garden's people are not visitors admitted on sufferance but inhabitants whose nature has been fitted to the place, as the Fire's residents were fitted to theirs. The sūrah has already furnished the residence — rivers flowing beneath the Gardens, fruit provisioned, purified spouses, and the standing clause of permanence (2:25) — and verse 82 files the title deed: this furnishing is not metaphor offered to console but estate conveyed to owners. The term *aṣḥāb* also carries the company its root implies: the residents of the Garden are each other's, a companionship the recital will elsewhere describe in mutual facing and conversation, the society of the saved as part of the salvation. Against the private room of verse 76 — conspirators managing knowledge among themselves in fear — the Garden's company is the same human need for one another, transposed into a house where nothing needs managing: what the two-faced community sought in concealment, the residents of the Garden possess in open belonging.

**Forever, on Both Sides of the Line**

The closing clause is identical to the verdict's: *they will be there forever*. The shared eternity is the verse's answer to the numbered days, and it answers from the side of promise rather than threat. The claim of verse 80 capped the Fire at a countable term on the strength of an identity; the recital's actual doctrine removes the cap from both houses — the Fire's forever and the Garden's forever stand on the same grammar of permanence — and the effect on the reader is a single reorientation: nothing in the hereafter is temporary, so everything rides on which forever a life has earned. The permanence is also the verse's comfort in its deepest form, because the human grief the Garden answers is the grief of ending: every good the world gives is leased, and the lease's shortness poisons the holding. A Garden held forever removes the poison at its root — the sūrah's phrase *there forever* appears in its earliest promise (2:25) and returns here as the settled law, and the tradition reads the sequence as deliberate: the believer's smallest act inside the double condition is being stored against an unending balance, which is why the recital can ask a whole community to spend its wealth, its safety, its very selves (as verse 84 will demand of a covenant-people) without the arithmetic of loss ever closing. Forever on both sides of the line is the recital's way of making this life's every choice infinite-stakes and its every sacrifice infinite-return.

**The Universal Law in Place of the National Tariff**

Read against its occasion, the verse performs a substitution that is the passage's whole argument. A community claimed exemption by descent — the Fire will not touch *us*, the schedule set by who we are — and the recital answered by publishing the actual terms of both eternities: not lineage but belief and work; not a national tariff but a personal formula available to every person of every people. The substitution dismantles the claim at its root, because a doctrine of identity-privilege cannot survive contact with a law of universal eligibility: if the Garden's forever is purchased by belief and good works, then no community holds a monopoly on it and no community is exempt from its conditions — including the community hearing the recitation. That is the verse's edge for its own audience and for every later one: the believers of Madina are being given the promise in terms that also audit them. Belief and work are conditions, not badges; the residents of the Garden are defined by what they hold and do, and the recital that files this verse goes on, for two hundred verses more, to specify the work — the covenant terms, the rulings, the spending, the fighting, the honesty — because a promise with conditions is an assignment. The forever is certain; the double formula is the door; and the verse stands at the close of the recital's first great movement having replaced a people's false comfort with the only real one on offer: an eternity that cannot be inherited, and therefore cannot be lost except by abandoning the two things that earn it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:83

> And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel ˹stating˺, “Worship none but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy; speak kindly to people; establish prayer; and pay alms-tax.” But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away—except for a few of you—and were indifferent.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Charter of the Covenant**

With the eschatological interlude closed — the numbered-days claim rebutted, the two eternities filed — the recital returns to its central exhibit and quotes the covenant itself. *And remember when We took a covenant from the children of Israel*: the verse sets down the terms in the order a complete life requires them. First the vertical bond — *worship none but Allah*. Then the circle of obligation widening outward: *parents*, then *relatives*, then *orphans and the needy* — the claims of blood, of kinship, of helplessness. Then the whole of society in a single clause — *speak kindly to people*. And finally the two standing rites, *prayer* and *alms-tax*, the daily and the material disciplines that keep the charter in force. The exegetes recognize the list's genre immediately: it belongs with the Qur'an's great universal commandment-passages, the decalogue of Sūrah al-Anʿām (6:151–153) and the long ethical charge of Sūrah al-Isrāʾ (17:23–39), which the tradition counts among the *muḥkam* — the clear, foundational verses on which the rest of revelation stands. What is being quoted here is therefore not a tribal contract but the moral constitution of revealed religion itself, the same charter in every prophet's hand — which is precisely why its violation, filed in the verse's closing clause, indicts something deeper than one community's history.

**Allah's Right, the Servant's Right**

The charter's first term is its foundation, and the Prophet ﷺ once stated it as a paired doctrine of rights. Riding behind him on a donkey, Muʿādh was told: *"Allah's right on His slaves is that they should worship Him (Alone) and should not worship any besides Him. And slave's right on Allah is that He should not punish him who worships none besides Him"* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2856). The covenant of verse 83 opens with exactly this right — worship none but Allah — and the ḥadīth supplies the reciprocal: the servant who keeps the first term holds a promise against punishment, the divine counterpart to the human obligation. The pairing explains why the charter begins where it does. Every other term — kindness, speech, prayer, alms — is a branch of the first; a kindness performed for social credit, a prayer offered to be seen, an alms given to purchase standing all fail at the root the root-term plants: that the act belongs to Allah alone. The sūrah's own theology of forgiveness draws the same line from the other side: association with Allah is the sin whose forgiveness He has not placed in the ordinary economy (4:48). The covenant is thus offered on a single non-negotiable condition, and its fivefold social and ritual elaboration is what that condition looks like when it is lived — a structure the recital now holds up against the record of the people who received it first.

**The Four Claims of Kindness**

The social terms of the charter are ordered by nearness, and the ordering is instruction. Parents first: the Qur'an honors them with a standing emphasis — the command runs through the Book in passage after passage (17:23, 29:8, 31:14, 46:15) — and the exegetes note that the duty binds whether the parent believes or not, pointing to Abraham's restraint with his unbelieving father (19:42–48) as its outer limit case; the prophetic tradition crowns the mother specifically, in the saying that Paradise lies at the mothers' feet. Then *relatives* — in the Arabic *dhū al-qurbā*, the possessors of nearness — the ring of blood whose claims the Qur'an files again and again beside the poor (2:177, 4:36, 17:26). Then *orphans* — the *yatīm*, classically the child whose father has died, the minor stripped of its provider and protector, whose case the Book legislates at length (4:3–10, 6:152, 107:2). Then *the needy* — the claim of want itself, owing nothing to kinship, resting entirely on the covenant. The sequence walks outward from the household to the stranger, and its moral logic is deliberate: kindness is trained on the near and tested on the far. A community that keeps the inner rings while neglecting the outer has not kept the charter, and a community that performs for strangers while devouring its own orphans has performed, not obeyed. The four claims together define the covenant's horizontal face — and the recital's audience is being shown what Allah considers the minimum furniture of a just community, in terms no one hearing it could call particular to any tribe.

**A Goodly Word to All People**

Between the circle of kindness and the rites stands a clause so general the exegetes marked its generality expressly: *speak kindly to people* — to people, without qualification. Al-Ṭabarī's reading is explicit that the command applies to all human beings, not to the community's own members only, and the interpreters gather under it the whole ethics of the tongue: the call to tawhid, the commanding of the right and the forbidding of the wrong (3:104), ordinary courtesy in ordinary exchange. The clause's placement does quiet work against the passage just behind it. The recital has spent ten verses documenting crimes of speech — the word distorted after understanding (75), the two rooms' two scripts (76), the hearsay passed off as certainty (78), the book written by hands and warranted as divine (79), the claim about Allah made without knowledge (80). Against that catalog, the covenant's speech-term is the counter-law: one tongue, kindly used, owing the same honesty to every listener. The verse thereby answers the conspirators of verse 76 in advance — a charter that commands the goodly word *to people* cannot be kept by a community that speaks one language in the meeting and another in the private room. Speech in the covenant is not decoration on the moral life but its most public organ, and its kindness is not softness: the same mouth owes the call to monotheism, which is the hardest and kindest thing it can say.

**Prayer and Alms-Tax: The Ritual Seal**

The charter closes as the sūrah's own address to the believers closed at its start — with prayer and zakāh, the pair the recital has joined since verse 43, where the community hearing this history was told: *establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and bow down with those who bow down* (2:43). The pairing is the covenant's machinery: prayer keeps the first term alive in the body's daily rhythm, alms-tax keeps the kindness-terms alive in the property's annual circulation — the vertical bond rehearsed five times a day, the horizontal claims discharged as an obligation rather than a mood. The exegetes note a grammatical feature of the verse that carries theological weight: an alternate reading puts the first term in the third person — they worship none but Allah — with the imperatives beginning mid-verse, one of the recital's characteristic shifts of address. Whether read as command or as covenant-statement, the terms are identical, and their identity with the Muslim community's own obligations is the verse's silent transfer: the charter taken from the children of Israel is the charter taken from every people given a revelation, the same five terms in the same order — God, kin, the helpless, the tongue, the rites. The recital quotes Israel's constitution to its new holders not as foreign history but as their own inheritance, with the record of the first holders attached as warning label.

**“Except for a Few of You”**

The verdict falls in the final clause: *but you turned away — except for a few of you — and were indifferent*. Three features of the sentence carry its weight. The address is second-person — the covenant is quoted to the generation that broke it as though they stood inside it, the recital's standing method of collapsing the distance between ancestral crime and present responsibility. The exception is recorded — *except for a few* — and the few matter to the verse's justice: the charter was kept by some, which proves it could be kept, and the exception separates the remnant from the mass the way Sūrah al-Māʾidah will separate them again — deceit always found on their part, *except for a few* (5:13). The few are the covenant's vindication and the many's indictment in one phrase: no generation can plead that the terms were impossible, because the impossibility is refuted inside its own ranks. And the closing word — *indifferent*, turning aside in aversion — names not the failure of the weak but the posture of the unbothered: not those who tried and fell, but those who turned away. The distinction is the verse's pastoral edge for every reader. The audit that follows this covenant through the coming verses will weigh the community's conduct, deed by deed — but the root failure it keeps returning to is this one word: a charter perfect in its terms, a few who kept it, a many who were indifferent, and a recital that files the whole scene in the second person so that no one hearing it stands outside the question of which group he belongs to.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:84

> And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant that you would neither shed each other’s blood nor expel each other from their homes, you gave your pledge and bore witness.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Covenant of Blood and Homes**

The recital moves from the universal charter to a specific bond, and the specificity sharpens the charge. After the five terms of verse 83 — worship, kindness, speech, prayer, alms — this verse quotes a covenant in two prohibitions: *that you would neither shed each other's blood nor expel each other from their homes*. The two protected goods are the most elementary a community possesses: life and dwelling, the person and the place the person belongs to. And the covenant's grammar makes both goods reflexive — *each other's* blood, *each other's* homes — so that the crimes it forbids are not crimes against strangers but against the self extended: the brother's blood is your blood, the neighbor's house is continuous with your own. The exegetes read the verse as continuing the account of the earlier Israelites, the covenant of the community's founding laid beside the charter of the previous verse — and the pairing is deliberate in its architecture. Verse 83 bound the community upward and outward, to Allah and to people; verse 84 binds it inward, to its own members, in the two things no member may take from another. A people whose charter is perfect but whose internal bond is broken has religion without community, and the recital is about to document exactly that condition — which is why this verse first fixes the bond's terms and, in its second half, its ratification.

**You Gave Your Pledge and Bore Witness**

The verse ends where a contract ends: *you gave your pledge and bore witness*. The double formula is legal language, and its doubling is the point — the covenant was not merely received but confirmed, and confirmed twice over. The pledge is the community's own act of binding itself; the bearing of witness, in al-Rāzī's and al-Ṭabarī's readings, is either direct attestation — we heard, we accept, we testify to this bond — or presence itself, the standing of the whole group at the event as its witnesses. Either way the effect is evidentiary: a covenant witnessed cannot later be disowned, because the disowning party is on the witness list. The recital's method of address presses the point home. *Your* covenant — the second person runs through the sentence, so that the pledge belongs to the community as a present fact rather than an ancestral event, and every generation that says *we are the people of that covenant* re-signs the witness roll in the act of saying it. This is the verse's quiet machinery for everything that follows: the coming indictment will not be arguing that the bond was unclear or unwitnessed. The terms were elementary — do not kill each other, do not expel each other — the pledge was given, the witnesses were the pledgers. What remains to be examined is conduct, and conduct against a witnessed covenant admits no defense of ignorance.

**The Group and the Individual: Two Ways to Inherit a Crime**

The verse's communal address raises the question the tradition faced directly: how can a later generation be bound, or indicted, by a covenant its ancestors ratified? The exegetical discussion distinguishes two inheritances. The first is passive implication — the way children suffer from parents' crimes, the way a household pays for its head's debts: a burden carried without choice. The second is active participation — and here the principle turns moral: where individuals glory in a group identity, holding its honors as extensions of the self, they expose themselves to the crimes attached to that identity as well. The boast and the burden are one package; a people that says *we are the chosen* has claimed the choosing and the chosen's conduct together. This is the mechanism by which the "sins of the fathers" pass justly to later generations — not by blood but by identification: the descendant who accepts the ancestral glory without repudiating the ancestral crime ratifies the crime, and his ratification is real because his acceptance of the glory was real. The verse's second-person grammar operates inside this logic. *We took your covenant* — the address treats the community across its generations as a single moral person, and the treatment is fair on the community's own premises: a people that remembers its covenant as *ours* has already merged its account with the covenant's.

**The Inheritance of Character**

Beneath the legal mechanism runs a social one, and the exegetes trace it plainly: people take the shape of the society around them. A generation that is malicious tends to raise children who copy its malice, because the child's moral vocabulary is the environment's — imitation transmits the vices of fathers as reliably as their surnames, and the Qur'an's standing rebuke of those who argue from ancestral practice (*we found our fathers doing this*) is aimed at exactly this transmission taken as justification. The converse holds with equal force: to be raised among truth-tellers, inside an environment that enshrines compassion and hands it forward, is a better inheritance than any estate — environments are the vessels in which a community's character crosses generations. The verse's covenant of blood and homes is therefore not only a prohibition but a piece of social engineering: a community that keeps it raises children for whom fratricide and expulsion are unthinkable, and a community that breaks it raises children fluent in both. The tragedy the recital documents is the second case running at scale — a people whose charter forbade shedding each other's blood, whose witness roll was signed, and whose later generations inherited not the charter's restraint but its violations, performing them with the confidence of custom. The individual's escape from that inheritance is named in the tradition and is narrow but real: repentance for one's own sins and a life of active virtue — the deliberate re-weaving of character against the received pattern.

**The Fire Next Door**

The discussion of communal responsibility keeps one sober limit in view, and the limit is the verse's darkest realism. Even the person who repudiates his community's crimes — who deplores them while still belonging, who keeps the covenant alone among covenant-breakers — may not escape the effects of the communal sin, any more than a man escapes the blaze that has taken his neighbor's house. The image is exact: communal corruption is a fire, and fires do not check title deeds at the property line. The righteous remnant of verse 83 — the *few* excepted from the turning away — lives inside this hazard: their exception saves their standing before Allah, but not necessarily their houses, their city, or their century. The tradition balances the bleakness with its own counterweight: a culture sunk in moral darkness can be rescued by an infusion of virtue — saints and sages in ordinary ages, prophets in the ages of revelation — though the average community retains the qualities of its founders rather than discarding them, and rescue is the exception history records rather than its rule. The two facts together give the verse its full pastoral register. Belonging to a good community is a protection no individual virtue fully replaces; belonging to a corrupt one is a hazard no individual virtue fully escapes; and the covenant of blood and homes is addressed to the community precisely because the community is the unit that either keeps its members safe or burns their houses down around them, whatever any single member intended.

**The Present-Tense You**

The verse's grammar carries its permanent application, and the exegetes mark the feature deliberately: the Qur'an addresses past and future generations in the present tense — *We took your covenant* — folding every generation of the community into the moment of ratification. The you of verse 84 is thus a standing address. Every community that claims a revealed charter has taken the covenant of blood and homes; every community whose members kill each other and expel each other has broken it with its pledge fresh and its witness list intact. The first hearers in Madina recognized the address in its historical form — the tribes and alliances of their own city about to be held against the covenant's terms — and every later hearer inherits the recognition in his own form: the factionalism that calls itself fidelity, the purges that call themselves discipline, the exile of the inconvenient that calls itself protection of the community. The two prohibitions are elementary because they are permanent — life and home are what any group's members may never take from each other, whatever the group's grievances — and the ratification clause is what makes the indictment inescapable: you gave your pledge, and you bore witness. The recital files the bond before filing its violation because the order matters to justice: no one will be shown the crime before being shown the signature. The signature is on the page, in the second person, witnessed — and the audit that follows reads conduct against it, verse by verse.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:85

> But here you are, killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin and aggression; and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you as captives, you still ransom them—though expelling them was unlawful for you. Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest? Is there any reward for those who do so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment? For Allah is never unaware of what you do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Here You Are: The Contradiction on Live Feed**

The verse opens with the signature of an accusation caught in the act: *but here you are* — the present tense of a crime contemporaneous with the recitation, quoted to perpetrators who can check the report against their own week. The charge is the covenant's exact inversion: *killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes* — the two prohibitions of the witnessed bond (84), violated in the same reflexive grammar, each other's blood, your own people's homes. The historical scene the exegetes supply is Madina itself in the generations before the Prophet's ﷺ arrival. Three Jewish tribes — Banū Qaynuqāʿ, Banū al-Naḍīr, Banū Qurayẓah — lived among the two great Arab tribes, Aws and Khazraj, whose wars ran for decades. When Aws fought Khazraj, the Jewish tribes fought across both battle-lines: Qurayẓah and al-Naḍīr with one Arab ally, Qaynuqāʿ with the other — so that Jew fought Jew, killed him, drove him from his house, and took him prisoner, all in the service of alliances that made enemies of co-religionists and brothers-in-arms of idolaters. The clause *aiding one another in sin and aggression* names the alliances' moral structure: cooperation exists — energetic, loyal, costly cooperation — but its object is transgression, and the verse's phrase pairs the two nouns the Qur'an keeps joined for forbidden collaboration: sin against Allah, aggression against people.

**The Ransom Paradox**

The indictment's turn is its strangest feature: *and when those expelled come to you as captives, you still ransom them*. The same community that drove out its own now pays to free them — expel with one hand, ransom with the other, the crime and its expiation performed by the same people in the same war. The exegetes locate the verse's central question in precisely this contradiction: believing part of the Book and disbelieving part refers, on al-Ṭabarī's reading, to the clash between the expulsion — which violates the Book — and the ransom — which accords with it. The paradox is not hypocrisy of the simple kind but of an intricate kind, and its intricacy is what makes the verse's question so cutting. The ransom is genuine virtue: freeing captives stands in the Qur'an's own ethic among the highest acts — Sūrah Muḥammad legislates the treatment of war captives as release *by grace or by ransom* (47:4) — and the Prophet ﷺ made it a standing command of the community's duty: *"Give food to the hungry, pay a visit to the sick and release (set free) the one in captivity (by paying his ransom)"* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5373). The verse does not fault the ransom. It faults the selectivity — a community that keeps the commandment which costs money and breaks the commandment which costs power, that honors the Book in the captive-market and tramples it on the battlefield, in the same week, with the same hands.

**“Though Expelling Them Was Unlawful for You”**

The parenthetical clause fixes the legal order of the two acts, and the order is the verse's jurisprudence in miniature: ransoming the captive is obedience; *expelling them was unlawful for you* — the expulsion had no warrant at any point, which means the ransom is not repairing a lawful act gone wrong but funding the aftermath of a crime. The community's own practice testifies against it: by ransoming the expelled, it admits the expelled were its people, owed the covenant's protection — the ransom is a signed confession that the expulsion breached a duty the ransomers themselves hold sacred. Al-Rāzī's alternative reading of the surrounding passage connects the partial belief to the prophecies of the coming Prophet, though he notes the immediate context does not require it; the expulsion-and-ransom contradiction remains the reading the verse's own wording carries. The clause's deeper function is to destroy the defense of consistency. A community that never ransomed could plead a coherent (if brutal) position; a community that ransoms has conceded the covenant's authority over captives and stands convicted of applying that authority selectively — honoring the Book where honor is cheap, suspending it where obedience would cost an alliance, a fortress, or a war. The recital's audit is exact: it does not charge them with rejecting the Scripture, but with rationing it.

**Some of the Scripture, the Rest Rejected**

The verse's central question generalizes the case into a permanent category: *do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest?* The wider sense of *kufr* the exegetes mark here is rejection and denial of specific truths rather than atheism of God — the expulsion and the alliances are hypocrisy and immorality enacted, and in the Qur'an's moral arithmetic such acts are inseparable from a measure of unbelief, because a truth one systematically disobeys is a truth one has functionally denied. Sūrah al-Nisāʾ will legislate the category in full: those who believe *in some and disbelieve in others* — the selective believers — are made disbelievers in truth by their selection (4:150–151). The mechanism the verse exposes is the treatment of revelation as a menu: the comfortable terms taken, the costly terms left, the selection itself performed by appetite rather than by the Book. And the selection is never random — it runs, in every age, along the line between commandments that cost money and commandments that cost power. The ransom costs money and was kept; the prohibition on expulsion cost tribal position and was broken. The verse's question is addressed to every community that keeps a Scripture, because every community that keeps one keeps it partly, and the partial pattern is legible the moment one asks which terms are honored and what each honored term costs.

**Disgrace Here, the Harshest Punishment There**

The sentence is doubled across the two worlds: *disgrace in this worldly life* and *the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment*. The worldly half is exposure — *khizy*, the shame of a community whose contradiction becomes public, its covenant-breaking visible to the very neighbors it made its allies; the recital itself is part of that disgrace, quoting the private arithmetic of expulsion and ransom in the open mosque for the city to hear. History ran the sentence to its letter in Madina's following decade, as tribe after tribe of the three lost its place in the city — the expulsion its own hands had normalized returning as its own fate. The otherworldly half carries the verse's distinctive superlative: not punishment simply but *the harshest* — a degree reserved here for the selective believers, and its logic reads back through the passage: one who never received the Book sins in ignorance; one who received it, ratified its covenant, witnessed it, and then rationed it has sinned against light, and the light aggravates the sentence. The closing clause returns the whole scene to the standing audit — *Allah is never unaware of what you do* (2:85) — the same sentence that closed the hardening of hearts at verse 74, framing this entire stretch of the recital: nothing in the two rooms, the battlefield, or the captive-market escapes the file, and the double punishment is filed against a crime the Judge watched completely.

**The Whole Book, or the Menu**

The verse leaves its audience with the choice its question implies, and the choice is the recital's demand on every Scripture-keeping community. Belief in the Book is not subscription to selected clauses; it is standing under all of them, including the ones that cost what the honored ones never touch. The Muslim community hearing the recitation was being vaccinated in real time: its own charter — the covenant of verse 83, the bond of verse 84 — contained the same costly terms, and the same wars, alliances, and exiles would come for it in its own generations, wearing the same justifications the verse strips bare. The ransom paradox is the verse's permanent diagnostic, and it works in both directions. Keeping the cheap commandments while breaking the expensive ones is selective belief condemned here by name; and performing the expensive ones as a cover for the cheap ones' violation — ransoming the captive the same hands expelled — is the aggravated form, because it dresses the rationing as piety. The verse's answer to both is the unrationed Book: every term in force, the alliance dissolved where the covenant forbids it, the expulsion undone where the covenant protects, the ransom paid where the covenant commands — and the whole held together by the clause that closes the audit: He is never unaware. What is kept and what is skipped is on the record, and the record's verdict is already quoted: disgrace here, the harshest punishment there, for those who believed in some of the Scripture and rejected the rest.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:86

> These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world. So their punishment will not be reduced, nor will they be helped.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Name of the Transaction**

Two sentences close the case the previous verse opened, and the first is a diagnosis: *these are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world*. The recital has reached the underlying form of every crime it has filed in this passage. The distortion after understanding, the two rooms' two scripts, the expulsion and the ransom, the covenant rationed — each is now named as one act wearing different clothes: a purchase. The verb is the market's own — buying and selling — and the sūrah has been building this economics of the sacred since its early verses: the signs exchanged for a cheap price (2:41), the souls sold for a price the sūrah elsewhere calls miserable indeed (2:102), the book written by hands and sold for a fleeting gain (2:79). Verse 86 states the general law behind the ledger: every sin against known revelation is a trade in which the Hereafter is the currency and the world's life the merchandise. The trade's structure explains the selectivity the previous verse indicted — the cheap commandments kept, the costly ones broken — because a trader selects by price: what the world pays for is bought, what it does not pay for is left on the shelf, and the shelf's contents are the covenant's expensive terms. The verse's demonstrative — *these are the ones* — points at a defined class rather than a moment of weakness: the people whose governing orientation has become the transaction itself.

**The Terms of the Trade, and Its Arithmetic**

The arithmetic of the purchase is the verse's unspoken exhibit, and the Qur'an files it wherever the trade appears.
