The recital has filed this clause in several forms — Allah never unaware of what is done (74), the Knower of what hearts conceal (77) — and each filing has marked a transition from exposure to judgment. Here the transition is complete: the challenge has been issued, the refusal predicted and explained, and the explanation placed inside a knowledge that cannot be appealed.

**The Two Certainties**

What the verse exposes, in its final analysis, is a mismatch between two certainties that ought to be one. The claimants possess a verbal certainty — exclusive paradise, articulated, defended, taught — and lack the practical certainty that would make it operative: the settled expectation that changes what a person wants. The commentators set the claim beside its cousin at verse 80, the numbered days of the Fire, and read both as one disease: confidence in excess of warrant, certainty manufactured where revelation was silent. The Islamic contrast the tradition draws is instructive in its structure rather than its details. The prayer the Prophet ﷺ taught for the moment of affliction is conditional — life if life is better, death if death is better (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6351) — and its conditionality is doctrinal: the believer's standing before Allah is real but unseen, hoped for but not held. Islam asks its saints for trust without claim; the verse's claimants had claim without trust. The two certainties come apart in exactly one place — the will — and the verse's test was built to find that place. A certainty that cannot produce its corresponding desire is a sentence repeated, not a belief inhabited; and the recital's judgment is that the community knew it, which is why the wish was impossible, and why the impossibility was itself the confession.

**The Test That Never Closes**

The prediction's permanence is the verse's transfer to every later reader. Unlike a prophecy about events — a battle, a reign, a conquest — this one is about a posture of the will, re-tested every time an exclusive assurance is examined against its holder's relation to death. The recital's audience inherits the instrument. Every community breeds its guarantees: salvation assured by membership, standing secured by ancestry, paradise reserved for the correctly affiliated — and every such guarantee can be put to the verse's question without argument, by watching what its holders want. The test discriminates cleanly between two kinds of religious confidence. The confidence that comes from received promise behaves like the conditional prayer: it faces death without seeking it, holding the outcome in Allah's knowledge and the hope in its own heart. The confidence that comes from manufactured entitlement behaves like the verse's claimants: absolute in statement, paralyzed at the boundary, unable to want what it says it has. The difference is invisible in doctrine and unmistakable in desire — which is why the recital tests at desire. *Allah knows the wrongdoers* closes the verse as it closed the case: the hands' record is held, the silence is witnessed, and the challenge remains open on the page for every generation that claims what its heart will not choose.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:96

> You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people, even more than polytheists. Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years. But even if they were to live that long, it would not save them from the punishment. And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Most Clinging of People**

The verdict of verse 95 becomes a portrait: *you will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people*. The address — *you will find them* — is directed at the Prophet ﷺ and through him at every observer, and its verb carries the sense of discovery upon examination: look at this community's actual behavior and you will find this, the way one finds a fact in evidence. The superlative is the verse's first shock. Among all peoples, in all their variety of attachment to living, these are the *most* clinging — and the comparison clause sharpens the shock into a paradox: *even more than polytheists*. The commentators press the paradox's logic. The polytheist addressed here is one without belief in a hereafter of reward: death, on his account, is annihilation or descent to a shadow-land, and attachment to life is therefore the whole of what his cosmology leaves him. If the people of an exclusive paradise cling harder than that, their behavior testifies against their doctrine more loudly than any refusal could: the man who expects annihilation clings because clinging is all he has; the man who clings harder while claiming paradise shows that, in the register of conduct, he expects annihilation too. The verse completes the challenge's work. Verse 94 asked for a wish; verse 95 predicted its absence; verse 96 documents the wish that is present instead — the wish for more life — and files it as the community's own refutation, observed, comparative, and public.

**A Thousand Years**

The second sentence gives the clinging its number: *each one of them wishes to live a thousand years*. The commentators divide on the number's reference and its sense. Grammatically, the wish can attach either to the Jews described at the verse's opening or to the polytheists of the comparison — the second reading would make the thousand years the idolater's wish, with the Jews exceeding even that; al-Rāzī notes the alternative construction but finds the primary reading the natural one. Historically, some exegetes connected the figure to Persian usage, citing the long-life greetings exchanged in that culture — blessings of ten thousand years spoken on ordinary occasions — and reading the verse as describing Zoroastrian-influenced expectation. Al-Rāzī prefers the simpler linguistic account: the thousand is idiom for the indefinite many, the way a language says *forever* when it means *as long as possible*. The weighing matters less than the wish's shape, which is the same under every reading: quantity invoked where quality is unavailable. A thousand years is not a plan but a panic's arithmetic — the longest number the imagination can carry, deployed against the boundary it cannot cross. And *each one of them* individualizes the panic: this is not a policy or a doctrine but a wish held person by person, the private prayer of every member, which makes it the truest available statement of what the community actually believes about death.

**What a Thousand Years Would Not Do**

The verse then runs the arithmetic to its end: *even if they were to live that long, it would not save them from the punishment*. The conditional is concessive — grant the impossible premise, the wish fulfilled, the millennium lived — and the conclusion is unchanged: the punishment arrives exactly where the extra centuries leave it. The sentence dismantles the wish from inside. Longevity is being treated by the wisher as a refuge, and the verse shows the refuge has no walls: death deferred is death still owed, and a thousand years of deferral changes the date without touching the destination. This is the recital's answer to the numbered-days doctrine of verse 80 arriving from a new direction — there, the Fire's term was imagined short; here, the life before it is imagined long; and both imaginations fail against the same fact, that the two terms are set by Allah and not by preference. The commentators add the psychological layer through a saying of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: the hypocrite is more covetous of the world than the idolater — and the explanation given is the gnawing awareness of consequences. The greed for life grows precisely where assurance is weakest; the man who is certain of paradise does not need a millennium, and the man who clamors for one is confessing, in the currency of desire, what verse 95 stated in the currency of prediction. The hypocrisy's delusion of safety has a truth beneath it — that his actions preclude the safety — and the truth is not fully hidden from him, which is why the clinging is *eager* rather than merely strong.

**All-Seeing of What They Do**

The closing clause repeats the audit formula with a shift of divine name: *Allah is All-Seeing of what they do*. Verse 95 closed with knowledge of the wrongdoers; verse 96 closes with sight of the deeds — the same surveillance described from its two sides, the ledger and the eye. The name *Baṣīr* carries the seeing that penetrates: not observation of surfaces but vision into the doing, its motives and its clinging included. The shift suits the verse's content. What verse 96 documents is visible behavior — eagerness for life, the wish for years, the observable contradiction between conduct and creed — and the clause files all of it under a sight that misses nothing. The verse's whole argument has been evidentiary: you will *find* them, look and see the comparison, hear the number of the wish; the closing clause adds that the finding is not only the observer's. Allah sees what they do — including the doing's inner shape, the fear beneath the eagerness, the disbelief beneath the profession — and the seeing is the warrant for the sentence to come. For the reader the clause installs the verse's permanent use: attachment to life is not hidden sin but visible testimony, and it testifies continuously. What a person's clinging says about his actual expectation of death is on display to every observer and recorded by the All-Seeing — which makes this verse the recital's instrument for reading any community, including one's own, by the single most reliable indicator available: how its members behave at the boundary of the life they claim not to fear losing.

**The Believer's Measure of Attachment**

Islam does not indict love of life as such, and the verse must be read with that distinction sharp. The prayer taught for affliction asks for life *while life is better* — life held as a good, received conditionally, surrendered when its better term arrives (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6351). The believer of the sūrah's own portrait sends his good ahead and finds it with Allah; his relation to years is stewardship rather than clutching. What verse 96 condemns is clinging as eschatological strategy — life accumulated against death, years pursued as a refuge from the audit, the millennium-wish as a substitute for the repaired record. The economics of the passage names the trade exactly: a thousand years purchased at the price of the Hereafter is verse 86's transaction conducted in the currency of time, and the verse's concessive clause publishes the exchange rate — the purchase fails even when it succeeds. The recital leaves its audience with the diagnostic in working order. Eagerness for life is a gauge, and its reading is honest: the stronger the profession of paradise and the stronger the clinging in the same person, the wider the gap between the two — and the gap is the verse's whole subject. The All-Seeing watches the gauge along with the deed, and the sūrah files the reading here so that no later claimant of guaranteed bliss can plead that the instrument was hidden from him.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:97

> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it—a guide and good news for the believers.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Objection That Named an Angel**

Two accounts preserved by the exegetes give this verse its occasion, and both carry the same improbable objection. In the first (Ibn Kathīr's report), a delegation of Jews tested the Prophet ﷺ with questions only a true prophet could answer; among them was the question of who brings him his message. When he answered *Gabriel*, they said they would have followed him had he named Michael — in their reckoning an angel of mercy — whereas Gabriel brings war, death, and destruction. In the second account, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, who used to sit with the Jews while they studied the Torah because he loved watching the two revelations confirm each other, was told by them that they held Muhammad ﷺ to be a prophet but would not follow him, because they were at peace with some angels and at enmity with others — and Gabriel belonged to the hostile side. ʿUmar was astounded: on the Jews' own telling, both angels stand at either side of God, and friendship with one while warring on the other was incoherent to him. He went to report the exchange to the Prophet ﷺ and found the verse already revealed. Whatever the exact occasion, the objection's shape is fixed: a refusal of the message grounded in a grievance against its courier — angelology deployed as an excuse at the point of decision, the first instance in the recital of a theology manufactured to carry the weight of a refusal.

**Michael and Gabriel in the Two Traditions**

The objection had a real history behind it, and the verse is stronger for knowing that history. In Jewish tradition Michael holds the preeminent angelic station: Israel's prince in the book of Daniel (10:13–21), Israel's advocate and, in later literature, the teacher of Moses. The two angels appear across that literature with complementary attributes — Michael paired with snow and Gabriel with fire, Michael called the merciful and Gabriel set over the powers, gentleness assigned to one and severity to the other. The midrashic tradition casts Gabriel as Sodom's destroyer, and a literature populated with fallen angels and distributed functions (the Enochic books above all) made room for a popular reading in which Gabriel's portfolio — destruction, death — marked him as an adversary of Israel while Michael served as its patron. It is fair to note, as the record requires, that Jewish literature as a whole holds Gabriel in positive regard; the enmity-tradition was a strand, not the consensus. But a strand was all the objection needed. The exegetes also preserve al-Rāzī's sharper diagnosis: at least part of the hostility to Gabriel flowed from the fact that Muhammad ﷺ was not of Israel — the angel's severity functioning as an excuse that masked displeasure at an Arab being chosen at all. On this reading the courier-objection is the lineage-objection of verses 89–90 in disguise, and the verse's answer addresses both at once: to fault Gabriel is to fault the God who sent him, since the courier's mission is entirely the Sender's will.

**Brought Down Upon Your Heart**

The verse's central clause describes the delivery, and its precision is theological: *he revealed this Quran to your heart by Allah's Will*. The destination is the heart — and the commentators mark the word's full range in Qur'anic usage: the heart is the seat of knowledge and understanding, not of sentiment alone, so the descent described here is the arrival of cognition at the organ of cognition. Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ states the same delivery in the same terms: the revelation the *trustworthy spirit* — Gabriel named by his title of trust — *brought down into your heart, O Prophet*, so that he might be one of the warners (26:193–194). The pairing of the two verses fixes the courier's identity beyond the objection's reach: the angel who brought this Book to this heart is the trustworthy spirit, and trustworthiness is his defining attribute in the Qur'an's own testimony. The clause *by Allah's Will* completes the answer's first movement. Gabriel has no independent mission, no private agenda, no war of his own against any people — he descends where and when Allah wills, which makes enmity toward him a category error with a moral core: the hostility is really aimed upstream, at the Will that sent him, and the verse says so by structure, placing the courier's act inside the Sender's permission before it names the message's qualities. The recital's audience hears the whole chain in one sentence — Will, courier, heart — and the chain has no loose link for an objection to catch.

**Confirming, Guiding, Giving Good News**

The message's three descriptors answer the objection's second layer — that the angel of war brings a message of destruction. *Confirming what came before it*: the Book this courier carries testifies to the Torah rather than assaulting it, which is a strange cargo for a destroyer; the confirmation-relationship the Jews of Madina had themselves invoked while praying for victory (89) is stamped on the message's face. *A guide*: the Book's function is direction, the Qur'an's standing self-description from the sūrah's opening verse. *Good news for the believers*: the message arrives as glad tidings — and the restriction to the believers is the descriptor's edge, because it locates the message's differing effects in its recipients rather than in its courier. The same descent is good news to one heart and trial to another, not because the angel carries two packages but because guidance received is guidance accepted. The verse thereby completes its answer without ever arguing about angels' temperaments: the courier is trustworthy, his mission is Allah's will, his cargo is confirmation and guidance and glad tidings — and an objection that survives all three is not about the courier. The recital has met this structure before, at verse 88, where the covered heart explained a refusal it could not justify; here the angel-objection is the same refusal wearing theology, and the verse's answer strips the costume by simply describing, clause by clause, what was actually delivered — to a heart, by a will, with a purpose no enemy of Israel could have chosen.

**The Standing Answer to Courier-Objections**

The verse's transfer runs through every age's version of the courier-objection, and the versions are numerous. A message refused because of its messenger's tribe, accent, class, or history; a revelation discounted because of the human instruments who carried or transmitted it; a truth weighed by the manners of its advocates rather than its own content — each is verse 97's objection with new names on it. The verse's method against all of them is fixed: examine the delivery chain and examine the delivery. If the chain terminates in Allah's will — if the message's source is divine and its transmission faithful — then grievances against the links are grievances against the Sender, and the Sender is not reachable by preference. And if the cargo is confirmation of prior truth, guidance for the present, and good news for the receptive, then the courier's portfolio is mercy whatever his other assignments may be, because this mission is the one that reaches the objector. The Muslims hearing the sūrah were being trained in a discrimination their own centuries would need: between objections that address a message and objections that address a messenger, between refusal with reasons and refusal with pretexts. The verse hands them the test in its own structure — follow the chain to the Will, read the descriptors on the cargo — and leaves the angel-objection where every pretext belongs: answered not by counter-argument but by description, exposed not as error but as costume.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:98

> Whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel, and Michael, then ˹let them know that˺ Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A List That Cannot Be Sorted**

The answer to the courier-objection arrives as an enumeration, and the enumeration's grammar is its argument: *whoever is an enemy of Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel, and Michael*. The list moves from the Sender to the two orders of His agents — angels and messengers — and then names the two angels the objection tried to separate, side by side, inside the same class. The construction follows a pattern the Qur'an uses deliberately: specification after generalization, where the named particulars do not stand outside the category but repeat it with emphasis. The commentators' linguistic warrant is the Book's own style — Sūrah al-Raḥmān mentions fruit and then dates and pomegranates, the particulars honored by naming after the general they belong to — and the principle settles the verse's first question before it is asked: Gabriel and Michael are not being distinguished from the angels as though they were something else; they are being exhibited as the case in point. The objection had claimed a position — at peace with some angels, at war with others — and the list dissolves the position by refusing its architecture. There is no sorting available here. The angels are one order, the messengers one office, Allah the source of both, and the two named angels stand where the objection placed its whole case: inside the class it tried to divide. Enmity aimed at any point of the list reaches every other point, because the list is not an aggregate of independently befriended parties but a single chain of agency terminating in one Sender.

**Why the Chain Has No Neutral Link**

The chain-logic deserves its full statement because it is the verse's theology in miniature. An angel has no mission of his own: he descends by Allah's will, carries what he is given, delivers where he is sent. A messenger has no message of his own on the same principle: the recital has been filing revelation as sent-down, brought-down, delivered-to-the-heart, at every station. Enmity toward a link in such a chain is therefore never confined to the link — it is enmity toward the origin, expressed at the point where the origin becomes visible. This is why the objection of verse 97 was incoherent in ʿUmar's instant reading of it: both angels stand at either side of God on the objectors' own account, so befriending one while warring on the other is befriending the court while declaring war on its king's business. The verse generalizes the incoherence into a law: whoever is an enemy of *any* of these — Allah, angels, messengers, this angel, that angel — stands in one position, because the enmity's object is always the sending, never merely the sent. The Qur'an elsewhere makes the same point from the messenger-side, where rejecting one prophet is rejecting the office itself; here it makes the point from the angel-side, where warring on a courier is warring on the Sender's will. The two sides meet in the verse's closing clause, and the meeting is the judgment.

**“I Will Declare War”: The Principle in a Ḥadīth Qudsī**

The tradition states the verse's principle in its most developed form, in a ḥadīth the commentators cite for its concordance and whose wording is preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī: *"Allah said, 'I will declare war against him who shows hostility to a pious worshipper of Mine'"* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6502). The ḥadīth's case is the *walī* — the pious servant, the friend of Allah — and its ruling is that hostility shown to the friend is received by the Patron as hostility against Himself, answered by a declaration of war. The verse applies the same structure at its highest altitude: if enmity to a righteous servant draws the divine war-declaration, enmity to the angels and messengers — the servants closest to the Throne, the agents of revelation itself — falls under the declaration with every aggravation the case allows. The two texts read together give the verse's final clause its full weight: *Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers* is not a matching of tempers but the execution of a standing law — the law that the Sender espouses His sent, that the Patron answers for His friends, that enmity toward the chain awakens the enmity of its Source. The ḥadīth continues into the same theology from the other side — the servant who draws near by obligatory and supererogatory deeds until Allah becomes his hearing, his sight, his hand — and the contrast frames the verse's warning completely: nearness to Allah is available through the chain by obedience, and enmity is incurred against the chain by hostility. There is no third position, and the objection of verse 97 tried to occupy one.

**The Enmity Returned**

The closing clause executes the symmetry: *then let them know that Allah is certainly the enemy of the disbelievers*. Three features carry its force. The knowledge-frame — *let them know* — makes the clause a notification rather than a threat in the ordinary sense: a statement of fact addressed to people operating under a false assumption about the consequences of their position. The enmity is named from Allah's side in answer to enmity from theirs, and the naming is judicial rather than emotional: divine enmity in the Qur'an's usage is justice in active opposition — the withdrawal of aid, the exposure to consequences, the treatment of persistent hostility as what it is — not passion, not vindictiveness, not the mirror-image of human grudges. And the object is generalized at the last step: *the disbelievers*, the class rather than the delegation. The verse began with a specific occasion — an objection about an angel raised in Madina — and ended with a standing ruling: enmity to the chain of revelation places its holder, whoever he is in whatever age, inside a relationship he did not intend to enter and cannot unilaterally leave. The symmetry is exact and it is the verse's whole answer: you have declared a friend-and-foe list among Allah's agents; Allah has answered with the only list that matters — His friends and His enemies — and the second list is populated by the first. Whoever wars on the court discovers the King's disposition toward warmakers, and the discovery is what the clause means by *know*.

**Michael Named, and the End of Selective Friendship**

The verse's final particularity deserves its own note: Michael is named. The objection had nominated him as the acceptable angel — the merciful one, the patron, the friend — and the verse's answer does not accept the nomination; it absorbs the nominee into the same list as Gabriel, the same class, the same protection, the same enmity incurred by hostility to either. The mercy-angel is thereby removed from service as an ally against the severity-angel, and the removal is the objection's total defeat. Selective friendship with the unseen is not a position that survives contact with the unseen's own order: the angels are not parties to be chosen among but servants to be accepted as sent, and the human who sorts them has sorted nothing except himself into or out of the verse's two classes. The recital's audience keeps the lesson beyond the angels. Every age attempts its own selective friendship with revelation — the merciful verses befriended and the severe ones warred upon, the comfortable commandments embraced and the costly ones opposed, a personal canon assembled from the preferences of the assembler. Verse 98 answers all of it with the list's indivisibility: the revelation is one chain from one Sender, and enmity to any link — verse, ruling, angel, messenger — is enmity answered by the Source. The two names stand at the verse's end as its exhibit: the friend claimed and the foe alleged, found at last on the same side, under the same Lord, protected by the same declaration of war against whoever makes enemies of the court's servants.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:99

> Indeed, We have sent down to you ˹O Prophet˺ clear revelations. ˹But˺ none will deny them except the rebellious.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Signs Sent Down, Clear by Description**

After the angel-exchange, the recital states the message's own quality in a single declarative sentence: *We have sent down to you clear revelations*. The noun is the Qur'an's standing word for its units — *āyāt*, signs — and the adjective *bayyināt* is its most honored qualifier: signs that are clear in themselves and clearing in their effect, the things that make plain. The commentators specify what the clarity consisted of for the verse's first audience: the signs of Muhammad's ﷺ prophethood — his personal qualities, the knowledge he possessed, the confirmation his message carried — evidence that should have been apparent, Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī note, to any believing Jew, meaning to anyone holding the Torah with the expectation the Torah itself installs. The descent-verb keeps the verse's chain-logic from the previous exchange intact: these signs are *sent down*, from the Sender the objection tried to reach past its couriers — and their clarity is therefore not a human achievement but a divine provision, the evidence supplied with the same Will that supplied the messenger. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ — *to you* — but the clarity is for everyone: a sign sent down to one heart is posted to the world, and the verse's second half treats it as publicly legible, which is the premise the whole sentence runs on.

**None Deny Them Except the Rebellious**

The restriction clause is the verse's judgment, and its exclusivity is total: *none will deny them except the rebellious*. The sentence does not say most deniers are rebellious, or that rebellion often produces denial — it makes rebellion the necessary condition of this denial, the only interior from which these particular signs can be refused. The epistemology installed here is the recital's own, consistent from its first movement: where evidence is clear, rejection is never evidentiary. Verse 75 charged distortion *after understanding*; verse 95 traced the unspoken wish to the hands' record; verse 97 exposed the angel-objection as a costume for lineage-grievance. Verse 99 gathers the pattern into a law: the āyāt are bayyināt, so denial is not a verdict about them but a disclosure about the denier. The clause's future tense — *none will deny them* — extends the law past its occasion: this is not a report about one delegation's refusal but a standing description of every refusal to come. And its logic carries a comfort as exact as its severity: if only the rebellious deny clear signs, then the persistence of denial proves nothing against the signs' clarity, and the believer's confidence in the revelation never has to borrow strength from its acceptance. The verse separates the message's quality from its reception completely — the first fixed by its Sender, the second diagnostic of its audience — and having separated them, assigns each its owner.

**Fisq: The Word for Exiting**

The class-name the clause uses is *fāsiq* — the rebellious one, the transgressor — and the word's root is worth its weight here. *F-s-q* carries the sense of exiting, of coming out from an enclosure; classical usage preserves the image in the mouse leaving its hole, and the Qur'an's moral vocabulary builds on exactly that image: the fāsiq is one who has come out from obedience, stepped outside the enclosure of the command. The choice of word locates the denial precisely. It is not error — the mistaken remain inside, looking; not ignorance — the ignorant have not been shown; not doubt — the doubting stand at the boundary. It is exit: a departure performed by the will after the signs have done their clearing work. The recital has watched the exit in stages through this passage: the covenant cast aside (a departure from the bond), the Book thrown behind the back (a departure from the inheritance), the messenger disliked for his message (a departure from the delivery), the angel befriended selectively (a departure disguised as loyalty). Each stage is fisq in the root's literal force — the same body stepping further outside — and the verse names the accumulated motion at last. Its diagnostic value for the reader is the mirror of its indictment: denials of clear revelation are not intellectual events to be argued with but departures to be recognized, and recognizing the category changes the response the recital counsels, from persuasion to witness — the signs remain sent down, clear, and the exit remains the exiters'.

**Clarity Does Not Compel**

The verse's two halves hold a tension the recital never resolves, because the tension is the truth it teaches: the signs are maximally clear and the denial is fully real. Clarity, in the Qur'an's epistemology, is not coercion. The bayyināt do their work on the eye and the mind; the will keeps its governance over what the person does with the seeing. This is the same structure verse 94's challenge exposed — a claim tested not by argument but by desire — and the same structure the hardening-verses filed: signs accumulate, responses divide, and the division happens in the organ that signs inform but do not commande. The verse's restriction clause is therefore not a limitation on the signs but a statement about their audience: given clarity this complete, the remaining variable is the receiver's posture, and the only posture that produces denial of the clear is the exited one. The pastoral consequence for the believing reader runs in two directions. Toward the denier: the verse forbids despairing of the signs' power when denial persists — the persistence is fisq's fingerprint, not the message's defect — and it equally forbids flattering the denier by treating his exit as a respectable alternative reading of clear evidence. Toward the believer: the verse makes reception a matter of staying put. The enclosure the fāsiq exits is where the bayyināt land, and faithfulness at this station is largely the refusal to step outside when a sign costs something — the discipline the challenge-verses tested by desire, restated as position rather than wish.

**The Consolation Addressed to the Messenger**

Read in its place, the verse is also pastoral speech to the Prophet ﷺ at the close of a long exchange of refusals. The angel-objection has just been answered; the challenges have been issued and their silence predicted; and this verse arrives to settle the messenger's own relation to the denial he lives inside daily. The settlement is in the sentence's two clauses: what you carry is clear — the defect your opponents allege in your message is a defect the Sender's own description excludes; and those who deny it are the exited — the refusal you absorb is testimony about the refusers, filed by Allah in their record rather than yours. The sūrah's consolations run in this register throughout: do not grieve yourself to death over denial (18:6); Allah guides and leaves astray by His knowledge, so do not consume yourself over them (35:8). Verse 99 adds the epistemic form of the same comfort: the clarity is a divine attribute of the message, not a human achievement of the messenger, and therefore the messenger's standing does not rise or fall with the audience's response. For every later carrier of this recitation the verse installs the same posture — the evidence's quality held as received fact, the denial's meaning read as diagnosis, and the self-location fixed inside the enclosure the rebellious exited: sent down to you, clear, and denied by none who stayed.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:100

> Why is it that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside? In fact, most of them do not believe.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Habit Written Into the Grammar**

The verse opens with a question whose particle — *kullamā*, every time — carries the entire indictment. Not once, not in a crisis, not under compulsion: *every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside*. The iteration is the finding. A single breach is an event with causes; a breach repeated at every covenant is a disposition, and the question form — *why is it that every time?* — asks the audience to read the repetition as evidence of what the community has become. The subject of the casting is precise in a way that matters: *a group of them* — farīq, a party, a faction. Not all, each time; a group, every time. The distribution is diagnostic of a community whose covenant-breaking has become institutional — always enough of them, at every station, to make the covenant inoperative, while always fewer than all, so that the exception keeps the accusation from being a blanket. The recital has been filing the stations: the charter of verse 83 turned away from, the witnessed bond of verse 84 violated in Madina's wars, the Torah's testimony to the coming prophet cast aside at his arrival. The verse gathers the stations into the pattern, and the pattern into a character diagnosis delivered in the tone of exhausted recognition — the question a prosecutor asks when the exhibits have run out and only the summary remains.

**Which Covenant? The Occasions and the Pattern**

The exegetes supply three historical referents and then transcend all three. The first: the Jews of Madina pleaded, against the Prophet's ﷺ call, that they had never made any pact or covenant concerning Muhammad specifically — a denial of any obligation toward him — and this verse was revealed against that plea. The second: the covenant in view is the old one, the promise the community had made to follow the prophet who was to come and give them victory over the idolatrous Arabs (the promise verse 89 recorded them praying by). The third: the betrayals of the alliance with the Prophet ﷺ himself — the covenants of mutual defense in Madina broken by siding with the Quraysh, the conduct the recital will address in Sūrah al-Nisāʾ as well (4:51–52's context). Al-Rāzī's note settles the method: the meaning is not restricted to any particular incident. The iterative grammar supports him — *every time* spans occasions, and the three referents the tradition preserves are instances of the law rather than its exhaust. The weighing is worth stating because it decides how the verse reads: taken as incident-report, it belongs to Madina's politics; taken as the tradition finally takes it, it is a standing description of covenant-people's covenant-conduct, with the incidents as its evidentiary base. The recital needs both readings at once — the occasions make the verse historical, the iteration makes it permanent — and the verse's grammar is built to hold them together.

**“Most of Them Do Not Believe”**

The second sentence delivers the cause, and the cause inverts the expected order: *in fact, most of them do not believe*. One might expect the sequence to run the other way — covenants broken, therefore faith lost — but the verse files disbelief as the ground and the casting as the growth. The habit of discarding bonds is not a failure of faith under pressure; it is what a community's life looks like when faith is absent and covenant-language remains in use. The word *most* does its precise work against the earlier exceptions: the few who kept the charter (83), the few excepted at every sealing (4:155's remnant) — most is not all, and the verse's justice needs the margin. But *most* also fixes the community's center of gravity: a people whose majority does not believe will produce, at every covenant, the group that casts it aside, because the casting is simply the majority's actual relation to the bond expressing itself when the bond is renewed. The clause completes the passage's epistemology of refusal: verse 95 located the unspoken wish in the hands' record, verse 99 located denial in rebellion, and verse 100 locates the broken covenant in unbelief — consistently, the recital traces outward behavior to the interior's actual content, and consistently finds that content other than what the profession claims. The covenant-language survives in the community's mouth; the belief that would make it binding does not survive in the community's chest; and the gap between the two is what *every time* measures.

**The Covenant as the Qur'an's Central Bond**

The weight of this verse depends on the weight of covenant in the recital's whole theology, and the sūrah has built that weight deliberately. Covenant in the Qur'an is not a contract between negotiating parties but a bond whose terms descend and whose acceptance is owed — Allah's covenant with Israel at the charter (83), the witnessed bond against blood and expulsion (84), the covenant of every prophet's community, and behind all of them the primordial taking of testimony from the children of Adam at 7:172, the covenant every person ratifies by existing as a creature of Allah. Breaking such a bond is therefore not breach of contract but rupture of relationship — which is why the sūrah's causal chain at verse 83's parallel in al-Māʾidah runs covenant-breaking directly into hardening of hearts: *for breaking their covenant, We condemned them and hardened their hearts* (5:13). The group that casts the covenant aside at every station is the same population whose hearts verse 74 found harder than stone, and the two verses describe one process from its two ends — the will's repeated exit producing the organ's settled stone. The recital's covenant-theology gives verse 100 its tragic register: each casting is not a fresh start but a deposit, and a community that casts at every covenant is, without noticing, completing the hardening its own history reports.

**Every Time: The Renewal Test**

The verse's iteration has a use for its hearing community, and the use is the reason it stands inside a recitation addressed to believers as much as to its historical subjects. Covenants are renewed constantly in the religious life — at every prayer, every Ramaḍān, every moment of clarity in which the heart re-signs its bond — and the verse's *kullamā* applies to the renewals with the same exactness it applied to Madina's treaties. The test it installs is behavioral and available to everyone: watch what happens to the covenant at the next station of cost. The group that casts aside is rarely the whole community and rarely announces itself; it is the party whose interest turns against the bond at each renewal, and its membership shifts, and every member knows the moment he joins. The verse's second sentence is the diagnostic for that moment — the casting is unbelief expressing itself, which means the small abandonment of a renewed bond is not a minor event but a reading of the heart's actual contents. For the community that received this sūrah, the warning was structural rather than tribal: nothing in the verse binds its law to Israel's lineage, and everything in the recital's second-person method applies it to whoever renews and casts. The covenant is made every time; the group forms every time; and most of them — the verse's permanent margin of sorrow — do not believe.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:101

> Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them— confirming their own Scriptures—some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs as if they did not know.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Messenger Who Confirmed**

The verse restates the arrival with its decisive credential attached: *a messenger from Allah has come to them — confirming their own Scriptures*. The confirmation-relationship is the recital's standing answer to the provenance objection — the new Book testifying to the old, the arriving truth vindicating the truth already held — and the verse positions it as the scene's aggravating circumstance. This was not a foreign claimant demanding surrender of an inheritance; it was the inheritance's own witness arriving with the inheritance's own marks upon him. Verse 89 filed the recognition at the arrival; verse 99 named the signs' clarity; verse 101 combines them into the setup for the crime it is about to describe: everything needed for acceptance was present, present in the community's own idiom, certified by the community's own Book. The sentence's *now* — the temporal particle marking the completed setup — functions like a courtroom's *and then*: the conditions are established, the evidence is entered, and the verse's second half records what the people of the evidence did with it. The recital's method throughout this passage has been to remove every excuse before filing every charge; this verse is the method in single-sentence form — credential first, conduct second, with no room between them for a defense.

**Behind the Backs: The Body-Language of Abandonment**

The central image is physical and exact: *they cast the Book of Allah behind their backs*. The Arabic idiom — نبذ وراء الظهر, to throw behind the back — describes not loss but disposal: the deliberate motion of a hand putting something away in the direction the eyes do not look. The image's precision is in its direction. A book dropped is an accident; a book shelved is respect without use; a book cast behind the back is refusal performed with the whole body — the object discarded to the region of non-attention, where it cannot be seen, consulted, or consulted-by-others. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān uses the same idiom for the same crime at its origin: *"Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture to make it known to people and not hide it, yet they cast it behind their backs and traded it for a fleeting gain"* (3:187) — and the pairing of the two verses gives the image its full anatomy: the Book was held in the hands, covenanted into custody, and the custody ended in a backward throw. The verse's grammar keeps the actors inside the Book's own community: *some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah* — the possessors disposing of their possession, the crime's peculiar shape. Outsiders cannot cast behind their backs a Book they never carried; the throw requires custody, which is why this verse indicts a betrayal available only to inheritors.

**Which Book Was Cast?**

The exegetes divide on the identity of the cast Book, and the division is fine-grained enough to matter. The phrase *the Book of Allah* could denote the Qur'an — the messenger's own revelation, rejected at his arrival. But the stronger reading, which al-Ṭabarī and the majority follow, takes it as the Torah, and the verse's own wording carries the argument: the subject is *those who were given the Book*, and what they cast is what they were given — their Scripture, specifically its testimony confirming this messenger, thrown behind the back at the moment the testimony became consequential. The two readings converge in practice, since casting the Torah's confirmation is casting the Qur'an's claim in the same motion; but the Torah-reading sharpens the indictment by locating the betrayal inside the community's most sacred possession. A parallel division runs over the subject: some exegetes restrict *those who were given the Book* to the learned — the scholars whose custody made the casting criminal in the full sense — while others (al-Qushayrī, al-Rāzī) extend it to all who take the Torah as their book and disregard what it says. The extended reading fits the verse's social anatomy better: the scholars cast first, at verse 75's station of informed distortion, and the casting became the community's posture when the majority followed the scholars' direction rather than the Book's. Both the object and the subject of the crime were disputed precisely because both were consequential — the Book's identity fixes which custody was betrayed, and the casters' identity fixes how far the betrayal reached.

**As If They Did Not Know**

The verse's final clause is its psychology: *as if they did not know*. The knowing is conceded by the sentence's whole structure — the confirmation was *their own Scriptures'*, the signs were clear (99), the recognition had occurred (89) — and the clause describes the performance of its opposite. *Ka-annahum lā yaʿlamūn*: the manner of the ignorant adopted by the informed, the posture of innocence worn over a record of comprehension. The recital has catalogued this performance at every station: the distortion *after understanding* (75), the private counsel that managed what public confession would concede (76), the covering laid over blessings received (90). The *as if* is the catalog's common form — a similitude maintained in public while the dissimilitude is known in private — and its cost is the verse's quiet statement: the performed ignorance must be performed continuously, against the performer's own memory, which makes it labor rather than lapse. The clause also fixes the legal character of the casting. Ignorance, actual and invincible, excuses; simulated ignorance aggravates, because the simulation is itself a second decision — the decision to make the first denial unanswerable. The verse indicts both decisions in three words, and the recital's audience keeps the diagnostic: wherever a community's conduct requires its members to behave as if they did not know what the community demonstrably knows, the *as if* is doing work, and the work is the casting of a Book behind backs that once carried it.

**The Anatomy of Abandonment**

What the verse describes is the mechanism by which a religious community abandons its own revelation without ever formally rejecting it, and the mechanism's subtlety is its danger. No book is burned in this verse; no council declares the Torah void; the confession of verse 76's meeting-room still says *we believe*. The abandonment happens in the direction of attention: the Book remains honored in statement while its operative testimony is thrown where consultation cannot reach it. The distinction the verse installs — between a Book held and a Book heeded — is the recital's permanent instrument for every custodian community. The Torah's confirmation of the coming messenger was in the Torah, known, located, quoted in private among the learned; the casting consisted in arranging public life so that this content never functioned. The verse's transfer to its hearing community is immediate and uncomfortable in the way all the recital's transfers are. Every Scripture-keeping people casts something behind its back: the ruling that costs, the testimony that would decide an argument the community has already settled otherwise, the verse that reads the community's own conduct. The casting is rarely announced and never feels like rejection — it feels like emphasis, like context, like the natural quiet of a text no longer quoted. The verse names it for what it is: the Book of Allah, in the custody of the people of the Book, behind their backs, in the posture of those who do not know — and the naming is the mercy, because an abandonment that can be named can still be undone, by turning the body around and picking the Book back up.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:102

> They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon. Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved. They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon. The two angels never taught anyone without saying, “We are only a test ˹for you˺, so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith.” Yet people learned ˹magic˺ that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband and wife; although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will. They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them—although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter. Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls, if only they knew!

**Expanded Commentary**

**What the Devils Recited**

The recital turns from the cast Book to what filled the vacancy, and the verse's opening names both the substitute and its authors: *they followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon*. The devils' activity is described with the same word the Qur'an uses for revelation's recitation — they *recited* against Solomon's kingdom, or, in the variant reading the exegetes preserve, recited regarding it or within its time — and the verbal echo is deliberate: against the Book cast behind the back stands a counter-recitation, a corpus taught, transmitted, followed. The setting is Solomon's reign, and the tradition's accounts of how the corpus entered circulation cluster around the king's death: writings describing the arts by which Solomon ruled, interred beneath his throne-platform, exhumed after his death and put to misuse — documents of power turned into manuals of manipulation, spread among people given over to their passions, circulating until the Prophet's ﷺ own time. The commentators are candid about the reliability gradient here — this verse's exegetical literature, more than any other's, gathers material startlingly incongruous with the tradition's standards, and the major commentators, Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī among them, reject the legends' speculative elaborations while retaining the verse's plain architecture. What the verse itself asserts is narrower and firmer: there was a devil-authored tradition of magic associated with Solomon's era, the people of this verse followed it, and the following was itself the disbelief the sentence structure implies — they traded a sent-down Book for a recited-up corruption.

**“Never Did Solomon Disbelieve”**

The verse interrupts its own narrative to clear a prophet's name, and the interruption's vehemence — *never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved* — marks what was at stake. In the surrounding traditions, Jewish and later popular accounts had woven Solomon's unmatched dominion into a magician's biography: the king who commanded jinn and wind rendered as a king who dealt in sorcery. The Qur'an's counter-testimony is absolute. Solomon's powers were conferred — the raging winds subjected to him, blowing by his command (21:81), the jinn and the devils in service, the kingdom none after him would hold — and conferred power is the opposite of usurped art: it arrives with its Source named, which is why its holder never disbelieved. The distinction the verse installs runs through every case of extraordinary capacity: powers granted by Allah point back to Allah and keep their holder inside faith; powers sought from the devils' recitation point back to the self and their price is the soul. Solomon is thus not merely exonerated but exhibited — the maximum case of divinely given power, held without a gram of disbelief, against which the magic-buyers' minimum purchase stands condemned. The clause's placement does further work: by clearing Solomon at the moment the devils are named, the verse assigns the disbelief precisely — *rather the devils disbelieved* — and makes the following of their recitation a participation in their disbelief rather than a neutral technical acquisition.

**Hārūt and Mārūt, and the Warning Built Into the Teaching**

The verse's most discussed element is its second curriculum: *what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon*. The exegetical literature around the two angels includes the legends the tradition itself flags as incongruous — angels sent down after boasting of human frailty, tempted by a woman of beauty (Venus in the legend's astrology), intoxicated into sin — and the major commentators reject these elaborations; al-Rāzī at one point even identifies the two with Gabriel and Michael. The sober reading the verse's own wording supports is cleaner and more instructive: the angels taught, and their teaching carried its warning inside it — *"We are only a test for you, so do not abandon your faith"* (2:102). No one was taught without first being told what the knowledge was: a trial, a double-edged instrument, dangerous in proportion to its power. The structure is the Qur'an's permanent law of hazardous knowledge. The hidden dimensions of the cosmos can be read — for wisdom, for healing, for good — and the same reading can be turned to severance and harm; the difference is not in the knowledge but in the receiver, which is why the knowledge is delivered with the test declared. Babylon as the setting is exact rather than incidental: the esoteric tradition associates this revealed-and-warned knowledge with the correspondence-sciences that originated in Babylon — the web of sympathies joining stars, minerals, plants, and human affairs, the foundation on which astrology, alchemy, and divination were built. The angels taught the science with its warning; the people kept the science and discarded the warning, which is the verse's account of how a test becomes a trap.

**Siḥr: The Range of the Word**

The verse's subject-term deserves its lexical range stated, because the range explains the verse's severity. *Siḥr* covers, in Arabic usage and in the exegetes' accounting, more than stage-magic: it includes sleight of hand and illusion; the manipulation of hidden forces toward a chosen effect; the attainment of knowledge of absent things — distant in space or time — by occult means; and, at the word's furthest reach, a persuasive eloquence so captivating it binds its hearers, which is why the Qur'an's opponents could accuse the recitation itself of being *siḥr mubīn*, manifest magic (10:2). The range gathers the verse's elements into one category: the devils' recitation (a counter-revelation binding hearts), the angels' warned science (hidden forces legible and steerable), the separation of spouses (effects in the world wrought by unseen means). What unifies the range is the bypass: siḥr in every sense reaches its ends around the ordained channels — knowledge without revelation, power without permission, persuasion without truth. The verse's judgment on the bypass is written into its economics, which arrive in the second half: the buyer of magic purchases harm, spends his soul, and forfeits his share in the Hereafter. The tradition's esoteric reading runs the same judgment inward — the magic here is the soul's defection from the heart and spirit to the ego's lower instruments, the turning from the *Solomon of the spirit* to the devils of the soul — and the inward reading keeps the verse's law portable: every age has its correspondence-sciences, its techniques for steering hidden forces past their warned limits, and the purchase-price is unchanged.

**The Rift Between Husband and Wife**

The verse names magic's signature effect, and the naming is a social diagnosis: *they learned from them what caused a rift even between husband and wife*. The marriage bond is the target because it is the load-bearing wall of human society — the first covenant between persons, the structure under every household, market, and generation — and an art whose showcase achievement is its severance is an art aimed at the social order's foundation. The commentators note how common this commission was in premodern societies, and the Qur'an's final sūrahs will keep their refuge-language trained on the same threat (113's introduction in the tradition). The verse's limiting clause then delivers its theology in a sentence that dismantles the art from inside: *their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah's Will*. The permission-principle is total: no technique, however ancient, however warned-about, however purchased, carries independent causal power — every effect runs through the same divine Will that runs every event, and the magician's real transaction is not with hidden forces but with the devils' recitation, buying a participation in disbelief at the price of a power he does not actually possess. The clause protects the verse's audience in both directions: against terror of the art (it harms only by the Will that also protects) and against temptation toward it (its exercise is disbelief's purchase, whatever its effects). Between husband and wife, the bond the recital's covenant-theology most resembles, the art's greatest recorded success is also its greatest recorded crime — and the Will that permits the rift is the same Will verse 186 will describe as answering the prayer of whoever calls.

**The Purchase and Its Price**

The verse closes with the buyer's ledger, in the sūrah's transaction-grammar: *they learned what harmed them and did not benefit them — although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter*. The learning verbs stack deliberately: they learned the art, they learned its harm, and they already knew its cost — knowledge at every level, purchase anyway, which is the recital's fixed portrait of informed self-destruction. The trade-clause then pronounces in the formula this passage has already established as the sūrah's verdict-idiom: *miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls, if only they knew!* — the same exclamation filed at verse 90 over the souls sold in envy, here over souls sold for severance-power. The commentators mark the verse's Faust-structure by name: the bargainer who trades the soul for unworthy worldly gain, the Western tradition's crystallization of the purchase this verse describes with its warning-clause intact. And the final *if only they knew* holds the verse's cruelest precision against its own premise — they already knew. The knowledge that should have blocked the purchase was present at the purchase, which locates the failure exactly where verse 75 located the distortion and verse 101 located the casting: not in the intellect's supply but in the will's direction. The devils' recitation found its followers among people fully informed about the Hereafter-share they were paying away — informed, and buying — and the verse's ledger stands as the recital's complete account of what informed purchase of the forbidden costs: harm without benefit in this world, no share in the next, and a soul spent against a knowledge that watched the spending.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:103

> If only they were faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, there would have been a better reward from Allah, if only they knew!

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Counter-Offer Filed Against the Purchase**

One sentence answers the ledger of verse 102, and the answer is structured as the offer the buyers never took: *if only they were faithful and mindful of Allah, there would have been a better reward from Allah*. The commentators state the comparison's terms plainly — Allah's recompense is better than what they purchased with their souls — and the verse's whole force is in the word *better*. Not merely other, not merely safe: better on the buyer's own axis of evaluation, better as return, better as acquisition, better in the currency the purchase was made in. The counter-offer thereby meets the magic-buyers inside their own economics rather than outside it: you sought gain, the verse says, and the gain you refused exceeds the gain you took — not in the Hereafter alone but at the moment of transaction, since the reward named is *from Allah*, held by the party whose possession nothing devalues. The conditional's mood carries the tragedy: *if only they were* — the offer is stated in the irrealis, the mood of the unactualized, which files what the counter-offer's status now is. It was available at the purchase; it remains the verse's content; and its unclaimed standing is the recital's quietest indictment — the better reward not withdrawn but bypassed, sitting in the offer while the buyers walked away holding harm.

**Faith and Mindfulness: The Two Conditions**

The offer's conditions are the pair the sūrah runs on: faith — *āmanū* — and mindfulness of Allah — *ittaqaw*, the taqwā that names the whole posture of guarded reverence, the life organized around the presence of the One to be guarded against offending. The pairing is not additive but structural, and verse 102's own scene demonstrates why both are needed. The magic-buyers' failure ran at both levels: they disbelieved in the share they knew they were forfeiting — faith's absence — and they crossed the warned boundary the angels' teaching had marked — taqwā's absence. The warning-clause built into that teaching, *we are only a test, so do not abandon your faith*, addressed precisely the two conditions together: the test required faith to be believed and taqwā to be passed. A knowledge of hidden forces without faith is a menu with no forbidden items; the same knowledge without taqwā is a boundary with no fear at its edge. The verse's conditions are therefore the exact complement of the purchase: faith answers the *no share in the Hereafter* the buyers knew and paid anyway, and mindfulness answers the *do not disbelieve* they heard and crossed. The pair also carries the sūrah's standing definition of the religion it offers — belief held as assent and enacted as vigilance — and its appearance here, at the end of the magic-episode, restates the definition against the episode's whole alternative: a life steered by unseen forces purchased from warned-against sources, set against a life steered by the Unseen Himself, received on faith and kept in fear.

**“If Only They Knew”: The Suspended Knowing**

The verse ends where verse 102 ended, on the same suspended phrase — *if only they knew* — and the repetition is the passage's hinge. Verse 102's clause landed against a stated fact: they *already knew* the buyer's cost, which made the closing *if only they knew* an irony — the knowing present and inoperative. Verse 103's clause lands against the counter-offer: the better reward is real, from Allah, available on two conditions — and the knowing of *that* is what remains missing. The two verses together complete the diagnosis of this community's epistemic tragedy: the knowledge they possessed did not save them from the purchase, and the knowledge they lacked concerned the only thing worth having instead. The recital has been building this portrait for thirty verses — distortion after understanding, wishes stopped by records, denials classified as rebellion, covenants cast by non-believers — and the doubled *if only they knew* names the pattern's essence: knowledge and faith are not the same possession, and the gap between them is the width of the will. The verse's exclamation is therefore not condescension but grief in grammatical form — the *if only* of a speaker watching someone choose the lesser good with full information about the greater, which is the one failure argument cannot repair, because argument supplies information and the information was already supplied.

**The Better Reward, Unnamed**

The reward the verse offers is not described, and the absence of description is the offer's rhetoric. Verse 102's merchandise came itemized: the rift between spouses, the harm without benefit, the share forfeited — the purchase's contents fully specified, and specified as loss. Verse 103's better reward carries no inventory: *a reward from Allah*, defined by its source alone. The asymmetry is deliberate and it teaches the two economies' natures. The devils' recitation sells named effects — precise, bounded, and hollow, every item a harm wearing a benefit's label. Allah's reward is named by its Giver because its contents exceed itemization: the recital has already filed samples of it — gardens with rivers beneath, whatever the heart's labor finds waiting with Allah — and its description-language consistently outruns list-making. The buyer between the two offers is therefore choosing between a specified small thing and an unspecified great one, and the choice requires exactly the two conditions the verse names: faith to trust an unseen reward's reality, taqwā to hold a warned boundary against a visible technique's allure. The unnamed reward is not vagueness but superabundance — and the verse's final service to its reader is making the comparison honestly: the purchase promises what it can specify and delivers harm; the offer specifies nothing and delivers from Allah. Between a named loss and an unnamed better, the recital asks its audience to locate the real ignorance — and it is not on the offer's side.

**The Offer Stands**

The conditional's tense — *there would have been* — reads as past, closing a case on people who chose; but the recital's whole method forbids taking its closures as final, because every verdict it files in the second person is filed to be re-heard. The offer's conditions are standing: faith and mindfulness remain available, the better reward remains from Allah, and the counter-offer is restated every time the verse is recited — which is to say, in every prayer that carries this sūrah's recitation forward. The magic-buyers of Madina are the verse's occasion, not its boundary; the purchase it condemns has successors in every technique of every age that promises steering of the unseen at a price the warned boundary forbids — and the counter-offer addresses each successor's buyers in the same irrealis, which becomes real the moment a buyer turns. This is the verse's structural mercy inside the passage's severity: verse 102's ledger closed with a soul sold and a share forfeited; verse 103 reopens the transaction from the credit side, stating the better that was refused in terms that remain purchasable. The sūrah's economics has now completed its first full circuit — the cheap price of verse 41, the fleeting gain of verse 79, the trade of verse 86, the miserable price of verse 90 and verse 102 — and at the circuit's end stands the only counter-entry the recital ever files: a better reward, from Allah, for faith and mindfulness. The knowing the verse wishes for its subjects is the knowing it offers its readers, and the offer's final clause is addressed to whoever is still choosing: if only they knew.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:104

> O believers! Do not say, “Râ’ina.” [Herd us!] But say, “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!] and listen ˹attentively˺. And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Word Banned for the Believers**

The recital turns, in a single verse, from the theology of selection to the vocabulary of the prayer-hall, and its subject is one word. *Rāʿinā* — in the believers' mouths a colloquial request for attention, something like *lend us your ear*, from an idiom current in the speech of the two cities: *rāʿinā samʿak*, attend to me with your hearing. The believers had been using it to the Prophet ﷺ in the ordinary way of people asking a teacher to slow down, to stay with them, to give them his regard. The verse legislates against it absolutely: *do not say rāʿinā — but say unẓurnā*. The command's scope deserves notice before its reasons: it addresses the believers themselves, the sincere users of the word, not its abusers. The legislation therefore is not about intent but about the word — a term the faithful meant innocently is withdrawn from the community's address to its Prophet ﷺ, and a substitute is installed in the same breath. Sūrah al-Nisāʾ records the other side of the word's history: some among the Jews twisted their tongues with it, saying *"We listen and we disobey"* and playing with *"Rāʿinā"* as an insult dressed in a request (4:46) — the same syllables carrying mockery in their mouths and innocence in the believers'. Between the two verses the word's career is complete: an ordinary idiom, a vehicle of abuse, and a revealed ban that removes the vehicle by removing the idiom.

**Why the Innocent Word Had to Go**

The exegetes give two grounds for the ban, and their weighing is instructive. The first is the idiom's own texture: in the usage of Makkah and Madina, *rāʿinā* carried a demeaning, familiar edge — the tone of one who herds cattle applied to one who is addressed as a shepherd of souls, impudence available inside an apparently neutral request. Al-Ṭabarī sets this verse with the Prophet's ﷺ standing practice of calling things and people by their noblest names, and connects it to the Qur'an's own etiquette-legislation in Sūrah al-Nūr: *do not treat the Messenger's summons to you as lightly as your summons to one another* (24:63) — the address of the Prophet ﷺ is not the address of an equal, and words whose idiom implies equality are barred from it regardless of the speaker's heart. The second proposed ground is the Hebrew wordplay — that the Jews exploited the word's resemblance to a term of abuse, and the ban removed their instrument. Al-Ṭabarī discounts this reading *for this verse* with a sharp argument: the command falls on the believers, who would not have adopted a phrase of insult they did not understand; the wordplay belongs to the 4:46 account of the abusers, not to the legislation addressed to the sincere. The weighing matters because it fixes the verse's principle: the ban protects the dignity of the address itself, not merely against one group's mischief. A word can be removed from sacred use because of what it sounds like in the culture's ear, even when every user means well — and the community's speech to its Prophet ﷺ is regulated at the level of idiom, not merely at the level of intention.

**Unẓurnā and the Command to Listen**

The substitute comes with its own instruction: *say unẓurnā, and listen attentively*. The verb *unẓurnā* — regard us, attend to us, and in other contexts wait for us, as in the Day-scene where the hypocrites beg the believers to *wait for us so that we may have some of your light* (57:13) — carries the same request as *rāʿinā* with the demeaning idiom stripped out: the believers may still ask the Prophet's ﷺ regard, still ask him to pace himself to them, still ask for the audience a learner needs. The content of the request survives; its cultural packaging is replaced. The verse's second imperative then completes the instruction: *and listen* — which the exegetes read as listening in its full sense, hearing that includes obeying, the same hearing-and-obedience the covenant demanded and the community of verse 93 refused with its inverted formula. The pairing of the two commands gives the verse's positive program: ask respectfully, then listen obediently. The speech-legislation is not only protection of the Prophet's ﷺ dignity but formation of the believers' learning posture — a community that addresses its teacher in the idiom of regard and receives his teaching in the idiom of obedience has structured its education as worship, and the verse's small lexical surgery is the recital's way of building that structure at the level where language lives.

**The Punishment Clause**

The verse ends with a sentence that appears to change subject entirely: *and the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment*. The shift is not as abrupt as it reads. The commentators locate the clause's referents in the word's abusers — the mockers who turned an idiom into an insult, whose wordplay Sūrah al-Nisāʾ files as playing with words and discrediting the faith — and on that reading the clause seals the legislation with its sanction: the same syllables that cost the believers a vocabulary change cost their abusers a sentence. But the clause's generality — *the disbelievers*, unnamed, unqualified — extends its coverage past any single occasion, and the extension is the verse's structural point. Speech that toys with the honor of revelation's bearer is not a misdemeanor of manners; in the recital's taxonomy it belongs to disbelief and draws disbelief's penalty. The verse has thus legislated in both directions at once: to the believers, whose innocent idiom is withdrawn lest dignity suffer by proximity; to the mockers, whose calculated idiom is answered with the punishment-clause. Between the two audiences stands the principle the whole verse enacts — that the words a community uses toward its Prophet ﷺ are themselves religious acts, weighted, audited, and legislated, and that the recital cares about the texture of address closely enough to ban a single word and install a better one in its place.

**The Discipline of Substituted Words**

The verse's transfer runs to every community's vocabulary. Religions accumulate idioms — forms of address, honorifics, casual phrases around sacred things — and the idioms drift: familiarity erodes the reverence they once carried, and outside tongues learn to hide abuse inside them. Verse 104 is the recital's precedent for managing the drift, and its method is precise. It does not lecture on reverence in the abstract; it names one word, bans it, and supplies its replacement — legislation at the granularity of vocabulary, where reverence actually lives. The method implies a standing audit for the community that receives it: which of our words for sacred things carry, in the culture's ear, a tone we would not choose if we heard it from outside? Which idioms of intimacy have become idioms of cheapness? The believers of Madina did not know their word had a demeaning register — the revelation knew it for them, which is the verse's quiet claim about the reach of revealed legislation: it regulates what sincere users cannot self-diagnose. And the installed substitute teaches the replacement's spirit: *unẓurnā* keeps the request and drops the contempt, which means the discipline is not silence but better speech — reverence is not the absence of familiar address but its purification. The listening-command attached to the substitute completes the verse's curriculum for every generation: ask in the words respect provides, and hear as those who intend to obey — while the punishment-clause stands over the whole economy of words, a reminder that in the recital's accounting, speech about the sacred is never merely speech.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:105

> The disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord, but Allah selects whoever He wills for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Coalition of One Negative Wish**

The verse begins with a survey of the opposition, and the survey's finding is remarkable for its unanimity: *the disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord*. Two camps that agree on almost nothing — the scriptural monotheists of Madina and the idolatrous Arabs of Makkah, whose mutual relation the recital has already documented as warfare and contempt — converge on a single desire, and the desire is negative: not that they possess some good, but that the Muslims lack it. The verse's construction puts the negation first: what unites the opposition is not a shared creed but a shared withholding, the wish that no good descend on this community. The analysis matters because it diagnoses opposition at its root. Doctrinal conflict can be argued; interest-conflict can be negotiated; but a will organized around another's deprivation is not reachable by either means, because the Muslims' gain is precisely what it refuses. The recital has watched this refusal operate at every station: the private counsel managing what the believers might be told (76), the ransom-paradox funding captives while expelling neighbors (85), the resentment at grace's freedom (90), the wish to reverse belief itself (109, ahead in the file's own unfolding). Verse 105 states the common denominator behind all of them, and in stating it, frees the community's strategy: against a coalition whose bond is your deprivation, the response cannot be appeasement, because your flourishing is the thing the coalition exists to refuse.

**“Any Blessing from Your Lord”**

The object of the withheld wish is defined with a phrase whose every term works. *Any blessing* — *khayr* in its widest sense: every good, without specification, which makes the wish's breadth total — not opposition to particular Muslim advantages but to the category of Muslim advantage. *From your Lord* — the source named as the Muslims' own Lord, in the possessive form the recital uses for intimacy: the good that is begrudged is not wrested from a rival but descending from a Patron, which relocates the conflict entirely — the coalition's real quarrel is with the descent's Source. And the exegetes specify the blessing's primary referent in this context: the revelation itself and its wisdom, bestowed through the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ — the mercy the community actually received, which is why the verse's second clause answers in the same terms. The specification exposes the wish's futility in advance.
