The three streams are not rivals so much as strata: purity-commands, pilgrimage-rites, and survival-trials together compose the patriarch's received biography, and each stream's evidence is textual within the larger Qur'an. The weighing the verse itself supplies is structural — it reports the testing and the fulfillment without adjudicating the list, which tells the reader where the emphasis belongs: whatever the words were, they were completed, and the completion is what the office is built on.

**“I Am Making You a Role Model”**

The fulfillment is answered by an appointment: *I will certainly make you into a role model for the people* — an *imām*, the word whose root is the prayer-leader's standing and whose range covers every form of followed leadership, religious and political. The imām is defined by the direction of faces: the one whose pattern others walk in, whose standing others orient by. The appointment's emphatic form — *I will certainly make you* — carries the divine guarantee, and its object — *for the people*, unqualified — carries the scope: not for a tribe, not for a century, imāmah for humanity. The tradition's readings of the office deepen it. In Sunni usage the imām here is the leader in faith whose example is binding by excellence; in Shīʿī doctrine the word carries its technical weight — the bearer of the Muhammadan Light, designated by divine decree — and the fifth and sixth Imams of that tradition cited precisely this verse for the principle that Allah does not establish or permit an unjust imām. Both readings draw from the same clause of the verse, and the verse's own second half arbitrates: whatever the imāmah's metaphysics, its transmission is governed by the answer to Abraham's question — and the answer conditions everything.

**“And of My Offspring?”**

The patriarch's response to his appointment is immediate and generational: *what about my offspring?* — the question of every founder who has received an office: does it continue in the line? The question is not ambition but concern, and its asking is honored by being answered rather than rebuked; the answer, however, redraws the question's map: *My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers*. The exegetes read the reply at three depths. At the first, it is a qualification of eligibility: the wrongdoer — the tyrant, the unjust — does not deserve the covenant and cannot rightly hold the imāmah. At the second, it is a qualification of promise: an imām who does wrong would not receive the covenant's Hereafter-guarantee — the office may be held, the promise is forfeited. At the third, it is simply information: not all of Abraham's descendants will be virtuous — a fact Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt states outright: *We blessed him and Isaac as well. Some of their descendants did good, while others clearly wronged themselves* (37:113). The three readings converge on one doctrine, and the doctrine is the verse's hinge for the whole recital: the covenant runs on righteousness, not blood. The lineage question receives a moral answer — the office is transmissible in principle and conditional in fact, and the condition is personal rather than genealogical. The section just closed had documented the failure of the opposite assumption across a hundred verses; the section now opening states, at its patriarch's first station, the law that assumption violated.

**The Tested Pattern as Inheritance**

The verse's transfer is in the office's nature. An imām is followed, and what Abraham's imāmah makes followable is the tested pattern: commands received, commands fulfilled, appointment granted, concern for the line answered with a moral condition. Sūrah al-Furqān preserves the pattern as every believer's prayer — *our Lord, grant us pious spouses and offspring, and make us models for the righteous* (25:74) — the imāmah-words turned into supplication, the office opened to whoever prays for it on its terms. The terms the verse files are exacting and available: the test comes as commands (revelation, not speculation); the fulfillment is personal (Abraham's own hands, his own fire, his own son); the appointment is divine (no self-declared imām stands in this file); and the transmission is moral (the wrongdoer excluded at the patriarch's own threshold). The recital's audience — a community two generations old, already generating its own claims of precedence — received in this verse the constitution of religious authority as Islam holds it: leadership earned under examination, conferred by Allah, inherited only by the righteous, and measured at every generation against the man who fulfilled. The children of the covenant, hearing their own file closed at verse 123, now hear its root opened at verse 124 — and the opening sentence tells them, and every later claimant, that the covenant's first holder got it by passing a test, and keeps it by the answer given to his question about his children.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:125

> And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre and a sanctuary for the people ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer.” And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Place of Return and a Place of Safety**

The verse states the House's dual institution, and the two terms are its whole social theology. *A centre* — *mathāba*, the place of return, the point people come back to again and again: the word names not a location but a gravitational function, the station that draws repeated approach, that no visit exhausts and no pilgrim leaves for good. *A sanctuary* — *amn*, safety: the precinct where the hunted is safe, where the vendetta stops at the boundary. Al-Ṭabarī records the sanctuary's pre-Islamic operation: even a killer stood secure within its bounds, a practice the tradition reads as the continuation, in Arabian custom, of the status the House received at its institution. The two functions answer the two needs the House serves. The return-function serves worship's repeatability — a faith needs a point its body can revisit, a direction its face can find, a journey its calendar can schedule; the safety-function serves worship's precondition — the house of God must be a place where God's creatures are beyond reach of each other's violence. The pairing also reads against the verse two stations back: the masājid barred and ruined (114) were houses whose return-function was blocked and whose sanctuary-function was violated, and verse 125 files the original pattern those crimes inverted — the House made for return, made safe, owned by the One whose property verse 114 defended.

**The Standing-Place of Abraham**

Between the two institutions stands a specific commandment: *take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer*. The maqām — the standing-place — is identified in the tradition first as the physical station: the stone near the Kaʿbah said to bear Abraham's footprint, held in its enclosure beside the House to this day. The exegetes record wider readings — the maqām as the ḥajj-rites in their entirety, or as the pilgrimage's other stations, ʿArafāt, Minā, Muzdalifah — and the readings share a claim: whatever Abraham stood on or stood for in the House's service is consecrated as prayer-ground. The tradition preserves the commandment's occasion in two accounts. In one, the Prophet ﷺ took ʿUmar by the hand at the stone and said, *this is the standing-place of Abraham*; ʿUmar asked, *shall we take it as a place of prayer?*; the Prophet ﷺ answered that he had not been commanded to — and before the day's sunset the verse descended with the command. In the account ʿUmar himself narrated, preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, he wished aloud to the Prophet ﷺ, *I wish we took the station of Abraham as our praying place* — and the revelation came: *and take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 402), one of the three matters in which ʿUmar reported his Lord agreed with him. The two accounts differ in who spoke first, and the difference is immaterial to the verse's fact: the prayer-site at the patriarch's stone is legislated here, in a form — *you may take* — that some exegetes read as imperative and others as declarative, the community's practice settling the reading. The stone's function completes the verse's Abrahamic architecture: the imām of verse 124 leaves a footprint, and the footprint's place becomes the community's prayer-ground — leadership followed literally, at the point of standing.

**“Purify My House”**

The verse's second half records the charge laid on the builders: *We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House*. The covenant-verb — *ʿahidnā* — makes the purification a commissioned trust, and al-Ṭabarī specifies the content: cleansing the House from idolatry and from doubt. The two objects of purification define the masjid's negative and positive conditions — no false object of worship inside it, no false posture of heart toward it — and the charge's tense carries its history: for Abraham, purification meant maintaining the House in the state it was instituted in, a standing custodianship; the tradition then records the custody's long erosion, the idols' arrival, and the restoration — the Prophet ﷺ returning the House to its Abrahamic condition at the conquest, the charge fulfilled a second time by the descendant of its first trustees. The purification-clause also binds this verse to verse 114 with a knot the recital ties deliberately: the House's existence is for the circlers, the meditators, the bowing and prostrating — and whoever fills it with anything else, or bars anyone from these, is charged with the ruin the earlier verse sentenced. *My House* — the possessive is the clause's warrant: the purification standard is not the trustees' preference but the Owner's purpose, and the purpose is named in the three classes the charge serves.

**The Three Classes of Worshipper**

The House's beneficiaries are listed in three participles, and the list covers the body's whole liturgical range. *Those who circle it* — the circumambulators, the ṭawāf whose walking orbit makes the House the fixed center of a moving devotion, the rite that is the pilgrimage's signature. *Those who meditate in it* — the *ʿākifūn*, from a root meaning both devoted-to and resident-in: the retreaters, whose worship is stationary presence. The tradition built an institution on the word: *iʿtikāf*, the practice of spending set days inside the mosque in prayer and remembrance, established by the Prophet's ﷺ own retreats in the last ten nights of Ramaḍān, and behind it the Sufi discipline of seclusion — the *khalwah* whose genealogy the exegetes trace to this participle. *Those who bow and prostrate* — the prayer's two defining movements, the liturgy in its daily form. The three classes are the House's complete population: the circling movement, the abiding stillness, the rhythmic prayer — procession, retreat, and worship gathered in one precinct, each class served by the purification, each class's exclusion a violation of the charge. The list also quietly legislates the House's schedule: it is not a monument visited but a masjid inhabited, and its trustees' duty is measured against the three forms of occupancy the Owner names.

**Father and Son, Jointly Entrusted**

The charge names two trustees, and the second name is the verse's argument to its audience: *Abraham and Ishmael*. The patriarch of verse 124 and the son whose line the Arabian hearers claimed are joined in one custodianship — the House built and purified by both, its covenant held by both, its prayer-ground marked by one and legislated for all. The joint trusteeship does precise polemical work in the recital's Madinan moment. The Israelite claim ran through Isaac's line exclusively; the Arabian claim ran through Ishmael's; the verse files the House as the two brothers' common work, under their common Father's God, which makes the House older than the division and superior to both claims. The purification-charge addressed to both also states the recital's covenant-law from verse 124 in operative form: the office descends through righteousness held jointly, not through lineage held exclusively — and the wrongdoer's exclusion the patriarch heard applies to every trustee of every generation, of either line. For the Muslims hearing the sūrah — a community praying toward this House within months of the verse's revelation, their qibla legislation about to arrive — the verse installed their direction's full pedigree: the House they faced was not a Makkah landmark but a divine institution, made center and sanctuary, charged to two prophets, purified for three classes of worshipper, its patriarch's footprint legislated as their prayer-site. The community's newest practice was given the oldest title-deed in the recital's possession.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:126

> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure and provide fruits to its people—those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day.” He answered, “As for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves for a little while, then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire. What an evil destination!”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Patriarch's Civic Prayer**

The verse records the second of Abraham's two prayers for the House's setting, and this one is urban: *my Lord, make this city secure and provide fruits to its people*. The petition's two terms are the two goods a settlement lives by — safety and supply — and their order is doctrinal: security first, because provision cannot be enjoyed where fear governs, and worship cannot be gathered where the roads are unsafe. The city is Makkah, the barren valley the patriarch had settled his household in with the prayer Sūrah Ibrāhīm preserves: *our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a barren valley, near Your Sacred House, so that they may establish prayer — so make the hearts of people incline toward them, and provide them with fruits, so perhaps they will be thankful* (14:37). The two prayers are one petition across decades: the valley without cultivation asked for fruit, the city asked for security, and both asked on the House's account — the settlement's goods requested for the sake of the worship it hosts. The same sūrah preserves the prayer's third term, the patriarch's fear for its interior: *make this city secure, and keep me and my children away from the worship of idols* (14:35) — security and provision bracketing the one danger that would void both, the idol inside the safe, fruit-bearing town. The verse's prayer is therefore a complete civic theology in one sentence: safety for the body, fruit for the body's life, and — in the clause that follows — the qualification that reveals what the body's goods are for.

**The Qualifier and the Answer That Widens It**

Abraham restricts his petition: *those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day* — the security and the fruits asked for the believers of the city. The divine answer accepts the prayer and exceeds its restriction, and the exceeding is the verse's central instruction: *as for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves for a little while, then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire*. The disbeliever is not excluded from the city's provision; he is included in it, for a while, and the while is named as a while. The amendment teaches three things at once. Provision is not a verdict: the fruit of Makkah falls on believer and disbeliever alike, so neither prosperity nor its absence reads as divine approval — the doctrine the sūrah will legislate in its own terms against every reader who mistakes supply for standing. The patriarch's intercession is honored past its own scope: Abraham asked for the believers, and the answer shows the asking was received in a generosity wider than the ask — the city's economy cannot be run on the prayer's exclusion, because the world's economy is not run that way. And the enjoyment is structured as respite: *a little while*, then the destination — the worldly provision of the disbeliever is not a share but a span, and the span's end is filed in the same sentence: *what an evil destination!* The verse thereby answers, in advance, the theology of verse 80's claimants and every successor who reads worldly inclusion as otherworldly insurance: the Fire's condemned were fed too.

**The Sanctuary Declared**

The prayer's first term — *secure* — received its historical ratification in the tradition's most documented declaration. On the day Makkah was taken, the Prophet ﷺ stood in the city and stated its status: *"Allah has made Mecca a sanctuary, so it was a sanctuary before me and will continue to be a sanctuary after me. It was made legal for me — that is, I was allowed to fight in it — for a few hours of a day. It is not allowed to uproot its shrubs or to cut its trees, or to chase or disturb its game, or to pick up its lost things except by a person who would announce that publicly"* (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1833) — with the tradition's single recorded exception, when al-ʿAbbās asked for the idhkhir-grass used by the goldsmiths and for graves, and the Prophet ﷺ granted it. In another formulation of the same announcement, the tradition dates the sanctity to the day the heavens and the earth were created and extends it to the Day of Resurrection, with the killing inside it permitted to no one before or after. The declaration's content is Abraham's petition made law: the city *secure* — not merely peaceful by circumstance but inviolable by statute, its safety a ruling rather than a condition. The statute's granularity in the ḥadīth — the shrub, the tree, the game, the lost article — extends the sanctuary past human blood to the city's whole living furniture, and the few-hours exception of the conquest confirms the rule by marking its only breach as unique, dated, and closed. The verse's prayer is thus answerable in the historical record: asked at the House's founding, legislated at the city's return, and the *āmin*-root binding it to verse 125's *amn* ties the city's security to the House's sanctuary as one institution.

**Fruits in the Barren Valley**

The petition's second term carries the geography's standing miracle. Makkah sits in a valley the patriarch's own prayer described as without cultivation (14:37) — no orchards, no fields, no water-command of its own — and the fruit asked for it is not agricultural produce but commercial and pilgrim provision: the goods carried in because the House draws the carriers. The prayer's mechanism is stated in 14:37 itself — *make the hearts of people incline toward them* — the fruit routed through inclination, the supply created by love of the destination, and the history the verse's audience knew ran exactly on that mechanism: the caravans of winter and summer, the market fairs of the pilgrimage season, the barren town fed by its own drawing-power. The recital's audience was also hearing the petition's purpose-clause, which 14:37 states and verse 126 assumes: *so that they may establish prayer*, *so perhaps they will be thankful*. The fruits are instrumental — provision for a worshipping settlement, supply ordered to gratitude — and the instrumental ordering is what the answer's second half enforces from the other side: the provision arrives for all, but it is received rightly only where the gratitude runs, and where it does not, the enjoyment is booked as respite and the destination as evil. The verse leaves the two receptions standing side by side in one city: the believer fed and thankful, the disbeliever fed and respite-held, the same fruit, the same security, two destinations — and the difference between them located, as the recital always locates it, in what the fed heart does with the feeding.

**The Respite and the Destination**

The answer's structure — *a little while, then* — is the Qur'an's grammar of respite, and its logic runs through the whole passage this section belongs to. The enjoyment granted the disbeliever is real and it is temporary, and both facts are load-bearing: real, because the verse does not promise the world's deprivation to the unbelieving — Makkah's fruit-fed history included its idol-decades; temporary, because the while is bounded by the *then*, and the *then* carries the destination-clause with its verdict-word — *what an evil destination*, the same exclamation-form the recital has filed at every trade's settlement (86, 90, 102). The respite-doctrine answers the question every reader brings to a secure, fruit-fed city of mixed belief: why does the provision continue where the gratitude fails? And the answer is the verse's own: because the continuation is part of the sentence, not its suspension — the enjoyment is the little while in which return remains possible, and its littleness is what makes the destination evil rather than merely unfortunate. The patriarch's prayer and the divine answer together give the recital's audience the complete civic theology: pray for your cities' safety and supply; expect the prayer to be answered past the boundaries of your asking; do not read the answer's breadth as endorsement; and hold the destination-clause over every enjoyment — the little while named little, the then named then, and the evil destination named evil, in the same breath that grants the fruit.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:127

> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael, ˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord! Accept ˹this˺ from us. You are indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Raising the Foundations**

The verse narrates the building, and its verb carries the tradition's whole debate about the House's age. *Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael* — the verb *yarfaʿān*, raising, lifting up — describes work on foundations that exist rather than ground broken anew, and the exegetical literature preserves the lore that accounts for the difference: accounts of a much more ancient origin for the Kaʿbah, going back to Adam — the father, having ceased to hear the voices of the angels after his fall, praying for their return and receiving the promise of a House on earth around which people would circle as the angels circle the Throne; the House sent down, standing through the early ages, withdrawn or buried at the flood, and its foundations brought to light again by Abraham and his son rather than built from nothing. Al-Ṭabarī's own position on the lore is characteristically careful: he recounts the stories and judges them unreliable as actual history, while many other commentators hold them true. The weighing does not need to settle the archaeology to read the verse, and the verse's own wording holds what all readings share: the raising was commissioned, joint, and prayerful, and its object was *the House* — definite, known to the builders, an entity whose identity preceded their work on it. Whether the foundations were Adam's or bare ground, the recital files the patriarchs as the House's raisers, and their raising as the act the following clause turns into worship.

**The First House**

The Qur'an states the House's rank in its own terms, and the statement is the verse's doctrinal anchor: *surely the first House of worship established for humanity is the one at Bakkah — blessed, and a guidance for all people* (3:96). The name *Bakkah* is the verse's own antiquarian evidence — an alternate form of Makkah that the tradition connects to the biblical Valley of Baca in the Psalms (84:6), a link the commentators note across the two scriptural archives. The firstness claimed is of establishment *for humanity* — the earliest house set up for human worship, which is compatible with the Adam-lore and independent of it: whatever the foundations' age, the House's standing as humanity's first appointed sanctuary is the Qur'an's own assertion. Sūrah al-Ḥajj supplies the building's commission from its other end: *when We assigned to Abraham the site of the House* (22:26) — the location designated, the builder placed at the designated point, with the charge that follows in that verse running exactly parallel to verse 125's purification-command. The two verses together fix the building's theology: the site is assigned, not chosen; the House is established, not invented; and the raisers' work, however monumental in its labor, is execution of a divine plan whose firstness, blessedness, and guidance-function belong to the plan rather than to the masons. The verse's audience — a community praying toward this House, months from legislating the direction permanently — received in these clauses their qibla's full credentials: first, blessed, guidance, assigned, raised by the two names their own genealogies traced to.

**“Accept From Us”**

The builders pray while they build, and the prayer's single petition is the verse's spiritual center: *our Lord, accept from us*. The request names the work's actual risk. Construction can fail structurally — but the patriarchs, raising a house whose site was assigned by Allah, do not pray about walls; they pray about standing. The deed's acceptance is not guaranteed by the deed's correctness: an act can be complete in its performance and unaccepted in its account, and the prayer confesses the gap — acceptance belongs to the Receiver, not to the act's arithmetic. The tradition's grammar of acceptance runs through the recital: the fast accepted, the charity received, the pilgrimage *mabrūr* — each pairing a completed human act with a requested divine response, and each keeping the response on mercy's side of the ledger. The prayer's timing is its instruction: it is spoken *during* the raising, not after it — the builders' hands moving while their tongues ask, the acceptance sought for work in progress, which makes the prayer a continuous liturgy of labor rather than a closing ceremony. The two Names that seal the petition state the acceptance's mechanism: *You are indeed the All-Hearing* — the prayer reaches its addressee, the asking is not spoken into vacancy; *the All-Knowing* — the work and the intention behind it are both held in knowledge, the seen stones and the unseen sincerity registered together. The hearing answers the prayer's utterance and the knowing answers the prayer's unspoken content, and the pair is the builders' complete warrant: nothing in the raising — not the effort, not the fear of inadequacy, not the intention no colleague can verify — falls outside the two attributes the petition names.

**The Two Builders**

The verse joins the two names in one sentence of joint labor, and the joining is the recital's genealogical politics at its most concrete. Abraham, the imām tested and appointed at verse 124; Ishmael, the son of the Arabian line, named here not as attendant but as co-raiser — the foundations lifted by both, the prayer said by both (the verse's grammar puts the petition in their shared mouth), the acceptance sought for both. The tradition's accounts of the building divide the labor between them — one laying stones, one handing them, in the reports the exegetes preserve — and whatever the division's details, the verse's headline is partnership: the House's construction belongs to the two lines' common ancestor-pair, and the prayer over it is a single prayer in a dual voice. For the recital's Madinan audience the fact carried its full charge. The Israelite claim ran through Isaac; the Ishmaelite line ran to the Arabs; the House now being raised in the narrative stood as the work of both brothers under their father, its purification-charge (125) laid on both, its acceptance-prayer uttered by both — an institution older than the division of the lines and jointly owned across it. The verse thereby performs, in narrative form, the covenant-law verse 124 stated in doctrine: the office and the trust descend through fulfillment and righteousness, held here by father and son together, with the wrongdoer — of either line, of any generation — excluded by the answer Abraham received. The two builders pray as one party, and the House they raise is, in the recital's design, the standing rebuke to every later monopoly of the patriarchs.

**The Prayer That Outlives the Building**

The verse's final reach is its prayer's permanence. The walls the patriarchs raised have been rebuilt, damaged, and re-raised across the millennia — the tradition records the House's repairs through pre-Islamic and Islamic centuries — but the petition spoken during the first raising has never left the building's liturgy: *our Lord, accept from us* is recited at the House by every generation of its servants, and the two Names that seal it govern every act performed there. The prayer's transfer extends past the precinct. Every worker for the sacred — the teacher mid-lesson, the giver mid-gift, the builder of any house where Allah's Name is mentioned — inherits the verse's posture: labor in motion, acceptance in question, the request made during the work rather than after its showcase, and the warrant located in the Hearing and the Knowing rather than in the work's visible quality. The verse installs this posture as the recital's labor-law, and its two clauses — the raising and the asking — are never separated in it: no building scene without the prayer, no prayer without the building underway. The patriarchs' fear was not that their work would fall but that it might not be received, and the fear is the verse's gift to every builder after them — the anxiety that keeps the deed for Allah, spoken in the sentence that asks Him to take it. The petition continues beyond this verse, and the House stands as its answered monument: accepted, purified, made center and sanctuary, first of the houses and guidance for the people — the acceptance asked in humility and filed, by the recital's own telling, in the permanence of what was built.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:128

> Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You and from our descendants a nation that will submit to you. Show us our rituals, and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Petition to Be Made Submitters**

The builders' prayer continues, and its first petition is its most remarkable: *our Lord, make us both fully submit to You*. The request is for submission spoken by submitters — the patriarch who fulfilled every commandment (124) and the son laboring at the House asking to be *made* muslimūn, the participle of a transitive verb: the ones submitting, in the state the verb's form describes as produced rather than self-generated. The exegetes mark the word's significance precisely: *muslim* here is the active participle tied to *islām*, the submission that verse 132 will name as the prophets' bequest and the sūrah will legislate as religion's universal form — and the petition's transitive grammar carries the doctrine inside it. Submission is asked *from* Allah: the orientation of the self toward its Lord is itself a gift to be requested, not a possession to be declared. The prophets pray for what they already hold, which reads at three depths at once — increase of a state that admits of degrees, perseverance in a state exposed to trial, and the confession that the state's holder never owns it outright. The petition defines the prayer's whole theology in its first clause: the highest station in the recital's file — the tested, fulfilled imām — stands before Allah asking to be made what he is, and the asking is not deficiency but the station's proper posture. A submission that stopped asking to be made would already have become property, and property is the category the previous section's hundred verses dismantled.

**A Nation That Submits**

The prayer's second petition extends the first across generations: *and from our descendants, a nation that will submit to You*. The word *umma* names not a family but a community — a people gathered by a shared orientation, the term the Qur'an uses for the constituted bodies of religious history. The petition is the patriarch's answer to his own question at verse 124: asked whether the covenant would run through his offspring and told it does not extend to wrongdoers, Abraham now prays the only prayer that question permits — not that his descendants hold the office by blood, but that a nation of them be *made submitting*, the covenant's condition fulfilled in them by the same grace requested for himself. The exegetes ground the petition's scope in a general principle: kin hold the first claim on a person's care and concern — al-Rāzī's note, anchored in the Qur'an's own command to the believers: *protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones* (66:6). The patriarch's prayer models the principle at its prophetic height: the imām's first congregation is his line, and the line's good is not its precedence but its submission. The petition's wording also carries the recital's covenant-law forward: a nation *that will submit* — the qualifying participle attached to the community as its defining mark, so that the nation asked for is constituted by the posture rather than the genealogy, and every later member qualifies by the same clause. The prayer thus builds, inside the House-raising scene, the community that will inherit the House — an umma defined at its founding petition as submitters-made, descendants in form, muslims in content.

**“Show Us Our Rituals”**

The third petition asks for the liturgy itself: *show us our rituals* — *manāsik*, the word whose range the tradition sets out as the pilgrimage-rites, the sacrificial practice, and worship's forms in general. The verb — *show us* — is the petition's doctrine: the rites are seen before they are performed, given before they are invented. No prophet in the recital designs his community's worship; the forms descend, are assigned, are shown — as the House's site was assigned (22:26) and the standing-place legislated (125). Sūrah al-Ḥajj states the principle across the communities: *for every community We appointed a rite of sacrifice, so that they may pronounce Allah's Name over the livestock He has provided* (22:34) — appointment and provision from one side, pronouncement from the other, the liturgy's two-party structure fixed. The petition's humility is its instruction for the recital's audience: the patriarchs, custodians of the first House, ask to be shown how to worship in it — the builders requesting the liturgy of their own building. The question embedded in *our rites* is equally instructive: which forms belong to this House, this community, this covenant? The prayer leaves the answer entirely with Allah, and the answer arrived in the tradition's record as the complete ḥajj — the circling, the running, the standing, the sacrifice — held in Islam as Abrahamic institution, its forms received, its showing granted. Between the submission asked in the first petition and the rites asked in the third stands the prayer's complete order: orientation first, form second — the submitting heart before the shown ritual, because the rite without the orientation is the empty house of verse 114's indictment, maintained in stone and abandoned in function.

**“Turn to Us”**

The fourth petition is the prayer's most tender clause: *and turn to us in grace* — *tub ʿalaynā*, the tawba-verb in its divine direction. The tradition's grammar of tawba is reciprocal, and the reciprocity is the clause's whole content: the human being turns toward Allah in repentance, and Allah turns toward the human in acceptance — one word, two motions, the meeting named from each side. The sūrah filed the mechanism at its origin-station: Adam received words from his Lord and the turning was accepted (2:37) — the first repentance, its vocabulary given, its reception guaranteed. The patriarchs' use of the verb carries no claim of known sin; it is the servant-posture in its pure form — the creature asking the Lord to keep the relation turned, the face-to-face of grace maintained, whatever in the servants' state requires the turning. The two Names sealing the petition are chosen from the prayer's own request: *the Accepter of Repentance* — *tawwāb*, the intensive form, the One whose turning is abundant, repeated, ready; *Most Merciful* — *raḥīm*, the mercy that meets the turning where it lands. The pairing is the verse's theology of return in two words: the request to be turned to is addressed to the One whose Names already answer it, which is the recital's standing structure of duʿāʾ — the petition built on the attribute that grants it, the asking shaped by the Giver's self-description. For the community hearing the prayer, the clause legislates the liturgy's interior: rites shown, submission made, and over both the continuous turning — the worship that keeps asking to be received, at the House whose builders never stopped asking.

**The Prayer's Architecture**

Read as a whole, the petition sequence is a complete religious life in four requests, and the sequence is the verse's gift to every supplicant after it. Submission — the orientation asked as gift. A submitting nation from the descendants — the transmission asked as grace, the faith's crossing into the next generation held in the same petition as one's own. Rites shown — the form asked as revelation, worship received rather than composed. Turning accepted — the relation asked as mercy, the whole structure enclosed in continuous return. The four petitions cover the religion's four dimensions — the self, the community, the practice, the relation — and their order is instructive: the self's orientation precedes the community's formation, the community's formation precedes the liturgy's showing, and the liturgy stands under the turning that alone keeps it alive. The tradition connects the prayer's horizon to the petition the next verse files — the messenger asked for from within the submitting nation — and the connection shows the architecture's reach: the four requests build the community that the fifth petition will ask to be guided from within. The recital's audience received the sequence as a template. The Muslim supplicant praying at the House, or toward it, prays inside a liturgy whose founding prayer was for submission, for children who submit, for rites shown, for turning granted — and every clause remains petition, none of them possession, which is the posture the patriarchs modeled with their hands on the stones and the verse preserves with their words still unfinished.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:129

> Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, AllWise.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Messenger From Among Them**

The builders' prayer reaches its final petition, and the petition names the community's future guide: *our Lord, raise from among them a messenger*. The preposition carries the prayer's whole ecclesiology — *from among them*, minhum: the messenger requested is not sent at the nation from outside but raised up from within it, of its substance, speaking its tongue, sharing its valley and its House. The request completes the sequence begun two verses back: a submitting nation asked for (128), and now, from that nation's own body, the guide whose office will keep it submitting. The verb — *raise* — is the Qur'an's standing word for prophetic commissioning, and its vertical sense belongs to the petition: the messenger is raised the way the foundations were raised at verse 127, a lifting from within the material, the community's own stock elevated to its guidance-office. The recital's audience heard the petition with its answer in their ears: Sūrah al-Jumuʿah states the fulfillment in near-identical terms — *He is the One Who raised for the illiterate people a messenger from among themselves* (62:2) — the ummī community of the sūrah's own portrait (2:78's illiterate, the nation that neither writes nor calculates, in the Prophet's ﷺ description) receiving the raised messenger the patriarchs asked for. The petition is the recital's bridge across the centuries: the House's builders praying for the House's future congregation's guide, and the guide arriving from among the congregation, in the lineage the prayer named — the answer carried by the son whose co-labor verse 127 had just honored.

**The Three Offices**

The petition defines the messenger's work in three verbs, and the three are the complete prophetic pedagogy. *Who will recite to them Your revelations* — the delivery office: the āyāt brought and voiced, the revelation placed in the community's ears, the same recitation-verb whose cognates the sūrah has used for the Book's own presence among its people. *Teach them the Book and wisdom* — the instruction office: not delivery but formation, the text explained, applied, turned into knowledge the community can operate. *And purify them* — the transformation office: the souls themselves worked on, the tazkiya that makes the taught knowledge livable. The three verbs' sequence is the pedagogy's order: revelation arrives, teaching unpacks it, purification realizes it — and the recital's own answer-verse confirms the sequence by naming the same three functions of the actual Messenger: *We have sent you a messenger from among yourselves — reciting to you Our revelations, purifying you, teaching you the Book and wisdom, and teaching you what you never knew* (2:151). The petition and the answer match function for function, which is the tradition's certainty about this verse: it is the Prophet Muhammad's ﷺ origin-story in prayer-form, his mission requested before his lineage existed, his three offices specified by the patriarchs' tongue. Every carrier of the recitation after him inherits the offices in descending degree — reciting what was delivered, teaching what was explained, seeking the purification the offices exist for — and the verse stands as the community's job-description, written into its founder-grandfather's prayer at the House's foundation-stone.

**The Book and the Wisdom**

The second office's two objects carry a pairing the Qur'an deploys as a fixed formula, and the formula's breadth is the tradition's evidence for its meaning. The Book — *al-kitāb* — is read most often as the Qur'an, the delivered text in its written-recited form. The wisdom — *al-ḥikma* — is understood in the exegetical tradition as the Sunnah: the Prophet's ﷺ exemplary sayings and doings, the Book's embodied commentary — or, more broadly, the knowledge and understanding of the religion the Book's delivery produces (al-Ṭabarī's range). The pairing's recurrence across the Qur'an settles its import: the Book and wisdom are named together as what Jesus received (3:48, 5:110), as what the Children of Israel were given (45:16), as what the House of Abraham received (4:54) — a formula, in the tradition's reading, for revelation's two modes wherever it descends: the text delivered and the understanding given, the word and its realization, the recitation and its application. The pairing also answers, in its structure, the communities the recital has just documented failing: a Book held without wisdom is the Torah rationed and cast behind backs (85, 101) — text preserved, understanding refused; and wisdom claimed without the Book is the desires called guidance (120). The petition asks for both offices in one messenger because the community's health requires both hold — and the answer's history is the tradition's demonstration: the Book memorized in ten thousand chests, the wisdom recorded in the Sunnah's corpus, the pairing maintained as the two hands of one inheritance.

**The Purification**

The third office is the petition's goal-term, and its placement last marks it as the work's completion: *and purify them*. Tazkiya — the verb of purification and growth at once — names the soul-craft the messenger performs: cleansing from the coverings the recital has catalogued (the sheathed hearts, the drunk-in calf-love, the black-marked mat-weaving), and growing the soul toward the states the recital promises (the white hearts the trials cannot harm, the no-fear-no-grief formula's holders). The purification-office is what separates the messenger from the librarian: a deliverer of texts transmits; a purifier transforms, and the petition asks for both because a community holding the Book unchanged is the recital's documented tragedy — the Torah in custody, the hearts hardened, the covenant cast at every station. The office's mechanism is the recital's own: the revelations recited do the purifying as they are received — the message that softens skins and hearts at Allah's mention (39:23's operation), the signs clear for people of sure faith (118) — and the messenger administers the reception, pacing the delivery to the community's capacity, as the Prophet ﷺ did with the companions whose formation the tradition records year by year. The petition's three verbs now show their architecture: recitation supplies the purifying agent, teaching supplies its application, purification is the effected state — and the community that receives all three is the umma the patriarchs asked to be made submitting (128), submitting not in name but in cleansed hearts.

**The Answered Prayer**

The verse's final clause seals the petition with the two Names that grant it: *indeed, You are the Almighty, All-Wise* — ʿazīz, the Mighty whose power raises messengers from illiterate valleys; ḥakīm, the Wise whose placing of the raise answers purposes the petitioners do not see. The Names are the prayer's theology in closing position: the request is made to power that can and wisdom that knows where — and the history between the petition and the recital's present is the Names' demonstration. The prayer was answered beyond its askers' vision: the messenger raised from among them carried the recitation to the world, the ummī nation became the tradition's ten thousand memorizers, the House the builders raised became the direction of a billion daily prayers. Sūrah al-Jumuʿah extends the answer past the first congregation — the messenger sent to them *and to others of them who have not yet joined them* (62:3), the prayer's reach covering every generation the recitation now includes. The verse's transfer is therefore not aspirational but locative: every reader of this sūrah stands inside the answered petition — the revelations recited to them its delivery-office, the Book and wisdom taught to them its instruction-office, the purification offered them its third office, all three running from a prayer spoken over foundation-stones by two builders who asked, for a nation not yet born, exactly the guidance that arrived. The recital files the prayer at the House's raising so that its congregation never forgets its own origin: asked for, before existing — and the asking's Names, Mighty and Wise, are the guarantee the congregation recites when it wonders whether the answer still holds.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:130

> And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool! We certainly chose him in this life, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question That Answers Itself**

The verse turns from the patriarch's prayer to the reader's position with a rhetorical question of the recital's most compressed kind: *who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool?* The question expects no candidate, and its expecting is the argument: after the file just presented — the test fulfilled (124), the imāmah appointed and its lineage-condition set (124), the House raised and purified (125), the city's security and fruit prayed (126), the building accepted (127), the nation and its messenger requested (128–129) — the rejection of this faith is not a position with reasons but a failure of the organ that weighs reasons. The word for the failure is *safaha*, and its sense is specific: foolishness as lightness, the mind that has lost its ballast, the self squandered by its own holder — the Qur'an's idiom *the fool in himself* describes a deficiency located in the person's own substance rather than in his information. The verse thus completes the passage's polemic by diagnosis. The recital has met rejection with analysis at every station — the distorters' understanding, the traders' arithmetic, the demanders' hearts — and here, at the patriarch's station, the analysis collapses into a single term: whatever else the rejection of Abraham's faith can be called, it cannot be called judgment. The question-form leaves the reader holding the examination: the file is open, the evidence is the preceding six verses, and the only question remaining is about the examiner's own organ.

**Millah: The Faith Named**

The object of the possible rejection — *the faith of Abraham* — translates *millah*, the term the recital defined at verse 120 as a community's whole way: not a creed held but a pattern lived, the total order of belief, practice, and direction. Abraham's millah is therefore everything the file just documented: the submission asked as gift, the commands fulfilled under test, the House and its rites, the prayers for nation and messenger, the covenant held on righteousness rather than blood. The Qur'an's contest over this millah is its historical occasion: the communities of Madina each claimed the patriarch — the Jews through the Israelite line, the Christians through their scripture's genealogy, the Arabs through Ishmael and the House — and each claim implied that Abraham's faith was that community's property. The verse answers every claim at once by naming the millah independently of all of them, and Sūrah Āl ʿImrān states the independence as doctrine: *Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian; he submitted in all uprightness, and was not a polytheist* (3:67). The patriarch's faith precedes the denominations that claim it — the uprightness, the ḥanīf-posture, the submission — and the verse's question thereby acquires its full edge: the communities rejecting the Messenger who carries Abraham's millah forward are rejecting, by the recital's account, the faith of their own claimed ancestor, and the rejection is filed not as theological difference but as the fool's lightness.

**Chosen in Both Worlds**

The verse's second sentence states the patriarch's standing in the two worlds, and the double statement is the rejection-question's warrant. *We certainly chose him in this life* — the iṣṭifāʾ, the selection the Qur'an records for a short list of its figures: Mary chosen above the women of the worlds (3:42), Moses chosen for the message (7:144), Adam (20:122), the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the sūrah of the Angels (35:32), the prophets collectively (6:87) — and Abraham, chosen with the emphatic *certainly*, his selection spanning the worldly life in office, honor, and function: imām, builder, answered supplicant, the direction of a community's prayer. *And in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous* — the second-world term of the selection: not merely saved but enrolled, placed among the ṣāliḥūn, the company the patriarch's own prayer-work kept naming. The two clauses together answer the millah-contest from the standing side: the faith whose rejection is foolishness is held by a man doubly certified — chosen here, righteous there — and the certification is divine speech, not communal claim. The verse also quietly settles the lineage-question of verse 124 from the patriarch's own side: the covenant did not extend to the wrongdoers among his offspring, and the patriarch himself stands at both worlds' head — the office's first holder, whose holding is the pattern every claimant of his name is measured against. Chosen, fulfilled, enrolled: the three verbs of the patriarch's file leave the rejection-question with no respectable answer, which is exactly what the question asserts.

**The Continuity of the Two Laws**

The exegetes read the verse as the recital's statement of continuity between the patriarch's law and the Messenger's, and the reading is the verse's structural function in the sūrah. Al-Qushayrī's note states the principle: the Law of Muhammad ﷺ retains the Law of Abraham except where it abrogates it — the continuity qualified by the naskh-doctrine the sūrah legislated at verse 106, so that the two mills stand in the relation the recital's own jurisprudence defines: one religion across its dispensations, its forms adjusted by the Owner of the kingdom (107), its substance unchanged. The concrete evidence runs through the passage just filed: the ḥajj-rites held in Islam as Abrahamic institution — the circling, the standing-place, the showing requested at verse 128 — and the tradition's tracing of the bodily purities, the grooming and cleanliness disciplines, back to the patriarch's fulfilled commands (124's first exegetical stream). The continuity-reading gives the verse's question its second edge. The millah is not a museum-piece the communities honor while practicing otherwise; it is a living law, carried forward in the rites the Muslims of Madina were performing and the Messenger they were following — so rejecting the Messenger is not preserving Abraham's faith but abandoning its transmission, the chain the verse's own six-station file documented link by link. The fools the question names are, in the recital's Madinan moment, precisely the claimants who honored the patriarch's name while rejecting his millah's arrival — and the verse files the contradiction as the definition of safah: lightness toward the heavy thing one claims to hold.

**The Fool and the File**

The verse's transfer runs to every reader who meets the patriarch's file, because the rejection-question is permanent in its form. Abraham's millah reaches each generation through its transmission — the rites, the prayers, the submitted orientation, the covenant-on-righteousness law — and each generation faces the question in its own terms: the rejection is rarely announced as rejection; it wears the forms the recital has documented — the millah honored in name and rationed in practice, the patriarch claimed while his tested pattern is declined, the House revered while its Owner's commands behind the back are cast. The verse's diagnosis covers all of it: safah is not the dramatic apostasy but the lightness — the loss of weight that lets a person hold a claim and a conduct that contradict, the organ failing while the vocabulary remains. Against the lightness the verse sets the file's heaviness: commands fulfilled under fire and knife, foundations raised with prayer mid-labor, a nation and a messenger asked for across centuries of unseen future, a city's fruit requested for people not yet born. The patriarch's faith is the weightiest thing in the recital's archive — every petition paid for in obedience — and the question's force is proportional: only lightness rejects weight. The recital leaves the reader with the examination running: whichever community's child one is, whichever patriarch's name one carries, the verse asks the single question that sorts the claimants — does the millah one claims have weight in the hands, in the rites, in the fulfilled commands? The fool is not who rejects Abraham; the fool is who claims him and lives light.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:131

> When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The One-Word Command**

The verse files the patriarch's defining moment in its smallest possible form: a command of one word. *When his Lord said to him: Submit* — *aslim*, the imperative of the same root whose participle the builders' prayer requested at verse 128 (*make us submitters*). The command's singularity is its content: not a list, not a ritual, not a doctrine — the whole religion in one verb, the orientation before the specification. The recital does not date the scene; the tradition's accounts place this command at various stations of the patriarch's life, and the undated narration is the verse's method — the moment abstracted into pattern, every prophet's commission reduced to its root. The root-command also explains the prayer of verse 128 in retrospect: the patriarchs asked to be *made* muslim because the making had been *commanded* — the imperative arrives first, and the submission that answers it remains, at every station of its holder's life, a thing asked for. The verse's structure is thus the religion's own in miniature: Lord, command, servant, answer — four terms, no fifth, and the whole of what the recital has legislated across a hundred verses stands inside the exchange. The commands fulfilled at verse 124 — the purities, the rites, the trials — are this command's specification; the fire and the knife were its tests; and the one word remained the sum, which is why the verse can state the patriarch's entire standing in one sentence of dialogue.

**“I Have Submitted”: The Answer in the Perfect Tense**

The response is as short as the command and carries one grammatical feature the exegetes mark: *aslamtu* — I have submitted — the perfect tense, the completed act. The answer does not say *I will submit* and does not negotiate terms, delay, or conditions; it reports the submission as already accomplished at the moment of speaking, the response and the command meeting without interval. The recital's audience knew the contrast-answer: the community of verse 93, commanded under the raised mountain to hold firmly and obey, replied *we hear and disobey* — the same command-structure, the split response. Between the two answers the recital's whole moral geography lies: the perfect-tense *I have submitted* and the inverted *we hear and disobey*, the patriarch's file and Israel's file, the millah and its rejection. The answer's object completes its scope: *to the Lord of all worlds* — the submission directed not to the command's occasion but to the Commander's universal lordship. The phrase — *rabb al-ʿālamīn* — is the recitation's own opening address, the Fātiḥa's second line (*all praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds*), and its appearance in the patriarch's mouth ties the Muslim's daily prayer to the patriarch's defining answer: every reciter of the Fātiḥa speaks the object of Abraham's submission in every prayer of his life. The worlds named are the plural of every realm — human, jinn, angelic, seen, unseen — and the submission is to the Rabb of the whole plurality, which is the verse's quiet completion of the millah-contest: a faith whose object is the Lord of all worlds cannot be any single community's property, because its object owns the claimants.

**Islām Before Islam**

The verse's verb is the recital's evidence for a claim the whole Qur'an makes: the submission named here is older than the name the Muslim community carries. The tradition states the principle plainly — *islām*, while the proper name of the religion brought by Muhammad ﷺ, is generalized in the Qur'an to mean the primordial religion, the true religion as such, the fundamental orientation of the soul toward God that is universal and stands among the bequests the prophets leave their children. The verse is the principle's founding exhibit: Abraham, centuries before the Mosaic law and centuries more before the Qur'an, receives the command *aslim* and answers *aslamtu* — and the exchange is the same religion the recital's own community bears by name. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān legislates the identity's exclusivity from the other side: whoever seeks a way other than islām, it will not be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he is among the losers (3:85) — the submission-pose named as the only accepted orientation across every dispensation. The verse thereby performs the recital's genealogical politics in one dialogue: the patriarch is not a proto-Jew, not a proto-Christian, not an Arab ancestral cult-figure — he is a muslim in the Qur'an's precise sense, the first word of whose religion is the word commanded to him, and every community that claims him claims a submitter, which is a description of posture rather than of party. The command's universality is its inheritance-law: the millah passes to whoever answers it, and the answer has never been restricted to a lineage — the same lesson verse 124's covenant-condition stated in legal form, here stated in dialogue.

**Submission as Response, Not Achievement**

The verse's deepest instruction is in its sequence, and the sequence reverses the usual grammar of religious accomplishment. The command comes first; the submission is the answer. Abraham's aslamtu is not a self-generated attainment — not a discipline achieved, a state climbed to, a perfection manufactured — but a response to being addressed, the servant's word after the Lord's. The theology inside the sequence is the recital's own at every station: guidance descends before response rises (the signs sent down, the Book revealed, the messenger raised), and the human act that saves is reception rather than production. The petition of verse 128 now reads as the sequence's prayer-form — *make us submit* — asking from Allah what Allah commanded toward: the command creates the obligation, the grace creates the ability, and the perfect-tense answer holds both in one word. This is why the patriarch's submission can be commanded to increase (128) without contradiction: the achieved state is itself a received state, and reception continues for as long as the address continues. The verse leaves its reader with the exchange as model. The command arrives in every life in its own forms — the ruling that costs, the direction that changes, the truth that requires the perfect tense — and the verse files the only two answers the recital recognizes: *I have submitted*, spoken to the Lord of all worlds, or the inversion verse 93 preserved. Between the two lies the whole distance the sūrah has been measuring since its opening verses, and the patriarch's answer stands at the far end of it — one word commanded, one word returned, and the worlds' Lord named in the returning, which is the shortest complete religion the recital ever files.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:132

> This was the advice of Abraham—as well as Jacob—to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this faith; so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Bequest**

The verse records the patriarchs' final act as fathers, and the act is a genre the Qur'an treats with standing seriousness: the *waṣiyya*, the deathbed counsel — *this was the advice of Abraham, and Jacob likewise, to his children*. Two names, two generations-apart scenes, one instruction: the verse joins the millah's founder with the Israel-line's father — Jacob, grandson of Abraham, the patriarch whose twelve sons became the tribes the recital's hundred verses addressed — and joins them in the same act of transmission. The pairing is the verse's ecumenical stroke: the father claimed by the Arabs and the father claimed by Israel are shown doing one thing, saying one sentence, to their children — and the sentence is not about lineage, land, or precedence but about the faith's survival in the sons. The waṣiyya's solemnity in the recital's culture is its setting: the last words, spoken at the edge of the world's business, when the speaker's remaining property is truth. What the patriarchs spend that property on is the verse's ranking of goods — not estates, not offices, not the covenant's external marks, but the orientation of the children's souls. The tradition reads the bequest as the prophets' standing practice, the submission-pose of verse 131 transmitted at every prophet's deathbed to every prophet's house, and the two named here stand as the pattern's twin exemplars: the millah's founder and the tribes' father, the root and the trunk, both closing their files with the same charge.

**“Allah Has Chosen This Faith for You”**

The counsel's first clause states the children's position, and the statement is grace before demand: *indeed, Allah has chosen for you this faith*. The verb is the iṣṭifāʾ of verse 124 and verse 130 — the divine selection, the same word used of the patriarch's own choosing — now applied to the religion itself as the children's portion. The clause's theology is precise in its prepositions: the faith is chosen *for you*, *by Allah* — the religion arrives as gift before it stands as task, the selection divine before the holding is human. The verse thereby installs the correct order of the religious life: the children are not told *choose this faith* but *this faith has been chosen for you* — their freedom operates inside a prior grace, the way the patriarch's own submission was commanded before it was answered (131). The named object — *this faith*, the millah in its submission-form — is the religion verse 131 defined: islām as the primordial orientation, the universal pose, what the prophets bequeath. And the choosing's agent answers the millah-contest one final time from inside the family scene: the faith the patriarchs transmit is not a tribal inheritance but a divine selection — held by the children not because their fathers held it but because Allah chose it for them, a ground that stands for every generation the choice reaches and falls away for every claim that cites the fathers alone. The counsel's first clause is thus the recital's whole doctrine of election in one sentence: chosen by Allah, chosen for the children, chosen as this — the submission the dialogue of verse 131 enacted.

**“Do Not Die Except in Submission”**

The counsel's second clause is its famous imperative, and its form is the verse's most striking feature: *so do not die except in a state of full submission*. Death is not chosen — no one commands the hour of his dying — and the command therefore addresses what the hour arrives to find: the state, not the event. The imperative is a command about living whose term is set at dying: arrange the whole of life so that death, whenever it comes, comes upon a submitter. The tradition named the doctrine this verse legislates — the good ending, ḥusn al-khātima — and its logic is the recital's own anthropology: the state at death is the sum of the life's direction, the heart's last posture continuous with its practiced posture, and the one who lives submitting dies submitting by the same necessity that verse 93 filed in the other direction: the heart made to drink its loves carries them past the boundary. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān legislates the identical clause to the Muslim community directly: be mindful of Allah as He deserves, *and do not die except in submission* (3:102) — the patriarchs' deathbed counsel converted into the ummah's standing law, which is the verse's proof that the waṣiyya was never addressed to one family. The command's severity is also its mercy: it makes every moment continuous with the last one, so that the deathbed requires no emergency conversion — the submitter arrives at death already in the state death is commanded to find. Between the two clauses the counsel's whole architecture stands: the faith given by selection, the life ordered toward the exit — gift and task, grace and vigilance, in the two sentences a dying father spent his last words on.

**Fathers, Children, and the Recital's Own File**

The verse's scene reads against the file the recital has just closed, and the contrast is its polemical edge. The Children of Israel are the children of this counsel — Jacob's sons and their descendants, addressed in the second person across a hundred verses — and the record between the bequest and the recital's present documents what children can do with a father's last words: the covenant cast at every station (100), the Book behind the backs (101), the hear-and-disobey (93). The verse does not draw the contrast explicitly; its structure draws it. The bequest was total — the faith chosen, the exit commanded — and the transmission's failure was therefore not the fathers' but the children's, which is exactly the covenant-law of verse 124 operating in narrative: the office and the promise do not ride the blood; each generation receives the counsel and answers it individually. The pairing of Abraham with Jacob sharpens the point across both lines: the Arabs' father and Israel's father gave the same charge, so neither line's children can plead a defective bequest — the counsel was perfect on both sides of the family, and the audit of verse 123's individualism runs on the children's answers alone. The verse thereby closes the recital's long argument with the claimants of the patriarchs: you hold the bequest's text and dispute its content; the content is submission, the exit-command is plain, and the ancestors named are witnesses against every child who received the waṣiyya and died in another posture. The counsel stands unrevoked in both houses, which is why the verse can state it once for two fathers: the millah's transmission has one wording, and the wording is the same at every deathbed the recital files.

**The Counsel to Every Child**

The verse's transfer is in its address: every reader is somebody's child, and the waṣiyya reaches whoever inherits a faith. The counsel's two clauses are the inheritance's two questions. Has the faith come to you as chosen — received as selection before it is held as identity, the gift-order of verse 128's petition intact? And is your life arranged toward the commanded exit — the daily posture continuous with the deathbed posture, the submission practiced at the scale of hours so that it stands at the scale of the end? The recital's audience heard both questions with their own bequest in hand: the Qur'an itself is a waṣiyya to its hearers, this sūrah's hundred-verses-plus of covenant, audit, and patriarch-file the counsel's elaboration, and the Messenger ﷺ raised from the prayed-for nation (129) its living transmitter. The verse installs the community's self-understanding as children of a bequest — not owners of a property but heirs of a charge, with the charge's terms stated: the faith is chosen for you, so do not die except in submission. Between the two patriarchs' deathbeds and the recital's Madinan moment, the counsel travels unchanged, which is the verse's final proof of the millah's identity: what Abraham said to his children and Jacob said to his, the sūrah says to its — one sentence, three generations of speakers, one posture required of every hearer, and the exit-command running until the Day verse 123 described, where the states the deaths found are filed, and no soul arrives except as it lived.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:133

> Or did you witness when death came to Jacob? He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?” They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers— Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac—the One God. And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Witness Question**

The verse opens by putting its audience on the stand: *or did you witness when death came to Jacob?* The question — the recital's challenge-form, familiar from verse 80's pledge-demand and verse 94's death-wish — is addressed to the claimants of the patriarchs, and its first function is evidentiary. The disputants of Madina spoke for Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes; the verse asks whether they were present at the scene that defines the patriarchs' faith — the deathbed of Jacob — and the answer is known: they were not. Their claim rests on report, and the report they do not carry is being recited to them now, in dialogue, with the questions and answers intact. The verse thereby installs the recital's authority over the patriarchs' legacy: whatever the claimants assert about their ancestors' religion, the Qur'an files the founding scene itself — the actual question the dying father asked, the actual answer the twelve sons gave — and the filing is the testimony the absence of witnesses cannot rebut. The *or* of the opening continues a challenge-sequence, and its continuation is the verse's method: the counsel of verse 132 stated the bequest in summary; verse 133 stages it, so that the bequest is no longer reported but performed — the waṣiyya heard in the room where it was given, with the recitation itself as the only reliable witness present. The audience of every later age stands in the claimants' position: no one since has been present at that deathbed either, and everyone since receives the scene from the same testimony.

**The Dying Father's Question**

Jacob's question to his children is the verse's center, and its wording is a deathbed's whole priorities in one sentence: *what will you worship after me?* Not who will lead you, not how will the tribes be ordered, not what will become of the estate or the covenant's external marks — the object of worship, and its survival past the father's presence. The question assumes the danger the patriarchs' counsel has been legislating against: religion held in a father's presence can be held by proximity, and the deathbed is the test of whether the sons hold the God or the household. The interrogative *what* rather than *who* — *mā*, the thing-question — carries a theological precision the exegetes mark: the question asks after the object of worship as such, the reality to be worshipped, not yet its name; and the sons' answer supplies the identification. The scene also completes verse 132's counsel in dramatic form: the bequest commanded *do not die except in submission*, and the deathbed question examines the command's transmission — will the state survive me? Jacob asks what every bequeather actually asks, and the verse files the asking as the patriarchs' final office: not the transfer of property but the examination of orientation, conducted at the one moment when pretense is most expensive, with the sons' answer to be lived after the room empties. The recital's hundred-verses file of the tribes' subsequent history is, from this scene's vantage, the long record of the answer's keeping and losing — and the verse preserves the answer in its founding purity so that the record can always be measured against it.

**The Sons' Answer**

The reply is the verse's creed, and its structure moves in three steps. *We will worship your God* — the personal term first: the sons receive the faith as their father's God, the deity of a lived relationship they were raised inside, the continuity of the household's worship. *And the God of your forefathers — Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac* — the historical term second: the fathers named, the lineage's three patriarchs listed in an order the verse makes remarkable. Ishmael stands between Abraham and Isaac — the Arabian uncle named among the fathers, in a list the Israel-line's descendants speak, and the inclusion is the recital's genealogical reconciliation in the sons' own mouth: the House's two builders (125, 127) are both ancestral to the worship confessed here, the family's two lines joined in one God-list. The exegetes note the verse's noun-choice with matching care: *your God* translates *ilāh*, the common noun for deity, not the proper Name — the sons confess the object's oneness before they speak its name, and the confession's third step states the oneness: *the One God* — *ilāhun wāḥid*, the singularity that makes the three fathers' God one God rather than three household deities. The answer closes where the whole section has been heading: *and to Him we submit* — the islām-clause, the patriarchs' counsel (132) answered in the patriarch's own house, the submission-pose of verse 131 spoken by the twelve. Sūrah Yūsuf preserves the same confession from one son's mouth a lifetime later: Joseph in the Egyptian prison following *the faith of my fathers — Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob* (12:38), the list recurring, the submission restated — the deathbed creed become the tribes' standing formula in its best son.

**The Patriarchs Cannot Be Owned**

The verse is the recital's argument, in narrative form, against every exclusive claim on the patriarchs, and the argument's force is that the scene is the claimants' own. The Qur'an's general case runs through this section: Abraham was neither Jew nor Christian (3:67); his millah is submission, held by whoever answers its command (130–131); the covenant excludes the wrongdoer of any line (124). Verse 133 supplies the case's decisive exhibit — the deathbed itself, with the Israel-line's own father asking the worship-question and his own sons answering in the terms the recital legislates: one God, the fathers' God including Ishmael, and submission to Him. The answer the tribes' founder received is the answer the Qur'an preaches, which makes the Madinan claimants' rejection of the Messenger a rejection filed against their own founding scene: the patriarchs, in the tradition's reading, were followers of the pure religion of Abraham — primordial monotheism, which is to say islām in the verse's own closing word — and the communities that claim them while rejecting the submission-formula contradict, the recital asserts, the only witnessed testimony about what the patriarchs actually transmitted. The verse's witness-question thus inverts at its close: the claimants were not present at Jacob's deathbed, but the recital was — and what it reports is a creed with no exclusivity clause in it, no lineage-reservation, no millah-property: the God of all the fathers, one, submitted to. The patriarchs belong to whoever holds their sons' answer, and the answer's text is quoted here in full, so that the belonging is adjudicated by the scene rather than the claim.

**The Scene as the Section's Seal**

Verse 133 closes the recital's Abraham-cycle, and the closing scene gathers the cycle's whole argument into a room. The test and its fulfillment (124) end in the question every fulfillment faces: will it survive into the children? The imāmah conditioned on righteousness (124) stands confirmed: the office passed through the answer, not the blood. The House built and purified (125), the city prayed for (126), the building's acceptance requested (127), the submitting nation and its messenger asked (128–129) — every petition lands in this scene's confession: the nation submitting, in its patriarchal nucleus, answering at the deathbed of Israel's father. The millah beyond denomination (130), the one-word command answered in the perfect tense (131), the bequest commanding the submitted exit (132) — all three verified in the sons' closing clause: *to Him we submit*. The recital seals the section with the formula its next movement will legislate for the Muslim community in the same terms, and the seal's message to every claimant of every patriarch is the verse's standing challenge: the witness-question runs against all of them — you were not present, the testimony is recited, and the testimony contains the creed. Whoever holds the creed holds the fathers; whoever rejects it is rejected by the scene, whatever his lineage. The deathbed of Jacob remains the recital's examination-room for every child of the patriarchs, and the twelve sons' answer remains on the record — your God, the God of Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac, one God, submitted to — waiting at every generation's exit for the voice that will speak it as its own.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:134

> That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The File on Abraham Is Closed**
