The long appeal to Abraham that began with his covenant and his imamate has just ended with his deathbed, and this verse draws the line under the whole account. "That was a community that had already gone before" — *qad khalat*, they passed, they are gone, their case is finished. The generation of the patriarchs lived, chose, believed, struggled, and died, and what they accumulated went with them into their own reckoning. The sentence is not a dismissal of the ancestors; the sūrah has spent the previous verses honoring them. It is a transfer of attention. The ancestors cannot act for you, so the question that remains is what the living will do. Every appeal to a golden past eventually reaches this floor: the past is a record, not a proxy, and records are read by those who must still write their own.

**Kasab: Deeds as Property**

The verb the verse uses for what the dead and the living alike hold is *kasaba*, to earn — and the same root, depending on context, carries the sense of committing or perpetrating. The double edge is deliberate. A deed in the Qur'an's moral economy is not an event that evaporates; it is an acquisition that attaches to its doer the way a purchase attaches to a buyer. What a person "earns" becomes his property in the only ledger that survives death, and the property can be a burden as easily as a treasure. The vocabulary of earning also explains why the verse phrases both halves identically — *for them* what they earned, *for you* what you earned. There is no qualitative difference between the ancestors' account and the descendants': the same verb governs both, the same ownership rules apply to both, and the same audit awaits both. Death closes the earning, not the ownership; what was acquired remains acquired, held by the dead in a custody no living relative can reach into. That is why the verse can say so flatly that "for them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned": the sentence structure of ownership. Their earnings are in their hands; yours are in yours. No transfer mechanism exists between the two accounts, in either direction.

**No Soul Carries Another's Load**

The principle stated here in the language of earnings is stated elsewhere in the language of burdens. The sūrah of the Star records, as if reciting a creed already known, *"˹They state˺ that no soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another, and that each person will only have what they endeavoured towards"* (53:38–39). Two claims in two clauses: liability is non-transferable, and reward is proportional to effort. Together they seal the verse's argument. A sinner cannot offload onto his ancestor, and an heir cannot withdraw from his ancestor's balance. The Qur'an presses this point precisely because ancestral credit was a live currency in its first audience — lineage was identity, protection, and prestige, and the claim to have righteous forefathers functioned as a kind of moral insurance. The verse cancels the policy.

**A Community, Not a Clan**

The word for what has passed is *ummah* — a community defined by what it held together, its faith and its way, rather than by blood alone. That choice of word quietly redefines what the heirs inherit. From an *ummah* that has gone before, the living receive a direction: the creed it lived by, the pattern of its submission, the guidance it carried. What they do not receive is its credit. The distinction matters because the same sūrah has already fixed the rule at the top of Abraham's story: when God made him a leader for humanity, the imamate was explicitly withheld from wrongdoers among his own line — *"˹He said,˺ 'And ˹so will˺ some of your descendants ˹also˺.' ˹Allah˺ said, 'My covenant does not ˹extend to˺ the wrongdoers'"* (2:124). Rank in God's economy runs through conduct, not chromosomes. A clan boasts of its dead; a community continues their work.

**Why the Sentence Will Return**

This exact sentence appears again, word for word, seven verses later (2:141), and the repetition is structural rather than redundant. Between the two occurrences falls a dense argument: rival invitations to join one sect or another, the community's own full confession of faith, the exposure of the claim that the patriarchs were Jews or Christians. The verse here states the principle before the case is argued; its twin restates it after the case is closed. The effect is a bracket — the dispute about who owns Abraham is opened and shut between two identical judgments. When the second occurrence arrives, the sentence will no longer be information. It will be a verdict. The reader who notices the bracket understands that everything between its arms has just been ruled out of order.

**The Earned Inheritance**

If ancestral credit is unavailable, what remains of the ancestors is their example — and the example is itself an earned thing, offered for imitation rather than for claiming. Abraham did not bequeath righteousness the way a man bequeaths land; he demonstrated a path, and the path is open to whoever walks it. This is why the sūrah can honor the patriarchs so highly in one breath and strip their descendants of every inherited privilege in the next. Honor belongs to the dead for what they earned; obligation belongs to the living for what they will earn. The verse thus performs a double liberation: it frees the living from despair over ancestors who sinned, and it frees them from complacency about ancestors who were righteous. Both moods are refusals of work. What the verse demands is work — your own, beginning now, in an account no one else can touch.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:135

> The Jews and Christians each say, “Follow our faith to be ˹rightly˺ guided.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “No! We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright—who was not a polytheist.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Invitations, Neither a Choice**

The verse reports a dueling pair of claims: the Jews say follow our faith, the Christians say follow ours, and each promises that its road is the road to guidance. These were not two offers on one table from which a neutral shopper might choose. Each community was speaking for its own religion alone, and each treated the other's invitation as void — the claim is exclusive on both lips. The Qur'an's answer refuses the terms of the contest entirely. It does not adjudicate between Jerusalem's synagogue and the church, because the argument as framed assumes that guidance arrived with one of these institutions. The reply reaches behind both, to a faith older than either name: the *millah* of Abraham. By declining to choose between the two sects, the verse dissolves the question they were fighting over.

**The Millah of Abraham**

*Millah* denotes a creed, a way of religious life held by a community — and here it is identified with Islam itself. This is not an isolated gesture. The command to follow Abraham's faith recurs at the close of the Meccan sūrahs: *"Then We revealed to you ˹O Prophet, saying˺: 'Follow the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not one of the polytheists'"* (16:123); *"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ 'Surely my Lord has guided me to the Straight Path, a perfect way, the faith of Abraham, the upright'"* (6:161); and Abraham's way is called the best faith in the company of doing good and full submission (4:125). The pattern is consistent: whenever the Qur'an needs a name for the religion it preaches that predates every sect, it names Abraham's. The prophet whom all three traditions claim belongs, in the Qur'an's telling, to none of them and authorizes the one that follows him in substance.

**Ḥanīf: Inclining Away from Every Party**

The word attached to Abraham here is *ḥanīf*, and its etymology is famously strange. The root can mean to be lame or crooked, and it can also mean to incline toward; Semitic cognates carry unflattering senses — hypocrite, vile, pagan, heathen in the sense of neither Jew nor Christian. Christian Arabic writers used it of Muslims, sometimes with those negative echoes intact. Yet in the Qur'an the word is uniformly a title of honor. The likely path of meaning is a reversal: one who inclines away from a group is reproached by that group, and praised when the group is judged to be in error. A ḥanīf is therefore someone not bound to a party's limitations, distortions, and tribal loyalties — not hidebound, not sectarian to the detriment of universal truth. Grammatically the word appears in the Qur'an almost always in the indefinite accusative, describing the state one is in when believing or worshipping: upright, as a ḥanīf, in the condition of pure undivided devotion.

**The Uprightness Written Into Human Nature**

That condition corresponds to what the Qur'an calls *fiṭrah* — the unspoiled primordial nature God gives every human being. The sūrah of the Romans ties the two together in one command: *"So be steadfast in faith in all uprightness ˹O Prophet˺—the natural Way of Allah which He has instilled in ˹all˺ people. Let there be no change in this creation of Allah"* (30:30). To be ḥanīf is not to join a new sect but to return to the orientation the soul shipped with. The same word governs worship in the sūrah of the Clear Proof — serving God *"with sincere devotion to Him in all uprightness"* (98:5) — and standing upright for God without association in the sūrah of the Pilgrimage (22:31). Judaism and Christianity, on this reading, are particularizations of a universal religion, and each particularization accumulated what the ḥanīf inclines away from.

**Not the Pilgrim, Not the Circumcised**

Early exegetes tested narrower definitions of ḥanīf and rejected them for good reasons. Some proposed "pilgrim," but pilgrimage to the House was performed by the pagan Arabs too, so the label would have included idolaters. Some proposed "follower" in the sense of one who kept Abraham's practices such as circumcision, but circumcision was kept by the Jews, so the label would have collapsed into one of the very parties the verse is declining. Al-Ṭabarī settled on the sense of straight, upright following of Abraham's way. He added a clarification that matters: the verse does not imply that the prophets before Abraham lacked uprightness; Abraham is named here because God made him an imam of pure monotheism with a standing role for all monotheists after him — the same imamate granted in 2:124. The name anchors a lineage of faith that runs through conduct, not through the boundary markers the sects were trading.

**The Ḥunafāʾ Already in Arabia**

The word was not a Qur'anic invention landing on deaf ears. Even among the non-Muslim Arabs of the Prophet's time, the quality of being ḥanīf was associated with Abraham, with renouncing idols, and with leading a moral life, and the biographical literature remembers individual Arab seekers who abandoned idolatry for a monotheism traced to Abraham before the revelation ever reached them. It was never a label for Jews or Christians, and it never denoted an organized group with meetings and membership — it named a posture. That is precisely why the Qur'an's answer works in this argument. When the two sects say follow us, the reply names the one thing both had already conceded was older and purer than their dispute: the upright devotion of Abraham, which no party owns and which every party is measured against.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:136

> Say, ˹O believers,˺ “We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us; and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants; and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and other prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them. And to Allah we all submit.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Creed That Leaves Nothing Out**

This is the community's confession of faith in a single sentence, and its architecture is deliberate. It moves in widening circles of revelation: God Himself first; then what has been revealed to this community; then what was revealed to the patriarchs — Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and Jacob's descendants; then what was given to Moses and Jesus; then what was given to the prophets as a class, unnamed and unnumbered. No era of revelation is skipped and no prophet is dropped. The confession is spoken in the first-person plural — *we* believe — because it is not a private opinion but the standing statement of a community, recited by each generation in its own voice. Its final clause folds the whole inventory into a single posture: and to God we submit. Belief is enumerated; then it is enacted.

**The Descendants: Grandsons and Tribes**

The word rendered "his descendants" is *asbāṭ*, whose singular *sibṭ* means grandchild — a precise genealogical note, since these are Jacob's grandchildren through his sons, the ancestors of the twelve tribes of Israel. The sūrah of the Heights records the division itself: *"We divided them into twelve tribes— each as a community"* (7:160). Placing the asbāṭ inside the creed accomplishes something the sectarian argument of the previous verses could not: the tribes that the Torah's guardians prized as their exclusive inheritance are here enrolled as recipients of revelation alongside everyone else. They are honored — revelation came to their line — but they are not privileged. In a confession that ends with "we make no distinction," even the twelve tribes hold their place as peers of Ishmael, the ancestor the Arabs claimed, and of the prophets who never had a tribe to name after them.

**No Distinction in Believing**

"We make no distinction between any of them" is a statement about belief, not about rank. The Qur'an elsewhere acknowledges that God *"chosen some of those messengers above others"* and raised some high in rank (2:253), and the believers' creed later in this same sūrah repeats the no-distinction clause in the same sense (2:285). What is excluded here is selectivity: believing some prophets and disbelieving others, accepting the ones your tradition kept and discarding the ones it lost. That selective habit is exactly what the sūrah denounced earlier, rebuking those who believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest (2:85). A creed that admits Moses but refuses Jesus, or honors Jesus but refuses Muhammad, has not made a theological judgment; it has made a tribal one. The confession closes that door: every prophet is believed, because every prophet came from the same Lord.

**One Religion From Noah Onward**

The creed's comprehensiveness rests on a theology of continuity stated explicitly elsewhere: *"He has ordained for you ˹believers˺ the Way which He decreed for Noah, and what We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what We decreed for Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, ˹commanding:˺ 'Uphold the faith, and make no divisions in it'"* (42:13). One religion, four named stations, one command — and the prohibition of division inside the command itself. On this account the confession of this verse is not the membership oath of a new party competing with older parties. It is the same faith every prophet brought, recited by the community that refuses to divide it. The sects fractured the inheritance; the creed gathers it back up, which is why it can name Abraham, Moses, and Jesus in one breath without embarrassment or appropriation.

**The Same Words, Again and Again**

The formula proved to be the community's fixed statement rather than a one-off sentence. Āl ʿImrān carries a nearly identical confession — *"We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants"* (3:84) — and the sūrah of the Women commands belief in God, His Messenger, the Book sent down to him, and the Scriptures sent down before (4:136). The repetition across sūrahs, in Mecca and Medina, shows the creed functioning as the believers' answer whenever faith is demanded of them: when the People of the Book say join us, when the pagans ask what you worship, when the community defines itself in prayer. A statement repeated this many times in the Book ceased to be commentary and became liturgy — the shortest complete account of what a Muslim believes, recited in the plural because it is held in common.

**Submission as the Seal**

The creed ends where it began in God, but with a verb instead of a noun: "And to Allah we all submit." The inventory of revelations could have closed with a summary — this is our faith, this is our book. Instead it closes with an act. *Islam* here is not a second belief added to the first; it is the first belief standing up. To believe in God and every prophet He sent is to owe Him the whole of one's direction, and the confession pays the debt in its last four words. The placement also answers the sects implicitly. The Jews said follow our faith, the Christians said follow ours, and each named an institution; the confession names a posture — submission to the Lord of all the prophets, without distinction, without a party between the servant and his God. The verse after this one will state the consequence: whoever believes as this creed believes is guided.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:137

> So if they believe in what you believe, then they will indeed be ˹rightly˺ guided. But if they turn away, they are simply opposed ˹to the truth˺. But Allah will spare you their evil. For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Condition Stated Once, Plainly**

The verse converts the confession of the previous verse into a single conditional with two exits and no third door. If they believe *in the like of* what you believe, they are guided; if they turn away, they are in opposition. The phrase "in the like of" has been read carefully by the exegetes, because taken crudely it would imply that the object of the believers' faith has a "like" — and Islamic theology holds that nothing resembles God. Al-Ṭabarī therefore explains it as affirmation of the same things: the People of the Book should believe the very realities this community believes, God and all His revelations without distinction. Al-Rāzī adds a second layer with historical bite: believing "the like" can mean believing the Torah and Gospel in their undistorted state — the scriptures as originally given rather than as edited by the hands the sūrah has already accused (2:75). On either reading the condition is not a vague sympathy but a full assent, and the guidance promised is the guidance the believers already possess.

**Shiqāq: Turning Away as Fracture**

The word for what the refusers do is *shiqāq* — literally a splitting or fracture, and by extension an attitude of active opposition and hostility. The Qur'an uses the same root consistently in this hardened sense: those who differ regarding the Book are *"totally engrossed in opposition"* (2:176); the wrongdoers are *"totally engrossed in opposition"* (22:53); the disbelievers stand *"˹entrenched˺ in arrogance and opposition"* (38:2); and the one who denies what is from God has *"gone too far in opposition"* (41:52). The choice of word matters. Turning away from this creed is not classified as a legitimate alternative, a different path among paths. It is named as rupture — a deliberate break made against known truth. The verse thus refuses the comfortable modern category of "equally valid options": belief here yields guidance, refusal yields schism, and the two outcomes are not morally symmetrical.

**A Guarantee Before the Community Had Power**

Between the two exits the verse places a promise: "But Allah will spare you their evil." When this was revealed the Muslim community in Medina was small, surrounded, and internally infiltrated; its opponents had wealth, alliances, and rhetorical skill. The guarantee that their evil would be sufficed away was not a description of present strength but a pledge against a future the community could not yet see. The verb is *kafā*, to suffice — to be enough for a need. God is announced as enough against the opponents' evil: enough that their scheming will not destroy the community, enough that its members need not buy safety by diluting the creed. The promise is total because the sufficiency is divine; no quantity of opposition exhausts it, which is why the verse can state it in one clause and move on.

**The Family of Sufficiency**

The Qur'an returns to this sufficiency in register after register. God is sufficient as a Reckoner over the trusts of orphans (4:6); sufficient as Guardian and Helper against enemies (4:45); sufficient for the Prophet and the believers who follow him (8:64); sufficient in battle, when He drove back the confederates *"in their rage, totally emptyhanded"* (33:25). The believers' own liturgy of sufficiency is the sentence *"Allah is sufficient for me"* placed on the Prophet's tongue when the adversaries turn away (9:129), and the older formula *ḥasbunā Allāh* — God is enough for us — which Āl ʿImrān records the believers saying when told a great army had gathered against them (3:173). Each instance is a variation on the promise of this verse: whatever the form of the evil — financial, military, rhetorical — the sufficiency covers it.

**Two Men and Two Fires**

Ibn ʿAbbās linked that formula to two moments of extreme danger, and the report is preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (4563): "Allah is Sufficient for us and He is the Best Disposer of affairs" was said by Abraham when he was thrown into the fire, and it was said by Muhammad when the people told the believers that a great army was gathering against them — and it only increased their faith. The two men faced the same arithmetic: overwhelming force on one side, nothing visible on the other. In both cases the sentence was not a denial of the danger but a declaration about the size of God beside it. Read against this verse, the arc is exact. The promise that Allah will spare the believers their opponents' evil was made in Medina when the community was weak, and its first great test — the confederate army at the Trench — ended with the enemy driven back without a battle, the sufficiency demonstrated rather than argued.

**All-Hearing, All-Knowing**

The verse seals with two names: He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing. The pairing is not decorative; it names the two faculties the besieged community most needs God to have. All-Hearing: the mockery is audible to Him, the taunts about the qiblah, the whispered "he follows our religion," the slander of a community too small to answer every voice. All-Knowing: the schemes are visible to Him, the private plotting that never reaches speech, the intentions behind the arguments. A guarantee against "their evil" would be worthless if God could be misinformed about it, so the names certify the guarantee. The enemies are not being spared attention — they are being heard and known with a completeness their victims cannot match, and the case is in hands that will not lose evidence. The community's job, in this verse's own logic, is not surveillance or counter-plotting but belief: hold the creed, and the sufficiency holds the rest.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:138

> This is the ˹natural˺ Way of Allah. And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way? And we worship ˹none but˺ Him.

**Expanded Commentary**

**One Word, One Occurrence**

The verse in Arabic opens with two words only: *ṣibghat Allāh* — the dye of God, or as this translation renders the sense, the natural Way of God. The root *ṣabagha* means to dye, to plunge cloth into coloring liquid, and more generally to cause someone to enter into something. *Ṣibghah* is the dye itself, or the coloration it leaves. This is the word's only occurrence in the entire Qur'an — a hapax — and the singularity is part of its power: a term with no prior Quranic usage to lean on, chosen once, for this one place, at the climax of the argument about whose religion is true. Because the word is unique, the exegetes have read it in several directions at once, and the readings turn out to converge rather than compete: God's coloration is His nature stamped on the soul, His unchanging way with creation, His religion, and His purification, all in one image.

**The Color Worn From Birth**

The primary reading takes the dye as the *fiṭrah* — the primordial nature every human being bears the way a cloth bears its original color. Al-Thaʿālibī's explanation is exact: the ṣibghah is the upright religion God instilled in human nature, the religion named in the sūrah of the Romans — *"the natural Way of Allah which He has instilled in ˹all˺ people"* (30:30) — the same verse that uses the word *ḥanīf* which appeared in the answer about Abraham's faith three verses back (2:135). The chain of connection is deliberate: the faith of Abraham, the upright, is the faith of unspoiled nature, and God's dye is that faith as a fact of creation rather than a choice of sect. A person does not acquire the color at conversion; he is dipped in it at his making, and every religion that arrives later either matches the dye or paints over it.

**An Answer to a Rite**

The reading was sharpened by the religious landscape of Arabia, where Christian communities practiced baptism as the rite of entry into faith — immersion in water as the sign of belonging. Some commentators understood this verse to answer that rite directly: God's baptism, His dyeing of the soul at creation, is superior to any water a church administers, because the divine coloration is original, universal, and indelible, while the human rite is later, particular, and external. The question the verse poses — "who is better than Allah in ordaining a way?" — is rhetorical in the strictest sense: there is no candidate. Every instituted rite, on this reading, is measured against the instituting act of God Himself, who dyed the whole species in the color of upright recognition of Him before any priest existed to pour water. The claim is not that rites are worthless but that they are second — responses to a coloration that came first.

**The Dye as God's Unchanging Way**

A second family of readings takes ṣibghah as *sunnat Allāh* — God's wont, His unchanging manner of acting toward the world. The Qur'an uses the phrase repeatedly and always with the same emphasis on constancy: *"˹This has been˺ Our way with the messengers We sent before you. And you will never find any change in Our way"* (17:77), and *"˹This is˺ Allah's way, already long established ˹in the past˺. And you will find no change in Allah's way"* (48:23). Under this reading the verse says that the religion being preached is not an innovation but God's established procedure: the way He has always colored souls, sent prophets, and judged communities. The rhetorical question that follows then carries a historical weight — who is better than God at this, than the One whose method has never varied across the whole procession of nations the sūrah has just recounted?

**Religion, Purification, and One Image**

Other exegetes heard in ṣibghah simply God's religion (*dīn*), and others heard purification — the dye as the washing that cleanses. Al-Rāzī mapped the grammatical options with care: the phrase can stand as an imperative, "follow the dye of God"; it can reach back to Abraham's creed in 2:135 as the thing to be followed; or it can attach adverbially to the confession of 2:136, "we believe in God — dyed, as it were, in His religion." The interpretations are complementary rather than contradictory, because the image of dyeing contains them all at once. Dyeing is a religion's entry rite, a purification, a permanent change of state, and the revealing of the cloth's intended color. A single well-chosen metaphor can carry a whole theology, and this one carries the theology of the passage: God's coloring of the human soul is original, it is His own doing, no rival can match it, and the sects that quarrel over it are arguing about whose water is better while the dye was never water's to give.

**"And We Worship None but Him"**

The verse ends by dropping the metaphor and speaking plainly: and we are His worshippers. The shift from image to declaration does the final work. All the readings of ṣibghah — nature, wont, religion, purification — issue in one posture, and the posture is worship of the One who does the dyeing. The first-person plural continues the voice of the community's confession from two verses earlier: this is what we say, we who believe without distinction between the prophets. The grammar of the whole movement is worth naming: the creed was stated (2:136), its consequence for others drawn (2:137), and now its ground is given — the coloration of God Himself — and its fruit declared: worship. A religion that began as a list of things believed ends as an act performed. That is the shape the sūrah wants faith to have, and the hapax at its center is the pivot on which belief turns into belonging.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:139

> Say, “Would you dispute with us about Allah, while He is our Lord and your Lord? We are accountable for our deeds and you for yours. And we are devoted to Him ˹alone˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Arguing About God With God in Common**

The question the verse puts in the Prophet's mouth is designed to stop an argument by exposing its absurd shape. Would you dispute with us *about Allah* — while He is our Lord *and your Lord*? Both sides of the dispute already stand on the same premise: there is one Lord who owns both communities. The quarrel, then, is not about whether God exists or whose God is real; it is being conducted, oddly, about God Himself — His choices, His sends, His preferences — by parties who agree on who He is. The rhetorical question names that oddity. Disputing about a person behind his back presupposes you know him; disputing about God while calling Him your Lord presupposes a knowledge of His ways that neither disputant actually possesses. The verse does not forbid the discussion; it re-frames it, moving the contested matter out of God's essence and into the only place where evidence exists: the deeds of the disputants themselves.

**What the Dispute Was Actually About**

The historical substance of the argument is recoverable from the context and the commentaries. The Jewish communities of Medina objected to a prophet arising outside the Children of Israel — revelation, in their theology, had a lineage, and this claimant came from the wrong family tree. The idolatrous Arabs, for their part, objected on grounds of social rank: if heaven were going to send a man, it would send one of higher station than the orphan of Mecca — the same protest the Qur'an quotes elsewhere, *"If only this Quran was revealed to a great man from ˹one of˺ the two cities!"* (43:31). Both objections share a structure: they are claims about how God ought to distribute His favors, and the sūrah answers that distribution is His alone — *"You give authority to whoever You please and remove it from who You please"* (3:26). The dispute about Allah is, on inspection, a dispute about Allah's freedom. The verse's reply — He is your Lord as much as ours — concedes the relationship and denies either party a veto over it.

**Our Deeds and Yours**

Having named the true object of the quarrel, the verse disengages with a formula that recurs across the Qur'an: to us our deeds, to you yours. The same words appear when denial hardens into deadlock — *"If they deny you, then say, 'My deeds are mine and your deeds are yours. You are free of what I do and I am free of what you do!'"* (10:41) — and when submission is offered and refused: *"I have submitted myself to Allah, and so have my followers"* (3:20). The formula is not indifference and not relativism. It is the closing of a case that cannot proceed: each party's deeds will be answered for by that party, so further argument about whose deeds please God is litigation without jurisdiction. What the formula preserves is accountability — "we are accountable for our deeds and you for yours" — and what it refuses is the merger of accounts that the disputants wanted, in which one community's standing vouches for or condemns another's.

**The Prophet Who Ended the Same Argument Before**

The pattern is older than Medina. When Abraham's people argued with him, he answered with the identical move: *"Are you arguing with me about Allah, while He has guided me?"* (6:80) — the shared God named, the guidance located in the arguer's own experience rather than in the opponent's theory, and the fear transferred from the idols to the Lord who encompasses everything in His knowledge. The sūrah of the Cow itself stages the earliest version, the man who disputed with Abraham about his Lord (2:258), undone not by superior information but by the direction of the sun. This verse places Muhammad in that exact succession: the same argument, the same adversaries in new costumes, the same answer. Reading 2:139 alongside 6:80 shows that the Qur'an understands religious dispute as a repeating event with a fixed prophetic response — name the common Lord, present your own guidance, separate the accounts, and stop.

**Devoted to Him Alone**

The final clause is the verse's real edge: *wa-naḥnu lahu mukhliṣūn* — and we are sincere, devoted, purified in intention toward Him alone. The root carries *ikhlāṣ*, sincerity in the technical sense of a motive unmixed with anything other than God. Placed at the end of an argument verse, it identifies what actually terminates disputes: not the winning of points but the purity of the disputant. A person who argues to be seen winning cannot disengage, because the argument itself has become his object; a person devoted to God alone can state the separation of accounts and mean it. The clause also answers the *shiqāq* named two verses earlier (2:137) — opposition is a mixed motive at work, and sincerity is its cure. The community's position in the quarrel is thus not a stronger claim but a cleaner heart: we do not need to defeat you, because our devotion does not run through your defeat.

**The Graceful Argument**

The method of this verse is codified in the sūrah of the Spider, in the Qur'an's standing rule for interreligious speech: *"Do not argue with the People of the Book unless gracefully, except with those of them who act wrongfully. And say, 'We believe in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed to you. Our God and your God is ˹only˺ One. And to Him we ˹fully˺ submit'"* (29:46). The resemblance to 2:139 is structural: begin from the shared — one God, one Lord of both communities; state the creed without polemic; keep the accounts separate; reserve firmness for those who argue in bad faith. Grace (*aḥsan*) is the manner, not the message: the common ground is asserted first because it is true, and the separation follows because it is necessary. This verse is that procedure in its earliest Medinan form — a dispute about God settled by pointing at God, at the deeds of the disputants, and at the sincerity that needs no verdict from either.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:140

> Or do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants were all Jews or Christians?” Say, “Who is more knowledgeable: you or Allah?” Who does more wrong than those who hide the testimony they received from Allah? And Allah is never unaware of what you do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Claim the Calendar Refutes**

The verse puts the sectarian argument of the preceding verses to its simplest test: were Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes Jews or Christians? The question is not rhetorical decoration — it is a chronology. Āl ʿImrān presses the same point with the calendar made explicit: *"O People of the Book! Why do you argue about Abraham, while the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until long after him? Do you not understand?"* (3:65). The Torah is the book of Moses; the Gospel is the book of Jesus; both came centuries after the patriarchs lived and died. To call Abraham a Jew is to attach him to a law he never received; to call him a Christian is to attach him to a gospel he never heard. The verse's own conclusion, stated in the companion sūrah, is the flat denial: *"Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian; he submitted in all uprightness and was not a polytheist"* (3:67). The labels arrived late, and the patriarchs predate them all.

**"Who Is More Knowledgeable: You or Allah?"**

Between the question and the condemnation the verse inserts what may be the sharpest sentence in the whole passage. Who has better knowledge — you, or God? The question admits exactly two answers, and both are fatal. If God knows better, then His testimony about who Abraham was stands, and the claimants are overruled by the only authority competent to speak. If the claimants know better, they have set their knowledge above God's — a position no believing Jew or Christian can occupy without abandoning his own creed. The force of the sentence lies in its brevity: it does not argue the chronology again or cite the patriarchs' practices; it simply forces the opponent to choose between deferring to divine knowledge and claiming to exceed it. Every dispute about revelation eventually arrives at this fork, and the verse's placement of it here makes it the hinge between the historical argument and the moral charge that follows.

**Words That Did Not Yet Exist**

The anachronism can be sharpened with the history of the labels themselves. "Jew" derives from Judah, the son of Jacob whose name passed to his tribe, then to the southern kingdom, then to the religious community that took shape around the Torah centuries after Moses — the identity is downstream of events Abraham could not have witnessed. "Christian" is younger still: the book of Acts records that it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:26) — a name coined by outsiders, in a city, in the generation after Jesus, more than a millennium after Abraham's death. Neither word existed while the patriarchs lived, and neither community's founding document had been revealed when they died. The Qur'an's question — were they Jews or Christians — is therefore not a theological puzzle but a factual impossibility, and the fact that both sects nonetheless claimed the patriarchs shows what the claims were really doing: not reporting history but annexing it.

**A Testimony Hidden From Allah**

The charge that follows names the mechanism of the annexation: who does more wrong than those who hide a testimony they hold from Allah? The *shahādah* — testimony — is understood by the exegetes in two converging senses. It is the testimony God placed in their own scriptures: the descriptions of the coming prophet and the records showing that the patriarchs lived before the sectarian identities existed, so that the Qur'an testifies to the same truths their books uphold. And it is God's own testimony, borne in revelation, that these prophets were neither Jewish nor Christian. Concealing either is the same act, and it is the act the sūrah has been building toward since its early addresses: do not mix truth with falsehood or hide the truth knowingly (2:42); why do you mix the truth with falsehood and hide it knowingly (3:71)? The wrongdoer superlative — who does *more* wrong — marks concealment of known testimony as a peak category of injustice, because it injures not the concealer but everyone he might have guided.

**Why the Patriarchs Were Worth the Fight**

The intensity of the verse is proportionate to the stakes. Abraham is the founding figure of monotheism itself; whoever owns him owns the legitimacy that flows from him. Both sects claimed him because both needed their faith to be primordial rather than novel, and the claim to Abraham was the claim to be the original religion. The Qur'an's answer does not merely deny the claim; it relocates the inheritance. The people closest to Abraham, in Āl ʿImrān's formulation, are those who followed him, and this prophet, and those who believe (3:68) — proximity by following, not by labeling. That is the substance of the ḥanīf answer two groups of verses back (2:135): the patriarch's legacy belongs to whoever walks his road of upright devotion, and it is forfeited by whoever merely files him under a party name he never knew.

**"And Allah Is Never Unaware"**

The verse closes with the refrain of surveillance: Allah is never unaware of what you do. The concealment charge and the closing line interlock. Hiding testimony works only where witnesses can be managed — where the audience does not know what was hidden, and the hider can count on the gap. The refrain annuls the gap: the One from whom the testimony comes is watching the act of concealment, and the case file is complete on His side even when the public record is doctored on theirs. The same clause ends the qiblah verdicts that follow in this passage (2:144, 2:149), which is why the refrain functions as the passage's signature: every dispute about who is guided, who owns Abraham, and which direction is true is being conducted in full view of a Judge who cannot be deprived of evidence. For the concealer it is a warning with no appeal; for the community accused and outargued, it is the assurance that its case does not depend on winning the argument in the street.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:141

> That was a community that had already gone before. For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be accountable for what they have done.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Same Sentence, Spoken Twice**

This verse is a word-for-word repetition of 2:134 — the same community that passed, the same earnings, the same disclaimer of accountability. Verbatim repetition within a single argument sequence is rare enough in the Qur'an that its occurrence here demands an account. It is not filler and not a scribal doubling; the two placements carry different weights because they follow different material. The first occurrence came immediately after Abraham's deathbed and the injunction to die in submission (2:132–133), where it cut the nerve of genealogical reliance. The second comes immediately after the exposure of the anachronistic claim that the patriarchs were Jews or Christians, and after the charge of concealing testimony (2:140). The sentence has not changed; the case around it has. Read the first time it was a principle announced; read the second time it is a judgment pronounced.

**The Bracket That Closes the Argument**

Structurally the two occurrences form an inclusio — a bracket enclosing the densest block of sectarian polemic in the sūrah. Inside the arms of the bracket lie the rival invitations of the Jews and Christians (2:135), the community's full confession of faith (2:136), the two exits of belief and opposition (2:137), the dyeing of God (2:138), the disengagement from disputing about God (2:139), and the chronological demolition of the patriarch-annexation (2:140). Everything argued between the brackets is answered by the sentence that closes them. The ancestors whose ownership was fought over are a finished community; their earnings are settled; the living are back where they started, holding only their own accounts. The rhetorical effect is that of a courtroom: evidence heard, claims examined, and then the same ruling that opened the session restated from the bench as the verdict — no new argument required, because the principle was never in dispute.

**Ring Composition and the Second Landing**

Repetition as a structural device — saying the frame twice so that the material between is heard as enclosed — belongs to the Qur'an's own compositional habits, and here it does precise work. When the sentence first appeared, a reader could still hope that the ancestors' merits might be reachable, that lineage might be leveraged into standing. Seven verses later, after the sects have been shown claiming patriarchs who predate their very names, the identical sentence lands as confiscation. The community that passed took its earnings with it, and the claimants who fought over its name have fought over an estate that closed with its death. Nothing about the words changed; the argument between the two occurrences converted an observation into a dispossession. This is why the verse should never be read as a mere duplicate of the first — the duplication is the point, and the second instance carries the accumulated weight of everything it brackets.

**Slow Deeds and Fast Lineage**

The principle has a prophetic commentary that sharpens it into a single image. In a long report preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (2699a), Abu Hurayrah narrates the Messenger of God closing a catena of teachings with this sentence: whoever is slowed by his deeds, his lineage will not speed him up. The image is of a race in which a man of noble ancestry is falling behind on merit, and his pedigree — whatever its glories — exerts no forward force. The ḥadīth states exactly what the verse's bracket states: earnings are personal, and lineage is inert. A descendant of prophets walks at his own pace; an heir of the patriarchs' name carries none of the patriarchs' speed. Placed beside 2:141, the report converts the theological rule into a warning addressed to the very audience of the polemic — and to every later reader tempted to borrow velocity from the dead.

**Two Contexts, Two Edges**

The double placement of the verse gives it two distinct applications, and both were live in the sūrah's first audience. At its first occurrence the edge is turned against genealogical complacency: the children of Abraham by blood or claim cannot cash his righteousness, because that community's account closed with its death. At its second occurrence the edge is turned against sectarian appropriation: the claim to own the patriarchs — to make them retroactive members of a party — has just been shown to be chronologically impossible and morally culpable, and the verdict repeats to seal the exposure. One sentence, two boasts, one refutation. And the verse carries a third edge that neither occurrence spells out but both imply: it applies to the Muslims' own reverence for the patriarchs. Honor them, follow their faith, recite their story — but expect no transfer of credit. The bracket encloses the believers too.

**Neither Their Merit Nor Their Guilt**

The final clause deserves its own weight: you will not be accountable for what they have done. The disclaimer runs in both directions, and the second direction is the merciful one. Not only can ancestral virtue not save a descendant; ancestral sin cannot damn him. The sons are not punished for the fathers — a principle the Hebrew scriptures state in their own idiom when Ezekiel insists that the son shall not bear the father's iniquity nor the father the son's (Ezekiel 18:20), and the Qur'an states it in the idiom of burdens elsewhere: no soul bearing a load will bear another's (53:38). Between the two directions stands the individual, unrepresented and unabsorbed: no clan behind him to claim his case, no ancestry beneath him to carry his weight. This is the anthropology the whole bracket has been defending — the human being as a personal account, opened at birth, closed at death, audited by a God who never confuses one ledger with another.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:142

> The foolish among the people will ask, “Why did they turn away from the direction of prayer they used to face?” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “The east and west belong ˹only˺ to Allah. He guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question Predicted Before It Was Asked**

The verse arrives in the future tense: the foolish among the people *will ask* why the believers abandoned their former direction of prayer. Al-Rāzī notes that the future form does not exclude the past — it characterizes the question as a standing trait of the objectors as much as it predicts an event, the way a proverb says "the fool will say" because the fool always says it. The word for the objectors is *sufahāʾ*, the light-witted, those whose judgment lacks ballast, and al-Ṭabarī reports that some commentators identified them specifically as the hypocrites, whose question was not a search for reasons but a cynical probe — asked not to be answered but to unsettle the newly converted. The verse's foresight is itself part of its argument: the question is predicted, classified, and answered before the questioners finish asking it, which places the objectors inside a script they did not write.

**What the Question Assumed**

The question — why did they turn away from the qiblah they used to face — carries a buried premise: that the earlier direction had an intrinsic claim on loyalty, and that leaving it required a justification owed to the askers. The premise treats the qiblah as property of a place. The answer refuses the premise rather than the question. Nothing in the east or in the west obligates God, and no direction possesses sanctity in itself; a direction is a qiblah because God commanded it, and it ceases to be one when He commands otherwise. Had the verse offered a historical reason — the Jews boasted, the Prophet longed for Mecca — the objectors would have gained the ground they wanted: that the direction is negotiable in light of human motives. Instead the reply is theological and closes the negotiation: the points of the compass belong to Allah, and He guides whom He wills to a straight path. The same ownership was declared in this sūrah's earlier statement that the east and the west belong to God (2:115); here it becomes the answer to a challenge.

**Sixteen or Seventeen Months Toward Jerusalem**

The historical frame of the question is well documented in the exegetical sources. After the emigration to Medina the Prophet prayed toward Jerusalem for a period the reports place between thirteen and twenty months, with most specifying sixteen or seventeen. The accounts differ on the Meccan period: some hold that in Mecca the community faced the Kaʿbah, shifted to Jerusalem briefly after the migration, then returned to the Kaʿbah; others maintain that Jerusalem was the direction even in Mecca. What is common to the reports is that the Jerusalem orientation was observed in Medina for a substantial, counted stretch — long enough for it to become "the qiblah they used to face" in the questioners' mouths, and long enough for the change to be a genuine test rather than an administrative adjustment. The variation in the counts is itself honest historiography: the tradition preserved the disagreement rather than smoothing it, which is how the reports of this period usually behave on matters of duration.

**The First Ruling Ever Changed**

Within the science of *naskh* — the abrogation or supersession of a ruling by a later revelation — the change of the qiblah holds a paradigmatic place. It is regularly cited as the first instance of abrogation in the chronological order of revelation, and it carries a technical peculiarity the commentators flag: what was superseded was not a Qur'anic verse but a direction established through the Prophet's practice, making this a case of the Qur'an abrogating the Sunnah. The doctrine that makes such change coherent is stated in this same sūrah: *"If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten, We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything?"* (2:106). The qiblah case became the working example in the legal literature because it is undeniable, datable, and communal — a whole congregation's practice reversed by revelation, with the theological account already in place to explain it.

**The Mosque of the Two Qiblahs**

The change left a physical mark on Medina that survives. A few kilometers from the Prophet's Mosque stands Masjid al-Qiblatayn — the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs — so named because, as the exegetical sources report, a caller arrived while a congregation was mid-prayer to announce the newly revealed command, and the worshippers turned within the prayer itself to face the new direction. The building has been reconstructed in recent times, but its name and its site preserve the memory of the single most literal turning in Islamic history: a community reorienting its bodies while its prayer was still in progress. The story matters theologically as well as topographically. It shows the change executed at the scale of an ordinary neighborhood congregation, not only at the Prophet's own mosque, and it embodies the verse's lesson in obedience: the direction was not their choice before, and it was not their choice now, and the turn was made without the prayer being broken.

**Qubāʾ Turns at Dawn**

The most firmly attested report of the event is in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (403): ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar narrated that while the people were offering the dawn prayer at Qubāʾ near Medina, someone came to them and said that revelation had come to the Messenger of God that night ordering him to face the Kaʿbah — so turn your faces toward it. Those people had been facing al-Shām, the direction of Jerusalem, and they turned toward the Kaʿbah. The detail that they were mid-prayer at Fajr, that the news arrived from a single messenger, and that the whole congregation rotated on the strength of his word, gives the event its texture: the qiblah changed not in a council but in a village mosque at dawn, on trust in a report, with the prayer continuing through the turn. Bukhārī filed the report under the chapter on praying mistakenly toward a wrong direction without repeating the prayer — the legal conclusion the event itself generated.

**Pointing the Whole World at One Point**

Once a single building became the direction for a global community, the practical problem of finding it from anywhere on earth produced a scientific literature. An early method treated the worshipper as facing one wall of the Kaʿbah extended indefinitely, dividing the world into sectors each oriented to a different wall; since the Kaʿbah's corners align with the cardinal directions and its faces were associated with the summer sunrise and with Canopus, the navigation star, the heavens themselves were recruited into the calculation. Later methods grew mathematical: the great-circle route — the shortest path over the sphere — which from North America begins northeast and curves steadily toward the southeast, against the older sector method's simple southeasterly bearing; the constant-compass rhumb line as a third candidate; astrolabes and armillary spheres as instruments. All are used somewhere today. And a reported saying of the Prophet — whatever lies between the east and the west is qiblah — was read as granting latitude where exact determination is impossible, so that the obligation is orientation toward the House, not surveyor's precision. The fools' question about one village's turning ended by generating a science that turns every village toward the same point.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:143

> And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community so that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you. We assigned your former direction of prayer only to distinguish those who would remain faithful to the Messenger from those who would lose faith. It was certainly a difficult test except for those ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah. And Allah would never discount your ˹previous acts of˺ faith. Surely Allah is Ever Gracious and Most Merciful to humanity.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wasaṭ: The Middle That Means the Best**

The community is made *ummatan wasaṭan* — a middle community, rendered here "upright" — and the middle in Arabic idiom is not the mediocre but the choicest. A ḥadīth cited by the commentators reports the Prophet explaining "middle" as "just," and a saying current enough that some counted it a ḥadīth declares the choicest part of anything to be its middle. The social image behind the idiom is concrete: when a people gather around their leader, he stands at the center, so to name a man the middle of his people is to name him one of their finest. Al-Rāzī adds that the *wasaṭ* of anything is its choice part. The verse therefore confers a rank, not a location: this community is placed at the just center of the religious possibilities ranged around it, and the center is where the best of each extreme survives and the distortion of each is refused.

**The Ethics of the Center**

The commentators worked out what the middle means in practice, and their examples are the classic pairs. Courage is the mean between recklessness and cowardice; generosity is the mean between prodigality and miserliness — virtue as the disciplined midpoint of two failures. Applied to the religious traditions, the same schema yields the community's defining claim: where Judaism is read as emphasizing law and Christianity as emphasizing love and mercy, Islam is presented as holding the balance between them; where one tendency collapses into the external observance alone and another into the interior alone, the middle community keeps exoteric and esoteric together, this world and the Hereafter in one ledger. Some extended the image to geography, noting the lands of Islam across the middle belt of the inhabited world. The theological core is the first pairing: the center is a discipline, maintained against the pull of every excess, and it is what qualifies the community for the office the verse next names.

**Center of the Earth, Center of the Peoples**

The opening word "and so" — *kadhalika* — ties this rank to what preceded it, and the commentators read the tie two ways. Either: just as the Kaʿbah is the center of the earth, so you are the middle people — the community's position among nations mirroring its House's position among places. Or: just as We guided you to the straight path, so We made you a middle community — the uprightness of the creed producing the uprightness of the collective. Both readings converge on a single claim: centrality is given, not achieved. The community did not earn the middle by negotiation between the sects it declined to join; it was made middle by the same act that assigned its direction of prayer. The verse's own logic supports this — the very next sentence describes God assigning the qiblah as an instrument of His knowing and testing — so the community's character and its compass are one gift, dispensed together.

**Witnesses Over Humanity**

The purpose of the middle position is an office: *so that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you*. To be a witness is to hold real standing in the judgment of a thing, by virtue of knowing it — the same weight the Qur'an gives bodily testimony on the Last Day, when hands speak and feet testify to what their owners earned (36:65). The commentators connect the office to the Day of Judgment directly: this community will testify to the faithfulness of earlier prophets in delivering their missions, even where those prophets' own peoples will not confirm it — the witness structure of 4:41, where a witness is brought from every community and the Messenger as witness over his. The sūrah of the Pilgrimage states the same arrangement in nearly the same words: *"so that the Messenger may be a witness over you, and that you may be witnesses over humanity"* (22:78). A chain of testimony runs through the office: God's knowledge to the Messenger, the Messenger's life to the community, the community's account to the nations.

**Allah's Witnesses on Earth**

The witnessing is not wholly deferred to the Last Day. In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (1367), Anas ibn Mālik narrates that a funeral procession passed and the people spoke well of the deceased, and the Prophet said, "It has been affirmed." Another passed and the people spoke ill, and again he said, "It has been affirmed." When ʿUmar asked what had been affirmed, the Prophet answered: this one you praised, so Paradise is affirmed for him, and that one you spoke ill of, so Hell is affirmed for him — *you people are Allah's witnesses on earth*. The report shows the community's witness-function operating at the scale of a single funeral: the collective judgment of those who knew a life carries evidentiary weight before God. Read against 2:143, the ḥadīth is the earthly installment of the eschatological office — the middle community testifies now, in its streets, and will testify then, over humanity.

**The Qiblah as the Sorting Instrument**

The verse then explains what the change of direction was for: *We assigned your former direction of prayer only to distinguish those who would remain faithful to the Messenger from those who would lose faith*. Al-Ṭabarī preserves the reactions the test extracted. The hypocrites jeered: what is wrong with you? You adopt one direction, then you swap it. The Jews read the turn toward Mecca as nostalgia: Muhammad longs for his homeland; had he stayed with our direction, they said, we would have taken him for the awaited one. The Meccan idolaters drew the opposite comfort: Muhammad has wavered in his faith. And within the community itself some asked the anxious question the verse answers: what about our brothers who died facing Jerusalem — what of their prayers? To all of it the verse responds at once: the direction was never the point; it was the instrument of separation, and God would never discount your faith — the prayers already offered toward the old qiblah remain valid, believed, and recorded. The test was hard, the verse concedes — except for those God guided.

**"That We May Know"**

The phrase "only to distinguish" renders a construction that says literally *that We may know* — and the theologians handled it with care, because God's knowledge is eternal and nothing can add to it. Al-Ṭabarī records the readings. The first: "so that We may observe" — knowledge of a thing as existing requires the thing to exist, and God knows eternally what will happen but observes it happening in time; the trial produces the known thing, not the knowledge. The second: "so that My friends and partisans may know" — actions are attributed to a leader whose followers perform them, as people say ʿUmar conquered Jerusalem though he never besieged it; the divine first person covers the community's own seeing. Al-Rāzī adds a third with a pastoral motive: "so that you will all know," with God's use of the first person softening the verdict — *We shall know* falls less harshly than *you will know* when what is known is someone's disbelief. The underlying problem is the one the Qur'an poses wherever it speaks of testing — do people think they will be left to say "we believe" without being tried (29:2) — and the answer is the same: the outcome is known to God before the test, and the test is real anyway, because justice requires the deed to exist, not merely to be foreseen. The verse closes on the character of the Tester: Ever Gracious, Most Merciful to humanity — the sorting is severe, and the sorter is kind.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:144

> Indeed, We see you ˹O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven. Now We will make you turn towards a direction ˹of prayer˺ that will please you. So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque ˹in Mecca˺—wherever you are, turn your faces towards it. Those who were given the Scripture certainly know this to be the truth from their Lord. And Allah is never unaware of what they do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Face Lifted to Heaven, Seen and Answered**

The verse begins with an image unique in the Qur'an's legal passages: God watching the Prophet's face turn upward in longing. *We see you turning your face towards heaven* — the gesture of a man who hopes for a revelation he has not been given, who cannot ask in words for what he wants and so asks with his whole posture. And the answer matches the gesture: *Now We will make you turn towards a direction that will please you*. The phrasing is tender in a way legislative verses rarely are — the new qiblah is defined not first by its sanctity or its history but by the fact that it will please the one who hoped for it. The sequence teaches something about prophethood that the polemics around the qiblah had obscured: the Prophet does not legislate his preferences, but God attends to them, and when the preference is for God's House the answer comes as revelation rather than initiative.

**Why He Hoped**

The exegetes preserve several accounts of the hope behind the lifted face, and they compose rather than conflict. Al-Ṭabarī reports that the Jews of Medina were saying, "He follows us in our religion and uses our qiblah" — and the Prophet was displeased by their arrogance, not because the direction was wrong but because the boast made obedience look like discipleship to men. Al-Rāzī adds two further motives: love for the House of Abraham, the sanctuary his forefather in faith had built, and the hope that the Arab tribes would incline toward Islam if their ancestral sanctuary became the direction of prayer. On the origin of the Jerusalem orientation itself the sources differ: a few hold that the Prophet chose it on his own judgment to build a bond with Medina's Jewish population, while most maintain that he was instructed by God to face Jerusalem and then commanded to change. The majority reading is the stronger, because the verse's own logic — a divinely seen longing answered by a divinely decreed turn — presumes that both directions were decrees, and because the sūrah treats the earlier qiblah as something God assigned (2:143), not as a diplomatic choice.

**From Your Face to Your Faces**

The command moves in one verse from the singular to the plural: *turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque* — and then, *wherever you are, turn your faces towards it*. The first clause establishes the Prophet's own direction; the second universalizes it across the community and across geography. "Wherever you are" is deliberately unqualified: the command travels with the believer to every climate and coordinate, which is what made the qiblah a problem in spherical geometry rather than a local custom. The object is the Sacred Mosque — not merely the Kaʿbah's stone cube but the sanctuary around it, described in Āl ʿImrān as the first House of worship established for humanity at Bakkah, a blessed sanctuary and a guide for all people (3:96). The community is turned, in other words, toward the oldest house of God on earth — the House whose foundation Abraham and Ishmael raised, and whose claim to precedence the sūrah has already argued (2:127).

**A Command Given Before the Mosque Was Free**

One historical fact sharpens the verse: at the moment this command was revealed, the Sacred Mosque was in the hands of the very idolaters who had expelled the community — and would remain so for several more years, until the conquest of Mecca in the eighth year after the emigration. The believers were ordered to face a sanctuary they were barred from, held by enemies who had profaned it with idols. The command therefore functioned as prophecy and promise before it functioned as geography: to pray toward the Kaʿbah while the Kaʿbah was occupied was to enact the certainty that the House would return to those who faced it. The qiblah became a daily rehearsal of a future the community could not yet see, which is one reason the change could serve as the sorting test described in the previous verse — only those guided by Allah could keep praying toward a distant, occupied, promised direction.

**The People of the Book Know**

The verse then turns on the objectors with an assertion about their knowledge: *Those who were given the Scripture certainly know this to be the truth from their Lord*. Al-Ṭabarī explains the content of what they know: they know that Mecca is the true qiblah for this community — which means, in his reading, that they know the Prophet is right in his claims generally, so that their opposition to the change of direction is not a scholarly objection but one more instance of intransigence. The knowledge claim rests on the Islamic premise that the earlier scriptures carry descriptions of the coming prophet and his community, including the tokens of his mission. The verse does not argue the point here; it asserts it and moves to the closing clause. The assertion sets up the next verses, which will describe this same recognition in the simile of a father knowing his own children, and the concealment of it by a party among them.

**Never Unaware**

The verse ends with the passage's recurring signature: *And Allah is never unaware of what they do*. The clause answers the specific frustration embedded in the qiblah controversy. The objectors' weapon was speech — boasts, taunts, insinuations that the change of direction proved instability or hankering after homeland — and speech can be deniable, adjustable, aimed at different audiences. The closing clause withdraws that protection: the Speaker behind the revelation is tracking the doings behind the words. For the community the clause is the other kind of assurance, the one it needed when its prayers toward Jerusalem were questioned and its dead were worried over — nothing done in obedience is unseen, and the same surveillance that records the objectors' evil records the believers' turn. The verse thus completes the movement begun two verses earlier: the fools' question was answered theologically (the directions belong to God), the community's rank was declared (witnesses, middle, tested) — and now the longing of the Prophet is satisfied with a direction that will please him, a command binding on all his followers wherever they stand, and a warning to everyone who knows the truth and argues against it anyway.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:145

> Even if you were to bring every proof to the People of the Book, they would not accept your direction ˹of prayer˺, nor would you accept theirs; nor would any of them accept the direction ˹of prayer˺ of another. And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, then you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Evidence Has a Limit, and This Verse Names It**

The qiblah verses have so far argued: the directions belong to God, the change was a test, the new direction pleases the Prophet and the Scripture-people know it is true. This verse stops arguing and states a fact about the opponents that no further argument can alter: *even if you were to bring every proof*, they would not accept your direction. The conditional is maximal — every sign, every kind of evidence exhausted — and the refusal survives it. The sūrah of Jonah states the same law with its mechanism exposed: *"Indeed, those against whom Allah's decree ˹of torment˺ is justified will not believe—even if every sign were to come to them—until they see the painful punishment"* (10:96–97). The point is not that evidence is worthless; the qiblah passage is itself full of evidence. The point is that evidence persuades only where the will is open, and against a closed will the total argument and the partial argument produce the identical result. The verse liberates the community from the obligation of endless proof: there comes a term after which further demonstration changes nothing, and knowing that term saves the believer from mistaking every refusal for his own failure to argue well.

**The Qiblah as the Border of a Community**

The refusal is specifically about direction because direction is specifically about belonging. Jews traditionally face Jerusalem; Christian churches were historically oriented toward the east and the rising sun; and to face a community's qiblah is to be inside it, while to face another's is to be outside. The commentators draw the consequence bluntly: to say that someone follows a different qiblah is tantamount to excluding him from the religious community in question. The qiblah is thus not one ritual detail among many but the community's spatial signature — the bodily form of its creed. This is why the verse treats the three directions as mutually impossible rather than negotiable: *nor would you accept theirs; nor would any of them accept the direction of another*. There is no shared direction and no compromise bearing, because a direction adopted by negotiation would belong to no one's faith. The incompatibility stated here is not a lament but a clarification of what was never on the table.

**Facing Our Qiblah, Praying Our Prayer**

The identity function of the direction was fixed in the community's own law by a report preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (393). Maymūn ibn Siyāh asked Anas ibn Mālik what makes a person's life and property sacred, and Anas answered with the Prophet's words: whoever says none has the right to be worshipped but Allah, faces our qiblah, prays our prayer, and eats our slaughtered animal — that person is a Muslim, and has the same rights and obligations as other Muslims. Three marks, and one of them is the direction of prayer: the confession of the tongue, the orientation of the body in worship, and the shared table of what is slaughtered in God's name. The ḥadīth shows what the verse's incompatibility means in practice — the qiblah is a constitutive marker of the community's boundary, so accepting another community's direction would not be a gesture of goodwill but an act of defection from the creed's visible form.

**Desires Against Knowledge**

The verse's second half shifts from the opponents to the Prophet — and through him, as always with such addresses, to the community: *if you were to follow their desires after all the knowledge that has come to you, you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers*. The two terms are chosen to be exact opposites. *Ahwāʾ* — desires, caprices, whims — is the plural of a word denoting what the soul inclines to without warrant; *knowledge* is what arrives from God with warrant. The religious life, on this verse's schema, is governed by one or the other, and there is no tertium: a direction of prayer is either received as knowledge or adopted as desire. The same warning brackets this section of the sūrah from its start — *if you were to follow their desires after all the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against Allah* (2:120) — and recurs in the Medinan sūrahs with the same architecture: do not follow their desires over the truth that has come to you (5:48); if you followed their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, none would protect you from Allah (13:37). The repetition marks a standing danger rather than a historical one: the pull toward the opponents' ways does not cease when the argument is won.

**The Severity of the Address**

That the warning is addressed to the Prophet — who would never follow their desires — has a double function the exegetes recognized. It states the law at its maximum severity: if even the recipient of the knowledge would become one of the wrongdoers by trading it for desire, the calculation for anyone holding less knowledge is correspondingly bleaker. And it protects the community's future by putting the principle beyond personal exemption: no one's spiritual rank insulates him from the category. The wording refuses mitigation — *you would certainly be one of the wrongdoers*, not "you would be excused" or "you would err slightly." Knowledge, in this economy, is not credit but responsibility; the more clearly the direction has been shown, the graver the wrong of turning from it toward what merely feels agreeable. The verse thus completes the qiblah's moral: the direction was assigned by God, it is known by the Scripture-people to be true, it will not be accepted by those who refuse, and for those who have accepted it there is no legitimate road back — only knowledge followed, or desire obeyed and the name of wrongdoer earned.

**No Middle Direction Exists**

Read as a whole, the verse closes a door that the controversy might otherwise have left ajar: the door of the negotiated middle. Since each community's direction is its boundary, and since the boundaries are divinely assigned rather than humanly chosen, no ecumenical compromise-bearing is available — neither a physical direction between Jerusalem and Mecca nor a theological averaging of the creeds that face them. The community's task is not convergence toward a shared center but faithfulness to its own revealed orientation, coupled with the race in good deeds that the passage will soon command. This is the verse's practical legacy for interreligious life as the Qur'an frames it: honest incompatibility at the level of the boundary, and competition in virtue at the level of conduct — never a faked agreement about direction, because a faked direction would be desire wearing the clothes of knowledge.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:146

> Those We have given the Scripture recognize this ˹Prophet˺ as they recognize their own children. Yet a group of them hides the truth knowingly.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Simile Taken From the Certainties of Blood**

The verse describes the knowledge of the Scripture-people with the strongest simile available in human experience: they recognize it — or him — *as they recognize their own children*. The comparison is chosen for its epistemic quality, not its warmth. A father among many children does not infer which is his; he knows by a familiarity that precedes argument, that survives any stranger's contradiction, that he could not be talked out of even if he wanted to. The recognition the verse attributes to the learned among the People of the Book is of that order — immediate, intimate, unmistakable. This is not the tentative conclusion of an investigation but the settled knowledge of long acquaintance: they have handled the descriptions in their own scriptures the way a parent has handled his child, and the features match. The simile simultaneously honors and convicts: it honors their knowledge by calling it certain, and it convicts their silence by making that certainty undeniable even to themselves.

**What Is Recognized: the Direction or the Man**

The exegetes divided over the object of the recognition. Al-Ṭabarī read it as the truth of the Kaʿbah's qiblah, following the previous verse's assertion that those given the Scripture know the new direction to be the truth from their Lord. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī read it as recognition of the Prophet himself — known through the prophecies in the Bible, and known further by his presence, his character, the signs he brought, and the truth of his message. The second reading subsumes the first: recognition of the qiblah's truth depends on recognition of the Prophet's truthfulness, since Jerusalem had been a legitimate direction for a time by his own practice, and nothing about the Kaʿbah's stones compels assent apart from the authority of the one who turns the community toward it. The translation's insertion of "this Prophet" follows that logic. Either way the verse's charge is unaffected: the knowledge exists, it is child-certain, and it is being managed.

**The Same Recognition, Stated Twice More**

The Qur'an returns to this claim with variations that confirm its centrality. The sūrah of the Cattle states it almost identically and draws the darker conclusion: *"Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize him ˹to be a true prophet˺ as they recognize their own children. Those who have ruined themselves will never believe"* (6:20) — recognition that does not issue in faith is self-ruin, not a neutral state. The sūrah of the Heights locates the recognition textually: the followers of the unlettered Prophet are *"the ones whose description they find in their Torah and the Gospel"* (7:157). The three verses together give the claim its full structure: the recognition is in the books they carry (7:157), it operates in their minds with parental certainty (2:146), and its rejection is a spiritual catastrophe rather than an honest error (6:20).
