The Shāfiʿī school read the saʿy as a *rukn* — an indispensable component — of the pilgrimage, without which the ḥajj is incomplete; the Ḥanafī school read it as recommended rather than obligatory, the removal-of-blame phrasing suggesting permission more than requirement. The dispute is textual and honest: a verse that says "no blame" can legislate or can merely license. Those who made it a pillar cited a prophetic report directing the pilgrims to perform the crossing, on the ground that God has prescribed this running — and in practice the question never divided the community's performance: adherents of all schools perform the saʿy, so the disagreement lives in the books while the hills carry the same traffic. The case is a good specimen of how Quranic legislation works through the tradition: the verse sets the rite inside the symbols of God, and the Sunnah supplies the operating detail.

**The Lesser Pilgrimage and the Volunteer**

The verse legislates for two journeys at once: the *ḥajj*, the pilgrimage of the appointed days, and the *ʿumrah*, the lesser visit performable at any other time of year. The ʿumrah contains a shortened set of the ḥajj's elements — entering the state of consecration (*iḥrām*) in the two cloths, circling the House, and crossing between the two hills — and most scholars, especially those who hold the saʿy obligatory, read the verse's closing clause, *whoever does good willingly*, as a reference to it: the ʿumrah is the volunteered good, since it is not an obligatory rite like the ḥajj. The reading gives the sentence its point — beyond the required, there is the willing, and the willing is not left unrewarded. The hills thus stand over two economies at once: the obligation every pilgrim owes and the supererogation every lover adds, one rite serving both the debtor and the devotee.

**Appreciative and Knowing**

The verse closes with two names aimed at the volunteer: *Allah is truly Appreciative, All-Knowing*. *Shakūr* — Appreciative — is God described in the language of gratitude: the One who accepts the small and returns the large, who treats the willing extra as a debt He has chosen to owe. Paired with *ʿAlīm*, All-Knowing, the name covers the unseen portion of voluntary good — the ʿumrah performed when no one knew, the crossing of the hills done in exhaustion, the intention hidden inside the act. The Appreciative does not need the act publicized, and the Knowing cannot miss it. The two names together answer the verse's occasion one final time: the Companions who hesitated over the hills were worried how their rite would be *regarded* — by custom, by scruple, by the memory of idols. The verse ends by relocating the regard: the audience of the saʿy is the Appreciative, the All-Knowing, and in that audience a willingly done good is never lost.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:159

> Those who hide the clear proofs and guidance that We have revealed— after We made it clear for humanity in the Book—will be condemned by Allah and ˹all˺ those who condemn.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Crime the Passage Returns To**

The sūrah has named this crime before — hiding the truth knowingly (2:42), hiding the testimony received from Allah (2:140), the group that recognizes the Prophet as a father recognizes his child and conceals anyway (2:146) — and now it returns to it with the full weight of a formal sentence. The elements are stated in order: the thing hidden (*clear proofs and guidance*), its origin (*that We have revealed*), the aggravating circumstance (*after We made it clear for humanity in the Book*), and the penalty (*condemned by Allah and all those who condemn*). The aggravating circumstance is what makes the crime what it is. Concealing something obscure is a failing; concealing something God Himself clarified — published, made plain, written down for humanity in the Book — is an act against the clarity itself. The concealers are not withholding a secret they possess; they are fighting a disclosure God has already made, and the verse treats the fight as the essence of the offense.

**General Crime or Historical Case**

Al-Rāzī weighed two readings of the verse's scope and the tradition preserves both. The general reading: it is sinful for any person to obscure a truth of religion — the scholar who hides a ruling, the teacher who softens a doctrine for comfort, the witness who stays silent when his silence misleads. The historical reading: the verse addresses the People of the Book around the Prophet, and specifically the occasion when Muslims asked a group among them to point out the description of the coming prophet written in their own Book, and they refused. Al-Ṭabarī adds a third shade: the concealment of the truth of Islam itself — undercutting it, calling it false, failing to make known the foretelling of the Prophet that their scriptures contain. The readings are not rivals; the historical case is the general crime's first and fullest instance. The verse is revealed about a specific refusal and legislates about a category, which is how the Qur'an's occasions of revelation typically work: the event is the case law, the wording is the statute.

**Condemned by Allah**

The penalty begins with the divine condemnation — *yalʿanuhumu Allāh* — and the curse in Quranic usage has a fixed meaning the exegetes state plainly: being distanced from God and driven away from His mercy. The curse is not a wish of harm but an exclusion of closeness; the one cursed is placed outside the radius in which mercy operates. That the sentence opens with God's own curse sets its scale — no human condemnation can add to it and no human acquittal can subtract from it. The concealment was an act against guidance, which is mercy's road; the penalty is therefore the withdrawal of exactly what was fought. The symmetry is exact in a way the verse leaves unargued: the hider of mercy's directions is hidden from mercy. What makes the sentence dreadful is not pain but distance — the curse of this verse is the same state the Qur'an elsewhere describes as God not speaking to them on the Day nor purifying them (2:174), the administrative silence of heaven toward those who administered silence on earth.

**And by All Who Condemn**

The second half of the penalty widens the condemning court to everything able to curse. The exegetes identified the *cursers* in three candidate bodies. Some said the beasts of the earth — the animals who are deprived of rain and provision because of the sins of men, and who feel the weight of the concealers' crime in their own skins. Others said the angels and the believers, whose curse is their invocation of God's curse upon those He has cursed — the reading that 2:161 makes explicit, where the curse of God, the angels, and mankind all together falls on those who die disbelieving. Al-Rāzī added the denizens of Hell, who will curse the concealers for misleading them into the same fire. The three readings compose into a single picture: a verdict ratified across creation — by the creatures who suffer its consequences, by the beings who know its falsity, and by the damned who followed it. No concealment is private; every hidden truth has downstream victims, and the verse gives them all a voice in the sentence.

**The Fellowship of the Concealers**

The verse belongs to a family the Qur'an returns to whenever religious knowledge is traded or buried. Those who hide what Allah revealed, trading it for a fleeting gain, *"consume nothing but fire into their bellies"* (2:174) — the concealed truth becomes the fuel of the concealer. The covenant of the Scripture-people to make the Book known and not hide it was answered by casting it behind their backs and trading it for a miserable profit (3:187) — concealment as covenant-breaking, with an ancient signature on the promise. And the Messenger's arrival is described as *"revealing much of what you have hidden of the Scriptures"* (5:15) — the prophetic mission itself framed partly as an un-concealment, a forced disclosure of what was buried. Read with these, 2:159 is not an isolated threat but one station in a sustained campaign: revelation discloses, some hide what was disclosed, the hiding is cursed from every side, and a later prophet uncovers it again. The clarity God made in the Book is fought, but it is never defeated.

**Why Concealment Draws the Widest Curse**

Among the sins the sūrah names, few draw a curse of this breadth, and the reason is structural: other sins damage their doer and their immediate victims, but the concealment of guidance attacks the means by which any victim could be saved. The murderer kills one body; the concealer of the proofs endangers every soul that needed the hidden truth to find its way. Knowledge in the Qur'an's economy is a trust held for others — the scholar holds what the seeker cannot reach alone, and the holding is a stewardship, not a possession. This is why the penalty is communal in its prosecution: creation, angels, believers, and the damned all have standing in the case, because all were downstream of the concealed stream. And it is why the very next verse opens a door — the exception of repentance — whose conditions will match the crime: the public harm must be publicly undone.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:160

> As for those who repent, mend their ways, and let the truth be known, they are the ones to whom I will turn ˹in forgiveness˺, for I am the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Exception That Reopens Every Case**

The curse of the previous verse was total — God and all who curse — and this verse begins with the word that keeps totality from meaning finality: *except*. The concealers are cursed; the concealers who turn are received. The exception is not an afterthought softening a harsh rule; it is the rule's designed horizon, placed one verse away so that no reader can encounter the curse without meeting the door beside it. The sūrah's whole treatment of sin runs on this pattern — the offense stated at full severity, the return opened at full width — and here the pattern governs the very crime the passage cares most about, the hiding of guidance. Even that is forgivable. Even the war against clarity can be ended by the one who waged it. The verse's position teaches the community how to hold its own condemnations: nothing said against a sin may be said in a way that closes repentance from it, because God Himself pronounced the curse and Himself attached the exception.

**Three Movements, Not One**

The exception is conditioned, and the conditions are three: they repent, they mend, they clarify. The first is the turn itself — *tābū*, the heart's reversal of direction. The second, *aṣlaḥū*, carries the sense of putting things right, repairing what the sin damaged: the amended life, the restored practice, the corrected habit. The third is specific to this crime and is what gives the verse its jurisprudence: *bayyanū* — they make clear, they address and declare the very truth they had concealed. Al-Ṭabarī's explanation is exact: the repentant concealers must publish what they suppressed. The three conditions map onto the sin's three dimensions — the inward turn answers the intention, the mending answers the behavior, the clarification answers the public harm. A concealment is not undone privately, because it was not committed privately: it operated on other people's knowledge, and its repair must operate there too. The verse thereby establishes a principle larger than its case: repentance must match the injury. Stolen wealth is repaid; hidden truth is announced; the returning sinner retraces the exact road of his sin, undoing it step by step.

**One Root, Two Directions**

The verse's grammar enacts its theology in a single root. "They repent" and "I will turn to them in forgiveness" translate the same verb — *tāba* — turned by its prepositions: the servant turns *to* God (*tāba ilā*), and God turns *upon* the servant with acceptance (*tāba ʿalā*). The reciprocity is in the word itself: the movement of return is one motion with two ends, and the divine end is what makes the human end possible. The sūrah showed the mechanism at humanity's first sin: *"Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord, so He accepted his repentance"* (2:37) — the words themselves given before the asking. The same verse names God *Tawwāb* — the Accepter of Repentance, in the intensive form that denotes repeated, habitual, overflowing acceptance: not one who accepts once, reluctantly, but one whose nature is to keep accepting. The legal verses of the sūrah of the Women frame the boundaries — repentance accepted for those who sin ignorantly and turn soon after (4:17), and the question that makes despair illogical: *"Why should Allah punish you if you are grateful and faithful?"* (4:147) — but it is this verse's intensive Name that carries the whole doctrine: the door is not merely open; the Doorkeeper is described as leaning toward it.

**The First Person of Acceptance**

The verse shifts suddenly into the divine first person: *they are the ones to whom I will turn, for I am the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful*. The surrounding passage speaks of God in the third person or the majestic plural — We revealed, We made clear; cursed by Allah. Here the acceptance is personalized: *I*. The shift is the verse's tenderness. A curse pronounced in the third person can be heard as a verdict of the system; forgiveness spoken in the first person can only be heard as the welcome of a Person. The sinner returning from concealment does not re-enter a mechanism but meets a Speaker, and the Speaker names Himself twice in the same breath — Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful — as if the return needed two guarantees rather than one. The pairing also orders the gifts: the *tawbah* accepts the turning, the *raḥmah* covers what the turning cannot repair, since no clarification fully un-rings the years a truth stayed hidden. Acceptance handles the crime; mercy handles the residue.

**Against Despair, Against Presumption**

The verse stands between two errors the tradition policed with it. Despair: the concealer who reasons that his sin was against clarity itself, that he fought God's disclosure, and that such a case admits no pardon — the verse answers that the worst category of hiding is inside the exception. Presumption: the concealer who reasons that since God is the Accepter of Repentance, his private sorrow suffices and his published lie may stand — the verse answers with the third condition, which is precisely the one presumption refuses. True repentance from concealment costs the concealer his audience's revised opinion of him; he must stand before the same people he misled and say, what I hid was this. The cost explains why the three conditions are inseparable: a turn without mending is emotion, mending without clarification is self-improvement, and only the three together are the tawbah this verse accepts. God's first-person promise is then waiting at the end of all three — *I will turn* — the intensive Accepter meeting the completed return, and mercy absorbing the rest.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:161

> Surely those who disbelieve and die as disbelievers are condemned by Allah, the angels, and all of humanity.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Conditions and the Closed Door**

The verse states its subject with two joined conditions: those who disbelieve, *and die* as disbelievers. The second condition is what gives the verse its finality — and its justice. Disbelief alone, held by a living person, stands under the exception of the previous verse as long as breath remains; the door of repentance closes at death, not at sin. The sūrah will state the closure explicitly in its law of repentance: the return is not accepted from those who go on doing evil until death approaches (4:18), and the whole economy of 2:159–160 assumed a living audience. What this verse describes is the completed case — rejection carried through the whole span allotted for reconsideration and delivered, unrepented, to the far side. The conjunction of the two conditions also identifies the verse's true subject: not the disbeliever as a category of people walking the earth, but the fixed outcome of a life whose direction never turned. The community reading it is being shown the terminus of the road it was just offered the exit from.

**The Curse of God**

The penalty repeats the curse of 2:159 and completes its definition: *upon them is the curse of Allah* — the distance from His mercy made permanent. In the earlier verse the curse fell on an act, the hiding of clear proofs; here it falls on a settled state, disbelief consummated by death. The exegetes' definition governs both: to be cursed is to be driven away from God and excluded from His mercy. The permanence is new. A curse on an act can be lifted by the act's undoing — the repentance that clarifies — but a curse on a completed life has nothing left to undo it with; the material of repentance is time, and the verse's subjects have spent theirs. This is why the passage ordered the verses as it did: the act cursed (159), the door opened (160), the closed case sentenced (161). A reader who meets 161 without 160 will hear despair; a reader who meets both will hear the exact boundary — mercy is infinite in width and finite in duration, wide as any sin, long as any life.

**The Angels and the Curse They Voice**

The second curser is the angels. Al-Ṭabarī explains the sense: the curse of the angels and the believers is their invocation of God's curse upon those God has cursed — creatures ratifying the verdict of their Lord, echoing in the unseen what He has pronounced in the seen. The angels' participation is not additive to the divine curse but expressive of the order it establishes: the beings nearest the Throne, who know what the concealers and disbelievers refused to acknowledge, are aligned against the refusal. The sūrah of the Confederates states the same alignment in a curse-verse of its own — God curses the disbelievers and prepares for them a Blaze, and the angels' testimony belongs to that economy. A person rejected by heaven's court is not facing a private divine displeasure but a settled disposition of the entire unseen world, in which every conscious being that knows the truth he denied stands where the truth stands.

**All of Humanity**

The third curser is *al-nās* — mankind, all together — and al-Rāzī worked through its possible scopes with care. It may mean all people in the plain sense: humanity's collective verdict against the settled denier of its Lord. It may mean some people, since the definite plural in the Qur'an often covers a part. And it may mean something sharper: one's own allies and the people one misled, cursing him in the Hereafter for the misguidance he spread — the followers disowning the followed, the scene this same passage will stage two groups of verses later. Al-Rāzī's synthesis gathers the readings: since all human beings curse what is intrinsically vile, those who die disbelieving come to bear the curse of all in one way or another — directly from the righteous, retrospectively from the misled, universally from anyone who sees the case as it is. The verse that began with heaven's curse ends with earth's, and between them nothing stands for the cursed one: not God, not the angels, not mankind.

**A Verdict for the Hereafter, Not a License for the World**

Al-Qurṭubī drew a boundary around the verse that the tradition took seriously: the curse it describes belongs exclusively to the Hereafter. His reasoning was functional — a curse is a kind of prodding away from disbelief, a communication of disapproval meant to move its object; it is of no use directed at someone dead or insane, who cannot be moved by anything. The verse therefore describes what awaits, not what believers should perform; it is eschatology, not a command to action in this world. He grounded the limit in prophetic practice: the Prophet forbade cursing a person undergoing a legal punishment or one who had sincerely repented — a curse is leveled only at a state deserving of it, and one does not heap insult on a man already under sentence or already returned. The sūrah of the Spider supplies the Hereafter scene the verse points to: on the Day of Resurrection the allies of falsehood *"will disown and curse one another"* (29:25). The discipline this produces is precise: the believer may know that God's curse rests on settled rejection without being licensed to curse the living, among whom the door of 2:160 stands open until the last breath.

**The Full Range in Four Verses**

Read in its sequence, this verse completes a moral map drawn with unusual care. The crime: hiding what God clarified, cursed by God and every curser (159). The exception: repentance, mending, and disclosure, met by God's first-person acceptance (160). The closed case: disbelief carried through death, cursed by God, the angels, and mankind together (161). And in the next verse the sentence executed — abiding, unalleviated, unrespired (162). The map's two poles are separated by a single hinge, and the hinge is a life: while it lasts, the curse of 159 is escapable through 160; when it ends in rejection, the curse of 161 is total. The verses give no third region, no partial damnation for partial belief, no posthumous appeal. The clarity is itself a mercy — the boundary is published in advance, from every pulpit of the passage, so that no one can say at the end that the two outcomes were not shown side by side while there was still time to walk between them.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:162

> They will be in Hell forever. Their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be delayed ˹from it˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sentence in Three Clauses**

The verse executes the curse of its predecessor in three flat statements: abiding in the Fire, no lightening of the punishment, no respite from it. There is no rhetoric in the verse and no narrative — the sūrah has moved from description to sentence, and sentences are delivered in clauses. The first fixes duration: *khālidūn fīhā*, abiders in it, dwellers with no term. The second fixes intensity: the punishment will not be lightened — no mitigation, no anesthesia, no interval of relief inside the sentence. The third fixes execution: nor will they be delayed — no postponement, no stay, no gap between the verdict and its landing. Together the three clauses close every avenue a prisoner of any court scans for: an end date, a commutation, a delay. The verse's power is that it closes all three in eleven words and moves on, the way the next verses will move on to the creed that all this sentence exists to vindicate.

**A Formula the Qur'an Repeats**

The middle clause is a fixed formula, and its recurrence is deliberate. The traders of the Hereafter for this world: *"their punishment will not be reduced, nor will they be helped"* (2:86). The cursed of Āl ʿImrān, in wording identical to this verse: *"They will be in Hell forever. Their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be delayed"* (3:88). The wrongdoers of the Bee, when the punishment comes: *"it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be delayed"* (16:85). The disbelievers of the Originator, with the harshest addition: in the Fire *"they will not be ˹allowed to be˺ finished by death, nor will its torment be lightened for them"* (35:36) — and the sūrah of Ornament repeats the same pairing at 43:75. The repetition is not redundancy but jurisprudence: the same verdict stated in the same words across sūrahs establishes that this is one settled ruling, not a local threat. When the Qur'an sentences, it sentences identically everywhere, and the identical wording across Meccan and Medinan revelation marks the ruling as constitutional.

**Abiding: The Question the Tradition Argued**

The first clause — forever — carries the heaviest theology, and the classical tradition argued it rather than merely asserting it. The sūrah had already met the rival claim in its early verses: the assertion by some among the Scripture-people that the Fire would touch them only for numbered days (2:80), an assertion the sūrah answered by demanding their proof. On the other side stood philosophical speculations, some tracing to early voices, that the Fire's torment might eventually exhaust itself or that its inhabitants might cease. The exegetes answered from the text's own machinery: al-Ṭabarī argued from the verse of regret a few verses ahead — the disbelievers' wish to return will not remove them from the Fire (2:167), and a wish that never ceases marks a state that never ends; the abiding-verses state their duration without exception, and the exceptions the Qur'an does contain ("except as your Lord wills," 11:107) were read by the mainstream as covering the disobedient believers who exit, not the settled disbelievers who do not. The mainstream position held: for those who die in rejection, the Fire is without term. The argument's shape matters as much as its conclusion — the tradition treated the duration of Hell as a question answerable from revelation's grammar, and this verse is the grammatical anchor: *khālidūn*, abiders, a participle with no clock attached.

**No Lightening: The End of Hope's Arithmetic**

The second clause deserves precision, because lightening is what suffering naturally hopes for. The punished do not first hope for release — release is unimaginable from inside a sentence of abiding; they hope for reduction, a lighter day, a numb hour. The verse closes that hope first, before it can form. And 35:36 closes its back door: they will not be finished by death — the one release every sufferer retains, the body's collapse, is withdrawn, so that the capacity to suffer is maintained at full strength inside a punishment never lightened. What remains, in the Quranic scenes, is only the wish of 2:167 — the second chance that will not come — and the conversations of the Fire's inmates cursing one another (7:38–39), speech without remedy. The clause is thus the cruelest of the three by mercy's own logic: hope exists to be answered or abandoned, and a punishment defined as unlightenable leaves its subjects the single dignity of knowing their case exactly, which is what the verse, by stating it plainly here, extends to every reader while there is still a verse like 2:160 to act on.

**No Respite: The Term Expired**

The third clause — nor will they be delayed — uses the language of respite, *yunẓarūn*, from the same root as the respite granted to Iblīs at humanity's first temptation: delayed until the appointed Day. The contrast is the verse's hidden argument. The whole drama of this world runs on delay — the sinner respited, the tyrant's rope lengthened, the test administered across a lifetime of granted time. Respite is the world's constitution; its withdrawal is the Hereafter's. The Day of Judgment is elsewhere called the Day on which no soul can avail another and no intercession is accepted, and the delay that structured probation ends at its door. Those described in this verse spent their respite as the previous verses described — hiding the proofs, dying in rejection — and the sentence now states the consequence in the respite's own vocabulary: the time granted is used up, and what was delayed *for* them is delayed *from* them no longer. The punishment arrives at the exact moment the probation ends, with nothing between.

**Why the Severity Sits Beside the Creed**

The verse's placement is part of its meaning. It closes a four-verse sequence that opened with the curse on concealment and passed through the open door of repentance; and two verses later the sūrah will state, in the calmest sentence imaginable, *your God is one God* (2:163), followed by the seven signs of creation and the analysis of love. The severity and the creed are not juxtaposed by accident. The unlightened, undelayed, endless sentence is what is at stake in the confession — the Fire is the cost of the wrong answer to the question 2:163 asks, and the passage wants the reader to feel the weight of the question before it is posed. This is the Qur'an's standard architecture of ultimacy: mercy and wrath stated at full strength, neither diluted by the other, both real, both published, with the door of repentance standing open between them for as long as the reader has breath. The eleven words of this verse are the wall behind the door — and the door, in the previous verse, was described in the first person of God.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:163

> Your God is ˹only˺ One God. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Creed Between the Curse and the Signs**

After four verses of curse, exception, and sentence, the sūrah stops and states the ground of everything it has just legislated and threatened: *your God is one God*. The placement is architectural. The concealment that drew the curse, the repentance that opened the door, the abiding that closed the case — all of it presupposes an answer to the question of who God is and how many there are, and the passage now supplies the answer in the shortest complete creed the Qur'an contains. The verse reads like the still point of the section: no narrative, no occasion, no addressee beyond the possessive *your* — just the statement itself, delivered after the fires have been described so that the reader understands what the statement is worth. A creed recited in comfort is a formula; a creed recited between the curse and the signs is a position taken with full knowledge of both consequences.

**Ilāh, Not Allāh: The Grammar of the Claim**

The verse's wording was noted closely by the exegetes for a grammatical reason with theological consequences: in all three of its mentions of deity, the word used is *ilāh* — the common noun for a god, a divinity, anything worshipped — rather than *Allāh*, the supreme personal Name. *Your ilāh is one ilāh; there is no ilāh except Him.* The choice enacts the argument. To say "Allah is one" could be heard as a claim about one deity among others, a tribal statement about the God of the Arabs or of Abraham's line. To say "no *ilāh* except Him" is to sweep the entire category of the divine — every object any people has ever worshipped or could worship — and then to empty it, leaving one. The negation of the generic noun is what makes the confession exhaustive: it does not rank Allah above other gods; it denies that the other gods exist as gods at all. The Name that remains after the category is emptied is referred to by pronoun — *except Him* — the personal standing where the categorical ended.

**Wāḥid: One in a Sense That Excludes Parts**

Al-Ṭabarī unpacked the word for one — *wāḥid* — as carrying more than arithmetic: the unique, the one not made up of parts, the one without equal or like. Each of the three senses does separate work. Unique: there is no second of His kind, so no comparison between Him and anything is comparison between peers. Without parts: He is not composite, not divisible, not assembled — which excludes every genealogy of the gods, every pantheon's family tree, every theology that makes divinity a substance shared out among persons or emanations. Without equal or like: nothing in existence answers to Him as a counterpart, which is why the sūrah's later Throne verse will ask, rhetorically, whether any names or beings can be produced as His partners. The oneness confessed here is therefore dense — numerical, structural, and comparative at once — and the Qur'an's shortest sūrah will spend four verses restating exactly these three: One and Indivisible, the Sustainer needed by all, never begetting nor begotten, and with none comparable to Him (112:1–4). This verse is that sūrah in miniature, embedded in the middle of the longest one.

**The Two Mercies at the End**

The creed closes with two names: *al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm* — the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. Their position after the severity of the preceding verses is the verse's pastoral genius. The confession could have ended with power — the One is also the Omnipotent, and the curse-verses had just displayed His authority. Instead the defining attributes appended to the oneness are the two intensives of mercy: *Raḥmān*, mercy as a total disposition, vast and encompassing; *Raḥīm*, mercy as an act, particular and repeated. The effect on the creed is decisive: the God whose oneness is confessed is not a bare unity but a unity whose innermost published character is compassion. The sinner who passed through 2:160's first-person acceptance arrives here to find that acceptance built into the Name; the reader who flinched at 2:162's unlightened punishment learns that the sentence flowed from a mercy that was refused to its limit, not from a deity indifferent to its subjects. Monotheism in this verse is not only the claim that God is one; it is the claim about what the One is like — and the like is mercy wearing two intensities.

**Among the Most Recited of Verses**

The tradition recognized the verse's density by its use: it stands among the most often recited verses of the Qur'an, quoted in prayer, in dhikr, and on the lips of the dying. Its confession has a history of confrontation attached to it. The sūrah of the Ranks records the other reception of the same sentence: *"For whenever it was said to them ˹in the world˺, 'There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Allah,' they acted arrogantly"* (37:35) — the creed that this verse states in calm is the creed whose first hearing provoked the Meccan elite's scorn, because its exclusivity dethroned every ancestral god at once. The two verses frame the confession's worldly fate: accepted by the believers as the summary of everything, refused by the arrogant as an intolerable narrowing. And within this sūrah the creed looks forward as well — to the Throne verse, which will open with the same formula of divinity and build the whole architecture of God's knowledge and power upon it, and to the seven signs of the verse that follows immediately, which will exhibit the one God's handwriting across creation, from the alternation of night and day to the clouds held between the sky and the earth.

**The Axis of the Sūrah**

This verse is the pivot on which the sūrah's argument turns. Everything before it has been preparing a people — the creed confessed (2:136), the dyeing of God (2:138), the disengagement from disputes about Him (2:139), the truth from the Lord (2:147) — and everything after it will be demonstrating the confession: the signs in creation (2:164), the analysis of love and its misplacements (2:165), the food laws that protect the confession from inherited falsehood (2:168–173), the legislative arc running to the Throne verse and beyond. The curse-verses, for their part, now read as the confession's negative space: what happens to those who hide it, die against it, and are sentenced under it. A single sentence — your God is one God, no god but Him, the Compassionate, the Merciful — is thus the thesis the sūrah spends its length defending, illustrating, and legislating around. The reader who holds this verse holds the key to every section that follows, because every section that follows is either a proof of the oneness, a consequence of it, or a law for those who confess it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:164

> Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth; the alternation of the day and the night; the ships that sail the sea for the benefit of humanity; the rain sent down by Allah from the skies, reviving the earth after its death; the scattering of all kinds of creatures throughout; the shifting of the winds; and the clouds drifting between the heavens and the earth—˹in all of this˺ are surely signs for people of understanding.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Seven Signatures on One Page**

The verse that follows the confession of the one God exhibits His handwriting, and it does so as a list — seven items, gathered under one verdict. The creation of the heavens and the earth; the alternation of day and night; the ships that sail the sea with what benefits mankind; the water sent from the sky reviving the earth after its death and scattering every kind of creature in it; the shifting winds; the clouds held in service between sky and earth. The list is the Qur'an's characteristic method of proof: not syllogism but inventory. Each item is public, daily, and free of charge to observe; none requires initiation or literacy; all are visible to the Bedouin and the sailor alike. The verdict that closes the inventory — *surely signs for people of understanding* — assigns the seven not as decoration but as evidence, each one an *āyah*, a sign in the same word the Qur'an uses for its own verses. Creation is thus a second scripture read with the same faculty as the first, and the confession of 2:163 is its conclusion stated in advance.

**The Occasion: A Sign Demanded, Seven Given**

Al-Ṭabarī preserves the challenge behind the verse. Some among the idolaters demanded a sign — asking, in one report, that the hill of Ṣafā be turned to gold; and others asked, in astonishment at monotheism, how a single God could encompass the concern of all mankind. The verse is the answer to both. To the demand for a spectacular sign it responds by naming seven signs already installed, older than the demand and larger than any miracle of the sort requested: a golden hill would be one strange object, while the rain that revives the dead earth is a standing resurrection performed annually over the whole planet. To the astonishment at one God managing all people it responds by exhibiting a creation in which one system already manages everything — the same winds and clouds and rains serving every latitude at once, the alternation of day and night running on schedule across all longitudes. The management the questioners doubted is the management they live inside. The requested sign was refused because the refuse would have been smaller than the grant.

**The Ships: The Only Made Thing in the List**

Among the seven, the ships stand out for a reason the commentators mark: they are the only human-made items — and their inclusion deepens rather than dilutes the list. A ship is human craft at its most audacious, a constructed thing entrusted to an element that can swallow it; the very possibility of seafaring, and its permanent precariousness, is a reminder of God. The Qur'an returns to the ship as a sign across its whole length — the Lord *"Who steers the ships for you through the sea, so that you may seek His bounty"* (17:66); the ships sailing *"smoothly through the sea by the grace of Allah so that He may show you some of His signs"* (31:31) — and it uses the sea for its sharpest psychology of belief: aboard a storm-buffeted ship, the same people who associate partners on shore cry out to God alone in sincere devotion (29:65), and when the waves come over them like mountains their devotion is total, until deliverance lands them back in shirk (31:32). The ship in this verse is therefore a double sign — of the ingenuity granted to humanity and of the fragility that keeps that ingenuity honest. The sailor knows what the land-dweller forgets: how thin the floor of human competence is, and what lies beneath it.

**A Series the Qur'an Keeps Repeating**

The seven signs are not a one-off catalogue; they are elements of a series the Qur'an assembles again and again. The alternation of night and day appears with the creation of the heavens and earth in Āl ʿImrān's great sign-verse (3:190) and in Jonah (10:6); the revival of the earth after its death recurs in the Bee (16:65), the Spider (29:63), the Romans (30:19), the Originator (35:9), and the Kneeling (45:5); the ships appear in at least seven sūrahs. The sūrah of the Romans gathers a comparable series in a single passage (30:20–27), and the Kneeling's version ends, like this one, on the shifting winds and the provision sent down. The repetition has a purpose: the signs are being taught as a curriculum rather than cited as a proof-text, returned to until the reader's ordinary day — morning, weather, harbor, harvest — is reorganized around them. A sign seen once is an argument; a sign the Book keeps pointing at becomes a habit of sight, and the habit is what the phrase *people of understanding* names.

**Winds, Clouds, and the Language of Service**

Two of the seven signs are meteorological, and both are described in the Qur'an's vocabulary of subjection. The winds are *shifted* — turned, dispatched, varied — and the Qur'an elsewhere names them among God's blessings and messengers (7:57, 15:22, 25:48, 27:63, 30:46); the exegetes also noted the root-kinship of *rīḥ*, wind, and *rūḥ*, spirit, both carrying the sense of breath and life in motion. The clouds are *subdued* — held in service between the heaven and the earth, neither collapsing down nor dispersing up, suspended in the one region where rain can reach the living. The same vocabulary of subjection (*taskhīr*) runs through the Qur'an for everything pressed into human service — the sea, the night and day, the sun and moon. The theological claim inside the imagery is precise: the weather is not a wild force tolerated by civilization but a conscripted workforce, its shifts assigned by the One whose unity the previous verse confessed. The person who reads the sky as machinery reads only half the sign; the sky is machinery in obedience, which is why its obedience is evidence about its Owner.

**Understanding as the Organ of Sight**

The verse's closing qualification — *for people of understanding* — locates the bottleneck of belief not in the signs but in the seer. The seven items are given to everyone; they are seen as signs only by those who possess *ʿaql*, the intellect that binds observations into meaning — the same word the Qur'an uses in its constant rebuke: will you not understand, will you not reason. The inventory format makes the point structurally: seven items are listed precisely so that no single one can be dismissed as coincidence, since a pattern of seven public regularities, all serving life, all interlocked — rain feeding crops feeding creatures, winds driving clouds driving ships — is the shape of a design and not of an accident. The verse thus ends where 2:163 began, from the other direction: the confession says the God is one; the signs say the management is one. Understanding is the faculty that meets in the middle — the organ by which a person looking out of a window at weather arrives, if he is honest about what he sees, at the sentence of the verse before: your God is one God.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:165

> Still there are some who take others as Allah’s equal—they love them as they should love Allah—but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more. If only the wrongdoers could see the ˹horrible˺ punishment ˹awaiting them˺, they would certainly realize that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is indeed severe in punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Equals Loved With Divine Love**

The verse describes the inner structure of shirk, and the description is not about belief but about love. Some among people take *andād* — equals, rivals, competitors, the same word the sūrah used in its early challenge (2:22) — and they love them *as God should be loved*. The exegetes mapped the possible senses and the range is instructive: they love their idols the way believers love God; they obey their leaders the way God should be obeyed; they love these equals as they themselves claim to love God, dividing the love between heaven and its rivals; they glorify and follow human agencies with the total allegiance owed only to the Divine. All the readings share one claim: shirk is not primarily an intellectual error about how many gods exist but a misplacement of the heart's supreme attachment. The idolater may never formulate a theology; he performs one, in the structure of his loves — and the verse prosecutes the performance.

**The Believers' Love Is More Ardent**

Against the divided love the verse sets a comparison: *but the believers love Allah even more* — *ashaddu ḥubban*, stronger in love. Al-Rāzī's explanation is arithmetic rather than emotional: the love of the believers burns hotter because it is undivided, poured entirely into one true object, while the affection of the associators is split among rivals and is, in crisis, revealed as opportunistic — the same people who love their idols in ordinary times call on God alone when the ship is overwhelmed (31:32). The comparison quietly redefines strength of love as concentration. The idolater's affection may be passionate in each of its channels, but a passion distributed among competing objects is weaker at every point than a passion gathered into one; and it fails the only test that matters, since at the wave like a mountain the rivals are forgotten and the true love surfaces — proving all along which object the heart had actually ranked first. The believers' greater love is thus not a claim about feelings' temperature but about loyalty's unity: one object, no reserve, no emergency exit to a second.

**The Qur'an's Theology of Love**

This verse is the Qur'an's first great statement about the love between God and human beings, and the Book returns to it with a developed doctrine. The test of love is made practical: *"If you ˹sincerely˺ love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive your sins"* (3:31) — love validated by following, and answered by being loved in return. The community is defined by mutual love: Allah *"will replace them with others who love Him and are loved by Him"* (5:54). And love is put to its sharpest test in the sūrah of Repentance: if parents, children, siblings, spouses, wealth, trade, and cherished homes are *more beloved to you than Allah and His Messenger and struggling in His Way*, then wait for God's command (9:24) — the ranking of loves made the criterion of faith itself. Beyond these, the Qur'an speaks dozens of times of what God loves and does not love — the virtuous, the repentant, the patient, the just, on one side; the transgressor, the arrogant, the corrupter, on the other — so that divine love is not a sentiment but a moral alignment. Human love for God is described far less often than God's love for people, and the asymmetry is theological: every true love of God is downstream of His love first.

**"You Will Be With Those Whom You Love"**

The practical consequence of love's ranking was given by the Prophet in a report preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (6171). Anas ibn Mālik narrated: a man asked, when will the Hour be established, O Messenger of God? The Prophet said: what have you prepared for it? The man answered: I have not prepared much prayer or fasting or alms — but I love Allah and His Messenger. And the Prophet's answer was that a person will be in the company of the ones he loves. Anas added: nothing after Islam made us happier than that sentence. The report is the verse's eschatology in pastoral form. If love determines company — and the verse shows love determining even a person's gods — then the poor in deeds have one remaining capital: the direction of their love. The man who could not produce works produced an attachment, and the attachment was accepted as his ticket of proximity. Read with 2:165, the ḥadīth completes the picture from both ends: love misplaced binds a person to what he loves in punishment, and love rightly placed binds him to the Beloved in company. The Hour, in this teaching, does not sort people into strangers; it delivers each person to the object of his supreme love.

**Two Kinds of Love, and the Higher One**

The commentators used this verse to draw the classic distinction in the Islamic science of the heart. The first kind is desirous love — *ḥubb al-hawā* — loving a thing for what it does for the lover: God loved for His gifts, worship performed for its rewards. This love is legitimate and incumbent on all believers, since glorification, obedience, and righteous behavior are pursued in it for the peace and happiness God gives. The second kind is love for the sake of the beloved — arising not from benefit but because the perfection, beauty, and goodness of the beloved ignite the heart without intermediary. The higher lovers want the acts God loves not for what they gain but because He loves them; abandoning a thing the Beloved loves costs them more than serving their own interests ever would. The Sufis named the two poles metaphorical love (*majāzī*) — romance, the world, the self — and true love (*ḥaqīqī*), love of God alone and of all other beings through Him. Al-Rāzī added the epistemology of the higher love: one loves God to the degree one knows Him, and knowledge arouses love in return — even slight familiarity with the Beloved kindles the desire to know more, and that desire is itself love's signature. The discipline built on this circuit is *dhikr*, constant remembrance: the lover banishing from the heart all that is not the Beloved.

**Power Unveiled Too Late**

The verse ends by projecting the whole economy of love onto the Day: *if only the wrongdoers could see* — when they see the punishment — *that all power belongs to Allah and that Allah is severe in punishment*. The conditional is tragic in structure: the knowledge is certain and the timing is fatal. The rivals they loved as equals will be unveiled as powerless — the bonds cut, the leaders disowning the followers in the scene the next verses stage — and the power they had attributed to the loved objects will be seen residing wholly in the One they ranked second. An alternate reading reported by the exegetes turns the clause into an address to the Prophet: *if you saw* the wrongdoers when they see the punishment, you would see that power belongs entirely to God — the vision given to the reader rather than the wrongdoer, making the verse a warning delivered to whoever can still re-rank his loves. The severity named at the end is the verse's final argument against misplacement: love allocates allegiance, allegiance allocates destiny, and the severity of the punishment is simply what love-of-the-powerless amounts to when power arrives. The believers' stronger love is stronger because it was placed where the power actually is — before the seeing was forced.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:166

> ˹Consider the Day˺ when those who misled others will disown their followers—when they face the torment—and the bonds that united them will be cut off.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Day the Leaders Retract**

The verse stages the first scene of the disowning it announced at the end of the previous verse: the wrongdoers see that power belongs wholly to God — and here is what that sight contains. *When those who were followed disavow those who followed.* The exegetes identified the parties at several levels: the leaders of idolatry and their adherents; the devils and the human beings who obeyed them; and, in al-Ṭabarī's most comprehensive reading, all who led and all who followed in the ways of error across the whole life of the world. The identification matters less than the structure, because the structure is universal: every hierarchy of misguidance — teacher and disciple, chief and clan, opinion-maker and crowd — is shown dissolving at its foundation on the Day. The disavowal is total: the leader does not merely decline responsibility; he repudiates the relationship itself. The followers he cultivated, flattered, and used become, at the moment of torment, strangers he refuses to have known — and the refusal is the verse's first revelation about the nature of false authority: it was never a bond, only a use.

**The Bonds Cut: Asbāb Severed**

The second clause names what is destroyed with the relationship: *the bonds that united them will be cut off*. The word — *asbāb*, plural of *sabab* — is rich, and the exegetes worked through its senses: a rope, a means of obtaining something, a cause. Applied to the scene, the asbāb are everything by which the two groups were joined and helped each other in the world — the bonds of love, friendship, blood, tribal solidarity, common interest. In the world these were ropes: means by which the follower gained protection and the leader gained numbers, by which the clan defended its own and the party rewarded its loyal. On the Day every rope is severed at both ends. Al-Ṭabarī records a second reading with a sharper edge: the asbāb are the groups' *deeds* — which remain sound in the Hereafter if they were righteous, but are cut off when they were evil, so that the means which served them in the world become means that serve nothing at all. Al-Rāzī adds the practical consequence: there is no way left to stave off the punishment or escape its consequences. The verse thus describes not only a social collapse but a logistical one — the infrastructure of mutual help, which the world mistook for strength, removed entire.

**Why the Bonds Fail**

The failure is not an arbitrary punishment bolted onto the scene; it is the bonds' own nature finally displayed. The sūrah of the Spider states the principle from the idols' side: they were taken *"only to keep ˹the bond of˺ harmony among yourselves in this worldly life"* — and the same verse delivers the verdict: *"But on the Day of Judgment you will disown and curse one another"* (29:25). A solidarity built around the exclusion of God is built around nothing, and when the nothing is unveiled, the solidarity has no floor. This is the inverse of the love the previous verse described: the believers' love, directed wholly at God, binds them to the only Being whose power survives the Day — and, as the reports of loving for God's sake describe, outlasts it in company. The associators' bonds, directed at powerless objects and mutual advantage, dissolve with those objects. The verse's theology of friendship is therefore strict and complete: every human tie is a rope whose strength equals the strength of what it is tied to, and the Day of Judgment is simply the occasion on which the anchorage of every rope is tested at once.

**Satan's Speech and the Fire's Conversations**

The scene this verse opens is filled in elsewhere in the Qur'an with dialogues that carry the disowning to its last word. In the sūrah of Abraham, after judgment is passed, Satan addresses his followers directly: *"Indeed, Allah has made you a true promise. I too made you a promise, but I failed you. I did not have any authority over you. I only called you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me; blame yourselves. I cannot save you, nor can you save me"* (14:22) — the arch-leader disavowing not only his followers but his own former partnership, confessing the call was persuasion without power. In the sūrah of the Heights, the Fire's inhabitants enter group cursing group until they are all gathered, and the followers ask God to multiply their leaders' torment — only to be told the doubling has already fallen on all (7:38) — whereupon the leaders turn on the followers: *you were no better than us* (7:39). The mutual disowning is thus shown from every angle: Satan disowns the humans, leaders disown followers, followers attack leaders, and the attack is answered with the leveling insult. The verse of this passage is the summary headline under which all those dialogues are filed.

**The Torment Seen Together**

One clause of the verse fixes the setting with precision: the disowning happens *when they face the torment* — both parties seeing it, simultaneously. The timing is not incidental. In the world, the leader's authority rested partly on his apparent confidence about the unseen — his claim to know how things really are, his dismissal of the warning. The shared sight of the torment destroys that residue: the followers see that the man they trusted is as exposed as they are, and the leaders see that their following is now only an audience to their failure. The disavowal is spoken in full view of the thing both parties spent their lives explaining away. This is the verse's deepest cruelty and its deepest justice: the relationship of misguidance was founded on a shared denial of this exact sight, so the sight's arrival dissolves the relationship automatically — no argument needed, no trial of the bond, only its founding condition reversed. They face the torment together as they faced the warning together; but the facing is now alone-in-company, each group watching the other watch the Fire, with every rope between them cut.

**Reading the Scene Back Into the World**

The verse is eschatological, but the tradition reads it as instruction for the living, because the disowning reveals what the bonds already were. Every reader is positioned by it to audit his own ropes: the loyalties he holds that would survive a test of truth, and the loyalties that are really arrangements of advantage wearing love's language. The leaders the verse describes had followers who loved them as equals to God (2:165) — a love the leaders accepted and exploited, and a love the Day converts into the leader's own panic-stricken repudiation. The warning to the follower is sharper than the warning to the leader, because the follower's sin was trust misplaced: he gave to a human authority the reliance owed to God alone, and the verse shows him the receipt. The community that hears this in the world is being trained in the discrimination the Day will enforce anyway — attach yourself to what cannot disown you, tie your ropes to the One whose power the wrongdoers will see belongs wholly to Him, and treat every solidarity that asks you to exclude His commands as a rope already half-cut.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:167

> The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, “If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us.” And so Allah will make them remorseful of their misdeeds. And they will never ˹be able to˺ leave the Fire.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Wish for Revenge, Not for Return to God**

The followers' cry is the verse's whole psychology, and its content is startling on first hearing. Given the chance to return — *if only we could have a second chance* — they would not say: we would believe, we would follow the messengers, we would pray. They say: *we would disown them as they disowned us*. The wish is for symmetrical betrayal. The followers, having seen the leaders' repudiation, want nothing so much as to repay it — to stand where the leaders stood and cast them off in their turn. The tradition notes the alternative reading's implications and the mainstream takes the wish at face value, and the face value is devastating: even at the door of a second life, the heart formed by misguidance produces the currency of misguidance. The wish exposes what their following really was all along — not conviction but attachment, not belief but belonging — and belonging, once betrayed, wants only revenge. A repentance that begins with the leaders' disowning would be a return toward God; this wish never mentions Him, which is why the verse grants it nothing.

**The Second Chance That Defines the First**

The *karr* — the return, the second turn at the world — is the Hereafter's most requested impossibility, and the Qur'an's treatment of the request is consistent: the return is asked for, is refused, and the asking itself becomes part of the punishment. In the sūrah of the Believers the same plea is staged at the moment of death — send me back, that I may act rightly in what I left behind — and answered as mere words, with the partition of the barzakh standing between the speaker and the world until the Day they are raised. The theological work of these refusals is done on this side of the grave: the wish for a second chance is proof that the first chance was real. If the world were not the turn — the only turn in which deeds are earned — no one in the Fire would ask for it. The followers' cry thus retroactively confirms the sūrah's whole moral architecture: the test announced in the verses of patience (2:155), the doors of repentance open while breath lasts (2:160), the sentence closing at death (2:161). The Fire's population does not dispute the fairness of the arrangement; they dispute its finality, and the dispute is the arrangement's vindication.

**Deeds Displayed as Regret**

The verse's middle clause describes the mechanism of the punishment beyond the Fire's own torment: *thus does Allah show them their deeds as a source of regret* — *ḥasarāt*. Al-Ṭabarī preserves two readings of the display. In the first, the wrongdoers see what they would have possessed in the Hereafter had they acted righteously — the reward's shape rendered visible beside the deprivation, so that the knowledge itself is the torment. In the second, they see the houses of the Garden and long for them, while the Garden's own inhabitants see them and ask God to bless them — two populations looking at each other across the distance the deeds fixed. Both readings agree on the structure: regret here is not a mood but an exhibit. The deeds are *shown* — presented, made visible in their consequences — and the showing is divine action, part of the sentence. This is the Qur'an's answer to the question of how remorse functions after death: in the world, remorse can convert into amendment; here, amendment is closed, so remorse converts into nothing and consumes its subject. The deed that was light enough to commit is now heavy enough to look at forever.

**The Conversations the Fire Cannot End**

The verse belongs to a series in which the Qur'an gives the Fire a social life — one that inverts every comfort of the world's false societies. The followers ask that their leaders' torment be doubled, and are told the doubling has already fallen on all (7:38); the leaders answer that the followers were no better (7:39); Satan disowns everyone, confessing he had no authority, only a call that was answered (14:22); the allies of idolatry curse one another on the Day (29:25); and here the followers wish to disown in return. The pattern is exact: the Fire is populated entirely by failed relationships, and its inhabitants' only remaining activity is the litigation of those failures. Speech continues — accusation, excuse, wish — but no speech there is performative: nothing said in the Fire changes anything in the Fire. The world's conversations at least could convert into repentance, reconciliation, return; the Fire's conversations are the residue of that power, spoken after the power expired. This verse contributes the series' saddest entry: the wish to betray, which is what love-of-the-wrong-object becomes when it can no longer be anything else.

**"And They Will Never Leave the Fire"**

The verse ends with the clause that al-Ṭabarī wielded in the classical argument for the Fire's endlessness: their regret and their desire for another chance will not remove them from the Fire. The reasoning is textual and severe: a wish that persists is a wish unfulfilled, and the verse reports the wish without reporting its grant — so the state continues, wanting and not leaving, forever. Read with its neighbors, the clause is the third hammer in a row: the cursed condition fixed at death (2:161), the abiding without lightening or delay (2:162), and now the impossibility of exit stated in the plainest verb available — *they shall not leave*. The Qur'an's eschatology of permanence is not built on a single proof-text but on this accumulation: duration clauses, refused-wish scenes, and explicit non-exit statements reinforcing one another across sūrahs. And the accumulation is addressed, like all of it, to the living: every statement of the Fire's finality is published while its readers still hold the one thing the Fire's population has lost — a turn in the world, in which the deeds are still being chosen, the ropes still being tied, and the second chance still going by its real name, which is the first.

**The Verse's Place in the Argument**

Within the passage, this verse completes the love-arc begun two verses earlier. The equals loved as God should be loved (2:165) were the leaders and objects of the followers' devotion; the disowning scene (2:166) showed the devotion's leadership side collapsing; this verse shows the followers' side collapsing into the wish for revenge. Misplaced love is thus traced through its whole lifecycle — attachment, exposure, betrayal, and the desire to betray in return — and every stage is worse than the last, until the exit closes. Against this arc the passage has quietly set the only alternative it will name: the believers whose love is more ardent because it is undivided, and the reports of those who love one another for God's sake, whose bond is the one kind the Day does not cut. The verse does not preach the alternative; it finishes the autopsy of its opposite. The reader is left holding the comparison unspoken — bonds that survive the Day and bonds that become the Day's litigation — and the sūrah, characteristically, moves on to law: what to eat, what to avoid, how to live while the turn lasts.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:168

> O humanity! Eat from what is lawful and good on the earth and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. He is truly your sworn enemy.

**Expanded Commentary**

**An Address to Everyone, About Eating**

The verse's first word sets its scope: *yā ayyuhā al-nās* — O humanity. Not O believers, as so much of this sūrah's legislation begins, but the whole species, addressed on a matter that concerns the whole species identically: eating. The command is permission shaped as imperative — *eat from what is lawful and good on the earth* — and its audience is universal because its subject is the human table. The Qur'an's choice to open its food legislation with an address to everyone is deliberate theology: before eating is a matter of Islamic law, it is a matter of human existence, and the rules that will follow are presented not as the sectarian restrictions of one community but as the sane management of an appetite all people share. The earth is named as the source — *on the earth* — which makes the verse a statement about provision as well as permission: the food is already here, spread out, lawful in its origin, and the eating commanded is a reception of what has been furnished rather than an acquisition of something scarce.

**Halāl and Tayyib: Two Conditions on the Table**

The verse qualifies the food twice, and the two qualifications are distinct. *Ḥalāl* — lawful — is the legal category: what the Shariʿah permits, from a root whose range of meaning includes to untie, to set free, to unbind, the exact opposite of *ḥarām*, the forbidden and bound. *Ṭayyib* — good — adds the qualitative dimension the exegetes specify: pleasant, agreeable, wholesome, delicious. The pairing has generated a whole ethic: the merely permitted is not automatically the good, and the tradition reads ṭayyib as covering both the clean-and-wholesome and the decently-acquired — food lawful in kind but stolen in fact is not ṭayyib. The double condition answers the two ways eating goes wrong: the wrong thing, and the right thing wrongly gotten. It also frames the occasion of the verse's revelation, preserved by al-Qurṭubī: three tribal groups — Thaqīf, Khuzāʿah, and Banū Mudlij — had declared certain animal foods off-limits to themselves, binding what God had loosed, calling ḥarām what was ḥalāl ṭayyib. The command to eat is aimed at that self-starvation in God's name: the verse's first target is not indulgence but invented prohibition.

**Footsteps, Not Foot**

The second command names the danger with an image that has no better equivalent in English: *do not follow Satan's footsteps* — *khutuwāt*, the plural of a step, the tracks in sequence. The idiom, which the Qur'an repeats (2:208, 6:142, 24:21), was explained by the commentators as the concrete picture of yielding to temptation: nobody leaps to evil in one bound; the person walks into it, one printed track at a time, each step small enough not to alarm, each landing exactly where the previous step pointed. The plural is the whole doctrine — sin as a path rather than an event, with a walker who notices each individual footfall and never the direction. Applied to the verse's occasion, the footsteps are visible: an ancestral scruple about one animal is a single step; the scruple hardened into custom is the second; the custom declared divine law is the third; and the worshipper starving at a table God spread is the destination. This is why the food command and the footsteps warning share one verse: the invented prohibitions of the tribes were not eccentricities but tracks — Satan walking them slowly toward the point where human authority usurps the divine right to forbid.

**The Enemy Declared**

The verse closes by identifying the walker whose tracks these are: *he is truly your sworn enemy* — the manifest, declared, avowed enemy. The Qur'an repeats the formula at every station of Satan's campaign: God's own reminder in the Garden — *"did I not tell you that Satan is your sworn enemy?"* (7:22); Jacob's warning to Joseph about the brothers' plot — *Satan is a sworn enemy to humankind* (12:5); the command to speak what is best, because Satan sows discord — *a sworn enemy to humankind* (17:53); the Day's reproach — *"Did I not command you... not to follow Satan, for he is truly your sworn enemy"* (36:60). The insistence serves a military purpose: footsteps can be followed by mistake, but an enemy's movements cannot be mistaken once the enmity is known. Every small step of the path — the harmless scruple, the pious-sounding addition, the cautious extra prohibition — carries the signature of a declared adversary, and the verse transfers the reader's attention from the size of the step to the identity of the walker. Nobody following a sworn enemy's tracks is taking a neutral stroll.

**"I Made It Lawful; They Made It Unlawful"**

The footsteps of this verse have a prophetic description, preserved in a sermon-report in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (2865) from ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār: the Messenger of God said that Allah commanded him to teach the people what they did not know, including the divine words — the property I conferred on them is lawful for them; *My servants were created by Me inclined to pure devotion (ḥunafāʾ), until the satans came and pulled them away from that religion, forbidding what I had permitted and commanding them to set up partners against Me*. The report is this verse's commentary from the unseen side. The default of creation is a lawful table and an upright heart; the satanic intervention is precisely the double corruption this verse forbids — the invented prohibition (making unlawful what God loosed) and the association (worshipping what is not God). The tribes' scruples about animals were therefore not minor legal opinions but instances of the primordial sabotage: at every point where human religion starts forbidding what God permitted, a satanic footstep has been matched, and the walker is following a track laid at humanity's first fall.

**The Morsel and the Prayer**

The tradition attached one further consequence to eating within these two conditions. A Companion asked the Prophet how a person becomes one whose supplication is answered, and the answer was: purify your food, and your calling will be heard. A forbidden morsel, he warned, bars the eater's prayer for forty days; and flesh grown on unlawful earnings deserves nothing but the Fire. The report links the table to the sky by a chain the verse's own logic supports: the person walking Satan's footsteps toward forbidden food has taken the enemy's provision into his body, and the body funded by the unlawful prays with borrowed breath. Eating ḥalāl ṭayyib is thus not a private hygiene but a condition of the community's whole worship — which is why the verse that legislates it addresses all humanity, and why the believers will be given their own version of it in the verses ahead, with gratitude added as the table's second course.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:169

> He only incites you to commit evil and indecency, and to claim against Allah what you do not know.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Enemy's Full Job Description**

The previous verse declared Satan an enemy; this verse publishes his methods, and the list is exhaustive in its brevity — *he only incites you* — with "only" doing doctrinal work: there is no portion of his program that is benign, no counsel he gives that carries a grain of good. The three items named cover the field of human failure completely. Evil — *sūʾ*, the bad act in general, whatever harms its doer. Indecency — *faḥshāʾ*, the shameful in particular, the sin that exceeds evil's ordinary measure and offends the public sense of decency. And saying about God what one does not know — speech concerning the Divine undertaken without warrant. The sequence ascends in gravity: from act to shameful act to false theology, and the climax reveals the verse's real subject. Satan's campaign against human beings is not primarily a campaign of temptation toward pleasures; it is a campaign of corruption through unauthorized religious speech — and the food prohibitions the tribes invented, which the previous verse answered, are the case in point.

**Faḥshāʾ and Its Counter-Command**

The second item has its own vocabulary history in the Qur'an. That Satan commands indecency is stated again in this sūrah's verse on charity — *"The Devil threatens you with ˹the prospect of˺ poverty and bids you to the shameful deed ˹of stinginess˺"* (2:268), where even miserliness is classified inside faḥshāʾ — and in the sūrah of the Light: *"Whoever follows Satan's footsteps, then ˹let them know that˺ he surely bids ˹all to˺ immorality and wickedness"* (24:21). Against these stands the Qur'an's counter-command, stated with matching insistence: God forbids indecency, wickedness, and aggression (16:90); the prayer itself restrains from indecency and wickedness (29:45). The two lists confront each other as programs: what Satan bids, God and the prayer forbid, and the human being stands between the two commands with no neutral ground. The breadth of faḥshāʾ — covering sexual shame in its most common usage but extending to every act of excessive foulness, including the stinginess that abandons the needy — shows that indecency in the Qur'an's sense is a category of excess: the sin that goes beyond disobedience into ugliness, the act that degrades the actor in other eyes as well as in God's.

**The Worst Command: Speech About God Without Knowledge**

The third item is the verse's summit, and its placement last is an argument. To say about God what one does not know is to legislate in His name without His word — to declare permitted what He forbade, forbidden what He permitted, or to describe Him in terms no revelation supplied. Al-Ṭabarī connected this clause directly to the sacrificial customs of the Arabs that the sūrah of the Table dismantles item by item: the specially released she-camel, the one vow-protected, the one whose newborn was reserved — none of which God ever ordained — *"But the disbelievers just fabricate lies about Allah, and most of them lack understanding"* (5:103). The two verses name the same crime from two sides: the fabricated ruling is the lie about God, and its engine is the saying-without-knowing. The severity of the classification is intelligible: murder destroys a body, indecency degrades a person, but false theology corrupts the religion itself — every generation downstream inherits the invented prohibition as divine, and the lie acquires the authority it counterfeited. This is why the sin the verse ranks highest is committed most confidently: the tribes that forbade their cattle did so in God's name, with reverence, certain they were pious.

**The Three Zones of the Human Person**

Read structurally, the three incitements map onto the three zones in which a human being can fail. Evil operates in the zone of appetite — the act the desire pulls toward. Indecency operates in the zone of social shame — the act that exceeds appetite's privacy and wounds the community's moral sense. Saying about God without knowledge operates in the zone of creed — the word that misrepresents heaven itself. The mapping shows the campaign's completeness: Satan does not need a person to fail in all three zones, because a failure anchored in any one gives him a foothold in the others. The appetite-corrupted person eventually justifies himself; the shame-corrupted person eventually redefines decency; and the creed-corrupted person — the verse's climactic case — eventually commands the other two zones in God's name. The footsteps imagery of the previous verse is thus completed: the tracks lead through all three zones, and the walker who follows long enough will be led to speak about God what he does not know, which is where the path terminates and where the enemy's real work — not the temptation of individuals but the falsification of religion — is done.

**Knowledge as the Only Defense**

The verse names its own antidote in the wording of the third item. The sin is not saying about God what is false — a person can utter a false statement about God in honest ignorance and stand under the general hope of forgiveness; the sin is saying *what you do not know*, the speech that proceeds without knowledge whether or not it happens to land near the truth. The criterion is thus epistemic: religious claims require a warrant, and the only warrant the Qur'an recognizes is what God has actually sent down. The believer's defense against the footsteps is not stronger willpower but better information — knowing what revelation permits before adding prohibitions, knowing what it describes before describing God further. This is why the food verses that follow this one are structured as they are: a universal permission to eat of the lawful and good (2:168), the exposure of Satan's program (2:169), the ancestral refusal of revelation named as the obstacle (2:170), and then the revealed list itself — short, explicit, four items — closing the space where unauthorized speech operates. The verse condemns the method; the coming legislation removes the occasion, because where God has spoken plainly, saying about Him what one does not know has nowhere left to stand.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:170

> When it is said to them, “Follow what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “No! We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.” ˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance?

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Summons and the Refusal**

The verse is built as a dialogue in two lines. The summons: *follow what Allah has revealed* — the entirety of the religious demand compressed into one verb and one object. The refusal: *No! We only follow what we found our forefathers practicing* — the word "no" stated flatly, then the substitute source named. The exchange is not a debate but a substitution revealed: the question was never what to follow but whom to follow it from, and the answer exposes that for the refusers, the source has already been chosen and is not God. The verse's "them" is wide — al-Rāzī read it as covering the idolaters and possibly the People of the Book, al-Ṭabarī tied it to the food customs of the preceding verses — and the width is justified by the reply's familiarity across all the audiences the Qur'an addresses. Invented prohibitions, ancestral rites, inherited scruples: in every case the same sentence stands behind them, and this verse quotes it in the exact form it is actually spoken.

**The Question the Answer Cannot Survive**
