The verse does not argue with the refusal; it asks one question, and the question is lethal: *would they still do so, even if their forefathers had absolutely no understanding or guidance?* The conditional strips the ancestral appeal to its working assumption — that the fathers knew something the sons do not, that custom carries encoded wisdom. The verse invites the refusers to suppose the assumption false: the fathers understood nothing and were not guided. If the supposition changes nothing — and the flat "No!" of the first line suggests nothing would change — then custom was never the real authority; it is a preference wearing authority's clothes. The argument's force is that the refusers cannot answer the question either way. If they admit the fathers might have lacked guidance, the reason for following them dissolves. If they insist the fathers certainly had guidance, they have claimed a knowledge of their ancestors' inner standing that no descendant possesses — which is itself saying about God and the unseen what one does not know, the very sin the previous verse ranked highest.

**A Campaign Across the Whole Qur'an**

This verse is one station in the Qur'an's most persistent polemic. The sūrah of the Table repeats the exchange nearly verbatim — *"When it is said to them, 'Come to Allah's revelations and to the Messenger,' they reply, 'What we found our forefathers practicing is good enough for us'"* — with the same killing question appended: *"˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had absolutely no knowledge or guidance?"* (5:104). Luqmān's version adds the eschatological stake: the same refusal — *"No! We only follow what we found our forefathers practicing"* — *even if Satan is inviting them to the torment of the Blaze* (31:21). The sūrah of Ornament gives the ancestral creed its full formula — *"We found our forefathers following a ˹particular˺ way, and we are following in their footsteps"* (43:22) — and records the warner's question answered by total rejection (43:24). Abraham's people confess the same ground: *"We found our forefathers worshipping them"* — and Abraham's verdict: *"Indeed, you and your forefathers have been clearly astray"* (21:53–54). Pharaoh's court dresses the same refusal in political suspicion (10:78). The repetition across Meccan and Medinan sūrahs shows the Qur'an treating ancestral religion not as one error among many but as the error's default chassis — the structure every false religion installs itself inside.

**Custom as Satan's Slowest Footstep**

The previous two verses supply the connection this verse makes explicit by position: the ancestral refusal is where Satan's footsteps arrive when they are walked for generations. The first step is a scruple — one animal avoided, one practice added; the second is the scruple's hardening into custom; the third is the custom's consecration as religion; and the fourth is the verse's scene, where the summons to revelation is refused because the custom now has ancestors to vouch for it. The sūrah of Luqmān names the walker in this exact context: following the fathers *even if Satan is inviting them to the Blaze* (31:21) — the ancestral road revealed as the enemy's road, its antiquity the measure not of its truth but of how long the footsteps have been followed. This is why the food occasion matters: the tribes' prohibitions were small, local, and pious-sounding — the least alarming form the corruption can take — and the verse's dialogue shows what small pious-sounding corruptions become when time is added: an authority that answers revelation with "No."

**What the Qur'an Does Not Say About Fathers**

The polemic requires one clarification, because the Qur'an itself honors ancestors of a certain kind. The faith of Abraham is held up as the creed to follow (2:135), and the community's confession names Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, and Jacob as recipients of revelation (2:136) — fathers followed, explicitly, across the centuries. The difference between that following and this verse's refusal is precise and instructive: Abraham is followed because what he followed is known — revelation recorded, a faith transmitted in its content, an uprightness documented by God Himself. The ancestral religion of this verse is followed because it is ancestral — its content never examined, its warrant never requested, its fathers' understanding assumed rather than established. The Qur'an's criterion is thus not lineage against lineage but warrant against inheritance. A forefather who received revelation transmits light; a forefather who merely practiced custom transmits habit; and the verse's question separates the two by asking whether the habit was ever lit. The Muslims' own fathers in faith pass the test because God testified for them; the refusers' fathers fail it because no one can testify for them, and their children never asked.

**The Living Edge of the Verse**

The dialogue is quoted in the past, but its structure is permanent, and the tradition reads it as addressed to every generation's refusers. The summons — follow what Allah has revealed — arrives in every age with its scripture complete and its law accessible; the refusal arrives in the same words with new content: not only the fathers' cattle-prohibitions but the community's settled practice against the clear text, the inherited opinion defended after the evidence is shown, the "we have always done it this way" that answers correction with genealogy. The killing question applies unchanged: would you still follow, even if the practice had no understanding or guidance behind it? The verse's pastoral function for believers is therefore a mirror before it is a window — the refusers it describes are outside, but the reflex it exposes is inside everyone, since every person inherits practices he has never examined from people he cannot audit. The command to follow revelation is, on this verse's logic, a command to keep auditing: to hold every inherited act up to the revealed text until it either passes or is dropped, so that no reader ends up quoting the refusal with his own mouth while believing he is quoting his fathers' piety.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:171

> The example of the disbelievers ˹not responding to the Messenger’s warning˺ is like a flock not comprehending the calls and cries of the shepherd. ˹They are wilfully˺ deaf, dumb and blind so they have no understanding.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Parable of a Voice and a Flock**

The verse answers the dialogue of the previous one with an image. The summons was given and refused; this verse explains what the refusal looked like from the caller's side, and the explanation is a parable: the disbelievers' case is that of one who calls to what hears nothing but a call and a cry. The dominant reading, preserved by al-Ṭabarī, pictures the preacher as the shepherd and the summoned as the flock — the voice reaches the animals, who hear the sound and do not hear the meaning; the call lands on ears that register volume but not message. Al-Rāzī records the inverted reading: the parable describes the idolaters' own prayers to their idols, calls addressed to objects that hear only as dead matter hears — the sound arrives, the comprehension never does. The grammar sustains both, and the two readings compose: the disbelievers are the flock when the Prophet calls them, and they are the futile caller when they call their gods. The verse's genius is that one image convicts both directions of the community's speech — hearing without understanding when addressed, speaking without being heard when addressing.

**Hearing That Stops at the Ear**

The flock simile isolates the exact point of failure with anatomical precision. The animals are not deaf in the physical sense — the shepherd's voice provokes movement, attention, the shuffle of the herd toward feed or shelter. They hear. What they lack is the faculty that converts heard sound into understood speech, and the verse locates the disbelievers' failure at the identical joint: revelation reaches them as it reached every listener — audible, intelligible in its language, accompanied by arguments they could repeat. The failure is downstream of the ear. This is why the parable stings rather than insults: it does not say the disbelievers are beasts, but that their reception functions like a beast's reception — complete at the sensory level, absent at the level of meaning. The sound of the Qur'an was heard in Mecca's streets; its claims were debated in the assembly; its words were memorized by enemies who found them inimitable. All of it arrived. None of it was heard in the sense the shepherd needs, and the verse's second sentence names that deficit as the disbelievers' chosen condition.

**Deaf, Dumb, Blind — and Responsible**

The three deprivations are the sūrah's established formula for the closed heart. Its opening portrait used the identical triad: *"They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺"* (2:18) — with the crucial insertion that governs every use: *wilfully*, the deafness they do not wish to cure. The sūrah of the Spoils states the verdict from the divine side: *"the worst of all beings in the sight of Allah are the ˹wilfully˺ deaf and dumb, who do not understand"* (8:22) — and the sūrah of the Night Journey shows the condition's eschatological permanence: dragged on their faces on the Day, *deaf, dumb, and blind*, with Hell as their home (17:97). The pairing of incapacity language with voluntariness is the Qur'an's careful anthropology: the organs named are not the body's but the heart's, and the heart's deafness is acquired by repeated refusal until it becomes a nature. The flock in the parable cannot choose to understand; the disbelievers could have, and did not — which is why the parable describes their reception rather than their guilt, and the triad that follows describes their guilt as a state they own. The similitude's limit is the verse's deepest point: they are *like* the flock in hearing, and worse than the flock in accountability, because the flock was made so and they made themselves.

**The Qur'an's Animal Parables**

This simile belongs to a deliberate register in which the Qur'an figures insensibility to revelation through animals. The sūrah of the Congregation: those entrusted with the Torah who failed to carry it are *"like a donkey carrying books"* (62:5) — the most exact image of contact without comprehension, the load of meaning borne on a back that cannot read it. The sūrah of the Heights, on the man given the signs who clung to the earth: his example is the dog that pants whether chased or left (7:176) — appetite unchanged by every circumstance, the restless pursuit that no outcome instructs. The three parables form a graded series: the flock hears the call and misses the meaning; the donkey carries the book and never opens it; the dog pants identically in pursuit and in rest. Each is a portrait of revelation's reception blocked at a different joint — hearing, carrying, wanting — and each keeps the animal world's innocence as the foil: the donkey is not blamed for its books, but the scholar who resembles it is. The register's restraint matters: the Qur'an never says its opponents *are* animals; it says their case is *as* an animal's case, leaving the difference — the will — as the whole of the indictment.

**Comfort for the Caller**

The parable has a second addressee, and the tradition hears it clearly: the Prophet himself, and every caller after him. The preceding verses had staged the refusal's full social force — the flat "No!", the ancestral fortress, the killing question unanswered. A caller who has watched his summons dissolve against custom can only conclude one of two things: that the message failed, or that he failed. The verse forecloses both. The shepherd's call in the parable is everything a call should be — audible, purposeful, aimed at the flock's good — and the failure sits entirely in the receivers' incapacity to convert sound into meaning. The deficiency is located in the organ of reception, not in the voice or its owner. This is the same consolation the qiblah passage delivered in other terms — Allah will spare you their evil, He is All-Hearing of their taunts (2:137) — and it governs the Qur'an's whole theology of preaching: the messenger's duty is delivery in the clearest available words, the outcome belongs to the hearing God created and the heart God does not force. The caller who understands the parable preaches without needing conversion statistics to validate his faithfulness, because the verse has already validated it: the call was right; some of the flock could not hear; the shepherd keeps calling.

**Sound, Meaning, Response**

The verse's anatomy of hearing yields its practical doctrine in three stages: sound arrives, meaning is comprehended, response follows. The flock fails at the second stage, and the sūrah's earlier triad shows the stages' moral weight — the deaf refuse the sound's meaning, the dumb refuse the response's confession, the blind refuse the sign's direction. Revelation's reception is thus a sequence in which each stage requires the previous one's honesty, and the disbelievers' condition is the sequence arrested at its first link by will. The verse leaves the remedy implicit in its grammar: a parable about hearing invites the hearer to check his own hearing. The reader of this verse is inside the address — the calls and cries reach him too, in the same words — and the difference between him and the flock is not the clarity of the call but what he does at the second stage. The understanding the verse names at its close (*they do not understand*) is the faculty the Qur'an everywhere appeals to and everywhere assumes can be exercised: the ear that receives, the heart that comprehends, the will that answers. The parable's flock has the first organ only. The verse exists so that no reader settles for less than all three.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:172

> O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided for you. And give thanks to Allah if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Same Permission, Narrowed and Warmed**

Four verses earlier the command to eat went out to all humanity: eat from what is lawful and good on the earth (2:168). Here it is given again, to the believers alone, with two changes that carry the verse's whole message. The food is now described not as lawful-and-good in the abstract but as *the good things We have provided for you* — the provider named, the provision personalized, the table set by a Host. And to the permission is added an obligation the universal address did not contain: *give thanks to Allah*. The narrowing from humanity to believers is not a restriction of the food but an intensification of the relationship. All people may eat the lawful; believers are told that their eating is reception — that every meal is a gift arriving from a Giver who has furnished the earth and furnished their access to it. The verse thus converts the biological act the whole species shares into the covenantal act only the believers perform: eating as worship, the table as an altar of gratitude.

**The Ṭayyibāt: What God Did Not Forbid**

Al-Ṭabarī's definition of the good things is a definition by negation, and the negation is the doctrine: *ṭayyibāt* are the things God has not forbidden or singled out as sinful. The default of creation is permission. The earth was furnished before the prohibitions were legislated, and the legislative list — the four items the verse after next will name — is an exception carved out of an ocean of the allowed. This definition answers the occasion the surrounding verses had exposed: the tribes that forbade animals to themselves, the ancestors whose customs bound what God had loosed, the footsteps that walk pious people toward invented prohibitions (2:168–170). Against all of them the verse states the table's constitution — what God did not forbid is provision, not suspicion; the good things are good by divine manufacture, and the believer's first act toward his food is not scrutiny of its permissibility against human custom but reception of it against divine generosity. The satanic program named two verses back — making unlawful what God made lawful — is here countermanded in a single noun: the ṭayyibāt, the good things, plural and abundant, spread across an earth that was created to feed its inhabitants.

**Thanks as the Test of Worship**

The second sentence attaches gratitude to the eating with a conditional that reads as a test: *give thanks to Allah if you truly worship Him alone*. The condition does not doubt the believers' worship; it defines it. Gratitude is not an appendix to worship, a polite addition performed after the meal and the prayer — it is worship's own substance in the presence of a gift, and the verse makes the substance explicit: the one who worships Allah alone gives thanks to Allah alone, at the table where the alone-ness is most tangible. The logic binds the two halves of the creed together. Worship directed at rivals produces thanks to the rivals — the ancestors credited for the customs, the idols thanked for the harvest, the stars credited for the rain; and the invented prohibitions of the previous verses were exactly such misdirected reverence, scruples offered to sources other than God. The believer's thanks at the meal is therefore the smallest daily act of tawḥīd: the acknowledgment that this provision came from the One confessed in the creed of 2:163, and that the acknowledgment is owed to no one else. Eating without thanks is not a neutral act in this verse's economy — it is the food's provider left unnamed, which is the silence where shirk grows.

**The Verse Quoted by the Prophet**

This verse holds a distinction rare in the Qur'an: it was used as a proof-text by the Prophet himself, in a report preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (1015). Abu Hurayrah narrated the Messenger of God saying: *O people, Allah is good and accepts only what is good. Allah commanded the believers as He commanded the messengers* — and he quoted the sūrah of the Believers: *"O messengers! Eat from what is good and lawful, and act righteously"* (23:51) — *and He said: 'O you who believe, eat from the good things We have provided for you'* (2:172). Then he described a man long journeying, dishevelled and dusty, who raises his hands to the sky crying *O Lord, O Lord* — while his food is unlawful, his drink unlawful, his clothing unlawful, his nourishment unlawful: *how can he be answered?* The ḥadīth reads this verse as law with consequences: the command to eat the good things governs the whole body, and the body governs the prayer. The traveler has every title to an answer — the journey, the distress, the raised hands — and one disqualifier: unlawful nourishment standing between him and the sky. The verse's table is thus load-bearing for the community's entire worship; the supplication the fasting tongue utters is funded by what the hand ate.

**Manna and the Two Tables**

The command to eat the provided good things has a precedent in this same sūrah's history of the Israelites: the clouds shaded them, manna and quails were sent down, *"Eat from the good things We have provided for you"* (2:57) — the identical formula, spoken over the wilderness table. And the verse records what followed: *the evildoers did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves* — the same provision, received by one generation with transgression and rebellion. The two tables stand beside each other in the sūrah deliberately: provision plus gratitude is this verse's covenant; provision plus self-wronging was that generation's failure. The difference is not in the food — both tables were furnished by the same Provider with the same class of good things — but in the second course, which is thanks. This is why the verse makes gratitude conditional on worship rather than optional for it: the manna generation had the permission and lost the benefit, and the believers are handed both in one sentence so that the history is not repeated at their own tables. Every meal offers the choice the wilderness offered: eat and remember the Provider, or eat and wrong the self.

**The Shortest Food Law**

Structurally, the verse is the pivot of the whole food passage, and its brevity is its jurisprudence. The permission: eat the good things provided. The obligation: give thanks. The condition: if it is Him you worship. No list, no detail, no casuistry — the verse before it described the enemy's methods, the verse before that exposed the ancestral refusal, and this verse answers both with the positive law of the table in two sentences. The detail comes next, and comes short: the four prohibitions of the following verse, framed by necessity's exemption and closed with forgiveness and mercy. The architecture is a teaching about law itself — permission vast and stated first, prohibition narrow and stated second, gratitude woven through both. A reader who holds this verse holds the spirit in which the coming list is to be read: not as a fence closing the earth's bounty but as four exceptions proving the rule, spoken by the Provider over a table He furnished, to guests whose only required speech is thanks.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:173

> He has only forbidden you ˹to eat˺ carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity —neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—they will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Word "Only" and the Short List**

The verse opens with a restriction on restriction: *He has only forbidden you* — four items, and the four exhaust the divine prohibition of food. The "only" is the verse's argument in one word. Against the tribes that forbade whole classes of their cattle to themselves, against the ancestral customs that bound what God had loosed, against the footsteps that walk the pious toward invented prohibitions, the revealed law presents a list so short it can be memorized in a breath: carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in another's name. Everything else on the earth's table stands under the permission of the previous verse. The brevity is jurisprudence and theology at once — a religion whose food law is four exceptions to a universal permission cannot be accused of strangling life with scruple, and the contrast with the surrounding polemic is exact: the human additions were many, anxious, and false; the divine prohibitions are few, reasoned, and final. The tradition's summary of the verse's effect on the table is that God loosed the earth and marked four doors closed.

**The Four, One by One**

Each prohibition carries its own logic, and the classical readings drew it out. Carrion — *al-maytah*, the dead thing — is flesh whose death no one governed: an animal that died of disease, accident, or age, its body a site where the processes of decay and unknown illness have already worked; the prohibition of the unslaughtered dead is the prohibition of the uncontrolled. Blood — the flowing blood, as the sūrah of the Cattle will specify — is the life-fluid the ritual draining removes, prohibited in its gathered form. Swine is the single animal named as forbidden in its own flesh, a prohibition the Qur'an repeats without elaboration and the community received without exception. And what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah is the prohibition whose object is not hygiene but worship: the meat is physically sound, but the act that produced it was an offering to another — idolatry performed at the animal's throat. The four thus span the categories of concern: the unsafe, the unfit, the excluded by decree, and the consecrated to a rival. The last is the deepest, which is why the many jurists' permission of the food of the People of the Book turns on its absence: their slaughter names God, not an idol.

**The Name Over the Throat**

The fourth item establishes the positive ritual the community performs at every slaughter: the pronouncing of God's Name. The sūrah of the Pilgrimage legislates the same act over the sacrificial camels — *"pronounce the Name of Allah over them when they are lined up ˹for sacrifice˺"* (22:36) — and Islamic practice fixed the formula as the *basmalah* spoken at the cut. The theology is precise and answers the meal's deepest question: who made this death lawful for my life? The animal dies because a human needs it; the Name declares that the taking happens under God's permission and in His direction, converting a killing into a receipt. Meat from which the Name is absent is not thereby carrion in the physical sense; it is meat whose killing belongs to no one's stated accountability — or worse, to a named rival. This is why the verse's list ends with the dedication-prohibition rather than beginning with it: the first three items protect the body and the decree; the fourth protects the meaning of the act, and meaning is the verse's real subject. The table of the believers is a table at which every death has been declared to its Owner, and the declaration is what separates eating from mere consumption.

**The Necessity Clause**

The second sentence bends the law toward life: *but if someone is compelled by necessity — neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need — they will not be sinful*. The clause is the Qur'an's standing principle that the prohibition serves the human being and not the reverse: when the choice is the forbidden food or death, the food is commanded by the same law that forbade it. The two qualifiers prevent the clause from becoming a loophole. *Neither driven by desire* — *ghayra bāgh*, where the word carries both coveting and rebellion: the eater must not be using necessity as a cover for appetite, reaching for the forbidden because it is forbidden or because he wants what others may not have. *Nor exceeding immediate need* — *wa-lā ʿād*, transgressing the measure: enough to survive, not enough to feast; the necessity opens the door exactly as wide as the danger requires and no further. Al-Ṭabarī recorded a third reading of the transgression-qualifier with social teeth: some understood it to exclude the rebel and the highwayman — the person journeying in disobedience to God, for whom even necessity earns no license, since he may not provision his crime with the law's mercy. The mainstream reading keeps the clause general — necessity is necessity, whatever road the starving person is on — and the disagreement itself shows how carefully the tradition guarded the balance: mercy wide enough to save a life, discipline tight enough to survive the mercy.

**A Ruling the Qur'an States Three Times**

This verse is one of the Qur'an's most exactly repeated laws, and the repetitions mark its constitutional status. The sūrah of the Bee states it in near-identical words: *"He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"* (16:115). The sūrah of the Cattle states the principle without the list: *"Why should you not eat of what is slaughtered in Allah's Name when He has already explained to you what He has forbidden to you—except when compelled by necessity?"* (6:119). And the sūrah of the Table, in the Medinan period's final legislation, expands the list to its full detail — carrion, blood, swine, the dedicated-to-others, the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen, the gored, the partly eaten by predators, the altar-sacrificed, the divining arrows — with the same necessity exemption standing (5:3). The expansion confirms rather than revises: the later verse elaborates the carrion category into its modes of death and keeps the fourfold core intact. A law repeated verbatim across Meccan and Medinan revelation, then detailed without disturbance, is the tradition's picture of a ruling beyond abrogation — the food law's permanent floor.

**Forgiving and Merciful as the Law's Frame**

The verse closes with the two names — All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — and their placement is the final lesson. They follow the necessity clause rather than the prohibitions, covering the eater who crossed the line under compulsion, the one who erred in measuring his necessity, the one whose past meals were eaten before the law arrived. A food legislation could have closed with vigilance: Allah watches what enters your mouths. This one closes with absolution, and the absolution is attached precisely where human beings will fail — at the boundary cases, the famines, the mistakes, the years of ignorance before the permission and prohibition were revealed. The whole passage from the address to humanity to this verse is thereby framed by mercy at both ends: the enemy declared (2:168), his methods exposed (2:169), the ancestral refusal refuted (2:170), the uncomprehending flock parabled (2:171), the believers' grateful table set (2:172), and the four doors closed with the key of necessity in the lock and forgiveness on the frame. The community that receives this law is told, in the act of receiving it, that its Lawgiver expects to be thanked at the table and expects to forgive at its edges — and both expectations are mercy.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:174

> Indeed, those who hide Allah’s revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain consume nothing but fire into their bellies. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment, nor will He purify them. And they will suffer a painful punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Concealment Gets Its Price Tag**

The curse-verses on concealment (2:159–162) return here with a new element: the motive. The concealers are not merely hiding; they are hiding *for a price* — trading the Book for a fleeting gain, the same traffic the sūrah condemned in its portrait of the editors of Scripture: woe to those who write the book with their own hands, then say "this is from Allah," to sell it for a little price (2:79). The verse renders the transaction with a physical image of unusual violence: what they swallow is not the gain but fire — they *consume nothing but fire into their bellies*. The parallel in the sūrah of the Women fixes the same image to a neighboring crime: those who devour the property of orphans are, in truth, eating fire into their bellies (4:10). Both verses run the same accounting: the wealth sought by corrupting religion is not lost, not confiscated, not merely forbidden — it is *converted*. The price of the hidden truth arrives in the belly as the Fire that truth would have saved them from, and the conversion happens now, invisibly, at the moment of the profitable sin.

**God Will Not Speak to Them**

The second penalty is the withholding of speech: Allah will neither speak to them on the Day nor purify them. Āl ʿImrān states the identical sentence over those who trade God's covenant and their oaths for a fleeting gain: *"Allah will neither speak to them, nor look at them, nor purify them on the Day of Judgment"* (3:77) — the same crime drawing the same threefold withdrawal, with the look added there. But the Qur'an also describes God speaking on the Day — questioning all of them about what they used to do (15:92–93), questioning those to whom the messengers were sent and the messengers themselves (7:6), and telling the damned *"Be despised in there! Do not ˹ever˺ plead with Me ˹again˺!"* (23:108). Al-Rāzī harmonized the texts with precision: the plain sense of this verse and 3:77 is total silence, but in light of the questioning-verses it must describe a punishment within speech — God will not speak to them words of peace and welcome. He compared it to the intimacy of a king, whose displeasure is shown by exile and the cutting off of contact, and suggested the angels will be the ones who speak to people that Day. Al-Ṭabarī read it as God not saying things agreeable to them; al-Qurṭubī added the linguistic observation that Arabs say "he did not speak to him" of a man who is angry. The speech withheld is not communication but favor — and for souls arranged entirely toward God, the withdrawal of His address is itself the fire.

**Nor Will He Purify Them**

The third clause withholds purification, and the verb *zakkā* carries the double sense the exegetes exploited: to purify, and to *declare* purified. On the first reading God will not cleanse them — will not set right their evil deeds, will not accept their deeds as He accepts those of the purified. On the second He will not praise them or call them clean, which answers the sūrah's own command not to elevate yourselves as pure (53:32): the self-declared pure are the ones God will not vouch for. The two readings compose into a single exclusion — from cleansing and from commendation — and al-Rāzī drew from it the verse's deepest claim: the punishment of indignity and humiliation is worse than physical punishment, because distance and separation from God constitute the worst suffering in Hell. The concealers sold God's words for money; the sentence pays them in the same currency inverted — the words of God withheld, forever, which is what their money was always for.

**The Anatomy of the Fleeting Gain**

The phrase *fleeting gain* deserves the weight the verse places on it. The gain is characterized not by its size but by its duration — little and passing, a price that cannot be spent twice, in a market that closes at death. Against it the verse sets what was sold: revelations, clear proofs, guidance — goods whose value the sellers themselves acknowledged, since concealing something proves you know it is worth hiding. The trade is therefore never between equals but between the eternal and the temporary, and the verse's economics are exact: the fire in the bellies is not a punishment added to the bargain but the bargain's true content revealed. This is the same accounting the sūrah applied to the traders of the Hereafter for this world (2:86) and the covenant-sellers of Āl ʿImrān, who will have *no share in the Hereafter* (3:77) — a phrase that reads as the balance sheet: their share was taken early, in cash, and the account is closed. The one who hides revelation for money does not earn money and lose heaven; he exchanges one for the other at a rate the verse exists to publish.

**The Speech-Withheld as Mirror of the Crime**

The correspondence between crime and penalty is tighter than general justice requires, and the tradition read it deliberately. The concealers silenced a revelation — they took words God spoke and removed them from circulation, managing what the community would hear. Their sentence is the same act performed on them, by God, at the one moment when speech is everything: He will not speak to them. They made His words unavailable for a price; He makes His words unavailable without price, without appeal, on the Day when every other voice has been collected. The Qur'an's punishments consistently carry this mirrored structure — the fire eaten now answers the money eaten then; the silence then answers the silencing now — and the mirroring is itself information: it tells the reader that the penalty is not arbitrary severity but the sin's own logic run to its end. The concealer chose a world where God's speech is a commodity he controls; the Day gives him the fixed form of that world, where God's speech is simply absent and he has only what he paid for.

**Placed Between Patience and the Law**

The verse's location in the sūrah is part of its argument. It arrives after the patience-triad with its formula of return and its blessings (2:154–157) and before the great definition of righteousness (2:177) and the legislation of retaliation, bequest, and fasting that follows. Between the patient poor who say *to Allah we belong* and the community about to receive its civil law stands the figure of the religious profiteer — the scholar-class sinner whose crime is the precondition of every other corruption, since a community can only be misled where guidance was withheld. The sūrah has now named this figure from every side: the truth hidden knowingly (2:42), the testimony concealed (2:140), the recognition like a father's knowledge of his child (2:146), the curse and its exception (2:159–160), and here the price, the fire, and the silence. The legislation that follows — blood-money, bequests, the fast — is addressed to a community whose knowledge is assumed intact, and this verse is the guarantee that its keepers were warned: the words you carry are not inventory. They are the speech of the One who can withhold His own.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:175

> They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment. How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire!

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Trade Restated as Double Loss**

The verse repeats the accounting of the one before and sharpens it into symmetry. There, the concealers ate fire for a fleeting gain; here the same transaction is itemized in two pairs: they purchased error at the price of guidance, and punishment at the price of forgiveness. The doubling is deliberate and complete. In the first pair the object sold is cognitive — guidance, the knowledge of the way — and the object bought is its exact negation, misguidance. In the second pair the object sold is soteriological — forgiveness, the standing the revelation existed to offer — and the object bought is its exact negation, punishment. Nothing was gained in either exchange; in each, a good was surrendered for its opposite. The verse thus refines the economics of 2:174: the fleeting gain was never really in the ledger, because what the traders actually acquired were the two negatives. The money was the excuse; the misguidance and the punishment were the merchandise delivered.

**The Verb of Purchase**

The Qur'an's word for this transaction — *ishtaraw*, they purchased — belongs to a family the Book uses with bitter consistency for bad spiritual trades. The same verb described those who sold God's covenant and their oaths for a fleeting gain (3:77), those who trade the Hereafter for this life (2:86), and elsewhere those who purchase diversionary talk to mislead from God's way. The choice of commercial language is not decorative; it imports the whole apparatus of the market into the moral life — price, preference, exchange, profit — and then audits it. A market transaction is rational when the buyer values what he receives more than what he pays; the verse's claim is that these traders paid guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment, meaning they paid more than they received by an infinite margin, and did it knowingly, since the concealment of 2:174 presupposed knowledge of exactly what was being sold. The image convicts not only the sin but its stupidity: the Qur'an's profiteers are never shrewd operators but men who cannot do arithmetic, and the market metaphor exists to show every reader the ledger they are keeping with their own choices.

**"How Persistent They Are in Pursuit of the Fire"**

The verse's exclamation has taxed the commentators precisely because its surface is strange: what is praised — or mocked — is the traders' *patience*, their steadfastness, in relation to the Fire. The readings recorded by al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī converge on a rhetorical question: what drove them to the deeds that brought them near the Fire? — or, what gives them such patience toward the Fire that they abandon truth for falsehood? The common sense, in al-Rāzī's summary, is simply: what made them do this? The irony is the engine of the sentence. Patience — *ṣabr* — is the sūrah's supreme virtue: the instrument the believers were commanded to take up (2:153), the quality whose bearers receive blessings and mercy (2:157), the grace promised good news (2:155). Here the same constancy appears in inverted form: a steadfastness in ruin, an endurance that spends itself hastening toward punishment. The traders have the virtue's structure — persistence through difficulty toward a goal — and the vice's direction. The exclamation thus does double duty: wonder at the magnitude of their self-destruction, and a warning that constancy itself is morally neutral until its object is named.

**Patience Toward the Fire, Patience Toward God**

Set beside the patience-verses of this very passage, the exclamation draws the sūrah's full contrast. The believers were told they would be tested with fear and hunger and loss, and commanded to endure — a patience whose object is God's will and whose outcome is blessings, mercy, and guidance (2:157). The concealers exhibit the mirror image: they endure too — the labor of editing scripture, the management of secrets, the years of profitable concealment — and their endurance is real, disciplined, and social. The difference is the direction: one patience walks toward God through difficulty; the other walks toward the Fire with the same steady step. The verse's rhetorical question — what patience do they have toward the Fire? — asks the reader to look at the misbelievers' industry and recognize it as misplaced devotion. Nobody sins lazily at this level; the great corruptions require the great virtues, perverted. This is why the Qur'an reserves its harshest astonishment not for the weak sinner but for the energetic one: the traders' persistence is the measure of what guidance would have made of them.

**Forgiveness Sold Back**

The second pair of the trade deserves its own attention, because forgiveness is the sūrah's standing offer. The passage immediately before ended with the Accepter of Repentance speaking in the first person (2:160), and the whole legislative arc about to begin — retaliation with its pardon, bequests with their equity, the fast with its ease — is forgiveness made institutional. The concealers are described as having held forgiveness and exchanged it: the revelation they hid was the vehicle of pardon for their communities, and by selling it they sold their own access to what it carried. The exegetical point is structural: guidance and forgiveness are the two goods revelation brings — knowledge of the way and absolution on the way — and the trade named here surrendered both at once, which is why the penalty of 2:174 fell on both faculties: the fire answers the belly's gain, the withheld speech answers the guidance, and the withheld purification answers the forgiveness. Each element of the sentence corresponds to an element of the sale. The verse is not adding imagery to the previous one; it is displaying its itemization.

**The Question Left With the Reader**

The closing exclamation is addressed, grammatically, to no one — it is wonder spoken aloud, the way a bystander says *how could he?* over a ruin. That unaddressed quality is its pedagogy. The verse does not answer its own question; no reason is given for the trade, because none exists that survives statement — that is the point of calling it a purchase of error at guidance's price. The reader is left holding the question and is expected to apply it: what am I persistently walking toward, and at what price did I buy the direction? The sūrah will keep posing the same audit in different currencies — wealth traded for the Hereafter, oaths traded for gain, the self traded for appetite — and every instance inherits this verse's arithmetic. The Fire here is not only the destination but the disclosure: it is what every bad trade actually delivers, named at last by its real name. The traders of 2:174 thought they were selling religion for money; the verse corrects the invoice — they were buying the Fire, and paid for it with everything that could have saved them, and kept paying, patiently, to the end.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:176

> That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth. And surely those who differ regarding it are totally engrossed in opposition.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reason Clause**

The verse begins with *that is because* — the formula by which the Qur'an attaches a verdict to its ground — and the ground given here justifies everything the previous two verses sentenced. The traders ate fire, sold guidance for error, and walked patiently toward punishment *because God sent down the Book with the truth*. Al-Ṭabarī read the connection precisely: the punishment applies because of their treatment of God's Book. The causal structure is worth slowing on, because it inverts a natural expectation. One might expect the sentence to be grounded in the harm the concealment did others — the communities misled, the guidance lost. The verse grounds it instead in the Book's origin: it was revealed *in truth*, and everything about the crime follows from that attribute. A lie hidden is a misdemeanor; the truth hidden is treason against reality itself. The concealers did not merely wrong their audience; they set themselves against the mode in which God chose to enter human affairs — truthful speech — and the sentence measures accordingly.

**The Book Sent Down in Truth**

The phrase *in truth* — *bi-l-ḥaqq* — is a standing description of revelation's descent, and its sense is layered. The Book is revealed with truth as its content: what it says corresponds to what is. It is revealed with truth as its purpose: not for play, not for profit, not for one faction's ascendancy. And it is revealed by the One whose speech cannot be otherwise — the truth of the Book is downstream of the truthfulness of its Sender, which is why trading it for a fleeting gain is not a commercial act but a contradiction: the seller's own conduct declares the Book worthless while his knowledge (the knowledge that made concealment profitable) declares it true. This is the inner ruin the previous verse's pairs described — guidance exchanged for error is the intellect contradicting itself; forgiveness for punishment is the will contradicting itself — and 2:176 supplies the reason both contradictions were possible: the Book came in truth, and truth can be recognized and refused in the same act. Revelation does not compel assent; it makes assent and refusal both meaningful, and this verse is the hinge between the two.

**Which Book?**

The exegetes asked whose Book the verse means, and the answers widen its reach. It could be the Qur'an — the Book the concealers around the Prophet were trading against. It could be the Torah and the Gospel, which on the Islamic account attest to the Prophet's truth, so that "differing regarding it" covers the questions of interpretation and distortion the sūrah has been prosecuting since its early verses (2:75). Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī both allowed the most comprehensive reading: the Book as God's Book collectively — Torah, Gospel, and Qur'an together — one revelation in successive installments, so that differing regarding it is differing regarding the whole enterprise of heaven's speech. The comprehensive reading is the strongest, because the passage's subjects have been plural throughout: the People of the Book who hide the testimony (2:140), the group that recognizes and conceals (2:146), the concealers cursed by all who curse (2:159). A single Book in three descents is exactly the object such parties can all be said to differ regarding, and it makes the verse the summary judgment on the whole sectarian argument the sūrah opened — the claim and counter-claim of Jew and Christian (2:135) resolved by the identity of what they were all given.

**Shiqāq: The Opposition Engrossed**

The verse's second clause names the condition of those who differ: they are in *shiqāq baʿīd* — far schism, deep opposition, the fracture-word the sūrah used of those who turn from the community's creed (2:137). The word's career in the Qur'an is consistent: the wrongdoers *totally engrossed in opposition* (22:53), the disbelievers *entrenched in arrogance and opposition* (38:2), the denier who has *gone too far in opposition* (41:52). Each instance pairs schism with a qualifier of depth or distance, and the image is spatial: opposition as a position taken far from something — not disagreement at close quarters, where correction is possible, but rupture with distance built in. The addition here, *regarding the Book*, identifies the axis of the rupture: the difference is not about weather or wages but about the one object whose whole function is to end differences. A book revealed in truth exists to be the common reference; differing *regarding it* is therefore not using a shared standard differently but destroying the standard — which is why the verse assigns no ordinary disagreement but far schism. The parties who quarrel over the Book have quarreled their way out of the only court that could have settled them.

**Differing About It, Not Differing With It**

The preposition carries a distinction the classical readers marked. To differ *with* someone regarding a text can be honest exegesis — the sūrah itself has modeled disagreement handled with grounds, reporting the exegetes' divisions and weighing them. What the verse condemns is differing that has the Book as its object in the sense of its casualty: readings that distort (2:75 — a group hears the word of God and then knowingly corrupts it after understanding it), concealments that subtract (2:174), trades that price it (2:175). The far schism is thus not pluralism but sabotage — difference manufactured from a text whose truth is known to the manufacturer. This is why the verse lands where it lands in the sequence: the traders' sentence (2:174–175), the reason (176), and then immediately the sūrah's positive counterpart — the definition of righteousness (2:177) that begins by believing in the Book and the prophets without distinction. The two verses are a diptych: far schism regarding the Book on one panel, and on the other the creed that holds every book together, makes no distinction between the messengers, and turns belief into the worked righteousness of orphans, travelers, captives, and pledges kept.

**The Distance Called Far**

The final word of the clause — *far* — deserves its own weight, because distance in the Qur'an's moral geography is measured from God. The wrongdoer is elsewhere described as having gone astray *far* (4:116's phrasing of distant error), and the Fire's own name for its inmates' condition is remoteness — the curse the previous passage defined as being distanced from mercy (2:159, 2:161). Schism regarding the Book is far, then, in the same sense: every act of distortion, concealment, and sale moves its author a measurable distance from the truth he still holds the text of, and the distance compounds, because each generation of readers inherits the corrupted copy rather than the clear original. The verse's causal opening now reads as its consolation too: *that is because God revealed the Book in truth* — the revelation's truth is not damaged by the traders, since truth does not depend on its handlers; the damage is entirely in the distance the handlers walked. The Book remains true where it is; the schismatics are simply far from it, and the far is where the punishment of 2:174–175 was already located. The reason clause thus closes the case the same way it opened it: the Book in truth, the differing in distance, and the sentence as the arithmetic of the gap between them.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:177

> Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets; who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives; who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and keep the pledges they make; and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity, and in ˹the heat of˺ battle. It is they who are true ˹in faith˺, and it is they who are mindful ˹of Allah˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Not the Direction but the Whole Life**

The verse opens by declining a definition. Righteousness — *birr* — is not in turning faces east or west. The occasion the reports preserve explains the target: after the migration to Medina the Muslims observed the Jews praying westward toward Jerusalem and the Christians eastward, in the period when the qiblah itself had been the community's defining dispute (2:145). The verse does not abolish the direction — the sūrah had just spent a dozen verses fixing it by revelation — but it refuses to let the direction be the sum. *Birr* is defined by the exegetes as obedience to God well established in the heart, or the total of the acts of obedience and devotion that bring a person near Him; the same word names the duty owed to parents in the phrase for filial devotion. The structure of the verse is therefore a correction of proportion: orientation is a part of righteousness, and a commanded part; the whole is the architecture this verse builds — creed, charity, worship, covenant-keeping, and endurance — of which the facing is one brick.

**The Five Articles Before the Deeds**

The definition begins in belief, and the list it gives became canonical: belief in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets. These five are the principal articles on which the Islamic creedal statements are built, and they reappear as a unit in the sūrah of the Women's command to believe in Allah, His Messenger, the Book revealed to him, and the Scriptures revealed before (4:136). Their fullest canonical exposition is the famous ḥadīth of Gabriel, preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb: the archangel, appearing as a traveling man, asks the Prophet to define *īmān*, and the answer enumerates belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the divine decree in its good and its evil — the same list, with the decree added. The ordering in this verse is instructive: God first, then the Day that gives moral life its horizon, then the unseen agents, then the books, then the messengers — creed before conduct, because the conduct that follows is unintelligible without it. The righteous are not defined as those who *do* the listed deeds but as those who *believe* the listed truths and do the deeds out of them.

**Wealth Given While It Is Still Loved**

The first deed named is charity, and its qualifier is the verse's psychological core: giving wealth *despite loving it* — or, on the reading that takes the pronoun as God's, *because of love for Him*. Al-Ṭabarī's explanation covers the first sense: parting with property even when one fears poverty or yearns for what wealth provides. The phrase has a twin in the sūrah of Man, where the righteous feed the poor, the orphan, and the captive — *and give food despite their desire for it* (76:8). The gift counted here is the one that costs, made while the hand still prefers to keep. The recipients are then listed in the order of social nearness and need: kinsfolk first — charity begins where obligation bleeds into love; orphans, whose guardianship the sūrah has legislated repeatedly; the indigent; the wayfarer stranded among strangers; the beggars; and the freeing of captives — wealth spent not on a person but against an institution, buying human beings out of bondage. Many jurists noted that this giving must be *beyond* the zakāh, since the alms-tax is listed separately later in the same verse: first the costly charity of love, then the fixed levy of law. The recipient list recurs at 2:215 and 4:36 and across the Qur'an's legislation of war-booty — one standing roster of the people a righteous economy is measured by.

**Prayer, Alms, and the Kept Pledge**

Three more acts complete the worship section: establishing the prayer — not performing but *establishing*, the word that denotes the settled, regular, communal maintenance of the rite; giving the zakāh, the fixed purifying levy that makes charity law rather than mood; and keeping pledges when they are made. The third is the verse's social keystone. The oath and the promise are the instruments by which human beings extend their wills into the future and bind themselves to others — contracts, treaties, vows to God, words given in marriage and market — and the righteous are defined as those whose spoken word survives the change of their interests. The Qur'an's insistence on this virtue runs through its portraits of the prophets — Ismāʿīl, who kept his word to his people — and its laws require the same fidelity of ordinary believers in 5:1 and throughout. Placed between the ritual duties and the patience that follows, covenant-keeping bridges the verse's two halves: it is worship performed in the medium of other people's trust, and it is the first form the coming patience will have to take, since the pledge is hardest to keep precisely when keeping it hurts.

**Patience in the Three Extremes**

The final deed is the sūrah's standing virtue, now specified by its three testing grounds: patience in misfortune (*baʾsāʾ*), in hardship (*ḍarrāʾ*), and in moments of peril. Al-Ṭabarī's glosses separate them: misfortune as challenges like poverty — the loss of means; hardship as matters like sickness — the loss of health; and the moments of peril as battle, the meeting of the enemy, the hour when the body's fear argues against the will's resolve. The three grounds cover the full geography of affliction — the purse, the body, the battlefield — and together they recall the test announced at 2:155 with its fear and famine and loss of property, life, and crops. The verse thus closes its definition where the passage began: the righteous are the patient of 2:155–157, described now in full dress. And the peril-clause points forward with deliberate timing: the sūrah is about to legislate retaliation (2:178), then war itself (2:190 onward), and the community about to receive those laws is first told that the law's operators must be defined by patience — in the feud's heat, in the wound's pain, in the battle's first hour.

**The True and the Mindful**

The verdict that closes the verse is double: *it is they who are true, and it is they who are mindful of Allah*. The first word — *ṣadaqū*, they were truthful, they proved sincere — answers a question the verse's own opening raised: who is telling the truth about righteousness? Not the one who points at his direction of prayer but the one whose creed, charity, worship, pledges, and patience are on record. Truthfulness here is demonstrated rather than claimed, which is why the sūrah elsewhere reserves the same word for those whose faith survives testing. The second — the reverent, the *muttaqūn* — names the quality the whole sūrah has been circling since its second verse, the Book given as guidance to the mindful. The restrictive construction of both clauses ("it is *they*") excludes the counterfeits the passage has just catalogued: the concealers who traded the Book (2:174–176), the far-schismatics, the direction-merchants of righteousness. Between the traders of revelation and the definition of birr the sūrah has drawn its clearest boundary line — righteousness is a life structured by believed truth, costly giving, established worship, kept words, and endured extremes; and the verse leaves no direction of the compass, east or west, with any excuse to stand in for it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:178

> O believers! ˹The law of˺ retaliation is set for you in cases of murder— a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female. But if the offender is pardoned by the victim’s guardian, then bloodmoney should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously. This is a concession and a mercy from your Lord. But whoever transgresses after that will suffer a painful punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Law Given Into a Feud**

The verse must be read inside the system it replaced. Pre-Islamic Arabia ran on the tribal vendetta: a killing was an injury to the clan, the clan's honor demanded blood, and the demand escalated far beyond the original crime — a tribe might answer one murder by killing many members of the killer's tribe, and might deliberately overbid the victim's status, taking a free man for a slave, a man for a woman, a notable for a person of low station. The feud thus served two economies at once: revenge for the past and prestige for the future, with the original crime quickly irrelevant as each retaliation justified the next. Into that escalating arithmetic this verse introduces the principle of equivalence: the retaliation is set — *kutila*, prescribed, written — as life for the life taken, person for person, and no more. The commentators are explicit that the verse's function is limitation: responsibility follows the nature of the crime precisely, so that retaliation can neither fall short of the crime nor exceed it. The feud's engine — the honorable escalation — is removed at the root.

**"A Free Man for a Free Man"**

The three pairs have been misread as a tariff of inequalities, and the classical exegetes took care to close that reading. The verse was not understood to mean that only a man may be executed for a man, or that a woman's murder goes differently unavenged; nor does it make anyone but the perpetrator responsible for his act. The pairs state the equivalence rule against the vendetta's status-inflation: for the free man killed, the free man who killed him — not his whole tribe, not a substitute of higher rank; for the slave, the slave; for the woman, the woman. Each pairing forbids the specific excess the tribes practiced in that category. The wording implies that the retribution for a crime against a woman could neither fall short of nor exceed what the crime warrants — her life carries the same protection of the law, and the law's arithmetic refuses both the feud's overkill and any discount of her blood. Read against the practice it answers, the verse is leveling rather than ranking: it is the first time Arabian blood-debt was put on scales that weighed only the deed.

**The Three Options of the Heir**

The verse's legal machinery places the homicide's outcome in the hands of the victim's next of kin, with the state holding the sword. Islamic law's developed doctrine gives the heirs three courses: demand retaliation (*qiṣāṣ*), carried out only by the authorities — the verse is understood to exclude vigilantism entirely; accept the blood-money (*diyah*), a monetary composition; or forgive outright. The options are mutually exclusive in effect: once one is executed, the other two are cancelled — an heir who has taken the diyah cannot afterward demand the life, and the reverse holds. Some jurists declined to treat retaliation and blood-money as equal alternatives in cases of clear, intentional homicide, holding that capital punishment must then follow; most left the choice with the heirs. A minority position recorded by Ibn Kathīr allowed the killer himself to refuse the composition and submit to the punishment against the heirs' will. The detailed literature that grew from this verse — direct versus indirect causation, standards of evidence, the manner of execution, the amount and payment schedule of the diyah, the state's role — is the measure of how much jurisprudence one sentence of revelation generated: the schools differ on the branches while the trunk, equivalence with the heir's option of mercy, is common to all.

**The Pardon and the Courteous Payment**

The second sentence legislates the mercy-case in two directions. *If the offender is pardoned by the victim's guardian* — the wording is notable: the pardoner is called the offender's *brother*, a term of kinship the law keeps alive at the moment of maximum enmity — then let the pardon be followed honorably and the payment rendered with goodness. The exegetes read the double adverb as binding both parties: the heir who pardoned for money must not harass or inflate, and the offender's side must not delay or diminish; the settlement is to be performed with the courtesy that makes it a reconciliation rather than a truce. And the verse names this arrangement itself a gift: *that is an alleviation from your Lord, and a mercy*. The alleviation, as the commentators specify, is the very existence of the blood-money option — that homicide, the gravest of crimes, admits of composition at all. The comparison with the Torah's own retaliation law was drawn by the exegetes: Deuteronomy instructs the eye-for-eye court to show no pity (Deuteronomy 19:21), while the Qur'an's parallel in the sūrah of the Table pairs the same lex talionis — a life for a life, an eye for an eye — with the sentence that whoever waives it charitably finds it an expiation for him (5:45). Rabbinic tradition too incorporated composition into its practice; the Qur'an's contribution is to make the merciful exit explicit, named, and rewarded.

**Transgression After the Settlement**

The verse closes by legislating against its own abuse: whoever transgresses after that has a painful punishment. The classical reading fixes the case with precision — the heir who accepts the blood-money and then kills the offender anyway. The settlement extinguished the claim; the killing after it is not retaliation but plain murder, and the jurists drew the consequence: for that killer, execution becomes mandatory and no blood-money may be accepted from him. The clause completes the verse's architecture by protecting the peace the payment bought. A composition system survives only if the composition is final — if the seller of his vengeance can resell it in blood afterward, no offender would ever pay, and the feud returns through the back door of the settlement. The transgression-after-pardon is therefore the one crime the verse punishes without option: the heirs lost their mercy-privilege the moment they took the money, and the state's sword becomes unconditional. The pain threatened here is not only the punishment of the Hereafter but the removal of the very mercy the verse called an alleviation — the transgressor exits the system of pardon and re-enters the system of the feud, with the law now against him instead of the feud.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Moral Sequence**

The placement of this legislation is argument. The verse before defined righteousness as creed, costly charity, established prayer, kept pledges, and patience in misfortune, hardship, and battle (2:177); the verse after will give the retaliation's rationale — life in the qiṣāṣ (2:179). Between the definition and the rationale, the sūrah installs the law that most needs both: the killing-law, given to a community of ex-feuders whose patience is about to be legislated for the battlefield. The sequence teaches that the retaliation is not an isolated penalty but a chapter of birr — the kept pledge includes the settlement signed over a grave, and the patience in moments of peril begins with the heir who could take blood and takes money, or who could take money and forgives. The Qur'an's criminal law here is continuous with its ethics: the same heart that gives wealth despite loving it is being asked to give vengeance despite loving that too, and the verse that demands the exchange supplies, in its own title for the arrangement, the reason it can be endured — an alleviation from your Lord, and a mercy.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:179

> There is ˹security of˺ life for you in ˹the law of˺ retaliation, O people of reason, so that you may become mindful ˹of Allah˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Life in the Law of Death**

The verse states in nine Arabic words what legal philosophy elsewhere needs volumes for: *in the qiṣāṣ there is life for you*. The paradox is the point — the law whose content is killing is announced as an instrument of living, and the exegetes unpacked the claim in three movements. Al-Ṭabarī's summary gathers them: the exemplary punishment deters future crimes, so lives that would have been taken are never endangered; it places a concrete value on human life, teaching the community that a life costs a life, which is the only price the potential murderer understands; and because the maximum revenge is limited to the actual perpetrator, with vendettas forbidden, the law itself preserves the lives the feud would have consumed — the relatives, the tribesmen, the escalating substitutes of the old system. A law of death produces life by all three routes at once: by frightening the would-be killer, by dignifying the potential victim, and by capping the aftermath. The verse is thus not an apology for severity but a claim about severity's economy, stated so compactly that Arabic rhetorical tradition has treated it as inimitable — the whole case for capital law carried in a single sentence.

**The Proverb It Outclassed**

The classical commentators measured this verse against the Arabs' own wisest saying on the subject, a proverbial line roughly rendered "killing is what wards off killing" — the ancestral formula the pre-Islamic Arabs considered the summit of legal wisdom. The comparison was always resolved for the verse, and the reasons given are instructive. The proverb is circular: it names killing twice, making the cure and the disease the same word, and it addresses only the deterrence function. The Qur'an's sentence is wider in every direction — it speaks of life where the proverb speaks only of killing; it names the institution (*al-qiṣāṣ*, the lawful equivalent) rather than the act, distinguishing the court's measured retaliation from the feud's murder; and it includes the audience inside the benefit, *for you*, making the law a possession of the community rather than a threat against it. The rhetorical verdict the tradition drew is theological: a sentence that outperforms the concentrated wisdom of a language's proverbial stock, in fewer words, is doing something proverbs cannot. The verse invites to be read as evidence — of the Book's inimitability in the very passage that legislates its hardest law.

**People of the Kernels**

The address that follows — *O people of reason*, ūlū al-albāb — is one of the Qur'an's honorifics, and its literal sense is an image: possessors of the *lubb*, the kernel inside the shell. The nut symbolism carries the epistemology: wisdom lies deeper than the surface, and the one who would be nourished by a thing must crack through to its inner truth. The title recurs wherever the Qur'an wants its hardest thinking done — in the pilgrimage's provisions (2:197), in wisdom's gift (2:269), over the verses precise and elusive (3:7), before the signs of the heavens and the earth (3:190), in the stories of the prophets (12:111), and a dozen places more. Its use here is pointed: the law of retaliation is exactly the kind of ruling whose surface — a killing commanded — repels the shell-level gaze, and whose kernel — life multiplied by deterrence, valuation, and limitation — is available only to the reader who cracks it. The verse does not address everyone; it summons the readers capable of holding a paradox, and it makes the holding itself an act of the intellect it honors.

**The Value the Law Sets**

The second of al-Ṭabarī's reasons — the concrete value placed on life — deserves expansion, because it is the verse's most modern-seeming claim. A community without the qiṣāṣ prices life implicitly and erratically: the feud priced it by honor, so a notable's life cost several commoners'; the bribe prices it by wealth; the tyrant's caprice prices it by mood. The retaliation law fixes one exchange rate — a life for the life taken, whoever the taker and whoever the taken — and the fixing is itself the valuation. When the price of a life is stated in lives, every member of the community carries the same price on his head, slave and free, woman and man, notable and nobody, and the equivalence the previous verse legislated becomes a declaration of equal worth performed in the idiom of penalty. This is why the verse can promise *life for you* — plural, communal: the security is not only the individual's lowered chance of being murdered but the collective knowledge that the law values each member identically. The deterrence protects bodies; the valuation protects persons; and the second is the deeper gift, since a community that has learned its poor are priced the same as its notables has learned something the feud could never teach.

**So That You May Be Mindful**

The verse ends by assigning the law a purpose beyond safety: *so that you may become mindful of Allah* — taqwā, the same end the fast will be given (2:183) and the same quality the bequest-legislation will call an obligation upon the reverent (2:180). The claim is strong: penal law is moral education. A retaliation system run by the state, bounded by equivalence, opened to pardon, and priced at life-for-life trains its community in precisely the dispositions taqwā names — restraint at the moment of rage, deference to a standard above the self, the habit of seeing every act answered. The feud trained the opposite virtues: initiative in vengeance, loyalty to the clan over the truth, escalation as honor. The law replaces the curriculum, and the verse states the pedagogy's goal: not merely a safer Arabia but a God-fearing one. This is also the verse's quiet answer to the objection that severity is unspiritual — the qiṣāṣ is not the enemy of mercy but its infrastructure, since the pardon-option of 2:178 is only meaningful where the right to punish is real; mercy without a sword behind it is not forgiveness but weakness, and the taqwā the verse aims at is built from both instruments, the fixed retaliation and the open pardon, working on the same heart.

**The Whole Arithmetic in One Line**

Read with its predecessor, the verse completes the sūrah's first legislation of blood. 2:178 built the machinery — equivalence against the feud, the heir's three options, the courteous settlement, the punishment of post-settlement transgression — and 2:179 supplies the machinery's reason for existing, so that the law is received not as a code of vengeance sanctioned but as an instrument of life deployed against vengeance. The Torah's own arithmetic is enlisted in the same direction elsewhere in the Qur'an: the ordinance given to the Children of Israel that whoever takes a life unjustly is as if he killed all humanity, and whoever saves a life is as if he saved all humanity (5:32) — the same valuation logic, the same weighting of each life with all lives. The Qur'an's shorter sentence does the same work inside penal law: one life taken is a wound to the whole body, and the measured answer to it is what keeps the whole body alive. The people of the kernels are asked to see it — the killing in the law and the life in the killing — and the seeing is itself the first exercise of the mindfulness the law exists to produce.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:180

> It is prescribed that when death approaches any of you—if they leave something of value—a will should be made in favour of parents and immediate family with fairness. ˹This is˺ an obligation on those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Deathbed Gets a Law**

The verse uses the sūrah's legislative verb — it is *prescribed*, the same word that set the retaliation (2:178) and will set the fast (2:183) — and applies it to the hour of dying. When death approaches and the dying person leaves *khayr*, something of value, a bequest is to be made for parents and near kin in fairness. The word *khayr* — good — standing alone for property is established Quranic usage: whatever good you spend is for your own sake (2:272); the sūrah of the Chargers describes the human being as fierce in his love of good things, meaning wealth (100:8). The law's trigger is thus twofold: the approach of death and the existence of something to leave. The exegetes read the second condition as limiting the first — the bequest-legislation addresses those who die holding property, and it does not disturb the prior claims on that property, since debts and financial obligations must be discharged from the estate even after death. The verse installs the will as the dying person's last lawful act: a final disposition, bounded by fairness, supervised by the community, and owed to the people closest in blood.

**Parents and Kin, in Fairness**

The beneficiaries are named in an order that carries moral weight: parents first, then the near relatives. The fairness qualifier — *bi-l-maʿrūf*, in what is honorable and fitting — governs both the amounts and the manner, and the early commentators pressed its social edge: bequests are to be made first to relatives and only secondarily to others, and those who left relatives in need while bequeathing property to strangers were severely condemned. The ruling answers a standing temptation of the deathbed — the wish to make a grand gesture to a friend, a teacher, an institution, while the family that will survive the testator inherits poverty. The Qur'an's economy of charity consistently orders the claimants by nearness: the same roster of kinsfolk, orphans, and the poor structures the giving of 2:177 and 2:215 and the kindness-command of 4:36. Fairness here is therefore not equality but proportion to claim — the parent's claim, the child's, the dependent relative's — assessed by the honorableness the word *maʿrūf* denotes: what the community's best judgment recognizes as right, without the need for a schedule.

**The Two Limits the Law Grew**

From this verse the jurists developed the bequest's two famous restrictions, and both have textual anchors. The first: a bequest may not exceed one-third of the estate. The proof-text is the report preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (1295): Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, gravely ill in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage and wealthy with only a daughter to inherit, asked the visiting Prophet whether he might give two-thirds of his property in charity — no; half — no; and the Prophet set the ceiling: a third, and even a third is much. Then the reason: it is better to leave your heirs wealthy than to leave them poor, begging from people. The second restriction: no bequest may be made in favor of a person who already inherits by the Quranic shares — the widely transmitted prophetic saying "there is no bequest for an heir." Together the two rules protect the fixed inheritance system from the deathbed's affections and grudges: the shares of 4:11–12 stand untouched by wills, and the will's own space — the third, the non-heir — is preserved for exactly the cases the shares cannot reach.

**Was the Verse Abrogated?**

The second restriction generated one of Islamic legal theory's most instructive debates, because it appears to collide with this verse's own command to bequeath to parents and kin — who are usually heirs. Three positions are recorded. Some held the verse wholly abrogated by the inheritance-verses of the sūrah of the Women, which assigned the shares directly. Others — al-Ṭabarī among them — held it partially abrogated: superseded for those entitled to a fixed share, still in force for relatives outside the quota system. A third group, including the Shīʿī jurists, denied abrogation entirely, harmonizing the texts and reading the verse as fully operative. Beneath the positions lies a constitutional question: the saying "no bequest for an heir" is Sunnah, and its acceptance as binding showed al-Qurṭubī that the Sunnah can abrogate the Qur'an — a position others rejected on epistemic grounds, since a report carrying less certainty than the Qur'an's transmitted text cannot repeal its ruling.
