Al-Qurṭubī himself acknowledged that this ḥadīth is the only text preventing full harmonization, and harmonizers proposed readings such as restricting the verse's parents and kin to those who would not inherit anyway — a disbelieving parent, for instance, outside the quota system. The debate is the verse's living afterlife: a single sentence about the deathbed became the test-case for how revelation's two sources relate.

**Before the Shares: The Arabian Background**

The verse also marks a transition in property history. Before the Quranic legislation, Arabian inheritance was agnatic — the male line took the estate, with custom excluding women and minors from succession entirely. The Quranic shares reorganized the field around fixed quotas for named relatives, including the women the custom had passed over: the male's share twice the female's, the daughter's half or two-thirds, the parents' sixths, the spouses' quarters and eighths (4:11–12) — all disbursed, as those verses repeatedly insist, *after the fulfilment of bequests and debts*, which is this verse's institution embedded in the arithmetic. The customary agnatic heirs were thereby demoted to a secondary position under Sunni law, inheriting the residue after the quota shares; Shīʿī law rejected agnatic priority altogether, distributing the remainder by proximity of blood-kinship through both male and female lines. Within that architecture the bequest of 2:180 holds its office: the testator's personal word, operating in the third, reaching the people and purposes the fixed shares do not name — the law's provision for the dying heart, fenced so it cannot trample the heirs.

**An Obligation on the Mindful**

The verse closes by naming its addressees' quality: this is an obligation upon the reverent — upon the people of taqwā. The formula does ceremonial work. A bequest is the one legal act performed at the moment when all other sanctions are failing: no court compels the dying, no reputation is being built, no force can reach a man on his bed. The law that governs that hour must therefore be carried by the one virtue that survives it — the fear and mindfulness of God — and the verse says so, assigning its execution to conscience. The same formula will return over the retaliation's rationale (so that you may be mindful, 2:179) and the fast's purpose (2:183), building the passage's pattern: each law is given, then grounded in taqwā. The dying testator who bequeaths in fairness, within the third, without cheating an heir, performs the definition of righteousness the previous verses supplied — the kept pledge extended to the pledge no one will be alive to enforce. The verse's placement between the murder-law and the fast is exact: blood regulated, property regulated, appetite next — and over all three, the same Presider, the mindful heart.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:181

> But whoever changes the will after hearing it, the blame will only be on those who made the change. Indeed, Allah is AllHearing, All-Knowing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sin Transferred**

The verse legislates for the moment after the deathbed: the will has been made, heard, and recorded, and the testator is gone. If anyone now alters it, the sin of the alteration falls *only* on those who altered — the wording is exclusive and deliberate. The transfer answers a question the situation itself raises: when a bequest is changed, whose account carries the wrong? Not the dead man's — his act was completed in fairness or in its absence, and the verse of exception that follows (2:182) shows the law's concern for his possible fault separately. Not the heirs who suffer from the change — they are its objects, not its agents. The sin attaches to the changer and stays there, undistributed: the executors who adjusted a figure, the witnesses who "remembered" different terms, the relatives who intercepted a bequest before it could operate. Al-Qurṭubī's reading of the verse establishes the rule's shape: a bequest validly made cannot be altered — the dead man's word acquires, at his death, a legal inviolability, and the living hands that touch it take on the whole of the touching's guilt.

**Hearing as the Trigger of Responsibility**

The condition in the verse — *after hearing it* — is not incidental but constitutive. The alteration condemned is the knowing one: the changer heard the will, from the testator's mouth or the witnesses' attestation, and then changed what he had heard. Hearing creates custody; custody creates the duty of fidelity; the change breaches both. The same structure governs the bequest's attestation in the sūrah of the Table, where two just men are to be called as witnesses when death approaches (5:106) — the institution exists precisely so that the hearing is official, the will is not a private whisper, and any later alteration is provably against a heard text. The verse thereby protects the dying in the only way law can protect the dead: by deputizing the living. The witnesses, the executors, everyone within earshot of the bequest become its custodians, and the sin-clause tells them that custody is not honorary. What was heard must be delivered; the delivery is now their act, and its corruption is their sin alone.

**What the Verse Does Not Forbid**

The prohibition has a boundary the jurists drew carefully, and the boundary completes the law rather than weakening it. Al-Qurṭubī distinguished altering a valid bequest from correcting an invalid one: a bequest is not protected by this verse when it was itself unlawful, and such a bequest can be cancelled or modified without incurring the sin. The two examples he gives define the category — a bequest exceeding the third is reduced to the third; a bequest directing something forbidden, such as the gifting of wine, is nullified. The principle underneath is that the verse guards the testator's *lawful* word, not his wordlessness before the law: a will is inviolable inside the boundaries the previous verse set (the third, the non-heir, the fairness), and outside them it carries no protection, because the dead have no right to command sin. This reading is what connects 2:181 to its successor: the changer condemned here alters a bequest against the heirs' rights for his own ends, while the intervener excused there alters a bequest that was itself engineered against those rights. Same physical act — changing the will — opposite moral valence, distinguished entirely by which direction justice runs.

**All-Hearing of the Quiet Crime**

The verse closes with the two names, and their fit to the case is exact. The bequest is among the quietest of legal events: spoken on a deathbed, heard by two or three, committed to memory or a private page, and then tested at a moment when its author cannot testify. The alteration is quieter still — a number adjusted, a name omitted, a document lost, a witness persuaded — performed precisely where human oversight is thinnest, since the one person who could say *that is not what I said* is beyond saying anything. Against that structural invisibility the verse stations the two divine attributes: Allah is All-Hearing — He heard the will as it was spoken, in the room, in its exact words; All-Knowing — He knows the change, the changer, the motive, and the difference between the heard text and the delivered one. The names do the evidentiary work the case cannot otherwise have: the crime of altering a bequest is almost perfectly concealable from people and perfectly unconcealable from God, so the verse's deterrence is the same one the concealment-passages used (2:174) — the surveillance that survives every witness's death. The changer heard; God heard the changer. The sin is on those who alter, and the recording of it is on the One who does not die when the testator does.

**The Dead Man's Word as Continuing Act**

Underlying the verse is a legal-moral conception worth naming: the bequest is treated as the testator's act still in progress. Islamic law generally holds that a person's obligations survive him — debts are paid from the estate, wrongs are answered from what he left, the hajj owed may be performed on his behalf — and the will is the instrument by which the dying extend their agency past death. To alter the will is therefore not to adjust a document but to intercept a person: the dead man is still speaking through it, still giving, still discharging the duties of fairness the previous verse imposed, and the changer's hand falls on the speech itself. This is why the sin is charged so exclusively and so heavily — it is a wrong done to one who cannot complain, in the name of one who cannot consent, and it converts the community's most vulnerable legal moment, the interval between the deathbed and the distribution, into a test of exactly the virtue the surrounding verses keep naming: the mindfulness of God in transactions no one else can audit. The verse's economy of blame — *only on those who alter* — is finally a protection for everyone else in the room: the heirs need not fear the will's corruption, the witnesses know their attestation binds someone, and the dead keep the one power the law can still give them, a word that stands.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:182

> Whoever suspects an error or an injustice in the will and brings about a ˹fair˺ settlement among the parties will not be sinful. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Exception That Guards the Exception**

The previous verse made the will inviolable and charged every alteration to the alterer; this verse opens the one door through which alteration may lawfully pass. Whoever *fears* — suspects, apprehends, has ground to worry — an error or an injustice *from the testator himself*, and then sets matters right between the parties, carries no sin. The structure is deliberate and rare: a prohibition (2:181) immediately qualified by its necessary exception (2:182), so that the law's severity against changers cannot become a shield for a corrupt will. The sin the previous verse assigned to the changer is here lifted from the corrector, and the distinction between the two actors is the verse's entire content. Both change the document; one changes it against justice for gain and bears the sin alone; the other changes it toward justice against a wrongful instrument and bears none. The verse thus completes the bequest-legislation by installing a remedy inside the rule — the dead man's word is protected, but only insofar as his word was just.

**Janaf: The Error and the Injustice**

The two words the corrector may fear — *janaf* and *ithm* — cover the will's two failure-modes. *Ithm* is sin proper: a bequest commanding something forbidden, directing wine or stolen property, exceeding the third with no heir's consent. *Janaf* is subtler, and the exegetes illustrated it with the case that defines it: a dying man leaves property to his son's wife, meaning thereby to enrich the son himself — a will that looks lawful on its face (the son's wife draws no fixed share) but is engineered to route property to someone the law excludes, violating the rule that legal heirs receive no bequests. Al-Qurṭubī records a prophetic report built on the verse's own word, branding *janaf* in wills a grave sin. The classification matters: the testator who commits janaf is not breaking a rule in plain sight but manipulating the rules' gaps — using the bequest's freedom to defeat the inheritance's fairness. It is the deathbed's version of the concealment the passage behind this one prosecuted: form preserved, substance subverted, the letter honored while the intent is smuggled. Against this engineered will, the verse arms the community.

**The Duty of the Living**

The correction the verse authorizes is not optional housekeeping but a communal obligation. Al-Qurṭubī states it as a communal charge: where a will's evident purpose is to sidestep the Quran's fixed shares of inheritance, the community must revise or void it. The actors are named with legal precision: *between them* refers to the heirs; *him* — the one who fears and sets right — is the trustee administering the will, its attesting witnesses (5:106), or whoever holds the charge, though some readings place the initiative with the heirs themselves. The no-sin clause then explains itself against the general rule: altering a will would ordinarily incur the sin of 2:181, but here equity outranks the dead man's directive — the correction is not alteration in the forbidden sense because it does not defeat the dead man's lawful word; it defeats his unlawful one, on behalf of the very system his word attempted to outmaneuver. Al-Rāzī's formulation gives the principle its edge: the corrector acts *for* the testator's real interest and *for* the heirs' right simultaneously, and a change that serves both against a documented injustice is the law repairing itself, not a person overriding the law.

**The Names That Close the Triad**

The bequest-legislation ends where it began, with mercy named: Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful. The two names do specific work here. Forgiveness covers the testator — the man whose will erred or inclined, who perhaps repented too late or never knew his bequest was janaf; the verse corrects his instrument without adding his sin to the changers' accounts, and the forgiveness named leaves his case with God rather than with the estate. And forgiveness covers the corrector — the executor who must judge a dead man's intentions, who may fear wrongly, who may adjust a will that was innocent after all; the no-sin clause is generous precisely because the judgment is hard, and the merciful names assure the hesitant intervener that an honest correction made in fear of injustice stands under pardon even where his fear proved mistaken. The triad of verses thus closes as a complete legal-moral unit: the command to bequeath in fairness (2:180), the protection of the bequest against the greedy living (2:181), and the correction of the bequest against the unjust dead (2:182) — each guarded from the abuse its own emphasis invites, and all three framed by the same names.

**Charity While the Blood Is Warm**

The commentators closed this passage with a caution that protects the verse from a misreading: none of this bequest-legislation diminishes the superior virtue of giving while alive. The tradition prizes the charity given when the giver is *ṣaḥīḥ shaḥīḥ* — healthy and avid, in the full grip of life's attachment to wealth — and reports the Prophet's comparison: the dying donor resembles a man who gives only once his own appetite has been sated. The deathbed gift comes cheap; the healthy gift costs. The jurists fixed the practical boundary: during life a person may dispose of his property freely, in any measure he wishes — the one-third restriction binds only the bequest, the posthumous gift, not the living hand. The distinction keeps 2:182 in perspective: the will is the law's provision for the dying, a bounded instrument fenced against janaf; it is not the main channel of generosity, and the believer who waits for his deathbed to be fair has already spent the years when fairness was costly. The verse forgives the corrector and regulates the testator; the tradition beside it exhorts the healthy — and the three together describe a community in which property is disciplined at death, corrected after death, and given away, ideally, long before.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:183

> O believers! Fasting is prescribed for you—as it was for those before you—so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Kutiba**

The verse begins with the sūrah's legislative formula — *kutiba ʿalaykum*, it is written upon you, it is prescribed — the same verb that established the retaliation in cases of murder (2:178), and the formula carries the same weight here: fasting is not recommended, not ancestral custom, not a spiritual option; it is written. The obligation it creates became, in its final form, the fast of Ramadan, counted by all the schools of law among the five pillars of Islam: complete abstinence from food, drink, and sexual relations from dawn until sunset, across every day of the lunar month. The verse that prescribes it is addressed to the believers specifically — O you who believe — where the food permission had gone out to all humanity (2:168); the fast belongs to the covenant community, and its prescription dates, the exegetical sources record, to shortly before the Battle of Badr, in the second year of the Hijrah — the same season of legislation that gave the community its qiblah. A people turned toward the Kaʿbah, given its murder-law and its wills-law, now receives the law of its months: the body itself enters the legislation.

**As It Was for Those Before You**

The prescription arrives with a company clause: fasting was prescribed for those before you as well. The exegetes identified the predecessors at several scopes — the Christians, the People of the Book generally, or all peoples in general — and the clause does its work at every scope. It answers the objection the new obligations invited: this is not a burden invented for you, not a novel austerity by which this community is tested more harshly than the righteous of history. The fast is old — older than the qiblah controversy, older than the sects, recognizable in the practice of the very communities whose claims the sūrah had just adjudicated. The clause also establishes the fast's ecumenical intelligibility: a discipline every prophetic tradition received is a discipline about something universal in the human condition, and what it addresses — appetite's sovereignty over the will — is the same in every generation that practiced it. The believers are enrolled in an ancient order rather than initiated into a private one, and the enrollment is itself consolation: the difficulty ahead has been borne before, by people the Qur'an elsewhere honors, under the same prescription's essential form.

**So That You May Become Mindful**

The purpose clause names the fast's product: taqwā — mindfulness, reverence, the guarded consciousness of God that the sūrah has made the end of every law it legislates. The retaliation was given so that the community might become mindful (2:179); the bequest is an obligation on the mindful (2:180); and the fast is prescribed so that perhaps the fasting will produce the same quality. The fit between the discipline and the goal is exact, and it is why the verse needs no elaboration. Taqwā is the state of a person whose actions are governed by an unseen standard — who abstains from what he could take because a Presence he cannot see forbids it. Fasting is that state rendered physical and continuous: for the whole bright day, with food in reach and appetite intact, the fasting person abstains from what is otherwise lawful to him, and no observer can tell whether he is fasting — the discipline's compliance is invisible, its inspection internal. A month of this is a month of practiced taqwā, the heart learning by repetition that the unseen command outweighs the visible opportunity. The other pillars have public forms — the prayer is seen, the alms are counted, the pilgrimage is traveled; the fast alone is a secret between the servant and his Lord, which is why the tradition reports, in the sacred ḥadīth of the fast, God saying that every deed of the human being is for himself except the fasting — it is for Me, and I reward it.

**The Hunger That Teaches**

The pedagogy of the fast runs through the body, and the verse's prescription takes the whole body as its classroom. Hunger and thirst are the two appetites no human can argue with; for one lunar month the believer argues with them anyway, daily, and wins by abstention rather than satisfaction. The training generalizes immediately: the appetite that is refused at noon is the same faculty that must refuse the forbidden morsel of 2:168, the bribed judge of 2:188, the illicit gain of 2:174 — the fast is a rehearsal of every refusal the law will later demand, performed in the easiest case, where the refused thing is lawful and only the hour forbids it. The tradition drew the same conclusion from the fast's effects on speech and temper, requiring the fasting person to abstain from false and idle talk as well as food, so that the discipline covers the tongue and the appetite together. This is taqwā being manufactured: not the abstract reverence of doctrine but the drilled reflex of a body that has learned, thirty times running, that a command can stand between it and its desire — and a body that has learned this in the small case is being prepared for the large ones the sūrah is about to legislate, on the battlefield where appetite's cousin, fear, will make the same demands in the opposite direction.

**The Ease Already in the Prescription**

The verse prescribes absolutely, but the legislation it opens is famous for the exemptions built into its following verses — the ill, the traveler, those who bear the fast only with difficulty, all provided for with alternatives of makeup days and feeding the poor. This verse states the obligation without stating the concessions, and the sequence is deliberate: the command comes first in its full weight, so the community receives the fast as written law rather than as negotiable advice, and the ease arrives afterward as the Lawgiver's own qualification — God intends ease for you, the coming verse will say, not hardship. The pedagogical order matters. A law announced with its exemptions already attached is received as a suggestion; a law announced in full, then softened by the One who announced it, is received as authority tempered by mercy — and the tempering teaches more about the Legislator than an originally soft law ever could. The believers of Medina heard the prescription whole, and heard the easements as gifts; the structure produced the Ramadan the tradition describes, a month whose severity is undertaken with joy, precisely because the joy is the mercy inside the severity, legislated in that order.

**A Community Between Two Laws**

The verse's placement completes a legislative triptych that defines the new community from three sides. Blood was regulated — the feud replaced by equivalence, pardon, and mercy (2:178–179). Property was regulated — the deathbed governed by fairness, custody, and correction (2:180–182). Now the body is regulated — appetite governed by the month, the day, and the unseen standard of taqwā. The three laws answer the three domains in which human societies destroy themselves: violence, wealth, and desire; and the same purpose-clause runs through all three, so that you may be mindful. The fast is the triptych's central panel in a further sense — it is the one discipline every believer performs personally and daily, the retaliation being the rare case and the bequest the final one, and it therefore carries the community's moral formation through the ordinary month rather than the exceptional event. Between the sūrah's food permissions and its coming war-legislation, this verse installs the training ground: a people learning, one hunger at a time, that what God has written upon them is written for what it makes of them — and what it is making here, the verse says in its last word, is the reverent.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:184

> ˹Fast a˺ prescribed number of days. But whoever of you is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺. For those who can only fast with extreme difficulty, compensation can be made by feeding a needy person ˹for every day not fasted˺. But whoever volunteers to give more, it is better for them. And to fast is better for you, if only you knew.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Days, Numbered**

The verse opens by describing the fast as *numbered days* — ayyām maʿdūdāt — and the commentators divided over what those days first named. One reading, recorded by al-Ṭabarī, identifies them with the days of Ramadan itself, the verse being a compact statement of the month-fast with its exemptions. The other reading identifies an earlier, shorter obligation: before Ramadan was legislated, the community is reported to have kept three days of fasting each month along with the fast of ʿĀshūrāʾ, the tenth of Muḥarram — and this verse, on that account, prescribed those numbered days, with the Ramadan-verses that follow superseding them. The ʿĀshūrāʾ practice is well attested: the reports describe the Muslims fasting the tenth of Muḥarram, with some connecting it to the Jews' fast on that day, others to the day Noah's ark came to rest on the mountain. Al-Bukhārī preserves the decisive exchange (2004): the Prophet came to Medina and found the Jews fasting ʿĀshūrāʾ because it was the day God saved the Children of Israel from Pharaoh, for which Moses fasted in gratitude — and he answered, *we have more right to Moses than you*, fasting the day himself and commanding the fast (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2004). The numbering matters for another reason: a fast of counted days is a fast with an end, and the Qur'an's first word about the discipline is that its duration is finite, bounded, and known in advance — the ease-theme of the whole legislation stated in its opening noun.

**Was the Earlier Fast Obligatory?**

The three-days reading generated a secondary question the exegetes pursued honestly: if those numbered days preceded Ramadan, was their observance an obligation? Opinions differed. Some held the three days a genuine duty, later lifted by the month-fast. Others maintained no fast was ever obligatory before Ramadan. Al-Ṭabarī weighed the reports and gave the decisive methodological verdict: there is no reliable report that any specific fast before Ramadan was ever an obligation — the evidence simply does not establish it, and the question is left where the evidence leaves it. What the tradition unanimously affirms is the continuation of the practice as merit: the three days each month remained a beloved observance of the Prophet and the righteous after Ramadan was legislated, never abrogated as a voluntary act because it was never established as a compulsory one. The scholarly episode is a small exhibit in the Qur'an's own evidentiary ethic — the exegetes distinguishing what the reports compel from what they merely permit, and refusing to legislate certainty where transmission is silent.

**The Sick and the Traveler**

The exemption clause is the verse's operative law: whoever among you is sick, or on a journey, fasts a number of other days instead. The structure is substitution, not cancellation — the missed fast is not forgiven but *deferred*, kept as a debt to be discharged in healthier or settled days. The jurists read the clause as requiring the concession to be used where the harm is real: the sick person for whom fasting impedes recovery, the traveler whose journey meets the law's threshold, are not merely permitted to break the fast but in many readings expected to, since the verse grants them the exemption as a gift from the same hand that gave the obligation. The details the schools developed — what degree of illness, what distance of journey, whether the traveler may fast if he prefers — belong to the verse's afterlife, and the next verse will carry them forward; here the principle stands: the law of the fast is written for bodies, and bodies differ, so the law differs with them. A numbered fast with numbered makeup days is an obligation that has done arithmetic on human weakness and legislated for it.

**Those Who Can Bear It Only With Difficulty**

The third clause — *and upon those who can bear it only with difficulty is a redemption: the feeding of a poor person* — was read in two directions, and both readings are classical. The first, reported from the early community and recorded by al-Qurṭubī, treats the clause as an original option: in the fast's earliest legislation, whoever wished could feed a poor person for each day and not fast at all — a concession later withdrawn by the Ramadan-command that whoever is present in the month should fast it (2:185), which abrogated the choice and left the feeding only for those incapable. The second reading, which al-Qurṭubī preferred on the grammar, finds no abrogation: the root ṭ-w-q here denotes the ones who bear the fast with hardship rather than the ones who merely could but need not — the chronically ill whose condition will not lift, the elderly whose strength is spent — and for them the feeding of a poor person per day is not a purchased exemption but the substitute duty their incapacity creates. On this reading the makeup-days clause covers the temporarily unable, and this clause covers the permanently unable, and the two together leave no body without a law. The grammar that supports it is the reading's own evidence: the difficult-bearing are those for whom the fast remains possible but punishing, and the verse prices that punishment at a meal.

**Whoever Volunteers More**

The clause that follows — whoever volunteers good, it is better for him — was explained by al-Qurṭubī in two concrete directions. The volunteer may feed more than the minimum: a poor person for each day becomes two, and the extra is his own merit. Or he may keep feeding beyond the redemption, giving the poor even when the law's requirement is already discharged. The voluntariness is the verse's hinge between duty and virtue: the feeding is fixed at one poor person per day, but the good above the fixed amount is welcomed without limit, and the verdict on it is unambiguous — it is better. The same verse thereby answers a question the exemption system always raises: whether concessions cheapen devotion. They do not; they relocate it. The one who cannot fast feeds; the one who feeds beyond the requirement has taken the fast's inner logic — hunger transferred into generosity — further than the fasting itself would have. The law's floor is exact, and above the floor the verse opens the voluntary ascent that the whole sūrah's charity-legislation has been describing since the spending-verses of its opening.

**Fasting Is Better for You, If You Knew**

The verse closes by returning to the fast itself with a comparative verdict: to fast is better for you, if you only knew. Al-Qurṭubī's glosses gather the comparison's terms. Better than the redemption — for the one capable of both, the fast outvalues the feeding, because the discipline does to the soul what the substituted meal cannot. And better even within the exemptions: for the traveler and the sick person for whom fasting is not severely harmful, keeping the fast outranks taking the concession — a ruling the exegete attributes in its general form to the practice of the Companions, noting that the details differ and that knowledge of them rests with God. The clause *if you only knew* is the verse's tenderness toward the exempted: the concession is real, the permission is God's own, and still the fast is named the better path for those it does not harm, because its goods — the practiced taqwā, the tasted hunger, the secret kept between the servant and the Lord — are known fully only to those who have kept it. The verse ends where the prescription began: numbered days, numbered exemptions, numbered redemptions, and above all the arithmetic a comparative the reader is invited to verify by fasting.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:185

> Ramaḍân is the month in which the Quran was revealed as a guide for humanity with clear proofs of guidance and the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺. So whoever is present this month, let them fast. But whoever is ill or on a journey, then ˹let them fast˺ an equal number of days ˹after Ramaḍân˺. Allah intends ease for you, not hardship, so that you may complete the prescribed period and proclaim the greatness of Allah for guiding you, and perhaps you will be grateful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Month Defined by Its Book**

The verse names the month and defines it — not by its fast but by its revelation. Ramadan is the month in which the Qur'an was sent down, as guidance for humanity, with the clear signs and the criterion. The priority of this definition is the verse's first lesson: the month is sacred because of what entered the world through it, and the fast is the human response to that entry, not its cause. The exegetes described the descent in two stages, following the Qur'an's own accounts elsewhere: the Book was sent down in its entirety to the guarded tablet in heaven — the preserved original of 85:22 — and thence to the lowest heaven of this world, from which the angel Gabriel brought it to the Prophet passage by passage, occasion by occasion, across twenty-three years. The month's connection to that descent is fixed by the Night of Power within it — the night better than a thousand months, on which the sending down occurred (97:1–2) — so that every Ramadan reenacts, in its fast and its recitation, the month the Book arrived. The believers do not merely fast in Ramadan; they fast in the anniversary of revelation, and the traditional month-long recitation of the whole Qur'an in the night prayers keeps the definition audible.

**Guidance, Clear Signs, Criterion**

The three descriptors the verse gives the Book map the ways a revelation guides. *Hudan* — guidance — is direction itself, the road named. *Bayyināt* — the clear signs, the manifest proofs — are the evidence along the road, the verses and demonstrations that make the direction recognizable as true rather than merely asserted. *Furqān* — the criterion, the separator — is the instrument of judgment, the standard by which right is distinguished from wrong, case by case. The same triad describes revelation's function throughout the Qur'an, and its presence here explains why the month of the Book is kept by the body: a criterion is not only read but practiced, and the fast is the practice in which the separation between the lawful and the forbidden is felt hourly — the morsel permitted at sunset and forbidden at noon is furqān made edible. The verse thus ties the month's two contents together: the Book that separates truth from falsehood, and the fast that trains the will in every smaller separation, so that the community holding both learns the criterion with its mind in the recitation and with its hunger in the day.

**Whoever Is Present, Let Him Fast**

The command that follows is the legislation's completion: whoever of you is present in the month, let him fast it. The wording — present, witnessing the month — was read against the exemptions of the previous verse, and the reading fixed the law's shape. Al-Qurṭubī records the decisive consequence: this command abrogated the option, reported in the early community, of feeding a poor person instead of fasting; from this verse forward the fast is the duty of everyone present and able, and the feeding remains only for those who cannot. The exemptions are then repeated in the same breath — the sick, the traveler, the same number of other days — and the repetition is legally significant: the concession survives the tightening. The month-fast is now universal in obligation and particular in application, binding on the present and the well, lifted for the journeying and the ill, with the deferral arithmetic unchanged. The jurists' debates over the clause's details — how sick, how far a journey, whether the traveler fasts if able — are the verse's working-out in the schools, with opinions differing as they do; but the structure is the verse's own and admitted by all: presence in the month triggers the fast, incapacity suspends it, and the suspended days are kept as a debt to the same law.

**Ease Intended, Not Hardship**

The reason clause is among the most-quoted sentences in Islamic legal literature: *God desires ease for you, and does not desire hardship for you*. The clause is not decoration; it is a hermeneutic key the jurists applied across the law. The exemptions of illness and journey are instances of the desired ease — the same Lawgiver who commanded the fast removed it from the bodies it would harm, and the removal is as much His will as the command. The principle generalizes: no hardship is laid upon you in the religion (22:78), and the Prophet's standing instruction to his envoys was to make things easy and not difficult, to give glad tidings and not drive people away. The verse thereby installs mercy inside the legislation's logic — the fast is severe and the severity is bounded by the same hand, so the believer receives both the discipline and its limits as one gift. This is why the exemptions are not experienced as loopholes in the tradition but as evidence: the concession proves the Legislator's intent, and the intent explains why the obligated fast is undertaken joyfully rather than resentfully. A law whose author has declared that He desires ease is a law whose every harshness carries its own measured scope.

**Completing the Number and Proclaiming the Greatness**

The verse's final movement gives the month its ending: complete the number, and magnify God for having guided you. The completion was read two ways, both operative. The first: complete the count of the fast's days — whether the month arrives at twenty-nine or thirty, its number is completed by the sighting that ends it, and the makeup days of the exempted complete their number in turn. The second: complete the obligations the month carries, so that nothing of the prescribed period is left unperformed. Then the magnification — *takbīr* — which the tradition located at the month's close in the chanting of *Allāhu akbar* on the way to the festival prayer, the community proclaiming God's greatness aloud after thirty days of proclaiming it silently, by hunger. The clause states the reason for the proclamation: *for having guided you* — the takbīr is gratitude for the guidance, which is the same word the verse used for the Book itself. The month thus ends as it began, in the vocabulary of guidance: the Book sent down as guidance, the fasters magnifying God for having guided, the whole legislation framed as one course in being led. And the last word opens beyond it — that you may be thankful — placing the completed fast on the same footing as every blessing the sūrah has legislated gratitude for, the month's hunger resolving into the community's thanks.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:186

> When My servants ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about Me: I am truly near. I respond to one’s prayer when they call upon Me. So let them respond ˹with obedience˺ to Me and believe in Me, perhaps they will be guided ˹to the Right Way˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question of Distance**

The verse arrives in the fast-legislation as an answer to a question the reports preserve in several forms. Some Companions asked, *Where is our Lord?* — and at what hour should we call upon Him? Others report a Bedouin's question with the same architecture: is our Lord near, that we should whisper to Him, or far, that we should cry out? The occasion matters because the answer addresses distance directly, and the answer is a first-person declaration from God: *I am near*. Al-Rāzī noted the theological labor the verse performs — it repels the imagination of divine remoteness that makes prayer feel like shouting into vacancy, and it does so in the simplest possible grammar. No mediation is commanded, no ritual apparatus interposed, no time-window assigned; the question of where and when collapses into the assertion of nearness. The verse's placement inside the Ramadan passage deepens the collapse: the fasting community, which has spent its days refusing lawful things for an unseen Commander, is told that the Commander is near — that the unseen is not the far, and that the intimacy the hunger has been practicing all month is reciprocated on God's side by proximity.

**The Answer Without "Say"**

The verse carries a structural distinction visible on the page of the Qur'an itself. The sūrah is full of questions routed through the Prophet — they ask you about the new moons, *say*… (2:189); they ask you what they should spend, *say*… (2:215); they ask you about fighting in the sacred month, *say*… (2:217); they ask you about wine, about orphans, about the Hour — each time the answer is handed to the Prophet to deliver, the command *qul* interposed between question and reply. Here alone in the sequence, when the servants ask about God Himself, the *say* is absent: the verse moves directly from the question to *I am near* — God answering in His own person, without the prophetic relay. The commentators marked the difference and read it as intimacy legislated into the syntax: on every other subject the revelation speaks about God; on this one God speaks. The servant who asks where his Lord is receives not information transmitted but presence declared, and the first-person voice — *innī*, I, am — is itself the answer's content. The nearness is not a fact about God reported by a prophet; it is God's own word in the moment of asking.

**I Answer the Call of the Caller**

The declaration expands into a promise with the structure of reciprocity: when My servants call, I answer — *I respond to the call of the caller when he calls upon Me*. The same promise grounds the Qur'an's great invitation elsewhere: call upon Me, I will respond to you (40:60); and its most urgent case is named in the sūrah of the Ants — who answers the distressed when he calls upon Him (27:62). The answering here is unconditional in form: the caller calls, and the response is given; no merit-clause qualifies it, no worthiness-test precedes it. The tradition supplied the mechanics of what answering means — the request granted, or averted evil substituted for it, or reward stored against the Day — but the verse's own claim is the bare reciprocity: the call does not fall into silence. This is the fast's hidden dialogue made explicit. For a month the believer has been addressing an unseen Lord with his whole bodily state, and the verse assures him that the address arrives: the nearness is not spatial metaphor but responsiveness — God is near in the manner of one who answers. The servants who asked *where* are told *how*: not at a place, but in the responding.

**Be Kind to Yourselves: The Voice and the Shout**

The nearness-verse generated one of the tradition's most practical corrections. Al-Bukhārī preserves the scene (6384): on a journey, the people raised their voices in proclamation and supplication until the Prophet called out — *O people, be kind to yourselves; you are not calling one who is deaf or absent — you are calling the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, and He is nearer to you than the neck of your riding animal*. The report applies this verse to volume: the shout assumes a distance the verse denies. If God is near, hearing, and seeing, then the raised voice does not improve delivery — it only exhausts the caller, and the exhaustion is the unkindness to the self the Prophet named. The correction reeducates the worshiper's imagination: prayer is not transmission across a gap but address to a Presence, and the Presence requires neither amplification nor repetition to hear. This is why the Qur'an's own instruction on the manner of calling pairs humility with secrecy — call upon your Lord humbly and in secret (7:55) — and why the tradition prized the silent dhikr and the night's whispered prayer: not because God hears them better, but because they confess what the loud prayer forgets — that the One called upon is already near, already hearing, already answering.

**Nearer Than the Vein**

The nearness declared here has a whole geography elsewhere in the Qur'an, and the verse is its legal center. God is closer to the human being than his jugular vein (50:16) — nearer than the body's own instrument of life; closer than the people between whom and their hearts He intervenes (8:24); and at the hour of death closer still — when the soul reaches the throat, We are nearer to him than you, though you do not see (56:85). The nearness has its eschatological form too: David's repentance was sealed with nearness and a beautiful return (38:25), and the Garden's own inhabitants are addressed by the name that repeats it — peace be upon you for your patience, the near ones. And the name itself, *al-Qarīb*, the Ever Near, stands among the divine names, paired with the All-Hearing in the very verses of this sūrah's Abraham-passages (34:50). Set against this constellation, the servants' question about location reads as the perennial human mistake — imagining transcendence as absence — and the verse's answer as its permanent correction: the God above the throne is the God nearer than the vein, and the fasting servant's whispered call travels a distance of zero.

**Let Them Respond to Me**

The verse closes by turning the reciprocity into a command: since I answer when they call, let them respond to Me, and believe in Me, that they may be rightly guided. The response demanded is not another calling but the whole life's answer — obedience answering the nearness, belief answering the response. Al-Rāzī read the clause within the fast's own context: the ease God legislated in the fasting — the exemptions, the bounded days, the answered prayers of the fasting hours — calls for the servants' answering faithfulness in return; the concession and the command are two movements of one covenant. The word for respond is the same root as the promise — God *yastajīb* to the caller, and the callers are to *yastajībū* to God — so the verse builds a circuit of answering: the call goes up, the response comes down, and the human response climbs again as belief and obedience. The final clause names the circuit's destination: that they may be guided. The guidance here is not the Book-guidance of the previous verse but its appropriation — the guided direction lived, the nearness trusted, the answered caller answering back. The question *where is our Lord?* receives its complete answer in a sequence: He is near; He responds; respond to Him; and the responding is itself the way.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:187

> It has been made permissible for you to be intimate with your wives during the nights preceding the fast. Your spouses are a garment for you as you are for them. Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves. So He has accepted your repentance and pardoned you. So now you may be intimate with them and seek what Allah has prescribed for you. ˹You may˺ eat and drink until you see the light of dawn breaking the darkness of night, then complete the fast until nightfall. Do not be intimate with your spouses while you are meditating in the mosques. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not exceed them. This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to people, so they may become mindful ˹of Him˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Rule and Its Early Hardship**

The verse legislates by easing, and the reports behind it describe what was eased. In the fast's first years the night was not free: food and marital relations were permitted only until the night prayer, after which the fast effectively began — one school of reports even describing abstinence through the entire month's nights, with the concession coming only in response to the community's failure to keep it. The case the tradition names most often is ʿUmar's: he confessed to the Prophet that he had approached his wife after the night prayer, and the answer came that he had not been firm in holding to the original restriction — a rebuke accompanied by relief, since the verse that followed made the whole night lawful. Al-Qurṭubī preserves the companion case of Qays ibn Ṣirmah, who worked his land all day during Ramadan, came home exhausted, and — his wife having gone to fetch food while he slept, which under the old rule ended his eating for the day — passed out; the next day's collapse in the Prophet's presence brought the question of the rule's severity into the open. Against this background the verse's opening verb is significant: it has been *made permissible* — a permission granted, an earlier narrowness lifted by the same authority that imposed it.

**They Are a Garment for You**

The easing arrives with the Qur'an's most intimate marriage image: your wives are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them. The exegetes read the metaphor in both directions — the covering, the protection, the mutual envelope spouses provide one another, each concealing what the other would not wish exposed and each warming what the other cannot warm alone — and the reciprocity is the image's heart: the garment clause runs both ways in a single sentence, making the marriage a mutual indwelling rather than a one-sided shelter. The choice of metaphor serves the law beside it: the night before the fast belongs to the marriage, and the marriage belongs to both parties equally. The verse had legislated the fast as a full day's abstinence from food, drink, and sexual relations; this clause restores the third to its night, and in restoring it describes what is restored — not an indulgence tolerated between obligations but the spouses' mutual covering, itself a good the fast's daytime suspension now protects by bounding rather than destroys. The tradition drew the practical consequence the commentators state plainly: the concession is a relaxation within the worship, so that the month of the body's discipline is also the month of the marriage's lawful warmth.

**He Knew You Were Deceiving Yourselves**

Between the permission and its image stands a diagnosis: *God knew that you were deceiving yourselves* — betraying yourselves, as the word's root suggests — and He turned to you and pardoned you. The self-deception named is the community's under the old rule: the reports of ʿUmar and others describe believers failing the night-restriction and then bearing the failure as guilt, and the verse identifies the double harm — the rule exceeded the people's constancy, and the exceeding produced not merely infractions but self-betrayal, the worshiper at war with his own nature inside his own devotion. God's knowledge of this is the verse's tender clause: the Lawgiver watched the community deceiving itself, and the response was not enforcement but *turning* — the same word the repentance-passages use, God turning to the sinner — followed by pardon. The legislative easing is thus framed as an act of mercy rather than retreat: the law changed because the Lawgiver knew, turned, and forgave, and the new permission arrives inside that sequence. The verse teaches a principle of revelation's dealing with human weakness: the command is not adjusted to appetite, but the community's honest failure is met by a mercy that re-legislates — the fast remains, the night is freed, and the self-deception ends.

**Seek What God Has Ordained**

The permission is then enlarged: be with them now, and seek what God has ordained for you. The exegetes read the seeking in two directions, both rooted in the word's usage. It is the seeking of children — the marital night open to the generation the fast's daytime rule suspends, the ordinance of progeny continuing its course through the holy month. And it is the seeking of the Night of Power within those same nights — the night better than a thousand months, on which the Qur'an was sent down (97:1), sought by the worshiper in the month's latter part even as the marriage keeps its rights in the month's every night. The double reading composes the verse's vision of Ramadan's darkness: it is not a void between fasted days but a field of ordained goods — the children conceived, the night-prayer kept, the decree-night watched for — and the concession that freed the night for the marriage freed it for all of these at once. The wording *what God has ordained for you* keeps the emphasis where the easing placed it: the night's goods are not tolerations of the flesh but ordinances of the Lawgiver, licensed from the same hand that licensed the day's abstinence, so that the believer moves between the two without contradiction — the fast's discipline by daylight, the ordainment's warmth by dark, both commanded, both worship.

**The White Thread and the Black Thread**

The verse's most famous detail fixes the fast's beginning: eat and drink until the white thread of dawn becomes distinct from the black thread of night. The idiom — the two threads as the first light against the last dark — was initially taken literally by some Companions, and al-Bukhārī preserves the case of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim (1917): he placed a black cord and a white cord under his pillow and watched them through the night, unable to tell one from the other, until the Prophet explained that the verse means the darkness of night and the whiteness of dawn. The report does double duty. It documents the community's scrupulosity — a man watching cords rather than guess at his fast's boundary — and it models the Qur'an's idiom being read as idiom: the threads are the horizon's two colors, not two objects, and the distinction is the true dawn's lateral spreading light against the night. The other reports of the verse's descent add the phenomenon's detail: the light of dawn appearing in the sky, the tops of mountains and houses catching illumination, the white thread emerging from the black. The resulting law is the fast's daily architecture — from true dawn to sunset, the boundary marked by light itself, so that every fasting community reads its obligation off its own sky, and ʿAdī's cords remain the tradition's emblem of literalism corrected by the Prophet's own exegesis.

**Retreat, Limits, and the Signs Made Clear**

The verse closes with three clauses that frame the whole legislation. First, the boundary on the concession: do not approach your wives while you are in retreat in the mosques — the *iʿtikāf*, the practice of staying in the mosque for days of prayer and remembrance, which the Prophet observed in Ramadan's last ten days, and twenty days in the year of his death. The retreat suspends even the night's permission: the mosque-stayer has left the marriage's hours entirely for worship, and the law marks that leaving as inviolable. Then the formula: *those are the limits of God — do not approach them*. The wording is deliberately stronger than transgression-language: the limits are not merely not to be crossed but not to be approached, the believer stationed away from the boundary rather than balanced on it — the same precaution the sūrah applied to the property of orphans and the sacred months. And finally the verse's own purpose: thus God makes His signs clear to people, that they may be mindful. The clarity is the gift — the fast's hours defined, its nights freed, its exemptions itemized, its retreat bounded, nothing left to guesswork — and the clarity serves the same end every law in this passage has served: taqwā. The verse that opened by easing the marriage-night closes by fencing it, and between the easing and the fence the whole Ramadan stands legislated: the day of discipline, the night of ordinance, the mosque of retreat, and over all of them the limits made clear by the God who knew, turned, and pardoned.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:188

> Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly, nor deliberately bribe authorities in order to devour a portion of others’ property, knowing that it is a sin.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wealth Gets Its Food-Law**

The verse arrives between the fast-legislation and the war-legislation, and its position is its argument: after the month that trains the body to refuse lawful food at forbidden hours, the sūrah legislates the permanent refusal — wealth that may never be consumed at any hour, by anyone, however lawfully it is served. The prohibition's first clause is general and mutual: consume not one another's wealth *by the false* — the word *bāṭil* covering every mode of taking that is void, wrongful, or deceptive: theft and fraud, usury and gambling, false contracts and withheld wages, the whole economy of taking what the taking does not entitle. The mutuality matters: *between you* makes the property of every member of the community sacred to every other, and the verse thereby completes the food-legislation it follows — 2:168–169 commanded eating of the lawful and the good and forbade the steps of Satan; this verse extends the same lawfulness from the plate to the purse. The fast trained appetite's obedience for thirty days; this verse legislates appetite's obedience for wealth, where the hunger is less honest and the temptation better dressed.

**Nor Offer It to the Judges**

The second clause narrows to a specific machinery: nor proffer it to the judges — literally, nor throw your wealth to the rulers, so that you may consume a portion of people's wealth in sin, knowingly. The verb's image is of the bribe as something flung toward the bench: wealth deployed not as payment for goods but as ammunition aimed at justice itself. The crime the clause describes is two-staged and both stages are indicted. The first stage is the private injustice — the claim to a portion of another's property that the claimant knows he does not own. The second is the instrumentalization of the court: the bribe exists to convert the unjust claim into a legal victory, to make the machinery of right adjudicate a wrong. The verse's final words — *and you know* — fix the culpability at its maximum: this is not error or disputed entitlement but knowing sin, the briber fully aware that what he seeks from the judge is another's property. Al-Qurṭubī's gloss draws the clause's sharpest edge: even if a judge sincerely decides in the briber's favor, the ruling is not lawful for him, because he knows it to be false in fact — the courtroom's verdict cannot launder a claim its claimant knows to be void.

**The Ruling That Cannot Make Lawful**

From that gloss grows the verse's central legal-moral doctrine: the separation of legal title from moral right. A court decides on evidence and procedure; it can be deceived, out-lawyered, or bought; and when it is, its judgment transfers possession but not entitlement. The tradition's proof-text is the report al-Bukhārī preserves from Umm Salamah (2680): the Prophet said — *I am only a human being, and people bring their disputes to me; some of you may be more eloquent in argument than others, so I may judge in favor of the one whose eloquence prevails. If I give someone what is in truth another's right, I am only giving him a piece of the Fire — let him not take it.* The hadith universalizes the verse's case: the judge is human, the eloquent litigant may win unjustly, and the prophetic verdict converts the ill-gotten award into its substance — fire, the same conversion 2:174 applied to the concealers' gain and 4:10 to the devourers of orphans' property. The briber of 2:188 has purchased exactly this: a favorable ruling that is, before God, a coal. The verse and the report together establish that the law's outer verdict and the soul's inner standing run on separate tracks, and the bribe is the attempt — always futile on the second track — to make the first serve the second's crimes.

**The Corruption of the Instrument**

The clause indicts more than the briber, and the tradition read it that way. A judicial system that can be proffered wealth is a system whose officers are for sale, and the Qur'an's legislation against bribery has its counterpart in its legislation of judges — the sūrah of the Table's command to judge by what God has sent down and its portrait of those who judge by other than it (5:44–45), the sūrah's own instruction that disputes be brought to God and the Messenger rather than managed privately. The bribe's social damage exceeds its private crime: each purchased verdict teaches the community that verdicts are purchasable, and the teaching destroys the instrument that 2:178–179 had just made the alternative to the feud. The retaliation-law replaced blood-vendetta with courts; the courts exist only while their judgments are trusted to track justice rather than money. The briber therefore commits a double betrayal — of the neighbor whose portion he covets and of the system whose integrity his neighbors' lives depend on — and the verse's placement immediately after the qiṣāṣ and bequest legislation is exact: blood regulated, wills regulated, and now the regulator itself, the court, fenced against the wealth that would capture it.

**The Economy of the Fast**

The verse's adjacency to Ramadan is not incidental, and the commentators felt the connection. The fasting month trains the believer in abstention from the lawful — food, drink, intimacy — for a bounded time, for God; this verse commands abstention from the unlawful — other people's wealth — for all time, for the same God. The pedagogy runs from the easier refusal to the harder: if the body can be taught that a morsel permitted at sunset is forbidden at noon because God said so, the hand can be taught that wealth obtainable by bribe is forbidden always because God said so. The *and you know* of the verse addresses the same faculty the fast disciplines — the knowing appetite, the desire that understands perfectly well what it is doing — and the Ramadan just legislated is its annual school. The tradition reinforced the link by requiring the fasting person to fast from false speech and wrongful action as well as food, and by warning that the hunger of the one who does not abandon falsehood gains him nothing with God. The verse stands, then, as the fast's civil code: the month ends, the abstention continues — the plate returned to lawfulness at the ʿīd, the purse never opened to the false.

**Knowing as the Aggravator**

The last words of the verse deserve final weight, because they mark its difference from the errors of property the law also governs. Islamic jurisprudence legislates extensively for honest dispute — contested inheritances, unclear contract terms, mistaken boundaries — and provides courts precisely for cases where knowledge is genuinely divided. This verse is not addressed to those cases. Its target is the taker who *knows*: the claimant aware that the portion is another's, the briber certain his eloquence is purchasing what he has no right to. The knowledge clause strips the crime's usual camouflage — the self-narratives of entitlement, the *it's complicated*, the *technically I'm owed* — and leaves the act naked: a knowing hand, reaching past a known line, using the law's own instruments to do it. The same clause explains the verse's severity of framing: sins of ignorance are the ones repentance most readily reaches, and the sūrah has legislated repentance generously (2:160, 2:182); the knowing consumption of another's wealth is the sin committed with the conscience fully briefed, and its only remedy is the piece of Fire's return — restoring the portion before the verdict of the higher court, where no eloquence prevails and every ruling tracks the truth.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:189

> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about the phases of the moon. Say, “They are a means for people to determine time and pilgrimage.” Righteousness is not in entering your houses from the back doors. Rather, righteousness is to be mindful ˹of Allah˺. So enter your homes through their ˹proper˺ doors, and be mindful of Allah so you may be successful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question and the Redirect**

The verse follows the sūrah's familiar question-form — they ask you — and its answer performs a characteristic move: it declines the question as posed and answers the need behind it. The reports about what was actually being asked vary — some describe curiosity about the moon's waxing and waning, its physical mechanics; others describe a practical inquiry about the new moons' function — but the answer is the same in every case: *they are means of timing for people, and for the pilgrimage*. The redirect is the verse's method. Speculation about the celestial mechanism is not forbidden, but it is not what the community needs legislated; what it needs is to know what the moons are *for*, and the verse supplies the for: the religious calendar. The same pattern governs the sūrah's other question-verses — the inquiry about spending answered with the list of recipients (2:215), the inquiry about the sacred month answered with the hierarchy of sins (2:217) — revelation answering in the register of practice rather than theory, turning every question toward the life it must govern. The moon asked about as an object is answered as an instrument, and the instrument's user is the worshiper.

**The Moon That Is Seen, Not the Moon That Is**

The verse's word — *ahillah*, the new moons, plural of hilāl — denotes specifically the visible crescent, and the distinction is astronomical as well as legal. The Islamic month does not begin at the astronomical new moon, when sun and moon share the sky and the lunar disc is dark and invisible; it begins with the first sighting of the waxing crescent after sunset. The mechanics the tradition describes are exact: the moon's orbit is inclined to the ecliptic, so the dark conjunction-moon passes north or south of the sun unseen; as it moves eastward in its orbit its angular distance from the sun grows, and when that separation and the timing after sunset suffice, the thin crescent becomes visible above the western horizon — the hilāl whose sighting opens the month. The law attaches itself to this visibility deliberately: a calendar keyed to an invisible conjunction would require calculation invisible to the herdsman and the Bedouin, while a calendar keyed to the seen crescent can be kept by any community with clear western sky. The means-of-timing the verse names is thus a timing *for people* — the phrase is emphatic — an instrument calibrated to human eyes rather than to abstract astronomy, which is why the sighting, and not the computation, remained the law's trigger across the tradition.

**Timing and Pilgrimage: The Calendar Built**

The two functions the verse names — timing for people, and the pilgrimage — cover the religious year's architecture. The lunar months order everything the community must date: Ramadan's fast begins with a crescent and ends with a crescent (2:185's completing of the number); the hajj belongs to months appointed (2:197), whose first is another sighting; the ʿīds, the zakāh-year, the ʿiddah of widows and divorced women (2:234), the months of the truce and the sacred months — all run on the hilāl's arithmetic. The pilgrimage is named separately because it is the calendar's summit: the one act of worship whose timing is collective and continental, drawing every community's sighting into a single convergence at a single place in a single month. By making the moons the means of both daily timing and the great gathering, the verse installs the sky itself as the community's clock and its compass-measure of seasons — a calendar not legislated by priests nor adjusted by rulers but posted monthly on the western horizon, where the herdsman reads it as reliably as the astronomer. The answer to the questioners is thus larger than the question: the moon they wondered at is the instrument by which the entire worship-life of the ummah keeps its appointments with God.

**The Back Doors of Yathrib**

The verse's second half turns abruptly from sky to architecture: it is not righteousness to enter houses by their backs. The reports behind the clause describe an actual practice. Among the pre-Islamic Arabs — the Anṣār of Yathrib are named in the accounts — a returning traveler or a person in a state of ritual consecration would not enter his house by its door; he would scale the back wall or have a breach made, treating the ordinary entrance as forbidden in his condition. Other reports connect the practice to the ihram of pilgrimage or to returning from the festival rites; al-Qurṭubī collects the variants and their common shape: a scruple that had attached itself to doorways, a superstition of thresholds. The verse's verdict is total: the practice is not righteousness — not a higher piety but a misplaced one, an act of devotion performed in the wrong element. The clause then states the true substance: righteousness is the taqwā itself, the mindful reverence of God — and from that substance the practical instruction follows almost as corollary: enter the houses by their doors. The superstition is not merely tolerated-with-disapproval but routed by a definition: the back wall is not holiness, the door is, because the door is where God put the entrance.

**The Spiritual Reading: Houses and Their Doors**

The Sufi exegetes, with Ibn ʿAjība at their head here, read the clause as the allegory its concreteness invites: everything in the religious life is a house with an appointed door, and the house is not entered by its back. Ibn ʿAjība's schema names the three houses and their nine doors — the house of the sharīʿah, entered by repentance, obedience, and reverence; the house of the ṭarīqah, by sincerity, purification, and virtuous character; the house of the ḥaqīqah, by concentration, contemplation, and gnosis. The principle generalizes beyond the schema: the knowledge that comes without its discipline of study, the spiritual station sought without its obedience, the intimacy with God attempted without the prayer He appointed — each is the back wall, and each fails for the same reason the Yathrib climber's scruple failed: it approaches a true destination by an unappointed route, mistaking the difficulty of the approach for its legitimacy. The verse's genius is to make the smallest of superstitions — how one enters one's own courtyard — carry the whole epistemology of worship: there are doors, the doors are known, the doors are God's, and the climb over the wall is not extra piety but refused piety, the piety that will not accept being directed.

**Enter by the Doors, and Be Mindful**

The closing commands gather both halves of the verse into one ethic. *Enter the houses by their doors* is the general principle extracted from the specific practice — appointed means for appointed ends, the lawful route however plain against the dramatic shortcut. *And be mindful of God, that you may prosper* attaches the principle to the sūrah's governing virtue and its governing promise: taqwā as the way, success — falāḥ — as the end, the same pairing the sūrah's opening gave its very first description of the guided (2:5). The two halves of the verse now read as one lesson in two registers. The moon: a wonder asked about as spectacle, answered as instrument — the celestial body's meaning is its function in the worshiper's calendar. The door: a scruple performed as extra-devotion, answered as error — the threshold's meaning is its appointment by the Lawgiver. In both cases the verse disciplines religious imagination toward obedience: not what seems marvelous (the moon's phases, the wall's ascent) but what has been made a means (the timing, the door). The questioners who came asking about the sky are sent home with a calendar and a doorway, and the verse's last word promises that the homecoming — through the door, by the months, in mindfulness — is where the prospering lives.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:190

> Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you, but do not exceed the limits. Surely Allah does not like transgressors.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Permission, and the Dispute About It**

This verse opens the sūrah's legislation of war, and the tradition debated whether it opens the Qur'an's. The exegetes record the question directly: is this the first verse revealed permitting the Muslims to fight, or does that priority belong to the sūrah of the Pilgrimage's permission — granted to those being fought, for they have been wronged (22:39)? The reports supporting each are given, and al-Ṭabarī declines to decide, finding the narrations insufficiently conclusive — a characteristic exercise of his evidentiary discipline. What the verse's own context supplies is the setting: the reports of occasion place it in the period of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, when the Prophet and his Companions set out for the ʿumrah unarmed and were turned back, and the settlement's terms left the community's relationship to Meccan violence unresolved. The legislation that follows addresses a people who have been persecuted, expelled, and fought for thirteen years, who have just been barred from their own sanctuary by treaty rather than battle — and the first word of the war-law to such a people is a limitation, not a license: fight *those who fight you*.

**In the Cause of God**

The command's first phrase sets the war's final cause: fight *in the path of God*. The formula excludes every other motive the Arabian battlefield offered — tribal honor, booty as end, vengeance as appetite, prestige as currency — and names the one legitimate aim: the cause that is God's, which the surrounding verses will define as the ending of persecution and the securing of worship (2:193). The cause-clause is thus the verse's first limit and its most comprehensive: a war fought in God's path is answerable to God's stated ends, and any operation serving another end has left the permission even if it keeps the vocabulary. The tradition heard the clause as governing conduct continuously, not merely intentions at the outset — the fighter in God's path is the one the reports describe as asked whether he fights for courage, for zeal, or for show, and answered that only the one who fights so that God's word is uppermost fights in God's path. The verse installs that test as law: the cause is named before the conduct because conduct untethered from a named cause degenerates into the very transgression the second clause forbids.

**Against Those Who Fight You**

The permission's object is reciprocal: those who fight you — and the classical exegesis built the whole defensive architecture on the phrase. The one who does not fight you is not within the permission; the fighting is answer to fighting, not initiation of it. The verse that follows will extend the reciprocity spatially — expel them from where they expelled you — keeping the response tied to the injury's geography as well as its fact. The tradition's elaboration is extensive and consistent with the clause: the reports prohibit the killing of women, children, monks and hermits, the chronically ill, the aged, and the peasants not participating in hostilities; Ibn ʿAbbās is cited stating the categories flatly — do not kill women, children, the old, or those who offer peace. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote to his commanders on the verse's principle: do not fight those who do not fight you. The phrase thereby becomes the root of the Islamic law of war's discrimination principle — the distinction between combatant and non-combatant — and the verse's reciprocity is not merely a casus belli rule but a targeting rule: the permission reaches the fighters and stops at the boundary of the fighter's person.

**Do Not Exceed the Limits**

The second command is the verse's famous prohibition: *do not transgress* — the iʿtidāʾ whose forms the tradition enumerated. The exegetes read the non-transgression as governing every excess the reciprocity could invite: killing beyond the combatants, retaliation beyond the injury, pursuit beyond the need — and the Qur'an's own parallel legislation of retaliation states the standard it applies here: if you retaliate, retaliate with the like of what was done to you (16:126); the recompense of evil is evil like it (42:40). The verse's closing names the divine disposition toward the excess: God does not love the transgressors — the same formula the food-legislation used of the wasters (2:168) and the sūrah will use again, marking transgression not merely as forbidden but as forfeiting love. The prohibition's placement is the verse's structural point: the permission to fight and the ban on exceeding it arrive in one breath, so the community never holds the license without holding its limit. Every war-law that follows — the Sacred Mosque's clause, the persecution's ranking, the cease-fire's acceptance — is the working-out of these two clauses together: fight the fighters, and fight them within bounds.

**The Verse Beside Its Neighbors**

Read against the Qur'an's wider peace-legislation, the verse's limits show their framework. The sūrah of the Examined Woman distinguishes the two populations precisely along this verse's line: God does not forbid you from being kind and just to those who did not fight you over religion nor expel you from your homes — God loves the just (60:8); what is forbidden is alliance only with those who fought and expelled and abetted (60:9). The peace-orientation is legislated independently: if they incline to peace, incline to it (8:61); the good-and-evil asymmetry of the sūrah of Explained in Detail commands repelling evil with what is better, until the enemy becomes as an intimate friend (41:34); and the patience-counsel to the Prophet himself is to bear what they say and depart from them courteously (73:10), with the reminder that he is not there to compel anyone (88:22). Against this background 2:190 is not an isolated permission but a bounded exception inside a scripture whose default is patience, kindness to the non-fighting, and peace when peace is offered — the exception's boundaries drawn by reciprocity and non-transgression, and its exercise governed by the cause that alone makes it God's.

**The Sanctuaries and the Sequence**

The verse's setting at Hudaybiyyah also charges what follows it. The community addressed had just been prevented from the Sacred Mosque without battle; the next verse will legislate the Mosque's special regime — no fighting at it unless attacked there — and the third will name the war's ultimate object: the end of fitnah, the persecution that had driven the community out and barred it from its sanctuary. The sequence thus moves from the general permission (fight the fighters, without excess) to the sacred exception (the Mosque's inviolability) to the war's terminus (persecution ended, religion God's alone) — and every step is limitation rather than escalation. The verse that opens Islamic war-law opens it, in other words, by naming the war's enemies as the people already at war with the believers, its conduct as bounded by non-transgression, and its cause as God's rather than theirs. A permission shaped this way is a permission designed to end wars rather than multiply them — which is what the treaty-context of its descent suggests it was first given to do: to arm a community for the fighting already imposed on it, and to forbid, in the same sentence, every use of the arms beyond that need.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:191

> Kill them wherever you come upon them and drive them out of the places from which they have driven you out. For persecution is far worse than killing. And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque unless they attack you there. If they do so, then fight them—that is the reward of the disbelievers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Permission's Scope and Its Symmetry**

The verse extends the previous verse's permission into the field, and its two commands are drawn with deliberate symmetry. *Kill them wherever you find them* — the fighting is not restricted to set-piece encounters; the combatant met anywhere within the war's theater is within the permission. And *expel them from where they expelled you* — the geography of the response is the geography of the injury: the expulsion of the believers from their homes and their sanctuary licenses the reciprocal expulsion of the expellers, and licenses exactly that, no further.
