Between the two giving-clauses and the guarding-clause the whole of a Muslim's wanting is gathered: provision for the road, arrival at the end, and safety from the ruin that swallows both. The verse quotes it without commentary because the quotation is the commentary: against the single-horizon soul, the double-horizon sentence stands complete.

**Ḥasanah: The Beautiful Good**

The word the prayer uses for its two gifts — *ḥasanah* — carries more than the translation's "good." The root ḥ-s-n bears the sense of beauty: the ḥasanah is the beautiful thing, the good that is also fitting, radiant, whole. The righteous predecessors elaborated its content, and the tradition's glosses gather the concrete and the comprehensive: good in this world has been read as a righteous spouse — the prayer's most intimate petition — as sufficient and lawful provision, as security, health, and the ability to worship; good in the Hereafter as the Garden itself, with everything the name contains. The word's generosity is its point: the prayer does not itemize because the ḥasanah includes every beautiful thing the two worlds hold, and the asker commits the itemization to the Giver. The Qur'an's own usage confirms the breadth — Moses prays ordain for us good in this life and the next (7:156); the virtuous are told that for those who do good in this world there is goodness, and the Home of the Hereafter is better (16:30); Abraham is granted good in this world and stands among the righteous in the next (16:122). Each instance carries the same double grant in the same beautiful word, and the pilgrim's petition inherits them all.

**The Prophet's Most Frequent Supplication**

The verse's duʿāʾ is not merely a Quranic sentence but the Prophet's own habitual prayer, and the report is among the best-attested in the tradition. Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim preserves it (2690): Qatādah asked Anas ibn Mālik which supplication the Messenger of God made most frequently, and Anas answered that his most constant prayer was this — O Allah, grant us the good in this world and the good in the Hereafter, and save us from the torment of the Fire. Anas added his own practice to the report: whenever he made any supplication he included this one within it, so that every prayer he ever prayed carried the Quranic petition folded inside it. The identification is explicit in the sources — this is the verse's prayer, the duʿāʾ of 2:201, spoken by the Prophet more than any other words of asking. The report settles the verse's status in Muslim practice: not a text to be admired but a sentence to be repeated, the petition its Revealer chose to make the most-repeated petition of His Messenger. The pilgrim at Minā who prays it is praying the prayer the Prophet prayed most, at the stations the Prophet taught him, with Anas's inclusion as the model of how to carry it into every other asking.

**The Prayer's Life in the Community**

From the verse and the report grew a practice that runs through Muslim worship to this day. Ibn Kathīr notes that this supplication is frequently repeated by Muslims in their individual prayers and appears constantly in the books of collected duʿāʾ — and its most iconic placement is inside the hajj itself: the pilgrims recite it during the circuits of the Kaʿbah, traditionally in the stretch between the Yemeni Corner and the Black Stone, so that the Quran's prayer is spoken at the Quran's house in the rhythm of the tawāf. The verse thereby completes a circle with its context: revealed as the pilgrims' petition at the rites' end, it became the pilgrims' petition at the rites' center, and through them the daily petition of the whole community — at weddings and funerals, after the obligatory prayers, in the qunūt of calamity, in the private asking of the night. The comprehensiveness explains the adoption: a prayer that holds both worlds and the Fire's guard is a prayer that never needs replacing, suitable to every condition because it asks for everything that matters in the order that matters. The tradition's verdict on it is implicit in Anas's practice — the sufficient prayer, the one into which every other prayer can be folded.

**Against the Truncated Asking**

Set beside the previous verse's single-world prayer, this petition defines the Islam of the tongue. The first group asked for this world and received its limits — no share in the Hereafter; this group asks for both and, the next verse will state, receives a portion from what it earned. The contrast is not between material and spiritual temperaments: the second prayer is *more* material in one sense, since it asks for this world's good explicitly, naming what the ascetic might disdain to request. The difference is the horizon and the order. The truncated prayer treats the world as the whole; the whole prayer treats it as the first half — requested, valued, and outranked in the same sentence. And the third clause does further work against a third error: the prayer that asks for both goods without the Fire's guard would be a prayer of presumption, as though the goods were owed; the guarding-clause keeps the asker in the posture the whole passage has trained — the pilgrim who asked forgiveness at his rite's summit (2:199), who remembers God more ardently than his fathers' boasts (2:200), and who now requests everything while taking refuge from the one loss that annuls everything. Wanting whole, asking humbly: the verse's sentence is both.

**The Supplication as the Rites' Fruit**

The verse's position at the hajj-legislation's turning point makes the duʿāʾ the pilgrimage's stated product. The manāsik are completed (2:200); the remembrance replaces the boast; and the petition replaces the appetite. What the weeks of iḥrām, the plain, the surge, and the nights of Minā were for is now visible in a single sentence: a heart re-sorted in its wanting, praying with both horizons open and the Fire in view. The verses that follow will confirm the sorting — the portion earned by such askers, the reckoning swift upon it (2:202) — but the sort itself happens here, in the words. The tradition's reading of the prayer's clauses as a curriculum completes the picture: the righteous predecessors who read good in this world as a righteous spouse and lawful provision, and good in the Hereafter as the Garden, treated the duʿāʾ as the syllabus of a whole life — marriage, work, worship, death, judgment, all named or implied in three clauses. The pilgrim who learns the sentence at Minā carries home not a souvenir but a structure: every future asking already shaped by the double horizon, the beautiful good, and the guard against the Fire.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:202

> It is they who will receive a ˹heavenly˺ reward for the good they have done. Surely Allah is swift in reckoning.

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Portion of What Was Earned**

The verse settles the account of the two prayers. To the askers of the previous verses it assigns a portion — *nasīb* — from what they earned: the reward is not a gift unconnected to the asking but a share answerable to the work, and the word of earning — *kasb* — is the Qur'an's standard term for the deed that carries its consequence. Al-Rāzī records the exegetes' division over whose portion the verse names. Some read it as belonging to the second group alone — the ones who asked for good in both worlds receive their earned share in both. Others extend it to the first group as well — the single-world askers receive a portion too, in the world they asked for and nowhere else — so that the verse describes both settlements at once: the world-seeker's portion paid in the world, the both-worlds-seeker's portion paid in both. The comprehensive reading gives the verse its sharpest edge: the portion principle is universal, and every asker is paid from what he earned, with the asking itself counted among the earnings. The prayer is the work; the portion is its wage; and the wage's geography follows the prayer's horizon.

**The Duʿāʾ as Earning**

The verse's economics make supplication a labor with a yield, and the tradition took the claim seriously. The portion is *from what they earned* — the asker's own petition is his first earning, since the duʿāʾ that spans both worlds is itself an act of faith: it confesses that the world is not the whole, that the Hereafter is real, that the Fire is possible, and that the asking reaches a Hearer. The single-world prayer earns its narrowness — the horizon of the sentence becomes the horizon of the payment. The whole prayer earns its width: the good requested for this world is granted as provision counted in the portion, the good requested for the Hereafter is granted as the Garden counted in the portion, and the guard requested against the Fire is granted as the protection that makes both portions safe to hold. Nothing in the verse suggests the portion is proportioned to the prayer's eloquence or length — the earned share answers the prayer's content, the heart's actual wanting behind the words. This is why the previous verse could legislate a formula: a sentence that asks in the right order for the right things is an earning whose portion the verse now guarantees.

**Swift in Reckoning**

The second clause names the speed of the settlement: God is swift in reckoning — *sarīʿ al-ḥisāb*. The attribute answers an objection latent in the portion-principle: the wage is promised, but the payer's audit of the whole creation would seem to require an age — how can the account of every asker be settled at all? The swiftness is the answer, and it is an attribute the Qur'an repeats at exactly such junctures: the People of the Scripture did not dispute until knowledge came to them, and whoever denies God's signs should know that God is swift in reckoning (3:19). The reckoning's speed follows from the reckoner's nature: an audit is slow in proportion to the auditor's distance from his accounts, and God's distance is zero — He knows the portion before it is asked, the earning before it is made, the prayer before the tongue forms it. Nothing must be gathered, retrieved, or reconstructed; the account stands already complete in His knowledge, and the reckoning is therefore instantaneous. The exegetes drew the practical corollary in both directions: swift for the reward, so the asker is not kept waiting on his portion; swift for the audit, so the deferrer of repentance is not granted the delay he assumes. The Day's arithmetic is not slow justice but immediate disclosure.

**The Reckoning and the Supplicant**

The swiftness has a personal edge for the praying pilgrim, and the passage's own structure supplies it. The verse before the duʿāʾ-diptych commanded the pilgrim at his rite's summit to ask forgiveness (2:199); the verse before the diptych stationed remembrance at the rites' end (2:200); the nearness-verse of the fasting legislation promised I respond to the call of the caller (2:186). The whole context is a theology of answered prayer, and swift in reckoning is its final guarantee: the portion of the earned prayer is not filed for a distant processing but settled by a reckoning that outruns the asking. The believer who prays 2:201's sentence at Minā, between the Yemeni Corner and the Black Stone, in the night or the crowd, prays into an accounting already moving — the kasb registered, the nasīb assigned, the reckoning swift. The clause thus converts the portion-principle from a warning into a comfort: what you have earned is held for you by One whose audit needs no time, and the speed that makes the sinner's case fearful makes the asker's case sure. The two movements are one attribute — the reckoning is swift whether it convicts or pays, and the prayer decides which.

**The Verse as the Diptych's Hinge**

Structurally, this shortest of the three verses carries the whole weight of the settlement. Verse 200 quoted the truncated prayer and its verdict — no share in the Hereafter; verse 201 quoted the whole prayer without verdict; verse 202 supplies the verdict for the whole — and, on the comprehensive reading, for the truncated one too. The diptych's moral anatomy is thereby completed in a single sentence: the asking reveals the earning, the earning fixes the portion, and the reckoning delivers it swiftly. The verse's brevity is proportioned to its function — it adds no imagery, no narrative, no elaboration, only the accounting — because the accounting is all the two prayers lacked. The single-world asker was told what he would not have; the both-worlds asker is told what he will: a portion, earned, paid by a swift reckoning. And the portion-language quietly answers the hajj's own economics: the pilgrim has spent wealth on the journey (2:195's spending, 2:197's provisions), earned hardship on the road, and invested weeks in rites whose yield is invisible; the verse credits all of it to the account — the kasb includes the journey — and settles it with the speed that makes the invisible yield as certain as the visible cost.

**Under the Swiftness, the Whole Passage**

The attribute's shadow falls across the legislation that follows as well. The numbered days at Minā are about to be legislated with their easy options — depart after two days or stay to the third, no sin on either for the mindful (2:203) — and beneath the ease stands the same swiftness: every choice in the rite, like every clause of every prayer, is registered instantly and settled exactly. The passage that began with the sacred month's ledger (2:194) and the spending in God's cause (2:195) has been building one continuous accounting — the retaliation measured, the offerings priced, the prayers portioned — and swift in reckoning is the seal on all of it: the ledger is kept in real time, by a knowledge that never pauses to compile. For the pilgrim the seal is mercy; for the Ḥums-type heart that prays with one horizon it is warning; and for the reader of the sūrah it is the standing condition of every verse's legislation — that the laws are not ideals posted against time but accounts entered the moment they are kept or broken. The portion from what they earned is, in the end, the hajj's final rite: the prayer completed, the earning closed, and the reckoning already swift upon it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:203

> And remember Allah during ˹these˺ appointed days. Whoever departs swiftly on the second day is not sinful, neither are those who stay behind ˹till the third—seeking additional reward˺, so long as they are mindful ˹of their Lord˺. And be mindful of Allah, and know that to Him you will ˹all˺ be gathered.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Days Numbered**

The verse legislates the hajj's final station: remember God in the days numbered — the eleventh through the thirteenth of Dhū'l-Ḥijjah, which the pilgrims spend at Minā, the valley east of Mecca, and which the tradition calls the days of tashrīq, a word whose derivation is uncertain and whose sense the rites preserve: the three days after the Day of Sacrifice, not counting it. The station's central act is the stoning — the casting of pebbles at the columns (jimār) that represent Satan's three ambushes of Abraham on the road of the sacrifice — and the verse stations remembrance over the whole of it. The numbered days complete the pilgrimage's arithmetic: months appointed (2:197), a night at the sacred monument (2:198), a surge with the people (2:199), rites completed (2:200), and now days counted — three, named, and bounded, like the fast's numbered days before them. The numbering is the legislation's characteristic mercy: the rite has a defined end, the pilgrim knows his remaining obligation to the hour, and the remembrance that fills the days has a frame that keeps it from dissolving into the journey's fatigue.

**Remember God in Them**

The remembrance commanded in these days has a precise form in the tradition's practice: the takbīr — Allāhu akbar, God is greatest — recited while casting the pebbles at the columns and recited at the times of the prayers throughout the days. And the recitation is not the pilgrims' private liturgy: the takbīr of these days is performed by all Muslims, in every city, from the Day of Sacrifice until the last of the tashrīq days, so that the whole ummah's tongue moves with the valley's. The litanies are the same ones the fasting-legislation produced — the verse of Ramadan's completion commanded magnifying God for having guided (2:185), and the formula the tradition recites there is the formula recited here: Allāhu akbar, Allāhu akbar, lā ilāha illa'Llāh, wa'Llāhu akbar wa li'Llāhi'l-ḥamd — God is greatest, God is greatest, there is no god but God, and God is greatest, and to God belongs the praise — with other litanies added in some practice. The two festivals thus share one doxology: Ramadan ends in takbīr for the guidance, and the hajj's last days run on takbīr at the columns — the community praising at every summit its rites reach, the remembrance itself the rite's stated substance.

**Who Hastens and Who Tarries**

The verse's famous flexibility governs the days' length: whoever hastens on after two days — departing Minā on the twelfth — bears no sin, and whoever delays — staying through the thirteenth — bears no sin. The ruling created the hajj's one open option at its close: the pilgrim may complete the stoning in two of the three days and proceed to the farewell circumambulation at the Kaʿbah, by which the hajj is complete, or may remain for the third day's casting. Both courses are declared sinless, and the declaration's double negative is emphatic — no sin on him, no sin on him — legislating freedom where religious scruple would otherwise manufacture anxiety. The option answers real conditions: the caravans' departure schedules, the travelers' distances, the weak and the hurried; a rite drawing the whole inhabited world to one valley cannot require of every pilgrim the valley's maximum. And the option preserves the maximum's honor: the delay is not corrected or discouraged — it stands equally sinless, which in the tradition's reading means equally meritorious for the one whose circumstances allow it. The verse thus closes the hajj as it closed the fast: a fixed obligation with legislated margins, the strictness at the center and the mercy at the edges.

**For the One Who Fears**

The flexibility carries a condition, and the condition is the verse's hinge: the no-sin ruling is *for the reverent* — for the one who keeps his taqwā. The exegetes read the qualifier in complementary directions. It attaches to both options: the hastener is sinless only if his hastening is not a flight from the rite's discipline but a traveler's necessity kept inside piety, and the delayer is sinless only if his staying is not self-righteous display. It also attaches, in the stricter reading, to the departing specifically: the one who hastens must have kept the fear of God in his whole pilgrimage — the rafath, fusūq, and jidāl avoided (2:197), the rites completed for God (2:196) — for the exemption to cover his early exit. The condition thereby prevents the flexibility from becoming laxity: the option is not a discount on piety but a discount *for* the pious, the margin granted to the heart the rite has already formed. And the verse reinforces the point by repeating its command — be mindful of God — immediately after the options, so that both departures, the two-day and the three-day, are dispatched under the same taqwā, the only luggage whose inspection matters at the valley's exit.

**To Him You Will Be Gathered**

The verse ends by projecting the gathering at Minā into the gathering to God: know that to Him you will be gathered. The clause is the days' eschatological frame, and its fit to the setting is exact. The pilgrim at Minā stands inside the largest rehearsal the faith performs of the Day of Gathering — the nations assembled in one valley, ranked in tents like the ranks of the resurrection, performing the stoning of the devil who will be judged, awaiting the departure that resembles the final departure. The knowledge commanded is the rehearsal's lesson: this gathering disperses, that gathering does not; these days are numbered, that Day is not; this valley's exit is by the farewell circuit, that assembly's exit is by the portion earned. The clause also seals the passage's accounting-thread — the sacred month's ledger (2:194), the portion from what was earned and the swift reckoning (2:202) — with the destination of all accounts: the gathering to Him. The pilgrim who hastens after two days and the pilgrim who tarries to the third walk out of the valley under the same knowledge, and the verse leaves them both with it: the option was about days; the gathering is about the One who numbered them.

**The Hajj's Closing Verse**

Within the legislation's architecture this verse is the coda. After it the passage turns — abruptly, in the sūrah's manner — from the pilgrim's duties to the hypocrite's portrait (2:204–207), as though the completed hajj demanded the contrast: the community that has just been legislated through remembrance, flexibility, and taqwā is shown the man whose speech impresses and whose hand corrupts. The turn confirms the coda's function: the days numbered have produced a people defined by the takbīr on their tongues, the option in their law, the mindfulness in their hearts, and the gathering in their knowledge — and the verses that follow measure every claimant to that people against the portrait. The hajj-legislation's own arc closes in the verse's three movements: the remembrance commanded (the tongue's rite), the freedom granted (the law's mercy), the gathering announced (the heart's horizon). A pilgrim who has kept all three has carried the valley home: the takbīr that outlasts the columns, the ease that outlasts the days, and the knowledge that outlasts the dispersal — to Him you will be gathered, and the numbered days were the counting-down to it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:204

> There are some ˹hypocrites˺ who impress you with their views regarding worldly affairs and openly call upon Allah to witness what is in their hearts, yet they are your worst adversaries.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turn From the Pilgrim to the Impostor**

The sūrah makes one of its characteristic pivots here: the hajj-legislation closes with the pilgrims gathered at Minā, remembering God in numbered days (2:203), and the next movement opens on a man whose speech impresses and whose heart is war. The contrast is the point of the placement — the community that has just been legislated through remembrance, flexibility, and mindfulness is immediately shown its internal opposite, the person who performs the language of faith while carrying enmity inside it. The verses that follow (204–207) form a diptych: this portrait of the eloquent adversary, and its counter-portrait of the one who sells his soul for God's pleasure (2:207). Between the two figures the sūrah lays out the heart's two economies — the speech that markets the self, and the life that spends the self — and asks the reader, freshly returned from the valley of gathering, which trade he is in.

**The Speech About the Life of This World**

The portrait opens with the man's instrument: his manner of speaking about worldly affairs delights you. The verb carries the senses the exegetes list — to please, to evoke wonder, to delight — and its object is specified: not talk of God or the Hereafter but of *this world's life*, its affairs, its interests, its management. The hypocrite's eloquence is worldly fluency: he speaks the community's practical concerns — provision, politics, the arrangements of the road and the market — with a mastery that wins the listener's admiration. The specification matters. The sūrah's opening portrait of the hypocrites described their claim, we are only peace-makers (2:11); this portrait describes their competence. The dangerous deceiver is not the one who talks badly about sacred things but the one who talks brilliantly about worldly things and carries the brilliance into the sacred. The listener's admiration — the verse addresses the Prophet himself, *impresses you* — is the mechanism of the harm: the community is disarmed not by argument but by aesthetic surrender, the pleasure of a well-managed sentence doing the work a false doctrine could never do alone.

**God Called to Witness the Heart**

The portrait's second stroke is the oath: he calls God as witness to what is in his heart. The performance is total — the deceiver does not merely speak well; he sanctifies his speech, invoking God as guarantor of his heart's contents, saying in effect what God knows is in my heart. Al-Ṭabarī records the case attached to the verse: Akhnas ibn Shurayq of Thaqīf displayed a pretended eagerness for Islam, protesting all the while that God was witness to his heart — the oath of interiority wielded by a man whose interior was the opposite of his words. The invocation is the most religious form deception can take: it borrows the language of the heart's transparency that true believers use before God and installs it at the service of a lie. And it is unfalsifiable by design — no human listener can audit another's heart, so the oath to what the heart contains claims exactly the territory where the community cannot check. The verse exposes the mechanism by naming God's actual relation to it: the Witness invoked is witness against the swearer, since what is in the heart is precisely what God knows and the man's audience does not.

**The Fiercest of Adversaries**

The third stroke reverses the whole surface: yet he is your bitterest opponent. The phrase carries a second reading al-Ṭabarī preserves — most crooked in disputation — and the two readings compose into one diagnosis: the man whose eloquence impressed you is your enemy in both senses, the one who works against you in fact and the one who twists against you in argument. The reversal is the verse's structural heart. Everything the listener received — the pleasing speech, the worldly fluency, the sacred oath — is reclassified in the final clause as the equipment of hostility: the eloquence is the weapon, the oath is the camouflage, and the admiration the listener felt was the wound being inflicted. The verse thus trains a discernment the community urgently needed in Medina, where the hypocrites lived inside the city's walls, prayed in its mosque, and fought no open battle: the enemy who cannot be identified by his position must be identified by his pattern, and the pattern the verse gives is the disjunction — the sweeter the speech about this world, the holier the oath about the heart, the sharper the suspicion the clause commands.

**Occasions and the Universal Portrait**

The exegetes record specific occasions for these verses and then, characteristically, prefer the general reading. Beside Akhnas, al-Thaʿlabī reports another incident behind the revelation: Meccan men feigned eagerness for Islamic instruction and requested that a party of teachers be dispatched to them; the men sent were waylaid en route and killed. But Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, and al-Ṭabarī agree in treating the passage as universal teaching on the nature of hypocrisy rather than as a locked historical caption — the portrait is drawn to be recognized in every generation. The preference is methodologically significant: a verse tied to one impostor would arm the community against a man; a verse describing the type arms it against the form. And the form is durable — the eloquent manager of worldly affairs, the invoker of God as heart-witness, the adversary inside the admiration — recurring in every community that judges its speakers by their speech. The universal reading also explains the diptych's second panel: the one who sells his soul for God's pleasure (2:207) is no less a type, and the two figures stand as the permanent alternatives of the religious life — the self marketed in God's name, and the self spent in God's cause.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Architecture of the Heart**

This portrait belongs to the sūrah's long anatomy of interior corruption, which began in its opening pages — the hypocrites who say we believe in God and the Last Day while believing not, who seek to deceive God and the believers while deceiving only themselves without awareness (2:8–9) — and now, two hundred verses deep, returns with its mature instruments: not the crude claim of belief but the accomplished performance of it. The progression is pedagogical. The opening portrait warned against the lie; this one warns against the beautiful lie, the one that arrives with worldly competence and sacred oaths, that impresses before it deceives. The hajj-context sharpens the warning: the pilgrim has just spent weeks in the state where the interior is legislated — the intention no one can audit, the rafath and jidāl forbidden even in the tongue's smallest movement, the remembrance required where no crowd can see — and the verses that greet his return describe the antipode of that formation, the man whose exterior is perfected and whose interior is enmity. The sūrah's two hundred verses have been building the community's heart; these verses name the counterfeiter who has been studying the same blueprint from the other side.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:205

> And when they leave ˹you˺, they strive throughout the land to spread mischief in it and destroy crops and cattle. Allah does not like mischief.

**Expanded Commentary**

**When He Turns Away**

The verse follows the impostor out of the room. The portrait of 2:204 was drawn inside the encounter — the impressive speech, the oath to the heart, the listener's admiration — and this verse tracks what happens when the encounter ends: when he turns away, he strives in the land. The turning was read by the exegetes at two levels: the physical departure, his leaving the presence of those he has been deceiving, and the interior turn, the anger that shows the mask's underside. Both readings carry the same disclosure: the eloquence was a costume worn for an audience, and the audience's absence reveals the wearer. The verse thus completes the diagnostic pattern begun in the previous verse — the disjunction between the speech in your presence and the conduct out of it is the hypocrite's identifying mark. The community is taught where to look: not at the performance, which is flawless while watched, but at the interval, the going-away, the hours in which no admirer is present to be impressed. What a man does when he turns away is the report on what he was while facing you.

**The Striving That Spreads Corruption**

The verb of the verse is emphatic: he *strives* — yasʿā — in the land, and the object of his striving is fasād, corruption. The energy is the first surprise: the deceiver is not passive, not merely false, but industrious in his falsehood, working with the same diligence the believer owes to good. The word fasād carries the sense the exegetes fix — literally rot, and in Quranic usage corruption in the broadest sense: decadence, immorality, injustice, the undoing of what holds a land together. The verse's own illustration is concrete: some commentators describe a particular hypocrite who burned people's fields and hamstrung their donkey — the arson and the maiming as the portrait's case study. The striving against a whole land, not against individuals, marks the scale: this is not private malice but public sabotage, the deliberate rotting of a community's fabric. And the striving answers the previous verse's oath: the man who called God to witness the goodness of his heart spends his absent hours manufacturing corruption in the earth God made — the witness he invoked is witness to the interval.

**Tillage and Offspring Destroyed**

The verse names the corruption's two targets: he destroys the tillage and the offspring. The tillage — the harth — is agriculture, the crops, the planted fields; the offspring — the nasl — is livestock on the primary reading, and on some commentators' extension any progeny including the human. The two named things are the Arabian world's entire wealth: what the land grows and what the herds bear, the standing crop and the multiplying stock, the food of this year and the food of all years to come. To destroy them is not to injure a competitor but to attack the conditions of life itself — the scorched field does not belong to the enemy alone but to the future, and the hamstrung animal ends a lineage of provision. The modern readings the verse has generated follow the same logic outward: Muslims have interpreted such corruption-verses as condemning injustice in society and the destruction of the natural environment, citing the Qur'an's own summary — corruption has spread on land and sea through what people's hands have done (30:41). The hypocrite of this verse is the type of every agent whose striving leaves the land less fertile, the herds less numerous, the air and water and social trust less whole: fasād as the anti-cultivation, the unmaking of what God's provision grows.

**God Loves Not Corruption**

The verse's final clause states the divine disposition: God does not love the fasād. The formula — the negation of divine love — is the Qur'an's characteristic verdict-language, marking not merely prohibition but divine aversion: God does not love the transgressor (2:190), the waster, the arrogant boaster, the treacherous. Its placement here is strategic, because the hypocrite's whole performance is built on claiming God's favor — the oath that God knows his heart, the religious language of his impressive speech. The clause answers the claim from the side of God: whatever the man asserts about the divine knowledge of his interior, the divine love does not attend his work, and the work is what the verse has just described — striving corruption, destroyed tillage, ruined offspring. The negation also disciplines the community's discernment: you cannot audit his heart, but you can audit his harvest — the fields he leaves burned, the herds he leaves hamstrung, the trust he leaves rotted — and the divine non-love is pronounced over exactly that audit. The verse thereby hands the deceived a criterion that does not depend on eloquence: look at what his striving leaves growing, and what it leaves dead.

**The Anti-Economy of the Diptych**

Within the passage's architecture, this verse is the diptych's dark economy in full operation. The sūrah has just legislated an economy of cultivation and expenditure: spend in God's cause, the hands that withhold cast themselves into destruction (2:195); the pilgrim takes provision and seeks bounty without blame (2:197–198); the portion is from what is earned (2:202). Against that economy stands the hypocrite's: he spends nothing, earns nothing, and his one industry is the destruction of what others spend, earn, and grow. The tillage he burns is somebody's provision-command obeyed; the offspring he maims is somebody's bounty sought lawfully; the land he corrupts is the same land the verse of 30:41 describes as tasting the consequences of such hands. The diptych's second panel — the one who sells his soul seeking God's pleasure (2:207) — will complete the contrast from the other side: the believer's economy culminates in spending the self, the hypocrite's in destroying the harvest. Between the two, the verse's criterion of love divides them: the seller of the soul sells to a God who is kind to His servants; the spreader of corruption strives under a God who does not love corruption — and both dispositions are already, in this life, visible in the fields.

**The Verse's Standing Warning**

The warning this verse installs runs through the rest of the Qur'an's social teaching. The fasād it names — corruption pursued with striving energy, aimed at the land's fertility and the community's stock — becomes a category the scripture legislates against repeatedly: the punishment-verses of highway robbery and public disorder use the same word; the Pharaoh's administration is described as making corruption in the land; the sūrah's own opening portraits return to it at every recurrence of the hypocrites' type. And the ecological readings the tradition draws from it — injustice in society and destruction of the natural environment both named as fasād — extend the category to every scale of the modern world's corruption: the burned field is now also the cleared forest, the hamstrung donkey the collapsed fishery, the rotted trust the poisoned commons. The verse survives as the Qur'an's sharpest single indictment of productive-seeming destruction: the striving that looks like work, the eloquence that looks like leadership, the departure that leaves the land less alive. God does not love corruption — and the verse leaves the community the test by which to see it: whatever his speech in your presence, count the tillage and the offspring he leaves behind.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:206

> When it is said to them, “Fear Allah,” pride carries them off to sin. Hell will be their proper place. What an evil place to rest!

**Expanded Commentary**

**The One Sentence Every Counsel Needs**

The verse tests the portrait with the shortest possible intervention: when it is said to him, fear God. The counsel is the tradition's whole prophetic vocabulary in two words — the taqwā-command that every messenger brought his people, that the sūrah has legislated as the end of retaliation, bequest, fasting, and pilgrimage alike (2:179, 180, 183, 196–197). It is what a friend says to the eloquent impostor, what an elder says to the corrupter of the land, what the community says to its own admired speaker when the interval's report comes in. The verse's staging is precise: the admonition arrives, and what follows is the man's reaction to being told to fear God. Not to a refutation of his arguments, not to an exposure of his oath, but to the two-word counsel that names the only thing his whole performance lacks. The hypocrite's portrait is thereby completed by its response to correction — the surface was drawn in 204, the industry in 205, and here the interior's reflex, the movement of the heart when the heart is addressed directly.

**Pride That Seizes Him Into Sin**

The reaction is the verse's diagnosis: ʿizzah — pride, vainglory, the hot self-assertion — seizes him, and seizes him *into* sin. The grammar is violent in both directions: the pride is not his decision but his captor, the force that takes him; and its destination is not merely accompanied by sin but arrives at it, the carrying ending in the ithm. Al-Qurṭubī's lexicon of the word helps: ʿizzah in its rightful place is the honor that belongs to God, His Messenger, and the believers — the strength that comes from being right with the Divine; in this man it has become its counterfeit, the glory taken in the self's own standing, the prestige of the impressive speech and the invoked oath. The counsel to fear God strikes that counterfeit at its root — to fear God is to hold one's standing as borrowed — and the counterfeit defends itself by seizure: the admonished man does not consider the counsel but is carried off by his pride into the sin of rejection. The psychology is the tradition's standing account of how hypocrisy hardens: not through argument unanswerable but through glory unresigned, the ʿizzah that will not be a creature, the speaker who cannot afford to be corrected in front of an audience that admired him.

**Hell Suffices Him**

The verdict that follows uses the Qur'an's idiom of sufficiency: Hell suffices him — ḥasbuhu jahannam. The concept of sufficiency runs through the scripture in both registers, as the commentators note: God suffices the believer as guardian and helper, and in the negative register the punishment suffices the punished — it serves the purpose, it is enough, nothing need be added. The clause's economy is exact against the man's own economy: he who took so much — the admiration, the oath's credibility, the land's harvest destroyed — is paid in one sufficient thing. The sufficiency also answers his sufficiency-claim implicitly: the man whose speech said God knows what is in my heart claimed a divine endorsement; the verse returns the divine relation as the single provision of the Fire, enough for him as his portion, needing no supplement. The commentators cross-reference the formula's positive twin — if you turn away, the guidance has been delivered, and God suffices — to mark the symmetry: sufficiency is what the soul receives when it has chosen its one thing, and this man chose the self's glory, so the Fire is sufficient as its consequence.

**What an Evil Resting Place**

The verse's last clause inverts the imagery of rest: what an evil cradle, an evil place to recline. The word mihād carries the bed-sense — the cradle, the made-up couch, the place where a person settles as into their own element — and the Qur'an uses it elsewhere for Hell's furnishing, the bed of the arrogant. The inversion bites against the whole portrait: the man who impressed you with his talk of this world's life was arranging his rest in the world — the estates the Anṣār were tempted back to (2:195), the position his eloquence maintained, the comfort his corruption protected — and the verse names the resting place his choices actually furnished. Every act of the diptych's dark panel built this bed: the speech that marketed the self, the striving that rotted the land, the pride that refused the counsel — and the made bed is Hell, and the verdict on it is not merely punitive but aesthetic: what an evil resting place, spoken with the shudder of a person who has seen where the arrangement ends. The man who could not bear the two words fear God is given the sufficient and evil substitute, the couch of his own ʿizzah.

**The Circuit Completed: Speech, Act, Reaction**

The three verses now read as one closed circuit of hypocrisy. 2:204 gave the surface: the eloquent speech about worldly affairs, the oath calling God to witness the heart, the enmity beneath the impression. 2:205 gave the work: the turning away, the striving corruption, the tillage and offspring destroyed. 2:206 gives the reflex: the counsel to fear God, the pride's seizure, the sufficient Fire. Nothing is missing from the anatomy — what he says, what he does, and what he becomes when corrected — and the circuit's third stage explains why the first two are fatal rather than merely bad. A man who spoke well and corrupted badly might still be reached; the counsel to fear God is the reaching, and the verse reports it fails, not for want of clarity but by pride's reflex. The failure of correction is hypocrisy's defining difference from ordinary sin: the sinner who can still hear fear God retains the road back — the repentance-legislation the sūrah has spread through its length stands open — but the man seized by ʿizzah into sin has closed the road from inside, and the sufficiency of Hell is the verdict on a self that made itself unaddressable.

**The Portrait Against the Pilgrims**

The diptych's dark panel is now complete, and its frame is the hajj it follows. The pilgrims of 2:196–203 spent weeks in the state where the interior is legislated — the intention audited by God alone, the tongue fenced from rafath and jidāl, the boast of the fathers transferred to the remembrance of God, the petition taught to span both worlds. The man of 2:204–206 is the inversion at every point: his tongue perfected for the world's affairs, his oath profaning the divine witness, his boast reasserted in the pride that refuses counsel, his petition truncated to the world whose harvest he destroys. The passage has thus built its two citizens — the one who leaves the valley remembering God in numbered days and knowing he will be gathered to Him, and the one who leaves the encounter striving corruption in the land and being carried by glory into a sufficient Fire. The verse that follows will draw the second citizen of the diptych's bright panel — the one who sells his soul for God's pleasure — and between the sold soul and the sufficient Hell the sūrah will have completed its most compact moral map: the heart that spends itself and the heart that markets itself, the ʿizzah that seizes and the raʾfah that receives.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:207

> And there are those who would dedicate their lives to Allah’s pleasure. And Allah is Ever Gracious to ˹His˺ servants.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Soul Sold for Pleasure**

The diptych's second panel opens with the counter-figure: among people is the one who sells himself — his nafs, his soul, his self, his life — seeking the good pleasure of God. The verb is commercial and the verse means it: the same market-language the sūrah has used throughout — the traders who purchased error at guidance's price (2:16, 2:175), the concealers who sold revelation for a fleeting gain (2:174) — here receives its one holy instance. The seller is real, the merchandise is the highest thing a person owns, and the price is riḍwān Allāh, God's pleasure: not paradise as real estate, not safety as insurance, but the Divine good-will itself as the whole of the wanted. The transaction inverts the sūrah's bad trades completely. Those sold the eternal for the fleeting and received fire in their bellies; this one sells the fleeting — a life that ends regardless — for the eternal, and the verse's closing name will describe what the Buyer is: kind to His servants. The nafs sold is specified by the exegetes in its double sense, soul and life, because the sale runs at both levels: the self's desires given away, and where necessary the life itself laid down, in one undivided act of purchase-by-surrender.

**ʿUmar's Reading: The Man Who Enjoins and Is Slain**

The tradition's most cited application of the verse comes from the second caliph. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb is reported to have read the seller as a man who sets out to enjoin the right and forbid the wrong — and is killed for it. The reading connects the verse to the Qur'an's great civic precept, al-amr bi'l-maʿrūf wa'l-nahy ʿan al-munkar, the commanding of good and forbidding of evil, a theme legislated across the scripture: let there be a community among you calling to the good, enjoining the right, forbidding the wrong — those are the successful (3:104); the believers, men and women, are protectors of one another who enjoin the right (9:71); and a dozen places more. On ʿUmar's reading the sale of the soul is not mystical withdrawal but public speech with a lethal price: the one who stands before a tyrant, a corrupt assembly, a community bent toward the corruption of 2:205, and says fear God — the very counsel the proud man of the previous verse rejected — knowing the saying may end him. The nafs as life makes the reading exact: the enjoiner sells his life in the sentence he speaks, and the verse records the transaction as the highest commerce available to a believer.

**ʿAlī in the Prophet's Bed**

The sīrah supplies the sale's most famous instance, reported by al-Thaʿlabī and the historians in connection with this verse. On the night of the Hijrah, with the Meccan assassins posted around the house waiting to strike at dawn, the Prophet commanded ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib to sleep in his bed and cover himself with his green mantle, so that the watchers, peering through the door's hole, would see a sleeper and believe him still present. ʿAlī — a young man lying down in a targeted bed, under a mantle that identified him as the target — asked whether the Prophet would be safe, was assured, and lay down; when the assassins rushed in at the hour they had chosen, they found ʿAlī and not Muhammad. The report needs no embellishment in the verse's terms: a soul sold, in full knowledge, for the pleasure of God — the sale priced in a night's certainty of death and paid, by God's keeping, with the morning's life. The tradition adds other candidates to the verse's roster: the Companions who spent their wealth on the emigration, or lost it behind them in Mecca, selling property and homeland in the same transaction of the road to Medina. Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī gather the reports and keep, over all of them, the universal reading the passage prefers: whoever gives away his selfish desires or his life for God's sake has entered the virtuous bargain.

**The Virtuous Bargain**

The commentators' summary phrase for the verse — a virtuous bargain in the ultimate sense — states the economics the sūrah has been building since its opening pages. Every human being spends his nafs; the only question is the buyer. The traders of 2:16 spent their guidance on error and called the loss a trade; the concealers of 2:174 spent God's words on a fleeting gain and ate fire; the hypocrite of 204–206 spends his eloquence on this world's impression and is carried by pride into a sufficient Hell. The seller of this verse spends the same currency — the self, with its desires, its safety, its years — on the one counterparty whose payment does not fail: the good pleasure of God. The bargain's virtue is not that the seller receives more than he gives (he gives everything and receives a pleasure that is God's own) but that the transaction ends the selling: the self spent on the world must be re-spent forever, appetite renewing appetite, while the self sold to God is bought outright, and the buyer's name for the purchase follows in the same verse. The whole market-imagery of the sūrah — purchase, sale, trade, profit, loss — arrives here at its one transaction both parties will never regret.

**God Is Kind to His Servants**

The verse closes with the name that receives the sale: God is raʾūf — tender, deeply kind, full of pity — to His servants. The name's placement is the bargain's guarantee. A seller who gives his life fears one thing above all: that the price was wasted, that the buyer did not need the goods, that the sacrifice went unregarded. The verse answers with the divine tenderness: the Buyer of souls is not a hard master counting the minimum but the Raʾūf whose kindness precedes the sale — who made the servant, gave him the nafs he sells, and receives it with a tenderness the name denotes at its strongest in the Qur'an's usage. The clause also completes the diptych's contrast with the previous verse's ending: the proud man is paid with sufficiency — Hell suffices him, what an evil resting place; the selling man is received with tenderness — God is kind to His servants. The two panel-endings are the two divine dispositions the whole portrait-pair exists to display: the enough of judgment and the raʾfah of grace, each rendered to the heart that chose it. And the name binds the sale to the community: raʾūf bi'l-ʿibād, kind to the servants — plural — so that every seller in every generation sells into the same tenderness, and the bargain ʿAlī made in the Prophet's bed is open, at the same price, to whoever will lie down.

**The Diptych Complete**

The four verses now stand as one map of the heart's two economies. The first panel: the man whose speech about this world impresses, who calls God to witness a heart at war, who strives corruption in the land when he turns away, who is seized by pride into sin at the counsel to fear God, and for whom Hell suffices. The second panel: the man who sells his soul for God's pleasure — in the enjoiner's sentence, in the emigrant's bed, in the spender's emptied purse — received by the Kindness of God. Between the panels lies the hajj-legislation the diptych follows: the pilgrim who left the valley remembering God in numbered days, flexible in his options, mindful in his heart, gathered in his knowledge, walks now between the two figures and must recognize which one he has been becoming through the rite. The sūrah's method is visible in the whole arrangement — the law builds the community's shape, and the portraits test its heart — and the test this diptych administers is the market-question the sūrah has asked from its first pages: what is your nafs spending itself on, and who is receiving it? The eloquent self ends in sufficiency; the sold self ends in raʾfah; and the verse leaves no third buyer standing.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:208

> O believers! Enter into Islam wholeheartedly and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. Surely he is your sworn enemy.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Command to Enter Completely**

The diptych of the two men gives way to a direct address, and the address gathers the whole community: O you who believe, enter into the silm — completely. The command's first word raised the exegetes' longest question: silm literally means peace, and many read it here as submission — islām itself — acknowledging, as al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī do, that this is not the word's plain lexical sense but its contextual one. Others take it as obedience in the general sense: enter into the state of obeying God wholly. The readings converge on the act commanded: a total entry, the believer's full-person immersion in the religion rather than a partial occupancy of it. The adverb kāffah doubles the totality: it can be read as all together — the community entering as one body, undivided — or as altogether, modifying the entry rather than the entrants, so that the command reads enter into all of it, omitting none of its rites and commands. Al-Rāzī preserves both, and the verse holds them together without strain: the entry is complete in extent (all of the religion) and complete in company (all of the community), and either incompleteness is the foothold the second clause warns against.

**The Occasion: The Converts Who Kept Their Sabbath**

The reports behind the verse give the command its first case-study. Some narrations describe a group of Jewish converts — ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions are named in the traditions — who wished, after embracing Islam, to keep observing the Sabbath and other specifically Jewish practices that did not explicitly contradict Islamic teaching: continuing to abstain from foods the new law permitted, honoring the old holy day alongside the new. The verse answered the wish with the command to enter completely: the new submission is not an addition to the old observance but a replacement of it, and the convert who keeps one foot in the superseded law has not entered — he has leaned in the doorway. Al-Qurṭubī extends the reading to the People of the Book generally: the verse urges Jews and Christians, believers in Moses and Jesus, to convert en masse — the kāffah reading — to embrace Islam's totality rather than retain a partial continuity. The occasion and the extension agree on the principle: partial entry is no entry, and the religion admits no installment plans, because every retained reservation is a room of the house left unlit.

**The Entry of the Already-Believing**

For the believers already inside — the address's primary addressees — the command reads as deepening rather than conversion. Al-Rāzī states the sense: enter more deeply and completely into islām, omitting none of its rites and commands. The verse thus legislates against the most common failure of the established believer: the selective practice, the religion kept in its comfortable provinces while its demanding territories are left unvisited — the prayer maintained and the zakāh negotiated, the fast kept and the tongue unfasted, the hajj performed and the interval corrupted. The silm-as-peace reading adds a social dimension: the community that enters together enters into peace with one another, unfactionalized, the Ḥums-type separatisms of rank and lineage dissolved in the single entry — the same leveling the pilgrimage-verses just enacted at Minā. The command's grammar reinforces the totality: the entry is into the silm, not toward it or near it; the preposition of immersion, not approach. The believer addressed by this verse is told that his membership is not a status but a movement — an entering that is never finished, a going-in that must reach all the rooms, together with all the other entrants, until the house is fully inhabited.

**The Footsteps of Satan**

The second clause names what partial entry actually is: do not follow the footsteps of Satan. The phrase is the Qur'an's fixed formula — the same command the food-legislation carried (2:168), the cattle-rulings of the sūrah of the Cattle repeat it (6:142), and the sūrah of Light legislates it for the believers directly: whoever follows Satan's footsteps, he commands immorality and wickedness (24:21). The word khuṭuwāt — footsteps, tracks, the prints of a walked path — carries the formula's whole psychology: Satan's method is not the leap but the step. He does not invite the believer from the mosque to the Fire in one motion; he lays a track — the small concession, the reasonable exception, the reservation kept from the old life, the room left unentered — and each step is short enough to take. The verse's two clauses are therefore one argument: the incomplete entry *is* the first footprint. The convert keeping his Sabbath, the believer skipping a rite, the community splitting into factions — each has placed a foot on a track that leads, step by undramatic step, away from the house he thinks he still lives in. The manifest-enemy clause at the verse's end confirms the reading: an enemy declared, an enemy known, is countered by watching the path rather than the horizon — the footsteps, not the face.

**The Enemy Manifest**

The closing declaration — he is your manifest enemy — states the enmity's two properties at once. Manifest: the hostility is not hidden, not debatable, not subject to reassessment — Satan declared his program at the beginning, in the Qur'an's own narration of his expulsion: to sit for them on the straight path, to come from before and behind, to prove them ungrateful. The enemy who has published his methods is the enemy whose footsteps can be recognized, and the verse's command to watch the tracks presupposes the declaration's clarity. And *your* enemy: the enmity is personal and collective — aimed at each believer and at the community's entry as a whole, which is why the two clauses address the individual's completeness and the community's togetherness together. The sūrah's earlier food-legislation ended its own footsteps-command with the same declaration (2:168), and the repetition is the verse's pedagogy: the believer is reminded, at each legislative station, that the track exists and the enemy is known. Between the impressed speech of the hypocrite (2:204) and the total entry commanded here, the sūrah has drawn the whole geography of the heart's danger — the eloquence from outside, the footsteps from below — and stationed one command against both: enter, completely, together, and watch the ground you walk on.

**The Verse at the Passage's Hinge**

The placement of this command completes the movement's architecture. The hajj-legislation formed the community through rite (2:196–203); the diptych displayed the heart's two economies (2:204–207); and this verse issues the summons that both prepared: enter completely. The summons is addressed to believers — to people already inside the door — which is its sharpest feature: the rite-formed, portrait-warned community is told that its membership is still an entry, a movement not yet completed, a house with rooms it has not walked into. The verse that follows will state the stakes of faltering in that entry — if you slip after the clear proofs have come (2:209) — and the one after it the scene the slipper is waiting for. But the hinge-verse itself holds the whole demand in two clauses: the totality of the entry against the partiality of reservation, and the watchfulness of the path against the subtlety of the enemy. The community that left Minā knowing it would be gathered to God is now gathered to one command, and the command is the religion's own name turned into a verb: become what you are called — enter the silm, all of you, into all of it, with the enemy's footsteps visible on the ground at the door.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:209

> If you falter after receiving the clear proofs, then know that Allah is indeed Almighty, All-Wise. Waiting for Judgment?

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Slip After the Proofs**

The verse states the community's danger-case in one conditional: if you slip — after the clear proofs have come to you. The verb zalla is precise: not the rebellion of the defiant but the slip of the foot on smooth ground, the stumble of one who was standing, the error of one who was upright. The sūrah's vocabulary keeps the distinction sharp — the disbeliever rejects, the hypocrite conceals, the transgressor exceeds; the one who zalla was on the path and left it by a loss of footing rather than a decision of enmity. And the timing is the clause's aggravator: after the clear proofs — the bayyināt — have come. Al-Ṭabarī lists what the proofs comprehensively denote: the Prophet himself, the Qur'an, Islam as the embodied way, or all of them together. The slip is therefore never for want of evidence; it happens inside full illumination, which is why the sūrah has spent two hundred verses supplying the proofs — the legislative detail, the portraits, the stories, the hajj just completed — and why this verse guards the whole apparatus with a warning: the clearest light does not make the footing automatic. The proofs have come; the slip remains possible; the verse exists because the possibility is real for the people the proofs have already convinced.

**Then Know That God Is Mighty and Wise**

The conditional's consequence is striking in what it is not: no immediate threat of punishment, no enumeration of penalties, but a command to know — then know that God is Mighty, Wise. The two names are the verse's whole response to the slip. ʿAzīz — the Almighty, the Prevailing, the One whose might cannot be resisted and whose decree cannot be outrun: the name tells the slipper that the defection has not placed him outside power, that the proofs' Sender remains the unchallengeable, and that a slip inside His reach is not an escape from His reach. Ḥakīm — the All-Wise, whose every act and ruling carries wisdom whether or not the wisdom is visible: the name tells him that the legislation he stumbled against — the complete entry commanded, the rites imposed, the limits drawn — is not arbitrary burden but ordered good, and that the slip was not a correction of the law but a failure to see its wisdom. The pairing is the verse's therapy and its warning in one breath: Mighty, so the slip cannot be held against Him; Wise, so the slip cannot be justified against His law. The knowledge commanded is knowledge of God in exactly the two attributes the slipping heart most needs — power it cannot flee and wisdom it cannot improve upon.

**The Verse Against Despair**

Read beside the spending-verse of the same passage, this conditional performs a specific pastoral work. The sūrah had already named one self-destruction as the sinner's counsel of doom — the reading of 2:195 recorded by the exegetes, in which a person who believes his sin unforgivable goes on sinning, surrendering to moral despair instead of repenting. The slip-clause here could feed exactly that despair: I was given the proofs and I stumbled, so my case is closed. The verse's answer is the knowledge-command: the slipper is directed not into self-assessment but into theology — know God's might and wisdom rather than measure your own ruin. The direction matters because the two names hold the door open from both sides: the Mighty is the One whose strength the sūrah has repeatedly made the refuge of the weak, and the Wise is the One whose wisdom includes the repentance-legislation the sūrah has spread everywhere — the Forgiving turned toward every returner (2:160), the Forgiving and Merciful named over the pilgrim's istighfār (2:199). The verse thus refuses the slipper both escapes: it does not soften the slip into insignificance (the proofs were clear; the fall was real; the Might is over you) and it does not harden it into finality (the Wisdom that legislated the proofs legislated the return). Know, it says — and the knowing is the standing-up.

**The Footing of the Community**

The address is plural, and the slip it warns of is communal as well as personal. The clear proofs came to a community — the Prophet among them, the Qur'an descending on them, the legislation arriving verse by verse into their actual cases — and the community can slip where individuals slip: the rite kept in form while its wisdom drains (the boast returning after the remembrance, the prayer of this world alone replacing the double-horizon petition), the complete entry of 2:208 decaying into the provincial practice, the diptych's eloquent impostor admired again after his pattern was published. The verse's placement after the entry-command is deliberate: total entry is the footing, and the slip is what happens to the feet that stop walking into the house. The knowledge-command then reads as the community's maintenance — the regular re-knowing of the Might and the Wisdom that keeps the proofs from becoming furniture, the familiarity that precedes every communal zalla. The sūrah's own method models the maintenance: it re-states its proofs at every station, returns its names at every verdict, repeats its portraits — because a community that has received the bayyināt needs them re-delivered, not once but at every footing-risk, and the verse is the shortest form of that re-delivery: know.

**"Waiting for Judgment?"**

The translation's closing question — Waiting for Judgment? — marks the verse's forward edge, the point where the conditional opens onto the scene the next movement will unfold. The question hangs over the slipper in both of its possible postures. The one who slips after the proofs may still imagine time: the judgment deferred, the return postponed, the footing recoverable at leisure — and the question asks whether he knows what he is waiting for. And the community that holds its footing may still be tempted to treat the Might and the Wisdom as abstractions: powerful, yes; wise, yes — but at a distance, in a horizon not yet arrived — and the question reminds it that the horizon is the arrival, that the names it has just been commanded to know are the names of the One whose coming settles everything at once. The verse thus ends its conditional with a suspended interrogative, the two names named and the waiting named, and between them the reader's own posture: slipping or standing, the knowledge of the Mighty and Wise is knowledge of the One the question points toward — and the answer to the question is the scene that follows, in which the waiting ends.

**The Knowledge That Stands**

The verse's total demand reduces to its verb: know. Not perform more, not fear harder, not recover the lost ground by effort — know God's might and wisdom. The command identifies knowledge as the footing itself: the clear proofs came as knowledge, the slip happened despite knowledge, and the recovery is a knowledge deeper than the proofs' reception — the knowledge of who sent them and what His attributes guarantee. This is the same knowledge the hajj-legislation ended on: know that to Him you will be gathered (2:203); and the same knowledge the war-code ran on: know that God is with the mindful (2:194), severe in retribution (2:196). The sūrah's legislative stations all close in the commanded knowing, and this verse stations the knowing at the danger-point — the slip after clarity — because the knowledge of the Mighty and Wise is precisely what a slipping person has stopped having. The proofs inform the mind; this knowledge re-forms the posture: the heart that knows the Might cannot treat the slip as escape, and the heart that knows the Wisdom cannot treat the law as mistake. Between those two impossibilities the standing is rebuilt — and the verse, having rebuilt it, turns toward the horizon where all standing and slipping arrive.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:210

> Are they waiting for Allah ˹Himself˺ to come to them in the shade of clouds, along with the angels? ˹If He did˺, then the matter would be settled ˹at once˺. And to Allah ˹all˺ matters will be returned ˹for judgment˺.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Do They Wait for Anything Less?**

The verse answers the suspended question of the verse before with its full scene: do they wait for anything less than that God should come to them in the shadows of the clouds, and the angels, and the matter be decided? The interrogative's form — do they wait for nothing else but this? — carries the rebuke: what the waiters are deferring toward is not a negotiable future but the terminal event, the one arrival after which nothing remains to wait for. The verse thus names the posture it condemns: the life lived in the assumption that the decisive moment is indefinitely postponed, that the proofs can be received and slipped against (2:209) because the reckoning waits politely at the horizon. The clouds of the scene are the scripture's fixed apparatus of theophany — the same clouds the Day's own description uses: the day the heavens are split open with the clouds and the angels are sent down in ranks (25:25) — and the verse imports that whole imagery into the present tense of the waiting: what they wait for has a described form, a published manner of arrival, and a settled consequence, and the waiting is therefore not vagueness but appointment-keeping with their own end.

**The Coming in the Clouds, and Its Reading**

The exegetes handled the verse's grammar and its theology with equal care. Al-Ṭabarī records an alternate parsing: that God should come, and the angels in the shadows of the clouds — the cloud-apparatus attaching, on this reading, to the angels rather than to the Divine coming itself. Others read the coming as the coming of God's command or judgment: what arrives in the clouds is the thing God has promised or threatened, the decree's execution rather than a bodily transport. And the tradition fixed two settings for the scene: some connect it to the angels who come at the moment of death — the arrival each soul waits for privately, its matter decided at the last breath; others, al-Rāzī among them, read it as the description of the Day of Resurrection itself, with 25:25's split heavens and descending angels as the parallel text. The readings share a structure: an arrival, a cloud-apparatus, an angelic company, and a decision that the arrival renders irreversible. The variety is the verse's own invitation — the coming concerns every waiter at the hour that is his, the deathbed's or the Day's, and in both the shadows are the same shadows the scripture has already described.

**Not Movement, Not Place**

The commentators are careful — and the care is itself part of the verse's reception — to state what the scene cannot mean: it cannot imply that God moves from place to place, or is located in a place at all, since location would limit God and introduce change into His nature. The cloud-coming is therefore read, across the tradition's schools, either as the coming of the command and the angels (the created apparatus of the decisive hour), or as an arrival befitting the Divine majesty without modality — a real coming whose how no creature's categories contain. The theological precision serves the verse's rhetorical purpose rather than deflating it: the point is not that God travels but that the decisive hour arrives with the full weight of His authority, clouded and attended and final. The waiter who imagines the postponement safe because no visible arrival has occurred is answered by the scene's own grandeur — the heavens split, the angels ranked, the shadows filling the sky — an arrival that will not be missed, not deferred, and not survived as postponement. The verse's theology and its warning are one: the Coming is certain precisely because the Coming One is beyond the creaturely limits the waiters implicitly assume.

**The Matter Decided**

The scene's third element is the decision: and the matter has been decreed. Al-Rāzī explains the finality the clause carries: it refers to the Hereafter's decisive character — at that arrival the deeds have already been done, and there is no adding to them and no subtracting from them. The probation is over; the record is closed; the portion earned (2:202) is fixed. The Qur'an states the same closure in the sūrah of the Cattle's answer to the demand for visible angels: had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and they would be given no respite (6:8) — the angelic arrival and the decision's finality bound together there exactly as here. The clause is the verse's answer to the waiting posture at its root: what the deferrer is waiting for is the end of waiting — the hour whose whole function is to settle, after which no slip can be recovered (2:209), no entry completed (2:208), no soul sold (2:207), no portion altered. The matter decided is the swift reckoning arriving in scene-form: the audit the previous verses described as instantaneous disclosed at last as event — the clouds, the angels, and the book that no longer changes.

**To God All Matters Return**

The verse's final clause widens the decision into the cosmos's constant: to God all matters are returned. The formula is among the scripture's most repeated closures — to Him belong the matters' return in Āl ʿImrān, in the Spoils, in Hūd, in the Pilgrimage, in the Angels, in Iron (3:109; 8:44; 11:123; 22:76; 35:4; 57:5) — and its sense here is the waiting's refutation: the matters do not drift, defer, or belong to the interval; every affair is already in return-motion toward its Owner. The return is understood primarily as the Hereafter's gathering — the matters of every soul delivered back for the settlement — but its grammar holds the present tense too: the matter is returned at every moment of its existence, since nothing is ever out of His hands long enough to be lost. For the waiter the clause collapses the postponement's illusion: the arrival he defers toward is not a future interruption of the present order but the disclosure of the order the present already keeps — matters returning, accounts moving, the reckoning swift. The verse thus ends where the hajj-coda ended (to Him you will be gathered, 2:203) and where the whole sūrah's legislation has been pointing: every law a matter in return, every slip a matter in return, every prayer a matter already answered in the returning.

**The Verse Between Slip and Sign**

Within the passage's movement the verse holds the middle position between two addresses. Behind it: the command to enter completely, the warning of the slip after the proofs, the knowledge of the Mighty and Wise (2:208–209). Before it: the turn to the Children of Israel and their clear signs (2:211), the world made fair to the mockers (2:212), humanity's one community and the Book sent to judge its differences (2:213). The cloud-scene is the hinge between the community's internal danger and its historical lesson: the believers who might slip are shown the terminus their slipping defers toward, and then shown the people whose story proves the terminus real — the Israelites who received sign after sign and altered the favor after it came. The waiting-question binds both panels: the slipper waits as though the decision were far; the sign-recipients lived as though the favor were theirs to change; and the clouds arrive for both at the hour that ends both illusions. The verse leaves its reader with the posture the whole passage commands — the entry complete before the shadows fill the sky, the slip recovered before the matter is decided, the knowledge of the Mighty and Wise held until the return that holds every knower.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:211

> Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We have given them. And whoever trades Allah’s favour—after receiving it—˹for disbelief˺ should know that Allah is indeed severe in punishment.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question Put to History**

The verse turns from the cloud-scene to a standing witness: ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We have given them. The command to question is the verse's method — history summoned as testimony in the case the previous verses opened. The community that might slip after its proofs (2:209) is directed to the people who lived the slip at the largest scale the world has seen: a nation fed with signs, delivered by miracles, covenanted with God, and still the scripture's standing example of favor altered. The interrogative kam — how many — expects no number because the number is beyond counting; the question asks the witness to display its record, and the record itself is the argument. Al-Ṭabarī fixes the signs' identity: the miracles of Moses — the staff cast down and become a serpent, the hand drawn out white, the sea parted, the enemy drowned — the sign-cycle the sūrah of the Heights narrates at length (7:105–136). Each sign was a bayyinah, a clear proof in the exact sense 2:209 used for the proofs given this community: evidence so plain that rejection after it is not ignorance but choice. The verse thus establishes the comparison the passage needs — the proofs of this ummah against the signs of that — and asks the question whose answer is the warning.

**The Favor, and Its Alteration**

The verse's second movement names the crime: whoever alters the favor of God after it has come to him. The favor — niʿmah — was interpreted by al-Ṭabarī as the trust and covenant God made with the Children of Israel: the whole endowment of signs, scripture, prophecy, and election that constituted their national blessing. To alter it means, in the exegetes' primary sense, to deny it, to disbelieve in it — the favor received and then re-defined by its receivers as something other than what the Giver made it. The verb baddala carries the substitution-sense the Qur'an uses for the gravest exchange: not merely neglecting the favor but replacing it — and some commentators connect the alteration to the accusation of taḥrīf, the distortion of scripture, recorded at 2:75, where a group hears the word of God and then knowingly corrupts it after understanding it. The alteration is thus comprehensive: the covenant's terms renegotiated, the signs reinterpreted away, the Book's words adjusted toward the readers' desire. And the temporal clause is the crime's aggravator: after it has come to him. The favor was not altered in prospect or in ambiguity — it arrived, was received, was held, and was then changed in the holder's hands, which is the precise anatomy of the slip 2:209 warned this community against, drawn at national scale.

**The Severe Retribution**

The verdict clause repeats the formula the hajj-legislation closed on: God is severe in retribution — shadīd al-ʿiqāb. The same phrase ended the pilgrimage's concessions-verse (2:196), where it guarded the rite's interior against exploitation; here it guards the favor against alteration, and the repetition across the passage is deliberate — the two domains where the law has no human auditor, the pilgrim's intention and the covenant-keeper's fidelity, are the two domains the severe-retribution formula oversees. The severity answers the crime's shape: an alteration performed after full receipt is not weakness but transaction — the favor traded, the verse says in the translation's gloss, for disbelief — and a transaction is answered by a price. The sūrah has been building this economics since its opening: the traders who purchased error at guidance's price (2:16), the concealers who sold revelation for a fleeting gain and ate fire (2:174–175), the covenant-sellers of Āl ʿImrān whose trade earns them no share in the Hereafter and no divine speech on the Day (3:77).
