The Israelite alteration is the pattern's first national instance, and the severe retribution is the pattern's fixed consequence: the favor exchanged is not merely lost but avenged, because the exchange itself is the insult — the Giver's gift re-valued by the receiver as less than disbelief.

**Why the Question Is Commanded**

The command to ask has a purpose beyond polemic, and the verse's context supplies it. The passage has moved from the community's internal legislation — the hajj, the complete entry, the slip-warning, the cloud-scene — to its external orientation, and the question to the Children of Israel installs the new ummah inside an older story. The believers are not the first people given proofs; they are the latest, and the verse makes them inherit the whole archive: the signs of Moses are their inheritance-warning, the altered favor is their case-study, the severe retribution is their horizon. This is the same method the sūrah has used throughout — the Israelite narratives of the early verses (the calf, the covenant, the prophets killed) read as instruction for the new community rather than as history alone — and here the method becomes explicit: ask, it says; make the inquiry; hold the answer. The question also disciplines the community's self-understanding: the ummah addressed has just completed the hajj-legislation, the most elaborate rite-code in the sūrah, and might read its legislation as evidence of a secured standing; the verse reminds it that Israel had signs beyond counting and a covenant from God, and that neither the count nor the covenant prevented the alteration. Standing is kept, not inherited — and the asking is part of the keeping.

**The Signs and the Scripture's Own Case**

The verse's signs have a specific edge for a community whose central sign is a book. The miracles of Moses were public and physical — the staff, the hand, the sea — signs seen by multitudes and survived by no disputer; and the Children of Israel altered the favor built on them. The new community's clear proofs include a sign of a different order — the Qur'an itself, a bayyinah of speech rather than spectacle — and the verse's warning transfers without loss: the alteration Israel performed on signs it saw, a later generation can perform on a sign it reads, adjusting the Book's words toward desire, re-interpreting the covenant's terms, substituting for the favor a version of the favor that costs nothing. The sūrah has already legislated against exactly this on its own pages: the editors who write the book with their hands and say this is from God (2:79), the concealers who hide what was revealed (2:174), the far-schismatics who differ regarding the Book in truth (2:176). The question to Israel is therefore also a mirror: the clear signs given them and the clear proofs given this community stand under one law — received favor is kept by fidelity and lost by substitution — and the severe retribution named at the verse's end is pronounced over both archives, the sea parted and the Book revealed, against every hand that alters what it was given.

**Between the Clouds and the One Community**

Within the movement's architecture the verse is the bridge between the horizon and the history. The cloud-scene (2:210) showed the waiting its terminus; this verse shows the slipping its precedent; and the verses that follow will show the whole human story its shape — the world made fair to the mockers (2:212), humanity one community then divided, the Book sent down to judge the division (2:213). The Israelite question is the middle term: the case-history that proves the terminus is not theoretical. A people asked, given signs, altered the favor, met the severe retribution — the sequence in completed form, available for the asking. The community reading these verses between the hajj's end and the coming trials-verse stands at the sequence's second step: proofs received, favor held. The verse tells it what the third step can be and what the fourth is — and the command to ask is the instruction for staying at the second: keep inquiring of the archive, keep the case-history present, keep the alteration visible in the witness's own record. The signs given Israel are counted; the favor they altered is named; the retribution's severity is published — and the whole testimony is left standing at the door of every community the proofs afterward reach.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:212

> The life of this world has been made appealing to the disbelievers, and they mock the believers. Those who are mindful ˹of Allah˺ will rank above them on the Day of Judgment. And Allah provides for whoever He wills without limit.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The World Beautified**

The verse opens on the disbelievers' condition with a passive verb that does quiet theological work: the life of this world has been beautified — made fair, adorned — for those who disbelieve. The beautification is not their own achievement but something done to the world in their regard, and the exegetes' readings of the agent span the scripture's whole account of trial: the world is made fair by God as the test in which human choice is real; by Satan as the decoration he promised to spread; by the world's own glamour operating on the heart that has no second horizon. The verse needs no agent named, because its point is the effect: to the disbeliever this life arrives pre-adorned, its goods luminous, its losses intolerable, its horizon total. The beautification explains the mockery that follows — the man for whom this world is the whole beautiful thing can only treat the believer's other horizon as poverty of imagination — and it explains the sūrah's standing economics: the fleeting gain the concealers traded revelation for (2:174) is exactly this beautified life, and its beauty is the mechanism of every bad trade the sūrah has catalogued. The world is not evil in the verse; it is adorned — and the adornment is the trial, beautiful enough to be believed final.

**They Mock the Believers**

The adornment's social expression is the mockery: they ridicule those who believe. Al-Thaʿlabī records the occasions — the verse was revealed about the Meccan idolaters, or the Medinan hypocrites, or the Jewish leaders of Medina who belittled the Muslim community for its composition: the poor, the weak, the slaves and laborers who filled its first ranks while the notables stayed away. The mockery has a fixed structure the verse assumes: the disbelievers measure the believers by the beautified world's metrics — wealth, status, comfort — and find them losing, then announce the verdict publicly, as though the ledger of adornment were the only ledger. The Qur'an answers this scene repeatedly and consistently: the sūrah of the Mockers devotes its opening to the woe of every scorner who counts his wealth (104:1–2); the Garden's people will call down to the Fire's people asking what their counting availed them (74:40–47 in substance); and the reversal the mockers cannot see is the verse's next clause. The mockery is also, in the passage's own logic, the diptych's continuation: the eloquent hypocrite whose worldly speech impressed (2:204) is the mocker in his community-role, and the mocked believers are the sellers of their souls (2:207) — the verse names both groups' worldly standing and then overturns it in the Day's.

**Above Them on the Day**

The reversal is stated in a single future tense: those who are mindful — the muttaqūn — will be above them on the Day of Resurrection. The elevation is the mockery's exact answer: the ranking the world performed in reverse, the Day performs in truth. Al-Qurṭubī notes the tradition's elaborations — reports describing how the belittled and mocked believers will receive great fame and standing on the Day while their abusers are humiliated and punished — and the verse's own wording carries the whole: above them, a spatial verdict in a scene the scripture consistently describes in the spatial terms of rank, the Garden's people calling down to the Fire's, the elevated couches and the lowered abode. The taqwā named as the elevation's criterion completes the passage's thread: the reverent are the ones the hajj-legislation formed (2:196–203), the ones the flexible options were granted for (2:203), the ones God is with (2:194) — and the verse now publishes the community's true standing against its mockers. The mockery measured by adornment; the Day measures by mindfulness; and the measured are placed above not by retaliation but by the simple disclosure of what the two currencies were always worth.

**The Lowliest Better Than a World Full**

Al-Qurṭubī collects, under this verse, the report that gives the reversal its most concrete image — the exchange between Abū Dharr and the Prophet. Look around the mosque, the Prophet said, and find the most exalted man you can see: Abū Dharr looked and named a finely dressed man sitting in prominence. Now find the lowliest: he looked again and named a weak man in tattered clothes. Then the verdict, sworn by the One in whose hand his soul rested: the second man weighed, before God, more than a world filled with the first man's kind. The report is the verse's commentary in scene-form: the two men the mockery ranks, the adornment's champion and the taqwā's unknown, weighed against each other in the only scales that hold, and the lowliest not merely equal but outweighing a world filled with his exalted counterpart. The hyperbole is arithmetic rather than rhetoric — the verse's without-limit clause supplies its ground: if God's giving is beyond reckoning, then the worth He places in a single mindful soul can exceed any quantity of adorned ones, and the Day's above-them will be the public reading of a weight already assigned. The mosque scene is every community's scene: the dressed and the seated and the admired on one side, the tattered and the unnoticed and the reverent on the other, and the scales hidden.

**Provision Without Reckoning**

The verse closes with the clause that re-reads everything before it: God provides for whomever He wills without reckoning. The exegetes unfold the phrase's several senses, and each cuts against the mockers' ledger. God does not give a reckoning to anyone for what He does — the Provider answers to no auditor, and the adorned life's distribution is His alone. His infinitude needs no reckoning — He does not count His giving for fear it will dwindle, the treasury beyond arithmetic. The giving spans both worlds — provision in this life and provision in the next (al-Rāzī), so the adorned man's wealth is not the whole of what is being distributed. Some read the clause eschatologically: the elect who enter the Garden directly, without reckoning, their passage as unmeasured as the provision. And the clause alludes to the incommensurability of God's giving altogether — the tenfold and beyond of the good deed (6:160), the grain that sprouts seven ears of a hundred grains (2:261), the provision found beside Mary in the sanctuary, from God, who provides for whom He wills without limit (3:37). Every sense converges on one refutation: the world's accounting — by which the mockers measured and the believers lost — is not merely unfair but unreal, a local arithmetic inside a giving that has none.

**The Verse Between the Diptych and the One Community**

The verse's placement binds the movement's three panels into one argument. The diptych (2:204–207) showed the heart's two economies in individual form — the marketed self and the sold self. The slip-and-cloud verses (2:208–211) showed the community's footing and its horizon — the proofs, the waiting, the altered favor of the witness-people. This verse shows the two economies at social scale: the beautified world with its mockers, the taqwā with its mocked, and the Day with its reversal — and the following verse will widen the scene once more to the species, humanity one community then divided, the Book sent to judge (2:213). The through-line is the currency-question the whole passage keeps asking: what is the world's adornment worth against the portion earned (2:202), the sold soul's price (2:207), the favor not altered (2:211)? The verse's answer is the provision-clause — the giving without reckoning, in which the mockers' wealth is a measured thing inside the Unmeasured's hand, and the mocked believer's standing is a weight already placed. The reader carried from Minā's gathering through the hypocrite's portrait to this verse arrives at the community's charter against contempt: the adornment is real but reckoned by another arithmetic, the mockery is loud but brief, and the above-them of the Day is provision without limit made visible.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:213

> Humanity had once been one community ˹of believers before they lost faith˺. Then Allah raised prophets as deliverers of good news and as warners, and revealed to them the Scriptures in truth to judge among people regarding their disputes. And no one disputed the Scriptures except the very people who received them after clear proofs had come to them—out of jealousy. Then Allah, by His grace, has guided the believers to the truth regarding those disputes. And Allah guides whoever He wills to the Straight Path.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Humanity Was One Community**

The verse opens the whole human story in a single clause: mankind was one community — ummah wāḥidah. The exegetes' readings map the possibilities, and al-Ṭabarī notes that the exact chronology is not what matters. Some locate the unity in the period between Adam and Noah; some understand it as a unity in disbelief and degradation, later corrected through Noah and then Abraham; others describe a unity in submission — all humanity following one religion, one community of believers before the loss. Another reading takes the oneness as Adam himself: humanity began as a single person and became many, and the Qur'an does use ummah of one man — Abraham was an ummah, rendered in the common translation as a model of excellence, devout and upright (16:120). A further reading connects the one community to the pretemporal covenant of 7:172, when all Adam's descendants testified Am I not your Lord? and answered yes — the unity of that original acknowledgment. The readings agree on the verse's structural point: the story begins in oneness, and everything that follows — prophets, books, differences — is the history of that oneness lost and its truth recovered. The sūrah of Yūnus states the same opening with the divergence explicit: mankind was nothing but one community, then they differed (10:19).

**The Implied Difference**

The verse's logic turns on what the first clause leaves unsaid, and the commentators supply it: many read an implied phrase, so the sentence runs mankind was one community — *and then they differed* — whereupon God sent the prophets. The implication is necessary to the sequence, because the sending answers the difference: prophets are sent to correct error and adjudicate division, and al-Rāzī's argument is decisive — had humanity remained united in one true religion, the sending would be superfluous. The difference that intervened is not detailed, and the verse's silence is informative: the scripture consistently declines to romanticize the unity's duration or itemize the first fall, treating the divergence as the given condition the revelation addresses. Some exegetes read the earliest history as a time without the need for religion's commands and prohibitions, with prophecy becoming necessary at a later stage; al-Rāzī reports — disapprovingly — a view attributing the first period to unaided intellect, humanity knowing the Creator and the good by reason until pride and envy crept in and division made the prophets necessary. Against such views stands the tradition's own premise: Adam was himself a prophet, and the clear proofs began with the first man. The difference, on whatever timetable, is the hinge the whole verse turns on — unity, divergence, and the sending that follows divergence like the answer follows the question.

**Bearers of Glad Tidings and Warners**

The prophets are sent with a double office the Qur'an names as a fixed pair: bashīr — bearer of glad tidings — and nadhīr — warner. The two functions are the revelation's two hands: the good news that draws, the warning that drives, the Garden announced and the Fire announced, and no prophet sent with one hand only. With them — and the phrase binds book to messenger in one descent — God sent down the Book in truth, to judge between people in what they differed about. The Book here is read at two scopes: the general name for all the revealed books (al-Shaʿbī's reading), or the Torah specifically if the verse is tied to the Jews and Christians alone (al-Ṭabarī's alternative); the comprehensive reading carries the verse's universal frame better — one Book in successive descents, each installment in truth, each sent for the same adjudicating purpose. The phrase in truth is the same formula that grounded the far-schismatics' sentence (2:176): the Book descends bi'l-ḥaqq, its content corresponding to what is, its purpose the settlement of disputes by a standard no party controls. The verse thereby states revelation's job-description: not to decorate the difference but to judge it — the Book as court, the prophets as its bearers, the glad tidings and warnings as its two verdicts.

**Only Those Given It Differed**

The verse's most searching clause reports the trial's outcome: none differed concerning the Book except those who were given it — after the clear proofs came to them — out of mutual injustice and envy. The paradox is the scripture's standing grief: the difference did not arise from the Book's absence but from its presence; the disputants were not the uninformed outsiders but the informed recipients; the proofs were clear and the division came after. The sūrah states the same sequence of the People of the Scripture: they did not dispute among themselves out of mutual envy until knowledge came to them (3:19); and the sūrah of the Clear Proof repeats it: the People of the Book became divided only after the clear proof came to them (98:4). The motive named — baghy, the envious overreaching — identifies the difference's engine: not honest interpretive struggle but rivalry, the competition of parties who want the Book's authority for themselves. The commentators draw the general lesson: there is something near-inevitable, given human nature, about difference arising after revelation arrives — the truth given to a community becomes, in envious hands, the truth disputed by that community. The verse thus completes the warning of 2:211: Israel altered the favor after receiving it; here the whole pattern is generalized — the recipients are the differers, the proofs precede the division, and the envy is the difference's parent.

**Guided to the Truth by His Leave**

The verse's penultimate clause turns from the divided to the guided: then God guided those who believe to the truth of what they differed about, by His leave. The guidance is specific rather than general — not guidance to a new truth but to the truth of the disputed matter, the settlement the Book was sent to make and the divided recipients failed to receive: the community of believers is given what the envious receivers withheld from themselves. The phrase bi-idhnih — by His leave, by His gracious permission — marks the guidance's character: it is not earned by the believers' cleverness but granted by the Guide's initiative, the same gratuity the verse's last clause confirms. The sūrah of the Table states the framework the guidance operates in: to each community God ordained a law and a way, and had He willed He would have made you one community — but He tests you with what He has given you, so compete in good works; to God you all return and He will inform you of what you differed about (5:48). The verse of al-Baqarah is that framework's present tense: the differences are real, the competition is commanded, the final information is deferred to the Return — and in the meantime, by His leave, the believers hold the truth of the disputed matter, not as possession but as granted guidance.

**To the Straight Path**

The verse closes with the destination's name: God guides whomever He wills to a straight path. The ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm is the petition of the scripture's opening chapter — guide us to the straight path — and the verse answers the petition from the divine side: the guidance asked for is the guidance God wills to give, and the path asked for is the one this verse has been describing — the oneness recovered through the Book's judgment, the difference outrun by granted truth. The closing clause gathers the whole verse into its final shape: one community, then difference, then prophets and Book sent to judge, then the recipients' envious division, then the believers guided to the disputed truth, then the straight path as the guidance's name. The sequence is the theology of revelation in miniature — the human story as unity lost, adjudication sent, adjudication corrupted by its own recipients, and guidance preserved by grace in a community that asks for it. And the clause's last word is the passage's hinge to what follows: the straight path is not abstraction but legislation — the qiblah, the fast, the hajj, the war's limits, the bequest's fairness — the sūrah's two hundred verses of straight-path detail, with the trials-verse ahead confirming that admission to the path's end runs through the testing of its walkers. The one community's story closes where every community's story reopens: at the path, under the Guide, by His leave.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:214

> Do you think you will be admitted into Paradise without being tested like those before you? They were afflicted with suffering and adversity and were so ˹violently˺ shaken that ˹even˺ the Messenger and the believers with him cried out, “When will Allah’s help come?” Indeed, Allah’s help is ˹always˺ near.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question the Community Must Answer**

The verse opens with a question that dismantles an assumption: do you suppose you will enter the Garden without the likes of what befell those who passed before you? The interrogative form is not inquiry but correction — the community is addressed as people who have been entertaining, perhaps unconsciously, the idea that paradise is an inheritance of confession rather than an outcome of trial. The sūrah states the same principle twice more in identical terms: do you think you will enter Paradise while God has not yet proven who among you struggled and endured (3:142), and the sūrah of the Spider's opening — do people think they will be left to say "we believe" without being tested? We tested those before them (29:2–3). The three verses form a single doctrine of the tested faith: belief declares itself in words, and the trial verifies it in fact; between the declaration and the verification stands the whole life of the community. The verse's reference to those who passed before installs that verification in history — the test ahead is not novel but inherited, the same furnace every believing generation has entered, and its heat is not evidence of abandonment but of membership.

**The Trench, the Exile, and the Taunts**

The reports of occasion place the verse inside the community's hardest hours. Some connect it to the Battle of the Trench in the fifth year, when the confederated tribes besieged Medina and the Qur'an's own sūrah of the Parties remembers the days — when forces came against you and God sent a wind and hosts you did not see (33:9); others connect it to Uḥud in the third year, the defeat on the mountain. Al-Rāzī and al-Thaʿlabī preserve the social texture behind the shaking: the Emigrants were bearing the cost of exile — property left in Mecca, livelihoods interrupted, families divided — while the locals and the hypocrites taunted them, asking how long they would sacrifice themselves and their wealth for a cause that looked, by every worldly reckoning, like a losing one. The verse answers the taunt by relocating it in history: the question "when will this cost end?" is not a new question invented by Medina's cynics but the old question of every community under trial — asked, the verse will say, even by the Messenger and the believers with him.

**Misfortune, Hardship, and the Shaking**

The middle clause names the trial's two instruments and its effect: misfortune and hardship befell them, and they were shaken — zulzilū, the reduplicated verb of violent trembling, the same root the Qur'an uses for the earthquake of the Hour. The two instruments are the sūrah's standing pair: baʾsāʾ and ḍarrāʾ, the suffering and the adversity the definition of righteousness had already placed patience within (2:177) and the test-announcement had listed as fear, hunger, and loss (2:155). The shaking is the trial's real measure — not the affliction itself but the affliction carried to the point where constancy trembles. The verse is precise about how far the shaking went: so far that the Messenger and those who believed with him cried out. The extremity is stated without apology and without minimization; the trial of the prophets' communities reached the limit of human endurance, and the limit is where the cry comes. This is the verse's first consolation: the reader's own shaken faith does not place him outside the company of the faithful but inside it — the tremor is part of the record, recorded by God rather than hidden by Him.

**"When Will God's Help Come?"**

The cry is quoted: *When will God's help come?* The exegetes handled the question with care, because it issues from the Messenger and the believers together. Some read the Messenger here as Muhammad specifically; others took it generally — every prophet and his people at their trial's depth, since all the prophets encounter severe trials. Al-Qurṭubī records the reading that protects prophetic certainty: the Messenger knew the help was coming and the question sought its hastening — not doubt about whether but impatience for when. The Qur'an's parallel portraits confirm that prophethood does not exempt its bearers from the weight of trial: the messengers despaired and their people thought them denied, until Our help came (12:110); the breast straitened by what they say (15:97 in substance); the torment of the self over a people who will not believe (26:3 in substance); Job's affliction and his cry (21:83). The station of prophethood, in the Qur'an's presentation, includes human vulnerability to fear, sadness, and discouragement — and the verse quotes the cry rather than censoring it because the cry itself, at the trial's limit, is not disbelief but the last form of address to God: the question asked *to* Him, not about Him.

**Indeed, God's Help Is Near**

The answer is a single word of emphasis and a single adjective: *indeed — God's help is near*. The particle removes all hedging from the promise; the nearness does not specify an hour but a relation — the help is near to the cry, near to the limit, near to the shaking rather than distant from them. The verse's structure performs this: the cry and the answer share one sentence, with no intervening narrative, no condition inserted between the question and its response. The nearness is also the trial's hidden geography — the furnace the community enters is not a place God has left; the help is near *inside* it. The tradition drew the practical lesson for every generation under trial: the point of maximum shaking is not evidence of maximum abandonment but the classical position of deliverance, the hour the previous communities cried in and were answered from. For the verse's first hearers — the taunted Emigrants, the besieged city — the nearness was historical as well as theological: Uḥud was followed by the Trench, the Trench by its wind and its unseen hosts, and the wind by the road back to Mecca.

**The Verse as the Passage's Foundation**

The placement of this verse after the one-community history (2:213) and before the legislation of fighting (2:216) gives it an architectural office. The previous verse ended with the guidance granted by God's leave to those who believe; this verse states what the guided community must expect on the road — the trial of those before, carried to the shaking-point — and the verse after will legislate the obligation the community finds hateful. The sequence is pedagogy: guidance, then testing, then the hard command — the community is not given the command to fight before it is told what commands cost and what trials precede paradise. The verse also answers the mockery it will meet two verses on: the disbelievers for whom the world is beautified and who ridicule the believers (2:212) are exactly the taunters the reports describe, and the trial-verse tells the mocked that their shaking has a company, a purpose, and a near help. Between the one community of the past and the divided communities of the present, this verse installs the constant: every community that receives the truth is tried by it — and the trial's last word, spoken over the cry of the Messenger and the believers themselves, is the nearness of the help.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:215

> They ask you ˹O Prophet in˺ what ˹way˺ they should donate. Say, “Whatever donations you give are for parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and ˹needy˺ travellers. Whatever good you do is certainly well known to Allah.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question and the Shape of the Answer**

The verse belongs to the sūrah's great series of question-verses — they ask you, and revelation answers — and the shape of this answer is instructive. The question concerned spending: what should be given, and to whom. The reply does not begin with amounts, percentages, or categories of wealth; it begins with people. The answer names a list — parents, kinsfolk, orphans, the indigent, the traveler — and only then, in its closing clause, returns the whole matter to God's knowledge. The structure teaches the priority of charity's legislation: before the arithmetic of giving comes the geography of need, and the giving is defined by its recipients rather than by the giver's convenience. The exegetes note the verse's period: it is said to have been revealed before the institution of the formal alms-tax, and thus to govern ordinary charitable giving — the voluntary infāq that precedes and surrounds the fixed zakāh. The list it gives is therefore the community's first curriculum of generosity, taught by naming the claimants one by one.

**The Standing Roster**

The five named recipients are not an ad hoc list but the Qur'an's standing roster of the people a righteous economy is measured by. The same names recur wherever the scripture legislates giving: the definition of righteousness counted kinsfolk, orphans, the poor, the traveler, beggars, and captives (2:177); the kindness-command of the sūrah of the Women lists parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, neighbors near and far, the companion, the wayfarer, and those your right hands possess (4:36); the war-booty legislation assigns its fifth to God and the Messenger, the near relatives, orphans, the poor, and the traveler (8:41); and the sūrah of the Exile repeats the same five with its economic principle — so that wealth may not merely circulate among your rich (59:7). The recurrence is the point: the community is not given a different charity-list for each occasion but one list, installed across legislation, worship, and war alike, so that the same faces are seen in every distribution — the faces of the people the economy exists for.

**The Order of the List**

The list's sequence carries its own teaching. Parents stand first: charity begins at the root of the giver's own life, and the debt of nurture is the first claim on wealth — a priority the scripture reinforces everywhere, joining the worship of God to kindness to parents in a single breath. Kinsfolk follow: the circle of blood next, the relatives whose need the giver can see and whose claim the community's own fabric presses. Then orphans — the vulnerable whose protectors are dead, the class whose property this sūrah guards with its fiercest language. Then the indigent, the standing poor. Then the traveler — the stranger, the one cut off from his own support networks, whose claim arises from circumstance rather than relation. The movement is outward in widening circles: from the household, to the clan, to the unprotected, to the poor, to the passing stranger — and the widening is deliberate, so that generosity is trained in the order of natural attachment and then extended beyond it, until the unknown wayfarer stands inside the giver's obligation beside his own father.

**Whatever Good You Do, God Knows**

The closing clause returns the whole legislation to its unseen auditor: whatever good you do, God knows it. The same assurance stood inside the hajj-legislation — whatever good you do, God fully knows of it (2:197) — and in both places it does the same double work. It is a guarantee: the giving nobody sees, the relative supported quietly, the traveler relieved without witness — all of it is known, recorded, and answerable in reward; no act of charity is lost to the ledger for want of an audience. And it is a discipline: the knowledge of God audits the giving that *has* an audience, separating the charity performed for the eyes of people from the charity performed for the Face of God — the sūrah's recurring distinction, whose failure-mode it painted in the hypocrite who spends to be seen. The clause's placement after the list ties the two halves together: the recipients are named so the giving is directed rightly; the knower is named so the giving is motivated rightly. Direction and motive — the two coordinates of every act of charity — are fixed in one sentence.

**The Question-Verses as Classroom**

This verse is one of a dense cluster in which the community's actual questions are answered by revelation — the new moons and the doors of houses (2:189), the nearness of God to the caller (2:186), the sacred month's fighting (2:217), wine and gambling and the amount to spend (2:219), the orphans' affairs (2:220), menstruation (2:222). The cluster forms the sūrah's method of legislation: not a code delivered in the abstract but answers delivered to questions, the law growing at the points where the community's life actually presses against it. The question about spending — what should we give? — is the community asking to be directed in its daily economics, and the answer's form trains a habit: ask, and the revelation names the people. The method also honors the asking: the question is not rebuked as ignorance but answered as curriculum, and every generation inherits both the answers and the permission to bring its own cases to the text. The sūrah's legislation is thus dialogical — a community being formed through inquiry, with the roster of the needy installed at the center of the exchange.

**The Giver Between the List and the Knower**

Read whole, the verse places the giver between two presences: the visible claimants and the invisible Knower. The list makes the giving concrete — not "the poor" as abstraction but the father aging in the next room, the cousin fallen on hard years, the child whose guardian died, the beggar at the gate, the stranger whose caravan left without him. The knowledge-clause makes the giving pure — performed under an audit that sees the hand and the heart together. Between the two, charity becomes what the sūrah's whole economy intends: a transfer of wealth that is simultaneously an act of worship, directed to faces and offered to a Face. The verse that answers a simple question about spending thus carries the full moral architecture of Islamic giving — the priority of persons over amounts, the order of claims from kin outward, the surveillance that keeps the motive clean — and leaves the asker with a list to memorize and a Knower to remember. Whatever good you do, it ends; and the sentence is both the promise of reward and the standard the reward answers to.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:216

> Fighting has been made obligatory upon you ˹believers˺, though you dislike it. Perhaps you dislike something which is good for you and like something which is bad for you. Allah knows and you do not know.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Kutiba**

The verse uses the sūrah's legislative formula for the third time: it has been prescribed for you — the same verb that wrote the retaliation for murder (2:178) and wrote the fast (2:183). The formula's repetition builds the community's constitution in three obligations, and the third is the hardest: fighting. The sequence is itself instructive — the law of blood, the law of the body's appetite, the law of the body's risk — each *kutiba*, each written rather than suggested. But this prescription arrives with a clause its two predecessors did not carry: *though it is hateful to you*. The verse does not wait for the community to confess its aversion; it states the aversion inside the command, legislating over the top of a dislike it has already named. The candor is the verse's first gift: the believer is not required to feel enthusiasm for the obligation, not required to love what God has written — only to know that the writing stands over the feeling, and that the feeling itself has been seen, named, and answered rather than condemned.

**The Dislike Named, Not Rebuked**

The hateful-to-you clause has a precision worth marking. The Qur'an nowhere commands the emotional conversion of the reluctant fighter — there is no "fight and love it," no rebuke of the distaste as faithlessness. The dislike is treated as a fact of the human constitution, as real as the hunger the fast legislates over and the fear the battle produces. What the verse does is refuse the dislike a veto: the obligation is prescribed *while* the aversion is acknowledged, so the community learns to act from obedience rather than from appetite. The contrast with the hypocrites is immediate and structural: the diptych two movements earlier described the man whose speech delights while his heart is enmity (2:204) — the outward performance without the inner assent; this verse legislates the inverse, the inward reluctance carried by outward obedience. Between the eloquent impostor and the reluctant believer the sūrah has drawn its true line: God weighs what the hands do under the command, not what the feelings say about it — and the feeling of dislike, honestly held and honestly overridden, is closer to faith than the enthusiasm that performs.

**The Two Perhapses**

The verse's middle sentence is the scripture's great counsel on preference: perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you; perhaps you love a thing and it is evil for you. The double *perhaps* — ʿasā — is not weak uncertainty but the epistemic humility the verse commands: the human evaluations of good and bad are formed inside a visibility too narrow to be trusted with final verdicts. The sentence dismantles the authority of both feelings at once. The dislike is not evidence of badness — the prescribed fighting, disliked, may be the community's preservation; and the love is not evidence of goodness — the peace of staying home, loved, may be the road to the ruin the previous verse warned against. The two clauses together transfer the seat of judgment from the heart's preferences to the Legislator's knowledge, and they do it permanently: the sentence outlives its occasion and becomes the standing formula for every command the believer finds hard and every indulgence he finds sweet. The tradition's ascetic literature made the verse a hinge-text for exactly this reason — the discipline of suspecting one's own likings and dislikings, and of testing both against the revealed good.

**God Knows, and You Do Not Know**

The verse ends with the knowledge-clause that authorizes the whole transfer: God knows, and you know not. The formula is not a rebuke of ignorance in general but a specification of the gap that matters here: God knows the outcomes the fighting will produce — the persecution it will end, the community it will secure, the fitnah whose continuation the war-code named as worse than killing (2:191) — and the community knows only its own dislike. The clause is the epistemological ground of the two perhapses: the dislike-and-good and love-and-evil reversals are possible precisely because the divine knowledge spans the consequences and the human knowledge spans the moment. Read with the war-legislation behind it, the clause completes that legislation's frame: 2:190–193 bounded the fighting with reciprocity, proportionality, the sanctuary's immunity, and the cessation's pardon; this verse supplies the obligation's warrant — the bounded fighting is *written*, and its writing rests on a knowledge the commanded do not possess. The believer's posture is therefore fixed between two knowledges: he does not know why this war and not another feels right; he knows that the One who does know has prescribed it within limits He Himself drew.

**The Obligation's Jurisprudence**

The verse generated one of Islamic law's most consequential debates: whose obligation is fighting, and for how long. Some early commentators held the prescription bound the Prophet's Companions individually — fighting alongside him a personal duty of each — and became, after Islam's precarious beginnings passed, a communal responsibility: once the religion was no longer in danger of eradication, the universal prescription was lifted to the collective level, discharged when sufficient forces undertake it. The early generations divided further: Saʿīd ibn al-Muṣayyab deemed fighting in God's way an everlasting obligation, while Sufyān al-Thawrī called it a voluntary action. The practical case the commentators preserve is Ibn ʿUmar's: challenged for not joining the fighting of the First Civil War, he answered that the Companions fought in the Prophet's time when Islam was small and a man was tried in his religion — killed or tortured for it — but then Islam became great and there was no persecution left to fight. Al-Rāzī reports the consensus that crystallized: fighting, when called for, is a communal obligation — except when Muslim lands are invaded, where it becomes an individual obligation on all who can bear it. The debate is the verse's afterlife in jurisprudence: the *kutiba* stands, and its mode of binding is read through the community's actual condition, the same perhaps-principle applied to the law itself.

**The Verse Between Trial and Legislation**

The verse's placement completes the movement the trial-verse opened. The community was told it would be tested as those before were tested, shaken to the cry of *when comes God's help* (2:214); it was taught the roster of charity in the meantime (2:215); and now it receives the obligation the trial will chiefly run through — fighting, prescribed, disliked, defended by the knowledge-clause. The sequence trains a specific disposition: obedience under aversion, endurance under shaking, action under uncertainty of outcome. The verse that follows will take up the fighting's hardest case — the sacred month, the expedition that erred, the enemy's graver crimes — and the whole passage will legislate war inside a community whose feelings about war have been honestly legislated for. The reluctant believer of this verse is the same person the trial-verse shook and the roster-verse taught to give: one community, formed by trial, directed in charity, and commanded in what it dislikes — held together by the sentence that carries all three: God knows, and you know not.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:217

> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about fighting in the sacred months. Say, “Fighting during these months is a great sin. But hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah, rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque is ˹a˺ greater ˹sin˺ in the sight of Allah. For persecution is far worse than killing. And they will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith—if they can. And whoever among you renounces their own faith and dies a disbeliever, their deeds will become void in this life and in the Hereafter. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Expedition at the Oasis**

The verse answers a crisis, and the reports preserve its details. Roughly eighteen months after the Hijrah — before Badr — a scouting party under the Companion ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaḥsh went out against Meccan movements. At a watering-stop between Ṭāʾif and Mecca they encountered a caravan: a man was killed — ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥaḍramī — two captives taken, and the caravan's goods brought home. The killing, it emerged, had fallen on Rajab's opening day — sacred time — though the party had supposed Jumādā's final day still running — a confusion the crescent-based calendar made possible, since the month's beginning depended on the sighting the sūrah's moon-verse had legislated (2:189). The Prophet's response was immediate and severe: he declined the share of caravan-goods brought to him, and told the party that fighting in holy time was no order of his. The Quraysh seized the incident, condemning the breach and accusing the Prophet of transgressing the Arabian norm of the sacred months — spilling blood in the forbidden time. The affair was eventually resolved when the captives were ransomed back and ʿAmr's blood-price paid; and the verse descended, addressing all parties with a hierarchy of sins that neither side had calculated.

**The Scales: Grave, and Graver**

The verse's answer is a weighing, and its first weight concedes the accusation: fighting in the sacred month *is* grave — kabīr, great, a serious sin. The concession is total and comes first; the community's error is not minimized, excused by intention, or absorbed into the enemy's greater crimes. Only then does the scale take the other side: but turning people from the path of God, disbelieving in Him, excluding the faithful from the sanctuary, and driving out its people — these are graver in God's sight. The four named crimes are the Meccan system's actual record: the thirteen-year campaign of persecution, the boycott, the torture, the expulsion of the believers from their homes and their sanctuary, and the standing bar against the pilgrims the treaty had just enforced. Against that record the oasis-killing is weighed, and the verse's arithmetic holds both truths without collapsing either: the sin is real, and it is outweighed. The method is the Qur'an's moral calculus at its most disciplined — no side's crimes canceled by the other's, every act weighed in a single scale where the persecution of faith outranks the violation of a month, however sacred the month.

**Fitnah Is Graver Than Killing**

The weighing's summary clause repeats the war-code's foundational ranking: persecution — fitnah — is graver than killing. The same sentence stood inside the field-legislation (2:191), and its repetition here, in a case about an actual killing, is the verse's sharpest edge: the death of one man at the oasis is set against the campaign to destroy faith itself, and the campaign is named the greater evil. Fitnah in this usage carries the meaning the exegetes fixed — the trial and torture inflicted to make believers renounce their religion, the persecution whose end is apostasy, and in the commentators' gloss the idolatry the persecution aimed to restore. The ranking is not a discount on killing; it is a statement about hierarchies of harm: the killing of a body is terrible, and the killing of a soul's allegiance is worse, because it reaches past death into the eternity the war-code's whole legislation protects. The clause thereby answers the Quraysh's propaganda at its root: the party loudest about one bloodshed in a sacred month was the party operating a standing system of bloodshed against faith — and the verse measures the month's violator and the faith's persecutor in the same sight of God.

**They Will Not Cease**

The verse then states the enemy's objective as a permanent fact: the campaign against the community runs on, without pause, until apostasy succeeds — if it ever can. The clause is the war-legislation's intelligence report — the persecution named as not an episode but a program, bounded only by the enemy's ability, aimed not at territory or tribute but at the believers' faith itself. The conditional *if they are able* is not a softening but a realism: the objective stands whether or not the power currently matches it, and the community is instructed to plan against the objective rather than the momentary capacity. This is the verse's contribution to the whole war-code: 2:190–193 had legislated the fighting's limits and its end — fight until fitnah ceases; this verse confirms from the enemy's side that fitnah will not cease on its own, that the other program runs in the opposite direction with the same persistence. The two programs — the persecution aimed at apostasy, the fighting aimed at ending persecution — cannot both stop voluntarily, and the verse tells the community which one it is facing.

**The Apostate's Ledger**

The verse's final movement legislates the consequence of the enemy's success: whoever renounces his religion and dies in disbelief — the ledger of his deeds annuls itself across both lives, and the Fire becomes his lasting residence. The voiding is comprehensive: the whole ledger of a believing life — its prayers, its charity, its hijrah, its patience under trial — is annulled by apostasy carried to death. The exegetes note what the verse equally implies: the renouncer *can* return, and return restores him to the community, though some jurists held that certain obligations — notably the hajj — must be performed anew. And the tradition weighed carefully what the verse does and does not legislate about the community's treatment of the renouncer. The word irtadda is often translated as apostasy, but the commentators stress that mere change of religion is not, for many classical and contemporary scholars, a cause for communal punishment — in light of the Qur'an's own freedom-statements: the truth is from your Lord, so let whoever wills believe and whoever wills disbelieve (18:29); there is no compulsion in religion (2:256); to you your religion, and to me mine (109:6). On this reading the punishment the verse states is the Hereafter's, and the historical wars of Abū Bakr against the seceding tribes were directed at sedition — at apostasy amounting to a political act of destabilization, the changing of sides in a community where religion and polity were one — rather than at belief alone. The early authorities' practice points the same way: Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAlī, Abū Ḥanīfah, and al-Thawrī barred executing a woman for renunciation alone, a distinction that makes sense if the capital matter is the treason and the sword, not the private turn of belief the verse leaves to the Fire's ledger.

**The Verse's Full Answer**

Read whole, the verse answers four parties at once. To the community it concedes the sin of the sacred month and refuses to let the concession become despair — the greater crimes of the persecutors stand in the same scales. To the Quraysh it returns their propaganda measured: the month you invoke, you violate daily in graver ways, by barring the Mosque's people and hunting their faith. To the enemy's program it names the objective — persecution until apostasy — and legislates the community's endurance against it. And to the believer it states the one loss that outweighs every other: the renunciation that voids the ledger, the death in disbelief that makes the abiding Fire the residence. The passage's whole war-theology stands compressed here — the fitnah ranking, the permanence of the enemy's aim, the sacred things' inviolability, the freedom of belief with its eternal consequences — and the verse leaves the community with the scales in its hands: weigh the month's violation against the faith's persecution, weigh the deeds against the death, and know which losses the legislation exists to prevent.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:218

> Surely those who have believed, emigrated, and struggled in the Way of Allah—they can hope for Allah’s mercy. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verse of Comfort**

The verse descends, the reports say, directly into the crisis the previous verse addressed. When the ruling on the sacred month came down — the concession of the sin, the weighing against the graver crimes — ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaḥsh and his companions are said to have despaired, doubting that any merit remained for their action even though they had been absolved of crime; and this verse arrived as comfort and promise to them (al-Rāzī). The comfort's precision is worth seeing: the party had been told their act carried a sin, and their fear was that the sin had erased the sacrifice — the months of scouting, the risk of the mission, the service of the community's defense. The verse answers by naming, not the act, but the actors and their three defining deeds: those who believed, emigrated, and struggled in God's way. The mission's timing-error does not cancel the biography; the persons stand before God as the sum of their faith, their exile, and their striving, and it is to that sum — not to the single flawed operation — that the promise attaches.

**The Three Deeds**

The triad the verse names — belief, emigration, struggle — is the early community's complete biography in three verbs. Believed: the inner assent, the creed's foundation. Emigrated: the hijrah, faith made geographical — property left in Mecca, homes abandoned, the material cost of allegiance paid in full, the act that gave the community its calendar and its name (the Emigrants, al-muhājirūn). Struggled: the jāhadū, the striving in God's way with wealth and person — the expenditure the previous verses had legislated (2:195) and the fighting the verse before had prescribed (2:16). The three are joined by a single article — *those who* — making one class of people defined by all three together: the believing emigrant striver, the person whose faith cost him his home and whose home-loss issued in striving. The Qur'an returns to this triad repeatedly, and wherever it appears it carries the community's highest social-spiritual rank: the sūrah of the Spoils will give the emigrants who strove a promise of provision without measure, and the sūrah of Repentance will rank the strivers and emigrants at the summit of the believers' degrees. The verse here installs the triad as the identity the promise addresses.

**The Theology of Hope**

The promise itself is couched in a word the exegetes weighed carefully: they *hope* for God's mercy — yarjūn. Al-Rāzī unfolds both readings the word supports. The first is doctrinal: hope reflects the principle that no reward is certain, that everything remains in God's hands, that a person might still die a disbeliever — so the greatest deeds are completed not in certainty of payment but in hope of mercy. The verse thus refuses the community the merchant's confidence: even the believing emigrant striver does not hold God's reward as a debt but approaches it as a hope. The second reading is descriptive and practical: hope here indicates the attitude believers are called to hold — approaching God with hope and fear together, the two wings the tradition's spirituality never lets fly apart. The two readings compose: because the reward is not certain, hope is the correct posture; because hope is the correct posture, certainty is refused even to the triad's heroes. And the sūrah connects the hope to its earlier portrait of the humble — those who reckon that they will meet their Lord and to Him they return (2:46): the hoping and the reckoning describe both what believers do and what they are called to do, the expectation of the meeting shaping the life that precedes it.

**The Names That Receive the Hope**

The verse closes with the two names that make hope rational: God is Forgiving, Merciful. The pairing answers the party's case exactly. They feared the sin had voided the merit; the Forgiving — ghafūr — is the name that covers the sin, and the verse had already reported their absolution. They hoped the biography might still carry weight; the Merciful — raḥīm — is the name that receives the biography in mercy rather than measuring it in strict account. The names also complete the hope-theology from the other side: if no reward is certain because all is in God's hands, then the character of the hands is the whole question — and the verse names the character. The hope is not a gamble against an unknown disposition but a reliance on a declared one; the uncertainty concerns the servant's deeds, never the Lord's mercy. This is the same structure the pilgrimage-legislation ended on — the pilgrim commanded to ask forgiveness at his rite's summit and told that God is Forgiving, Merciful (2:199) — and here the structure consoles a community whose rite of war had carried an error inside its sincerity.

**Emigration as the Verse's Social Text**

The triad's middle term deserves its social weight, because the verse speaks to a community of displaced people. The Emigrants were the trial-verse's addressees in person: the property left behind, the taunts of the locals and hypocrites about sacrificing for a losing cause (2:214), the years of exile in a city not their own. To such people the verse names emigration as a constitutive act of faith — not a misfortune endured but a deed counted, ranked beside belief and striving in the single clause that defines the promised class. The hijrah's cost becomes its credential: the homes and wealth left in Mecca are not losses written off but expenditures credited to the same account as the striving. And the verse's hope-clause answers the exile's particular temptation — the sense of having paid everything and received nothing yet: the payment is seen, the biography is the promise's addressee, and the mercy hoped for is the exile's eventual homecoming in a form larger than Mecca. The community that would return to the Kaʿbah within years first received this verse, and its hope-structure — deeds counted, reward hoped, mercy named — carried the Emigrants through the remaining seasons of the taunt.

**The Verse Between the Scales and the Questions**

Within the movement's architecture the verse is the hinge between war and domestic law. Behind it: the trial (2:214), the charity roster (2:215), the fighting prescribed despite dislike (2:216), the sacred month's scales (2:217). Ahead: the question-verses of wine and gambling, orphans, marriage, menstruation, oaths, divorce, and nursing — the great household legislation that fills the sūrah's remaining pages. The hinge-verse carries the whole transition: the community that has been legislated for war is assured of its hope before being legislated for home. The triad itself spans both legislations — belief undergirds the household's rules, the emigration built the households that the rules will govern, and the striving includes the patience the domestic law will require. And the verse's final word-order leaves the community inside the names: Forgiving, Merciful — the same names that closed the bequest-legislation (2:182), the pilgrim's istighfār (2:199), and the cessation of hostilities (2:192). The hope for God's mercy is the atmosphere the whole sūrah breathes: every law given inside it, every error absolved under it, every biography — believing, emigrating, striving — received at last by it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:219

> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about intoxicants and gambling. Say, “There is great evil in both, as well as some benefit for people—but the evil outweighs the benefit.” They ˹also˺ ask you what they should donate. Say, “Whatever you can spare.” This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you ˹believers˺, so perhaps you may reflect

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Questions, One Method**

The verse continues the sūrah's question-legislation with two inquiries answered in one descent: what about wine and gambling? and what should we spend? The first answer is a weighing rather than a prohibition — in them is great sin, and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit — and the method of the weighing is the verse's first lesson. The revelation does not begin by declaring the two evils pure and simple; it concedes that benefit exists, places it on the scale, and then out-weighs it. The concession is rhetorically and morally load-bearing: a community that knows wine loosens the miser's purse and gambling feeds the poor (the benefits the exegetes will enumerate) is not asked to pretend otherwise — it is asked to hold both columns of the ledger and accept the verdict of the total. The second answer is equally a method: what to spend? *The spared* — the ʿafw, what can be given without strain. Both answers train the same faculty: judgment under complexity, the weighing of real goods against real harms, the refusal of both the zeal that denies facts and the indulgence that ignores totals.

**Maysir: The Gambling of the Arrows**

The verse's second term — maysir — denotes a specific Arabian practice the commentators describe in detail. The maysir was a game of arrows over meat: the players drew lots, and the loser was obliged to pay for the whole animal while receiving no portion of it — and was ribbed and chided in the bargain — while the winners distributed their shares to the poor as a public display of generosity. The institution is thus gambling clothed in charity: a mechanism of random extraction whose losses funded a spectacle of giving, ruinous to the loser and flattering to the winner's reputation. The exegetes note the broader terminology — gambling in general is qimār, of which maysir is one form — and the legal tradition's careful distinctions: wagering is forbidden outright, while games such as chess and backgammon, as idle pastimes, are frowned upon by many as spiritual distraction without being technically prohibited. The historical footnote the commentators add is telling: both games traveled from the Islamic world to the West, and — not being forbidden in the legal sense — both remained popular among Muslims, including devout ones. The verse's target is the wager's structure: wealth transferred by chance rather than by work, enmity manufactured by loss, and the poor made props in the winners' theater of generosity.

**The Benefits and Harms of Wine, Enumerated**

Al-Qurṭubī's enumeration of wine's benefits is remarkably candid: it aids digestion, makes the miserly magnanimous, gives boldness to the timid, brings color to the face, assists sexual capacity, and produces a short-lived feeling of well-being. The list reads like an honest inventory of what the drink actually offered its culture — medicinal, social, and psychological goods, none of them invented. Against it the same tradition sets the harms: intoxication's loss of the rational faculties, quarreling, violence, promiscuity, impaired judgment, and — the harm the Qur'an's final prohibition-verses will name first — the forgetting of God's remembrance. The verdict of the weighing follows the columns: the sin is greater than the benefit. The commentators note the extension the law drew from the term: though the verse names wine (khamr) specifically, Islamic law understands the ruling to cover all intoxicating drinks, following the prophetic definition that khamr is whatever clouds the mind. The enumeration's candor is the verse's enduring method-lesson: the ruling is not built on a pretense that the forbidden thing has no goods, but on a comparative judgment that its evils — especially the evil against the intellect and the remembrance — outweigh them.

**ʿUmar's Prayer and the Staircase of Prohibition**

The verse is the first of three steps in one of the Qur'an's clearest cases of gradual legislation, and the reports preserve the sequence with ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb at its center. Before the prohibition was declared, ʿUmar used to pray: O Allah, give us a clear, satisfying ruling about wine. This verse was revealed — in them is great sin and benefits — and was recited to him; and he prayed again: O Allah, give us a clear ruling about wine. Then came the sūrah of the Women's clause — do not approach the prayer while intoxicated (4:43) — and was recited to him; and he prayed a third time. Then came the sūrah of the Table's decisive verses — Satan only seeks to cast enmity and hatred between you through intoxicants and gambling, and to turn you from the remembrance of God and from the prayer; so will you not desist? (5:90–91) — and when they were recited, ʿUmar said: we have desisted. The sequence, preserved in the Sunan collections, is the legislation's own pedagogy: a community weaned off a deeply rooted habit not by a single command but by staged revelation — first the weighing that educated judgment, then the prayer-time restriction that built the habit of abstention, then the final question that asked for the community's own consent. The verse of the weighing is the staircase's first step, and its method — benefit conceded, sin out-weighing — prepared minds the flat prohibition would have met with resistance.

**The Objectives of the Law**

The weighing's rationale entered Islamic legal theory as one of its foundational cases. The harms named for intoxication — beginning with the loss of the rational faculties — made the ruling on wine a central proof for the maqāṣid al-sharīʿah, the objectives-of-the-law doctrine, in which the protection of the intellect stands as one of the essential ends the Law exists to secure, beside the protection of religion, life, lineage, and property. Gambling's harms were analyzed in the same framework: al-Rāzī notes that it creates enmity and despair, produces ill-gotten gains, and diverts from the healthy pursuit of profit — and the risk-structure of the wager entered Islamic financial theory directly, where certain transactions are invalidated for entailing excessive risk, a doctrine connected by financial theorists to the prohibition of ribā, itself discussed by some as carrying a severe form of risk — the usury-legislation this very sūrah will deliver (2:275–280). The verse thus seeded two entire disciplines: a theory of law's purposes built on the intellect's protection, and a theory of finance built on the wager's distinction — gain by chance versus gain by work — with the maysir of the arrows as its founding case.

**The Spared, and the Sentence Left Open**

The second answer names the measure of giving: *the ʿafw* — what can be spared, what comes easily, given without difficulty; the same word elsewhere carries the sense of pardon, and al-Rāzī notes both. The exegetes debated whether the directive concerns voluntary giving or a required duty — some holding it abrogated by the later institution of the zakāh, others seeing no contradiction between a fixed alms-tax and a standing command of charity beyond it. The practical ruling they draw is a middle-path economics: be neither miserly nor improvident; never impoverish yourself through giving — the same balance the sūrah of the Night-Walk states as an image: let not your hand be chained to your neck, nor let it be fully open (17:29). The answer expands the earlier spending-verse — which named the recipients (2:215) — by addressing the amount, completing the curriculum of giving with its two coordinates: to whom, and how much. And the verse's closing opens into the next: thus God makes the signs clear to you, that haply you may reflect — the sentence continuing across the verse-division into the two worlds the reflection is to span. The clarity and the reflection are the whole passage's method in one clause: the signs made clear, the ledger set out, the totals stated — and the mind left to do what clear signs exist for: to think, across this world and the next, about what out-weighs what.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:220

> upon this world and the Hereafter. And they ask you concerning orphans. Say, “Improving their condition is best. And if you partner with them, they are bonded with you ˹in faith˺. And Allah knows who intends harm and who intends good. Had Allah willed, He could have made it difficult for you. Surely Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sentence That Crosses the Division**

The verse begins mid-sentence — *upon this world and the Hereafter* — completing the reflection-clause the previous verse left open: thus God makes the signs clear, that you may reflect upon the two worlds. The verse-division falls inside a single grammatical unit, and the effect is deliberate: the reflection commanded over wine and gambling is given its object here, the two horizons across which the weighing must run. The exegetes connect the objects explicitly — the theme of the Hereafter's superiority is joined here to the intoxicants and the wager: the mind is to weigh the passing satisfactions and enduring damages these things breed, judging both against the two horizons (Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī). An alternative parsing is recorded: the clarity God gives spans both worlds at once. Either reading yields the same instrument: the two-worlds scale, the faculty the weighing-verse trained and this verse names. Every ruling that follows — the orphan's property, the marriage's gate, the household's law — will be legislation for people holding that scale.

**The Question About Orphans**

The verse then takes up the third of the cluster's questions: they ask you about the orphans. The occasion the reports preserve explains the question's urgency. The early community had received the scripture's fiercest property-legislation — the devourers of orphans' wealth eating fire into their bellies (4:10), the command not to come near the orphan's property except to improve it (6:152) — and the believers had responded with scrupulosity: guardians kept the orphans' property utterly separate, eating and drinking from completely distinct sources so that nothing of the orphan's might be touched. Al-Ṭabarī records the cost of the scruple: the separation became so burdensome that custodians sometimes withdrew from their wards altogether — and in the aloofness the property itself suffered, spoiling or falling into ruin. Another reading of the occasion looks behind Islam to a pre-Islamic custom: the Arabs had held it inauspicious, an ill omen, to eat with orphans or ride their mounts — a superstition of separation the verse also answers. Either way the question was real: how does a guardian obey the inviolability without destroying the estate — or the relationship — it exists to protect?

**The Economics of the Orchard and the Herd**

The answer's wisdom is embedded in a material fact the commentators supply: an orphan's inheritance in that economy was typically orchards and livestock — fruit trees and animals whose *value is maintained only through use*. An orchard unpruned and unpicked declines; herds unridden, unmilked, and unmanaged lose condition and fail to breed. The inviolability of the orphan's property, enforced as total hands-off separation, would have consumed the very wealth it guarded — the pedantic scruple producing exactly the ruin the legislation existed to prevent. The verse's ruling — set matters aright for them — legislates the estate's flourishing as the guardian's objective: the property is not a museum-piece but a working trust, and its improvement is the standard against which the guardian's every decision is measured. This is why the answer begins not with permissions or prohibitions but with a direction: iṣlāḥ, the setting-right, the making-whole — the same root-family as peacemaking (ṣulḥ) and righteousness (ṣāliḥ), the vocabulary of repair against its opposite, the corruption (fasād) the hypocrite-portrait had just described (2:205). The guardian stands between the two: his office is iṣlāḥ of the estate and of the child's place in the household.

**Intermingle — They Are Your Brothers**

The verse's permission follows: share life with the orphans — they are your brothers. The intermingling is defined concretely by al-Ṭabarī — one cup and one table, common animals, common household service — the full texture of a shared life under one roof. And this clause carries a precision the exegetes marked: the brotherhood does not wait upon the sharing, as though kinship began with common meals; it stands as a clarification that intermingling justly with their property carries no blame — the brotherhood stands whether or not the households merge. The orphan is a brother first and a trust second, and the property's inviolability exists to serve the brotherhood, not to replace it with segregation. The ruling thereby corrects both failure-modes at once: the devouring the fire-verse condemned, and the aloofness that ruins estate and relationship alike. Between the two errors the verse installs the household's real solution — the orphan eaten with, ridden with, served with, worked alongside, his property used exactly as use improves it, under a guardianship whose standard is his flourishing and whose intimacy is his right.

**The Corrupter and the Reformer, Known**

The latitude the verse grants is immediately fenced by its surveillance-clause: God distinguishes the spoiler from the repairer. The intermingling-permission hands the guardian enormous discretion — shared meals, shared mounts, estates managed in common — and discretion is where intention hides. The clause names the two intentions the sharing can carry: the corrupter who uses the intermingling as cover for consumption, drawing the orphan's wealth into the common pot precisely in order to eat it; and the reformer whose every act of use is the estate's improvement. No human audit can reliably separate the two — the common meal looks identical from outside — and the verse stations the separation with God. The clause continues: God could have imposed the crushing alternative — the scrupulous impossibility of total separation could have been commanded, and the guardians crushed under it; the mercy of the latitude is named as a willed divine choice, not an oversight. The closing names fit the architecture: Almighty — nothing escapes the power that could have imposed the hardship; All-Wise — the latitude is the wisdom's form, calibrated to human capacity and divine knowledge together. The guardian operates under both: free in the household's daily judgments, audited in every one.

**The Orphan-Legislation in the Sūrah's Whole**

This verse belongs to the scripture's longest sustained legislation for a single vulnerable class. The sūrah opened its social rulings with the orphan's property and its devourers (4:10's fire, echoed at 2:174); the definition of righteousness placed orphans second in charity's roster (2:177), and the spending-answer repeated the rank (2:215); the sūrah of the Women will legislate the estate's management across a whole passage (4:2–10); the Cattle's decalogue commands not approaching the orphan's wealth except to improve it, until maturity (6:152). This verse supplies the system's operating principle — improvement over isolation, brotherhood over segregation, intention audited by God — and its placement inside the question-cluster ties the orphan's welfare to the community's whole moral formation: the same people being taught to weigh wine against its benefits and to spare from their wealth for the roster are taught here that the roster's most vulnerable member is a brother in the house. The verse ends where the household-legislation that follows will begin: with the Almighty and Wise presiding over the intimate details of shared bread — the names that make the daily judgment of the guardian a matter of theology, and the orphan's flourishing a matter of divine interest.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:221

> Do not marry polytheistic women until they believe; for a believing slave-woman is better than a free polytheist, even though she may look pleasant to you. And do not marry your women to polytheistic men until they believe, for a believing slave-man is better than a free polytheist, even though he may look pleasant to you. They invite ˹you˺ to the Fire while Allah invites ˹you˺ to Paradise and forgiveness by His grace. He makes His revelations clear to the people so perhaps they will be mindful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Gate of the Household**

The verse installs faith as the condition of marriage, and in doing so it opens the sūrah's great domestic legislation — the rulings on intimacy, oaths, divorce, waiting periods, and nursing that fill the pages ahead. Before the household's interior is legislated, its gate is defined: do not marry the polytheistic women until they believe, and do not give your women to polytheistic men until they believe. The double prohibition is symmetrical in its condition — belief required of the man and of the woman alike before the marriage may proceed — and its placement is architectural. The community that has just been taught to weigh wine against its benefits, to spare from its wealth for the needy, and to treat the orphan as a brother is now taught that the most intimate of all human contracts is governed by the same faith that governs the rest: the household is not a private province exempt from the creed but the creed's primary site, and its founding act passes through the gate of belief.

**The Slave Better Than the Free**

Each prohibition carries its comparison, and the comparison dismantles the Arabian marriage market's two great currencies: status and beauty. A believing slave-woman is better than a free polytheist, though the free woman pleases you; a believing slave-man is better than a free polytheist, though he impresses you. The ranking is deliberate provocation: in a society that measured persons by freedom and lineage, the verse ranks the enslaved believer above the free idolater — not in legal rights but in the worth that matters for marriage. And the concession clauses are honest about the desire they overrule: *though she pleases you, though he impresses* — attraction is acknowledged as real, as felt, as insufficient. The verse does not ask the believer to stop finding the polytheist beautiful; it asks him to know that beauty does not carry a household and belief does. The comparison thereby legislates the marriage decision's true scale: against the market's axes of freedom and attractiveness, the verse sets the single axis of faith — and the slave on that axis outweighs the notable on the other.

**The Legal Development: The People of the Book**

The verse's ruling generated one of the passage's most discussed legal questions, because the sūrah of the Table permits what appears broader: the chaste women of those given the Scripture before you are lawful to you in marriage (5:5). The exegetes record the positions. Some held that 5:5 partially abrogated this verse's ruling, opening marriage with Jewish and Christian women while the prohibition against idolaters stands — a reading that arises only if the People of the Book were classed among the polytheists the verse names. Many maintained the simpler harmonization: the prohibition was never directed at the People of the Book at all, whose scripture and monotheism place them outside the verse's category. A minority held the reverse abrogation — that this verse cancels 5:5, forbidding marriage with any non-Muslim.
