The operative ruling in Islamic law follows the permissive readings: Muslim men may marry Jewish and Christian women, with some jurists extending the category to Zoroastrians and, in the Indian context, to Hindus. And the asymmetry the verse's second clause established became the law's settled position: the command not to give Muslim women to polytheistic men is understood consistently as barring marriage between a Muslim woman and any non-Muslim man. The verse thus stands as the household-gate's foundation, with 5:5 as its specified opening — faith the rule, the People of the Book the exception the scripture itself legislated.

**They Call to the Fire**

The verse's theological clause explains the gate's necessity: they call to the Fire, and God calls to the Garden and to forgiveness, by His leave. The calling is not imagined as preaching — the polytheist spouse rarely sets out to damn the household — but as the direction of a shared life: the values a marriage runs on, the gods a home honors, the ends a family's daily choices accumulate toward. Marriage is the verse's deep institution of direction, the arrangement in which two people call each other, day by day, toward whatever they severally serve; and a household founded across the divide of belief is founded across the divide of destinations. The clause's parallel structure states the two calls in their full scope: the Fire, against the Garden *and forgiveness* — God's call carries both the destination and the pardon for the road. The phrase *by His leave* keeps the calling gracious: the invitation to the Garden is not a transaction but a permission-granted gift, the same gratuity the previous verse's guidance and the trial-verse's help carried. The marriage-gate thus opens onto the whole eschatological geography the sūrah has been mapping — and the spouse is revealed as, in the deepest sense, a fellow-traveler toward one of the two destinations.

**The Signs Made Clear, That They May Remember**

The verse closes with the formula that has punctuated the whole passage: God makes His signs clear to people, that haply they may be mindful. The clarity-legislation and the taqwā-end are the sūrah's fixed pair — the same closing served the fast (2:185–187) and will serve the divorce-limitations ahead (2:230) — and its presence here marks the marriage-ruling as sign rather than mere rule: the gate of belief is legible as part of a coherent design, visible to the mind that reflects upon the two worlds the previous verse named. The mindfulness the verse aims at is precisely the faculty the domestic legislation will repeatedly demand: the guardian's intention audited by God (2:220), the husband's retention-or-release conducted honorably (2:229), the parent's weaning decided by mutual counsel (2:233). All of it requires people who have learned to see the revealed order as an order — clear signs read for their meaning, not mere commands obeyed without comprehension. The marriage-gate is the first sign of the household series, and its clarity is its mercy: the believer chooses his household's foundation with the design visible, choosing faith at the gate because the signs have shown him where each road's calling leads.

**The Verse in the Community's Formation**

Read within the movement, the verse completes the community's social architecture begun at the trial-verse. The believers were told their faith would be tested as the faiths before were tested (2:214); taught the roster of their charity (2:215); commanded in what they dislike (2:216); weighed in the scales of the sacred month (2:217); comforted with the hope of mercy (2:218); trained in the weighing of wine and gambling (2:219); instructed in the orphan's brotherhood (2:220). Now the household's gate: the intimate contract that will produce the next generation of the tested, the charitable, the obedient, the weighed, the hoping, the reflecting, the guardian-brothers. The verse's two comparisons — slave above free, belief above beauty — train the choosing heart in the community's inverted scale, the scale on which 2:212 had already ranked the tattered unknown above a world of the finely dressed. The marriage-gate is that ranking applied where it costs most: the desire of the eye overruled by the knowledge of the destination, the market's prices overruled by the Fire's and the Garden's callings — and the signs made clear so that the overruling is not mere submission but mindfulness, the household founded in the same reflective taqwā the whole passage exists to form.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:222

> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about menstruation. Say, “Beware of its harm! So keep away, and do not have intercourse with your wives during their monthly cycles until they are purified. When they purify themselves, then you may approach them in the manner specified by Allah. Surely Allah loves those who always turn to Him in repentance and those who purify themselves.”

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question and the Hurt**

The question-cluster continues with a matter the Arabian household needed legislated: they ask you about menstruation — and the answer opens with a single word of diagnosis: it is *adhā*, a hurt. The exegetes divided over the word's precise sense, and the division matters. Some read adhā as the discomfort the period causes the woman herself — the answer beginning, on this reading, with acknowledgment of her pain. Many others understood it as uncleanness attaching specifically to the menstrual blood. Still others glossed it simply as the blood, without attaching any notion of defilement to the woman. The three readings generate three different atmospheres for the ruling that follows: a law attentive to the wife's suffering, a law of ritual separation, or a law of practical timing. The legislation's actual content favors the restrained readings — what the verse prohibits is bounded, what it permits is broad, and the defilement it implies attaches to a flow, never to a person. The answer's structure follows the diagnosis: it is a hurt — therefore keep away, therefore do not approach — the ruling derived from the fact rather than from a mythology of pollution.

**Against the Background of Exile**

The ruling's context makes its moderation visible. The commentators record that before Islam, menstruating women in Arabia were not slept with in the same bed and did not eat from the same plate — a separation customs possibly shaped by the neighboring religious law: the prescriptions of Leviticus (15:19–33) and the Zoroastrian Vendidad (16), both of which mandated substantial isolation for menstruating women and ritual purification of objects they touched. Against that background of household exile — and the Arabian custom sitting somewhere inside it — the verse's ruling is a deliberate middle: it prohibits one act and returns everything else. The woman is not exiled from the bed in the sense of isolation, not separated from the table, not treated as a contaminating presence; she is approached in every manner except the one the hurt forbids. The tradition's reports fill in the practice: in many hadiths the Prophet is described as not staying aloof from his wives during their periods but showing them affection — kissing and fondling — short of intercourse. And the ruling on touch is explicit in the commentators' summary: apart from cleaning any item that menstrual blood contacts, Islamic teaching does not deem the touch of a menstruating woman unclean, and does not treat her as rendering anything unclean.

**The Boundaries of the Ruling**

The jurisprudence the verse generated is precise about both edges of the prohibition. Jurists are unanimous in forbidding vaginal intercourse during menstruation, and unanimous in forbidding anal intercourse at any time — the boundaries fixed by this verse read together with the tilth-verse that follows. Within those boundaries the verse's keep-away was understood as specific rather than total: other forms of contact and closeness remain lawful, and the commentators note that most schools allowed affection and fondling during the period. The verse also states the resumption's condition: do not approach until they are purified — a phrase read at two levels. Some interpret the purification as the cessation of the flow; the majority of the schools understand the verse to require, after cessation, the major ablution — ghusl, the ritual washing of the whole body — before intercourse resumes, with the Ḥanafī school allowing, under certain circumstances, resumption after the blood has ceased even before the ghusl. When the purification is complete, the verse restores the marriage's intimacy in full: go in unto them as God has commanded — the resumption itself a commanded good, the return to lawful intimacy within the manner God ordained. There is no formal expiation or punishment legislated for intercourse during menstruation, though some reports mention a monetary payment to the poor — a dinar or half a dinar — and the commentators classify the act as disobedience short of the major kind, from which the pious refrain.

**Your Menses Are Not in Your Hand**

The tradition preserves a scene that fixes the verse's atmosphere with unforgettable economy. Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim records it (298), from ʿĀʾishah: the Messenger of God said to her — bring me the small mat from the mosque. She answered: I am menstruating. And he said: *your menses are not in your hand*. The exchange is a ruling in miniature: the flow is located in the body, not in the hand that reaches; the woman in her period is not a contamination that spreads by contact but a person whose one bounded restriction leaves her hands — and her service, her presence, her household life — untouched. The report has been read in the legal tradition as addressing the mosque's boundary too: remaining inside the mosque and the retreat of iʿtikāf are restricted for the menstruating woman — restrictions the commentators connect more to protecting the mosque from blood-staining than to any defilement of the woman — while passing through and reaching into it stand. The verse's wider jurisprudence follows the same logic of bounded restriction rather than exile: the canonical prayer and the fast are suspended during the period (the fast made up later), the circumambulation of the Kaʿbah deferred, loud recitation and touching of the Qur'an withheld — suspensions of specific acts, never of the person's standing, her household, her affection, or her nearness to God.

**The Two Beloveds**

The verse ends where its subject most unexpectedly leads — in love: God loves those who repent, and loves those who purify themselves. The double object of divine love is the verse's theological summit. The repentant — the tawwābūn, the ones who turn and keep turning, the intensive form marking repeated return — are loved: the household's failures, the ruling's transgressions, the periodic lapses of a marriage and a life are met not merely with pardon but with love at the turning. And the purifiers — the mutaṭahhirūn — are loved: the ones who wash, who keep the purity the verse legislates, whose scrupulousness about the ghusl and the cleaned garment is itself an object of divine love. The pairing gathers the verse's whole movement: the hurt acknowledged, the boundary drawn, the resumption commanded, the purification required — and over all of it, at both its failure and its keeping, the same love. No other ruling in the passage ends so; the naming of love here transforms the menstrual legislation from a code of restriction into a chapter of intimacy with the Divine — the body's monthly cycle legislated inside a relationship in which both the turning back and the washing up are beloved acts.

**The Verse in the Household Series**

The verse's position in the domestic sequence completes its meaning. The marriage-gate legislated faith as the household's foundation (2:221); this verse legislates the body's cycle within the household; the verse that follows will legislate the marriage's intimacy itself and end in the meeting with God (2:223); and the oaths, the abstention-oath, the divorce, the waiting-periods, and the nursing will follow. Across the whole series the same method runs: a question from real life, an answer that acknowledges the fact (the hurt, the desire, the anger, the womb), a boundary that protects without exiling, a resumption that restores, and names of God — Forgiving, Merciful, Hearing, Knowing, loving the repentant and the pure — presiding over the details. The menstruation-verse is the series' clearest case of the method's genius: a subject the surrounding cultures handled with exile and pollution-mythology, the question-verses of other traditions left largely unaddressed, receives here a ruling of surgical narrowness wrapped in love — one act withheld while the flow lasts, everything else returned, and at the ruling's end the declaration that both the sinners' turning and the washers' purity are, in God's reckoning, objects of love.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:223

> Your wives are like farmland for you, so approach them ˹consensually˺ as you please. And send forth something good for yourselves. Be mindful of Allah, and know that you will meet Him. And give good news to the believers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Tilth**

The verse's central image is agricultural and its meaning generative: your wives are a tilth — harth, cultivated land, sown field — for you; come to your tilth as you will. The commentators read the symbolism straightforwardly: the tilth is the place of sowing, and the sowing's harvest is the child; the image locates the marriage's intimacy inside the same order as the field's — seed, soil, season, fruit — and by that locating, bounds it. A tilth is approached for what a tilth is for; the field's meaning governs the coming to it. Some exegetes took the verse as giving permission for any manner of vaginal intercourse, the symbolism referring to procreation as the act's natural end (Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī). The image also carries the whole ethic of cultivation the sūrah has been building: the hypocrite strives to destroy tillage and offspring (2:205) — the same two words, harth and nasl — while the believer comes to his tilth as a cultivator, and the verse that destroys and the verse that cultivates stand twelve verses apart, the field appearing in both as the measure of the heart.

**The Occasion: Two Customs, One Ruling**

The reports behind the verse preserve a clash of marital customs in the young community. The Emigrants from Mecca — Quraysh and their fellows — practiced intercourse in various positions; the Helpers of Medina held to a single manner and considered the others reprehensible. When Emigrant men married Helper women, the customs collided: one account names a Muhājir who married an Anṣārī woman and attempted his customary manner, and she refused him — the tradition preserves her objection in substance: we are approached in one way; do that, or keep away from me. The matter came to the Prophet, and this verse was revealed: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim records it from Jābir (1435) — the ruling permitting the positions, from the front or from behind, so long as it is in the one orifice; and in some narrations the Prophet summarized the verse in a phrase: a single orifice (al-Ṭabarī). The occasion is the verse's social theology: the woman's objection was not overruled by the husband's right but carried to revelation, and revelation answered with a ruling that bounded both customs — the Medinan restriction lifted, the Meccan license fenced by the orifice's singularity. Her refusal had legal standing; her case reached the Prophet; the household's dispute became scripture.

**The Grammar of Direction and Place**

The exegetes pressed the verse's grammar with care, and their conclusions bound the permission they found in it. Al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Ṭabrisī note that the Arabic construction — come to your tilth *annā*, whence or however you will — denotes direction and place, and they devote their commentary chiefly to the two questions the wording governs: which part of the body, and from which direction. They are emphatic about what the verse does not address: not when, not how in the sense of manner's morality, and not at whose behest the act takes place. The jurists' unanimity supplies the boundaries the metaphor implies: intercourse during menstruation forbidden by the previous verse, anal intercourse forbidden at all times — the permission of *as you will* operates entirely within the tilth's single sowing-place. The translation's rendering — approach them consensually as you please — draws from the occasion its governing spirit: the will of the verse is a bounded freedom inside a marriage whose disputes revelation takes seriously, the freedom of direction and place fenced by the field's own nature. The permission is real — the customs' narrowness overruled — and its fences are equally real, drawn by the same sentence that opens it.

**Send Forth for Your Souls**

The verse's second command turns the intimacy outward in time: send forth for yourselves — qaddimū, put forward, as one sends goods ahead to a destination. The exegetes read the sending as the performance of good deeds that will benefit the doer in the Hereafter, the same forwarding the Qur'an describes elsewhere: the day a soul finds what it did of good present (3:30 in substance), the provision sent ahead in the sūrah of the Cleaving and the Resurrection passages the commentators cross-reference. Within the marriage-context the command carries its immediate senses too: the child is the sending-forth par excellence, the soul's deposit into the future; and every act of the household — the affection kept lawful, the rights rendered, the kindness stored — is provision forwarded to the meeting the next clause names. The imperative transforms the verse's subject: the intimacy legislated is not a closed circuit of pleasure but a field whose harvest is forwarded — seed sown in the tilth of this world reaped in the soil of the next. The marriage, like the charity-verse's spending and the hajj's provisions, becomes an instrument of the two-worlds reflection the passage commanded (2:220): the household runs in this world and ships its yield to the other.

**Know That You Will Meet Him**

The verse's closing triad — be mindful of God, know that you will meet Him, give glad tidings to the believers — stations the whole ruling in eschatology. The meeting is the horizon the sending-forwards travels toward: the deeds forwarded arrive, and the spouses arrive, and the One met is the One whose tilth-legislation governed the household. The mindfulness commanded is the daily form of the meeting's knowledge — taqwā as the consciousness that the private is presided over, that the marriage's most intimate chamber is inside God's jurisdiction, that the permission of *as you will* is held under the audit of the meeting. And the glad tidings close the domestic series' first movement on its characteristic note of mercy: the believers — the ones who keep the gates, the boundaries, the forwardings — are given good news, the bashārah that runs through the sūrah from its opening pages (the glad tidings to the patient, 2:155) to its end. The bedroom verse ends in the evangelium: intimacy legislated, harvest forwarded, meeting certain, and over all of it the good news — the household's private law enclosed inside the public promise.

**The Verse Between Its Neighbors**

The verse's placement completes a pair with the menstruation-ruling and opens the series that follows. Before it: the question about menstruation answered with bounded restriction and beloved purification (2:222). After it: the oaths not made into hindrances (2:224), the oath against the wife legislated to four months (2:226–227), and the whole divorce-architecture (2:228–233). The pair 222–223 thus legislates the marriage's body in its two states — the cycle's suspension and the intimacy's permission — and both end where the series will keep ending: in the names and the meeting. The tilth-image holds the whole domestic legislation together: a field is a thing of seasons (the cycle), of bounded cultivation (the orifice), of forwarded harvest (the sending), and of the owner's audit (the meeting) — and the marriage that follows, through its oaths and estrangements and divorces and nursings, will be legislated as the care of that field in every weather. The verse's last word — the believers given glad tidings — leaves the household under the promise: the field cultivated in mindfulness, the harvest sent ahead, and the cultivators met, at the season's end, by the Giver of the news.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:224

> Do not use Allah’s Name in your oaths as an excuse for not doing good, not guarding against evil, or not making peace between people. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**God's Name Made a Barrier**

The verse prohibits a specific abuse of the holiest word: do not make God an *ʿurḍah* — a barrier, an obstacle, a thing set in the way — through your oaths, against righteousness, against taqwā, and against making peace between people. The image is architectural: the divine name, invoked in a sworn sentence, becomes a wall built across the road of good. A man swears by God that he will not speak to his brother, or will not give charity to a certain needy person, or will not mediate between two feuding kin — and thereafter the oath itself stands as the excuse: the good is not done, and the not-doing is religiously defended, since breaking a sworn oath feels like a greater sin than omitting the kindness. The verse names the mechanism and condemns it: the oath is not a shield for the omitted good but the sin's disguise, and God's name is not a warrant for withholding what God commands. The three goods named — righteousness, mindfulness, peacemaking — cover the oath-abuse's whole field: duties to God, duties of conscience, and duties between people, all three capable of being barricaded by a sentence sworn in the Divine name.

**The Oaths Condemned**

The exegetes specify the cases the verse targets: swearing never to speak to relatives, never to give charity, never to make peace between two people, never to perform some good deed — oaths against righteous behavior in every direction (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī). The list's first item has a social history: the sworn boycott of kin was an Arabian instrument of pressure, a man binding himself by God to silence against his own blood until some grievance was satisfied. The second and third items turn the same instrument against the community's charitable and reconciling life. In each case the oath performs a double wrong — the good withheld and the Divine name enlisted as guarantor of the withholding — and the verse's prohibition addresses both: the good must be done, and the oath that stood against it must not be honored at the good's expense. The legal tradition drew the practical rule from this verse together with its companions: an oath to disobey or to omit an obligation carries no binding force, and the swearer's duty is the good rather than the oath — with the expiation-legislation supplying the means of release.

**The Oath-Culture Corrected**

The verse legislates inside a culture dense with oaths, and the commentators note the culture's own ambivalence: even in pre-Islamic Arabia, immoderate oath-taking was counted a vice — the man forever swearing was suspected precisely because his sacred words were cheap. The Qur'an's own portraits carry the judgment: the sūrah of the Pen's list of the despicable characters to be obeyed-not includes the vain oath-monger — the habitual swearer, the one whose oaths are so frequent they mean nothing (68:10). And the sūrah of the Table legislates the oath's serious tier alongside its casual one: God does not take you to task for what is frivolous in your oaths, but He takes you to task for the oaths you have pledged in earnest — with the expiation defined: feeding ten poor people from the family's ordinary food, or clothing them, or freeing a bondsperson, or, for the one who cannot, fasting three days (5:89). The two verses together draw the oath's whole map: the casual invocation exempted, the deliberate pledge binding, the pledge against good dissolved with expiation — and over the whole territory, the name of God treated as the weight it is, neither banalized by frequency nor weaponized against the good it should serve.

**Hearing, Knowing**

The verse closes with the two names that preside over all speech-legislation: God is Hearing, Knowing. The pairing audits the oath from both ends. Hearing: the sworn sentence is a sound in the world, and the One whose name it invokes heard it — the words, the tone, the audience, the moment. Knowing: the intention behind the words is known — whether the oath was heat or calculation, whether the good it blocks was ever intended, whether the piety it claims is real. The names together defeat the abuse at its root: the man who swears against charity and then pleads the oath's sanctity is pleading before the Hearer of his swearing and the Knower of his purpose, and the verse leaves the plea in Their hands rather than in the community's. The same names closed the war-legislation's hearing of the cease (2:227's coming pair) and will preside over the divorce-resolutions ahead — the domestic legislation runs, clause by clause, under this surveillance: every word of the household spoken before the Hearing, every motive of the household held before the Knowing.

**The Oath-Block's Opening**

This verse opens a short block in which the sūrah legislates the whole life of the sworn word. Here: the oath misused against good. Next: the oath uttered carelessly, exempted from reckoning, with accountability reserved for what hearts have earned (2:225). Then: the oath sworn against a wife — the īlāʾ — bounded by four months and forced to resolve into return or divorce (2:226–227). The block's architecture is complete jurisprudence in four verses: the abusive oath, the empty oath, the harmful oath, and each one's ruling. Its placement matters: the oath-block stands between the household's intimacy-legislation (2:222–223) and the household's dissolution-legislation (2:228 onward), because the oath is the hinge between them — the speech-act by which a marriage's daily life can be poisoned or a divorce's drama staged. A community being taught to govern its bedrooms and its divorces is first taught to govern its swearing: the tongue that invokes God is the tongue that will pronounce the ṭalāq, and the verse that forbids making God a barrier to good is training the same organ that will soon hold a wife's fate.

**The Good That Must Pass**

The verse's deepest claim is about the relation between the sacred and the good: nothing sworn in God's name may barricade what God loves. The three named goods are not marginal favors but the legislation's own centers — righteousness and taqwā, which the sūrah has made the end of every law it wrote, and peacemaking between people, which the whole domestic legislation about to unfold exists to serve (the honorable retention, the graceful release, the reconciliation the waiting-period preserves). An oath against any of these is an oath against the scripture's own project, and the verse refuses such oaths the dignity of binding force. The believer is thereby taught a hierarchy: the Divine name is holy, the good is holy, and where a man's swearing has set the two against each other, the good passes and the swearing is expiated. The expiation-system exists precisely so that the passage costs nothing but the prescribed ransom — feeding, clothing, freeing, fasting — and the wall comes down. The verse ends, as its subject demands, with the hearing and the knowing: the walls we build with sacred words are heard being built, and known for what they block.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:225

> Allah will not hold you accountable for unintentional oaths, but for what you intended in your hearts. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Forbearing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Oath of Habit, Excused**

The verse draws the first great distinction of the oath-block: God does not take you to task for the *laghw* in your oaths — the careless, the unmeant, the words that pass the tongue without the will's signature. The exegetes' primary identification is sociolinguistic: the habit of swearing by God — wa'Llāh — as a filler of ordinary speech, an emphasis-reflex woven into daily conversation. The practice was common among the Arabs, the commentators note, and continues today among non-Arab Muslims and non-Muslim Arabs alike — a linguistic fossil of the same habit the verse addresses. The exemption covers it entirely: the tongue's reflex is not the heart's pledge, and God does not audit the grammar of custom. The distinction protects both the law and the language: without it, every conversational wa'Llāh would carry the oath's legal weight, the expiation-rulings would engulf daily speech, and the serious oath would be indistinguishable from the tic. With it, the sworn word keeps its gravity precisely because its trivial uses are pardoned — the verse's leniency is what makes its strictness elsewhere meaningful.

**The Honest Mistake, and the Angry Word**

Two further cases were gathered under the exemption by the commentators. The first: a person swears to something he believes true — I did not do it, he was there, the goods are mine — and later discovers the belief was wrong. The oath was sincere, the assertion false, and the verse exempts it: no expiation falls on the man whose heart meant truth and whose information failed. The second case al-Qurṭubī records: oaths taken in anger are excluded from the tasking — the word sworn in the heat that the cooled heart never willed. The two extensions share a principle with the habit-exemption: the oath's legal substance is the heart's commitment, not the mouth's output. Where the mouth ran ahead of knowledge (the honest mistake), ahead of temper (the angry oath), or ahead of intention entirely (the conversational reflex), the verse declines to hold the person to the sound. The jurisprudence this generated distinguishes the laghw from the muʿaqadah — the oath knotted in earnest, which the sūrah of the Table's legislation binds with its expiation of feeding, clothing, freeing, or fasting (5:89) — and the line between the two runs exactly where this verse draws it: through the heart.

**What Your Hearts Have Earned**

The verse's second half states the positive rule: He takes you to task for what your hearts have earned. The earning-language — kasb — is the sūrah's accounting term: the portion from what they earned settled the two prayers (2:202), the hypocrite's corruption was his striving's earn, the believer's good is sent ahead as earnings. Here the heart itself is the earning organ, and the oaths it knots are its kasb: the deliberate pledge, the intended commitment, the sworn word that the will stands behind. The verse thereby relocates the oath's jurisdiction from the tongue to the heart — a move consistent with the whole domestic legislation's surveillance-theology, from the guardian's intention known to God (2:220) to the concealment of the womb forbidden before the Last Day's reckoning (2:228). The heart's earnings are the real ledger: the reflex-swear adds nothing to it, the knotted oath adds its full weight, and the expiation-rulings that follow exist to let the heart unwind what the heart bound. The sūrah's final verse will legislate the same interiority as its closing principle — God does not charge a soul beyond its capacity, and the accounting runs on what the soul earned and sent ahead (2:286) — with this verse as its early statement in the grammar of swearing.

**Forgiving, Clement**

The names that close the verse are chosen for its subject with unusual precision: God is Forgiving — and Clement, Forbearing, ḥalīm. The forgiveness answers the laghw directly: the careless words are not merely unprosecuted but forgiven, covered by a name whose function is the absolution of shortfalls. The forbearance is the deeper fit. The ḥalīm is the One who does not answer immediately, who bears with the creature's rashness, whose punishment is delayed while the opportunity to return remains — and the verse's whole matter is rash speech: the tongue's reflexes, the anger's oaths, the honest errors. A strict auditor would task every uttered name; the Clement bears with the distance between human speech and human intent, and legislates from that bearing. The pairing also completes the oath-block's movement toward its hardest case: the forgiving and forbearing names stand here, before the īlāʾ-oath against the wife (2:226–227), so that the four-months legislation that follows is received inside clemency rather than severity — the oath that harms a marriage is bounded by a God who first declared His forbearance with the oaths that harm nothing.

**The Speech-Legislation's Inner Court**

Read with its neighbors, the verse forms the oath-block's inner court. The verse before governed the oath aimed at good — God's name made a barrier against righteousness, taqwā, and peacemaking, with the Hearing and Knowing presiding (2:224). This verse governs the oath aimed at nothing — the habit, the mistake, the heat — with the Forgiving and Clement presiding. The verse after governs the oath aimed at a marriage — the forswearing of the wife, bounded and forced to resolve (2:226–227). Across the three rulings the sūrah legislates the full spectrum of the sworn word by its object: against good, against meaning, against a person — and calibrates both the ruling and the divine names to each. The spectrum's lesson is the heart's jurisdiction throughout: the barrier-oath is condemned because the heart wields the name against the good; the laghw-oath is excused because the heart is absent from the words; the īlāʾ-oath is bounded because the heart's harm cannot be allowed to run without term. The tongue is legislated exactly in proportion to the heart's presence in its speech — and the Forgiving and Clement names assure the community that the proportion is kept by a mercy that has already, in this very verse, pardoned the vast majority of what human tongues do with the name of God.

**The Verse's Standing Comfort**

The exemption has carried pastoral weight across the tradition's life precisely because the habit it excuses is universal. The believer who counts his casual oaths and fears their tally is answered by this verse before he asks: the wa'Llāh of conversation is not on the ledger. The person tortured by a remembered oath sworn to a false belief is answered: the honest heart is not tasked. The man haunted by words sworn in rage is answered: the anger's output is excluded. The verse's comfort is not leniency for its own sake but the accuracy of divine audit — God takes the heart's earnings and leaves the tongue's noise — and the accuracy is itself the mercy: an audit that counted reflexes would drive the scrupulous to despair, and the sūrah's whole project (the hope of 2:218, the ease of 2:185, the latitude of 2:220) refuses despair as a legislative outcome. The Clement's forbearance with human speech is the atmosphere in which the serious oath can be serious: because the careless is forgiven, the knotted can bind; because the tongue's dust is pardoned, the heart's pledges carry weight — and the community learns to swear rarely, mean always, and expiate when meaning must be unwound.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:226

> Those who swear not to have intercourse with their wives must wait for four months. If they change their mind, then Allah is certainly AllForgiving, Most Merciful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Suspended Wife**

The verse addresses a specific pre-Islamic institution of harm, and the commentators describe it plainly: a man would stay away from his wife without divorcing her — swearing against marital relations and leaving her in a limbo that could last for years (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī). The suspended woman had neither of marriage's two goods: not its intimacy, since the oath withheld it, and not its exit, since no divorce freed her to marry another. She was a wife in law and a prisoner in fact — bound to a man who had sworn against the marriage's central act while refusing the word that would release her. The practice weaponized both the oath and the marriage: the oath's sanctity made the withholding feel irrevocable, and the marriage's bond made the woman's waiting indefinite. The verse abolishes the institution by giving its instrument a term: those who forswear their wives — who make the oath against relations — have four months. The number is not a permission for four months of suspension but a cap on it: the oath may not hold the marriage hostage beyond a bounded season, and at the season's end the swearer must be either a husband or a divorcer.

**The Four Months as Harm-Detection**

Al-Rāzī states the term's function with precision: the four months draw a line beyond which the abstention is taken as an intent to harm the wife. The reasoning reads the calendar as a diagnostic. A man angry with his wife may withdraw briefly — days, weeks — in the heat whose cooling the marriage normally provides; the withdrawal up to four months is within the range of a quarrel's natural history. A withdrawal that persists past the fourth month is no longer explainable as anger; it is a course of conduct, and its object is the wife's harm — the deliberate use of her suspended state as punishment or leverage. The verse thereby converts an invisible intention into a legible date: the community, the judge, and the wife herself do not need to read the husband's heart to know when harm has become his settled practice; the calendar reads it for them. The four months are, in effect, the law's instrument for distinguishing the marriage's weather from its poisoning — the temporary storm from the engineered drought — and the distinction is what makes the sequel's two exits just.

**If They Return**

The first exit is reconciliation: if they return — the resumption of marital relations — God is Forgiving, Merciful. The exegetes defined the return concretely: the resumption of intercourse itself; and they extended its validity — the return counts even where the husband intends it and is hindered by some obstacle, since the intent to harm has ceased; for some, bearing witness to the return suffices. The legal question the return generated concerns the oath itself: many understood the Forgiving-Merciful clause to mean that no expiation is necessary when the husband returns (al-Ṭabarī) — the reconciliation absorbs the oath without ransom; others held that some expiation, such as feeding the poor, remains due, since returning to the wife constitutes going back on the sworn word. The two readings compose a coherent policy: reconciliation is made as cheap as possible — the verse's names are forgiveness and mercy, not audit — while the oath's gravity is not entirely dissolved. The decisive point is the welcome: the swearer who comes back is met by the same names that closed the pilgrim's istighfār (2:199) and the comfort of the Emigrants (2:218), and the marriage that resumes after estrangement resumes inside pardon rather than under penalty.

**The Oath's Scope**

The jurists debated the boundaries of the īlāʾ — which oaths fall under the four-months law — and the debate maps the verse's concern. Some held the ruling applies only when the oath is made in anger with intent to harm: the man who swears against relations for another reason — protecting the well-being of a nursing child, for instance — stands outside the verse's ruling (Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabarī). Others extended it to any oath that keeps a man from relations with his wife, regardless of motive. Others extended further still: the forswearing need not concern relations at all but may cover any withdrawal intended to harm the wife — not speaking to her, not touching her. The three positions share the harm-criterion the four-month term installed and differ only on the harm's vehicles; the nursing-child exemption shows the criterion at work, since a withdrawal serving the child's welfare is not a withdrawal against the wife. The verse's legislative achievement is visible in the debate's shape: a pre-Islamic practice with no term, no definition, and no remedy became a bounded institution whose every boundary — which oaths, which motives, which harms — the law could now argue about, because the scripture had first made it a matter of law.

**The Deadline's Enforcement**

The sharpest question the verse generated is what happens at the four months' end: is divorce effected automatically by the lapse, or must further steps be taken? The commentators record the division — some maintained that upon the period's completion, divorce could be imposed by a judge at the request of the wife (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī). The judicial reading is the verse's protective machinery made concrete: the deadline does not merely define harm but empowers its victim — the wife who has waited out the term can bring the matter before the judge, and the judge can dissolve what the husband will neither live in nor leave. The automatic reading accomplishes the same release by operation of law. Either way, the verse's architecture guarantees the exit: the suspended wife's limbo has a date, and the date has teeth. This is the īlāʾ-legislation's whole innovation against the pre-Islamic institution — the years-long suspension became a four-month process with a judicial remedy at its end, the woman's freedom secured by the same calendar that measures her husband's harm.

**The Verse in the Household's Legislation**

The īlāʾ-verse sits at the hinge of the domestic series. Behind it: the marriage's gate of faith (2:221), the body's cycle and its beloved purifications (2:222), the tilth and the meeting with God (2:223), the oaths' general legislation (2:224–225). Ahead: the second exit — the resolved divorce, heard and known (2:227) — and the whole dissolution-architecture of waiting periods, counts, ransoms, and nursing (2:228–233). The verse's office in the series is to legislate the marriage's estrangement: not its daily friction, which the oaths-verses handled, and not its ending, which the divorce-verses will handle, but the suspended state between — the estrangement that pretends to be marriage. The four months force that pretense to choose, and the two exits the pair of verses provides — return under Forgiving and Merciful, divorce under Hearing and Knowing — cover the whole field: the marriage resumes or it ends, and what may not resume or end is the wife's captivity. The harm-criterion the verse installs will govern everything that follows — the retention that harms (2:231), the concealment of the womb (2:228), the taking-back of gifts (2:229) — making this short ruling the domestic legislation's declaration of principle: in the household God governs, no person's suspense may be another person's weapon.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:227

> But if they settle on divorce, then Allah is indeed All-Hearing, All-Knowing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Exit**

The verse is one of the Qur'an's shortest legislative units — a single conditional and a pair of names — and its brevity is its function. The previous verse set the īlāʾ-oath's term: four months, then reconciliation or continuation of the harm. This verse names the alternative to reconciliation: but if they resolve on divorce — the second exit, stated without elaboration because the elaboration is coming: the waiting-periods, the counts, the honorable retention and graceful release of the verses that follow. What the verse does here is close the option-set. At the four months' end there are exactly two doors — return, under the Forgiving and Merciful of the previous verse, or divorce, under this verse's Hearing and Knowing — and the third state, the pre-Islamic limbo of the suspended wife, has no door at all. The legislation's completeness is in the closure: every exit of the estranged marriage is provided, named, and assigned its divine names, and the exit that harms without term — the husband's indefinite withholding — is simply absent from the architecture. A law that leaves no room for the weaponized suspense has legislated exactly what the īlāʾ-verses exist to legislate.

**Resolve, Not Drift**

The verse's verb deserves its weight: they *resolve* — ʿazamū, the word of firm decision, settled intention, the knotting of the will. Divorce at the deadline is not to be a drifting, not a continuation-by-default of the estrangement that expired, not a sullen letting-the-marriage-lapse; it is a decision, taken with the same finality the word carries elsewhere in the Qur'an — the resolve of matters, the determination that precedes great acts. The requirement transforms the exit's moral quality. The husband who lets the suspended state slide into permanent abandonment has decided nothing and harmed endlessly; the husband who resolves has looked at his marriage, concluded that its reconciliation is not willed by him, and taken the lawful step that releases both parties into the dissolution-legislation's care. The ʿazm also answers the wife's position: a resolved divorce begins the waiting-period whose end she can see and after which her freedom is complete — the resolve is what converts her open-ended captivity into a bounded process. The verse thereby makes decision itself a duty of justice: where reconciliation is not chosen, the choosing of divorce is owed, and the owing is enforced by the names that follow.

**Hearing, Knowing**

The names presiding over the second exit differ from the names that presided over the first, and the difference is the verse's theology. Reconciliation was received by the Forgiving, the Merciful — names of welcome over the marriage resumed. Divorce is received by the Hearing, the Knowing — names of audit over the marriage ended. The Hearing attends to the divorce's word: the pronouncement is a speech-act, uttered and heard, with legal consequences that attach to its utterance; God hears the ṭalāq as the community's courts must, and the name guarantees that the word spoken in the household's privacy is spoken in the presence of the Hearer. The Knowing attends to the divorce's interior: the resolve behind the word — whether it is the settled decision the verb requires or the masked continuation of harm, whether the estrangement's history carried injustice into the dissolution, whether the wife's rights will survive the husband's decision. The two names together install the divorce inside the same surveillance the whole domestic series has run under: the guardian's intentions known (2:220), the oaths' hearts earned (2:225), the womb's secrets legible to belief in the Last Day (2:228 as it will legislate) — and now the marriage's ending heard and known. Nothing about the exit escapes the audit, which is why the exit can be left so brief: the One who hears and knows requires no elaboration here to protect the departing wife.

**The Pair as One Law**

The two verses are read in the tradition as a single legislation — the commentators treat 226–227 together, and their joint architecture repays the reading. One institution is abolished: the oath-suspension without term. One diagnostic is installed: four months as the harm-line. Two exits are opened: return with pardon, divorce with resolve. Two name-pairs preside: Forgiving-Merciful over the reconciliation, Hearing-Knowing over the dissolution. And one state is left without existence: the marriage that is neither lived nor ended. The pair's economy — a long verse and a short one, the machinery and the exit — enacts the law's proportion: the reconciliation, which the legislation prefers and facilitates, receives the fuller treatment and the warmer names; the divorce, which the legislation permits and polices, receives the brieest clause and the names of audit. The preference is legible in the structure without being stated: the return is made easy, cheap, and welcomed; the divorce is made deliberate, audited, and consequential — and between the two the suspended woman's release is guaranteed either way, since both doors open from the inside at the four months' end.

**The Divorce-Legislation's Threshold**

This verse is the threshold of the sūrah's divorce-code, and its position determines everything that follows. The waiting-period legislation (2:228) presupposes a divorce properly declared — resolved, heard, known — and its rules about the waiting, the return-right, and the womb's truthfulness all operate downstream of this threshold. The count-legislation (2:229) presupposes divorces that are decisions rather than harassments: twice, then retention in honor or release in grace. The harm-prohibition (2:231) exists because the threshold can be abused — the resolve reversed and re-declared as sport — and the Knowing at this verse is the abuse's standing witness. Read as the code's entrance, the verse performs the entrance's whole office: it establishes that divorce in this legislation is a grave, deliberate, divinely audited act — not a husband's casual instrument, not a drifting default, not a weapon of suspense. The tradition's famous description of divorce as the most hateful of permitted things to God finds its textual ground in exactly this architecture: permitted at the threshold, audited by the names, bounded by the counts, and preferred at every point by the reconciliation the previous verse welcomed — the permission real, and surrounded on every side by the machinery that makes its use deliberate.

**The Household Under the Names**

The verse leaves the estranged marriage — and the reader — inside the divine names, and the whole domestic series is now visibly a legislation of named presences. The marriage's gate stands under the clarity that produces mindfulness (2:221); the body's cycle under the love of the repentant and the purifying (2:222); the tilth under the meeting with God and the glad tidings (2:223); the oaths under the Hearing and Knowing of speech and the Forgiving and Clement of habit (2:224–225); the īlāʾ's return under Forgiving and Merciful (2:226); and its divorce under Hearing and Knowing (2:227). No chamber of the household — its founding, its bed, its quarrels, its estrangements, its dissolutions — is left outside a named relation to God; every act, from the sworn word to the resolved divorce, occurs in the presence of attributes that see its interior and answer its need. The brevity of this verse is thus not thinness but density: two names doing the work that lesser legislation would need paragraphs to do, because the Hearing requires no procedure to hear and the Knowing requires no evidence to know. The husband who resolves on divorce speaks his word into that hearing; the wife whose release the resolve begins stands under that knowing; and the code that follows will legislate their separation in the same light — heard, known, and bounded by the One who does both.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:228

> Divorced women must wait three monthly cycles ˹before they can remarry˺. It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they ˹truly˺ believe in Allah and the Last Day. And their husbands reserve the right to take them back within that period if they desire reconciliation. Women have rights similar to those of men equitably, although men have a degree ˹of responsibility˺ above them. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Waiting Legislated**

The verse opens the divorce-code with its central institution: the divorced women wait — three qurūʾ, three courses — before the divorce is final and remarriage possible. The waiting period, the ʿiddah, is the type of divorce the verse governs: the ṭalāq, declared by the husband — a period in which marital intimacy is suspended and the declaration stays reversible. The jurists' first question concerned the course itself — where the course's boundary lies: the flow itself, its stopping, or the full ablution that reopens prayer — a disagreement recorded by the commentators and left, characteristically, as a school-level detail. The waiting's functions are multiple and the verse legislates them in order. It is a period of clarity: the marriage's end is not instantaneous but processual, giving the decision time against the heat that may have produced it. It is a period of possibility: the reconciliation the clause that follows preserves. And it is a period of knowledge: the womb's truth established before any new marriage begins — the paternity-function the next clause addresses directly.

**The Womb's Truth**

The second clause legislates the waiting's evidentiary heart: the divorced woman may not hide what her womb contains — a pregnancy possibly begun — and the prohibition is enforced at the level of faith itself: belief in God and the Last Day is named as its sanction. The clause's structure is remarkable: the prohibition is enforced not by a procedure but by a faith-statement. Only the woman knows what her womb holds in those first weeks; no court, no former husband, no family can audit the knowledge; and the verse addresses the only auditor who can — her belief. The conditional *if they believe in God and the Last Day* makes the concealment's impossibility a matter of creed: the woman who believes stands before the Knower of the womb's contents and the Reckoner of the concealed truth, and the belief itself is the enforcement mechanism. The legal stakes are concrete: a concealed pregnancy would confuse the lineages — a child attributed to a new husband who is the former husband's, an inheritance misdirected, a blood-relation rendered strangers to each other — the whole genealogical order the marriage-legislation exists to protect. The ʿiddah's three courses serve exactly this certainty, and the clause binds the one person whose truthfulness the certainty depends on, binding her at the deepest level the scripture possesses: her faith.

**The Right of Return**

The third clause preserves the reconciliation the waiting exists to make possible: their husbands have the better right to restore them in that period, if they desire peace — the maʿrūf reconciliation, the restoration of the marriage. The right's logic follows the divorce's origin: the husband — initiator of the ṭalāq — holds the initiative of its undoing — the declaration was his, and within the waiting-period its withdrawal is his, conditioned on the desire for reconciliation rather than for harm. The condition matters and the verses that follow will enforce it: the return-right exists for peace, and its abuse — retaining to harm, the cycling of divorce and revocation as captivity — is legislated against at 2:231. The wife's position within this architecture is the jurists' noted asymmetry: her options for ending the marriage do not run through the ṭalāq but through the khulʿ, the divorce she initiates with a ransom, legislated in the next verse (and at 4:20). The waiting-period thus holds the marriage in a reversible state under the initiator's hand, with the reconciliation desired as the outcome the period prefers — the law's tilt toward preservation visible in the structure of the right itself.

**The Reciprocity Clause**

The verse's fourth movement is its most far-reaching: the women have obligations the like of what is owed to them, in what is honorable — and the men have a degree over them. The reciprocity-clause generated a range of readings the commentators preserve, and the range is the clause's wealth. Some read it as mutual duty: each side owes what the other owes — wives their part, husbands theirs, in honorable exchange. Some read it as the mutuality of intimate right: the wife's claim on her husband in this respect resembling his on her (al-Ṭabarī). Some read it as mutual protection from harm: the husband not harming the wife through endless cycles of divorce and reconciliation, the wife not harming the husband by concealing her womb — the two harms the verse itself has just legislated against, gathered into one principle of reciprocity. Others grounded it in the marriage's purpose: closeness, love, and peace shared between the spouses — with al-Rāzī's striking verdict that in this sharing, one might even say the woman's portion is more abundant. And Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have lived the clause in its most domestic sense: I adorn myself for my wife as she adorns herself for me. The clause installs, at the center of divorce-law, the marriage's own constitution — reciprocal rights and duties in maʿrūf — and makes the waiting-period's conduct a matter of that reciprocity rather than of the husband's prerogative alone.

**The Degree**

The degree-clause — a degree named for men over women — has been read by the commentators in directions that share a common structure: the degree is load-bearing rather than dignifying. Ibn ʿAbbās's reported reading is the most cited: the degree consists, he explained, in men's fostering of good relations and their largesse toward women in property and conduct — the upper hand is bound to incline against its own interest. On this reading the degree is noblesse oblige legislated: the advantage carries the obligation of self-disadvantaging generosity, the headship measured by what it gives up. Other readings the commentators record ground the degree in men's economic advantages and their corresponding obligations — the maintenance and clothing the marriage-law assigns — in their role in the community's defense, and in qualities such as physical strength. Al-Qurṭubī gathers the positions without collapsing them, and the verse's own closure — Almighty, Wise — places the degree's measure with God rather than with the degree-holder: the Mighty enforces the reciprocity the degree sits inside, and the Wise has ordered the household's asymmetry as an ordering whose wisdom is His to know. The degree, in the verse's architecture, never escapes the reciprocity-clause that precedes it: the obligations owed and owing are mutual and honorable, and the degree stands over that mutuality as responsibility, not exemption.

**The Soul's Waiting**

The commentators' spiritual reading extends the verse's whole architecture inward, following the Sufi exegetes' method: the marriage legislated here has its counterpart in the soul's own household. The nafs — the soul, the self — holds claims owed to it and claims it owes; the spirit (rūḥ) dominates the soul's powers, yet spiritual progress takes place precisely through the soul, not around it; and the discipline the verse legislates for the estranged couple applies to the person estranged from his own depths — gentleness with the soul, rest when rest is needed, the waiting-period against hasty dissolution, the reconciliation preferred over the divorce of the self from its own capacities. The wedding of the soul and the spirit is a standing motif of the tradition's spiritual literature, and the domestic verse is read as its legal shadow: as the marriage is kept honorable in its rights and degrees, so the soul's marriage to the spirit is kept in its mutual dues. The reading does not displace the law — the qurūʾ, the womb, the return-right, and the degree remain legislation for actual households, enforced by actual courts — but it completes the verse's reach: the same principles of bounded estrangement, honest knowledge, preferred reconciliation, and load-bearing asymmetry govern the community's marriages and the soul's interior, under the same Mighty and Wise.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:229

> Divorce may be retracted twice, then the husband must retain ˹his wife˺ with honour or separate ˹from her˺ with grace. It is not lawful for husbands to take back anything of the dowry given to their wives, unless the couple fears not being able to keep within the limits of Allah. So if you fear they will not be able to keep within the limits of Allah, there is no blame if the wife compensates the husband to obtain divorce. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, they are the ˹true˺ wrongdoers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Count That Ends the Cycle**

The verse's first clause installs the divorce-code's fundamental number: the divorce is twice. A couple can reconcile after a first declarative divorce and after a second; the third ends the marriage past recall — that third declaration being referred to either by this verse's release-in-grace or by the next verse's if he divorces her (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī). The count's target is the pre-Islamic abuse the surrounding verses keep circling: the man who divorced and revoked, revoked and divorced, holding his wife in serial waiting-periods — married in law, abandoned in fact, freed never. By numbering the declarations, the verse converts divorce from an instrument of indefinite control into a process with a terminus: each declaration costs the husband one of two revocable chances, and the third is the door that does not reopen. The legislation's deterrent logic is arithmetic: a man contemplating casual divorce now knows that every casual declaration spends an irreplaceable opportunity, and the husband who would use the ṭalāq as repeated punishment exhausts his power to punish precisely where the verse intends — at the third word.

**Retention in Honor, Release in Grace**

Between the counts the verse states the marriage's only two lawful postures: retain honorably — in maʿrūf — or release virtuously — in iḥsān. The formula is the divorce-code's ethical constitution. Retention in honor is the marriage maintained: the wife kept not as captive or servant but in the honorable exchange the previous verse legislated — the reciprocal rights and duties, the adornment Ibn ʿAbbās described as mutual, the closeness and peace al-Rāzī named. Release in grace is the marriage ended well: the divorce declared without spite, the rights rendered, the departure dignified, the ex-wife sent out with what the law assigns her rather than stripped of it. And the formula excludes the third posture — the retention in harm, the release in vengeance, the suspended state between marriage and divorce — which is exactly what the īlāʾ-verses abolished and 2:231 will legislate against by name. The two options together make every moment of a marriage's life and death a choice between two graces: how it is kept, or how it is released. The verse leaves no middle term because the middle is where the harm lives — the neither-kept-nor-released existence that the whole code exists to make impossible.

**The Bridewealth Not Taken Back**

The third clause legislates the divorce's economics in the wife's favor: it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them. The bridewealth — the mahr stipulated in the marriage contract — is the wife's property absolutely, and the husband-initiated divorce leaves it untouched: in the ṭalāq, the wife everything the wife owns stays hers. The clause's exception is narrow and specific: a marriage not consummated allows the return of half the stipulated amount (as 2:237 will legislate). And the clause carries an anti-abuse rule the commentators make explicit: the husband may not abuse his wife into purchasing her own release — refunding, through the manufactured "request," the mahr he had given — the pressure-divorce, in which cruelty manufactures the wife's "request" and converts it into a refund, is forbidden at its root. The economics complete the count's work: the man contemplating serial divorce now spends not only his revocable chances but nothing of his wife's wealth in the process — the declarations cost him opportunity, never her. The protection is total in its domain: what he gave at the marriage's founding remains hers at its ending, and the verse surrounds that remainder with the anti-coercion rule that keeps it real.

**The Khulʿ: The Wife's Door**

The exception-clause opens the code's other door: except where both parties fear the marriage cannot stay inside divine bounds — then no blame attaches to what she ransoms herself with. The khulʿ is the wife-initiated divorce, and its mechanism is the ransom: she returns some or all of the bridewealth to obtain her release. The commentators state the symmetry with unmatched clarity: the wife's property is material to the khulʿ procedure, while the husband's ṭalāq moves no property at all — the inverse of the marriage itself, where the wife collects the bridewealth as part of the contract and carries no financial responsibility within it. Put in the tradition's own formula, rephrased: the mahr is the price at which a man negotiates entry into marriage; the ransom is the price at which a woman negotiates her way out. The condition of the door is the fear named in the dual — that the two will not keep God's limits: the marriage's obligations of companionship and intimacy unsustainable, its prohibitions against abuse and adultery at risk. The jurists debated the fear's distribution: some require both spouses' fear; others hold the wife's fear sufficient while the husband's alone is not — if she wishes to remain and he does not, no khulʿ is permissible and he can take nothing of her property; others read the you-fear as the community's assessment of the pair, with some opinions granting the arbiters of 4:35 power to divorce or recommend divorce where reconciliation is impossible.

**The First Khulʿ**

The tradition preserves the door's first opening with documentary precision. The case is described as the first khulʿ in Islam: a woman brought her case to the Prophet, complaining of her husband — the reports carried by Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, and al-Ṭabarī describe her aversion to his physical appearance, while Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī preserves her words in another register (5273, and Ibn ʿAbbās's account at 5275–5276): the wife of Thābit ibn Qays said — O Messenger of God, I do not blame Thābit for any defect in his character or his religion, but I, being a Muslim, dislike to behave in an un-Islamic manner if I remain with him; in one account, I cannot endure to live with him; in another, I fear I may become ungrateful for God's blessings. Her complaint was not of abuse but of aversion — the fear that a marriage without love would drive her to contempt, and contempt to sin. The Prophet's ruling established the mechanism: will you return the garden he gave you as your mahr? She said yes — in one account, yes, and more. His answer fixed the ransom's measure: no, the garden alone — and to Thābit: accept your garden, and divorce her once. The case legislated the door's whole character: the wife's aversion received as sufficient ground, her property as the ransom, the excess refused, the release commanded — the marriage dissolved without blame on either, in the precise economy the verse had laid down.

**The Limits and Their Transgression**

The verse closes with the ḥudūd-formula that governs the whole code: these are the limits of God — do not approach transgression; whoever transgresses the limits of God, those are the wrongdoers. The limits are the rules the verse has just legislated — the count of two, the retention and release, the bridewealth's inviolability, the khulʿ's conditions and ransom — and the formula's force is the same as the fasting-legislation's (2:187): the limits are established, named, and fenced with the divine ownership. The commentary tradition filled in the limits' rationale with social wisdom: a bad marriage, al-Rāzī notes, can lead to further evils — adultery, social instability — and a couple starved of companionship slide toward bitterness, then toward sin; the discord the khulʿ answers (the nushūz of the marital-strife passages) is read from the verse's dual form as coming from both sides, or as originating in the wife's expressed hatred and aversion — the two readings complementary, since her aversion, even without ill-treatment by the husband, produces his resentment in turn. And the ransom's ceiling was debated: some jurists limit it to the bridewealth's amount; others allow any figure, since the verse names none — though even these consider it shameful and reprehensible to accept more. The closing verdict gathers everything: the transgressor of these limits — the serial divorcer, the coercer of khulʿs, the taker-back of gifts, the ransomer beyond honor — is named a wrongdoer in the same breath as the limits are named God's, and the household's law stands, like the fast's and the war's, under the single sovereignty the sūrah legislates everywhere: limits revealed, transgression defined, and the wrongdoer known to the Knower of the wombs and the Hearer of the divorce-words.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:230

> So if a husband divorces his wife ˹three times˺, then it is not lawful for him to remarry her until after she has married another man and then is divorced. Then it is permissible for them to reunite, as long as they feel they are able to maintain the limits of Allah. These are the limits set by Allah, which He makes clear for people of knowledge.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Declaration's Consequence**

The verse legislates the count's terminus: if he divorces her — the third declaration the previous verse's twice-counted structure leads to — she is unlawful to him afterward until a second marriage has intervened and itself ended in divorce; and then the former pair may reunite without blame. The rule's shape is absolute in its bar and open in its sequel: the third ṭalāq ends the marriage beyond the husband's own power to restore, and the only path back runs through a complete other marriage — contracted, lived, and ended in its own divorce. The bar is the count's enforcement: without it, the twice-limit of 2:229 would be a formality, since the third declaration could be issued and the wife remarried at the husband's convenience, the cycle of divorce-and-return resuming where the code intended it to stop. The intervening-marriage requirement makes the third word irrevocable in the only way human arrangements can be made irrevocable — by putting the wife's life, and her marriage to another, between the declaration and any possible return.

**The Deterrence Built Into the Bar**

The commentators read the rule as the deliberate completion of the code's anti-harm architecture: an extension of the logic limiting declarative divorce (2:229) and the forswearing of marital relations (2:226). Their reasoning is precise. Were the husband free to remarry his thrice-divorced wife, he would be free to declare three more divorces and repeat the process continuously — cycling her through serial waiting-periods, married on paper, never free in fact, barred from every other suitor. The prohibition against remarriage until she has married and been divorced by another caps the damage available to him at a finite sequence, and it deters the declaration itself: the prospect of recovering a wife who has meanwhile been another's is, in most cases, unlikely — and the unlikelihood is legislated on purpose. The third ṭalāq is thereby made expensive in the exact currency the abuser values: permanent loss. The man who used divorce as a leash finds at the third word that the leash has severed, and the severance is final in every direction the abuser measured — she is free, he is barred, and the return he counted on depends on contingencies no one controls. The code's whole deterrent logic — count, cost, finality — converges in this verse.

**The Intervening Marriage's Conditions**

The jurists drew the rule's necessary conditions from its wording and purpose. Most hold that the intervening marriage must have been real — entered and lived — before the first pairing may lawfully resume (al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī) — the marriage must be real, not a paper transaction, since a nominal contract divorced without consummation would circumvent the bar as easily as the serial cycling it prevents. The consummation-requirement keeps the intervening marriage's dignity intact in the law's own terms: the wife's second marriage is a true marriage with its full rights and its own possible future, not a legal device — and its ending in divorce must be that marriage's own real event. The verse's scope-clarification completes the conditions: this bar applies to the thrice-divorced pair; remarriage after a single declaration belongs to the different legislation the code will supply — the completed-waiting-period remarriage of 2:232, where the couple's honorable consent suffices and no intervening marriage is required. The three-declaration case and the single-declaration case are thus governed by opposite logics: the first barred absolutely until another life has intervened; the second open as soon as the waiting ends — the law's severity exactly proportioned to the abuse each case represents.

**If They Deem They Will Uphold the Limits**

The return the verse permits carries its condition: no blame on the two to return to each other *where both judge that the bounds of God will this time be kept*. The deeming is prospective — a judgment about the future marriage, not a nostalgia about the past one — and its object is the limits: the whole ḥudūd the code has legislated, the retention in honor and release in grace, the reciprocal rights, the counts observed. The condition transforms the permitted remarriage from a romantic reunion into a covenantal assessment: the twice-separated couple may return only on the expectation that the third time will keep the law — that the harms which ended the marriage twice will not end it a third. The jurists read the deeming as a serious estimate, and its presence explains the bar's mercy: the intervening marriage is not only the deterrent but the test — years have passed, another life has been lived, and the two who return do so as people with evidence about themselves rather than as people with memories. The limits-language ties the verse to its predecessor's closing formula, and the tie is the code's self-reference: the limits whose transgression made the wrongdoers (2:229) are the limits whose future observance conditions the return — the same law serving as both the bar's reason and the gate's requirement.

**Clear to a People Who Know**

The verse ends with the ḥudūd-formula's rarest qualification: The bounds are made plain, the verse closes, for those endowed with knowledge. The clarity-clause has run through the sūrah's legislation — the signs made clear that people may be mindful (2:187, 2:221), the verses made clear that they may reflect (2:219–220) — and each instance names its audience by the faculty the legislation requires. Here the faculty is knowledge: the divorce-code is addressed to knowers, and the address is the code's final instruction about itself. The machinery this verse completes — counts, bars, intervening marriages, ransom economics, prospective deeming — is intricate, and its intricacy is not accidental but pedagogical: a law this precisely articulated against the abuses it foresees demands readers who can hold its structure, trace its deterrents, and apply its conditions case by case. The people who know are the code's intended administrators — the judges who impose divorce at the īlāʾ's deadline, the arbiters who assess the khulʿ's fear, the jurists who debate consummation and ceilings and the dual of the limits — and the verse names them as the clarity's recipients because the limits' keeping depends on their knowledge as much as on the spouses' obedience. Between the clarity and the knowledge stands the code's whole claim: the household's hardest cases are not left to power or custom but legislated in detail, made plain, and entrusted to understanding.

**The Code's Keystones**

Read with its neighbors, this verse is the divorce-code's keystone — the piece that locks the arch. The count (2:229) gave the structure its numbers; the bar and its sequel (2:230) give the numbers their consequence; the harm-prohibitions that follow (2:231–232) give the consequence its manners — the retention without injury, the remarriage without obstruction; and the nursing-legislation (2:233) extends the code's care past the divorce to the children it produces. The keystone's own logic gathers everything: the marriage is a covenant whose dissolution must be deliberate (the counts), whose final dissolution must be costly (the bar), whose restoration must be reformed (the deeming), and whose whole law must be understood (the knowers). The wife the pre-Islamic practice suspended for years now has a calendar; the husband who cycled declarations now has a terminus; the couple who return now have a condition; and the community now has a code whose severity — the third word's irreversibility — is entirely in the service of its mercy: that no marriage be a prison, no divorce a weapon, and no return a repetition of the harm the limits were made clear to prevent.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:231

> When you divorce women and they have ˹almost˺ reached the end of their waiting period, either retain them honourably or let them go honourably. But do not retain them ˹only˺ to harm them ˹or˺ to take advantage ˹of them˺. Whoever does that surely wrongs his own soul. Do not take Allah’s revelations lightly. Remember Allah’s favours upon you as well as the Book and wisdom He has sent down for your guidance. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Retention-Abuse Named**

The verse legislates against the divorce-code's most specific cruelty, and al-Ṭabarī's description of the practice is exact: a man declares divorce, then takes his wife back just before the waiting period ends — revoking the declaration at the last permissible hour — then divorces her again when a new waiting period begins, and repeats the action in order to harm her. The cycling keeps the wife permanently inside ʿiddah: never married in fact, never free in law, her life organized around a waiting that renews itself at the husband's pleasure. The count-legislation of 2:229 barred the cycle's infinity — twice, then finality — and this verse bars its spirit: even within the lawful count, the revocation-right may not be exercised *as harm*. The ruling's wording covers both edges of the waiting period — when they have fulfilled their term, keep them honorably or release them honorably — and the double honorably makes the manner obligatory at both poles: the reconciliation near the term's end must be a real reconciliation, not a trap re-set; and the release at the term's end must be a real release, not a last-minute retraction. The harm the verse abolishes is thus not only the cycling but every use of the waiting-period's structure against the woman it was designed to protect.

**Do Not Take the Signs in Mockery**

The verse's second prohibition goes to the heart's posture: do not take God's signs in play — in mockery, as sport. Al-Ṭabarī supplies the case: the man who declares divorce and then says, I was only playing — the sacred formula treated as a game's move, the marriage's fate as amusement, the law's instruments as toys. The prohibition names the disposition that makes the cycling possible: only a heart that holds the divorce-declaration lightly can declare it serially, and only a man for whom the waiting-period is a lever rather than a person's season can work the lever for harm.
