Nothing in the preceding legislation was left deliberately obscure: the ambiguous middle-prayer, the withheld night, the unseen hour belong to a different divine pedagogy; here the signs are mubayyanāt, made plain, spelled out in cases and numbers and named parties. The exegetes connect this clarity to the code's burdens — a legislation of counts and waiting-periods and scaled provisions asks real patience, and the clarity is what makes the asking legitimate: the obligated party is never trapped by an unreadable rule. The formula also answers the code's internal complaints: the questions the sūrah has been fielding — they ask you concerning wine, orphans, the new moons — were met not with mysteries but with rulings, and the refrain states the pattern as a policy. God's dealing with this community, in its law, is dealing by clarification; the perhaps of the purpose-clause leaves the understanding free, but leaves it without excuse.

The clarity named here has a social dimension the code has just demonstrated. A law that assigns rights to widows, scales provisions by capacity, forbids secret commitments, and forbids the child's use as a weapon is a law that can be argued about in the open — every party to a domestic dispute can read his own position in it. Obscure legislation serves the powerful, who can afford interpreters; plain legislation arms the weak, who carry the text itself. The widow counting her months, the divorced woman owed her provision, the guardian auditing his own intentions — each has the clarified sign in hand, and the verse's seal tells them the plainness was deliberate: the signs were made clear *to you*, the plural including the code's every beneficiary, not only its jurists.

**The Hinge Between the Two Halves**

The verse's position is structural as well as rhetorical. Behind it, the sūrah's great legislative block — qiblah, fasting, pilgrimage, war, family — has run nearly unbroken from verse 183. Ahead, the sūrah's narrative mode resumes: the stories of the fleeing thousands, of the requested king, of the tested army, which carry the sūrah toward its second half. The one-sentence verse is the hinge between them, and hinges of this kind do interpretive work: the legislation just sealed is the community's law, and the narratives about to begin are the community's memory — law and memory, the two materials of a formed people, joined by a sentence that describes the first as made clear and the purpose of the clarity as understanding. The commentators read the transition as deliberate encouragement: the code trained the mind in God's legislative wisdom; the stories will train it in God's historical wisdom, and the same refrain-family will close them too. The verse asks nothing new of the reader — it only marks the moment where everything asked so far has been made plain, and waits to see if the understanding arrives.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:243

> Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who fled their homes in the thousands for fear of death? Allah said to them, "Die!" then He gave them life. Surely Allah is ever Bountiful to humanity, but most people are ungrateful.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First of the Stories**

The hinge-verse turns, and the sūrah's narrative sequence opens with a scene of pure paradox: thousands flee their homes *for fear of death*, and death is exactly what meets them — by direct divine command. *Allah said to them, "Die!" then He gave them life.* The two imperatives frame the whole event: the command to die arrives at the fleeing thousands in their thousands, and the giving of life follows — a resurrection inside history, witnessed, reported, and made a sign. The opening formula, *Have you not seen*, is the Qur'an's summons to the mind's eye: what follows is not presented as speculation but as a scene the hearer is to see, and its seeing is the lesson's vehicle. The commentators note the verse's function at this exact position: the legislation has just closed with a call to understanding (2:242), and the first narrative unit delivers the understanding's first object — a demonstration, in thousands of simultaneous deaths, of the proposition every preceding ruling assumed: that life and death are God's property, and that no human arrangement reaches them.

**Who They Were**

The tradition's account, recorded by al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī, places the scene among the Children of Israel: a community — a town's population or an army's multitude — that fled either a plague or a war, in circumstances the narrations describe as disobedience, seeking a place of safety. They left in thousands, the numbers themselves part of the sign: flight at that scale is a society's decision, not a panic's. Death overtook them anyway, all of them, and God then raised them — the narrations describe a prophet sent to or passing the scene, at whose intercession or by whose witness the thousands stood up alive again. The exegetes also record the position that treats the particulars as beside the point: who they were, when they lived, and where they fell matter less than the verse's demonstrative core — God kills and God gives life, the fleeing is futile, and the revival is grace. Both readings coexist in the commentaries without tension, since the narrative's historicity and its typology carry the same claim.

**The Plague and Its Protocol**

The plague-identification connects the verse to a body of prophetic legislation the commentators cite at this point. When plague breaks out in a land, the Prophet commanded, do not enter it; and when it breaks out in a land where you are, do not flee it (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī). The two rulings look like quarantine law and are also theology: the first refuses to carry the disease toward the healthy, the second refuses the flight this verse depicts — the departure *for fear of death* that the fleeing thousands undertook and that did not, in the event, save them. Al-Ṭabarī's commentary sets the command beside the verse precisely because the verse is the tradition's proof-text for the futility the plague-protocol assumes: death is not a geography one can leave, and the believer's posture in an epidemic is neither flight nor fatalism but stay-and-trust, since *Allah said to them, "Die!"* reaches the runner and the rester alike. The revival then supplies the protocol's second half: life, too, is not a geography — it is a word, and the same voice that commanded the dying commanded the rising.

**Ezekiel's Valley**

Some commentators see in this verse an allusion to the vision in Ezekiel 37 — the prophet set down in a valley full of dry bones, commanded to prophesy over them, and watching the bones come together, take flesh, and stand as an exceeding great army. The parallel is real and the differences are instructive, and the exegetes mark both. The biblical account gives no reason for the valley's dead — the bones are the whole house of Israel in its exile-despair, and their revival is a parable of national restoration; the Qur'anic account gives its thousands a specific motive, flight from death, and a specific end, the demonstration of God's command over life. Beyond the revival itself, al-Ṭabarī notes, the two accounts share almost nothing — no valley, no bones, no prophesying-over in the Qur'anic scene. The relationship is best read as the Qur'an's characteristic use of known material: a story circulating among the People of the Book, taken up, stripped of its parabolic machinery, and re-pointed at a single doctrinal fact.

**The Lesson the Verse Is Placed For**

Al-Qurṭubī states the verse's purpose with unusual directness: the theme is that God holds the power of life and death over human beings, that they cannot determine their own life and death, and that the Prophet and the believers are to take the lesson — especially, he adds, given what the verse's context makes plain about the struggles ahead of the community. The placement does the argumentative work. The sūrah has just legislated fighting, patience, spending, and the whole architecture of a community under pressure; the narrative sequence that begins here will run through a requested king, a tested army, and a giant felled by a boy. The fleeing thousands are the sequence's first exhibit and its negative example: a multitude that tried to solve the problem of death by moving, and learned that the solution was never spatial. Every story that follows — the army that drinks at the river, the few who stand against Goliath — is the verse's lesson lived forward: the fear of death managed by flight produces death; the fear of death surrendered to God produces, sometimes, an army that cannot be counted by its enemies.

**Bountiful, Ungrateful**

The closing clause generalizes the scene into a standing description: *Surely Allah is ever Bountiful to humanity, but most people are ungrateful*. Dhū'l-faḍl — the Possessor of bounty toward mankind — names the relationship the fleeing thousands had forgotten: the God they ran from was the God whose faḍl they ran inside, since life itself, the thing they were trying to save, was and remained His gift. The revival is the bounty's proof — death commanded and life restored, both acts of the same generosity — and the ingratitude is the scene's moral residue: *most people* neither flee-with-gratitude nor stay-with-trust but live as though life were a possession to be defended by technique. The clause sets up the whole narrative sequence's recurring rhythm, which the sūrah will strike again and again — divine bounty extended, human response divided, the few grateful and the many not — and it ends the verse the way the verse began it: with life and death in one hand, and the human task reduced to the single question of whether the hand is thanked.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:244

> Fight in the cause of Allah, and know that Allah is AllHearing, All-Knowing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Command Between Two Scenes**

Nine words in English and two clauses in Arabic: the imperative, and the knowledge attached to it. Its position is the first interpretive question, and the exegetes answer it two ways. Some read the command as addressed to the revived thousands of the preceding scene — the community God killed and then restored, now conscripted by the One who has just demonstrated that its life is His to give twice. On that reading the verse completes the story's logic: you fled death and found it; you were returned to life and life now carries its obligation. Others, al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī among them, press the grammar: the verb-form is a direct address, not a historical narration, and the command belongs to the believers hearing the sūrah — a standing injunction delivered through the story rather than into it. The second reading has carried the tradition, and it makes the verse the pivot on which the whole narrative sequence turns: the fleeing thousands are the object-lesson, and the imperative is the lesson applied.

**In the Cause of Allah**

The qualifier *in the cause of Allah* — fī sabīl Allāh — is the command's entire legislation compressed into three words. The fighting the verse orders is defined not by its enemy, its territory, or its grievance but by its direction: the way, the road, the cause that is God's. The sūrah's earlier fighting-legislation (2:190–193) supplied the content of the phrase — fight those who fight you, do not transgress, until persecution is ended and the religion is God's — and this verse restates that whole architecture as an intention-test. Al-Rāzī draws the implication the tradition kept repeating: the same act of arms, performed in the same battle, is fī sabīl Allāh or it is not, depending on the cause it serves and the heart it proceeds from — and the difference between the two is invisible to every witness except the One the second clause names. The phrase converts the verse from a military order into a criterion, and it is why the tradition could read the struggle, as al-Qurṭubī records, as spiritual as well as physical: the sabīl is wide enough for the soul's campaign against itself, provided the campaign is really God's.

**The Imperative's Weight**

Read against the sūrah's own history, the command marks a threshold. The permission to fight had come recently — *Permission ˹to fight back˺ is ˹hereby˺ granted to those being fought* (22:39) and the Baqarah's own fighting-verses — after years of Meccan patience under persecution; this verse is among the passages the exegetes cite as evidence of its post-permission revelation, since an imperative to fight presupposes the fighting's legitimacy already established. The sequence matters for the command's tone: it is not the eagerness of a new power but the obligation of a community that has learned, through the fleeing thousands and through its own thirteen years of Meccan endurance, that survival is God's gift and that gifts carry assignments. The imperative also stands bare — no enemy named, no campaign specified — which is why the general reading could carry it forward: whatever the community's battles, their legitimacy is measured by the sabīl-qualifier and their conduct by the knowledge-clause that follows.

**Fight and Know**

The two clauses are joined by a conjunction, and their joining is the verse's moral structure: *fight, and know*. Not fight because you know — fight while knowing, and let the knowing govern the fighting. The knowledge commanded is of two names: the All-Hearing and the All-Knowing. Samīʿ hears what the campaign produces — the battle-cry and the private complaint, the oath of sincerity and the muttered calculation, the words spoken over the wounded and the words spoken over the spoils. ʿAlīm knows what precedes the words — the cause the fighter actually serves, the resentment or devotion actually carried into the line, the intention beneath the intention. The commentators connect the pair to the fighting's characteristic temptations: war generates speech (boasting, rallying, bargaining) and war generates hidden motive (plunder, status, vengeance), and the two names cover both surfaces. The fighter is told that the audit of his campaign is total — acoustic and interior — and that the audit begins before the first blow.

**The Same Pair the Code Just Used**

The name-pair is not new to the sūrah, and its reappearance here does deliberate work. The Īlāʾ-verse closed with the Hearing, the Knowing (2:227) standing over the marriage's most private deliberations; the same pair now stands over the campaign's. The pairing's distribution across the code is instructive: God hears and knows wherever human acts have an unseen interior — the oath in the heart, the resolve about a wife, the intention in a war. Al-Rāzī's spiritual reading rests on exactly this continuity: the struggle legislated here, physical or inward, is subject to the same surveillance the domestic legislation invoked, and the fighter's sincerity is audited by the same names that audited the swearer's. The verse thus binds the sūrah's two great subjects — the house and the battlefield — under one divine attention, and its message to both is identical: the outward act is legislated; the inward cause is known.

**The Shortest of Commands**

The tradition noticed the verse's brevity and read it as density. After the twenty-verse code of marriage and divorce, after the four-months-and-ten, the halves and waivers and scaled provisions, the sūrah orders a campaign in a sentence with no subordinate clause — and then spends its second half on the names that supervise it. The disproportion is the point: the act commanded is simple to state and impossible to purify without the knowledge-clause, so the verse allocates its words accordingly. Ibn Kathīr reads it together with the narrative that follows — the requested king, the tested river-crossing, the few against the many — as one continuous instruction: the imperative states the duty, the story exhibits the duty's conditions, and the names guarantee the duty's audit. The believer addressed by the verse carries away three things: an order, a criterion, and two names — and the tradition's summary of all three is the phrase the verse itself supplies: fight in the cause of Allah, and know Who hears the fighting.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:245

> Who will lend to Allah a good loan which Allah will multiply many times over? It is Allah ˹alone˺ who decreases and increases ˹wealth˺. And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question That Is an Invitation**

The verse opens with a question that has no addressee's answer in it — *Who will lend to Allah a good loan?* — and the question-form is the invitation's genius. God, who owns the treasuries of the heavens and the earth, asks to borrow; the borrower names Himself and the loan's quality together: qarḍ ḥasan, a goodly loan, given willingly, from the lawful, without reminder or reproach attached. The commentators note the inversion the verse performs on every ordinary loan: in human lending the poor borrow from the rich, and the rich stipulate their terms; here the Rich asks the poor to lend, and the stipulation runs the other way — the loan must be *good*, and the repayment is promised at a multiplication no human creditor could offer. The transaction-language is not accidental; the Qur'an consistently frames the human relation to God as commerce — a bargain, a sale, a loan — and consistently assigns the guaranteed side of the ledger to God.

**One Verse, Two Readings, No Contradiction**

The verse's placement between the fight-command and the king-story gave the exegetes its first question: what is the loan for? One reading continues the preceding line of thought — the goodly loan is the effort expended and the risk undertaken in the struggle just commanded, the self and the wealth lent to God's cause on the campaign. Another reads the verse as beginning anew: the loan is charity, the giving of wealth to the poor and to religious causes, the ordinary economics of generosity. Al-Rāzī records the third position that harmonizes them — there is no contradiction between the two, since both are lendings to God and the verse's wording names neither exclusively. The harmonization has the verse's own support: the multiplication-promise attaches to the loan's quality, not to its use, and the decrease-and-increase clause that follows governs wealth in every deployment. The reader is left with a question whose every generous answer — purse or person, dirham or campaign — the verse accepts.

**Abū al-Daḥdāḥ's Garden**

The tradition's own answer to the question is a story. When this verse was revealed, the narrations collected by Ibn Kathīr relate, Abū al-Daḥdāḥ al-Anṣārī came to the Prophet and asked: does God truly seek a loan from us? The Prophet said yes, and Abū al-Daḥdāḥ asked for his hand, took it, and said: I have lent my garden to my Lord. The garden held six hundred date-palms, and his wife and children were living in it. He went to them and called his wife: Umm al-Daḥdāḥ. She answered: here I am. Leave the garden, he said, for I have lent it to my Lord. Her reply became proverbial: a profitable transaction — or words to that effect — and she moved herself and the children out. The Prophet's response, in the narrations, praised what Abū al-Daḥdāḥ now had: how many a date-cluster, heavy with pearls in Paradise, hangs for Abū al-Daḥdāḥ. The story is the verse performed: the question asked aloud, the loan contracted by handshake, the whole estate lent rather than a portion given, and the multiplication acknowledged before it arrived.

**The Loan Verses as a Network**

This is not the Qur'an's only loan-invitation, and the repetitions define the institution. The covenant with the Children of Israel made the good loan one of its conditions — *lend to Allah a good loan, I will certainly forgive your sins and admit you into Gardens under which rivers flow* (5:12); the sūrah of Iron asks the same question with the same multiplication and adds the honorable reward (57:11); the sūrah of Mutual Disillusion attaches the forgiveness and names God Most Appreciative (64:17); and the wrapped-in-garments sūrah repeats the call (73:20). The exegetes draw the network's conclusion: serving God and doing good is always, in the Qur'an's economics, a profitable transaction — and its inverse is legislated too, in the condemnation of those who sell God's signs for a paltry price (2:41). The two sides of the ledger give the loan-language its seriousness: every person is transacting with God constantly; the only question is the terms, and the verse's terms — a loan repaid many times over — are the generous side of a trade both sides must make.

**The Multiplication's Arithmetic**

*Which Allah will multiply many times over* — adʿāf kathīrah, multiples upon multiples — and the Qur'an elsewhere supplies the arithmetic's floor and ceiling. The floor is the sūrah of the Cattle's rule: *Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded tenfold* (6:160), while the evil deed draws one. The ceiling is this sūrah's own grain-parable — the spent-in-God's-way wealth likened to a grain growing seven ears, each with a hundred grains, and God multiplying further for whomever He wills (2:261). Between ten and seven hundred and beyond, the multiplication is undefined — which is precisely the invitation's form: a creditor who fixes the interest invites calculation; a creditor who says *many times over* invites trust. The commentators note that the verse's own second clause removes even the calculation's motive: since increase and decrease belong to God alone, the wealth kept back was never secure and the wealth lent out was never lost — the multiplication is not an addition to the lender's estate but a revelation of where the estate always stood.

**Contraction and Expansion**

*It is Allah ˹alone˺ who decreases and increases* — yaqbiḍu wa-yabsuṭu, He contracts and He expands — and the Sufi commentators found in the two verbs one of the Qur'an's central spiritual vocabularies. Qabḍ, contraction, and basṭ, expansion, name the soul's two alternating states: the heart's tightening, when provision narrows and worship goes dry and God feels withheld; the heart's opening, when both return. The states follow each other, the Sufis say, as night follows day, and they pair with fear and hope — the two reins that must be held in balance for the soul to travel. Some read the verse as a three-stage map of spiritual realization: purification, in which God withholds and strips; the acquisition of the virtues, in which He expands and gives; and return, in which the soul arrives at Him. Under another reading the contraction exposes the soul to God's Majesty and the expansion lets it taste His Beauty. The material sense remains — wealth decreases and increases by His hand alone — and the spiritual sense rides inside it: the purse and the heart contract and expand on the same divine schedule, and the loan is what a person does with the contraction while trusting the expansion.

**And to Him You Will Be Returned**

The verse's final clause closes the economics with the eschatology: the return. Every loan-language elsewhere in the Qur'an ends the same direction, and the ending is what makes the metaphor literal — a loan implies a meeting at repayment, and the meeting-place named here is the return to God. The commentators connect the clause to the two before it: the multiplication is promised because the repayment happens where God's ledger is the only one, and the decrease-and-increase is His because both are instruments of the same journey. The verse thus moves in three steps from invitation to cosmology — lend, for the terms are generous; do not clutch, for the clutching changes nothing; and prepare, for the settlement is not here. The return-clause also answers the question the verse began with, in the only register that finally matters: *who will lend?* is, at the end of the sentence, a question about who understands where he is going.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:246

> Have you not seen those chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses? They said to one of their prophets, "Appoint for us a king, ˹and˺ we will fight in the cause of Allah." He said, "Are you not going to cower if ordered to fight?" They replied, "How could we refuse to fight in the cause of Allah, while we were driven out of our homes and ˹separated from˺ our children?" But when they were ordered to fight, they fled, except for a few of them. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Summons to See**

*Have you not seen* — the formula that opened the fleeing-thousands scene (2:243) opens this one, and the repetition binds the two stories into a single exhibit. What the eye is summoned to now is not a multitude dying but a council deliberating: the chiefs — the malaʾ, the leading men — of the Children of Israel in the generation after Moses, bringing a political request to a prophet. The tradition identifies the prophet as Samuel, the last of the judges, and the period as the era before the monarchy: the tribes under Philistine pressure, their shrines violated, their leadership failing. The verse compresses the whole situation into its opening exchange, and the compression follows the pattern the previous scene established — the narrative will move from a human proposal to a divine demonstration, and the demonstration will concern not the enemy but the proposers.

**The Request and Its Biblical Twin**

*Appoint for us a king, and we will fight in the cause of Allah.* The request has a documented parallel the commentators cite: the elders' demand to Samuel in the first book of Samuel — a king to *go out before us and fight our battles*, so that Israel may be like the nations (1 Samuel 8:19–20). The two accounts share the structure — monarchy requested as a military solution — and differ in emphasis instructively. The biblical elders want to be like the nations, a king visible at their head; the Qur'anic chiefs frame the request entirely in terms of the divine cause: the king's function is to make their fighting possible, and their fighting's definition is fī sabīl Allāh. The Qur'an's version thus sharpens the coming collapse: these are not men asking for pomp but men pledging a holy war conditional on a commander — and the condition, once granted, will reveal what the pledge was worth.

**The Prophet's Counter-Question**

The prophet does not accept the pledge at face value: *Are you not going to cower if ordered to fight?* The question — hal ʿasaytum, might it be that you would not — is the tradition's anatomy of a promise made in comfort. He is not refusing the request; he is testing its grammar. The chiefs have said *we will fight* in the indicative, describing a future they imagine; the prophet translates the situation into its actual form — an order will come, and the question will be obedience, not inclination. The exegetes note the precision of his verb: to cower, to shrink back — the failure he names is not defeat in battle but flinching at the command. The counter-question functions in the narrative the way the river will function two verses later: a device for separating the said from the done before the doing begins. The chiefs answer it — and their answer, magnificent in its logic, will be the measure of their collapse.

**The Answer and the Collapse**

Their reply is the verse's rhetorical high point: *How could we refuse to fight in the cause of Allah, while we were driven out of our homes and separated from our children?* The argument is a fortiori and it is airtight — the double injury (exile and separation, homeland and family) supplies every motive a people could need, and the divine cause supplies the justification; what possible combination of reasons could produce refusal? The verse's next sentence is the whole point of the story: *But when they were ordered to fight, they fled, except for a few of them.* Between the answer and the order nothing changed except the arrival of the moment the answer was about. The commentators read the collapse as the counter-question vindicated in the smallest number of words the narrative could use: the prophet had asked whether they would cower; they had answered with their grievances; the order came; and the grievances proved insufficient — *save a few*. The exception-clause is the story's only hope and its recurring structure: the remnant that keeps the promise becomes the community that keeps the faith.

**What the Story Diagnoses**

The verse is a study in the difference between a people's reasons and a people's readiness. The chiefs' reasons were real — the expulsions had happened, the children had been taken — and real reasons, the narrative shows, do not automatically produce obedient men. Something between the grievance and the order converts resolve into flight, and the Qur'an's diagnosis, embedded in the story's structure, is that a pledge whose condition is external (give us a king) has located its power outside the pledge-makers: when the king comes and the order is issued, the men discover that they had promised a situation, not themselves. The few who do not flee are the counter-diagnosis: readiness that survives the command's arrival is an interior property, and the narrative sequence that follows — the tested river-crossing, the small company's maxim — will be entirely about producing and identifying such interiority in the community's fighters. The chiefs asked for a king to make them fight; the story gives them a king who finds out which of them can.

**God Knows the Wrongdoers**

The verse closes with the knowledge-clause: *And Allah has perfect knowledge of the wrongdoers*. The wrongdoers named are precise — not the enemy, not the fleeing crowd in general, but those whose flight constituted ẓulm: the pledge-breakers, who had invoked their expulsed homes and separated children as the guarantee of their fighting and then withheld the fighting the guarantee promised. The commentators connect the clause to the story's function for its first hearers: the community receiving this sūrah had its own chiefs, its own pledges, and its own approaching orders, and the knowledge-clause stands over all of them — the audit that caught the fleeing thousands (2:243) and will audit the fighters of the following verses begins here, at the council. The clause also does narrative work: God's knowledge of the wrongdoers is the story's quiet statement that the flight was seen, recorded, and named — and that the few who stood were seen too. Between the two sightings the verse leaves its reader with the question the prophet asked: what will you do when the order comes?

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:247

> Their prophet told them, "Allah has appointed Saul to be your king." They protested, "How can he be our king when some of us are more deserving of kingship than he, and he has not been blessed with vast riches?" He replied, "Allah has chosen him over you and blessed him with knowledge and stature. Allah grants kingship to whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing."

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Appointment and the Protest**

The request is granted, and the grant detonates the story's second crisis: the king named is Saul — Ṭālūt, his Qur'anic name carrying the length that the verse's answer will explain — and the chiefs' first response is not allegiance but objection. *How can he be our king when some of us are more deserving of kingship than he, and he has not been blessed with vast riches?* The protest has two grounds, and the exegetes note that both are claims about entitlement: we are more deserving — a claim of comparative right residing in the claimants — and he lacks wealth — a claim that the office requires an endowment he does not have. The men who pledged to fight under any king now contest the king given, and the contest reveals what the first verse of the story suspected: their pledge had been to an idea of command — a command like theirs, from their rank, resourced like their houses — and the appointment's actuality tests the pledge again before any order to fight has arrived.

**Saul in the Biblical Record**

The objection's historical basis is documented, and the commentators cite the parallel record. When Samuel first speaks to him, Saul himself argues his own improbability: *Am I not a Benjaminite, of the least tribe and the humblest family?* (1 Samuel 9:21). And after his anointing, the scripture records the same objection the Qur'an preserves: certain base men asked, *How can this man save us?* — they despised him and brought him no gift (1 Samuel 10:27). The Qur'anic account adds the genealogical detail the exegetes draw from al-Rāzī: Saul came from neither the kingly line — Judah — nor the priestly line — Levi — but from Benjamin, outside both pedigrees of power. The objection was thus, by the lights of its makers, entirely reasonable: the tribes had a constitutional expectation of where kings come from, and the appointment violated it. The narrative's whole design is to show that the expectation was the error.

**The Mirror of the Prophet's Own Rejection**

The commentators do not let the story stand alone, and the connection they draw is the verse's sharpest edge for its first hearers: the ground of the objection to Saul was the ground of the objection to Muhammad. The Quraysh's notables asked why the revelation had not descended on a great man of the two cities — wealth and station were their stated criteria; the Jewish tribes objected on lineage, the prophet from outside the prophetic houses. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī both note the parallel with the sūrah of ʿImrān's sovereignty-verse (3:26), where kingship is likewise God's disposal. The Israelite chiefs, in this reading, are not an ancient curiosity but a mirror held up to Mecca and Medina: every generation re-enacts the protest that divine election ignores human resumes, and every generation's protest is answered with the same two words the prophet answers with here — God has chosen. The story's placement in a sūrah addressed to a prophet whose own credentials were disputed on exactly these grounds is the placement's purpose.

**Knowledge and Stature**

The prophet's answer does not argue about wealth; it changes the criteria. *Allah has chosen him over you and blessed him with knowledge and stature* — the election named first, then its visible content: ʿilm, knowledge, and a widening of the body — the breadth and stature that made Saul, the biblical record adds, stand head and shoulders above the people. Al-Rāzī draws the philosophical distinction the pairing performs: knowledge and bodily capacity are intrinsic qualities — they inhere in the man, they are exercised in command, they cannot be borrowed — while wealth and lineage are extrinsic, accidental to the person, attached to him by circumstance rather than nature. The chiefs' objection had rested entirely on the extrinsic (he lacks wealth; we are more deserving by house), and the answer rests entirely on the intrinsic (he knows; he stands; and behind both, he was chosen). The verse thus legislates a theory of leadership in one sentence: the qualifications of command are the qualities of the commander, and their source is the election of God.

**Kingship Is Given**

*Allah grants kingship to whoever He wills.* The sentence is the objection's formal refutation: the chiefs had spoken of deserving as though kingship were a wage earned by pedigree, and the verse names it a gift conferred by will. The Qur'an's parallel statements gather around this one — the sovereignty-verse of ʿImrān, which gives dominion to whom God wills and takes it from whom He wills (3:26); the sūrah of Women's question — *do they envy people for what Allah has given them of His bounty* (4:54); and Joseph's prayer at the end of his own rise, *My Lord! You have surely granted me authority* (12:101) — the same vocabulary of grant, the same recognition that the office was received. The theological stake is the objection's root: if kingship is earned, the chiefs' resumes are valid grievances and God's choice is appealable; if kingship is given, the objection is not against Saul but against the Giver — which is why the verse's final clause names the Giver's two relevant attributes rather than answering the chiefs further.

**All-Bountiful, All-Knowing**

The closing pair answers the two grounds of the protest in order. Wāsiʿ — All-Bountiful, All-Encompassing, the Wide — answers the wealth-objection: the God who grants kingship is the God whose giving is not narrow, whose bounty exceeds the chiefs' arithmetic of endowments, and who can attach to an unrich man everything the office requires. ʿAlīm — All-Knowing — answers the deserving-objection: the God who chose knows the interior the chiefs' comparison could not see, the knowledge and the capacity and the fitness that no lineage-roll records. The exegetes note the pair's fitness to the story's coming trial: the wide bounty will be displayed in what the unwealthy king is given — the returning token of the next verse, the tested army, the victory — and the perfect knowledge will be displayed in what He knows of the men who objected, and of the few who did not. The verse leaves the protest formally answered and practically unresolved: the chiefs have been told who their king is and why; whether they will follow him is the question the narrative now walks toward.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:248

> Their prophet further told them, "The sign of Saul's kingship is that the Ark will come to you—containing reassurance from your Lord and relics of the family of Moses and the family of Aaron, which will be carried by the angels. Surely in this is a sign for you, if you ˹truly˺ believe."

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sign Announced**

The prophet's answer to the objection moves from argument to evidence: the appointment will be confirmed by a sign, and the sign is the Ark — the tabūt, the sacred chest of Israel's sanctuary-history, missing from the community's life, now promised back. The verse's structure is precise about what the sign does: it authenticates the kingship (*the sign of Saul's kingship*), and it authenticates the prophet who announced it — al-Ṭabarī reads the prophet's gesture as self-validating: the Ark returns while I am your judge, so believe my prophecy about your king. The narrations describe the Ark's history among the Israelites as one of loss — captured in battle, or hidden, or neglected into disappearance — and its return as an event that could only be divine: a lost national sanctuary restored, carried by angels, arriving as the credential of an unlikely king. The chiefs had asked for deservings and resumes; the answer gives them a miracle with a luggage-list.

**Sakīnah: The Reassurance Inside**

The Ark's first content is *reassurance from your Lord* — sakīnah, the tranquility-word the Qur'an reserves for divine calm sent into human hearts. The commentators divide on its mode here: an object inside the Ark whose presence arouses tranquility, or the sakīnah itself — the quality, contained. Al-Rāzī notes the grammar permits a third reading: the Ark comes *on account of which* there will be tranquility — the chest as the sign's vehicle rather than the calm's container. Whichever mode is meant, the word's Qur'anic network is fixed and martial: the sakīnah sent down upon the Messenger and the believers after the battle's shaking (9:26), sent down again in the cave and at the treaty-year's crisis; the serenity sent into the believers' hearts *so that they may increase even more in their faith* (48:4). In every instance the word names God's answer to a community's fear — and its placement here, ahead of a campaign, tells the objecting chiefs what their king's real equipment is: not wealth, but the divinely-sent steadiness the Ark carries.

**The Relics of the Two Houses**

The second content is *relics of the family of Moses and the family of Aaron* — baqiyyah, a remnant, a remainder. The exegetes enumerate the candidates the tradition preserves: the staff of Moses — the rod that struck the sea and the rock (2:60); the fragments of the stone tablets brought down from Sinai, the broken pieces preserved after the first tablets' shattering (7:150); the manna of the wilderness years (2:57); and the vestments of the two brothers, including the sandals Moses was told to remove in the sacred valley (20:12). The list's significance is cumulative rather than archaeological: everything inside the Ark is a residue of revelation — objects that touched the founding events of Israel's faith, kept by God's people and lost by them, now returned. The two families named are the two offices of that founding — prophecy in Moses, priesthood in Aaron — and the remnant of both houses, riding in one chest, tells the objecting chiefs that the kingdom being authenticated stands in the line of both.

**Carried by the Angels**

The mode of the Ark's arrival is its own claim: *which will be carried by the angels*. The narrations describe the manner variously — the chest borne between heaven and earth in plain sight, or delivered by angelic carriage to the appointed place — and the variation does not touch the point: the return is visibly supernatural, performed in a mode no human caravan could imitate and no thief could stage. The angelic carriage answers the sign's evidentiary requirement exactly. A recovered artifact could be explained — found, bought, forged; an arrival carried by angels cannot. The commentators note that this is the verse's response to the chiefs' implicit demand for proof commensurate with the appointment's strangeness: an unlikely king is authenticated by an impossible event, and the impossibility is public, witnessed, and attributed — the angels are named so that no one can credit the prophet's politics with the chest's return.

**The Biblical Background and Its Divergence**

The exegetes are candid that much of the surrounding material is biblical, and the divergences are as instructive as the parallels. In the books of Samuel the Ark was captured by the Philistines, afflicted its captors with plagues until they returned it, and then sat for decades in a private house at Kiriath-jearim — a period the biblical record itself marks as religious decline, Israel indifferent to its own sanctuary; David would later say, *we did not turn to it in the days of Saul* (1 Chronicles 13:3). The Bible's chronology thus places the Ark's return long before Saul's reign and records its neglect during it; the Qur'an gives no chronology at all, and al-Ṭabarī records the reading that resolves the tension: the Ark's restoration to Israel's life — functionally, as a sign — occurs around this appointment, whether or not the chest had sat physically nearby. One Muslim narration adds that from its Philistine return until Saul's time the people were prevented from approaching the Ark, a single family guarding it: present but inaccessible, its blessing withheld. On every reading the Qur'an's interest is identical — not where the chest was, but what its coming means: a neglected sacred history returning as the credential of God's chosen king.

**A Sign for You, If You Believe**

The verse's closing conditional ties the sign to its receivers: *Surely in this is a sign for you, if you truly believe*. The conditional has a double edge the commentators draw out. For the believing, the sign is a sign — the returned Ark confirms the appointment and the community rallies behind its king. For the objecting, the same event confirms nothing, because a sign is not a proof that compels but an address that requires a hearer: the sakīnah it carries is for hearts disposed to be steadied, and the relics it carries speak only to those who remember the houses they came from. The verse thus ends the authentication where the objection began — in the chiefs' own interior — and hands them the decision the whole story has been building toward: the evidence has arrived, carried by angels, containing the reassurance their fear of the coming war will need; whether it functions as evidence is a property of their faith, not of the Ark. The next scene opens with the king on the march, and the sign's conditional will be answered not in argument but at a river.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:249

> When Saul marched forth with his army, he cautioned: "Allah will test you with a river. So whoever drinks ˹his fill˺ from it is not with me, and whoever does not taste it—except a sip from the hollow of his hands—is definitely with me." They all drank ˹their fill˺ except for a few! When he and the ˹remaining˺ faithful with him crossed the river, they said, "Now we are no match for Goliath and his warriors." But those ˹believers˺ who were certain they would meet Allah reasoned, "How many times has a small force vanquished a mighty army by the Will of Allah! And Allah is ˹always˺ with the steadfast."

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Test Announced Before the River**

The army marches, and the king's first act of command is to publish the coming test: *Allah will test you with a river*. The announcement itself is part of the test's design, and it marks the difference from every comparable trial in scripture — the men are told, in advance, exactly what will be asked of them and exactly what the asking means. The terms are stated with legal precision: whoever drinks his fill from it *is not with me* — the full drink severs the soldier from the army; whoever does not taste it *is definitely with me* — total abstention confirms belonging; and between the two, the concession — *except a sip from the hollow of his hands*, the single cupped handful permitted to the thirsty. The commentators note the concession's function: it distinguishes need from indulgence. The soldier who takes the handful acknowledges thirst and stops; the soldier who drinks his fill obeys it. The test measures not thirst but the thirst's governance — and the army knows, before reaching the water, that the water is not water.

**The Sifting at the Crossing**

The result is stated in the verse's shortest and most devastating sentence: *They all drank their fill except for a few!* The exclamation belongs to the revelation's own voice, and the numbers invert every expectation the chiefs' council began with: the army that marched out — the narrations describe it as large, and the tradition's numbers run into the tens of thousands — arrives at the far bank as a remnant. The verse's structure makes the river, not the enemy, the campaign's decisive engagement: Goliath's host has not yet appeared, and already the army has lost the overwhelming majority of its strength to a drink of water. The exegetes draw the sifting's lesson for the story's whole sequence — the chiefs who pledged and fled, the objectors who demanded a sign, the sign that came: every stage has separated the said from the done, and the river separates them finally and physically, with belonging to the army defined by a mouthful. The few who crossed with their king are the community the remainder of the narrative belongs to.

**Gideon's Water, Saul's Water**

The commentators set this scene beside its scriptural twin: Gideon's army at the water in the book of Judges (7:4–7), reduced by a drinking-test to three hundred men. The parallels are typological rather than historical — Gideon lived generations before Saul — and the differences are as structured as the similarities. Gideon's test was known only to Gideon: the soldiers were not told they were being sorted, and the criterion (lapping from the hand versus kneeling to drink) was applied after the fact, its meaning explained by God alone. Saul's test is proclaimed to the whole army, its criterion stated as a command, its consequence named as belonging or exclusion. Both tests reduce an army to a few so that the victory's attribution will be unambiguous — Judges states the purpose explicitly, that Israel might not boast against me, saying, my own hand has saved me — and both echo the Qur'an's wider water-motif, the parted sea of the exodus and the Jordan crossed before Jericho: the waters as the threshold where God's people are separated and reconstituted. The reenactment-reading follows naturally: sacred history repeating its forms, the river-test as a recurring station on the road God's armies travel.

**Two Voices on the Far Bank**

The crossed remnant divides once more, this time by speech. The first voice: *Now we are no match for Goliath and his warriors* — the arithmetic of the visible, conducted by men who have just passed a divine test and draw the wrong conclusion from it. The second voice belongs to *those who were certain they would meet Allah*, and the commentators define the certainty two ways that converge: certainty of the Hereafter — the meeting named in the verse as an appointment, not a possibility — and readiness for death, the soldier's state when the meeting is expected rather than feared. Their reasoning is the verse's famous maxim: *How many times has a small force vanquished a mighty army by the Will of Allah!* The grammar of the maxim is its argument — kam, how many, introducing not a hope but a record: the small-over-large is not an exception to be prayed for but a pattern to be counted, and every instance in the pattern carries the same attribution, bi-idhn Allāh, by God's leave. The two voices together state the campaign's real front: Goliath across the field, arithmetic inside the camp — and the second voice defeats the first before either reaches the enemy.

**The Company of the Certain**

The verse's designation of the second group — *those who were certain they would meet Allah* — is the story's theological center, and it explains the maxim's power. Certainty (yaqīn) about the meeting reorders the soldier's arithmetic completely: if death is an appointment kept with God, then the numerical disparity between two armies concerns only the manner of the meeting, not its fact or its outcome. The few who drank nothing at the river had already demonstrated the same ordering — thirst governed, appetite deferred, belonging chosen over comfort — and the maxim is that governance extended from the mouth to the mind. Al-Qurṭubī connects the certainty-clause to the fleeing thousands of the sūrah's earlier scene (2:243): those fled death and met it; these expect death and thereby meet God, and the difference between the two multitudes is the verse's whole instruction. The remnant that survives both sifts — the river's and the arithmetic's — is defined not by strength but by a settled relation to its own end, which is why so few have it and why the campaign needs so few.

**Allah Is with the Steadfast**

The maxim closes with the companionship-claim: *And Allah is always with the steadfast* — maʿiyyah, divine withness, attached to ṣabr. The formula is the sūrah's own standing promise, announced in its patience-verses — seek help through patience and prayer, for God is with the patient (2:153) — and its repetition here, in the mouth of the certain few, shows the promise functioning as doctrine under fire: not a comfort quoted after the battle but a premise used inside the arithmetic. The companionship is what makes the small-over-large record explicable — the mighty army fights alone in the sense that matters, and the small force does not fight at all alone — and it converts the maxim from battlefield folklore into theology. The verse's final word-order leaves the army on the far bank with the claim spoken: the river has sifted the indulgent, the maxim has answered the counters, and the companionship of God has been declared over what remains. What remains is very small, very certain, and — as the next moment will show — at prayer.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:250

> When they advanced to face Goliath and his warriors, they prayed, "Our Lord! Shower us with perseverance, make our steps firm, and give us victory over the disbelieving people."

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Advance and Its First Act**

The remnant advances to meet the host, and the verse records what the advancing men do first: they pray. The narrative could have moved straight to the engagement — the disparity is established, the maxim is spoken, the companionship of God is claimed — but the revelation inserts the prayer between the advance and everything after it, making duʿāʾ the army's first deployed formation. The commentators note the sequence's instruction: the men who were certain of meeting God begin the meeting's approach by addressing Him, and the address is not a formality tacked onto the campaign but its opening move. The three petitions that follow are the shortest complete theology of struggle the Qur'an contains, and their order — endurance, firmness, victory — is itself the lesson: the army asks for the interior before the exterior, for what happens in its own hearts and feet before what happens to the enemy. The few who crossed the river now cross the last distance on their knees.

**Pour Down Patience Upon Us**

The first petition's verb is a pouring: *afrigh ʿalaynā ṣabrā* — empty out, pour in abundance, patience upon us. The metaphor is rain and vessel at once: the ṣabr asked for is not the patience the men already possess, deployed and rationed, but patience as a divine downpour filling them beyond their capacity — the word choice the commentators contrast with ordinary requests for patience, which ask for endurance within existing strength. The petition acknowledges what the river-test proved: the human stock of steadfastness is finite, drinkable in a handful or gulped past its limit, and the army facing a host of giants knows its own stock has already been spent down to a remnant. What remains must be supplied from above, and the supplying verb is generous — not give us patience but pour it, the abundance-form that matches the disparity. The Sufi commentators read the petition as the station of the certain: the men who know they will meet God ask, before the meeting's battle, for the quality that makes the meeting survivable in either direction.

**Make Our Steps Firm**

The second petition is military and spiritual in one phrase: *thabbit aqdāmanā* — make firm our feet. The foot is the soldier's point of contact with the ground he must not leave; the firming asked for is against the flight the story has now twice witnessed — the chiefs who fled when the order came, the thousands who drank and were dismissed from belonging. The verb thabbit, from the root of fixing and confirming, is the Qur'an's word for the steadying of hearts under shaking — the believers' feet made firm is the standing that replaces the running, in the line and in the heart. The commentators connect the petition to the maxim spoken on the far bank: the small force's advantage is not mobility but standing, and standing against a charging host is precisely what unaided feet cannot do. The army asks, in four words, to be made the kind of force its own doctrine describes — the few who do not break — and asks it of the only party who has ever made anyone such.

**The Third Petition and Its Parallel**

*And give us victory over the disbelieving people* — the exterior request arrives last, and its placement after the two interior petitions is the verse's ethics of prayer: victory is asked for a people already asking to be made worthy of it. The petition has a documented twin, and the Qur'an itself preserves the parallel: at the battle of Uḥud's crisis, the sūrah of ʿImrān records the believers' prayer — *Our Lord! Forgive our sins and excesses, make our steps firm, and grant us victory over the disbelieving people* (3:147). The two duʿāʾs share their second and third petitions almost word for word, and the shared middle — make firm our steps — is the link the tradition treasures: the community of Muhammad praying the same prayer, in the same order, as the remnant of Saul. The parallel does interpretive work in both directions: it identifies the Ṭālut-army's prayer as the believers' standing battle-duʿāʾ, and it reads Uḥud's shaken ranks into the story's remnant — a small force facing a large one, asking not for numbers but for feet.

**What the Prayer Does Not Ask**

The three petitions are bounded by everything they omit, and the omissions are as instructive as the requests. The army does not ask for reinforcements — no angels, no tribes, no belated arrival of the drinkers it left at the river. It does not ask for weapons, or terrain, or the enemy's confusion. It does not ask why the disparity exists or protest the smallness it was sifted into. The commentators note the prayer's economy: three requests, all of them qualities rather than quantities, two of them interior — and the single exterior request placed last and aimed at the enemy's unbelief rather than the enemy's numbers. The prayer thus performs the maxim it follows: a force that believes the small-over-large record asks, accordingly, not to be made large but to be made firm. The omission of every material request is the army's final sifting — the river separated the indulgent from the disciplined, the far bank separated the counters from the certain, and the prayer separates those who still expect God to change the arithmetic from those who expect Him to change the arithmeticians.

**The Duʿāʾ Preserved**

That this prayer is written down, in the revealed Book, is its own final lesson, and the commentators draw it: the Qur'an archives the words of God's servants at their moments of extremity, and the archive is an instruction. The duʿāʾ of the remnant joins the book's standing collection — the prayer of the patient (2:153's company), the prayer of those shaken at Uḥud (3:147), the prayers of Abraham, of Jonah, of Zachariah — each preserved as a form the community may inhabit. The preservation teaches that prayer under disparity is not a private resource but an inherited one: the believer facing his own Goliath does not need to compose a theology of the few from scratch, because the few have prayed before him and their words were kept. The verse's placement — between the maxim and the outcome the narrative now carries — makes the prayer the story's hinge: everything the sifting produced converges into these three petitions, and what the petitions ask for is exactly what a remnant needs to remain one. The army advanced, it prayed; the Qur'an, characteristically, wrote the prayer down and let the advancing speak for itself.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:251

> So they defeated them by Allah's Will, and David killed Goliath. And Allah blessed David with kingship and wisdom and taught him what He willed. Had Allah not repelled a group of people by ˹the might of˺ another, corruption would have dominated the earth, but Allah is Gracious to all.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Rout by Leave**

The engagement is dispatched in three words: *they defeated them* — and the words that follow carry the verse's entire weight: *by Allah's Will*, bi-idhn Allāh. The rout's attribution is fixed before its description: the remnant won because the winning was permitted, the same leave the maxim on the far bank had invoked — the small-over-large record whose every entry carries the same signature. The narrative then names the stroke that decided it: *David killed Goliath*. The Qur'an assumes the story its hearers knew — the young shepherd, unarmored, declining the king's sword, taking five stones from the brook and one of them from the sling; the giant felled in the forehead, the host's collapse at its champion's fall (1 Samuel 17). The commentary tradition adds the detail the verse's economy implies: David, the youngest present, was the army's champion against Goliath, and the duel — one boy against one giant — condensed the whole campaign's disparity into a single exchange decided, like the campaign, by leave.

**The Boy and the Two Inheritances**

The verse's second movement turns from the battle to the victor: *And Allah blessed David with kingship and wisdom*. The dual gift is read by al-Ṭabarī as a double inheritance: wisdom means the prophethood — David inherits the prophetic office of Samuel, the story's announcing prophet; kingship means the throne — he inherits the royal office of Saul, whose line the narrative will not continue. The shepherd thus gathers into one person the two authorities the tribes had held apart, and the gathering is the verse's quiet answer to the chiefs' old objection about pedigree: the man who ends up holding both offices came from neither house, chosen the way Saul was chosen, for what God knew. The Qur'an's David-portrait continues elsewhere — the sūrah Ṣād's account of him as authority in the land, commanded to judge with truth and warned against desire's misdirection (38:26) — and the kingship-plus-wisdom pairing here is that portrait's origin-story: the office and the character to carry it, granted together, at the moment of the sling.

**Taught Him What He Willed**

The third clause widens the gift: *and taught him what He willed*. The teaching's content is unnamed, and the naming is withheld deliberately — the tradition associates David with the Zabūr, the Psalter, with the mountains and birds joining his praise, with the craft of mail taught by divine instruction (21:80); the verse subsumes all of it under a single principle: what God teaches, He teaches by will, and the recipient's qualification is election rather than curriculum. The commentators connect the clause to the story's leadership-theology: Saul was increased in knowledge and stature (2:247), David is taught what He willed — both men carry endowments whose measure and timing belong to the Giver. The clause also frames the coming verses' subject, the messengers and their preferments: before the sūrah generalizes the principle — some messengers raised above others — it exhibits it in one career, a boy given a kingdom, a prophethood, and an education no school administered. The will that chose the unlikely king chooses the unlikely champion, and teaches him out of the same freedom.

**The Repelling Principle**

The verse's fourth movement steps back from the story to a law of history: *Had Allah not repelled a group of people by ˹the might of˺ another, corruption would have dominated the earth*. The principle — God repels some people by means of others — is the Qur'an's answer to the question every holy war narrative raises: why does the divine administration run through human conflict at all? The verse's answer is counterfactual and total: without the repelling, the earth's corruption would not merely occur but prevail — the fa-sada that consumes societies would go unchecked, and the checking is done, in God's arrangement, by human forces set against one another. The parallel statement in the sūrah of the Pilgrimage specifies the repelling's stakes in the register of worship: *Had Allah not repelled some people by means of others, destruction would have surely claimed monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques in which Allah's Name is often mentioned* (22:40). The two verses together state the principle's scope: the repelling protects the earth's order and the earth's sanctuaries, and it protects them through exactly the kind of event the story just narrated — a remnant set against a host.

**Who Repels Whom**

The commentators press the principle for its mechanics, and the readings they record span the visible and the hidden. Some say the repelling runs through the spiritual hierarchy: the abdāl, the Substitutes — forty souls, al-Qurṭubī records, an inward order through whom, the exegetes hold, God's grace and shielding reach the world, each vacancy at a death silently filled by another. Others read it socially: the prayerful repel the punishment due to the unprayerful, the pious hold back the consequences of the impious, the obedient check the evil of the disobedient — al-Ṭabarī's version of the same economy. A ḥadīth the exegetes cite states the exchange as a list: God turns away the punishment owed by the prayer-less through the one who prays, and likewise through the almsgiver, the faster, the pilgrim, and the striver for those who leave each act undone. The readings agree on the structure: the earth's habitability is a function of the righteous operating inside it, and their operations — visible battles, invisible prayers — are the repelling by which corruption is denied its dominance.

**Gracious to All**

The verse closes by naming the repelling's source: *but Allah is Gracious to all* — dhū faḍlin ʿalā'l-ʿālamīn, the Possessor of bounty toward the worlds. The name answers the counterfactual's darkness: the sentence begins with the corruption that would have dominated and ends with the generosity that does not let it, and the bounty's range — the worlds, not the believers, not the remnant — includes the repelled and the repellers, the defeated host and the boy with the sling. The echo with the fleeing-thousands scene is deliberate: that story closed on God's bounty toward mankind and mankind's ingratitude (2:243); this one closes on the same bounty, extended through a war, over all worlds. The story-unit that began with a multitude dying for fear of death ends with the principle that keeps the earth alive through the few who did not fear it — and the principle's engine, the verse's final word insists, is not necessity but faḍl. David will reappear in the Qur'an as judge, psalmist, and king; the verse that installs him installs, around his career, the standing explanation of why history has heroes at all: the earth would corrupt, and God is gracious, so He sends the few against the many, by His leave, until the leave runs out.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:252

> These are Allah's revelations which We recite to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth. And you are truly one of the messengers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Address Turns**

The story ends, and the verse turns from the story's world to the Prophet's: *These are Allah's revelations which We recite to you*. The shift of addressee is the verse's whole function — everything narrated since the fleeing thousands (2:243) has been third-person history, and the seal now makes it second-person property. The demonstrative tilka, those, gathers the whole sequence: the thousands killed and revived, the council and its pledge, the appointment and the protest, the Ark and its angels, the river and the remnant, the prayer and the rout — and names all of it āyāt, signs, the same word the code's closing refrain used for the legislation just completed (2:242). The recitation is placed in God's own voice with the Qur'an's characteristic grammar of revelation: We recite — the divine first-person performing, in the verse itself, the very reciting it describes. The Prophet is told, in the act of being told, that what he has been reciting to his community is not his narrative but a delivery — and the delivery's source is named so that its authority is not his to defend.

**In Truth**

The recitation's qualifier — bi'l-ḥaqq, in truth — does double work, and the commentators divide it between the two. The first work is ontological: what has been recited is true, the stories are accounts of what was, not edifying inventions; the Qur'an's parallel declaration in the sūrah of ʿImrān states the claim at its strongest — *Certainly, this is the true narrative, and there is no god worthy of worship except Allah* (3:62), the story's truth and the creed's truth in one sentence. The second work is purposive: the reciting is *in truth* in the sense of *for truth* — the stories are delivered not as antiquarian interest but as vehicles of the revelation's claim, each carrying the doctrines the sūrah has been legislating: God's command of life and death, the hollowness of pledges untested, election over pedigree, the few and the many, victory by leave. The two readings converge in the verse's context: the Prophet's recitation of these stories to a community containing their skeptics is itself an act of truth-telling, and the qualifier arms him for it — the stories he tells are true, told truly, and told for the truth they carry.

**The Consolation Reading**

Al-Ṭabarī records the verse's pastoral dimension: the stories of 2:243–251 were sent, on this reading, to hearten the Prophet against the enemies pressing him — the past's messengers and prophets, he is reminded, endured trials of the same shape. The reading fits the sequence's content precisely. The fleeing thousands faced death and were commanded onward; Samuel's council pledged and collapsed; Saul was appointed to a nation that disputed his right to exist as king; the remnant faced a disparity their own ranks could not bear. Every scene is a mirror of the Prophet's circumstance — a messenger with a pledged community that keeps failing its pledges, facing enemies who dispute his appointment on grounds of wealth and pedigree — and the verse's seal tells him that the mirrors were sent on purpose. The consolation is not that the past prophets won easily but that they were where he is: outnumbered, objected-to, dependent on leave. The sūrah's earlier consolation-verse had promised the believers help until the last messenger despaired (2:214); this verse delivers the help in narrative form, addressed to the messenger himself.

**You Are Truly One of the Messengers**

The seal's second sentence moves from the recitation to the reciter: *And you are truly one of the messengers*. The declaration is credential and comfort in one clause, and its logic runs through the stories just sealed. The man reciting accounts of councils he never attended, campaigns he never marched in, and prayers he never overheard — reciting them in truth, with the precision of a witness — is performing the defining activity of the office the verse names: carrying revelations he did not compose. The commentators connect this evidentiary structure to the Qur'an's standing argument from the unseen: the Prophet's knowledge of these histories, unlearned from any book and undelivered by any teacher, is itself among the signs he recites — the recitation authenticates the reciter in the same sentence that authenticates the recitation. The emphatic inna — *you are truly* — answers the objection the sūrah has been fielding since its opening: the disputer who denies the messenger is answered, at the story-sequence's close, with the story-sequence itself held up as his credential. He is one of them — of the messengers the stories carry — and the stories are the proof.

**The Seal on the Narrative Unit**

Structurally, the verse closes the first block of the sūrah's narrative mode, and its closing formula becomes the block's signature. The pattern it establishes — story delivered, then the delivery addressed to the Prophet in truth — governs how the sūrah's remaining narratives will be read: not as digressions from the legislation but as its counterpart, the memory doing for the community's courage what the code did for its conduct. The verse's two sentences mark the boundary between them: the revelations are God's property recited (not the Prophet's material composed), and the reciter is a messenger (not a storyteller). Both claims are aimed at the same disputer — the hearer tempted to reduce the narrative to legend and the reciter to legend-collector — and both are stated at the exact point where the temptation is strongest, after a sequence whose marvels run from mass death to angelic carriage. The sūrah now carries its Prophet, sealed and credentialed, into the narrative's second movement: the messengers themselves, and the preferments among them, which the following verse takes up from the word this one ends on.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:253

> We have chosen some of those messengers above others. Allah spoke directly to some, and raised some high in rank. To Jesus, son of Mary, We gave clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit. If Allah had willed, succeeding generations would not have fought ˹among themselves˺ after receiving the clear proofs. But they differed—some believed while others disbelieved. Yet if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another. But Allah does what He wills.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Preferment and the No-Distinction Creed**

The verse opens on a claim that sounds, to the creed-trained ear, like a contradiction: *We have chosen some of those messengers above others*. The sūrah's own closing confession will have the believers say *We make no distinction between any of His messengers* (2:285), and the same no-distinction formula governs belief elsewhere in the Book (2:136, 3:84). The tradition's resolution, which the exegetes state as settled doctrine, distinguishes two objects: belief makes no distinction among the messengers in their truthfulness, their prophethood, and their protection from sin — every one of them maʿṣūm, every one of them to be believed in without exception — while God's preferment ranks their missions, not their persons. The sūrah of ʿImrān supplies the ranking's formula: *They each have varying degrees in the sight of Allah* (3:163). To believe all and to acknowledge the degrees is not double-bookkeeping but one creed with two clauses: the messengers are equal in what they are, and differentiated in what they were sent with and given.

**The Three Axes of Difference**

The commentators enumerate the axes along which the missions differ, and the enumeration fills the verse's general claim with content. First, earthly power: some messengers were given kingdoms — Solomon's dominion over men, jinn, and wind — while others, Jesus among them, were given none; the office's worldly reach varies without the office's worth varying. Second, the kinds of signs: Moses' staff and sea, Solomon's command of the wind and the speech of birds, Jesus' healings and the table sent down — each messenger's miracles are his own, different in kind and not merely in count. Third, scope of sending: in Islamic belief the earlier prophets were sent to their own peoples, while the Prophet Muhammad was sent to humanity entire — a difference of mission-width the tradition reads as the ground of his own rank. The verse's two named examples map onto the axes: Moses, spoken to directly, carries the sign-privilege; Jesus, given proofs and the Spirit, carries the support-privilege; and the raised-in-ranks clause, left unnamed, is where the tradition places the widest mission of all.

**The One Spoken To**

*Allah spoke directly to some* — the kalām-privilege, and the tradition identifies its bearer without hesitation: Moses, the kalīm Allāh, the one to whom God spoke. The identification rests on the Sinai accounts — *When Moses came at the appointed time and his Lord spoke to him* (7:143) — where the speaking is unmediated, without the angelic embassy that carries revelation to every other prophet. The exegetes mark what the privilege does and does not imply: it does not make Moses the highest-ranked (the tradition's ranking places the highest elsewhere), and it does not imply a divine mode of speech like human voices — the theology of the attribute is contested ground the verse does not enter. What the verse's syntax does is place the speech among the preferments: it is one of the things God gave, a gift in the list of gifts, and its listing answers the communities who disputed it — the claim's fact is asserted here as calmly as a ledger-entry. The direct speech, in the Qur'an's economy, is not a metaphysical curiosity but a mission-endowment: the law-giver of Israel received his law mouth-to-ear, and the verse records the receipt.

**Raised High in Ranks**

*And raised some high in rank* — the clause is deliberately unspecified, and the tradition has read the specification two ways. The general reading takes it as the verse's own summary principle: beyond the named privileges — the speech, the proofs, the Spirit — God elevates some messengers by degrees whose content the verse withholds, the ranking being His to assign and His to know. The specific reading, dominant in the commentaries, identifies the highest of the raised: the Prophet to whom the sūrah is being recited, raised above the ranks by the widest mission, the complete Book, and the intercession the tradition attaches to his station — and the verse's placement immediately after his credential-seal (*you are truly one of the messengers*, 2:252) is read as pointing the unnamed clause at the named addressee. Both readings keep the verse's discipline: the preferments are divine acts, listed without envy and without appeal, and the ranks are assigned by the One the verse's final clause will name as doing what He wills. The unspecified elevation is the creed's safeguard — the ranking is believed because it is revealed, and its details are known where they are known and left where they are left.

**The Proofs and the Spirit**

The verse's one named messenger after Moses is Jesus: *To Jesus, son of Mary, We gave clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit*. The proofs — the bayyināt — are the visible signs catalogued elsewhere in the sūrah and in the Table: the healings of the blind and the leper, the quickening of the dead by God's leave, the bird of clay breathed into life, the table sent down (5:110). The support is the same pairing the sūrah stated in its address to Israel — *We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit* (2:87) — and the Spirit's identity is the exegetes' question. Al-Rāzī records the three identifications the tradition carries: the angel Gabriel, the Spirit who brought the revelation and strengthened the prophets; the spirit God breathed into human being (15:29), the life-principle in its divine origin; and the Gospel itself, the revelation given to Jesus. The three, he notes, share one quality — each is life-giving, whether the quickening of bodies or the nourishment of hearts and intellects — and the sharing is the identification's real content: whatever the Spirit is, its function in Jesus' mission is the same, the divine reinforcement carried alongside the proofs. The word's root, qudus, carries purity as well as holiness: the support named here is the clean, uncreated side of every miracle the verse's Jesus performs.

**Had God So Willed**

The verse's second half turns from the messengers to their aftermath, and its refrain begins: *If Allah had willed, succeeding generations would not have fought among themselves after receiving the clear proofs*. The subject is precise — not the pagans but the generations after the messengers, the communities of revelation, fighting each other *after* the bayyināt arrived: the very proofs the verse just named as gifts became the occasion of war, because clarity divides as surely as it guides. The refrain has its network, and the network is the doctrine: *If Allah had willed, He would have made you one community, but His Will is to test you with what He has given each of you* (5:48); *Had your Lord so willed, He would have certainly made humanity one single community, but they will always choose to differ* (11:118); and the sūrah's own earlier statement that humanity was one community before it differed, the messengers sent with the Book to judge between them (2:213). The verse adds nothing to the mechanism and removes nothing from its hardness: difference after revelation is willed — not approved, not authored in the sense of commanded, but permitted inside a will whose alternative (one undiffering community) is named and declined.

**Some Believed, Others Disbelieved**

The division's shape is stated in the verse's shortest sentence: *But they differed—some believed while others disbelieved*.
