The two parties exhaust the field, and the commentators read the exhaustiveness as diagnosis: after the clear proofs, there is no third position — no neutral ground between belief and disbelief once the bayyināt have arrived, which is why the aftermath of every mission is conflict rather than indifference. The fighting named twice in the verse is this bifurcation carried into history: communities of the same revelation, holding the same proofs, turning them against each other. The second *had God so willed* — repeating the first almost verbatim — has been read as emphasis and as escalation: emphasis, because the refrain doubled insists that the difference itself, and not merely its violence, stands inside the divine permission; escalation, because between the two refrain-clauses the verse inserts the belief-disbelief split, so that the second clause covers not just the fighting's possibility but the division's. The tradition holds both readings without choosing, and the verse's structure rewards both: the willed difference and the willed-against fighting are two layers of one permission.

**But Allah Does What He Wills**

The verse's final sentence is the refrain's resolution and the whole preferment-doctrine's ground: *But Allah does what He wills*. The clause answers the objection the verse's first half invites — if some messengers are raised and some are not, if the speech is given to one and the Spirit to another, if the proofs arrive and the communities fight anyway — who adjudicates the arrangement? The answer declines adjudication: the will is the last term, and the verse places it last. The commentators are careful about what the clause does not say: it is not arbitrariness dressed as sovereignty, since the same verse names what the will has actually willed — gifts, proofs, support, clarity — and the Qur'an elsewhere attaches the willing to wisdom (2:269, 3:74 in the tradition's citation). It is, instead, the closing of every appeal: the ranks are not negotiable by the ranked, the difference is not litigable by the differers, and the fighting after the proofs is not excusable by its participants, since the proofs they fought over were given. The verse ends where the story-sequence began — with a divine administration whose dispositions are seen, named, and not explained away — and leaves its hearer with the only response the administration has ever asked for: belief on one side of the difference, and the deeds that follow.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:254

> O believers! Donate from what We have provided for you before the arrival of a Day when there will be no bargaining, friendship, or intercession. Those who disbelieve are ˹truly˺ the wrongdoers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Spend Before the Day**

The narrative sequence closes on the messengers and their preferments, and the sūrah turns to its addressees with an imperative built on a deadline: donate *before the arrival of a Day*. The spending commanded is min mā razaqnākum — from what We have provided you — and the phrasing reclaims the wealth at the moment of its use: what the giver spends was never his except by provision, and the verse spends it for him before the Day spends it without him. The deadline is the verse's engine. Al-Ṭabarī states the mechanism plainly: the Day named is the Day of Judgment, when the time for performing good deeds has passed — the spending commanded here is possible only in the interval, and the interval is what the verse is selling. Spending from God's provision is one of the sūrah's founding descriptions of the believer — the portrait at its opening lists belief in the unseen, the prayer, and spending from what is provided (2:3) — and this verse returns that founding mark to the community as an urgent command with an expiration date attached.

**The Three Currencies Refused**

The Day is defined by three refusals, and each names a currency the world runs on. No bargaining — the world's transactions: ransom, price, negotiation, the deal struck at the margin. No friendship — the world's networks: the ally who intervenes, the connection who vouches, the kinship that opens doors. No intercession — the world's hierarchies of access: the patron who stands between the accused and the judge. Every ordinary strategy for surviving judgment — pay, know, be vouched for — is voided in one clause, and the voiding is total because the three currencies exhaust the three ways influence moves among people. The Qur'an states the same economics elsewhere: the sūrah of Abraham orders the believers to donate *before the arrival of a Day in which there will be no ransom or friendly connections* (14:31); the sūrah of the Believer pictures the Day *when the hearts will jump into the throats* and the wrongdoers have *neither a close friend nor intercessor to be heard* (40:18). The verse's function is to price the interval: while bargaining, friendship, and intercession still exist among people, the one transfer that reaches past the Day is the donation made before it.

**The Intercession Question**

The third refused currency deserves the precision the commentators give it, because the Qur'an's intercession-teaching is not a flat denial. The sūrah's own early verse stated the Day's rule absolutely — *No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken, and no help will be given* (2:48) — while other verses condition intercession rather than abolish it: who can intercede with God except by His leave. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī record the reconciliation here: the ability to intercede is unavailable, on this Day, to the disbelievers — the refusal is scoped to those who refused God. The tradition's picture of the Day includes intercession exercised by permission — above all the Prophet's intercession for his community and for the world, attached to the praiseworthy station promised him (17:79) — and the theological literature extends the permission to others by rank, al-Ghazzālī among the saints and the faithful, the Shīʿī tradition through the Imams. The verse's clause, read in that light, does not erase the institution but empties it of everything the world meant by it: no intercession that is bought, owed, or leveraged — only what the Judge permits, to whom He permits, for whom He permits.

**Friends Become Enemies**

The friendship-refusal has its own Qur'anic elaboration, and the elaboration sharpens the warning. The sūrah of Ornaments states it as a reversal: *Close friends will be enemies to one another on that Day, except the righteous* (43:67). The exception is the verse's hidden door: the friendships that survive the Day are the ones that were already righteous — bonds whose content was the good rather than the useful. The sūrah of Smoke adds that on the Day *no friend will avail a friend in any way*, and the sūrah of the Stairways pictures the loyal friend not asked about by his loyal friend (70:10) — each soul too occupied to plead another's case. Read together, the network-verses tell the believer something actionable in the interval: the worldly friendship that will be worthless on the Day is the friendship of mutual advantage, and the only social capital that crosses is the righteousness shared — which is why the verse's command is a command to spend: the donation is precisely the act that converts wealth, the most worldly of currencies, into the only form that the refusals do not touch.

**The Wrongdoers Named**

The final clause fixes the blame's location: *Those who disbelieve are truly the wrongdoers*. The identification is the Qur'an's standing equation — kufr as ẓulm in its fullest sense — and its placement after the Day's three refusals assigns the wrongdoers their fate precisely: the people for whom there will be no bargaining, no friendship, and no intercession are named here, and the naming is the verse's warning to the believers who still hold the interval. The commentators connect the clause to the command's logic: the disbeliever is called a wrongdoer because he misappropriated what was provided — the wealth that was God's provision spent as though it were self-earned, kept as though keeping were ownership — and the Day's refusals are the foreclosure on that misappropriation. The believers are addressed as believers and commanded to donate; the disbelievers are described in the third person and condemned. Between the two sentences stands the whole meaning of the verse's timing: the addressees can still choose which sentence describes them, and the donation is the choosing.

**The Verse as Threshold**

Positioned where it sits, the verse opens the sūrah's second great theme-block — spending — and opens it with the eschatology that will govern every spending-verse to come. The parables of the grain and the garden, the prohibitions on reminders and injury, the ranking of secret over public, the recipients who do not beg: all of it operates inside the deadline this verse states. The three refusals also gather the sūrah's earlier material — the Day described in its opening eschatological verses, the intercession-question raised at 2:48, the spending-from-provision commanded from 2:3 — and compress it into a single imperative. The reader is left with the verse's arithmetic, which is deliberately simple: everything a person owns is provided, everything provided can be donated, everything donated before the Day crosses it, and on the Day the three currencies of the world are refused to everyone. The command is therefore not a tax on the believer's wealth but the only available exchange rate — and the wrongdoers named at the end are the ones who waited for a better one.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:255

> Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him, the EverLiving, All-Sustaining. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who could possibly intercede with Him without His permission? He ˹fully˺ knows what is ahead of them and what is behind them, but no one can grasp any of His knowledge—except what He wills ˹to reveal˺. His Seat encompasses the heavens and the earth, and the preservation of both does not tire Him. For He is the Most High, the Greatest.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Greatest Verse**

Āyat al-Kursī — the Verse of the Pedestal, sometimes rendered the Throne Verse — is arguably the single most widely known verse of the Qur'an, named for the kursī it mentions and recited by Muslims setting out on journeys, seeking protection spiritual and physical, and memorized among the first passages a child learns. Its standing is prophetic, not merely popular. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (810), the Prophet asks Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: O Abū'l-Mundhir, do you know which verse of God's Book is the greatest? Ubayy answers by reciting this verse — *Allāhu lā ilāha illā huwa'l-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm* — and the Prophet strikes his chest and says: may knowledge gladden you, O Abū'l-Mundhir. Other narrations call the verse a quarter of the Qur'an, direct the Companions to recite it before sleep, and promise — in a report of the Sunan collections — that whoever recites it after every obligatory prayer is kept from Paradise only by death. The tradition of its protective recitation has a famous story behind it: Abū Hurayrah, set over the Ramadan alms-store, caught a night-thief three times running, and the third time released him in exchange for words of benefit — recite Āyat al-Kursī when you go to bed, and a guardian from God will stay with you and Satan will not approach you until morning. The Prophet's verdict, in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (2311): he told you the truth, though he is a liar — the thief was Satan himself.

**The Living, the Self-Subsisting**

The verse opens with the shahādah's Qur'anic form — God, there is no god but He — the phrasing that dominates the text's own declarations of unity (2:163, 3:2, and many more), and then names the two divine titles the tradition counts among the mothers of the Names, ummahāt al-asmāʾ. Al-Ḥayy, the Living, occupies in Islamic theology a place the commentators equate with Being itself: a living thing, al-Rāzī formulates it, is one able to fully actualize all its perfections — and the theological cascade runs from there, God's Power directed by His Will, His Will determined by His Knowledge, all of them depending on His Life. Al-Qayyūm, the All-Sustaining, is an intensive form from the root of standing and establishing: God subsists through Himself, and — the second half of the intensity — all things subsist through Him. The two names together state the verse's whole architecture: a Life that cannot lapse and a Subsistence that cannot be borrowed, which is why the next clause denies the lapse's slightest forms.

**Neither Slumber Nor Sleep**

The negation is graded: sinah, the doze — the light slipping at the edge of wakefulness — and nawm, deep sleep. Neither overtakes Him, and the commentators connect the wakefulness-clause to the verse's later statement that preservation does not tire Him: the same sovereignty described twice, once as unfailing awareness and once as unfailing maintenance. The denial of sleep is not a physiological remark but a custodial one: a guardian who sleeps is not a guardian, and the verse's God keeps the heavens and the earth the way wakefulness keeps a trust — without interruption, without lapse, without relief required. The clause also carries the epistemic side: His awareness of the creation never pauses, which means no moment of any creature's existence falls outside it — the sleeplessness is total surveillance in the exact sense the word's Latin root implies, a watching-over that does not blink.

**Ownership and Permission**

*To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth* — the ownership-clause grounds the intercession-clause that follows, and the intercession-clause is the verse's great reconciliation. The sūrah's earlier Day-verse had denied intercession flatly (2:48); here it is affirmed conditionally: *Who could possibly intercede with Him without His permission?* The rhetorical question concedes nothing to the intercessor — the permission is God's, wholly — and everything to the institution: intercession exists, and it exists as a function of the leave. The tradition's supreme instance is the Prophet's intercession on the Day of Judgment, for his community and for the world, attached to the praiseworthy station (17:79); theologians like al-Ghazzālī extend permission-granted intercession to the saints and ordinary believers according to rank, and Shīʿī doctrine places the Imams at its center. The commentators' deepest observation is structural: every prayer one person makes for another already assumes intercession — the angels' forgiveness-prayers for the believers (40:7), Jacob's promised prayer for his sons (12:98), the command to the Prophet to seek forgiveness for the faithful — since to pray for another is to believe God answers. Intercession, on this reading, is a special kind of supplication, and the verse's permission-clause is its charter: no one stands before God for anyone except by His leave — and His leave is why anyone stands.

**The Knowledge That Cannot Be Grasped**

*He knows what is ahead of them and what is behind them* — the phrase's referents are read three ways by al-Rāzī and the tradition: the Hereafter ahead and the world behind; what comes after death and what preceded creation; the deeds yet to be done and the deeds already done. The pronoun covers both the would-be intercessors and those interceded for — every party to any plea, past and coming. Then the verse closes the knowledge in the other direction: *no one can grasp any of His knowledge — except what He wills to reveal*. Knowledge here, the commentators note, is used in the sense of the known — the content rather than the faculty — and the exception-clause is the Qur'an's standing epistemology: the unseen is disclosed only where God approves its disclosure, *except messengers of His choice* (72:27); the angels' own confession is the verse's echo from the sūrah's opening — we have no knowledge except what You have taught us (2:32). The intercession-clause and the knowledge-clause are thus two statements of one rule: no access to God's court and no access to God's knowledge except by His leave and His will — and both accesses, the verse affirms, are real.

**The Pedestal**

The kursī is the verse's famous crux. Some read it as the place of the feet — the footstool before the throne — but the commentators find the rendering problematic: in the cosmological reports the kursī is not beneath the ʿarsh but below it in rank and above the cosmos — the Throne encompasses the Pedestal, and the Pedestal encompasses the heavens and the earth — an order that collapses if the kursī is a footstool, which sits in front of a throne rather than under it. The report from Ibn ʿAbbās states the encompassment as scale: the seven heavens and the earth beside the kursī are like a ring thrown into a wilderness. Others read the Pedestal metaphorically — knowledge, sovereignty, authority — the way "the crown" names the monarch. The tradition's discipline about both readings is the verse's own lesson in theological method: neither pure allegory, which lets the reader's desires into the text, nor literalist anthropomorphism, which assigns God location and limbs. The verse ends the question where it ends everything: the Seat — however named — encompasses both worlds, and *the preservation of both does not tire Him*, the keeping of everything that exists being, to the Keeper, without cost.

**The Most High, the Greatest**

The two closing names gather the verse's movement. ʿAlīy, the Most High — exalted above the intercessors who stand only by leave, above the knowers who grasp only what is willed, above the cosmos the Seat encompasses. ʿAẓīm, the Greatest — the magnitude the ring-in-the-wilderness report tries to picture and the tireless-preservation clause proves. The verse's whole structure ascends to them: unity declared, life and subsistence named, sleep denied, ownership stated, permission required, knowledge fenced, the Seat measured against the worlds — and then the two names that say what all the clauses were saying: nothing in the verse's inventory is on His level, and everything in it stands by Him. It is fitting that the tradition's most-recited verse is a verse about keeping: the Living who cannot lapse, the Sustainer on whom all subsistence leans, the preserver whom the preservation of two worlds does not tire — recited by travelers because the road is a place of lapse, by sleepers because sleep is the small death, by the frightened because fear is the doubt that anything is being kept. The verse answers the doubt in one sentence's worth of names: He is the Most High, the Greatest, and neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:256

> Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood. So whoever renounces false gods and believes in Allah has certainly grasped the firmest, unfailing hand-hold. And Allah is AllHearing, All-Knowing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sentence and Its Grammar**

Lā ikrāha fī'l-dīn — *no compulsion in religion* — is among the most cited sentences in the Qur'an, and its first interpretive question is grammatical: is it descriptive or prescriptive? Read as description, it states a fact about faith itself — religion cannot be compelled, because belief coerced is not belief; the heart under threat produces compliance, not īmān. Read as prescription — *let there be no compulsion* — it legislates the fact, forbidding what would in any case be futile. The traditional commentaries carry both readings without conflict, and the second clause supplies the reason either way: *the truth stands out clearly from falsehood* — rushd has become distinct from ghayy, and what is distinct does not need to be imposed. The Qur'an's parallel statements gather behind this verse: *Had your Lord so willed, all people on earth would have certainly believed. Would you then force people to become believers?* (10:99); and the command to say: *Whoever wills let them believe, and whoever wills let them disbelieve* (18:29). The compulsion-verses share one assumption — that faith is a seeing, not a yielding — and this verse states the assumption as a principle of law.

**Rushd and Ghayy**

The two nouns of the reason-clause carry more than the translation shows. Rushd, rendered *truth* here, is the word for sound judgment, right direction, maturity — the same root as the rightly-guided (rāshid) and the growth-toward-sense that the sūrah of the Cave attaches to the orphans' treasure; ghayy, rendered *falsehood*, carries error but also transgression and seduction — going astray as an active falling-away. The clause thus says more than true-is-distinguishable-from-false: it says maturity is distinguishable from seduction, sound direction from the stumble. The verb — *stands out clearly* — is in the perfect: the distinction has been completed, accomplished by the revelation's own clarity, which is the sūrah's recurring claim (thus God makes His signs clear). A clarity this complete changes the function of force: where the road forks visibly, compulsion adds nothing to the seeing and subtracts everything from the chooser.

**The Occasions of Revelation**

The narrations behind the verse are specific and domestic, and they matter for its scope. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī record three occasions, all involving children and belonging. In the first, Muslim parents had children among the Banū Naḍīr — the Jewish tribe exiled from Medina after its plotted betrayal — and asked whether they might force the children into the Muslim community; the background is a pre-Islamic custom of Yathrib, where women whose infants kept dying vowed that any child who survived would be raised Jewish, and it was such vowed children who now stood between two communities. In the second, a Muslim man's two sons were converted by merchants and left for Syria as Christians. In the third, Muslims who had been wet-nursed by Jewish families wanted to depart with the exiled clans, and their families were forcing them to remain. In every account the verse arrives to stop a compelled belonging — and in every account the compelling party is the one with the better religion, which is precisely why the case is hard and the ruling general.

**Scope, Jizyah, and the Abrogation Debate**

The jurists asked how far the principle reaches, and the commentary records the debate honestly. Some sources restrict the verse to the People of the Book, or to anyone from whom the jizyah-protection tax may be taken (9:29's legislation) — noting that the idolatrous Arabs were not offered the option of remaining idolaters, and reading the no-compulsion rule as governing the recognized protected religions. Others claimed the verse was abrogated by the fighting-commandments, the sword-verse of sūrah 9 among them. The commentators answer the abrogation-claim on chronology: all three occasions of revelation follow from conflicts with the Jewish tribes — conditions resulting from banishments already carried out — so the verse is late, not early, and cannot have been repealed by verses whose campaigns preceded it. The deeper answer is doctrinal: compulsion in religion negates taklīf, the accountability before God that gives both this life and the Hereafter their meaning — and an ethical pronouncement of that kind is not subject to abrogation at all. The record adds a historical observation: forced conversions in later Islamic history, while not unknown, count as rare exceptions to the rule — the fighting Muslims carried out was, like the occasions of this verse show, motivated by political circumstance rather than by the desire to convert.

**Ṭāghūt and the Handhold**

The verse's second half describes the act of faith in two movements: renouncing ṭāghūt and believing in God. Ṭāghūt — rendered *false gods* — is built on the root of rebellion and trespass: al-Rāzī glosses it variously as Satan, as soothsayers and magicians, as idols, as any being who rebels against God and is followed in the rebellion; the longer treatment waits in the sūrah of Women (4:51). The renunciation comes first in the syntax, and the order is the theology: the handhold is grasped by a letting-go. The image — *the firmest, unfailing hand-hold* — has its parallel in the sūrah of Luqmān: whoever submits to God and does good *has grasped the firmest hand-hold* (31:22). The commentators identify the handhold as faith itself or as the shahādah-word, and they note the precision of *unfailing*: the Arabic break it denies is the fracture that does not show — the handhold that fails imperceptibly, the faith that parts silently under strain. What is grasped, the verse promises, does not give way even slightly, and the grasping is available to whoever performs the two movements — renounce, believe — with no one compelled into either.

**All-Hearing, All-Knowing**

The closing pair is the sūrah's audit-seal, set here over the verse's two interiors. The hearer of the shahādah-word is God — the confession spoken under a sword and the confession spoken in freedom reach the same hearing, and the name quietly completes the no-compulsion rule: since God hears the heart's speech directly, human coercion adds nothing to His knowledge and cannot manufacture what He alone receives. The Knower knows the renunciation's sincerity — whether the ṭāghūt let go of was outward or inward, whether the handhold was grasped or clutched at. The pair also answers the occasions of revelation: the parents wondering about their vowed children, the families forcing the wet-nursed to stay, the fathers watching sons leave for Syria — every party to those disputes is heard and known, and the verse releases them all from the work of adjudicating each other's hearts. Religion under this seal is a matter between the grasping hand and the Knowing God; the community's law is only to keep the space clear — no compulsion — and let the clarity of rushd from ghayy do what clarity does.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:257

> Allah is the Guardian of the believers—He brings them out of darkness and into light. As for the disbelievers, their guardians are false gods who lead them out of light and into darkness. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Walī**

The verse opens with a single relational noun carrying the weight of everything that follows: God is the walī of those who believe — guardian, protector, ally, friend, patron; the word holds all of them at once, and the tradition's glosses move across the range. A walī is the one who stands nearest with power to help: the guardian of an orphan, the protector of a client, the ally of a confederation, the friend whose friendship has consequences. Assigned as the believer's walī, the name gathers the sūrah's whole theology of care — the All-Sustaining of the preceding verse, the wakeful preservation that does not tire — into a personal relation: the God who keeps the cosmos keeps the believer, and keeps him as a walī keeps his charge, near, responsible, and effective. The symmetry the verse then builds is exact and inverted: as the believers have God, the disbelievers have their awliyāʾ too — the ṭāghūt just renounced in the handhold-verse — and the two guardianships produce two opposite migrations.

**Out of the Darknesses, Into the Light**

The movement ascribed to God's guardianship is an extraction: *He brings them out of darkness and into light*. The Arabic's asymmetry is the image's first teaching, and the commentators mark it: the darknesses are plural — ẓulumāt — while the light is singular, nūr. Error, in the Qur'an's idiom, is many; truth is one. The plural darknesses are the unbelief's varieties — the idols, the doubts, the appetites, the inherited errors — and each extraction is particular: this believer out of these darknesses. The singular light is the destination's unity: one faith, one direction, one God. The symbolism runs through the whole Qur'an, and this verse is its most explicit statement of movement — elsewhere the sūrah of the Table names the Book *a light by which Allah guides* (5:16), the sūrah of Light builds the symbol into its greatest verse — *Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth* (24:35) — and the extraction-formula recurs: out of the darknesses into the light at 14:1, 33:43, 57:9, 65:11. Al-Ṭabarī records the majority gloss plainly: light is faith and guidance, darkness is denial and error — and the bringing-out is the work of the walī, not the achievement of the brought.

**The Reverse Migration**

The verse's second sentence is its most disturbing symmetry: the disbelievers' guardians *lead them out of light and into darkness*. The migration is real and it runs backward — and its starting point is the verse's quiet claim about unbelief: it begins in light. The ṭāghūt-guardianship does not operate on people who never saw; it takes people who did — the clarity established in the preceding verse, the rushd distinguished from ghayy, the handhold within reach — and leads them out of it. The commentators read the reversal as the work of false patronage: whatever is followed in rebellion against God performs, for its followers, the inverse of God's walāyah — it has the shape of guardianship (devotion given, direction taken, trust extended) and the function of undoing. The plural returns in the destination as in the cause: out of the one light, into the darknesses — the single truth abandoned, the many errors entered, each idol and appetite its own chamber. The symmetry denies any neutral ground: every person is migrating, under one guardianship or the other, and the verse's two sentences are the two itineraries.

**Guardianship as Pedagogy**

The bringing-out and the leading-out share a structure the exegetes draw out: both are gradual, both are relational, and both are performed on the person rather than by him. Light and darkness in this idiom are not information but states — a person is in them, and getting out requires a hand. The believer's extraction is the history of revelation itself: the Book sent *that you may bring people out of the darknesses into the light, by their Lord's permission* (14:1) — the messenger's mission defined as the same bringing-out the verse ascribes to God, since the walī's work runs through the means the walī appoints. The disbelievers' leading-out has its ministers too: the callers to the ṭāghūt, the merchants of Syria in the occasion-narrations of the preceding verse, the inherited customs of Yathrib's vowed children. The verse's pastoral instruction is to audit one's guardianships — to ask of every attachment that shapes the heart's direction whether it is extracting toward the one light or conducting toward the many darknesses — because the migration is underway either way, and nobody travels unaccompanied.

**Residents of the Fire**

The closing sentence states the second itinerary's end: *It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.* The residence-language is the Qur'an's term of permanence — ahl, inhabitants, the Fire as a dwelling rather than an event — and its placement here completes the verse's symmetry one final time: the guardianship determines the migration, the migration determines the residence. The commentators connect the permanence to the guardianship's nature: the ṭāghūt followed in this life becomes, in the idiom of the reversal, the company kept in the next — the darknesses entered one by one close into the single dark of the Fire, and the extraction refused becomes the confinement chosen. The verse's own logic supplies the final contrast with the preceding āyah: the handhold-verse ended with the hearing and knowing God over every grasp; this verse ends with the residence over every letting-go. Between the two endings stands the whole of the sūrah's account of faith — a hold and a being-held, or a leading-out and a being-led, with no third road through the darknesses.

**The Verse in Its Sequence**

Positioned between the no-compulsion verse and the debate of Abraham, this āyah is the sequence's hinge: the handhold-verse declared faith uncoercible because clarity has been established; this verse explains what happens to the clarity under the two guardianships — received as extraction or reversed as seduction. The Abraham-narratives that follow will exhibit both migrations in person: the king who is led out of what he knew into dumbfoundment, the passers-by and the prophets brought out of question into certainty. And the verse supplies the frame the sūrah's coming legislation will assume: the spending-parables, the giving-without-injury, the charity by night and day — all of it is the extracted person's conduct, the behavior of someone whose walī has brought him into the light and who walks, in the light's idiom, as one being kept. The residents of the Fire are named once, at the verse's end, and the sūrah returns immediately to the living work of the illuminated: the debates, the resurrections, and the grain that multiplies.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:258

> Are you ˹O Prophet˺ not aware of the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord because Allah had granted him kingship? ˹Remember˺ when Abraham said, "My Lord is the One Who has power to give life and cause death." He argued, "I too have the power to give life and cause death." Abraham challenged ˹him˺, "Allah causes the sun to rise from the east. So make it rise from the west." And so the disbeliever was dumbstruck. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The King Who Argued**

The verse opens on the Qur'an's only recorded debate between a prophet and a reigning king, and it withholds the king's name. The commentators commonly identify him as Nimrod, but they are candid about the identification's standing: it rests on folkloric material, he is named in no ḥadīth, and his place even in the biblical record is ambiguous. The anonymity is arguably the point — the argument matters, the arguer's biography does not. What the verse supplies instead is the debate's cause: *because Allah had granted him kingship*. The grammar admits two readings, al-Rāzī notes — the sovereignty could belong to Abraham (whose descendants were given a mighty kingdom, 4:54) or to the antagonist — and the majority takes it as the king's: the power that God gave him became the ground from which he disputed God. The verse thus opens with its diagnosis already embedded in its syntax: kingship, a divine grant like every authority, is the instrument of the argument against its Giver.

**My Lord Gives Life and Causes Death**

Abraham's opening statement is a definition of lordship in two verbs: *My Lord is the One Who has power to give life and cause death*. The formula — God gives life and causes death — recurs across the Qur'an as the standing description of the divine monopoly (2:28 among its earliest instances in this sūrah), and Abraham deploys it as a test of the word rabb itself: whoever holds life and death holds lordship, and lordship belongs to whoever holds them. The king's answer is the verse's masterpiece of sophistry: *I too have the power to give life and cause death*. The narrations supply the performance behind the claim — the king brings two men, kills one and spares the other: there, life given and death caused, a ruler's prerogative demonstrated on the spot. The mimicry is exact in vocabulary and empty in substance: the pardoned prisoner was not given life but left alive, and the executed man's death was an inflicted event, not the withdrawal of a sustaining hand. The king has seized the words and released the meaning — which is the verse's picture of how power argues.

**Bring It from the West**

Abraham's rejoinder does not contest the mimicry; it changes the terrain. *Allah causes the sun to rise from the east. So make it rise from the west.* The commentators note the move's construction: the first claim could be counterfeit because life and death, in human hands, have look-alikes — the pardon, the execution, the reprieve. The sun has none. Its rising is a daily, public, unbuyable fact with no administrative substitute, and the challenge transfers the debate from a domain where sovereignty can perform imitations to a domain where it cannot perform anything. The single imperative — make it rise from the west — is the whole refutation: not an argument to answer but a task to attempt. The verse's next word records the result in one passive verb: the disbeliever was dumbstruck — buhita, confounded, struck silent. He does not concede, does not argue further, does not strike back; the debate simply ends where the pretense can no longer follow. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī read the silence as the verse's epistemology: against the sign that cannot be mimicked, falsehood has no next move.

**The Nature Full of Signs**

The encounter exhibits a theme the commentators name explicitly: Abraham's triumph exposes the ruler's pretense *and* demonstrates that the natural world is full of God's signs. The debate's two rounds are two kinds of evidence — the first the hidden governance of life and death, disputable because invisible; the second the visible governance of the heavens, indisputable because daily — and Abraham's shift between them is the Qur'an's method in miniature: when the invisible sign is contested by a counterfeit, move to the sign whose counterfeit is impossible. The patriarch's career runs on these celestial observations: the sūrah of the Cattle will show him reading guidance in a star, a moon, and a sun that all set (6:76–78), concluding that lordship cannot belong to what does not stay. Here the same sky supplies the refutation of a king. The natural sign, in the Qur'an's usage, is not decoration for the argument — it is the argument's strongest form, because it is addressed to every eye at once and cannot be pardoned, executed, or administratively arranged.

**The Pharaoh Parallel**

The commentators set this king beside his archetype: the debate between Moses and Pharaoh, whose claim escalates to the direct announcement — *I am your lord, the most high* (79:24). The two rulers fail in the same shape and differ in degree. Pharaoh asserts the lordship outright and is answered by signs he can watch and cannot touch — the staff, the hand, the plagues, the sea; Abraham's antagonist asserts only the two verbs and is answered by a single sentence about the sunrise. In both stories the ruler's power is real — the execution happens, the kingdom stands — and in both, the reality of the power is precisely what tempts it into the claim. The verse's causal clause names the temptation's source: *because Allah had granted him kingship*. The grant is not the sin; the argument from the grant is. The Qur'an's kings are not condemned for ruling but for reading their rule as self-derived — the same misreading the handhold-verse diagnosed in the ṭāghūt, the rebel followed in his rebellion, whose guardianship leads out of light and into darkness.

**No Guidance for the Wrongdoers**

The verse closes with the withheld gift: *And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people*. The sentence explains the dumbfoundment's permanence — the king is silenced but not converted, confounded but not guided — and states the verse's final theorem: guidance is not the automatic prize of losing an argument. The wrongdoer's non-guidance is the Qur'an's standing account of the hardened heart: the ẓulm that takes God's grant and argues from it, that mimics the divine verbs on prisoners, closes the road the signs open. Al-Rāzī connects the clause to the debate's structure: the signs did their work — the counterfeit was exposed, the sun was named, the silence fell — and what remained missing was the reception the wrongdoing had disabled. The verse leaves its reader with the encounter's whole geometry: a prophet with no army, a king with one; a claim tested on a prisoner, a claim tested on the sunrise; an argument that ended in a word, and a guidance that did not follow the word. The sūrah's next scene will show the same two forces — death and life, doubt and certainty — at work on a ruined city and a hundred-year sleeper, where the questioning is honest and the guidance, accordingly, arrives.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:259

> Or ˹are you not aware of˺ the one who passed by a city which was in ruins. He wondered, "How could Allah bring this back to life after its destruction?" So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years then brought him back to life. Allah asked, "How long have you remained ˹in this state˺?" He replied, "Perhaps a day or part of a day." Allah said, "No! You have remained here for a hundred years! Just look at your food and drink— they have not spoiled. ˹But now˺ look at ˹the remains of˺ your donkey! And ˹so˺ We have made you into a sign for humanity. And look at the bones ˹of the donkey˺, how We bring them together then clothe them with flesh!" When this was made clear to him, he declared, "˹Now˺ I know that Allah is Most Capable of everything."

**Expanded Commentary**

**The City on Its Roofs**

The second scene of the life-and-death sequence shifts from a debate to a solitary ride: a passer-by comes on a city *in ruins* — the Arabic picture is precise, the roofs collapsed and the walls fallen in on top of them, and the word khāwiyah carrying, the commentators note, the double sense of fallen and emptied. The ruin is total in the way ruins of great places are: not a village abandoned but a civilization folded in on itself. The passer-by's question is the verse's hinge, and its tone has been debated from the first: *How could Allah bring this back to life after its destruction?* Read as doubt, it is the hardest question faith faces — not whether God can raise the dead in general but whether God will restore what history has actually destroyed, the particular city, the particular loss. Read as wonder, it is the mind standing at the edge of the conceivable. The verse answers the question the only way the Qur'an ever answers such questions — not with a proposition but with an experience: the questioner is made into the evidence.

**Who Passed By**

The tradition offers identities and the commentary records them all: Ezra, most commonly — the ʿUzayr of the narrations, connected to Jerusalem's destruction and restoration; Ezekiel, whose biblical vision of the valley of dry bones supplies a parallel the exegetes themselves note; even Khiḍr, the unnamed servant of the cave-sūrah. Al-Rāzī preserves the fourth reading that dissolves the question: not a prophet or saint at all but a disbeliever, shown the resurrection's reality directly. The Qur'anic text's own reticence — *the one who passed by* — is why the translators' notes and the classical renderings hedge the pronouns: the story's identity-interest is minimal and its demonstration-interest total. Whoever asked the question, the answer was the same hundred years of death, and whoever he was, he came back with the confession the verse ends on. The anonymity functions like the king's in the preceding verse: the debate's antagonist is unnamed because his title is the point, and the rider is unnamed because his question is the point — every reader who has looked at a ruin and wondered how God could restore it has, in the verse's grammar, already passed by the city.

**A Day or Part of a Day**

The resurrection's first datum is the sleeper's own estimate: *How long have you remained?* — *Perhaps a day or part of a day.* The question-and-answer pair is the Qur'an's standing instrument for measuring the dead's experience of time, and it appears at the two other great awakenings: the sleepers of the cave, roused, ask each other *How long have you remained asleep?* and answer themselves *perhaps a day, or part of a day* (18:19); and the resurrected soul, questioned on the Day — *How many years did you remain on earth?* — will answer with the same collapsed arithmetic (23:112). The three passages state one doctrine of death's duration: from inside, the interval is nothing — a day, a part of a day — however the outside counts it. The correction that follows is therefore not about the man's honesty but about the two clocks: *No! You have remained here for a hundred years!* The century has passed over him and not through him; his estimate is what a hundred years of death feels like, and the verse preserves both numbers because both are true — the calendar's and the sleeper's.

**The Food and the Donkey**

Two proofs are staged for the awakened man, and their contrast is the scene's construction. First the untouched: *look at your food and drink — they have not spoiled*. The hundred years have passed beside his provisions without touching them — the commentators note the food's freshness as the miracle's quiet half, time arrested around the sleeper's own belongings. Then the dismantled: *look at your donkey* — and the donkey is bones. The verse's longest imperative unfolds the reconstruction as a spectacle: *look at the bones, how We bring them together then clothe them with flesh* — the assembly watched bone by bone, the clothing watched layer by layer, the rider watching his mount reassemble. The exegetes debate whether the bones-clothing clause describes the donkey's revival or the man's own reconstitution, al-Rāzī recording both; on either reading the demonstration is the same — resurrection shown not as announcement but as procedure, the steps visible, the agent named. The man who asked how God could restore a collapsed city is given a collapsed body to watch rebuilt, at a scale where every movement of the rebuilding can be seen.

**A Sign for Humanity**

The scene's purpose-clause is attached to the spectacle: *We have made you into a sign for humanity*. The commentators test the clause against an obvious inference — that being made a sign means being made a prophet — and refuse it with a counterexample from the Qur'an itself: Pharaoh too was made a sign (10:92), the drowning king preserved as a lesson, and he is the opposite of a prophet. The sign-status is about the person's evidentiary function, not his rank: this man's century of death and his minute of waking are now public property, a datum the community can carry. And the tradition softens the question behind his original wonder: if the rider is a prophet, his how-could-Allah is not pernicious doubt but the same spirit as Abraham's request in the verse that follows — *show me how You give life to the dead* — the question of one who believes asking to see. On that reading the two scenes are one movement: the passing rider and the patriarch both ask the how of resurrection, and both are answered with demonstrations — one with a century of his own death, the other with four birds and a call.

**I Know That Allah Is Able**

The confession that closes the verse is the scene's whole yield: *Now I know that Allah is Most Capable of everything*. The commentators mark the shift precisely — the verse's first sentence held a question about possibility (*how could Allah*), and the last holds knowledge of power (*I know that Allah has power over all things*). The distance between them was not an argument but a hundred years, a jar of unsoured drink, and a donkey reassembled under its owner's eyes. The knowledge named is not abstract omnipotence but omnipotence verified in the particular case the questioner had doubted: this city, this body, this ruin — the restoration whose how was unimaginable has been performed on the questioner himself. The verse's instruction, read with its neighbor, completes the pair the sūrah set out to teach: the king argued about life and death and was confounded by the sun; the rider wondered about life and death and was answered by his own bones. The first would not be guided — wrongdoing closes the reception; the second asked and was shown — and his showing ends where every demonstration in the Qur'an ends, with the knower naming what he now knows: God is, over everything, able.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:260

> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, "My Lord! Show me how you give life to the dead." Allah responded, "Do you not believe?" Abraham replied, "Yes I do, but just so my heart can be reassured." Allah said, "Then bring four birds, train them to come to you, ˹then cut them into pieces,˺ and scatter them on different hilltops. Then call them back, they will fly to you in haste. And ˹so you will˺ know that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise."

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question of the Friend of God**

The third life-and-death scene is a request: Abraham — the patriarch the Qur'an will call God's friend, the man who broke the idols and walked out of the fire — asks to be shown how God gives life to the dead. The verse supplies no occasion, and the commentators record the possibilities the tradition gathered: he had seen, on a seashore, the creatures of sea and land and air feeding on one another, and wondered how resurrection would reassemble pieces scattered through so many bodies; or the request grew from his debate with the king, the demonstration lending his message force; or it connects to the sacrifice of his son; or it seeks confirmation of his own station. The plurality is the verse's first teaching: the how-question is legitimate wherever it arises, and the Qur'an preserves it in the mouth of the last person whose faith needed propping. The divine response treats the question accordingly — not as an accusation to answer but as a faith to confirm: *Do you not believe?*

**The Answered Answer**

*I do — but just so my heart can be reassured.* The commentators hear the exchange as an implicit affirmation wearing the form of a question: you believe, then — so the asking is not doubt's asking. What Abraham names is the heart's dimension: faith held in the mind seeking settlement in the breast. The tradition's vocabulary for the sought state is rich and the verse's word — yaṭmaʾinna, be at peace, be settled — is the same root as the sūrah of the Dawn's invitation, *O tranquil soul, return to your Lord* (89:27), and the sūrah of Thunder's axiom, *in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find comfort* (13:28). Al-Rāzī's reconciliation of the patriarch's asking with the patriarch's peace became the standard reading: spiritual knowledge has degrees, and Abraham is describing passage from one depth of understanding to the next — not hesitation about God's existence or power but the desire, no believer ever finishes having, to witness more of God's self-disclosure. The Prophetic verdict on the whole scene is the famous sentence in the ḥadīth collections — we are more entitled to doubt than Abraham — which defends the patriarch by relocating the question: if this asking counts as doubt, the doubt belongs to everyone before it belongs to him; and in truth it was not doubt but an entreaty for more knowledge. The Qur'an commands the same entreaty of its own Prophet: *My Lord, increase me in knowledge* (20:114) — a prayer that highlights not his ignorance, the commentators note, but God's limitlessness.

**The Four Birds**

The demonstration is ordered in a sequence of imperatives, and the sequence's second step is the tradition's great grammatical debate. *Take four birds and make them inclined to you* — the verb, in the majority reading, means to cut them up, though al-Rāzī records the difficulty the prepositional phrase then carries (cut them *to you*?). On the majority reading the rite runs: four birds — the commentaries list peacock, eagle, raven, and rooster, with other lists preserved — are cut into pieces, the pieces distributed on four mountains, read as the four cardinal directions, and then called. What is called reassembles: the scattered parts return into their forms and come flying, in haste, to the caller. On the second reading, recorded as the translation's alternative, no killing occurs at all: Abraham first draws each bird to himself — tames them, habituates them — then stations them alive on the mountains, then calls them home. The reading transforms the demonstration from reassembly into return: the resurrection pictured as the reunification of souls and bodies with the ease of a man calling birds that come running to the voice they know. Both readings end at the same verse-word — *in haste* — and both make the call, not the cutting, the demonstration's center.

**The Birds of the Self**

The allegorical reading of the four is one of the commentary's most transmitted: the birds are the soul's four — the eagle, lust for food; the rooster, lust for sex; the raven, excessive curiosity; the peacock, vanity — and the rite is their scattering and recall, the self's appetites dispersed on the mountains and summoned back under the caller's command. Al-Rāzī preserves the reading while noting that the commentaries carry many different bird-lists, each generation assigning its own quartet of vices. The spiritual interpretation follows the verse's own invitation: resurrection demonstrated on birds becomes resurrection demonstrated on the heart — the revival of dead hearts through the Spirit, as the gloss has it — and the haste of the returning birds becomes the appetite's speed when the purified will calls it. The four-mountains geography serves the reading: the cardinal directions are the self's four quarters, and the caller standing at the center is the heart obeyed at last by what it feeds. The literal demonstration and the allegorical one are not rival accounts but the same sign at two scales — the bodies reassembling on the hills, the soul's birds reassembling in the breast.

**The Most Hopeful Verse**

The scene's closing gift is not in the demonstration but in its manner. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said of Abraham's question and God's gentle response to it: there is no more hopeful verse in the Qur'an than this one. The hope is grammatical: the patriarch asks to see, and God does not rebuke the asking — He answers it, supplies the birds, the mountains, the call, and ends the instruction with the knowledge it was meant to produce: *and know that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise*. The conversation partner of Ibn ʿAbbās offered his own candidate for the most hopeful verse — the sūrah of the Throngs' proclamation: *O My servants who have exceeded the limits against their souls! Do not lose hope in Allah's mercy, for Allah certainly forgives all sins* (39:53) — and the tradition keeps both nominations, each marking a different frontier of hope: the forgiveness that exceeds the sin, and the answering that exceeds the question. Between them the verse's own promise is the quieter one — that the heart's need for reassurance is not a defect of faith but one of its appetites, and that God's response to the appetite, in the case of His friend, was not patience but a demonstration.

**Almighty, All-Wise**

The two closing names seal the rite's double character. ʿAzīz — the Almighty — is the power the demonstration displays: the pieces recalled, the dead reassembled, the mountains obeyed by what flies between them; the might is shown not as force but as summons, the omnipotence whose instrument here is a voice calling birds. Ḥakīm — the All-Wise — is the demonstration's design: the four and the mountains and the haste, the choice to answer a how-question with a how-answer, the pedagogy that lets the seeker perform the resurrection he asked about with his own hands and his own call. The pair also answers the verse's opening question by refusing it: *do you not believe?* was not asked because the belief was doubtful but because the wisdom wanted the belief to have a body — a rite, a scene, a memory of birds in haste. Abraham asked to see how God gives life to the dead; he was shown how by being made the one who calls. The verse's final word to its own reader is the same instruction in the same names: the how is knowable, the knowing is given, and what is asked of the knower is the call — and the certainty that follows it, that God is Almighty, All-Wise.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:261

> The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a grain that sprouts into seven ears, each bearing one hundred grains. And Allah multiplies ˹the reward even more˺ to whoever He wills. For Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Resurrection to Agriculture**

The life-and-death sequence closes with birds returning at a call, and the sūrah's great spending-section opens with a seed. The transition is the verse's first lesson: resurrection and charity run on the same divine logic — the small thing given over to the earth's keeping comes back multiplied, and the arithmetic in both cases belongs to God. The parable's form is agricultural through and through: one grain, planted, becomes seven ears, and each ear carries a hundred grains — a seven-hundredfold return stated not as a miracle but as a harvest, the ordinary mystery of the seed performed at its most generous reported yield. The commentators note the parable's precision: it describes what spending *in the cause of Allah* is like, and every element maps — the grain is the deed, small and single; the planting is the giving, which buries the deed where it cannot be retrieved or displayed; the multiplication is God's, who owns the increase the way He owns the rain. The spent dirham, in the verse's picture, is not lost but sown.

**The Multiplication Beyond the Parable**

The seven-hundred is a floor, and the verse says so in its second sentence: *Allah multiplies even more to whoever He wills*. The commentators connect the clause to the Qur'an's wider reward-arithmetic: the sūrah of Light promises that God rewards the best of what they did *and increases them from His bounty*, providing without reckoning (24:38); the sūrah of the Cattle sets the baseline — the good deed rewarded tenfold, the evil deed with one (6:160). Between ten and seven hundred and beyond-reckoning, the parable's field has no fence, and the will named in the clause is the same will that grows the seed: the increase is not a wage computed but a harvest willed. The tradition preserves the Prophet's own statement of the range — God multiplies the son of Adam's good deed tenfold up to seven hundred times, and beyond, except the fast, which is God's own and He rewards it as He wills (in the ḥadīth collections) — and the exception proves the parable's point from the other side: the deed most hidden, most purely between the doer and God, has the one reward no arithmetic is printed for.

**Seven Hundred Camels**

The narrations gathered around this verse include one that translates the parable into the desert's own currency. A man came to the Prophet leading a camel and said: this camel is given in the way of God. The Prophet's answer, Ibn Kathīr records: on the Day of Judgment you will have seven hundred camels. The report does the exegetical work of the parable in a single exchange — the gift of one animal answered by the promise of the parable's exact multiplication — and it fixes the arithmetic's direction: the seven hundred is not a spiritualized metaphor for satisfaction but a real ledger-entry in the currency given. The commentators read the concrete promise alongside the more abstract ones deliberately: the Qur'an's reward-language moves between the garden's rivers and the camel's count because the spenders it addresses hold both kinds of wealth, and the parable of the grain is itself the bridge — a promise stated in seeds that applies to camels, dates, dirhams, and the day's labor alike. Whatever is sown in the cause, the verse's arithmetic runs on it: one becomes seven hundred, and the will of God runs past the number.

**All-Bountiful**

The verse's first closing name is al-Wāsiʿ — rendered here *All-Bountiful*, and the commentators note the word's double register: the Wide, the Encompassing, and the Generous whose giving has width. The name answers the parable's implied question — where does the seven hundred come from, when the seed contains one? — by naming the source's capacity: the increase comes from the One whose bounty is wide enough that a single grain's return does not narrow it. The exegetes connect the name to the multiplication-clause structurally: God multiplies for whoever He wills *because* God is Wāsiʿ — the will to increase is not constrained by scarcity on His side, and the clause's open-endedness (whoever He wills) is the width's grammatical form. The name also answers the giver's secret fear, which every spending-verse in this section will address in turn: that the gift diminishes the giver. The parable's field belongs to the Wide One; what is sown in it is received by a capacity that the sowing cannot deplete.

**All-Knowing**

The second closing name pairs the width with precision: *All-Knowing* — ʿalīm, the name the verse's agricultural image requires, since a harvest is a reckoning. The Knower knows the grain sown — its size, its quality, the hand that released it — and knows what it became: which of the seven hundred belongs to which act of giving, and which giving was for the cause and which was for the eyes of men. The pairing of Wāsiʿ and ʿAlīm is the section's founding statement, and the spending-verses that follow are its unfolding: the reminders that annul charity (2:264), the secret giving that is better than the public (2:271), the recipients who do not beg and are known by their mark (2:273) — every clause presupposes a God who is wide enough to multiply every gift and knowing enough to distinguish every gift's interior. The parable thus ends where the sūrah's whole ethics of spending begins: the deed is buried like a seed, invisible after its planting, and the invisibility is not a loss but the condition of the harvest — the All-Knowing keeps the account the earth keeps the grain.

**The Parable's Place in the Section**

This verse is the section's title, and its position sets the terms for everything that follows. The next verses will legislate the manner of giving — no reminders, no injury, kind words better than wounded charity — and the quality of what is given, from the good things earned and produced; they will rank the secret over the public, name the recipients too dignified to beg, and warn against the rock that yields nothing. All of it elaborates the parable's single claim: spending in the cause is planting, and planting has conditions — the seed must be good grain rather than chaff, the soil must be receptive rather than stone, the sower must not dig the seed back up to show the neighbors where it went. The verse's agriculture is thus the section's ethics in one image: what is sown in sincerity, from the good, and left in the earth of God's knowledge, returns at seven hundred to one — multiplied further for whoever He wills — and the will that multiplies is the will that knows exactly what was planted, by whom, and why.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:262

> Those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah and do not follow their charity with reminders of their generosity or hurtful words—they will get their reward from their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Conditions**

The parable stated the harvest; this verse states the conditions under which the harvest stands, and it states them as a single sentence with two clauses joined. The first clause is the spending itself — *those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah* — the parable's own subject, the grain sown. The second is the negative condition that follows the sowing: *and do not follow their charity with reminders of their generosity or hurtful words*. The two named spoilers — mann, the reminding, and adhā, the injury — are both post-gift phenomena: neither occurs in the giving but after it, in the speech that follows the transfer. The verse's syntax enacts the prohibition: the giving comes first, the following comes second, and the second undoes the first. Al-Rāzī states the mechanism the verse legislates against: exulting in one's generosity, or reminding the needy of their neediness, destroys the virtue in the charitable act — not partially but totally, the way the fiery whirlwind of the coming parable does not prune the garden but consumes it. The deed is completed at the handoff; everything said afterward either leaves it intact or burns it.

**Mann: The Reminder**

The first spoiler is the gift's afterlife in speech: the reminder. Its forms are catalogued by the commentators in the everyday register — the giver who mentions his generosity in company, who brings up the past gift in a present argument, who lets the recipient feel the weight of the favor at every meeting, who tells the poor man's neighbors who fed them. The reminder's operation is economic as well as moral: the gift transferred wealth, and the mann transfers it back — the recipient's dignity becomes the payment, collected installment by installment in every mentioning. What the giver keeps after the reminder is not the virtue of the charity but its receipt, and the receipt is precisely what the parable's planting forbade: the seed dug back up to be shown. The tradition's diagnosis is that mann converts the transaction's direction — the giving was for God's cause, and the reminding reveals it was for the giver's standing; the verse's condition thus tests the first clause, since spending *in the cause of Allah* and spending for the echo of one's own name cannot both describe the same completed act.

**Adhā: The Injury**

The second spoiler is broader and blunter: hurtful words — the rebuke of the asker, the contempt in the handing-over, the sigh that accompanies the gift, the characterization of the recipient in the act of relieving him. Al-Rāzī's commentary pairs it with mann as the two mouths of the same sin: the reminder wounds after the fact, the injury wounds during it. The verse's placement of both under one prohibition has a structural logic the section will confirm — the coming verse will prefer a kind word and forgiveness to a charity followed by injury (2:263), which means the giving without the wound is not the whole standard; the standard is the giving that carries the wound-free word inside it. The commentators connect the injury-prohibition to the recipients the section will later describe — the poor too constrained to beg, known by their mark (2:273): the people the verse protects are precisely those whose asking costs them most, and an adhā delivered to such a person taxes the very restraint that made them worthy of the gift.

**Their Reward With Their Lord**

The promised reward is phrased with a preposition that does the verse's theological work: *they will get their reward from their Lord* — ajruhum ʿinda rabbihim, their wage is *with* their Lord, deposited in a location the verse's two spoilers cannot reach. The commentators draw the contrast implicitly: the reward of the reminding-giver was collected on the spot, in the gratitude and deference of the recipients and the audience — which is why nothing remains with God. The reward of the un-reminding giver was never collected anywhere visible, and therefore stands entire *with* the Lord — the same custody the grain-parable assumed, the seed left in the earth of God's knowledge. The phrase also personalizes the transaction: the reward is not an amount but a relationship — *their* Lord, the رب who is theirs specifically, the guardian-language of the preceding verses (2:257) applied now to the ledger. The giver who refused to cash his gift in human acknowledgment has, the verse promises, exactly one creditor and exactly one payer, and the payment is kept by the One who watched the refusal.

**No Fear, No Grief**

The sentence's final clause is the Qur'an's formula of arrived security: *there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve*. The pair covers the two directions of the heart's disturbance — fear facing the future, grief facing the past — and its recurrence across the sūrah marks it as the language of final states: the believers addressed at the Garden's promise (2:25), the faithful of every revelation who believe and act rightly (2:62), the sūrah's closing portrait of the night-and-day givers (2:274). Applied here, the formula does precise work against the two spoilers: the reminder-giver lives in fear — of the gift forgotten, the gratitude expired, the standing unacknowledged — and the injuring-giver lives in grief's neighborhood, the enmity his words planted. The un-reminding giver is released from both economies: he has no future to fear because his reward is with his Lord, and no past to grieve because nothing he gave has been taken back in speech. The no-fear-no-grief clause is thus not a generic comfort but the spoilers' exact negation — the peace of the person whose generosity has no afterlife in anyone's memory but God's.

**The Verse as the Section's Rule**

Read as legislation, the verse is the spending-section's constitution in one sentence: the deed, its protection, its reward's location, and its reward's effect. The verses that follow are its commentary in both directions — the comparison that ranks the kind word above the wounded gift (2:263), the command that voids the charity of the preening giver and his rock (2:264), the garden that doubles its fruit for the sincere (2:265), the old man's ruined orchard (2:266), the command to give of the good (2:267), the secret giving that acquits sins (2:271). Every one of them elaborates a term this verse states: what following the charity means, what the cause of Allah requires, what with-their-Lord keeps, what the un-fearing and un-grieving do with their wealth. The tradition's summary of the whole is the verse's own shape — giving is easy, the commentaries say in effect, and the difficulty of the section is everything that happens after the hand opens: the words that follow, the audiences that watch, the memory that collects. The verse legislates the hand and the silence together, and promises, for both kept, the reward no reminder can reach and the peace no injury disturbs.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:263

> Kind words and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allah is Self-Sufficient, Most Forbearing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Better Thing**

The verse performs an act of ranking so counterintuitive that its whole function is to reorder the giver's arithmetic: *kind words and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury*. The comparison is not between giving and not-giving — the verse assumes the charity happened, the transfer completed, the need met — but between a completed gift with a wound attached and two things that cost no dirhams at all: the honorable word and the pardoning of what the asker did. Al-Rāzī supplies the scenario the verse legislates: the poor person asks, and the asked cannot or will not give; what is owed then is not the gift but the word — an honorable reply — plus forgiveness for whatever harm the asking carried, whether the asker's manner was rough or the request itself caused embarrassment. The ranking's shock-value is deliberate: a refused request answered with kindness outranks a granted request poisoned by injury, which means the section's true currency was never the amount transferred. The wounded gift is worth less than nothing given gently — less, the verse says, than two words and a pardon.

**The Honorable Word**

Qawl maʿrūf — the word the translation renders *kind*, and the code's own standard-term: maʿrūf, the recognized-good, the same measure that governed the divorced women's treatment (2:229), the nursing provision (2:233), the compensation scaled by capacity (2:236). The honorable word at the door of the un-given is thus not a softer substitute for the gift but the code's regular instrument applied where the gift cannot be: what the community's decent practice recognizes as the right saying to a person in need. The commentators' examples fill the term — the reply that preserves the asker's dignity, the promise of future help if it is honest, the explanation that does not shame, the greeting that treats the asking as no disgrace. The word is *better* than the wounded charity for a reason the verse's ranking makes structural: the maʿrūf-word continues the relationship — the asker may return, the giver may give later — while the injury inside the gift ends it, converting the recipient into a debtor of dignity who will not ask again. The section's economics reappear inverted: the grain sown multiplies (2:261), the gift with adhā burns (2:262), and the honorable word, sown without a gift, outperforms both when the gift was going to carry its wound.

**Forgiveness of the Asking**

The verse's second no-cost gift is directed at a harm the Qur'an quietly assumes: asking can injure the asked. Al-Rāzī names the two forms — the manner of some askers is rough, and some requests embarrass — and commands the pardon: one should be kind and gentle with the poor, and if their asking causes trouble or discomfort, forgive them for it. The legislation is remarkable for what it refuses to do: it does not criminalize the importunate asker, does not rank the deserving from the undeserving, does not make the giver's patience conditional on the recipient's grace. It asks the person with the power in the exchange — the one who has been asked — to absorb the friction the asking generated. The commentators connect this to the section's coming portrait of the truly poor: the ones too constrained to beg, known by their mark, who do not ask importunately (2:273) — the verse here handles the cases where the constraint failed, where need did make the asking rough or persistent, and assigns the roughness to the forgiveness of the asked rather than to the account of the asker. The dignity the silent poor keep by not asking, the asking poor keep by being pardoned.

**Why the Wounded Gift Loses**

The ranking requires the injury-gift to be worth less than the word-without-gift, and the mechanism is the verse's assumed theology of giving. The charity followed by injury has already failed the preceding verse's condition — the reward that stands is with the Lord, and the adhā collects its payment from the recipient instead — so what remains in the verse's comparison is not a rewarded deed versus an unrewarded one but a completed good against a spoiled good and two intact small ones. The spoiled gift also does active damage the honorable word does not: it teaches the poor that asking costs humiliation, and it teaches the giver that giving buys superiority — two lessons that shrink every future exchange between them. The word-and-forgiveness, by contrast, leave both parties whole: the asker unshamed, the asked unburdened, the relationship open. The verse's better is thus a better in total effect, not merely in intention — the arithmetic of a community where gifts can wound and refusals can heal, summed across every door.

**Self-Sufficient**

The first closing name indicts the wounded gift at its root: Ghaniyy — Self-Sufficient, the One who needs nothing from anyone. The giver who injures has made his gift into an instrument of return — acknowledgment, deference, remembered favor — and the verse answers him with the name of the Giver his gift was supposedly for: God is Ghaniyy, beyond every need, which means the gift given for His sake has no collection mechanism at all; its entire return is with Him (2:262). The commentators tie the name to the section's direction of travel: God does not need the charity, and He does not need the honorable word either — both are legislated for the community's fabric, and the Ghaniyy-name frees the giver from the only temptation that produces adhā: the sense that the recipient, or God, owes something back. Al-Rāzī's cascade in the coming verse (2:268) begins from the same point: the soul that gives expecting return gives badly, then gives less, then gives nothing. Ghaniyy is the name that stops the cascade at its first step.

**Most Forbearing**

The second name is the verse's own subject applied to God: Ḥalīm — the Forbearing, the One who does not answer injury with immediate consequence. The pairing with Ghaniyy is the section's signature move — the same pair closed the oaths-verse (2:225) — and here it does a precise work: the Self-Sufficient One has nothing to gain from the gift, and the Forbearing One does not strike the giver who spoiled it. The ḥilm named over the verse covers both parties in the exchange: the rough asker is pardoned because God Himself forbears with far greater offenses, and the injuring giver is not annihilated for his adhā but given the section's remaining verses — the rock and the garden, the secret and the public, the good things to spend — as the road back. The commentators read the name's placement as the verse's final ranking inverted: the kind word and the forgiveness are better than the wounded charity, and both are imitations of the divine conduct named in the closing pair — the Self-Sufficiency that gives without needing return, the Forbearance that absorbs without retaliating. The giver who cannot manage the gift without injury is asked to manage, first, the word — and to learn from the two names why the word, un-costly and un-collected, is where the section's whole ethic begins.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:264

> O believers! Do not waste your charity with reminders ˹of your generosity˺ or hurtful words, like those who donate their wealth just to show off and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. Their example is that of a hard barren rock covered with a thin layer of soil hit by a strong rain— leaving it just a bare stone. Such people are unable to preserve the reward of their charity. Allah does not guide ˹such˺ disbelieving people.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Do Not Annul**

The command's verb is the verse's center: lā tubṭilū — *do not waste*, do not nullify, do not void. The charity is assumed to have happened; the transfer is complete; and the verse legislates over its aftermath with the language of cancellation. The two annulment-instruments are the pair the previous verse named — reminders of generosity and hurtful words — and the verb assigns them their true power: they do not reduce the charity or discount it but void it, the way the sūrah's own war-legislation used the same root of deeds that come to nothing. The annulment-theology is the verse's first instruction: a completed good can be unmade by a following evil, and the unmaking is total rather than proportional. The commentators will read the coming garden-parable (2:266) in exactly these terms — the old man's orchard as the lifetime of good works, the fiery whirlwind as the annulment arriving at the worst possible hour — and this verse is that parable's command-form: what the whirlwind does to the garden, the reminder does to the gift.

**The Show-Off**

The verse then widens from the spoiling believer to the corrupted giver outright: *like those who donate their wealth just to show off and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day*. The riyyāʾ-giver — the spender li-ruʾāʾi'l-nās, to be seen of men — is the section's negative pole, and the verse diagnoses him with two coordinated failures. The first is the substitution of audience: the gift is performed for human eyes, which makes the eyes the paymaster and the seen-ness the wage. The second is the belief-structure that permits it: no faith in God, who would have been the actual recipient, and no faith in the Last Day, which would have been the actual payday.
