The commentators connect the portrait to the sūrah of Small Kindnesses — those who pray and are heedless of their prayer, who act to be seen and refuse even the small courtesies (107:4–7): the same riyyāʾ governing worship there and wealth here. The verse's comparison — *like those* — does a specific work for its believers-addressed audience: the reminder-giver is not the show-off, but he is *like* him, because the reminder reveals the same appetite — the gift completed for God's sake cannot need its echo among people, and the giver who needs the echo has quietly changed his paymaster.

**The Rock and the Rain**

The parable is geological: *a hard barren rock covered with a thin layer of soil hit by a strong rain — leaving it just a bare stone*. The commentators read the image's three elements against the giver it depicts. The ṣafwān — the smooth, hard stone — is the heart on which nothing grows: not evil soil but no soil, the surface that cannot receive a seed. The dust upon it is the deed's appearance: a film that looks, from a distance, like ground — the show-off's charity has the color of generosity and covers nothing. And the downpour is the test: the same rain that doubles the fertile garden's yield (2:265) strips the dust from the stone, and the stripping is not an attack but an exposure — after the rain, the rock is what it always was. The commentators read the downpour variously as the Day of Judgment, as death, as the reckoning's scrutiny; every reading keeps the parable's mechanics: the rain does not create the barrenness but reveals it. The show-off's charity and the reminder-giver's charity are one substance — dust on stone — and the verse's weather is coming for both.

**No Power Over What They Earned**

The sentence after the parable states the loss in the ledger's own terms: *such people are unable to preserve the reward of their charity* — they have no power over anything of what they earned. The verb kāsabū, earned, is the Qur'an's word for the deed-as-acquisition, and the verse's claim is that the acquisition has slipped their hands: what looked like an asset deposited by the gift was never held. The commentators connect the clause to the section's custody-theology from two verses earlier — the un-reminding givers have their reward *with their Lord* (2:262), a deposit in a keeping nothing can reach; the show-offs chose a different custodian, the audience, and the audience's memory is the dust on the rock: present while it is watched, gone at the first real weather. The clause also answers the giver's own arithmetic: the riyyāʾ-giver did earn something — the seen-ness, the praise, the standing — and the verse concedes the earning precisely to void its preservation: everything collected in the world's currency stays in the world's currency, and the Day is a jurisdiction where that currency is not legal. The power they lack is the power to carry anything across.

**No Guidance for Such People**

The verse's final clause is its heaviest: *Allah does not guide disbelieving people*. The non-guidance echoes the king's dumbfoundment two scenes earlier (2:258) — the same withheld guidance, the same ẓulm-shaped cause — and its application here to the giver rather than the arguer extends the verse's diagnosis into the ethics of wealth: the show-off's disbelief is not a doctrinal position but a structure of the heart, the audience-instead-of-God that functions, in the verse's judgment, as kufr whatever the tongue professes. The commentators read the clause against the believers-addressed opening deliberately: the command not to annul was given to believers because the annulment-pattern, followed far enough, is the disbeliever's pattern — the reminder, the injury, the performance, the dust-deep faith that survives no weather. Guidance is named at the verse's end as the thing at stake in the section's smallest transactions: how a gift is closed, what is said at the door, who the giver imagines watching — these are not manners but orientation, and the orientation is either toward the One who sees in secret or toward the eyes the rain will wash away.

**The Parable-Pair**

This verse and the next form a matched diptych the commentators treat as one teaching in two images: the same rain falls on both grounds. The downpour that strips the rock doubles the garden's fruit; the identical weather of trial, reckoning, and time produces, on the two substances, exposure or multiplication — which locates the entire difference in what was there before the rain. The section's legislation between the parables (the honorable word, the forgiveness, the secret giving, the good grain) is the agriculture of the heart's soil: the practices that deepen it. And the diptych's addressees are not two populations but one: the believer commanded not to annul his charity carries, in every gift, a little dust and a little ground, and the verse's warning is that the rain will report the ratio. The show-off is held up not as another kind of person but as the same person fully dust — the giver whose every act was surface — and the bare stone is what the section asks every reader to check his own ground against, before the weather does.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:265

> And the example of those who donate their wealth, seeking Allah's pleasure and believing the reward is certain, is that of a garden on a fertile hill: when heavy rain falls, it yields up twice its normal produce. If no heavy rain falls, a drizzle is sufficient. And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Garden on the Height**

The diptych's second panel reverses the first in every element: where the rock was flat, hard, and shallow, the garden sits on a rabwah — an elevation, a fertile height. The commentators work the topography carefully, because the hill is not decoration but argument. Al-Qurṭubī records the agronomy behind it: certain slightly raised grounds collect rich soil and flourish, and — crucially — a garden on a height has no stream running through it, so it depends entirely on the sky: nothing waters it but rain. Al-Rāzī presses the point into a difficulty and a resolution: a hilltop garden is exposed to wind and beyond the reach of irrigation, while a garden in a hollow drowns; he prefers to read rabwah from its root — to rise, to grow — as the fertile ground whose crops rise, and argues the best garden stands on level earth. The readings converge on the image's function: the sincere giver's heart is ground that cannot be watered by the world — no stream of audience-approval reaches it — and depends, for every drop of its fruitfulness, on what falls from above.

**The Two Motives**

The verse names what the garden's owners spend for, in two clauses: *seeking Allah's pleasure and believing the reward is certain*. The commentators read the second clause — the translation's *believing the reward is certain*, literally a confirmation in their souls — in three directions, each recorded: the givers act from confirmed faith, the certainty of īmān itself (Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī); they act from confirmation of God's truth, the ṣidq that answers the show-off's lie (al-Zamakhsharī); or they confirm their charity's placement — taking care where they put it, checking that it lands and is used properly (al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī). The three readings describe one disposition from three sides: the heart settled about God, settled about the promise, and settled enough to be careful with the deed. Pleasure-seeking — ibtilāgh riḍwān Allāh — is the first clause's content, and it is the show-off's motive inverted: the riyyāʾ-giver's pleasure-sought is human and immediate; this giver's is divine and deferred, which is why the second clause matters — only certainty about the unseen reward makes an unseen audience sufficient. The verse's psychology is exact: nobody spends against a merely probable return; the garden grows on the soil of yaqīn.

**The Rain's Double Arithmetic**

The parable's weather completes the diptych: *when heavy rain falls, it yields up twice its normal produce. If no heavy rain falls, a drizzle is sufficient.* The same downpour that stripped the rock to bare stone doubles the garden — and the verse adds the economy's second clause: even the light rain, the ṭall, the drizzle and dew, does the garden's work when the heavy water is withheld. The commentators draw the full accounting. The garden's yield does not depend on the rain's amount but on the ground's quality: abundant grace produces abundance, and scarce grace still produces — the sincere deed multiplies in seasons of trial and survives in seasons of drought. The image answers the giver's two fears at once: that his small gift will not matter (the drizzle suffices) and that his circumstances will not permit the great one (the doubling waits on the soil, not the season). Read against the rock, the arithmetic becomes the section's whole theology of intention: identical weather, opposite outcomes, because the difference between dust-on-stone and garden-on-height was settled before the first drop fell — at the moment the giver chose his audience and confirmed his certainty.

**The Date That Becomes a Mountain**

The tradition's most transmitted comment on this verse's multiplication is the Prophet's own image. He said, in the report carried by both Ṣaḥīḥs: whoever gives in charity the equivalent of a date, from lawfully earned wealth — and God accepts only the lawful — God accepts it with His right hand and nurtures it for its giver as one of you nurtures a foal, until it becomes like a mountain. The ḥadīth is the grain-parable (2:261) and the garden-parable in one scene: the smallest possible gift, a single date, and the largest possible increase, the mountain — with the mechanism named as tending. God's handling of the sincere deed is the breeder's handling of the young animal: patient, daily, growth-oriented, the increase invisible at any single observation and undeniable across the season. The verse's twofold yield and drizzle-sufficiency are this nurture's agricultural form; the ḥadīth is its zoological form; and both fix the same two conditions — the date must be lawfully earned (the coming verse's good-things legislation), and the nurturing is God's own act, which is why no season's drought and no audience's indifference can interrupt it.

**Seeking the Pleasure**

The first motive-clause deserves its own weight, because riḍwān — God's pleasure — is the Qur'an's name for the destination beyond reward. The sūrah of Man's portrait of the righteous gives the motive its purest formulation: *We feed you only for the sake of Allah, seeking neither reward nor thanks from you* (76:9) — the givers who refuse both currencies the show-off collects. This verse's formulation is deliberately below that summit and above the rock: seeking God's pleasure *and* believing the reward is certain — the pleasure sought and the reward expected, neither excluded. The commentators do not force the two apart: the reward-certainty is what keeps the pleasure-seeking honest, since a giver who doubts the promise will inevitably start collecting visible returns. The Face-of-God idiom the coming verses will use (2:272) is the same orientation — the giving whose direction is God, whose confirmation is internal, and whose weather comes entirely from the sky. Between the mountain-nurtured date and the 76:9 summit, the verse locates the sincere giver's ordinary state: not the purity that refuses reward but the certainty that makes reward's deferral bearable.

**All-Seeing of What You Do**

The closing name is the section's recurring seal — the same All-Seeing that ended the nursing legislation (2:233) and the half-dowry ruling (2:237) — and its placement here is the diptych's final stroke. The rock and the garden are distinguished by what rain reveals; the givers they depict are distinguished by what only the Seer witnesses: the pleasure sought or the audience courted, the certainty confirmed or the return calculated. The verse's parable runs entirely on surfaces — soil, dust, water, fruit — and its closing name withdraws every surface from the record: the seeing that governs the yield is the seeing of interiors, and the doubling or the stripping is its verdict made agricultural. For the giver the name is the section's comfort and its demand at once: the drizzle-season gift nobody noticed is seen, and the mountain it is becoming is seen too; the dust-film on the stone that fooled the neighbors was never deceiving the Seer. The garden on the height, watered only by sky, watched only by God — the verse leaves its reader standing in it, holding a date, deciding what the ground is.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:266

> Would any of you wish to have a garden with palm trees, grapevines, and all kinds of fruits with rivers flowing underneath and as they grow very old with dependent children, a fiery whirlwind hits the garden, burning it all up? This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so perhaps you will reflect.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question Nobody Would Answer Yes**

The verse takes the form of a question addressed to each hearer individually — *would any of you wish* — and the question's construction makes the answer impossible: no one wishes the described catastrophe, which means every hearer must imagine it as loss rather than choice. The garden described is the parable's maximum: date-palms and grapevines — the two capitals of Arabian wealth — with every kind of fruit, and rivers running beneath it, the water-supply the hilltop garden of the previous verse lacked. The image is the sūrah's own paradise-vocabulary deployed on earth: the Garden promised the believers is gardens under which rivers flow (2:25), and this garden has exactly that structure — which is why its destruction lands as sacrilege and not merely as misfortune. The commentators note the deliberate escalation across the section's parables: the dust on rock (2:264), the rain-fed garden on the height (2:265), and now the fully watered, fully stocked orchard at full maturity — the best possible case, positioned to receive the worst possible weather.

**The Hour of the Whirlwind**

The catastrophe's timing is the verse's real subject, and it is tripled. The owner is old — the garden's labor behind him, its fruit his remaining provision; he has weak progeny, the commentators glossing dhurriyyah ḍuʿafāʾ as young or helpless children and grandchildren who cannot work the land or replace it; and into this configuration comes the whirlwind — iḥṣār, the simoom-like wind — carrying fire, and the garden burns. Al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī both fix the point: the same garden destroyed in youth would be a setback and in childlessness a private grief, but destroyed at the end of a life, with dependents who have nothing else, it is total — the past's labor, the present's provision, and the future's inheritance consumed in one hour. The verse's rhetorical question works because the hearer automatically performs the arithmetic the owner can no longer redo: at that age, with those children, there is no replanting. The whirlwind does not subtract from the man's life; it annuls it — and annulment is precisely the section's governing verb, the lā tubṭilū the two preceding verses commanded against.

**The Giver's Reading**

The first interpretation the commentators give is the section's own: the parable depicts the giver who follows his charity with reminders and injury (2:264). The mapping is element by element — the garden is his lifetime of charitable deeds, the fruits are the rewards accumulating with the years, the fiery whirlwind is his boasting and his hurtful words arriving at the end of his life, and the weak progeny are the absence of any remaining good work that could intercede or rebuild for him. On the Day, in this reading, the man arrives with the record of a garden that burned: the annulment the verse commanded against has done to his charity exactly what the whirlwind does to the orchard — not at the moment of the reminder but at the moment of the reckoning, when the loss is discovered to have been total and the season for replanting is over. The reading gives the preceding diptych its third panel: the rock shows the gift that never grew, the hill-garden the gift that doubles, and the burnt orchard the gift that grew for decades and was killed in an hour — the worst of the three fates, because it wears the longest history.

**Ibn ʿAbbās's Reading**

The second interpretation, attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās and recorded by al-Qurṭubī, widens the parable beyond charity: it depicts the one who performed good works through a life and then turned to evil works at the end, the later wickedness wiping out the value of the earlier good. On this reading the garden is not one category of deed but a whole record — prayers, fasts, charities, patience — and the whirlwind is the closing apostasy or the final crimes, and the weak progeny are the deeds' inability, once annulled, to testify or to help. The two readings are not rivals but scopes: the giver-reading is the section's local application, and the Ibn-ʿAbbās reading is the general law the local case instantiates — the annulment-principle running on every accumulated good, of which the spoiling of charity is one instance. The sūrah of Hūd states the principle's positive mirror — *good deeds wipe out evil deeds* (11:114) — and the parable exists because the reverse direction operates too: the fire, like the water, does its work completely, and the verse's old man is the portrait of a record where the last hour outranked every preceding season.

**The Reflective Refrain**

The verse closes with the formula the family-code's seal used two dozen verses earlier: *This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so perhaps you will reflect* — the kadhālika-yubayyinu refrain with the reflection-verb, the pairing the wine-and-gambling legislation closed with (2:219) and the code's seal varied to understanding (2:242). The verb choice fits the parable: reflection — tafakkur — is the work the question-form demands, the hearer's slow imagining of the garden, the age, the children, the wind. The commentators note the refrain's function at parables throughout: at 2:266 it stands after a picture with no explicit application, leaving the mapping to the reflection commanded — the verse does not say the garden is your charity record; it asks whether you would wish it, and lets the wish expose what you already know the garden to be. The clarity named in the refrain is thus not the clarity of a labeled diagram but of a question that cannot be answered dishonestly: the signs are made clear precisely when the hearer can no longer pretend the parable is about someone else.

**Why the Section Needs the Fire**

The spending-section has now run its full rhetorical arc, and the burnt garden is its keystone. The parable of the grain promised multiplication (2:261); the conditions protected the deed from its aftermath (2:262–263); the rock exposed the deed that was never a deed (2:264); the hill-garden showed the weather of grace (2:265). What the arc lacked was the tragedy of time — the case where the deed was real, the growth was genuine, and the ruin came anyway, from inside the giver's own later conduct. The verse supplies it, and its supplied case is the one every long-term giver secretly fears: not the barren start but the late collapse, the record burnt on the eve of its presentation. The old man's helplessness — no strength to replant, no children strong enough to do it for him — is the eschatological moment's exact portrait, since the Day is when every account closes and no amendment remains possible. The reflection the refrain commands is therefore practical and immediate: the fire in the parable is lit by reminders, injuries, and late turnings — all three of which are choices still available to refuse, in the season where refusal still does something.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:267

> O believers! Donate from the best of what you have earned and of what We have produced for you from the earth. Do not pick out worthless things for donation, which you yourselves would only accept with closed eyes. And know that Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Sources of Wealth**

The verse legislates the material of giving, and its first clause catalogues the community's wealth in two streams: *from the best of what you have earned and of what We have produced for you from the earth*. The earned — mā kasabtum — is the wealth of acquisition: trade, labor, wages, the commercial economy of Medina's market. The produced-from-the-earth is the wealth of harvest: dates, grain, fruit, the agricultural economy the section's parables have been running on. The division is exhaustive for the verse's audience and deliberate in its grammar: the earned is attributed to the earners, and the earth's produce to God — *what We have produced for you* — a small asymmetry that quietly reassigns ownership at the moment the command to give is stated. The commentators read the pairing with the quality-command that governs both: the ṭayyibāt, the good things, are required from each stream alike — the merchant's best lawful profit and the farmer's best date-cluster, one standard across two economies. The verse's spending is thus not a levy on one class of wealth but a rule about quality at every source.

**What Ṭayyib Means**

The good things the verse commands are glossed by the commentators in three registers, and the three together define the standard. The wholesome-and-desirable: what the giver himself counts as good, the choice item rather than the stock. The acceptable: what one would not reject if it were offered — the verse's own second clause makes this the operative test. The lawful: the ḥalāl as against the forbidden, since wealth unlawfully acquired cannot be made good by being given away. The third register carries the tradition's harshest statements: the ḥadīth the exegetes cite here declares that God does not accept charity from unlawfully earned wealth — the servant who amasses wealth by forbidden means and donates it earns nothing by the donation, and the wealth's destination is unchanged; God, in the same report, erases evil with good but does not erase evil with evil. The three glosses interlock into the verse's ethics of the gift: the ṭayyib is simultaneously what the giver values, what the recipient would accept, and what the Law permits — and a donation failing any of the three fails the command, however large the amount.

**The Closed-Eyes Test**

The verse's sharpest instrument is its mirror: *do not pick out worthless things for donation, which you yourselves would only accept with closed eyes*. The ḥadīth-glosses state the principle bluntly — do not feed people what you would not eat yourselves — and the verse builds the test into the act of receiving: the khabīth-thing the giver selects is defined by the imagination of reversal, what the giver would take only with the eyes shut, in distaste, counting the transaction a loss survived. Al-Rāzī supplies the psychology behind the selection: the ideal is giving from the best, and the soul that begins by wanting to part only with the dregs is already on the slope the next verse will describe — the dreg-keeping that becomes the gift-withholding that becomes the giving-up. The closed-eyes test catches the slope at its first step, in the moment of choosing which item leaves the house: the verse does not ask the giver to feel generous but to perform a thought-experiment — would I accept this? — and to let the answer set the minimum. The Prophetic standard behind the test is the ḥadīth of the two Ṣaḥīḥs: no servant believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself — the love-of-self here functioning not as the ego's voice but as the measuring-rod the verse hands the ego.

**The Mosque's Date-Clusters**

Ibn Kathīr records the occasion that gave the verse its social photograph. A group of the Companions brought date-clusters from their palms and hung them in the Prophet's Mosque, on cords or poles, for the poorest of the community — the people of the veranda and the like — to eat from. It was an institution of open charity: the gift displayed where need walked daily. Then others, wishing to join the practice, brought inferior dates — clusters nobody would have chosen — and hung them with the good; and this verse was revealed, its closed-eyes test aimed exactly at the hung bunch. The occasion fixes three things about the legislation: the standard applies to voluntary public charity, not merely to zakāt's assessed dues; the comparison is social — the inferior gift hung beside the good one is a statement about the giver's estimation of the poor; and the mosque-wall is the verse's real setting, the place where the community reads each other's giving. The narrations preserve the rebuke's edge: the poor were to receive what the givers would have hung in their own homes for their own guests — and the verse makes the guest-standard the law.

**Piety's Price**

The verse's command has its summit-statement elsewhere in the Qur'an, and the commentators quote it here as the standard this verse legislates below: *You will never achieve righteousness until you donate some of what you cherish* (3:92). The relation between the two verses is the relation between the floor and the height — the Baqarah verse forbids the worthless and commands the good; the ʿImrān verse names the righteousness that begins where the cherished is released. The tradition preserves the Companions' response to that summit in the reports around its revelation — Abū Ṭalḥah's immediate gift of his most beloved property, his garden of Bayrūḥāʾ, upon hearing it — and the verse here builds the road to such responses by closing the opposite road: the soul that habituates itself to selecting the closed-eyes item trains its capacity for the cherished-release downward. The exegetes' moral-psychology of the section depends on this training-logic: giving is a faculty strengthened or atrophied by what it is repeatedly given, and the worthless-selection is the atrophy's daily exercise. The command of the good is therefore not fastidiousness about the poor's receipt — they would eat the inferior dates — but curriculum for the giver's soul.

**Self-Sufficient, Praised**

The closing names answer the verse's whole demand with the demand's own paradox: God commands the best and needs none of it. Ghaniyy — Self-Sufficient — states the needlessness: the ṭayyib-command enriches nothing divine, and the giver who calculates that God requires his good dates has misread the name. Ḥamīd — the Praised, the Praiseworthy — states where the giving's praise terminates: not in the giver's reputation (the rock's dust, 2:264), not in the recipient's gratitude (the reminder's collection, 2:262), but in the One whose praise is self-subsistent and who alone returns the gift's worth. The pair governs the quality-standard precisely: because God is Ghaniyy, the standard cannot be about His need — so it must be about the giver's formation and the recipient's honor; because God is Ḥamīd, the best is given where the giving is truly credited, and the closed-eyes item is not merely insufficient but misdirected — the worthlessness offered where all praise converges. The verse ends, as the section's verses keep ending, with a name-pair that restates its command as theology: give the good, because the Receiver of every gift is beyond every need of it and the only One whose praise makes a gift worth making.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:268

> The Devil threatens you with ˹the prospect of˺ poverty and bids you to the shameful deed ˹of stinginess˺, while Allah promises you forgiveness and ˹great˺ bounties from Him. And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing.

**Expanded Commentary**

**Two Voices at the Purse**

The verse stages the giver's interior as a contest of rhetorics, and the staging is symmetrical to the point of architecture. Satan *threatens* — yuʿidukum, promises-in-the-mode-of-menace — with poverty; God *promises* — yaʿidukum — forgiveness and bounty. The same verb-form serves both speakers, and the verse's genius is the reversal it exposes: the threat comes from the one who has nothing to give, and the promise comes from the One who owns the treasuries. The commentators' reading of the mechanism is precise: Satan makes the soul dread want, and the dread produces the withholding; God sets before the soul the remembrance of forgiveness and of generosity, and the remembrance produces the open hand. Ibn Kathīr states the verse's whole function in the section: it explains, at the interior level, the behavior the preceding verses legislated against — the dreg-selection of 2:267, the dust-film of 2:264, the reminders of 2:262 — all of which are the poverty-threat's downstream products. The section's ethics of giving had reached the point where external command was not enough; this verse opens the room where the commands are obeyed or sabotaged.

**The Threat of Poverty**

Al-Rāzī's analysis of the threat is the tradition's fullest map of the miser's descent, and it runs as a cascade. It begins with a distortion of the standard: ideally the person gives from the best of what he has, but the soul under the first touch of the threat wants to part only with the dregs — the closed-eyes item of the previous verse. From dreg-giving the descent continues: the fear of losing anything at all grows, and the giving stops — the charity is withheld entirely. Then the miserliness infects the rest of the soul, which arranges itself around keeping: holding what it desires, releasing nothing of value, the retention becoming the self's organizing principle. The final stage is the inversion of agency — passivity toward Satan's whispering becomes activity in sinning, the soul that stopped giving starts taking, until it ceases doing good at all and commits every manner of evil. The cascade's first step is the verse's whole warning: the poverty-threat does not arrive as a command to evil but as a piece of apparently prudent arithmetic — keep this, for the future is uncertain — and the arithmetic, obeyed repeatedly, becomes the character the last verse described as disbelieving dust on stone.

**The Shameful Deed**

The threat's second product is named in the verse's own translation-gloss: Satan *bids you to the shameful deed — of stinginess*. Faḥshāʾ is the Qur'an's word for the indecency, the excess that decency cannot look at — the word used for sexual transgression and for everything the moral sense finds grotesque. Its application here to miserliness is the verse's most radical naming, and the commentators hold it deliberately: the stinginess is not a weakness or a preference but an indecency, the soul's exposure of what should stay covered — the appetite that keeps while another's need stands at the door. The pairing with the poverty-threat defines the two movements of the same hand: the threat works on the future (you will want, later), and the faḥshāʾ names the present act (you are keeping, now) — fear as the motive, indecency as the deed. The tradition's moral vocabulary rarely escalates avarice this high, and the escalation is the section's doing: after the parables of the rock, the garden, and the burnt orchard, the verse can name the withholding what the parables showed it to be — the fire's fuel, the dust's source, the closed-eyes selection's engine.

**The Whisper and Its Counterpart**

The ḥadīth the exegetes cite at this verse gives the contest its interior acoustics. Satan has an instigation in the son of Adam, the Prophet said, and the angel has an instigation: as for Satan's, it is the promise of evil and the calling of the truth a lie; as for the angel's, it is the promise of good and the confirmation of the truth. Whoever finds the second in himself, let him know it is from God and let him praise God; and whoever finds the first, let him take refuge from Satan. The report supplies the verse's missing epistemology: the two voices are not equally audible, and the tradition gives their discrimination a test — the direction of the promise. The voice that promises good and confirms truth is the angel's register; the voice that promises evil (the poverty to come) while falsifying truth (the provision that is God's, the reward that is certain) is the satanic one. The verse's structure is now legible as the test applied: Satan threatens with a lie about the future and commands an indecency in the present; God promises the two truths — the forgiveness that covers the past and the bounty that answers the feared future — and the hearer's task is the ḥadīth's: recognize the register, praise or take refuge.

**Forgiveness and Bounty**

God's two promises are matched to the threat's two wounds. The poverty-threat wounds the future — you will lack — and bounty, faḍl, answers it: the provision's source is wider than the keeping can ever be, and the verse's own section has been parabling the width (the seven-hundredfold grain, the doubled garden, the mountain-nurtured date). The second wound is subtler and the commentators draw it from the section's context: the soul considering its giving-history — the dregs selected, the reminders spoken, the closed-eyes gifts — is wounded by its own record, and a promise of bounty alone would not answer the shame that keeps the hand shut. Forgiveness answers it: the past's spoiled giving is covered, and the hand may open without first solving its history. The two promises together are the verse's therapy of generosity — the future secured and the past absolved — and their pairing explains why the poverty-threat wins so often: it offers the miser a false solution to both wounds at once, keeping as security and keeping as erasure, and the verse exposes the double fraud.

**All-Bountiful, All-Knowing**

The closing pair repeats the grain-parable's names (2:261) and completes the verse's argument with them. Wāsiʿ — the Wide, the Bountiful — is the refutation of the poverty-threat in the form of a name: the One promising bounty is the One whose width the threat denies, and the verse asks its hearer to weigh a whisper against a name. ʿAlīm — the All-Knowing — governs the contest's hidden arena: which voice the heart is currently answering, whether the hand at the purse is moved by dread or by promise, whether the faḥshāʾ of keeping is being rehearsed in calculation nobody sees. The pairing also answers the ḥadīth's discrimination-test at its root: the human being cannot always tell the registers apart in himself — the prudent thought and the whisper sound alike from inside — and the All-Knowing is the verse's assurance that the ambiguity is not final: the Knower hears both voices and knows which one the soul is obeying. The section's spending-legislation thus stands between the two names it keeps returning to: the Wide, whose bounty outruns every threat of want, and the Knowing, whose audit makes the interior contest a matter of record — and the verse leaves the hand where the contest began, free to close or open, with the threat named, the promise stated, and both speakers identified.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:269

> Allah grants wisdom to whoever He wills. And whoever is granted wisdom is certainly blessed with a great privilege. But none will be mindful ˹of this˺ except people of reason.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Gift and Its Grammar**

The verse's opening clause is a sentence about giving that gives nothing to command: *Allah grants wisdom to whoever He wills*. The grammar is the sūrah's sovereignty-formula — the same structure as the kingship granted to whomever He wills (2:247) and the verses' distribution in the sūrah of ʿImrān — and its application here to ḥikmah makes wisdom a bestowal rather than an achievement. The commentators note what the formula excludes: wisdom is not accumulated by study alone, not purchased, not inherited by lineage, and not distributed by merit visible to men; it is given, and the giving follows the will. The verse's placement inside the spending-section is its first puzzle and its first lesson: between the contest of the two voices (2:268) and the audit of gifts and vows (2:270), the section pauses to name the faculty that reads both — the wisdom without which the threats and promises, the dregs and the good things, the parables of rock and garden, remain information rather than direction. The ḥikmah granted is the section's operating system, and the verse states its origin so that no reader mistakes it for his own.

**What the Wisdom Is**

The tradition's glosses on the verse's ḥikmah are a catalogue, and al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī preserve the range without collapsing it. The exegetical reading: knowledge of the Qur'an's meanings — its abrogating and abrogated, its ambiguous and determinate verses (the ʿImrān distinction at 3:7), its order of revelation, its licit and forbidden. The ethical reading: the fear of God, per the transmitted maxim that the beginning of wisdom is the fear of God. The cognitive readings: intelligence — ʿaql — and comprehension — fahm — the faculties the verse's own closing will name. The theological reading: some see in the verse an allusion to the power of rational demonstration, the wisdom that proves. And the disputed reading: prophethood itself — nubuwwah — which some commentators assign and others contest. The plurality is not indecision but the verse's method: ḥikmah is named as a genus whose species run from jurisprudence to fear to logic to revelation, and the common element the readings share is direction — knowledge that governs conduct. Al-Rāzī states the synthesis: wisdom as knowledge differs from right action, but wisdom proper is the combination — the understanding and the acting founded on it — which is why the verse's gift is called, in its second clause, much good rather than much information.

**Much Good**

*Whoever is granted wisdom is certainly blessed with a great privilege* — khayr kathīr, a good that is much, or much that is good, the Arabic holding both. The commentators weigh the clause against the section's arithmetic deliberately: the grain returns seven hundredfold, the garden doubles, the date becomes a mountain — and the verse assigns to wisdom a multiplication of a different kind, the good whose quantity is its quality. The ḥadīth the exegetes cite here is the tradition's famous permission of envy — there is no envy except in two cases: the man given wealth who spends it down in the way of truth, and the man given wisdom who judges by it and teaches it (in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī). The two cases are the section's two currencies — the spent wealth and the exercised wisdom — and the envy permitted for each measures its worth: these are the only possessions whose abundance in another's hands a person may rightfully ache for. The wisdom-case is doubled in the ḥadīth's own verbs: judged by and taught — the ḥikmah that governs its holder and the ḥikmah that governs through him, the private direction and the public teaching. The verse's much-good is thus the section's hidden premise: every ruling about giving — the quality, the silence, the secrecy, the recipients — is wisdom applied to wealth, and the applying is the gift.

**The Nourishment Reading**

Al-Rāzī adds the verse's psychological placement, connecting it to the verse before: the spirit or the intellect takes its nourishment from wisdom, while the ego's desires are fed by the indecencies the previous verse named. The two foods define the two souls of the section — the giver whose hand is opened by promise and the keeper whose hand is closed by threat — and the wisdom-verse states what the contest is actually over: not the dirham but the soul's diet. The reading gives the verse's grant its developmental logic: wisdom nourishes the faculty that recognizes the angel's register, that performs the closed-eyes test honestly, that hears the burnt-garden parable as self-description. Without it the section's commands are heard as restrictions; with it they are recognized as the appetite's proper objects. The commentators connect this nourishment-theme to the wider Qur'anic usage — wisdom as what settles the heart (the 13:28 comfort-language the tradition reads alongside) and as what the prophets were given in childhood (the sūrah of Maryam's Yahyā, granted ḥukm as a boy, 19:12) — a range that fixes the gift as simultaneously cognitive and constitutive: wisdom changes what the soul is hungry for, which is why its grant is called much good and why its absence makes every other gift dangerous.

**People of Reason**

The verse's closing clause restricts its own reception: *none will be mindful except people of reason* — ulū al-albāb, the possessors of the lubb, the intellect at its kernel rather than its surface. The term is the sūrah's own: the law of retaliation was addressed to the same people (2:179) — there is life for you in the retaliation, O people of reason — and in both places the naming does the same work: the legislation or the bestowal is stated openly, and its reception is assigned to the faculty that goes beneath the statement. Al-Rāzī and the tradition gloss lubb as the intellect purified of the desires' interference — the mind operating where the two voices of the previous verse have been discriminated — which makes the clause recursive in the section's exact sense: wisdom is granted to whom God wills; only the people of reason notice the grant; and the reason that notices is itself among wisdom's first fruits. The verse thus closes on the humility its opening commanded: the reader who recognizes wisdom in the section's rulings — who hears the closed-eyes test as protection rather than fastidiousness, the two voices as acoustics rather than mythology — is recognizing the gift he has been given, and the recognition is the mindfulness the clause names.

**The Verse Between Its Neighbors**

Structurally the verse is the section's hinge between the interior and the ledger. Behind it, the spending-legislation has run from the parables to the purse's private contest; ahead, the audit resumes — the gifts and vows known to God (2:270), the secret and the open ranked (2:271), the guidance-decoupling of the giving (2:272), the silent poor described (2:273). The wisdom-verse stands at the pivot and supplies both halves with their faculty: the interior contest requires the wisdom that discriminates voices, and the ledger requires the wisdom that remembers it is watched. The commentators' observation about the verse's sovereignty-grammar completes the placement: the grant being God's will, the section's demands are never addressed to the un-equipped — the giver commanded to select the good, to speak kindly, to give secretly, to recognize the dignified poor, is assumed to have been given, or to be being given, the ḥikmah the commands run on. The verse is thus the section's grace-clause in the literal sense: the statement that the faculty for all this giving is itself a gift — much good, granted by will, noticed by the reasonable, and exercised, once noticed, in exactly the transactions the surrounding verses legislate.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:270

> Whatever charities you give or vows you make are surely known to Allah. And the wrongdoers will have no helpers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Instruments Named**

The verse names two of the believer's transactions with God and places both under one knowledge: *whatever charities you give or vows you make*. The nafaqah is the section's standing subject — the spending legislated from the grain-parable onward, given freely in response to need. The nadhr, the vow, is its sibling instrument and appears here for the first time in the section: the binding promise by which a person obligates himself to an act of worship or charity he was not otherwise obligated to perform — the vow of the fast, the pilgrimage, the specified alms, classically conditioned on a hoped-for event: if God restores the sick child, such-and-such is owed. The two instruments cover the field of voluntary giving in both directions of initiative: the nafaqah begins in the moment's need and the giver's freedom; the nadhr begins in a prior speech and binds the future moment. The verse's pairing is jurisprudence compressed — whatever moves through either channel, in whatever amount, under whatever condition — is known; and the knowing is the section's recurring answer to the invisibility of most giving.

**Known Means Accounted**

The commentators give the verse's knowledge-clause its two operative meanings. Al-Ṭabarī: God knows it means He keeps the account of it — the record-entry that guarantees the reward no audience witnessed and no recipient can reciprocate. Al-Rāzī: the knowledge extends to the intention behind the act, great or small — the audit reaching past the amount to the interior the whole section has been legislating. The two readings are the two halves of the section's custody-theology: the reward of the un-reminding givers stands *with their Lord* (2:262) because the Lord's knowledge is the account itself, and the annulment of the reminder-givers is total (2:264) because the same knowledge recorded the spoiling speech. The vow receives the same treatment at its own pressure-point: the nadhr is speech about future action, performed before God as witness, and the verse's knowledge-clause is its enforcement mechanism — the promiser who forgets, minimizes, or quietly abandons his vow meets here the fact that the promise was heard where it was made. The jurists' subsequent legislation of vow-fulfillment — the conditions of validity, the obligation of performance, the expiations of failure — all presuppose the verse's clause: a vow is a real transaction because its recipient really knows it.

**The Vow's Theology**

The nadhr's place in the tradition is more delicate than its mention here suggests, and the verse's neutral-to-positive registration is worth marking. The prophetic reports about vows run in two directions: the ḥadīth collections carry the prohibition of the conditional bargain-vow — the vow does not bring about anything not already decreed, and it extracts from the miser what the miser's generosity would not — alongside the Qur'anic praise of vow-fulfillment, the sūrah of Man's righteous who fulfill their vows (76:7) and the Day whose evil is spreading. The verse here belongs to the second register: the vow is known to Allah — recorded, accounted, and in the section's logic, another form of the giving whose custody is divine. The commentators' synthesis reads the two registers as governing two different hearts: the vow that attempts to purchase a decree is the miser's instrument and avails nothing; the vow that binds the self to gratitude — Maryam's mother dedicating what is in her womb, the recovered sickbed's promised fast — is the speech of a heart already given, and its fulfillment is among the acts this verse assures are known. Between the two stands the verse's single clause, declining to sort the hearts because the Knower sorts them.

**The Wrongdoers and Their Helpers**

The verse's second sentence turns from the instruments to the persons who fail them: *the wrongdoers will have no helpers*. The commentators identify the ẓālimūn here with precision — al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī reading them as those who give for hypocritical reasons, the 2:264 figures whose charity was dust on stone — and extend the identification to the vow's own failure-modes: the promiser who does not perform, the giver who annuls, the person whose transactions with God were performed for witnesses other than God. The helperlessness is the Day's, and it is the section's eschatology stated in its social form: the wrongdoer's helpers — the audience whose approval he bought, the recipients whose gratitude he collected, the patrons whose causes his gifts advertised — are all persons whose help operates inside the world's three currencies, and the Day refuses all three (2:254): no bargaining, no friendship, no intercession. The clause thus gathers the section's warnings into one image of abandonment: the giver who spent for the eyes of men arrives where the men cannot see, and the vow-breaker who promised before God arrives before the God he promised — with the record the verse's first clause kept, and without a single helper the second clause declines to imagine.

**The Verse as the Section's Ledger-Line**

Short, austere, and positioned at the section's center of gravity, this verse functions as the ledger-line the surrounding parables and rankings write into. It comes immediately after the wisdom-verse — the gift that reads the transactions — and immediately before the ranking of secret over public giving: the knowledge-clause here is what makes the secrecy-ranking of the next verse possible, since a charity hidden from every creature is fully visible where the account is kept, and a charity displayed is fully discounted to what its display collected. The vow-mention extends the section beyond gift-economics into promise-economics, and the helperlessness-clause extends its eschatology from the burnt garden's owner to everyone whose dealings with God were mediated by other eyes. Read in the tradition's own terms, the verse is the section's statement of God's bookkeeping: every nafaqah entered, every nadhr registered, every intention inspected, every wrongdoer's file closed without endorsement. The two sentences leave nothing to negotiate — the instruments are known, the helpers are absent — and between them the verse hands the reader the only position the section ever offered: give as one whose gift is read by its Recipient, promise as one whose promise is held by its Witness, and let the helpers go, since the Day they would have helped in has already refused them.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:271

> To give charity publicly is good, but to give to the poor privately is better for you, and will absolve you of your sins. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Ranking**

The verse legislates the visibility of giving, and its structure is a ranked permission rather than a command: disclosure is good — ḥasan, affirmed, rewarded — and concealment given to the poor is better, and carries an absolution the public gift is not promised. The ranking does not denigrate the open hand; the commentators are explicit that public charity remains a genuine good, and the verse's better operates inside a scale whose lower rung is already approved. The two further conditions of the better case are noted by the exegetes: the hidden giving is specified as *to the poor* — the concealed gift aimed at real need, not at general benefaction — and its advantage is stated twice, once as betterness for the giver and once as the absolution of sins. The verse thus completes the section's movement inward: from what is given (the good things, 2:267), through what follows the giving (nothing injurious, 2:262–264), to where the giving is performed — in the open, lawfully, or in the secret, better. The interior direction of the whole section arrives here at its legislative point: the audience is itself a variable in the deed's worth.

**The Left Hand**

The tradition's commentary on this verse is dominated by one image. Many aḥādīth speak of the virtue of secret giving, Ibn Kathīr notes, often in variations of the saying: let the left hand not know what the right hand has given. The formula's most famous setting is the ḥadīth of the seven whom God shades under His shade on the Day when there is no shade but His — the just ruler, the youth raised in worship, the heart attached to the mosques, two who love each other for God's sake, the man tempted by rank and beauty who says I fear God, the one whose eyes flow in private remembrance, and the seventh: the man who gives charity so concealed that his left hand does not know what his right hand has spent (in the two Ṣaḥīḥs). The image's hyperbole is its instruction: the concealment that satisfies the standard is not merely from the neighbors but from the self's own record-keeping — the giving so unadvertised internally that the left side of the body is uninformed. The verse's better-for-you is measured against this image: every degree of the gift's privacy is a degree of the shade's proximity, because every degree removes an audience the deed could have been performed for.

**The Arithmetic of Ibn ʿAbbās**

The commentators preserve a quantified reading attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās that assigns the ranking its institutional nuance: for obligatory acts — the zakāt, the institutional alms — open performance is twenty-five times better; for voluntary, supererogatory giving, the private is seventy times better. The two ratios legislate two different goods. The open zakāt is public for reasons al-Rāzī lists: it sets the example the community imitates, it shows the poor that recourse exists among their neighbors, and it builds the open bond of provision between a society's members — the assessment's visibility is part of its justice, since a tax unseen is a tax unaudited. The secret nāfilah is private for the opposite reason: it is the sincerity-test, the giving that garners no prestige, where the only possible motive is the motive itself. The verse's ruling and the ratios agree in structure: the obligatory has a public function the voluntary does not, and the voluntary has an interior function the obligatory partly surrenders to administration. The juristic tradition runs on the same distinction — the zakāt paid publicly as norm, the ṣadaqah of the night as excellence — and the verse is the legislation both sides cite.

**The Absolution**

The betterness is then given its specific yield: concealment *will absolve you of your sins*. The commentators connect the verb to the expiation-vocabulary — kaffārah, the covering-and-effacing by which good deeds atone for evil ones — and quote the tradition's summaries: charity puts out sin as water puts out fire (the saying al-Ṭabarī records); and the Prophetic instruction, when you have done an evil deed, follow it with a good deed and it will wipe it away. The Qur'anic parallel is the sūrah of Hūd's axiom — *good deeds wipe out evil deeds* (11:114) — and the verse here assigns the wiping a specific location: the hidden gift. The commentators' logic connects the concealment to the absolution through the deed's purity: the sin-effacing power of charity runs at the charity's sincerity, and sincerity runs at secrecy — the gift with no audience has no alloy, and the unalloyed deed is the one the fire-quenching metaphor describes. The tradition's exchange preserved by al-Ṭabarī extends the absolution's scale: asked whether the remembrance of lā ilāha illa'Llāh counts among the good deeds that wipe, the Prophet answered that it is the best of good deeds — the covering-merit attaching to every unalloyed act of the tongue, the purse, and the heart, with the hidden charity among its purest forms.

**The Reading That Speaks First-Person**

Al-Ṭabarī records a variant that changes the absolution's speaker: in place of the third-person *it will absolve you*, some read the first-person plural — *and We will absolve you of some of your sins* — the promise arriving in God's own grammatical person. The variant is minor in text and major in register: the absolution becomes a speech-act of the Absolver, the deed's effect restated as the Giver's commitment. The commentators preserve both readings without adjudicating, and the section's theology keeps both true: the hidden charity effaces by its nature (the water-fire physics of the tradition) and effaces by promise (the covenant-language of the verse). The first-person reading also sharpens the verse's closing name: the All-Aware who sees the concealed gift is the We who absolves for it — the same divine attention operating as witness and as payer. For the giver the two readings carry one instruction: the concealment is not a loss of credit but a transfer of creditor — the audience foregone is replaced by a Recipient whose awareness the verse's final clause names and whose absolution, on the stronger reading, He pronounces Himself.

**All-Aware of What You Do**

The closing name is khabīr — the All-Aware, the expert-acquainted — the same name that sealed the widow's legislation (2:234) and the intercession-verse's interior (2:235), and its assignment here is exact. The hidden charity is, by construction, outside every human record: no witness, no receipt, no recipient's public gratitude, in the fullest form no left hand informed. The verse's ranking could therefore be read as a loss — the better deed is the one nobody can confirm occurred — and the closing name is the answer: the deed's confirmation exists, and its location is the divine awareness. Khubr carries the acquaintance-with-particulars that the concealment maximizes: the Aware knows the gift's amount, its recipient, the hour of its passing, and the intention's exact weather. The section's whole architecture closes on this name deliberately: the parables ran on what God does with unseen seeds (2:261), the annulments ran on what God records of following speech (2:264), the ledger-line stated that every instrument is known (2:270) — and the ranking-verse completes the system by making the unseen not merely recorded but preferred. The giver is left with the section's central inversion fully legislated: the visibility that makes a gift worth having in this world is the visibility that discounts it in the next, and the awareness that sees the concealment is the only audience whose seeing the verse calls good.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:272

> You are not responsible for people's guidance ˹O Prophet˺—it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills. Whatever you ˹believers˺ spend in charity, it is for your own good—as long as you do so seeking the pleasure of Allah. Whatever you donate will be paid back to you in full, and you will not be wronged.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Guidance Relinquished**

The verse opens with a sentence addressed to the Prophet that reads, in its position, as a correction: *You are not responsible for people's guidance — it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills*. The commentators supply the occasions, and all three concern charity at the boundary of the community. In al-Qurṭubī's first account, the Prophet had been giving charity to all who asked, and when the Muslim poor grew numerous he restricted the giving to Muslims — whereupon the verse arrived to lift the restriction. In the second, a Companion woman — the narrations name Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr in the related reports — had idolater grandparents asking her for support, and she declined to give until she asked the Prophet; the verse was the answer. In the third, Companions with relatives among the Jewish tribe of Qurayẓah refused them charity unless they converted. The three occasions converge on one question: does the recipient's faith condition the gift? And the verse's opening sentence answers by removing the question's premise — the giver is not the guide; guidance is God's assignment of Himself; the charity's legitimacy therefore cannot depend on a determination the giver has no authority to make.

**Charity Uncoupled from Identity**

The commentators state the verse's legal achievement in one formula: it uncouples charity from religious identity. The giving legislated here is not a mission-instrument — it does not purchase conversion, pressure it, or reward it — and it is not a loyalty-payment restricted to the in-group. The Qur'an's wider legislation confirms the uncoupling: the sūrah of the Examined Woman permits and commands the ordinary justice — *Allah does not forbid you from dealing kindly and fairly with those who have neither fought nor driven you out of your homes* (60:8) — and the verse here extends the kindness-and-justice to the purse specifically. The occasions' shared logic is the verse's second sentence: since guidance belongs to God's will, the giver who conditions his charity on the recipient's guidance is attempting to administer a province he does not govern — using the gift as leverage on a door only God opens. The tradition's practical ruling follows the verse directly: the obligatory alms run to the community's own poor, while the voluntary ṣadaqah crosses every boundary of belief — the idolater grandparent, the Qurayẓah relative, the asked-stranger all stand inside the verse's permission, and the giver's discernment is directed at the need, not the creed.

**The Night Charity of the Unknowing Hand**

The ḥadīth the exegetes cite at this verse tests the uncoupling at its most extreme. A man resolved to give charity and went out with his alms at night — and placed them, unknowing, in a thief's hand; the city talked in the morning, and he gave again, and the night's recipient was an adulteress; and the third night, a rich man. Each time the talk ran and each time he was answered: your charity is accepted — and perhaps, the reports reason, the gift will deter the thief from his thieving, prompt the rich man to give of his own wealth, and call the adulteress away from her sin. The story is the verse performed: the giver's knowledge of the recipients was zero, their worthiness was, by every social measure, negative, and the acceptance was total each time — because the deed's validity ran on the giver's intention and God's knowledge, not on the recipient's resume. The commentators draw the ruling the verse states as theology: *whatever you donate will be paid back to you in full* — the payment attaches to the spending, not to the spending's target, and the guidance-questions the giver cannot answer are precisely the questions the payment does not ask.

**For Your Own Good**

The verse's middle sentence turns from the recipient to the giver's ledger: *whatever you spend in charity, it is for your own good*. The commentators ground it in the Qur'an's standing principle — the sūrah of Explained in Detail states it flatly: *whoever does good, it is to their own benefit* (41:46) — and the principle does double work here. It answers the occasions' hidden arithmetic: the giving to the idolater-relative was not a loss to the community's boundary but a gain to the giver's own soul, since the deed's return is deposited with the doer whatever the recipient does with it. And it states the verse's condition: *as long as you do so seeking the pleasure of Allah* — the self-benefit runs on the God-direction, the same riḍwān-motive the garden-parable named (2:265) and the sūrah of Man's righteous voice in its purest form: we feed you only for God's sake, seeking neither reward nor thanks from you (76:9). The Face-of-God idiom the commentators attach here — spending ابتغاء وجه الله, seeking God's Face — is the section's highest motive-language, used at 2:272, 30:38–39, and 76:9: the gift whose direction is God's Face alone, with the recipient's identity, gratitude, and guidance all released from the transaction.

**Paid in Full, Not Wronged**

The verse's closing sentences are its contract-law: *whatever you donate will be paid back to you in full, and you will not be wronged*. The commentators read the fullness-clause against the section's earlier mechanics: the payment is the reward of the Hereafter, delivered without deficiency — the same custody the un-reminding givers were promised (their reward *with their Lord*, 2:262) now stated as a completed settlement. The wa-lā tuẓlamūn — you will not be wronged — is the contract's guarantee against the two frauds the section has been legislating: the fraud of the audience, which pays the show-off in perishable praise and leaves the ledger empty (2:264), and the fraud of the recipient's ingratitude, which the giver might fear has wasted the gift. Neither touches the payment: the gift to the thief is paid, the gift to the ungrateful is paid, the gift nobody saw is paid — because the payer is the Knower of the verse before, and the payment runs on His record rather than on the transaction's earthly reception. The verse's whole structure is thus a release: the giver is released from the guidance-question, from the worthiness-question, from the audience-question, and from the ingratitude-question — released into the single condition that remains, the Face-seeking — and every release is anchored in the two closing verbs: paid, in full, with no wrong done.

**The Verse in the Section's Architecture**

Positioned between the secret-giving ranking and the portrait of the dignified poor, this verse is the section's boundary-legislation: it defines whom the giving may cross (everyone, since guidance is not the giver's province), what the giving returns to (the giver's own good, under God's ledger), and what the giving requires (the Face-direction alone). The recipient-verse that follows will describe the specific poor the community must learn to recognize — the constrained, the silent, the marked — and the guidance-verse stands before it deliberately: before the section teaches the discrimination of need, it abolishes the discrimination of creed, so that the recognition commanded next operates on poverty and dignity rather than on belonging. The occasions of revelation give the sequence its historical edge — a community at war with some of the very relatives its charity-ethics now protects — and the verse's answer is the answer the whole section has been building toward: the gift is between the giver and God; the recipient stands in it as need, not as verdict; and the guidance of every heart involved, including the giver's, remains where the verse's first sentence placed it — with the One who guides whomever He wills.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:273

> ˹Charity is˺ for the needy who are too engaged in the cause of Allah to move about in the land ˹for work˺. Those unfamiliar with their situation will think they are not in need ˹of charity˺ because they do not beg. You can recognize them by their appearance. They do not beg people persistently. Whatever you give in charity is certainly well known to Allah.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Constrained Poor**

The verse describes the section's most delicate category of recipient: the poor whom poverty has made invisible. The opening participle — *too engaged in the cause of Allah to move about in the land* — carries, the commentators explain, the sense of a confinement: the verb connotes what hinders a traveler or prevents a setting-out. These are people whose commitment to the cause has cost them their mobility — and therefore their livelihood, since the working poor of the verse's world earned by moving: trade routes, day labor, caravan work. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī record the identification the tradition settles on: the People of the Veranda — ahl al-ṣuffah — the poor, homeless Companions who lived in the shaded portico attached to the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, known for their piety, devotion, and asceticism. They could not travel the earth, the commentators give two reasons, because they were too poor to equip a journey or because the roads outside Medina ran hostile — and their confinement *in the way of God* is read both ways: the ṣuffah-people held to the community's life when leaving would have meant safety or subsistence, and the verse honors the holding as the cause's own cost.

**Supposed Rich**

The verse's second sentence states the category's problem with unnerving precision: *those unfamiliar with their situation will think they are not in need, because they do not beg*. The taʿaffuf — the self-restraint, the keeping-oneself-away-from-asking — is the mechanism of the invisibility: the dignified poor are misread by every casual observer, and the misreading runs in the direction that starves them. The commentators draw out the social mechanics: charity in a community flows toward the visible claimant — the asker at the door, the voice in the market — and the restraint that makes a person worthy of admiration makes him absent from the distribution. The verse legislates against this flow with a reversal of evidentiary burden: the silence is not evidence of sufficiency but evidence of the specific need the community is commanded to seek out. The Prophetic ḥadīth the exegetes quote here is the category's definition: the truly indigent person is not the one who goes around receiving morsel after morsel from people — the visible beggar the community's charity reflexively feeds — but the one who has not enough, restrains himself, and does not ask people importunately (in the Ṣaḥīḥ collections). The verse and the ḥadīth together install a second poor behind the first: the fed asker and the unfed silent, and the community's duty to find the second.

**Known by Their Mark**

The verse's third sentence gives the finding its instrument: *you can recognize them by their appearance* — their sīmā, their mark. The commentators read the mark at two levels. The physical: the pallor of hunger, the traces of exertion and hardship on bodies whose need they will not voice — the signs the tradition elsewhere attaches to the righteous community, the mark on the faces from the trace of prostration (48:29), the sīmā-language repeated at the Day's recognition-scenes. And the level the commentators press: al-Rāzī records the reading of the mark as the manifestation of the soul in the body, especially the face — the dignity itself made visible, the restraint readable by the trained eye as exactly what it is. The ḥadīth the exegetes attach here is the tradition of spiritual discernment: beware the believer's firāsah, for he sees by the light of God — firāsah being, in the commentators' gloss, the perceptual skill by which the qualities of a soul are read through the form of the body. The mark of the truly poor, on this reading, is their humility and self-effacement made perceptible — present in the body but not of it — and the verse's instruction to the community is a training command: learn to see the need that presents as its opposite, because the presentation is the need's disguise and the seeing is the charity's first installment.

**Not Asking Importunately**

The verse's fourth sentence returns to the asking, and the tradition reads it as the category's legal boundary: *they do not beg people persistently* — the ilḥāf, the importunity, the pressure of repeated asking. The commentators supply the jurisprudence: the question of when asking becomes ilḥāf was measured by the fiqh tradition against a threshold of possession — a sum, forty dirhams in one transmitted measure, beyond which the asker's request is counted as importunate and blameworthy. The verse's silence-people stand at the far remove from that boundary: their restraint is not a refusal of asking at need but a refusal of the persistence that converts need into pressure. The two sentence-halves of the verse thus describe one ethics of the poor in its two registers — the dignity that does not ask, and the need that, when it asks, does not press — and the community's correlative duty in two registers: to see the unasked need (the mark), and to answer the asked need without making the asker pay in dignity (the 2:263 legislation of the honorable word). The verse is the section's complete circuit: the giving that begins in perception ends in the protection of the perceived.

**Whatever You Give, Allah Knows**

The closing sentence returns the verse to the section's ledger-line — *whatever you give in charity is certainly well known to Allah* — and the repetition from the audit-verse (2:270) is deliberate at just this point. The recipients the verse describes have no publicist: their need is unvoiced, their receipt unwitnessed, their gratitude — in the section's own legislation — not to be collected by the giver in any case. The charity that reaches them is thus doubly invisible: hidden by the giver's secrecy (2:271's better case) and hidden by the recipient's silence. The knowledge-clause answers both invisibilities with one verb: the transaction is known where it occurs, in full, with the mark's reading and the need's reality and the gift's arrival all registered. The commentators connect the clause to the verse's opening identification as well: the ṣuffah-people's confinement *in the way of God* was itself an unseen transaction — a poverty accepted for the cause's sake, invisible as charity and known as sacrifice — and the verse's closing assures both parties of the same record. The section's recipient-legislation ends where its whole ethics began: the giving is between the Knower and the known, the poor are to be sought rather than awaited, and the dignity the silent keep is the dignity the seeing are commanded to keep with them.

**The Verse and the Community's Eye**

Read as the section's closing movement before its final verse, this āyah completes the education the spending-legislation has been running. The parables taught the giver where his gift goes (the grain, the rock, the garden, the burnt orchard); the condition-verses taught what may not follow it (reminders, injury, annulment); the ranking-verses taught where to give it (the good things, the secret hand, past every boundary of creed); and this verse teaches whom to look for — the poor the community's own structures of visibility hide. The ahl al-ṣuffah identification gives the lesson its historical body: the portico's residents were the Prophet's own neighbors, fed from the gifts hung in his mosque (the date-clusters of 2:267's occasion), sustained by a community trained by exactly these verses to read the mark. The verse's permanent instruction is the training itself — that a community's charity is measured not by what it gives to the hand extended but by what it carries to the door not knocked, and that the carrying begins in the eye: the firāsah that sees by God's light, the mark read through the body, the silence recognized as speech. The section's final verse will describe the givers of night and day, secret and open; this verse has described the people their giving must find.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:274

> Those who spend their wealth in charity day and night, secretly and openly—their reward is with their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Four Quadrants of Giving**

The charity-section that has run from the grain-parable onward closes by completing its coordinate system: *day and night, secretly and openly*. The two pairs cross to make four quadrants, and the verse's claim is that the givers it praises have filled all four — every hour and every mode. The commentators read the doubling deliberately: night and day cover the axis of time, secret and open cover the axis of audience, and between them the verse exhausts the circumstances in which a gift can be given. Nothing is left outside: the urgent need at midnight and the assessed due at noon, the hand nobody saw and the hand the market watched. The section has legislated each quadrant separately — the ranking of the secret over the public (2:271), the open giving that remains good, the gift to the unseen recipient (2:272), the search for the silent poor (2:273) — and this verse gathers the legislation into a portrait of the person who has absorbed all of it: a giver for whom no hour is wrong and no audience disqualifying.

**The Quartet of ʿAlī and Abū Bakr**

Beyond the general import, the commentators record specific identifications. Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, and al-Ṭabarī preserve reports that the verse describes particular givers — ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq among those named — who are said to have distributed a sum in exactly the fourfold pattern the verse describes: a quarter by night, a quarter by day, a quarter in secret, a quarter in open. The reports function less as historical claims to verify than as the tradition's way of reading the verse's quadrants as a practiced discipline: giving as a deliberately diversified portfolio of occasions, so that no single mode dominates and the soul's attachment to any one audience — the night's privacy, the day's visibility — is broken by rotation. The specific-occasion reading and the general reading coexist in the commentaries without conflict, the verse's grammar allowing both: these are people who gave thus, and this is what all such giving earns.

**Their Reward With Their Lord**

The reward-clause repeats the section's custody-formula with precision: *their reward is with their Lord* — ajruhum ʿinda rabbihim, the same prepositional deposit promised the un-reminding givers (2:262). The repetition at the section's close is its final answer to the visibility-problem the whole passage has worked through: the four quadrants include two where no human ledger records anything — the night, the secret — and the verse assures both that the record exists, kept *with* the Lord, in a custody the giver's anonymity does not weaken and the recipient's silence does not erase. The commentators' earlier ruling that the hidden gift is better, and the open gift good, converges here in a single reward-location: whatever the quadrant, the payment stands in the same place, with the same Keeper — which is why the quadrants can be filled indifferently, the giver choosing between them by need's occasion rather than by reward's arithmetic.

**No Fear, No Grief**

The closing formula is the sūrah's language of arrived security, and its appearance here marks the charity-section's believers as having reached the state the formula names: *there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve*. The pair covers both directions of the heart's disturbance — the future's fear, the past's grief — and the section has already explained why its givers hold both: no future to fear, because the reward is deposited where nothing reaches it; no past to grieve, because nothing they gave has been taken back in reminders or injury. The same formula sealed the sūrah's early portrait of the faithful across the revelations — the believers, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians who believe and do good (2:62, 5:69) — and its assignment here places the complete giver in that same company of the secured. The verses ahead will name the opposite fate in its own formula — residents of the Fire, abiding — but this verse ends the section on the security-clause, and the givers it describes are the last people the charity-legislation leaves standing before the sūrah changes subject.

**The Total Giver**

Read as a portrait rather than a rule, the verse describes a disposition the section's fifteen verses have been constructing piece by piece. The good-things command (2:267) determined what he gives; the annulment-prohibitions (2:262–264) determined what he never says afterward; the garden-parable (2:265) determined why — God's pleasure and confirmed certainty; the burnt-garden parable (2:266) determined what he fears, and the fear corrected him; the ranking of the secret (2:271) trained his audience down to zero; the guidance-verse (2:272) widened his recipients past every boundary of creed; the mark-verse (2:273) sharpened his eye for the need that does not ask. The four quadrants are the resulting life: giving at every hour, in every mode, to every kind of need, from the good of what he has. The verse needs no new command to describe him because the commands have all been issued — it only states his schedule, his secrecy-range, and his deposit, and adds the two negations that define his interior: nothing ahead frightens him, nothing behind grieves him.

**The Section's Seal**
