The verse's position does structural work the commentators mark: it is the last of the charity-passages, the closing seal on the sūrah's longest continuous ethical legislation between the family-code and the ribā-passages that follow. The seal's form — a portrait plus a reward-formula — matches the section's opening parable, the grain that multiplies (2:261): the section began with the deed's growth and ends with the doer's security, the agricultural promise translated into the eschatological one. Between the two, every verse has been a condition or a protection of the deed, and the final verse is what remains when all conditions are met: the givers named, their quadrants filled, their wage with their Lord, their hearts emptied of the two things the section has been emptying them of all along — the fear of want that closes hands (the poverty-threat of 2:268) and the grief of the gift spoiled (the reminders and injuries of 2:262). The charity-section's last word is therefore its quietest: no drama, no parable, no command — only the four adverbs of a completed practice and the two negations of a completed peace.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:275

> Those who consume interest will stand ˹on Judgment Day˺ like those driven to madness by Satan's touch. That is because they say, "Trade is no different than interest." But Allah has permitted trading and forbidden interest. Whoever refrains—after having received warning from their Lord —may keep their previous gains, and their case is left to Allah. As for those who persist, it is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Devourers' Rising**

The sūrah's economy-legislation turns on its darkest case, and the verse opens with its eschatological image: the interest-eaters *will stand like those driven to madness by Satan's touch*. Al-Ṭabarī reads the standing as the rising from the graves — the resurrection of the ribā-devourer pictured as the epileptic's collapsing-and-rising, the body knocked down by an unseen hand and jerking upright, again and again. The ḥadīth literature the exegetes gather describes the Day's version of the devourer in harsher registers: raised choking, in a maddened state, or with a belly swollen to the size of a house, snakes visible inside it. The image's logic is retribution by resemblance: the trade that convulsed the debtor's household — debt compounding until possessions were swallowed — convulses its operator at the standing, and the touch attributed to Satan names the transaction's real counterparty. The verse's verb is worth holding: they *devour* — akala — the Qur'an's word for consumption that annihilates what it consumes, the same verb the orphan-wealth prohibition used (2:274's section's earlier fire, 2:210's devouring, 4:10's eating of the orphans' property): ribā is classified with the sūrah's consuming-sins, not its contracting-sins.

**Ribā: The Word and Its Two Kinds**

The verse's subject needs its definition, and the commentators supply it with unusual care because the usual translation misleads. Ribā means, in the root, increase, gain, growth — and "usury," understood as exorbitant interest or even any interest, is an imperfect rendering: not all interest is ribā, and not all ribā is interest. The Qur'an and the ḥadīth legislate two distinct transaction-types under the one name. The first is increase through deferment — ribā al-nasīʾah: a charge added to a debt at its maturity in exchange for time. The second is increase through surplus — ribā al-faḍl: an excess taken in the exchange of like commodities, gold for gold, or one grade of a staple for a better grade in unequal measure. The two types look nothing alike on the surface — one is credit's price, the other is a barter's imbalance — and the jurists spent centuries working out the single moral geometry they share; the verse's ruling covers both, which is why the tradition calls this passage one of Islamic law's most complex and multifaceted terrains.

**The Practice of the Age of Ignorance**

The deferment-type had a concrete pre-Islamic form the sources describe precisely. Imām Mālik records it in the Muwaṭṭaʾ: a man is owed a debt for a set term; when the term falls due he asks the debtor — will you settle, or will you increase? — pay now, or add to the debt and extend the time. If the debtor paid, the creditor took; if not, the debt grew and the term lengthened. The mechanism's engine was the doubling: the deferment-fee commonly doubled the principal across a year, and doubled again at the next deferment — the compounding the sūrah of ʿImrān legislates against directly: *Do not consume interest, multiplying it many times over* (3:130). The end-state of the mechanism was total: a debtor could lose every possession he had to the creditor through doubling upon doubling. Read against this practice, the verse's devouring-verb is not metaphor but description — the loan that began as help ended as the systematic absorption of the borrower's estate, and the resurrection-image gives the absorption its final form.

**The Slogan Refuted**

The verse names the devourers' argument and answers it in one movement: *That is because they say, "Trade is no different than interest." But Allah has permitted trading and forbidden interest.* The slogan's form is an equivalence-claim — bayʿ, ordinary sale, is mithl ribā, the same thing as the increase — and the traditional glosses preserve its historical voice: the Meccan creditor-class's defense of the practice, sale is only money-for-goods and ribā is money-for-money, both are trade. The refutation declines the terrain entirely. It does not argue the equivalence false on economic grounds; it states the legislative fact: God has allowed the one and forbidden the other, and the permission-and-prohibition are themselves the difference. The Qur'an's wider treatment supplies the economics the slogan hides — the sūrah of the Byzantines states it flatly: *Whatever loans you give, seeking interest at the expense of people's wealth will not increase with Allah. But whatever charity you give, seeking the pleasure of Allah—it is they whose reward will be multiplied* (30:39). The increase taken from people's wealth does not increase where increases are actually recorded; the two transactions are not the same because they run in opposite directions — one toward the debtor's loss, one toward the needy's gain.

**The Six Commodities and Bilāl's Dates**

The surplus-type's legislation is the ḥadīth's famous commodity-rule: gold for gold, silver for silver, wheat for wheat, barley for barley, dates for dates, salt for salt — like for like, equal for equal, hand to hand; and whatever exceeds that is ribā. The rule's operative story is Bilāl's dates: the Companion brought the Prophet choice dates, and asked their origin, learned he had traded two measures of common dates for one measure of fine — the Prophet's verdict was immediate: that is precisely the ribā; return to the seller, sell the common dates for money, and with the money buy the fine ones. The two-step sale, grounding the exchange in priced market transactions, is the rule's remedy for the invisibility of the surplus: unequal like-for-like hides its excess, and the market's money-prices expose it. The jurists then debated the commodities' shared legal attribute — measurability, fungibility, storability, edibility, or some combination — because the attribute determines how far the six-item list extends across other goods; the debate is the fiqh of ribā al-faḍl's first chapter, and it exists because the verse legislates a type whose instances no list can exhaust.

**Risk, Uncertainty, and the Permitted Exceptions**

The ribā-rules live inside a wider transaction-ethics the commentators describe here: the law of gharar, the unlawful uncertainty whose root is semantically tied to deception. The governing principle — one may not sell what one does not possess, what whose attributes are unknown, or what does not yet exist — carries its ḥadīth-list of instances: the unborn calf in its mother's womb, the unmeasured milk still in the udder, spoils sold before distribution, the diver's future catch. But risk, the jurists note, is present in every honest transaction, and the law therefore admits exceptions where social benefit outweighs the uncertainty — above all the forward sale of crops, payment now for delivery in one, two, or three years, which Medina's agricultural economy required and which the verse-section ahead will legislate in its documentation-rules (2:282). The Prophet permitted the forward sale under strict conditions — known quantity, known quality, known term — precisely so that necessity's exception would not become ribā's disguise. The ribā-prohibition is thus not a blanket risk-aversion but a calibrated economy of permitted and forbidden uncertainty, and the two ribā-types are its two forbidden poles: time priced against the debtor, and surplus hidden inside the like-for-like.

**Whoever Refrains After the Warning**

The verse's amnesty-clause legislates the prohibition's arrival: *Whoever refrains — after having received warning from their Lord — may keep their previous gains, and their case is left to Allah.* The commentators' rulings give the clause its exact reach: what is cancelled is the outstanding — the increases accrued and not yet collected at the warning's arrival; what has already been consumed is not reclaimed. The Prophetic statement attached to the clause fixes the formula: all the ribā of the Age of Ignorance is remitted; you have your principal; you neither wrong nor are wronged (the declaration made at the Farewell Pilgrimage's sermon, weeks before the Prophet's death). *Their case is left to Allah* covers the amnesty's interior: the desisting's sincerity, the past's weight, the heart's history with the practice — the file closed to human jurisdiction and left open with God. The clause is the verse's mercy-statement, and its timing is the tradition's observation: this passage is said to be among the very last revelations — some count it the last of all, with 4:176 and 5:3 the rival candidates — which the exegetes cite to explain why the ḥadīth record on ribā's fine mechanics is comparatively thin: the law arrived late, and its elaboration fell to the jurists of the following generations.

**Those Who Persist**

The final sentence closes the alternative: *As for those who persist, it is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.* The going-back — the return to the practice after the warning — is what the residency answers, and the verse's structure makes the persistence, not the past, the operative fact: the pre-warning gains were remitted, and only the post-warning return carries the Fire. The residency-language is the sūrah's permanence-formula, and its assignment here places ribā's operators in the company of the verse-sequence's other final residents — the apostates of 2:217, the darkness-led of 2:257 — while its occasion, an economic practice, is the sequence's sharpest statement that the ledger's deepest entries are commercial. The devourer's portrait is now complete in three strokes: the convulsed rising, the slogan refuted by permission-and-prohibition, and the residency earned by persistence after amnesty. Between the amnesty and the residency stands the verse's only open question — *their case is left to Allah* — and the case it leaves is every reader's own: what he will do with the increase in his ledger, now that trading has been permitted and this forbidden.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:276

> Allah has made interest fruitless and charity fruitful. And Allah does not like any ungrateful evildoer.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Two Verbs**

The shortest verse of the ribā-block is its thesis-statement, and it runs on two verbs set in deliberate opposition: God *blights* ribā and *causes charity to grow*. The first verb, maḥq, is the wiping-out, the effacement — the word for a decrease that is not subtraction but annulment, the barakah's removal leaving the amount intact and the substance gone. The second verb is where the verse hides its finest device, and the commentators mark it immediately: the form translated *makes fruitful* is ar-rabā — the verbal root of ribā itself. The increase-word the devourers used for their practice is used by the verse for its opposite: God's increasing belongs to the charity, and what the ribā calls increase is, in God's arithmetic, the blight. The single shared root does the whole argument — the two systems both claim to make wealth grow, and the verse concedes the verb to one of them and strips it from the other. Ribā is not increased wealth; it is maḥq wearing increase's vocabulary. Charity is not decreased wealth; it is the true rabā, the growth the word was always describing.

**The Blight's Operation**

The commentators read the blighting across both registers the sūrah has established. In the visible register, the ribā-estate carries the devourer's curse inside its own structure: the compounding that swallowed the debtor's possessions (3:130's doubling and redoubling) builds a wealth whose preservation requires the debtor's ruin, and the tradition's Prophetic saying quoted at the next verse states the visible end — ribā, even when it swells, ends in loss. In the unseen register — the one the section's parables have trained the reader to read — the blight is the dust-on-rock effect at the scale of an estate: amounts that looked like soil over substance, stripped bare by the downpour of the reckoning (2:264). The two registers converge in the parable-language the sūrah already supplied: the grain sown in charity multiplies to seven hundred (2:261), the garden on the height doubles under rain (2:265), and the orchard of a lifetime burns in an hour (2:266) — the ribā-wealth is the orchard whose fire was lit at its planting, and the verse's maḥq names the burning as already underway, invisible to the ledger and total in the fact.

**The Growth's Operation**

The causing-to-grow answers the blight point for point, and the section's own imagery supplies the mechanics. The date-given-in-charity is taken into God's hand and nurtured like a foal until it stands like a mountain — the ḥadīth the garden-verse's commentary carried; the single grain returns seven hundredfold and God multiplies beyond for whom He wills (2:261). The growth is not metaphorical in the tradition's insistence: the charity's increase is a real accretion in the only ledger that survives, deposited with the Lord (2:262, 2:274) where the maḥq cannot reach it. The verse thus restates the two preceding verses' eschatology as economics: the devourers' rising in convulsion (2:275) is the blight made visible at the standing, and the givers' no-fear-no-grief (2:274) is the growth made visible at the same hour. The sūrah of the Byzantines states the same opposition with the same verbs' logic — the interest seeking increase in people's wealth does not increase with God, while the charity seeking God's pleasure is multiplied (30:39) — and the two verses together are the Qur'an's complete rebuttal of the devourers' slogan: they claimed sale and ribā were one thing, and the answer is that ribā and charity are the two things, the false increase and the true.

**The Ungrateful Evildoer**

The verse's second sentence names the person the blight describes: *Allah does not like any ungrateful evildoer* — kaffār, the intensive of ingratitude-unbelief, paired with athīm, the intensive of sin. The double intensity is precise to the ribā-case, and the commentators draw out both halves. The ingratitude: the devourer's wealth arrived as provision — min mā razaqnākum, from what We have provided you, the giving-section's standing premise (2:254, 2:267) — and ribā is the provision turned against its own logic, the gift from God used as an instrument against God's other servants; the kaffār-name says the practice is not merely unlawful but unthankful at the root. The sin: the athīm-name carries the harm's ledger — the debtor's swallowed estate, the household's convulsion, the wrong the Farewell-formula abolished (neither wronging nor being wronged). The love-negation is the verse's relational verdict: the God who blights and grows is described here in His disposition — no love for this combination of names — and the disposition explains the two verbs' direction: the blighting and the growing are not mechanical but personal, the economy of a Lord who loves the grateful giver and does not love the ungrateful devourer.

**Why the Thesis Stands Alone**

The verse's placement between the devourers' portrait (2:275) and the believers' portrait (2:277) gives it the function of a fulcrum, and its brevity is the fulcrum's requirement. What precedes is the case of the ribā: its image, its slogan, its amnesty, its residency. What follows is the case of the community: belief, righteous deeds, the prayer kept, the alms paid, the reward deposited, the fear and grief removed. Between the two cases the sūrah needs one sentence stating the principle both are instances of — that God presides over two opposite arithmetic operations, effacement and increase, and assigns each to one of the two economies — and the sentence is this verse. The commentators' observation that the section's legislation (the commands to the believers in the next three verses) presupposes the thesis is exact: leave what remains of ribā (2:278) is a command that only makes sense to someone who believes the blight is real, and the respite-and-charity upgrade (2:280) is an invitation only attractive to someone who believes the growth is real. The one-line verse is therefore the block's axiom, and the axioms of divine economics, the Qur'an's structure suggests, fit in one line: two verbs, one root, two names of what a person can be.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:277

> Indeed, those who believe, do good, establish prayer, and pay alms-tax will receive their reward from their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Four Named**

The verse states the community's positive economy in four terms, and the terms' order is the verse's architecture: *those who believe, do good, establish prayer, and pay alms-tax*. The first pair is the sūrah's standard opening dyad — believed and worked the righteous — the interior assent and the deeds that verify it. The second pair names the two institutions: the ṣalāt established (āqāmū, the same causing-to-stand the prayer-verse commanded, 2:238) and the zakāt given. The commentators note the dyads' division of labor: belief and righteous work are personal and unlimited, while prayer and alms are the instituted forms the personal takes — the fixed stations of the day and the fixed levy on the year, the two pillars whose performance is measurable and whose neglect is public. The verse's listing is the same four that structure the sūrah's opening portrait of the successful (2:3–5: belief in the unseen, the prayer established, spending from the provision, belief in the revelation) — and the ring it closes is deliberate: the Book that began by defining the guided in these four terms ends its economy-legislation by restating the same four and attaching their reward.

**Alms Against Interest**

The zakāt-clause carries, in this position, a polemical weight the commentators make explicit: the institutional alms are the moral opposite of ribā, and the verse sets the opposition on the record. The two are inverse social machines. The zakāt moves wealth from the possessing to the needing as an obligation of faith — assessed, annual, distributed to the categories the sūrah of Repentance will list — while the ribā moves wealth from the needing to the possessing as an obligation of debt, compounding with time. The one treats the surplus as a trust whose release purifies (the root zakāh: to purify, to grow — both the blight-and-growth verbs of the previous verse gathered in one institution); the other treats the deficit as a revenue-source. The Prophetic saying the exegetes quote here states the opposition's arithmetic: the end of ribā, even where it seems to increase, is diminishment. Placed immediately after the blight-and-growth thesis (2:276), the verse's four terms read as the growth-system's specification — belief, work, prayer, alms are the four channels through which the true rabā flows, and the zakāt is the channel the devourers inverted.

**Their Reward With Their Lord**

The reward-formula is now so established in the section that its recurrence is itself meaningful: *they will receive their reward from their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve*. The custody-clause — the reward with, at, from the Lord — has sealed the un-reminding givers (2:262) and the four-quadrant givers (2:274), and its assignment here to the pillar-community extends the custody from the charitable act to the instituted life: the zakāt-payer's reward sits in the same divine keeping as the secret night-gift's. The no-fear-no-grief formula, which the tradition reads as the sūrah's language of final security, has by this point appeared across the revelations' faithful (2:62), the sūrah of the Table's parallel (5:69), the section's complete givers, and now the community's four-term portrait — and each recurrence narrows the distance between the formula's bearers until this verse, where it rests on the instituted believers themselves. The commentators' note that the verse's content parallels 2:62 and 5:69 sharpens the point: the security once stated for the faithful of every revelation is here stated for the community that keeps its two pillars — the same reward, the same custody, the same two negations, now as a description of institutional life rather than of creed alone.

**The Establishment-Verb**

The prayer-clause's verb deserves the attention the tradition gives it: āqāmū — they established, they caused to stand. The sūrah's prayer-guarding verse (2:238) commanded the keeping — ḥāfiẓū — of the prayers and their middle; this verse describes the community's characteristic act as the establishing, and the commentators gloss the difference as the difference between performance and institution: the prayer established is the prayer given standing — in the person's day (its times kept, its devotion honored) and in the community's space (its congregation maintained, its mosques built, its children taught). The same verb has run through the sūrah from its opening — those who establish the prayer (2:3) — and its reappearance in the economy-block is the verse's quiet structural claim: the market's ethics are anchored in the mosque's discipline. The zakāt-clause inherits the anchoring: the alms-tax is not occasional generosity but established giving — assessed, owed, distributed — the charity-section's free quadrants (2:274) crystallized into an institution that survives the moods of the giver.

**The Portrait Between Two Warnings**

The verse's position is the block's hinge: between the ribā-case's closing verdict — the ungrateful evildoer unloved (2:276) — and its opening commands to the believers, fear God and leave the remainder (2:278). The portrait does transitional work in both directions. Backward, it answers the devourers' residency with the community's security: the Fire's permanent residents on one side, the no-fear-no-grief on the other, and the four terms as the road between. Forward, it identifies who is being commanded: the leave-what-remains order, the war-declaration's warning, the respite-and-charity invitation are all addressed to the people this verse has just described — believers whose belief is established practice, and whose practice includes the alms that ribā inverts. The commentators read the sequence as pedagogy: the community is shown what it is (the four terms, the reward, the security) before being told what to do about the outstanding ribā in its ledgers (the commands) — identity before obligation, so that the obligation arrives not as an external imposition but as the four terms' own requirement. The verse is thus the block's mirror held up before its legislation: this is the community the coming commands assume, and the commands exist so that the mirror keeps matching.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:278

> O believers! Fear Allah, and give up outstanding interest if you are ˹true˺ believers.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Command's Two Halves**

The ribā-block's legislation proper opens with a sentence whose two halves the tradition reads as one command: *Fear Allah, and give up what remains of the interest*. The taqwā-clause is not decorative framing — the commentators treat it as the command's operative ground, the fear-of-God being the interior state whose absence produced the devourers' slogan and whose presence makes the relinquishment possible. The verb of the second half is dharaū — leave, abandon, let lie — and its object is mā baqiya, what remains: the remainder, the residue, the still-standing excess. The object's precision is the verse's first legislation: the command does not ask the creditors to disgorge their history (the amnesty of 2:275 covered what has passed — the previous gains kept, the case left to God) but to stop the machine where it stands — every accrued increase not yet collected, every deferment-fee on the books, every compounding clause in every ledger of the community, abandoned as of the command's arrival. The tradition's historical frame is the Farewell declaration the previous verse carried — all the ribā of the Age of Ignorance remitted, the principal alone retained — and this verse is that declaration's legislative form: the remission applied, creditor by creditor, to the outstanding balance.

**What Remains**

The exegetes work the phrase mā baqiya with juristic care, because the distinction it draws governs the whole transition. What remains is the increase that exists as claim rather than as possession — the amounts owed to the creditor under the ribā-terms and not yet paid. Those claims are voided: the debtor owes the principal and nothing beyond it, and the creditor's ledger is to be rewritten to match. What does not remain — what has already been taken — is treated by the amnesty-clause's rule: not clawed back, its case left to Allah (2:275), with al-Qurṭubī recording the consensus that past ribā was not open to reclamation. The distinction produces the transition's social shape: no retroactive confiscation, no debt-jubilee of principals, but an immediate and total stop to the increase-mechanism. The jurists read the same distinction into the repentance-clause of the next verse's formula — the principal retained, neither wronging nor being wronged — as the settlement this command's obedience produces: the creditor keeps his capital and loses his surplus; the debtor keeps his property and loses his compounding. What remains, on both sides, is the loan as the tradition understands it — an act whose return is with God rather than in the fee.

**If You Are Believers**

The verse's final clause is its sharpest instrument: *if you are true believers* — in tuʾminūn, the condition attached to the abandonment. The commentators read the conditional in the register the Qur'an reserves for such attachments: not a doubt cast on the addressees' faith but a definition of it. The faith named is being tested against its own content — the community that has just been described as believing, doing good, establishing prayer, and paying alms (2:277) is told that the outstanding ribā in its ledgers is incompatible with the description, and the conditional makes the incompatibility active: belief, if it is belief, gives up the remainder. The structure echoes the sūrah's own faith-verses — the handhold grasped by the renouncing and believing (2:256), the fear-of-God that the annulment-prohibitions assumed — and it does the same work here on the economy: faith is not a state that coexists with the increase-claims but a state that releases them. The tradition's ascetic commentators draw the clause's full edge: the verse makes the abandoned ribā the criterion, so that a believer's ledger is itself a testimony, and what remains in it after the command is the measure of what the in tuʾminūn found inside.

**The Taqwā-Frame**

The fear-of-God that heads the command connects the economy-block to the sūrah's whole legislation, and the commentators mark the connection deliberately: this is the same taqwā the code invoked at its thresholds — nearer to reverence in the waiver-ranking (2:237), the duty on those mindful in the provision-ruling (2:241), beware of Him in the heart-knowledge verse (2:235). The placement means that the ribā-relinquishment is legislated as an act of taqwā rather than as a commercial adjustment: what makes the abandonment possible is not economic argument but the feared-and-hoped relationship the sūrah has been installing since its opening portrait of the God-fearers (2:2–5). Al-Rāzī's cascade in the two-voices verse (2:268) is the psychology behind the frame: the soul that obeys the poverty-threat keeps and compounds, and the soul that fears God releases — the taqwā-clause is the command's statement of which fear it expects to find operative. The verse thus does not argue with the creditors' self-interest; it addresses the fear that outranks self-interest, and makes the argument's conclusion — leave the remainder — that fear's immediate act.

**The Community Addressed as Creditors**

One feature of the verse's address has drawn the commentators' notice: it speaks to believers as people who hold ribā-claims — the community's own ledgers, not the enemy's. The address assumes what Medina's economy actually contained: Muslim creditors holding pre-Islamic deferment-claims against Muslim and non-Muslim debtors alike, the mechanism of the Age of Ignorance still running inside the believing community's own books. The verse's legislation is therefore internal reform at its most concrete — a community ordered to rewrite its own contracts, cancel its own accrued income, and absorb the loss as the cost of the faith it claimed. The commentators connect this internality to the sequence's structure: the portrait-verse (2:277) described the community's four terms, and this verse tests the fourth — the alms-payters against the interest-takers are supposed to be the same people, and where they are not, the command makes them so by force of the conditional. No external enemy is named in the ribā-block; the war-declaration that follows is addressed to whoever among the believers does not comply — which is why the taqwā-frame comes first: the battlefield of this legislation is the believer's own ledger, and the fear of God is the only authority that can order a man to burn his own outstanding income.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:279

> If you do not, then beware of a war with Allah and His Messenger! But if you repent, you may retain your principal—neither inflicting nor suffering harm.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The War-Declaration**

The consequence of non-compliance is stated in the Qur'an's most severe formula: *then beware of a war with Allah and His Messenger*. The commentators mark the declaration's singularity — no other sin in the Qur'an is met with a war announced by God and His Messenger together, and the pairing is read as the measure of the ribā-persistence's gravity: an economic practice that convulses households and absorbs estates is treated as an armed posture against the divine order and its envoy at once. Ibn ʿAbbās's reported gloss carries the declaration into the eschaton: on the Day of Resurrection it will be said to the one who took ribā — take up your sword for war (al-Ṭabarī). Others read the formula's direction as descriptive rather than prospective: whoever persists has already made himself hostile to God and His Messenger, the war being the state his persistence constitutes (al-Qurṭubī). And the jurists drew from the declaration its this-worldly edge, recorded across the four exegetes: persistence in ribā after the warning can be cause for the legitimate authority to take up arms against the persisters — compelling the surrender of the ribā-gains, and fighting those who refuse to surrender them or desist. A sin legislated with imprisonment, confiscation, and campaign behind it: the declaration is the sūrah's statement that the devouring-economy is not a private vice but a public war.

**If You Repent**

Against the war stands the verse's other half, and the tradition reads the two halves as one instrument of mercy: *But if you repent, you may retain your principal*. The repentance named is the previous verse's abandonment performed — the remainder left, the claims rewritten — and its reward is the amnesty's exact content: the raʾs al-māl, the head of the wealth, the capital itself, retained in full. The commentators' jurisprudence is precise about what the retention means for both parties: the debtor remains liable for the original loan — the principal is not forgiven by the repentance but confirmed — while every fee, increase, and deferment-charge that accrued on it is cancelled. The creditor who repents is thus made whole in his capital and stripped in his surplus; the debtor who is released keeps his obligation to the amount actually received. The verse converts the repentance from an interior state into a settlement with arithmetic: here is what you keep, here is what you release, here is the war you exit — the same structure the Farewell-declaration carried (the ribā of the Age of Ignorance remitted, the principal retained) now stated as the standing terms on which any ribā-holder may come in from the war.

**Neither Wronging Nor Wronged**

The settlement's formula is the verse's most quoted clause: *neither inflicting nor suffering harm* — lā taẓlimūna wa-lā tuẓlamūn, you shall not wrong and shall not be wronged. The commentators note the formula's double fairness with care. The creditor is not wronged: his capital returns to him intact, and the repentance-clause exists precisely so that the prohibition does not become a confiscation — the religion does not make the abandonment of ribā a punishment of the lender's estate. The debtor is not wronged: the increase that was absorbing his possessions — the doubling and redoubling of 3:130 — stops at the principal, and the wrong of compounding is lifted from him forever. The two negations thus state the settlement as a symmetry, and the symmetry is the ribā-block's moral core: the forbidden transaction is the one that requires a wronging — the increase taken from the debtor's need is a wrong inflicted, and its cancellation without capital-loss ensures no wrong rebounds onto the creditor. The tradition reads the same formula as the economy's standing principle, the Prophetic declaration at the Farewell Pilgrimage using it as the ribā-amnesty's own closing words: you have your principal — neither wronging nor wronged — and the jurists extended the principle to the whole of muʿāmalāt: no transaction in the Islamic order may be built on either party's ẓulm.

**The Principal and the Loan's Nature**

The retention-of-principal ruling carries an implication the commentators draw out in the block's wider context: the legitimate loan, in this legislation, is a loan that returns exactly what was given. The Islamic tradition's ideal of the qarḍ — the loan — is therefore charitable in structure: money lent for a term, repaid in the same amount, the time-value surrendered by the lender as an act of the giving the section has been legislating (the invitation to turn the difficult debtor's respite into outright charity follows at the next verse). The profit-seeking uses of capital are not forbidden by this structure but channeled — into the trade God permitted (2:275's permission-clause), the credit-sale with its negotiated price, the lease, the partnership where profit and loss are shared — instruments in which the return compensates real risk or real exchange rather than time alone. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī both frame the principal-rule this way: the creditor's capital is protected because capital is legitimate property; the increase is cancelled because the increase was the wrong. The verse thus legislates not the abolition of lending but its purification — the loan restored to the form in which it can be, as the tradition insists, an act of charity with a contractual body.

**The Sequence's Position**

This verse and its neighbors form the block's enforcement-triad, and the triad's order is deliberate: the portrait of the pillar-community (2:277), the command to the believers to fear God and abandon the remainder (2:278), the war-and-repentance alternative (this verse), the respite-and-charity treatment of the struggling debtor (2:280), and the Day-return that seals the whole (2:281). The commentators read the movement as descending from the community's identity to its ledgers to its debtors to its final audit — each verse narrowing the frame: believers, creditors, debtors, souls. Within the triad this verse is the alternative-statement, the point where the command's two exits are named in full: persistence is war, repentance is settlement, and the settlement's terms are fixed at the principal. Nothing between the two exits is legislated — no partial compliance, no negotiated retention of some increase — and the binary is the verse's rhetorical force: the ribā-holder stands, in the moment of the command, at the fork the verse describes, and the fork's two roads have been named with their destinations, war on one side and neither-wronging on the other, with the principal waiting intact on the road of return.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:280

> If it is difficult for someone to repay a debt, postpone it until a time of ease. And if you waive it as an act of charity, it will be better for you, if only you knew.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Struggling Debtor**

The ribā-block turns from the creditor's sin to the debtor's distress, and its legislation begins with recognition: *if it is difficult for someone to repay a debt* — the ʿusrah, the straitness, the hard circumstance that makes the due date arrive against an empty hand. The verse does not treat the struggling debtor as a defaulter to be pressed but as a condition to be waited out: *postpone it until a time of ease*. The commentators mark the command's addressee and its force: the creditor who holds a matured debt against a debtor in genuine straits is ordered to grant the respite — the inaẓār, the looking-along, the patience of the term extended. The jurisprudence that grew from the clause distinguished the straitened debtor from the evasive one (the mūsil, the procrastinator with means, whose delay is ẓulm in the tradition's famous saying), and assigned this verse to the former: where the difficulty is real, the postponement is not the creditor's option but his obligation until the ease arrives. The verse thus completes the block's debtor-protection: the increase was cancelled at the principal (2:279), and now the principal itself is granted patience — the debt survives, and the debtor survives it.

**The Respite as Charity**

The verse's second movement converts the obligation into an invitation and ranks the conversion: *if you waive it as an act of charity, it will be better for you*. The waiving — the ṣadaqah-word the giving-section built its fifteen verses on — is applied here to the debt itself: the creditor may release not the increase (already cancelled) but the principal, turning the loan's remainder into a gift. The tradition's arithmetic of the respite makes the invitation's gradient explicit: a ḥadīth the exegetes cite states that whoever grants delay to one in difficulty is credited an act of charity for each day of the delay — the patience itself generating the giving's reward day by day — while the outright waiving is the section's own better, the excellence beyond the duty. Al-Qurṭubī's ruling fixes the two ranks' legal relation: the respite is commanded because the debtor's difficulty is real, but the principal remains the creditor's claim — the verse encourages the waiving without requiring it, since the lender's capital is legitimate property the law protects (the neither-wronged half of 2:279). The structure is the sūrah's characteristic ethics one final time: the floor legislated (postpone), the height pointed at (waive), and the better named without being imposed.

**The Loan's Charitable Nature**

The commentators read this verse inside the tradition's wider theology of the qarḍ — the loan — and the reading explains why the waiving is natural here in a way it would not be in a trade. Loans, in the Islamic scheme, were ideally charitable in kind: money lent for a term and returned in the same amount, the lender surrendering the time-value as his gift, while the profit-seeking uses of capital ran through other instruments — the credit-sale, the lease, the partnership — where return compensates risk or exchange rather than duration alone. The ribā-block has just legislated that scheme's boundary (the increase cancelled, the principal retained), and this verse legislates its summit: the loan that, at the debtor's distress, becomes a gift outright. The tradition's sayings gather around the summit — the man who relieves a believer's worldly distress relieved by God of the distresses of the Day; the lending described in the ḥadīth-collections as a deed whose reward runs ahead of the ordinary ṣadaqah, because the loan goes to the one too dignified to ask and the gift to the one who asks. The verse's if-you-only-knew is the same ranking stated as withheld arithmetic: the better-ness the waiving carries is visible from where the Day stands, and the verse invites the creditor to borrow that vantage now.

**If Only You Knew**

The closing conditional — *if only you knew* — is the verse's rhetorical hinge, and the commentators note its unfinished grammar: the apodosis is absent, the knowing left hanging over what it would change. The tradition reads the ellipsis as deliberate: had you known what the respite earns day by day, what the waiving weighs at the reckoning, what the debtor's distress is in God's sight — the sentence breaks off because the knowledge, if it arrived, would make the choice immediately and argument would be unnecessary. The formula matches the giving-section's whole pedagogy, which has consistently relocated the arithmetic from the visible ledger to the unseen one: the reward deposited with the Lord (2:262, 2:274, 2:277), the date nurtured into a mountain, the blight and growth operating where the amounts do not show (2:276). The creditor considering his struggling debtor is asked to perform the same relocation: the principal in his ledger is a visible amount, and the better the waiving carries is an invisible one — but the invisibility is an artifact of the vantage, not of the value, and the if-only-you-knew is the verse's promise that the vantage exists and is coming. The ribā-block ends its legislation on the word knew, and hands the whole matter, like the amnesty-clause before it, to the knowledge of God.

**The Block's Human Face**

Positioned between the war-declaration and the Day-return, this verse is the block's scene of ordinary mercy, and its placement is the sequence's final argument. The verses around it operate at the scale of systems — the devourers' resurrection, the blight and growth, the pillar-community, the war with God and His Messenger, the settlement at the principal — and this verse operates at the scale of two people: one who owes and cannot pay, one who is owed and can wait. The commentators read the scale-shift as the legislation's purpose: the ribā-prohibition exists for this scene, so that the creditor standing over the straitened debtor is standing inside an economy whose rules have already cancelled the increase, retained only the principal, ordered the postponement, and invited the waiving — every structural verse terminating in the concrete encounter the verse describes. The tradition's reports of the Prophet's own practice fill the scene: the debtor granted time, the debt remitted, the creditor counselled to accept less than his due. And the verse's two ranks — the commanded respite and the better waiving — leave the encounter with its whole moral range intact: justice at the floor, charity at the height, and between them the knowledge the closing word withholds, waiting for the Day to supply it.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:281

> Be mindful of the Day when you will ˹all˺ be returned to Allah, then every soul will be paid in full for what it has done, and none will be wronged.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Seal on the Economy**

The ribā-block closes as the sūrah's great legislative blocks have consistently closed — not with a new ruling but with the Day held up behind the rulings: *Be mindful of the Day when you will all be returned to Allah*. The commentators read the verse's function exactly: the passage on ribā ends with the reminder that all matters, economic ones included, will be accounted for in the Hereafter — the block's five legislative movements (the devourers' portrait, the blight-and-growth thesis, the abandonment-command, the war-and-principal settlement, the respite-and-charity invitation) all terminate in this single clause of return. The ittiqāʾ — the mindfulness, the same God-wariness that headed the command (2:278) — is now directed at a Day rather than an act, and the direction is the verse's legislation: the economy just governed is not a province life walls off from the fear of God but one of the fear's densest terrains, where every ledger-entry, every postponed term, every waived remainder is a transaction conducted in the Day's full jurisdiction. The tradition's report that this verse stands among the final revelations — cited by the exegetes among the passages said to be the last sent down before the Prophet's death — gives the seal a biographical weight: the economy's closing word is among the Book's closing words.

**Returned to Allah**

The return-clause's grammar carries the verse's first precision: *you will be returned* — the passive, the returning done to the returner. The commentators note the formula's kinship with the sūrah's own opening movement — how can you disbelieve, when you were dead and He gave you life, then causes you to die, then gives you life, then to Him you are returned (2:28) — and the kinship is the verse's argument: the return is not a journey the soul undertakes but an appointment it is brought to, the same divine passive that governed the first giving of life. The Day named is yawm — unspecified, undated, definite only in its certainty — and its content here is a single event: the return to God. Not the return to the earth, the tribe, the market, or the grave's silence but the return to the party every transaction in the block was secretly with: the Provider whose provision was spent or hoarded, the Warner whose warning arrived at the ribā-ledgers, the Lord whose principal-rule protected both creditor and debtor. The verse asks its reader to perform the block's whole economics as preparation for a meeting, and names the meeting's location as the meeting's meaning: to Him.

**Every Soul Paid in Full**

The Day's operation is stated in the verse's middle clause: *then every soul will be paid in full for what it has done*. The tawfiyah — the full paying-out, the completion of the wage — is the verse's economic verb, and its use at the Day's description is deliberate: the block that legislated debts, principals, respites, and waivers closes by describing the ultimate settlement in the same vocabulary. Every soul — kullu nafs, the individual in her singularity, the collective nouns of creditor and debtor dissolved into the unit that actually acted — receives the payment in full: nothing held back from the wage and nothing added to the bill. The commentators connect the clause to the resurrection of the devourers (2:275) as its double: the ribā-eater's convulsed rising and the soul's complete payment are the same Day seen from the two ledgers — the one whose increase was blighted arrives to find the blight total, and the one whose charity was grown arrives to find the growth counted to the last grain. What it has done — mā kasabat, what the soul earned — is the section's kasb-vocabulary applied at maximum scope: the earning includes the loans given and the increases abandoned, the respites granted and the debts waived, the principal retained without wronging and the surplus released without being wronged.

**None Will Be Wronged**

The verse's final clause is the block's own formula lifted to the Day: *and none will be wronged* — wa-hum lā yuẓlamūn. The commentators mark the echo deliberately: the same no-wronging that described the creditor's right at the settlement — you shall have your principal, neither wronging nor being wronged (2:279) — now describes every soul's position at the final audit. The parallel is the verse's quiet theorem: the settlement that the ribā-legislation imposed on the community's ledgers was a rehearsal of the Day's arithmetic, and the Day's arithmetic is the settlement's guarantee. Where the community's courts could only approximate the neither-wronging — the straitened debtor misjudged, the respite refused, the waiver uncredited — the Day performs it exactly: no soul overpaid, no soul underpaid, no increase surviving the blight, no charity lost from the growth. The commentators note the clause's double edge for the block's two parties: for the devourer who persisted, the no-wronging means the war-declaration's consequence arriving with full precision; for the repenter, the waiving creditor, the patient lender, it means the if-only-you-knew finally known — the better that was withheld from sight paid in full, to the last day of respite credited as the ḥadīth promised, to the last hidden gift found in the deposit with the Lord.

**The Individual Soul**

The verse's narrowing is its last structural gift: the block began with classes — the devourers, the believers, the creditors — and ends with the soul. Every economic identity the preceding verses assigned dissolves at the return into the single nafs that acted, and the singularization is the verse's pastoral point: no one stands at the Day as a member of a lending-house or a debtor-class, and the principal each soul carries is its own kasb. The commentators connect this narrowing to the sūrah's wider movement — the same every-soul formula runs through the Qur'an's Day-descriptions, and the sūrah's own later verses will restate it (what every soul has forwarded and left behind, 2:286's earned-and-perpetrated pair) — but here the narrowing serves the economy specifically: the ribā-block's hardest cases were always individuals inside systems, the creditor whose tribe's whole income ran on deferment-fees, the debtor whose distress the system called default. The verse hands both to the Day alone: what the system made complex, the soul's payment simplifies, and what the soul did — released or retained, waited or pressed, waived or devoured — is what the payment will be for.

**The Verse Between Two Legislations**

Positioned where it stands, this verse is also the hinge between the sūrah's two great documentary legislations: the economy-block it seals and the contract-verse that follows — the Book's longest verse, legislating the writing of debts. The commentators read the sequence as one argument: the Day-return verse establishes that every transaction is ultimately audited, and the documentation-legislation that follows builds the human audit to match it — the scribe, the witnesses, the written term, the small and great contracts recorded. The heavenly tawfiyah and the earthly kitābah are the two halves of one order: souls paid in full at the end, debts written in full at the beginning, and between them the mindfulness this verse commands — the ittiqāʾ that makes a merchant write honestly and a creditor postpone patiently, because both have read the same final clause. The ribā-block ends, and the sūrah's economic teaching continues into its documentation-form, with this verse standing at the door between them: the Day named, the return announced, the payment guaranteed complete, the wronging excluded — and the ledger of the world, in the verse's light, revealed as the draft of a document that will be settled to the last letter.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:282

> O believers! When you contract a loan for a fixed period of time, commit it to writing. Let the scribe maintain justice between the parties. The scribe should not refuse to write as Allah has taught them to write. They will write what the debtor dictates, bearing Allah in mind and not defrauding the debt. If the debtor is incompetent, weak, or unable to dictate, let their guardian dictate for them with justice. Call upon two of your men to witness. If two men cannot be found, then one man and two women of your choice will witness—so if one of the women forgets the other may remind her. The witnesses must not refuse when they are summoned. You must not be against writing ˹contracts˺ for a fixed period—whether the sum is small or great. This is more just ˹for you˺ in the sight of Allah, and more convenient to establish evidence and remove doubts. However, if you conduct an immediate transaction among yourselves, then there is no need for you to record it, but call upon witnesses when a deal is finalized. Let no harm come to the scribe or witnesses. If you do, then you have gravely exceeded ˹your limits˺. Be mindful of Allah, for Allah ˹is the One Who˺ teaches you. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Longest Verse**

This is the longest single verse in the Qur'an — a fact the tradition states with the gravity of a marker: the Book that runs from the Fātiḥah's seven short āyāt to its own final page reserves its maximum extension for the documentation of a debt. The commentators give the verse its occasion and its range together: it is said to have been revealed in connection with the agricultural forward sales practiced in Medina — payment now for harvests deliverable one, two, or three years out — but it applies generally to every deferred agreement, loans included: wherever payment and delivery do not meet in the same moment, the verse's machinery engages. The Prophetic rule the tradition attaches to the forward sale states the verse's minimum content: whoever contracts a forward sale should fix a known amount, a known measure, and a known term. The forward sale itself is the verse's exhibited exception to the wider prohibition on selling what one does not yet possess — permitted, al-Qurṭubī explains, because the farmer genuinely needs the funds for seed and care while his wealth stands in the ground in a yearly cycle, and because the social benefit outweighs the transaction's risk. The longest verse legislates, in other words, the longest transactions: the ones that stretch across years and therefore across the failures of memory, good faith, and life itself.

**Write It Down**

The command at the verse's head — *commit it to writing* — carries a precision the commentators draw out: the writing does not replace the living witness but serves the memory. Al-Qurṭubī states the legal hierarchy: in Islamic law the testimony is primarily oral and only secondarily written, and the document's function is to anchor the terms against the drift of recollection across the deferred period. The writing-command then generates the verse's first office: *let the scribe maintain justice between the parties* — the kātib positioned between the two as a third party with a virtue assigned, the bi'l-ʿadl justice being neither the creditor's amount nor the debtor's version but the transaction's own truth. And the office carries a duty and a dignity: *the scribe should not refuse to write as Allah has taught them to write*. The commentators read the refusal-ban as establishing contract-writing among the community's obligations — the jurists' classification is the communal duty, farḍ kifāyah: someone in the society must hold the skill and exercise it when called, though it is not every person's individual farḍ ʿayn. The clause's theology is the verse's quietest gift: the scribe writes *as Allah has taught him* — literacy itself named as a divine instruction (the same teaching-verb the verse's closing will reclaim), which makes the refused contract an ingratitude and the written one an act of the taught.

**The Debtor Dictates**

The verse's dictate-clause assigns the pen's source: *they will write what the debtor dictates, bearing Allah in mind and not defrauding the debt*. The choice of dictator is deliberate and the commentators explain it as protective arithmetic: the debtor — the party who owes, including the forward-sale's farmer-seller — speaks the terms because the creditor is more liable to describe a higher amount, and because the seller in these transactions is typically the weaker party, the one whose assets are non-liquid and whose need generated the contract. The dictation is bound to two restraints: the fear of God as Lord, and the fraud-ban — nothing diminished from what is actually owed. Al-Qurṭubī reads the assignment as the verse's balance-of-power device: the document's content comes from the mouth of the party with the incentive to understate, under an oath-like charge, in the presence of witnesses who will hear any understatement — the two possible frauds (creditor's inflation, debtor's diminution) checked by giving the pen to one and the ears to all. The incompetence-clause extends the protection to the dictator who cannot dictate: the feeble-minded, the minor, the one incapacitated by illness (the exegetes' three named cases) receives a guardian to dictate justly in his place — the verse's care reaching the parties the transaction would otherwise leave voiceless.

**The Witnesses**

The witnessing-legislation is the verse's most discussed clause, and the discussion repays care. Two men are called as witnesses; *if two men cannot be found, then one man and two women of your choice* — the doubling attached to its rationale in the verse's own words: *so if one of the women forgets, the other may remind her*. The commentators establish first what the exegetes agree on: the provision is peculiar to the commercial testimony this verse governs and differs from the Qur'an's treatment of testimony elsewhere — the sūrah of Light explicitly equates husband and wife as testifiers in the gravest of accusations (24:6–9), and the classical tradition, while generally excluding women from the corporal-punishment and qiṣāṣ cases, treated even there as preference rather than incapacity, admitting women's testimony when no male witness existed. The erring named is forgetting — a lapse of memory in the contract's particulars, not a character deficiency — and the classical readings of the reminder's effect ran in two directions: the reminded woman becomes legally equal to the man, or the two women together stand equal to him, the latter the more widely held. The modern and classical commentators converge in refusing the intrinsic-inferiority reading, and their structural argument is the verse's own: nothing here excludes a transaction between two women with two men witnessing; women in Islamic law transact sales and loans independently, without witnesses at all, across the whole range of ordinary commerce. The provision addresses, rather, the specific transaction's expertise-demand — the from-among-those-whom-you-approve phrasing signals competence in a domain, and complex multi-year forward contracts were, in the verse's society, a domain women rarely worked in. Al-Qurṭubī adds the social reading: participation of this kind was itself a major change for the women of the time, and the doubled presence functions as protection against bullying or manipulation in a long-term financial proceeding — while Abū Bakr ibn al-ʿArabī's recorded puzzlement (why could not one man remind one woman if she erred? he could not answer it) testifies that the tradition itself never settled the clause into a verdict on women's minds. The witnesses' duty-clause closes the paragraph symmetrically with the scribe's: *the witnesses must not refuse when they are summoned*.

**Small or Great, Written**

The verse's next movement kills the objection the documentation-command invites — the merchant's instinct that small deals do not merit the machinery: *You must not be against writing contracts for a fixed period, whether the sum is small or great*. The commentators read the small-or-great clause as a discipline of memory rather than of amount: it is the small deferred transaction whose terms are least likely to be remembered and most likely to be disputed, and the aversion-to-writing the verse forbids is precisely the false economy that skips the record where the record is cheapest and the loss most corrosive. The three benefits the verse then names are its own cost-benefit analysis: *more just in the sight of Allah, more convenient to establish evidence, and more likely to remove doubts* — the divine register first (the document as an act of the justice God sees), then the evidentiary (the record as testimony's anchor), then the psychological (the doubt removed from both parties' future). The spot-transaction exception follows and confirms the rule's logic: where the trade is hand-to-hand, delivered and paid in one moment, no writing is required — there is no deferred term for memory to fail across — though the verse still calls for witnesses at the deal's conclusion. The whole clause is a jurisprudence of the interval: documentation scales with time, because time is what corrupts the unwritten term.

**No Harm to Scribe or Witness**

The verse's penultimate legislation protects its own machinery: *Let no harm come to the scribe or witnesses. If you do, then you have gravely exceeded your limits*. The third parties the contract requires — the literate one summoned to write, the upright ones summoned to attest — are placed under the parties' protection, and the harm-ban is backed by the transgression-verdict: harming them is the verse's word for crossing into wrong. The commentators read the clause against the social realities the machinery creates: the scribe who writes a term one party dislikes, the witness whose testimony may decide a dispute — both are exposed to the losers' pressure, and both must answer the summons without refusal. The protection makes the refusal-bans operable: the scribe and witnesses can be commanded to serve only where serving is safe. The verse's closing movement then gathers everything into the theology that has governed it from the first clause: *Be mindful of Allah, for Allah teaches you. And Allah has perfect knowledge of all things.* The teaching-verb returns — the scribe wrote as God taught him, and now the whole community is addressed as God's taught: the documentation, the justice, the witnessing, the protection are a curriculum, and the taqwā is its disposition. The Knower of all things seals the verse that legislated against the failures of human knowing: the document exists because memory fails and doubt arises, and it is sufficient because the knowledge it approximates is, at its source, perfect.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:283

> If you are on a journey and a scribe cannot be found, then a security can be taken. If you trust one another, then ˹there is no need for a security, but˺ the debtor should honour this trust ˹by repaying the debt˺—and let them fear Allah, their Lord. And do not conceal the testimony, for whoever conceals it, their hearts are indeed sinful. And Allah ˹fully˺ knows what you do.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Journey Exception**

The documentation-legislation receives its case of impossibility: *If you are on a journey and a scribe cannot be found*. The commentators extend the clause's reach with a recorded variant reading — the absence is not only of the scribe but of the means: no writer available, or no materials to write with (al-Qurṭubī, al-Ṭabarī). The road is the verse's imagined scene, and it is exactly the scene where the deferred transaction most needs its machinery and least can have it: the caravan deal struck at a halting-place, the loan contracted between travelers, the forward-sale concluded far from the town's literate class and its paper. The verse does not suspend the transaction because the document is impossible; it substitutes — *then a security can be taken* — and the substitution preserves the contract-legislation's whole purpose through a change of instrument: where the written record cannot anchor the term, a held object anchors the debt.

**The Pledge in Hand**

The security named is the rahin maqbūḍah — the pledge in hand, the collateral physically seized and held by the creditor: property given by the debtor, or by the forward-sale's seller, as guarantee in the absence of the written, witnessed contract. The fiqh of the pledge that grew from this clause is one of the tradition's settled chapters — the pledge held, not merely promised; its value answering the debt at default; its care incumbent on the holder — and the Prophetic practice the tradition preserves gives the institution its most cited instance: the report in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī that the Prophet died with his shield pledged to a Jewish merchant of Medina against thirty ṣāʿ of barley for his household's food. The commentators draw the instance's lessons freely: the pledge's legitimacy across religious lines, its compatibility with the highest personal station, and its ordinariness — the Messenger's own household ran its grocery on the instrument this verse legislates. The pledge-in-hand thus completes the documentation-verse's architecture: the written contract for the settled community with its scribes, the seized collateral for the road without them, and the same deferred-debt protected across both geographies by whichever anchor is available.

**If You Trust One Another**

The verse's second provision rises above both instruments: *If you trust one another, then there is no need for a security, but the debtor should honour this trust by repaying the debt*. The commentators debate the provision's legal rank, and the debate is recorded in both directions: some held that this trust-clause abrogated the documentation-rules of the preceding verse — the higher ethic superseding the machinery; the many, whose position al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, and al-Ṭabarī all record, held that the clause applies specifically to the journey-case, and that in ordinary circumstances the written contract remains the norm. The majority reading preserves the verse's structure as a ladder rather than a repeal: documentation where possible, pledge where documentation is impossible, and trust — unsecured, undocumented, naked reliance on the other's fidelity — where the parties themselves can carry it. The trust-case's legislation falls entirely on the trusted party: *let him who is trusted deliver his trust, and let him fear Allah his Lord*. With no scribe, no document, no seized object standing behind the debt, the creditor's protection is the debtor's taqwā — and the verse accordingly names that taqwā with its fullest title, God his Lord, the fear that operates where no human instrument does. The ladder's top rung is thus not the absence of law but the law's interiorization: the contract written on the heart the documentation was invented to compensate for.

**Do Not Conceal the Testimony**

The verse's third movement turns from the debt's instruments to its witnesses, and its prohibition is the testimony's concealment: *do not conceal the testimony, for whoever conceals it, their hearts are indeed sinful*. The commentators connect the clause backward to the documentation-verse's summons — the witnesses who must not refuse when called (2:282) — and forward to its rationale: the whole machinery of writing and witnessing exists to make the truth available at the dispute, and the concealing witness defeats the machinery at its terminal point, holding in his memory the very fact the document was built to preserve. The sin-clause's organ is the verse's precision: the concealer's *heart* is named sinful — al-Ṭabarī and the tradition read the attribution as the sin's location and its totality, the heart being the seat whose corruption the concealment constitutes. The Qur'an's testimony-ethics elsewhere carry the same weight — the sūrah's own earlier verse legislated the witnesses' non-refusal and God's knowledge of what they do, and the sūrah of the Starving's picture of the record that leaves nothing out, small or great, unlisted (18:49) is the concealment-clause's eschatological guarantee: the withheld testimony is withheld from men only, and the heart that withheld it is registered.

**The Knower of What You Do**

The verse closes with the knowledge-clause the whole documentation-sequence has been building toward: *And Allah fully knows what you do*. The commentators read it as the sequence's enforcement-summary: the scribe's justice, the dictator's honesty, the witnesses' availability, the pledge-holder's care, the trusted debtor's fidelity, the testifier's disclosure — every actor in the contract-machinery has an interior the documents cannot capture, and the closing name captures it. The clause also answers the verse's ladder-structure with its final consolation: at the top rung, where trust operates without instrument, the creditor who relied and lost is not simply defrauded in an unenforceable deal — the transaction stands recorded where enforcement is perfect; and at every lower rung, where the document or the pledge may still fail (the forged term, the disputed collateral, the pressured witness), the same record stands behind the human machinery as its audit and its guarantee. The knowledge-verse thus completes the sūrah's documentary legislation the way the Day-return verse completed its ribā-legislation (2:281): the human instruments are commanded, calibrated, protected — and then handed over to the Knower, in whose knowledge the contract's final copy has been kept since the moment the scribe's pen, or the trusting hand, first moved.

**The Sequence's Completion**

Read with its two neighbors, this verse completes the sūrah's movement from the economy's morals to the economy's paperwork and back to the paperwork's morals. The ribā-block legislated the debt's ethics — the increase forbidden, the principal protected, the straitened debtor respited, the whole sealed at the Day (2:275–281). The documentation-verse built the debt's instruments — the writing, the scribe, the dictation, the witnessing, the harm-protections (2:282). This verse handles the instruments' limits and their interior: the road without a scribe, the pledge that substitutes, the trust that transcends, the testimony whose concealment is a sin of the heart. The three movements together are the Qur'an's complete treatment of the deferred obligation — its ethics, its documentation, and its conscience — and the verse's own structure enacts the completion: it descends from the ideal machinery to the emergency substitute, ascends from both to naked trust, and closes with the knowledge that holds all three levels equally. The believer who has traveled the sūrah's economy from the devourers' rising to the pledged shield and the trusted word now carries, the verse's closing clause assures him, a ledger kept at every altitude: documented where possible, secured where necessary, trusted where grace allows, and known — in every case, completely — to God.

## Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:284

> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Whether you reveal what is in your hearts or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it. He forgives whoever He wills, and punishes whoever He wills. And Allah is Most Capable of everything.

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sovereignty Premise**

The sūrah's closing movement opens by restating its property-law at the widest possible scale: *To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth*. The ownership-clause is the same formula āyat al-kursī carried (2:255), and its placement here does the same preparatory work: the accounting that follows is legitimate because the Accountant owns everything the account concerns — the wealth whose documentation the preceding verses legislated, the hearts whose concealments the testimony-clause policed, and the souls the Day-return verse (2:281) gathered from every economic identity into their singular kasb. The commentators read the clause as the ground of the verse's second sentence rather than its decoration: universal ownership makes universal accounting coherent, since nothing in any soul's contents falls outside the Owner's jurisdiction. The sūrah that began by describing the Book as the guidance in which there is no doubt ends its legislative career by naming the jurisdiction in which there is no outside.

**The Disclosed and the Concealed**

The verse's center is its audit-clause: *Whether you reveal what is in your hearts or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it*. Al-Ṭabarī records the specific reading first — the disclosure and concealment refer to the testimony the preceding verses legislated, the witness's moral responsibility to discharge his duty truthfully, whether he testifies openly or holds the truth back in his heart — and then the universal reading, which the tradition largely adopted: the clause covers the heart's entire contents, spoken or unspoken. The universal reading is what shook the verse's first hearers, and the reports the exegetes preserve are vivid: many Companions were distressed and grieved on hearing it, fearing they could never escape the reality it described; some worried it meant accountability for the fleeting thought itself; some wept from fear. The account of their distress is preserved together with its resolution — the two verses that follow, the sūrah's final pair, were revealed in part to quiet exactly this disquiet — and the pairing is the tradition's hermeneutic key to the whole closing: the audit-clause states the range of God's knowledge, and what follows states the range of His assignment.

**Accounting Is Not Punishment**

The tradition's clarification of the verse is precise and comes from al-Ṭabarī's own commentary: bring you to account need not mean punish. The muḥāsabah — the reckoning, the calling-to-account — is the Day's procedure, and in Islamic belief every person will first be brought to account for all his deeds before entering Paradise or Hell, except the elect who pass to Paradise directly (the sūrah's own verse on whom God wills among the reckoned-without-punishment, 2:212's discussion). The verse's forgiveness-and-punishment clause then names the accounting's two possible outcomes as divine dispositions: *He forgives whoever He wills, and punishes whoever He wills* — the will operating at the audit's end, not the audit's fact. The sūrah of the Cave's picture supplies the accounting's texture, quoted by the exegetes here: the record laid open, the wicked crying out — woe to us, what a book this is, leaving nothing out, small or great, but numbering it all (18:49). The verse's claim is thus total in knowledge and open in outcome: every heart-content is registered, and the registered stands before a will whose two movements are forgiveness and punishment — the dread the Companions wept at being the dread of the registration's completeness, which the verse affirms, and of the outcome's severity, which the verse leaves with the will that also forgives.

**No Abrogation, Two Descriptions**

Some held that the capacity-principle of the sūrah's final verse (2:286) abrogates this verse's audit-clause, and the commentators answer the claim on two grounds. The first is textual: there is no contradiction between the two — God's knowledge-and-reckoning of the heart's contents and God's not-tasking any soul beyond its capacity describe different relations (the audit's range and the obligation's measure), and both stand. The second is categorical: these are descriptions of God's acts, not legal rulings, and descriptions of the divine action are not subject to abrogation at all — naskh operates on commands and prohibitions, not on statements of what God knows, wills, and does. The clarification matters for reading the whole closing sequence: the verse is not a law later repealed but a doctrine permanently stated — the heart's contents are within the divine jurisdiction, full stop — and what the following verses adjust is not the jurisdiction but the community's burden under it. The Companions' weeping, on this reading, was a misreading of category: they heard a description of God's knowledge as an assignment to their hearts, and the sequence's remainder exists to separate the two — the knowledge total, the assignment capacity-bounded, the difference between them the mercy the final verses legislate.

**The Intentions Ḥadīth**

The tradition's operative commentary on the audit-clause is the ḥadīth the exegetes quote at length — the divine accounting of the heart's movements, in four cases. Whoever intends a good deed and does not perform it: God records it with Him as a complete good deed. Whoever intends it and performs it: God records ten good deeds, up to seven hundred times, and beyond. Whoever intends an evil deed and does not perform it: God records it with Him as a good deed — the tradition elsewhere explains, because he left it for God's sake. Whoever intends it and performs it: God records one evil deed. The commentators use the report to draw the distinction the weeping Companions needed: the accounting separates a psychological state from an executed choice — the difference between the concrete intention blocked by circumstance beyond the agent's control and the passing thought the heart sincerely struggles against. The unperformed good is rewarded as performed, the abandoned evil is rewarded as a good, the committed evil is recorded singly against the committed good's seven-hundredfold ceiling: the arithmetic of the audit, in the ḥadīth's form, is systematically tilted toward mercy — the same tilt the verse's forgiveness-whomever-He-wills clause names as the will's prerogative and the ḥadīth displays as the will's practice.

**Power Over All Things**

The verse's closing name gathers its three movements: *Allah is Most Capable of everything* — the qadr that owns the heavens and earth, registers the heart's concealed and revealed, and holds the forgiveness and the punishment in one will. The commentators connect the power-clause to the audit's feasibility: an accounting of every heart-content across every soul is an operation of infinite capacity, and the name states the capacity the clause assumes. The power is also the verse's answer to the sūrah's economic sequence, which ends here: the documentation legislated because human memory fails, the pledge because the road lacks scribes, the trust because instruments run out — and the divine power because nothing in the final audit depends on instruments at all. The God who teaches the scribe (2:282), who knows what the trusted debtor does (2:283), and who owns both worlds (this verse) is the God before whom the sūrah's last movement now begins — the believers' creed and their prayer, revealed, the tradition holds, into the very distress this verse's audit-clause created.
